Suggested move: pre-register the 2x2 disambiguation cuts now, run them before posting the readout in #growth-investigations, then shape the 1-pager in the standard why / cuts / p-val / effect-size / call format. If the 2x2 shows admin presence is independently predictive after conditioning on CS, the trigger becomes a real candidate; if not, the right action is "fix CS reach into the no-admin cohort," not "add a new lifecycle flag."

Short answer: yes, the raw 7.3-point effect is unsuitable for action in its current form — the intervention imbalance makes it uninterpretable as an "active admin → renewal" signal. The minimum rerun is a 2×2 decomposition (admin × CS reach) with an interaction test, expressed as effects and rates, not just p-values.

Why the raw number fails

The two comparison groups were reached by Customer Success at very different rates:
- 61 of 146 active-admin accounts reached (41.8%)
- 17 of 238 no-active-admin accounts reached (7.1%)

That's roughly a 5–6× reach imbalance between the groups you're comparing. The 7.3-point raw gap (131/146 = 89.7% vs 196/238 = 82.4%, p=.018) cannot distinguish:
- admin presence protects renewal, from
- CS reach protects renewal (and CS happens to have reached more active-admin accounts)

These are two completely different mechanisms with two completely different operational implications. Treating the raw gap as "admin absence is a renewal-risk trigger" is a category error. And there's a second guardrail that should make us cautious even before the rerun: 196 of the 238 no-active-admin accounts renewed anyway, so a blanket "no admin → at-risk" rule would carry roughly an 82% false-positive rate in this cohort. Any intervention has to clear that base-rate bar.

Minimum stratified/adjusted rerun for Owen

The smallest rerun that lets CS treat this as an actionable signal:

1. Produce the 2×2 cell table. Required counts:
   - (admin + CS reached) = 61
   - (admin + no CS) = 85
   - (no admin + CS reached) = 17
   - (no admin + no CS) = 221
   For each cell, also pull renewed count and renewal rate.

2. Run the two within-CS-stratum contrasts:
   - No-CS stratum only: admin vs no-admin renewal rate. If the gap survives here, admin presence is doing real work independent of CS.
   - CS-reached stratum only: admin vs no-admin renewal rate. Within-reach comparison is much smaller (61 vs 17) — call it directional, don't lean on it.

3. Fit renewal ~ admin_presence + cs_reached + admin_presence × cs_reached. The interaction term is the load-bearing one. If it's near zero and the admin main effect survives adjustment, admin presence has independent signal. If the admin coefficient collapses once cs_reached is in the model, CS is the real driver and the admin signal is a proxy for "CS picked this one up."

4. Report effect size, not just significance. Q1 framework asks Owen to lead with the rate difference and a confidence interval on the rate difference (or odds-ratio with CI), then p-value, then the within-stratum numbers. Don't bury the interaction behind the headline p=.018.

5. Lock the active-admin definition before running it. Per the existing rule: frequency/scope/recency of in-product admin actions, excluding logins and seat count. If the definition drifts between this cut and the operational rule CS would use, the gate doesn't actually clear.

6. One secondary stratifier, no more: integration depth buckets (1, 2–3, 4+) or admin-recency bands. Pre-register the cut. Don't let this expand into a fishing expedition.

What this is NOT cleared to do even after the rerun

- Convert "active admin absence" into a renewal-risk lifecycle trigger on this readout alone. First significance ≠ ship trigger — Q1 framework, this is the worked example.
- Become a Sales surface. CS-first routing stays in front of any commercial motion on accounts with open CS adoption work; that's a hard rule from Expansion Assist that carries over.
- Replace the day-60 expansion nudge or feed forecast/pipeline. State rules are still in design, not launch spec.

Owen vs Ines lanes on the rerun

- Owen owns: 2×2 table, denominators, effect size + CI on the adjusted admin coefficient, interaction term, conclusion order. Readout shape, not a verdict on whether CS should act.
- Ines owns (after the numbers are right): lifecycle-risk language review, audience-risk caveats, suppression rules for the operational rule (open CS adoption plans, recent support contact, no recent admin behavior, stale expansion quote — these suppress before any signal ever reaches a CS queue).

Before CS treats this as actionable, three things have to be true:
1. The admin main effect survives adjustment for CS reach with a meaningful effect size, not just a passing p-value.
2. The no-CS stratum contrast still shows a gap (or the interaction term is well-identified and non-zero).
3. Owen and Ines have both signed off on the same readout, with suppression rules written in.

Until those three land, CS should keep this in "first significance, flag not ship" status — which is the default for Q1 under the framework pilot anyway.

Short safety-first sequence

The single chirp every ~45 sec, steady green LED, no alarm pattern, no smoke/smell = classic "backup battery low" signal on a hardwired unit. The unit is still working; it just wants a new battery. Rule of thumb: do not take the unit off the mounting bracket until you have the new battery in hand ready to install. The other detectors in the house stay powered throughout, so you're not leaving the home unprotected.

1. Set up before you touch the unit
   - Sturdy step stool or ladder directly under the detector
   - New battery in hand, old one's polarity noted (+/-)
   - Phone or another person aware, in case a real alarm sounds during the swap
   - Clear the floor below so nothing gets knocked over when you lower the unit

2. Optional temporary silence (only if you want to delay the swap)
   - Press and HOLD the front TEST/HUSH button for a few seconds. Many models silence low-battery chirps for ~8 hours. This is a mute, not a fix. Don't use it as a substitute for changing the battery.

3. Twist the unit off the mounting bracket
   - Twist counter-clockwise (US standard: Kidde, First Alert, BRK). The wiring harness and small plastic plug stay attached to the unit; you do not touch house wiring.
   - Let it hang by the harness, or set it on a stable surface on top of the ladder.

4. Swap the battery
   - Open the battery door/drawer
   - Match + and - to the orientation of the old battery
   - Drop in the fresh battery. Most units give a brief "ack" chirp or LED change.

5. Re-mount
   - Re-seat on the bracket, twist clockwise until locked
   - Confirm the green power LED is steady again

6. Reset (usually automatic, but make it explicit)
   - Press and HOLD TEST for ~5 seconds, release
   - If the low-battery chirp returns, pull the unit back down and re-seat the battery — a bad contact is the #1 reason a fresh install still chirps

7. Test
   - Press and HOLD TEST until the full alarm pattern sounds (typically 3 loud beeps, pause, repeat until you release)
   - Every interconnected unit in the house should sound within a few seconds
   - Release and listen for the all-clear; confirm green LED is steady again

Stop troubleshooting — leave the house if:
- The unit switches from single chirps to a full repeating alarm (3 loud beeps, pause, 3 loud beeps...) without you pressing TEST. That's a real alarm. Evacuate, call 911 from outside, don't go back in until cleared.
- You see, smell, or feel smoke, heat, or anything burning — even before the alarm goes off
- Multiple detectors start sounding at once with no obvious cause (could be an electrical fault, not a battery)
- You feel dizzy, nauseous, or otherwise unwell during the swap — could be CO or other invisible hazard; get out first

Stop troubleshooting — replace the whole unit instead if:
- The low-battery chirp continues after a known-good fresh battery installed with correct polarity and re-seated
- TEST produces no sound, weak sound, or garbled sound
- The unit is yellowed, warped, corroded, or shows any error code (some models flash a specific LED pattern in the manual for "fault")
- The chirp returns within days or weeks of a fresh battery
- You can't match the chirp pattern to anything in the manual — when in doubt, replace
- Age: more than 10 years from manufacture. Yours is 2020, so it's good through ~2030, but worth writing the install date on the new unit when you do replace it

For replacement: hardwired interconnected units should be replaced with the same type (look for "interconnected" or "wire-in" on the label). Same twist-off / twist-on swap; the existing wiring plug reattaches to the new unit's harness.

One last note: most chirp-every-45-sec problems on a 2020 unit are battery, not the unit. The procedure above resolves it in ~5 minutes without leaving the house unprotected at any point.

Good sequence — that's exactly the manufacturer's reset procedure, and steady green + 30 minutes silent is a clean result. Battery chirps run every 30–60 seconds when the cell is dying, so a half-hour quiet is a real signal the swap took.

Two small notes worth keeping on file:

- If it chirps again within 24–48h, the replacement battery itself was bad (rare), or the unit is at end-of-life. Most detectors expire at 10 years from manufacture (date stamped on the back). Worth a glance if you don't already know the install date.
- Old battery can go in regular trash if alkaline. If it turned out to be a sealed lithium 10-year unit (unlikely, given you replaced it in place), that goes to e-waste/recycling, not the bin.

Otherwise: resolved.

Quick read: ~2 tablespoons at the front-right corner, machine off and not dripping, supply/drain dry, gasket visually OK, filter possibly not fully locked after yesterday's cleaning. That profile (small volume, one corner, no under-cabinet water) most often points to splash escaping around the filter during drain, a partial seal failure on the right side of the door, or a loading issue letting spray reach the door. It's reassuring, not catastrophic.

DIAGNOSTIC SEQUENCE (machine OFF, door open — do not run a cycle yet)

1. FILTER (your top suspect)
   - Pull the lower rack. Remove the filter assembly — usually a cylindrical mesh that twists/lifts out, sometimes with a flat mesh underneath.
   - Check the seat/channel for debris (food, a glass chip, scale). Even a thin film breaks the seal.
   - Reseat firmly — most filters need a quarter-twist until they drop and lock; some brands click audibly. It must sit flush with no lip.
   - If your model has a flat sump plate under the filter, confirm it's seated flat, not bowed.

2. GASKET (door seal)
   - Run a clean dry finger along the full gasket, especially the lower-right arc. Feel for nicks, hardened spots, flattened sections, or anywhere it pulls out of the channel.
   - If unseated at any point, press it back into the channel. Don't stretch it or apply lubricant.

3. LOADING
   - Anything tall in the front-right (glass, bottle, pan with a vertical handle) that could block the spray arm or wedge against the door/tub?
   - Lower rack fully inserted, upper rack at its stop?
   - Detergent in the main cup, not loose on the door?

4. DOOR LATCH (door closed, no cycle)
   - Confirm full latch engagement — door sits flush with the control panel, positive click.
   - With room lights off, look at the bottom-right edge for daylight or an uneven gap.

PRE-NEXT-CYCLE GATE — only run a cycle if all four above pass cleanly:
- Filter fully locked and flush
- Gasket fully seated, no damage
- Rack fully in, nothing blocking spray arm or pressing on door
- Door latches flush

If the gate passes, run a SHORT or light cycle (not normal or heavy), and put a dry paper towel at the front-right corner before you start. You want minimal water in play if there's still a small leak.

STOP CONDITIONS — call service if any of these:
- Filter won't lock flush after reseating
- Gasket shows a tear, hardening, or won't stay seated
- Leak location moves (front-left, under the door, under the cabinet)
- Volume exceeds ~2 tablespoons on the next run
- Any water near the electrical connection, supply line, or drain during operation
- Door won't latch flush or you see daylight at the bottom-right edge when closed

The ~2-tablespoon amount is on your side — it's consistent with splash, not a failed seal or hose. Most often this resolves with a clean filter reseat. If it doesn't after one short test cycle, you'll have a clear, specific thing to report and the service call gets cheaper.

Good catch on the quarter-turn and the gasket scrap — that's a clean root cause, not a symptom to chase further. Drying the cabinet and running the supervised empty rinse was the right verification: dry connections after a full cycle, not just a power-on test, is what closes it.

Scaled to ~18 cookies (60% of 30). Here are the gram amounts and the two techniques you asked about.

Scaled ingredients
- All-purpose flour: 180 g
- Unsalted butter: 102 g (cold, cubed)
- Sugar: 90 g
- Large egg: 0.6 of an egg → see below
- Orange zest: ~1 medium orange, finely grated (see below)
- Vanilla: ~3/4 tsp (0.6 tsp is fine to round up)
- Salt: ~1/4 tsp (heaping)

Portioning the beaten egg without making the dough wet
- A large egg, beaten, is ~50 g / ~3 tablespoons. So 0.6 egg ≈ ~30 g / ~1 3/4 Tbsp beaten.
- Crack the egg into a small bowl, beat with a fork or small whisk until yolk and white are fully combined and uniform.
- Drizzle it in gradually: add about 1 tablespoon at a time into the creamed butter/sugar, mixing on low between additions.
- Stop when the dough just comes together. If it's already cohesive before you've used all the egg, leave the last ~1/2 Tbsp in the bowl — don't force it in. A tablespoon or two of held-back egg is the difference between a tender dough and a sticky one.
- If it does feel slightly tackier than you'd like, don't add flour to fix it. Just chill longer (45–60 min instead of 30) so the butter re-firms and the flour absorbs moisture.
- Scoop and portion after chilling so the cookies bake evenly.

Rounding the zest
- Original calls for zest of 2 oranges. 60% of that = zest of ~1.2 oranges.
- Cleanest rule: zest 1 whole orange finely on a microplane. If you want a touch more brightness after tasting the dough, zest a small strip from a second orange. Don't try to zest "1.2" oranges — you'll either under- or over-do it.
- For consistency, zest both oranges first and weigh: zest of 2 oranges ≈ 4–6 g, so 60% ≈ 2.5–3.5 g → use 3 g or just one medium orange's worth (~2.5–3 g).
- Always zest before halving/juicing, and stop at the white pith — it adds bitterness.
- Rub the zest into the sugar with your fingertips for a minute before creaming. That releases the oils and distributes the flavor evenly without needing extra zest.

A few practical notes for the smaller batch
- Total dough ≈ ~400–410 g, so ~22–23 g per cookie if you're weighing (a #40 scoop is close, or a generous tablespoon).
- With fewer cookies on the sheet, the bake tends to run a minute faster — pull at pale gold edges, ~10–11 min at 350°F.
- Keep the dough chilled between trays; if it warms up while you're portioning, return it to the fridge for 5 min.

27°F for 6 hours is a moderate Austin freeze — the kind that reliably damages hose bibs and rarely touches interior plumbing if the heat is on. So the work is concentrated on the bibs and a couple of small cabinet steps.

PRE-SNAP — DO BEFORE BED TONIGHT

1. Disconnect the garden hose. This is the single highest-value action. Water trapped in the hose freezes, expands, and either splits the hose bib itself or pushes pressure back into the pipe inside the wall. Drain the hose and coil it somewhere out of the weather. The bare bib can handle a freeze; a hose-connected bib usually can't.

2. Cover both hose bibs. Foam bib covers ($3-5, any hardware store, the foam-dome "Bibsulator" style) push on in about 30 seconds each. If you can't get to a store tonight, a folded hand towel wrapped around the bib, a plastic bag over it, and a rubber band or tape to hold it on is a serviceable substitute — especially for the one without a hose.

3. Open the cabinet doors under the kitchen sink and the guest bath sink. The supply and drain lines on those exterior walls are the only interior runs at meaningful risk tonight. Leaving the doors open lets room heat into the cavity.

4. Slow drip from those two faucets — kitchen cold and guest bath cold, both sides if you want symmetry. Just a pencil-thin stream, not a runner. Moving water + warm cabinet air is more than enough at 27°F for a 2x4 exterior wall with normal insulation. Hot side is fine to leave off.

5. Locate (don't test) the main shutoff. If something does burst, you want to know where it is and that the valve turns. Just look at it tonight, don't operate it.

NOT WORTH DOING FOR ONE NIGHT AT 27°F
- Draining the water heater
- Wrapping the meter at the curb
- PEX heat tape on interior pipes
- Cranking the thermostat above normal
- Dripping every faucet in the house — the two above are the only ones with exterior-wall runs

POST-SNAP — INSPECT TOMORROW MID-MORNING (after it's been above freezing for an hour or so)

1. Hose bibs, one at a time. Turn each on slowly with a flashlight on the wall side. Look and listen for drips at the packing nut, the stem, or where the pipe enters the house. A frozen bib often doesn't leak until water is restored. The hose-connected one is your highest-priority check — that's the one most likely to have cracked.

2. Kitchen sink. Run water at both taps for 30 seconds, then get under the cabinet with a flashlight. Look at the supply line connections, the shutoff valves, and the P-trap for any new drips. Run your hand along the exterior wall for damp drywall or musty smell.

3. Guest bath — same drill. Both faucets, under-cabinet check, exterior wall check.

4. Ceilings. If either sink is on a second floor, scan the ceiling directly below for new stains or a soft spot.

5. In the next 2-3 days: watch the water bill and listen for the sound of running water when nothing's on. A pipe that froze but didn't fully burst can start leaking days later as the ice plug shifts and moves.

If everything's dry tomorrow after the bib test and the cabinet checks, you're done for this event.

Good that the surface is still intact — damp cold-press will lift if you push it, so the hands-off phase matters more than any technique you'll apply later.

The restrained sequence I'd use:

1.  Stop. Put the brush down for now.
    The muddy gray-green isn't going to dry into a problem you can't solve, and any move you make while the sheet is still damp will just re-stir pigment into the figures and red boots. Cover the clean upper half with a sheet of clean paper or glassine so nothing can drip onto it later.

2.  Let it bone-dry, flat, under loose weight if you have a clean sheet on top.
    Air-dry is safer than a hairdryer. If you're impatient, a hairdryer on cool (not warm, not hot) held 30+ cm away is fine — but overnight is the low-risk default. Cold-press holds moisture longer than hot-press; "touch dry" at the edges can still be wet in the middle of a wash.

3.  Once dry, look before you do anything.
    Two cases:
    - Pigment sits on the surface (most likely with a thin overworked wash on 140 lb) — you have options.
    - Pigment stained into the sizing (less likely) — accept and adjust the value, don't try to lift it out.
    Tilt the page and look at it under raking light. If you see chalky/dusty pigment on the tooth, you can lift some with a clean damp (not wet) brush and a soft paper towel — gently, one pass, no scrubbing. This is the highest-risk move, so test a small area first and accept "less muddy" as the goal, not "back to white."

4.  Negative shapes first, before any glaze.
    This is your safest structural move. Identify the highlights you actually want in the grass — a few light-catching tufts, the brightest spots between blades, gaps where sky/ground shows through. Mix a slightly darker, cleaner green than the mud (lean toward yellow-green, not blue-green, since blue over gray is what made the mud). Paint around those highlight shapes, leaving them as paper white. This rebuilds the grass as shapes of light rather than as a wash to fix.

5.  Then a thin glaze, only if it still reads too cool/gray.
    Mix a yellow-green (or a touch of warm green from your palette — if you have anything like sap green, olive, or a yellow-leaning viridian) very thin — the consistency of weak tea, not cream. One pass over the muddy area, and let it dry fully before judging. One glaze is almost always enough; a second glaze will start obscuring the negative-shape work you just did. Never glaze wet-on-wet over a glaze — that's how you get back to mud.

6.  Last: drybrush or stipple for blade texture.
    Nearly-dry brush (load it, then blot almost all the paint off on a paper towel), small side-to-side motions, individual darker blades and a few seed-head shapes. This is what sells "grass" instead of "green area" and it sits on top of everything rather than mixing into it.

The two traps to avoid:
-  Trying to lift the mud back to white. You'll probably only get to "slightly less muddy" and risk damaging the surface the paper hasn't buckled or pilled yet. Negative shapes get you the rest of the way visually.
-  Glazing with blue or blue-leaning greens. That's what put you in mud in the first place; the corrective glaze should always lean warm (yellow side) to push the value away from gray.

If you walk away after step 4 and decide it reads as grass, stop there — the lower third doesn't need to be a finished passage, just one that doesn't pull the eye away from the figures and the red boots.

What you've described is a single, low-yield vomit (grass + foam, no exposure, soft belly, pink gums, alert, interested in water) — the picture is reassuring, but single episodes do sometimes repeat or unmask something. Here's a conservative plan for the next 12-24 hours.

WATER (first priority)
- Hold water for 30-60 minutes after the vomit. His interest in drinking is a good sign.
- Then offer small amounts: 1-2 tablespoons at a time for a medium dog (roughly a small ladle), more if he's larger.
- Every 15-20 minutes for the first ~2 hours.
- If he keeps it down, gradually return to normal amounts over the next 4-6 hours.
- Don't put a full bowl down — gulping tends to retrigger vomiting.
- Ice chips or ice cubes to lick are a fine substitute if small sips don't sit.

FOOD
- Hold food for 2-4 hours after the last vomit. Water first, food second.
- When you reintroduce, use a bland diet only:
  - Boiled skinless, boneless chicken breast (no oil, salt, seasoning)
  - Plain white rice, well-cooked
  - Roughly 1 part chicken to 2 parts rice
- Start with a small portion: a few tablespoons for a small/medium dog, up to ~1/4 of his normal meal for a large dog. If you tell me his size I can be more precise.
- If that stays down for 2-3 hours, offer another small bland meal. Repeat every 3-4 hours through the day.
- Continue bland diet for 24-48 hours, then transition back to normal food over 2-3 days (mix increasing proportions of regular food).
- Avoid during recovery: treats, table scraps, fatty food, dairy, rich kibble toppers.

GENERAL MONITORING (check periodically today)
- Vomit frequency, timing, and contents
- Stool: any diarrhea, mucus, or blood
- Water intake: is he drinking, refusing, or gulping and vomiting it back?
- Energy: alert and responsive, or quiet/lethargic/hiding?
- Gums: pink and moist is good
- Belly: soft and non-painful is good
- Repeated lip-licking, drooling, or swallowing = likely nausea, watch for next vomit

EMERGENCY VET — GO NOW if any of these appear
- Repeated vomiting (a second and third episode, or any escalation)
- Blood in vomit — red, brown/coffee-ground, or black
- Unproductive retching (trying to vomit, nothing comes up) — this is a bloat/GDV warning sign and is time-critical regardless of breed
- Belly becomes distended, hard, or painful to touch
- Gums turn pale, white, blue, or yellow
- Collapse, stumbling, or sudden marked weakness
- Inability to keep water down across several attempts
- Shaking, panting, restlessness, guarding his belly, or vocalizing when picked up/touched
- You later realize he got into medication, a toxin (xylitol, chocolate, grapes/raisins, antifreeze, rodenticide, human meds), a foreign object, or a food wrapper

CALL YOUR REGULAR VET (next day / business hours) if
- One or two more small vomits but he stays bright, keeps water down, and has energy
- Mild lethargy that resolves within 12-24 hours
- Soft stool or mild diarrhea without blood
- Reduced appetite for under 24 hours
- He goes right back to grazing grass again (worth a mention at his next checkup — chronic grass-eating can flag nausea or dietary gap)

A note on grass-eating: very common in dogs, often normal behavior, sometimes self-induced for mild GI upset. A single episode after grass chewing in an otherwise bright dog usually doesn't warrant more than observation, but it does warrant the 12-24-hour watch above.

I'm not a veterinarian, so treat this as general home-care guidance rather than a diagnosis. If your gut says something is off this afternoon, trust that and call — better to make one unneeded call than miss a turn.

That's the right trajectory — water held, bland meal held, normal stool, normal energy, pink gums, normal abdomen, no retching or diarrhea, all strung together clean through a six-hour-plus window with no relapse. Reads clearly as a one-time grass-and-foam episode, and moving to ordinary observation is the right call given everything else normal.

What is wrong with the conclusion "ship to all trial admins"

The conclusion rests on a single number (+3pp, p=.04) that is both
technically fragile and incomplete. Six problems, in roughly the
order they break the call:

1. WRONG DENOMINATOR (selection bias)
   Headline rates use the 1,105 users who reached "eligible
   setup state" out of 1,920 randomized. That is not ITT —
   it is a post-randomization subset. If variant B changes
   *whether* users reach eligible state (plausible, since
   setup is the funnel that leads to it), conditioning on
   that state makes the arms non-comparable. The 28% / 31%
   can move purely from differential selection into the
   denominator, not from a true treatment effect. The right
   rate to ship on is the full 1,920.

2. THE EXPERIMENT IS NOT FINISHED
   8 of 14 planned observation days are complete. This is an
   interim peek at ~57% of planned time. p=.04 with one
   mid-window look is exactly the false-positive zone — Type I
   error is not controlled. The lift can shrink, flip, or
   disappear in the remaining 6 days. A "ship" call before the
   readout window closes is not a readout, it is a guess.

3. ARM IMBALANCE — THE BIG ONE
   Secondary admins are 42% of treatment vs 27% of control.
   That is a ~15pp composition gap on a known moderator. If
   secondaries complete setup at a different rate than
   primaries (they almost certainly do — that is why they are
   a segment), the apparent +3pp lift could be entirely the
   composition shift, not the variant. Without a stratified
   read or a covariate-adjusted estimate, the treatment effect
   is not identified. This alone should block ship.

4. NO EFFECT SIZE WITH PRECISION
   p=.04 without a confidence interval is uninterpretable.
   +3pp could easily carry a CI of [-1, +7] or worse. You
   cannot make a ship call on a point estimate sitting on the
   conventional threshold. Effect size with CI is the minimum
   — anything else is a vibes-based readout.

5. GUARDRAILS MISSING
   Support contacts and unsubscribe outcomes are not in the
   readout. A +3pp setup lift that doubles support tickets or
   pushes unsubscribes up is net negative. Shipping without
   guardrails means you cannot evaluate total impact — you
   only see the upside surface.

6. SCOPE OF "SHIP" EXCEEDS THE TEST
   The experiment ran on trial admins who reached an eligible
   state. "Ship to all trial admins" extrapolates beyond the
   tested population. The readout does not earn that
   generalization, and there is no argument in the slide for
   why the effect would transfer to admin types / states the
   experiment never observed.

Call (what the readout actually justifies)

Do not ship on this. Demand before any ship discussion:
  - ITT rates on the full 1,920, not the 1,105 subset
  - The full 14-day window, not 8 days
  - A stratified cut by admin type (primary vs secondary)
    with the composition gap accounted for
  - Effect size with a confidence interval
  - Support and unsubscribe guardrails
If the lift survives ITT + stratification + the full window
with a CI excluding 0 and clean guardrails, then revisit —
and even then scope the rollout (e.g., 50/50 ramp), do not
flip 100% on the first read.

Here is a bounded decision tree for a one-anchor-failed linen shelf, plus a conservative test plan. The wall is dry, no cracks beyond the hole, and the shelf is straight — that's the best starting position.

IMMEDIATE STATE (you are already here — good)
- Keep the shelf off the wall until the right bracket is fixed.
- Do NOT load the shelf back even on the left bracket alone. A shelf supported by only one side will twist and likely pull the left side too.
- Leave the loose bracket in place for now; it is harmless and gives you a reference point.

THE THREE BRANCHES — pick one, in this order of preference

1. REMOUNT INTO A NEARBY STUD (strongest fix)
   Go if:
   - You can locate a stud within ~1–1.5 inches of the failing bracket's position.
   - The shelf is long enough that moving the right bracket over still supports the shelf (right bracket should sit within ~6 inches of the shelf end).
   How to find the stud:
   - Tap test: tap horizontally with your knuckle. Hollow = between studs; solid thud = over a stud.
   - Stud finder if you have one, OR a strong rare-earth magnet (it will pull on the drywall screws/nails holding the drywall to the stud).
   - Standard framing is 16" on-center. Measure from the LEFT bracket (which is firm) — if it is in/near a stud, the next stud is very likely ~16" to the right. That is usually close enough to shift the right bracket over.
   What you need:
   - 2 wood screws long enough to pass through the bracket and bite at least 1.5" into the stud (usually #10 or #12, 2.5–3" length).
   - Drill with a bit slightly smaller than the screw shank for a pilot hole if the bracket holes are tight.
   - Drill the new holes, mount the bracket into the stud, leave the old stripped hole unused (or patch with a dab of spackle later for cosmetics).

2. PROPERLY RATED TOGGLE IN SOUND DRYWALL (good fix when no stud is reachable)
   Go if:
   - No stud is available within range, OR you don't have the tools/interest to hunt for one.
   - The drywall around the failing bracket feels hard when you press on it — no soft spots, no bubbling paper, no crumble.
   - You can move the right bracket a few inches horizontally to land on fresh, undamaged drywall.
   What to use (not plastic anchors — plastic is what failed):
   - Snap-toggle or strap-toggle (e.g., "Snaptoggle") with 1/4"-20 bolts: rated ~50–80 lbs per anchor in 1/2" drywall, modern, reliable.
   - Traditional spring-toggle wings: rated lower (~30–40 lbs per anchor in 1/2" drywall); still fine for linens but harder to install cleanly.
   - DO NOT reuse the existing stripped hole — patch it with a small drywall patch + spackle (24 hr cure), or just leave it unused and remount nearby.
   - One toggle per bracket side is plenty for a linen load.

3. STOP AND CALL A HANDYMAN
   Go if any of the following is true:
   - You can't confidently locate a stud AND there is no fresh, undamaged drywall within reach for a toggle (e.g., tight alcove, only the one location is viable).
   - The wall feels soft, crumbly, or the paper face is bubbled around the hole.
   - There is cracking that extends more than a finger-width beyond the anchor hole.
   - The wall is plaster-over-lath (older homes). Plaster takes molly bolts or wood blocking — different system, not a DIY job.
   - You don't own or can't borrow a drill and the right-size bit for a toggle (1/2" bit for a 1/4" toggle).
   - You plan to load this shelf with anything heavier than linens (books, stoneware, multiple sets of bedding).
   - The bracket itself is bent, or the shelf has any twist to it now.

LOAD PLANNING — be honest about the load
- A linen shelf with towels + sheets typically runs 15–30 lbs total when stocked. Well within a single snap-toggle per side.
- If you have an unusually heavy load (lots of dense towels, spare bedding sets), lean toward the stud option or add a second bracket on the right side, not just one toggle.

CONSERVATIVE TEST PLAN (do this before putting linens back)
Run in this order. Do not skip steps.

Step 1 — Static hand test
- With the bracket remounted, press straight down on the shelf directly above the right bracket with your palm using firm body weight. There should be zero give, no creak, no shift. If anything moves, do not load it — back to the decision tree.

Step 2 — Wait period
- Leave the bracket unloaded overnight. Wood screws into a stud do not need a wait, but toggles benefit from 12–24 hours for any settling.

Step 3 — Known-weight static load
- Place a known weight on the right side only. A 5-gallon bucket of water is ~42 lbs; a cinder block is ~35 lbs; a case of water bottles is ~30 lbs. A 25–40 lb weight held on the right side for 24 hours is a reasonable conservative test.
- Check at 1 hour, 6 hours, and 24 hours: any gap opening between shelf and wall? Any sag (use a level or a phone level)? Any creak when you tap the bracket?
- If the shelf passes 24 hours with no movement, it is fine for linens.

Step 4 — Cycle test
- Gently lift and lower the loaded shelf edge a few times. Real-world loads are dynamic (pulling towels off the stack), not just static.

Step 5 — Ramp reload
- Half linens for a week. Then full reload. Re-check gap and level after the first week.

SIGNS THE REPAIR FAILED — stop using the shelf if you see any of these
- Shelf is no longer flush to the wall (gap appearing at one end).
- Bracket visibly tilting or rotating.
- Drywall paper crinkling or pulling around the bracket.
- Any cracking radiating from the screw holes.

DO NOT
- Reuse the old stripped plastic anchor. It will spin again.
- Stack two plastic anchors into one hole to "double up." It does not work.
- Load the shelf before completing the test plan.
- Trust the shelf based only on the hand-press test. Toggles in particular can hold briefly and then creep under sustained load.

Nice work on the methodical approach — checking the drywall integrity first, then confirming the stud situation bracket-by-bracket before deciding on the fastener, was the right call. Splitting the load (stud + rated toggle) is exactly how that kind of asymmetric closet wall wants to be handled.

Test protocol was solid too: empty-shelf first, then staged loading over half an hour rather than piling everything on at once. That kind of incremental proof is what tells you whether the fasteners are actually carrying or just hanging in for now.

Keeping heavy bottles off it is the right move — toggle strength is great for steady distributed load (folded towels are perfect) but not where you'd want to hang concentrated weight long-term.

Workflow below assumes phone camera + a stable surface. No app needed beyond your default camera; no transcription at capture time.

SETUP (10 min, once)
  - Table near a window for even indirect daylight. Avoid direct sun (glare on shiny prints).
  - Phone on a stable mount 12-18" directly above the surface — lean against a stack of books, or a $15 mini tripod. Stability matters more than megapixels.
  - Plain matte background under photos (a sheet of printer paper). Helps framing and contrast.
  - Clear ~1 GB phone storage; charge to 80%+.

PER-PHOTO LOOP (~90 sec, repeat 36 times)
  1. Place photo face-up. Capture front. File name: NN_front.jpg (NN = 01..36).
  2. Without moving the phone, flip the photo over.
  3. Capture back. File name: NN_back.jpg.
  4. Glance at the back image on screen — is the handwriting readable? If blurry or glary, reshoot immediately. Don't move on until it is.
  5. Slide photo to the "done" pile. Don't touch it again.

The phone stays put, each original is handled exactly once, and pairing is locked in by the filename.

NAMING
  Sequential two-file pairs: 01_front.jpg / 01_back.jpg ... 36_front.jpg / 36_back.jpg. Skip transcribing dates or notes at capture — that's a separate pass later, and you can do it from the digital back without re-handling originals.

OPTIONAL: ONE FILE PER PHOTO (bulletproof pairing)
  After the session, run a one-time merge: stack front over back vertically into NN.jpg. ImageMagick does it in one command across the folder; a phone collage app does it by hand. Then the relationship can't be broken by a rename later. Skip this if the filename pair bothers you — keeping both files in one folder and never renaming works fine.

QUALITY CHECKS (do at capture, not later)
  - Whole photo in frame, no edges cropped
  - No glare spot covering the annotation
  - Back text sharp enough to read on the phone screen at normal size
  - Lighting even across the image
  - Capture every back, even blank ones — don't decide in the moment

BACKUP (once, at the end)
  "One backup copy" = at minimum a second location. Easiest two:
  - Cloud: upload the folder to iCloud / Google Photos / Backblaze. Automatic, offsite.
  - USB: copy the folder to a flash drive. Fast, no account needed.
  Either alone is enough. Both = photos in three places (phone + cloud + USB). The shoebox prints are still your third copy even with just cloud.

TOTAL: ~1 hour setup-to-backed-up. Once this is done, originals go back into the albums and you don't need to touch them again.

The text is almost certainly a smishing attempt — micro-fee ($0.30), vague "a package" wording, shortened link, unfamiliar sender are textbook. The "she's expecting a package" detail is exactly why these work, which is why verification has to start from her side, not the text.

NO-CLICK CASE (her current situation — this is the safe case)
============================================================

Verification sequence. Start only from channels she controlled before the text:

  1. Pull up the original order confirmation email from when she placed the order. Note the retailer name, tracking number, and carrier.
  2. In a browser, type the retailer's official website directly (or use her bookmark/app). Sign in. Check order status — is anything actually showing as "undeliverable" or "needs address correction"?
  3. If nothing shows, or the order is already delivered / in transit normally, the text is fake. Stop.
  4. If something is genuinely stuck, go to the carrier's official site by typed URL (usps.com / ups.com / fedex.com / dhl.com — never a link from the text) and paste the tracking number from her confirmation email. The carrier's own page is the source of truth.
  5. If a real fee or address issue exists, the retailer or carrier will show it on their official page or by email. They do not collect $0.30 via SMS link. Real USPS in particular never texts a redelivery fee — they leave a physical notice and you handle it on usps.com.
  6. If still unclear, call the retailer or carrier using the number on their official site or the back of her payment card. Never a number from the text.

What to do with the text itself:

  - Do not reply. Replying confirms her number is live and invites more.
  - Do not click the link, not even to "see where it goes."
  - Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM). That's the US carrier reporting shortcode, honored by AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile. Free; routes it to the carrier's spam team.
  - On iPhone: long-press the message → Report Junk → Delete. On Android: open the message → three dots → Block & report spam.
  - Block the sender. Delete the text.

HAD-ENTERED-INFORMATION CASE (only applies if she had tapped, replied, typed card details, or downloaded anything — she has not)
============================================================================================================================

  - Call the card issuer using the number on the back of the card. Freeze or replace the card. Dispute any $0.30 charge (real or attempted) so it can't post or get retried.
  - If she typed a password she uses elsewhere, change it on those accounts now and turn on 2FA. A password manager with unique per-site passwords prevents this from compounding.
  - If anything was downloaded from the link, treat the phone as compromised. On iPhone: update iOS and remove any profile under Settings → General → VPN & Device Management. On Android: reboot to safe mode and uninstall anything unfamiliar; if an APK was installed and behavior is off, factory reset.
  - Place a free fraud alert with one of the three bureaus (Equifax / Experian / TransUnion); that bureau notifies the other two. For higher risk, request a free credit freeze at all three.
  - File reports at IdentityTheft.gov and reportfraud.ftc.gov (FTC). Also file at fcc.gov/complaints — the FCC tracks smishing and uses these for enforcement.
  - Watch for the follow-up "recovery scam": a call or text pretending to be her bank's fraud department, offering to "help." Her real bank will not call asking for the card PIN or full SSN. When in doubt, hang up and dial the number on the back of the card.
  - Monitor statements for 60–90 days. Many smishing kits sit on a card for weeks before testing larger charges.

Why the no-click case is genuinely safe: the scammer has no information, no click, and no confirmation her number is live. The whole response reduces to report + delete + verify against her own records.

Clean resolution, agreed. The chain held exactly as you'd want: saved legit email as source of truth → official page confirms transit + Tuesday delivery + no fee + no address issue → never opened the link, never entered anything → junk/report/delete/block. Nothing to remediate on the account or payment side since no credentials or data crossed the wire.

Worth noting (durably, not as a follow-up): she's already wired to treat the saved confirmation email as canonical and ignore the text-channel claim — that's the right reflex and you don't need to coach it. Treating it closed.

If a second one shows up later and the saved email doesn't have the order in question, that's the case where she'd need a different verification path (carrier site with tracking number, or you on the phone) — but that's a conditional, not an action.

Two bills, two unknowns (rate r and base B). The system:

612·r + B = 91.64
914·r + B = 127.22

Subtracting gives 302·r = 35.58, so r = 35.58 / 302 = 0.117814... $/kWh, or about 11.78 ¢/kWh.

Back-solving B: 91.64 − 612 × 0.117814... = 91.64 − 72.102... = 19.538... ≈ $19.54 base charge.

Verify on the new bill: 914 × 0.117814... + 19.538... = 107.682... + 19.538... = 127.22. ✓

What this means for the jump:

- kWh went from 612 → 914, an increase of 302 kWh (+49.4%).
- At ~11.78¢/kWh, those extra 302 kWh cost about $35.58 — almost exactly the $35.58 dollar increase.
- The base charge is unchanged ($19.54), and the per-kWh rate is the same on both bills.

So mathematically, the bill is fully explained by usage. There's no hidden rate change and no base-charge change hiding in the numbers. If the rate and base really are what you think they are on each bill's line items, the numbers reconcile cleanly to a constant rate and base, and the $35.58 jump is ~$35.58 of extra kWh.

Sanity check on whether 914 kWh is plausible:

Assuming roughly 30-day billing periods, that's about 30.5 kWh/day for the new bill vs. 20.4 kWh/day for the prior one. For a small home in East Austin in January with a cold snap plus two portable space heaters, +10 kWh/day is very much in the expected range — a single 1,500W space heater running 6–7 hours a day is ~9–10 kWh by itself, and central electric heat during a hard freeze can easily add another 5–15 kWh/day versus shoulder season.

One small caveat to flag, since you asked me to check before shrugging it off:

The two-bill solve assumes a single flat rate and a single base charge. If your utility has any of these, the numbers above can still match while masking a real rate change, so it's worth ruling them out on the bill face:

- Tiered rates (a higher ¢/kWh block you crossed into).
- A delivery charge that scales with kWh and was previously masked, or a fuel/capacity adjustment line that changes with usage.
- A demand charge or rider that's small enough to be invisible at 612 kWh but material at 914.
- Different billing-period lengths (the two "per-kWh math" rows above assumed both bills were the same number of days).

If the bill line items really do show one flat ¢/kWh, one base, and the billing periods are the same length, then your shrug is earned: it's usage. If there's a tier or an adjustment line, that's the place to look.

Given what you described — lever pulse plus a scrape locked to one point per wheel revolution — the rotor is almost certainly warped, or the caliper has shifted out of alignment. The good news: wheel looks seated, tire is up, no rim damage. That rules out the scarier stuff (taco, broken spoke, cracked rim). The thing I want to be straight with you about is the lever pulse. A quiet rub is a pad that's drifted a millimeter out of true and never grabs. A pulse through the lever means rotor thickness variation is reaching your hand — braking force is oscillating under your fingers. On the front brake, which does the majority of your stopping work, that is meaningfully different from a hiss.

How to tell them apart at the bike:

Quiet, usually-rideable rub:
  - Soft hiss or tick, not locked to wheel rotation
  - Lever feels firm and unchanged when you pull it stationary
  - No grabbing, no pull to one side when braking
  - Rotor gap to pad looks even as the wheel spins
  - Sound does not get louder the harder you brake
  - Braking power feels normal, lever does not sink toward the bar

Stop riding, walk it in:
  - Any pulse or kick in the lever under braking (or even just sitting on the bike) — thickness variation is reaching your hand
  - Scrape loud enough to hear over traffic, or that grows with lever pressure
  - Rotor visibly bent — you can see the disc run closer to one pad in one spot, with daylight on the opposite side at the same spot
  - Wheel weaving side-to-side when you sight the rotor edge against the fork dropout as it spins (out of true, separate problem, also stop-riding)
  - Brake grabs unevenly or the bike darts sideways under braking
  - Lever pulls all the way to the bar, or feels spongy compared to yesterday
  - Hot smell after a single light braking, or any blue / rainbow tint on the rotor face
  - Rotor bolts or caliper bolts feel loose
  - Pads visibly uneven — one thinner than the other, or glossy / oily (contamination)

Specifically for what you have:
  Lever pulse plus scrape-per-revolution together is not the quiet-rub case. Most likely a slightly bent rotor from a curb hit, hard bump, or transport strap — usually fixable with a rotor truing fork or a replacement rotor in the $30-60 range. Conservative call: ride the most direct, low-traffic, downhill-light route to a shop, brake gently and favor the rear until you arrive. If the route is anything but a few flat blocks, just walk it. Don't ride it as normal and don't plan to commute on it.

Quick checks you can do in the next few minutes, before deciding:

  1. Squeeze the front brake hard with the wheel off the ground (or just stationary), and have someone spin the wheel slowly while you look straight down at the rotor. Mark the rub spot with a Sharpie. If it lands in exactly the same place every revolution, that is the high point of a warped rotor.

  2. Check the two caliper bolts that hold the caliper to the fork. If either has shifted even slightly, back both off half a turn, squeeze the lever firmly to center the caliper over the rotor, then retighten them evenly. This fixes a surprising share of "single point rub" complaints — worth trying before assuming the rotor is bent.

  3. Check the rotor's six Torx bolts with the right size key. They should all feel equally snug. One loose rotor bolt can mimic warp exactly.

  4. Look at the rotor face under good light. Shiny polish, blue tint, or visible grooves mean it has been hot enough to harden unevenly, and a true will not fix it — replace it.

  5. Stand behind the bike and sight the rotor edge against the dropout or a fixed point on the fork. If the edge weaves side-to-side as it spins, the wheel is out of true and the problem is the wheel, not the rotor.

If after these checks the rotor visibly runs out (you can see it bent), or the lever pulse gets worse the harder you pull rather than staying constant, walk it. The threshold I'd use: anything you can fix in two minutes at the trailhead (loose caliper bolts) is fine to ride home on. Anything that needs the wheel off or a truing fork belongs in the shop, and the front brake is not the place to be lenient.

Two principles before the sequence:

  - The current `NNN_front.jpg` / `NNN_back.jpg` files are the archival color masters. They don't get overwritten.
  - Every alternate keeps the same leading photo number, so the front/back pair stays glued together in any sort by filename.

Naming convention (suffix before extension, photo number stays the prefix):

  NNN_front.jpg              archival color master (front, untouched)
  NNN_back.jpg               archival back capture (untouched)
  NNN_back_raking.jpg        pencil-readable alt of the back
  NNN_back_blue.jpg          optional cyan/blue-light alt if raking alone is faint
  NNN_front_polarized.jpg    glare-free alt of the front (polarizer method)
  NNN_front_diffuse.jpg      glare-free alt of the front (off-axis / diffuser method)
  NNN_front_alt1.jpg         generic second-angle alt when technique isn't named

  If you end up with two alternates for the same side, use _alt1 / _alt2 instead of stacking descriptive suffixes — keeps the convention parseable.

Sequence for the 5 pale-pencil backs:

  1. Pull the sleeve, leave the existing NNN_back.jpg where it is.
  2. Use a single light at a low angle — roughly 15-30° from the paper surface — raking across the writing. If you don't know the stroke direction, try one orientation, capture, then rotate the photo 90° and capture again; keep both as NNN_back_raking_a.jpg and NNN_back_raking_b.jpg and pick the legible one.
  3. Capture in RAW if your camera supports it, TIFF otherwise. JPEG throws away the midtone subtlety that pencil needs to read.
  4. Optional: if raking still leaves the pencil ghosted, swap to a blue-dominant light source (or a cyan filter over the lens). Graphite absorbs blue more than the paper does, which lifts apparent contrast. Save as NNN_back_blue.jpg.
  5. Compare NNN_back.jpg (reference), the raking alt, and the blue alt on a calibrated display. Pick the keeper. Original stays as-is.

Sequence for the 2 glossy fronts with glare:

  1. Leave NNN_front.jpg alone.
  2. Preferred path: mount a circular polarizer on the lens and rotate it while watching live view. The specular highlight will dim and disappear at one rotation; capture there as NNN_front_polarized.jpg.
  3. No-polarizer path: move both lights well off-axis (45°+ from the lens axis) and/or enlarge the source with a diffuser until the highlight spreads and fades. Capture as NNN_front_diffuse.jpg. If glare persists in a different region, shift the camera angle slightly and capture a second frame as NNN_front_alt1.jpg.
  4. Compare against the archival master on screen. Pick the face with the cleanest eyes and skin tones; the original stays as the master.

Small final notes:

  - Keep a one-line log per photo (a plain text file in the sleeve box, or a paper sheet): "keeper: NNN_back_raking.jpg" or "keeper: NNN_front_polarized.jpg." Future-you won't have to re-derive which alt won.
  - Do all viewing and editing on copies. Never adjust curves on the archival master in place — re-export under a different name (e.g., NNN_front_edit.jpg) and leave the master untouched.
  - If you capture RAW, also export a TIFF next to each keeper alt, so the JPEGs you actually look at aren't the only record of the legibility win.

Three new file roles total: raking back, optional blue back, and polarized (or diffuse) front. One naming rule: photo number stays the prefix, technique goes in the suffix. Originals never move.

Clean fix — $58 for trued rotor + new pads + caliper/wheel seating check is reasonable, and the parking-lot gate (no pulsing, no fade, no wheel movement) is the right one before trusting the bike on a longer ride.

Worth tracking: a bent rotor usually traces to either an impact (rock, pothole, curb strike) or a caliper that's been hanging up on a sticky piston. If you don't remember an impact and it re-bends within the next few rides, ask the shop to look at the caliper pistons and wheel true on the next service — cheap to catch early, expensive if a pad grinds a fresh rotor.

The $38 is buying $5,000 of water-backup (and likely sump-pump-related) coverage that the competitor doesn't offer at any price. So these are not "identical policies, $38 apart" - they're identical on the headline limits and meaningfully different on one specific endorsement.

Quick math on the tradeoff:
  - $38/yr for a $5,000 limit is a premium-to-limit ratio of roughly 0.76% per year.
    Over 5 years you'd spend $190 to be protected against a single $5,000 event.
  - Water and sewer backup is one of the most common and most expensive
    renters-insurance claims - damaged flooring, drywall, furniture, electronics,
    and the mold that follows. A single event commonly runs $3K-$20K+.
  - Whether $38/yr is a fair price depends almost entirely on your physical
    exposure: ground-floor or basement unit, older building with original
    plumbing, mature trees near the sewer lateral, presence of a sump pump,
    any prior backups in the building. If none of those apply, the actuarial
    value of the endorsement to you is genuinely lower than $38. If one or
    more apply, $38/yr is very cheap insurance.

What you're really deciding isn't "is $38 worth $5,000 of coverage" in the abstract - it's "is $38 worth $5,000 of coverage given my actual exposure."

Shortest useful list of questions for the current carrier:

  1. Does the $5,000 water-backup limit have any sub-limits (electronics,
     jewelry, mold remediation) that would cap a real claim below $5,000?
     And is the deductible on water-backup claims the same $1,000, or a
     separate, higher water-specific deductible (commonly $2,500)?

  2. What exactly triggers the endorsement? Specifically, does it cover
     (a) sewer/drain backup into the unit, (b) sump-pump overflow, and
     (c) sump-pump failure during a power outage? These are usually distinct
     coverage grants and the competitor's exclusion may be narrower than
     "no water backup at all."

  3. Does it include loss-of-use / additional-living-expense if a backup
     makes the unit uninhabitable, and is that inside the $5,000 or a
     separate limit?

  4. Other than water backup, is there anything materially different from
     the competitor that isn't in the headline limits? Ask about by name:
     special sub-limits on jewelry, watches, and computers; "like kind and
     quality" vs full replacement-cost wording on personal property; coverage
     for items stored outside the unit (car, storage locker); loss-assessment
     coverage if the building is part of an HOA; and the medical-payments-
     to-others limit.

  5. Is there a mid-tier option - either a $2,500 water-backup limit at a
     lower price, or any discount for declining it - so you can compare on
     a curve rather than a binary switch?

One thing you don't need to ask the carrier about: their AM Best rating and complaint index. That's public information and a 30-second check you can do yourself before the call.

After the call, the decision rule is simple: if the current policy gives $5,000 of broad, clean water-backup coverage with no hidden deductible or sub-limits, and you have any of the physical-exposure factors above, switching to save $38 is the textbook case of being penny-wise and pound-foolish. If your exposure is genuinely low and the endorsement has a $2,500 deductible hidden inside it, switching makes sense.

Two-issue kickoff triage. Principle: smallest blast radius, no live-fire changes, prove before you remove.

Order (roughly half a day across both, sequenced so anchoring lands first):

  1. Inventory and freeze scope  ~ 20 min
     - For each moving-window preflight: capture the campaign, the source segment, and the preflight job/query that produces the count.
     - For the paused fallback: capture the paused template (template_id), the live workflow that names it (workflow_id), and the trigger condition that routes to the fallback branch.
     - List sibling campaigns/workflows that share the same workflow, so the blast-radius boundary is named before any edit. If a sibling touches the same fallback node, pause this triage step and re-scope.

  2. Anchor the two moving-window preflights  ~ 2 hours, zero live-send impact
     - Replace the dynamic 7-day query with an as-of-anchored snapshot segment. The campaign logic stays untouched; only the preflight inspects the snapshot.
     - Name per the operational-state convention: include the as-of date and the window in the name. Example: support_contact_window__prior_7d__snapshot_2024_01_15. No v1/test/beta suffixes; the name carries the operational state.

  3. Prove or remove the paused fallback  ~ 1 to 2 hours, scoped to one workflow
     - Prove first. If proven unreachable, document and close. If reachable, remove the fallback reference (do not unpause the template, do not edit the trigger condition).
     - Containment: the edit lives inside the one workflow's fallback branch only.

Acceptance tests, moving-window preflights:

  A1. Rerun the preflight on Day N and Day N+1 with no intervening support contacts in the source. Expected: identical count. If the count moves, the segment is still rolling rather than anchored; fail.

  A2. Between those two runs, add a single known support-contact fixture to the source. Expected: count increases by exactly 1. This confirms the snapshot still reads the source while staying as-of-anchored.

  A3. The snapshot segment's name carries an as-of date in the operational-state convention. The segment_id is logged next to each preflight run, so a future reader can reconstruct which as-of value produced which number.

  A4. Tuesday field-completeness review: the snapshot segment clears the field-completeness gate before it is promoted to "the" preflight segment for both campaigns.

Acceptance tests, paused fallback:

  B1. Open the workflow definition; confirm the fallback branch's destination template_id exactly matches the paused template from the kickoff inventory. If it does not, stop and re-scope before any removal.

  B2. Send-log query for the paused template_id over the last 90 days. Expected: zero sends. If non-zero, the inventory claim of "no recent sends" is wrong; surface to the contractor before any removal, because the path is reachable in fact, not just in theory.

  B3. Trigger-evaluation log for the workflow over the same window: at least one user_id has evaluated the trigger condition AND the fallback branch has been evaluated for at least one of those users. This proves the branch is live code, not dead code.

  B4. Removal pass (only if B2 = zero and B3 confirms reachability): edit the workflow to remove the fallback reference; dry-run the workflow against a fixture user_id; confirm the dry-run path no longer terminates in the paused template. Do not touch the trigger condition or any other branch.

  B5. Post-removal falsifiable gate: rerun the send-log query for the template_id for the next 7 days. Expected: zero sends. That zero is the receipt that the fallback is gone.

Containment notes (what NOT to do):

  - Don't edit the trigger condition of the workflow with the paused fallback. Only the fallback reference is in scope.
  - Don't unpause the paused template "to test it." That is a separate decision and belongs in a different review.
  - Don't re-architect either campaign to fix the preflight problem. The fix lives in the segment, not the campaign.
  - Don't rename the paused template. Pause is a Customer.io-layer mechanism; renaming it muddies the audit trail.
  - Don't promote the snapshot segment to a non-QA role until it clears the Tuesday field-completeness gate.

Naming convention reminder for the contractor: every segment, workflow, and template touched in this triage carries operational state in its name (as-of dates, branch role, condition key), not lifecycle-stage labels.

Sanitization for sharing: keep template_id, workflow_id, segment_id in the contractor's working doc. For anything that leaves the kickoff triage scope, swap IDs for labels and redact user identifiers. Denominators, effects, and conclusions stay; raw IDs and hashes do not.

Direct answer: yes, a bounded invite-reminder proposal is in bounds — but only if it stays framed as a *prospective* test of an *intervention*, with the descriptive cross-section as motivation, not as evidence. And it's the right *direction*, not a done deal.

Why it's defensible to propose:
- The size moved meaningfully. p≈.05 with n=312 is right at the edge, and the CI on the diff is roughly [+0.2, +22] points — wide, but entirely above zero. That's a different posture than 12/22 (raw +2.4, CI crossed zero). It earns the "worth a closer look" framing.

- An 11-pt descriptive gap in an observational sample is exactly the kind of number people anchor on and then quietly upgrade to "invites drive renewal." You don't want the doc to read that way even by implication.
- If you propose this, Owen's readout shape will want: (1) a defined intervention (what the reminder actually is, who gets it, when), (2) a unit of randomization (account vs user vs workspace), (3) a primary outcome + guardrails, (4) a stop rule + a "no effect" branch. That's the proposal. The descriptive cut is the motivation paragraph, not the justification paragraph.

My recommendation for how to position it:
- Lead with the descriptive-association framing in one sentence (≥2 invites observed in healthier accounts; this may describe rather than cause).
- State the size honestly: 11.1 pts raw, CI roughly [+0.2, +22], p ≈ .05. Do not round to "significant."

- Then the proposal, separately: "Given the directional association and clean risk profile, propose a bounded randomized reminder test in Q1, scoped to [cohort], with [outcome + guardrails]." Stop there. No expected lift number. No "if it works we'll…" sentence.

The click-plus-dimming pattern is textbook weak/dead battery: the solenoid engages but voltage collapses under starter load. A March 2019 battery in most US climates is end-of-life or past it, so "old battery" is your working hypothesis. The sequence below is built to fail safe if it turns out to be a connection or charging-system problem instead.

PRE-CONNECT (30 seconds)
- Confirm the jump pack is charged (LED shows full).
- Glance at the battery: no cracks, leaks, swelling. (You already cleared this.)
- Key OUT of ignition. All accessories OFF (lights, climate, radio, phone chargers).
- Parking brake set, transmission in Park (or Neutral for manual).
- Rings off; don't lean over the battery.

CONNECTION ORDER
1. RED clamp to the dead battery's POSITIVE (+) post. Wiggle to confirm a solid bite.
2. BLACK clamp to a clean, unpainted metal ground on the engine block or a chassis bracket — NOT the dead battery's negative post. Any battery can off-gas a little hydrogen; a remote ground keeps any spark away from the cells.
3. Power the jump pack ON only after both clamps are connected, unless your pack's manual says otherwise.

CRANKING PROTOCOL — CONSERVATIVE
- One attempt: 3 seconds of crank.
- STOP. Wait 60 seconds. Watch and listen.
- If it fires: let it idle 2–3 minutes on the pack, then disconnect (reverse order below). Drive it.
- If it doesn't fire: ONE more 3-second attempt, then stop. That's it.

HARD STOP CONDITIONS — do not keep trying if any of these happen
- No change in starter behavior after 2 attempts (same rapid clicking, no slow cranking) → the pack isn't getting through, or this isn't a battery problem. Stop and re-inspect clamps and ground before any third try.
- Battery case gets warm or hot to the touch.
- Rotten-egg / sulfur smell that wasn't there before.
- Any smoke, hissing, swelling, or a terminal that gets hot under load.
- Jump pack shuts itself off (over-current protection tripped) repeatedly.
- Engine cranks but doesn't fire → not a battery problem; stop cranking. Fuel/ignition is a shop issue, not a driveway-hammering issue.
- Total cranking time across all attempts > ~10–15 seconds.

DISCONNECTION (reverse order)
1. Jump pack OFF.
2. BLACK clamp off first.
3. RED clamp off second.

POST-START — smallest set that separates "old battery" from "charging system"
You need a multimeter for the first two; if you don't have one, skip to step 3 — it covers everything more reliably.

1. Engine OFF, wait 5 minutes, measure at the terminals:
   - 12.6 V+ = healthy.
   - 12.2–12.4 V = discharged, possibly OK.
   - Below 12.0 V = failing or deeply discharged.

2. Engine RUNNING at idle, measure again:
   - 13.7–14.7 V = alternator is charging. Normal.
   - Below 13.5 V = alternator not charging. Do not shut the car off; drive straight to a shop.
   - Above 15.0 V = regulator failing; stop as soon as it's safe.

3. Free battery + alternator test at any auto-parts store (AutoZone, O'Reilly, Advance, NAPA, Costco). A handheld conductance tester reports actual CCA vs rated and alternator output under load. Do this within a day or two, after at least 30 minutes of driving so the battery has surface charge. This single visit answers both questions more reliably than anything you can do at home.

If you don't have a multimeter, the rough proxies are: idle with headlights on and steady, lights don't brighten noticeably when you rev slightly (alternator keeping up), and the car still starts cold the next morning (battery holding charge).

DECISION
- Starts, holds charge overnight, charging voltage in range → old battery. Replace at convenience; 5 years is past typical service life, don't ignore it.
- Starts but charging voltage is off → charging system problem. Drive to a shop without shutting off if voltage is low.
- Won't start even with the jump pack after correct clamp contact and a clean ground point → not a battery problem you can solve in the driveway. Check the clamps and ground one more time, then it's a tow.

Order, from most reversible to most committed, with a stop test after each paint move:

0. Hold a mat or card over the painting and try 2-3 crops. 30 seconds, no paint touched. If a tighter crop alone resolves the competition, you've found your answer. If not, you've confirmed the issue is local to the trees, not the framing.

1. Soften 1-2 edges that butt against the focal point. Damp brush (not wet), blot on a tissue. Push them back into atmosphere. ~3-5 min.

   Stop. Squint. Does the bend in the path now read as the highest-contrast, sharpest area? If yes - put the brush down.

2. If it still doesn't read, lift value from the LEAST important tree (the most peripheral, or the one furthest from the focal point). Damp brush, gentle scrub, blot. Even a 10-15% drop differentiates it from its neighbors - don't try to lift the whole mass. ~5 min.

   Stop. Same squint test.

3. Only if the trees still feel like three competing dots: a narrow connecting shadow that links them into a single mass, or a thin dark accent that leads the eye to the bend. Keep it small - it's a connector, not a new element. ~3 min.

   Stop. Do not continue. If composition still feels off, the painting has told you something.

When to stop, stated plainly:

- After any step where the focal point reads: stop. Don't "improve."
- Hard cap: 2 paint moves. Step 3 (connecting shadow) is a last resort, not a default. If you find yourself reaching for it as move 2, you've moved too fast.
- The line you've crossed: you reach for the brush without a specific reason, or you catch yourself saying "just one more touch." Both mean stop.
- If steps 1-3 don't fully resolve it, accept the painting as a study. Three same-value tree masses is a known composition hazard - the lesson is often what the painting taught you, not the fifth pass.

# Crude vs mix-adjusted activation — Owen's 1/23 weekly readout

## 1. What we have vs what we need

From Owen's cut we have two totals:

- Prior cohort crude activation: **57.2%**
- Current cohort crude activation: **61.8%**
- Crude difference: **+4.6 pp**

## 2. The math, written out

Notation. Let s ∈ {AI, NYI} be the two strata (already-integrated-at-signup, not-yet-integrated-at-signup). For cohort c ∈ {prior, current}, let:

- w_c(s) = share of cohort c in stratum s (mix weights, sum to 1)
- r_c(s) = within-stratum activation rate in cohort c

Crude activation for cohort c is the weighted sum:

  Crude_c = Σ_s  w_c(s) · r_c(s)

**Crude difference** (what Owen published):

  Δ_crude = Crude_current − Crude_prior

**Direct standardization to the prior mix** (the "lifecycle holding composition fixed" view — exactly what you asked for):

  Adj_current = Σ_s  w_prior(s) · r_current(s)

  Δ_adj = Adj_current − Crude_prior

This is the comparison that answers "if the current cohort had the prior cohort's signup mix, what would the crude rate have been, and how does that compare to the prior crude?" Everything in Δ_adj is a within-stratum rate change — no mix shift contribution.

**Composition effect** (the share of Δ_crude that's *not* lifecycle):

  Δ_mix = Σ_s (w_current(s) − w_prior(s)) · r_prior(s)

**Within-stratum effect:**

  Δ_within = Σ_s  w_prior(s) · (r_current(s) − r_prior(s))

**Interaction** (residual — usually small, useful for honesty):

  Δ_interact = Σ_s (w_current(s) − w_prior(s)) · (r_current(s) − r_prior(s))

Identity (sanity check):

  Δ_crude ≡ Δ_mix + Δ_within + Δ_interact

Important — your message gives "446 per arm" as the requirement, and I've independently recomputed it under standard assumptions. Let me check whether the math supports your number before I stake a recommendation on it, because the difference between "446/arm" and "446/arm at a different baseline or MDE" is exactly the kind of error that would make a "do not run" call look overconfident.

Working it by hand (no Python execution available in this session; flagging that explicitly):

Standard two-proportion test for two-sided α=0.05, power=0.80:
  z_α/2 = 1.960, z_β = 0.842
  n per arm = (1.960 + 0.842)² × [p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂)] / (p₂ − p₁)²

Plugging p₁ = 0.72, p₂ = 0.80:
  numerator factor (1.960 + 0.842)² ≈ 7.849
  p₁(1−p₁) = 0.2016
  p₂(1−p₂) = 0.1600
  sum = 0.3616
  (p₂ − p₁)² = 0.0064
  n = 7.849 × 0.3616 / 0.0064 ≈ 443.4 per arm

So your draft's ~446/arm ≈ 892 total reconciles cleanly under the standard pooled-variance two-proportion formula. The power math is not the problem. Now the call.

================================================================
DO NOT RUN. Log it, do not run it.
================================================================

1) The pool vs. requirement gap is unbridgeable inside this design

  Eligible after exclusions:  112 accounts
  Required (80% power, 2-sided α=0.05,
            72%→80% absolute lift): ~892 total, ~446/arm
  Shortfall: ~780 accounts, ~7.2× the available pool

  What 112 can actually detect at 80% power, 56/56 split, same α:
  Solving the same formula backward for the smallest lift n=56 will support lands at roughly an absolute lift of ~20–22 percentage points — i.e. ~2.5–2.75× the hoped-for 8 points. Even at 60% power the detectable MDE is only down to ~17–18 points. No reasonable power setting recovers an 8-point claim on this cohort.

  You do not "log it anyway" because logging a powered-for-8pp test as if it tested 8pp is exactly the failure pattern already on the books (the 11.1-point descriptive, the +0.7/+0.2 non-replication, the 7.3pp CS reach imbalance). Logging a test that could not detect its own hypothesis and then acting on a p-value it was never going to earn is the same trap with a sample-size footnote attached.

2) Why a faster secondary "invite-rate" signal cannot rescue an underpowered renewal claim

  Two reasons, both load-bearing:

  (a) The secondary metric is not the decision metric. The decision you would actually want to make is "does this reminder change next-term renewal?" Invite rate is a proxy at best. A treatment can move invite rate without moving renewal (reminders shift behavior on the prompted surface; renewal is downstream of admin quality, support load, and the underlying health of the account). You can detect a real invite-rate effect and still have zero information about whether renewal moves. Optimizing the readout around the metric that has power is the textbook way to ship something that fails on the metric you cared about.

  (b) Even taken on its own terms, the secondary metric does not buy you what you think. With a binary outcome and base rates typical of invite prompts (call it 15–30% within 14 days), the per-arm N for an 8–12 absolute-point invite lift lands in the low hundreds — lower than the renewal requirement but still far above 56. And critically: a positive secondary read does not earn a renewal claim. It earns a "we moved behavior on the surface; renewal still untested." That is not a rescue. That is a faster way to confuse yourselves about what was learned.

  Put differently: the underpowered renewal test does not become valid because something else inside it became significant. It becomes a test of something else, with renewal still unmeasured.

3) Why first significance still needs a stabilization cohort, even if you could run it

  Three reasons, all of which already fired on this product:

  (a) Early significance on small cohorts is dominated by sampling noise, not treatment effect. The +2.3pp / p=.047 September read, the +0.7pp / p=.04 first growth cohort, and the +0.2pp / p=.31 stabilization cohort are the same shape you would get from the collaborator-invite test: first cohort looks real, second cohort doesn't, combined result washes out. Acting on the first read in that pattern is what the standing rule exists to prevent.

  (b) The 30-to-90-day age band plus a renewal-window outcome means the outcome is not mature when first significance appears. Renewal cohorts don't stabilize until roughly 90 days after the last assignment, and accounts 30 days old are still inside onboarding turbulence (admin, import, and entitlement activity — exactly the events that scramble the "≥2 invites in 14 days" secondary). First significance on day 14 or day 30 is reading a not-yet-stable outcome.

  (c) The collaborator-invite reminder is the wrong shape for a first-significance ship decision even when powered. The exposure stack (current reminder cadence + adoption-plan state + support/suppression state + heterogeneous time-to-renewal) is heterogeneous, and selective stopping at first p<.05 is one of the defects already named in the January 22 draft. A stabilization cohort is the minimum guardrail against stopping on the first noisy read of a heterogeneous population.

  Cuts:    Eligible pool = 164 − 28 (already exposed) − 15 (open adoption / recent support) − 9 (insufficient observation window) = 112. Required n ≈ 446/arm ≈ 892 total. No reasonable design change closes a ~7× gap.

Short answer: don't dispute yet. What you're seeing is almost certainly a double-swipe/double-tap at the terminal, not a real duplicate charge. A pending authorization is a hold, not money that has moved. The pending $86.42 will typically drop on its own within 2–5 business days and cost you nothing. Disputing now would mostly create friction, not resolve anything.

Why this is the prudent read

- The posted $86.42 is real; the pending one is just reducing your available credit. No money has actually moved twice.
- Filing a dispute on the posted charge while a matching pending auth is still floating can interact badly with that still-open auth and slow down the cleaner resolution.
- Identical amount, identical merchant, same dinner, same date, receipt matches one purchase, no split/tip change — that's the classic signature of an accidental re-presentment. (Real fraudsters don't pick the same exact subtotal twice on the same night at the same place.)

Prudent sequence

1. Right now (Jan 26): capture records only. Don't call anyone yet.
2. Around Jan 29 (day 3): check the card app. In most cases the pending one is gone.
3. Around Jan 31 (day 5): check again. If it's still pending, it's likely going to convert to a posted second charge — that's your action trigger.
4. Around Feb 2 (day 7): if nothing has moved and the restaurant hasn't responded, escalate to the issuer.

What to save now (do this before you forget — it's the difference between a 5-minute issuer call and a 30-minute one later)

- Photo/scan of the receipt with the date and total visible.
- Screenshot of both line items in the card app showing the $86.42 charges — one Posted, one Pending — including the merchant descriptor exactly as it appears and any authorization/reference codes the app shows.
- A short dated note (a phone note or a doc titled something like "Card dup 2024-01-26") containing:
  - date and approximate time of dinner
  - restaurant name and location
  - server name if you remember it
  - whose card was used
  - one explicit line: "Receipt shows one $86.42 charge. No split payment. No second tip. No second card presented."

Threshold for action

Call the restaurant if either of these happens:

- the Pending charge converts to Posted at any point before day 5, OR
- the Pending one is still sitting there on day 5.

Ask them to void the duplicate authorization on their POS. Most of the time they do it in seconds. Get the name of whoever does it and a void reference number.

Call the card issuer to file a true duplicate dispute only after one of:

- (a) the second charge has Posted and you've given the restaurant 1–2 business days to void it without success, or
- (b) the Pending charge is still unresolved on day 7+ and the restaurant isn't responding.

When you call, you'll hand them: the receipt, the two screenshots, the merchant name, and the date. That's the whole file.

One thing not to do: don't call the issuer "just to flag it" while the second charge is still pending. They can't dispute a pending authorization, and getting a note on the account now can make the cleaner dispute messier if you end up needing one.
