Two notes upfront before I dig in:

1. I don't have the two annual premium figures, so I can't run the dollar cost comparison yet — drop those in and I'll finish that part. Everything below doesn't depend on them.
2. This assumes both quotes list the same address, named insureds, and total personal-property coverage limit. If any of those differ between the quotes, that changes the comparison materially — flag it if so.

ACTUAL CASH VALUE vs REPLACEMENT COST — in real terms

ACV = what it would cost to replace the item today, minus depreciation. Depreciation is whatever the insurer decides the item has lost in value (age, condition, sometimes "obsolescence"). RC = the cost to buy a comparable new item today, no depreciation.

Worked against your actual items:

  - A 3-year-old laptop you bought at $2,800. RC for an equivalent today: roughly $2,800-$3,200. ACV: insurers commonly apply 20-40%/year on electronics, so the same machine might be valued at $1,400-$1,800. Same loss event, $1,000-$1,400 difference out of your pocket on the cheaper quote.

  - A bike bought for $1,800 two years ago. RC today for a comparable: $1,800. ACV: bikes depreciate slower than electronics (often 10-15%/year), so maybe $1,300-$1,500. Net recovery after deductible: on Quote B (RC, $500 ded) you recover roughly $1,300; on Quote A (ACV, $1,000 ded) you recover $300-$500 — not enough to make filing worth it, so you'd absorb the loss.

  - Watercolor supplies don't really depreciate in usefulness (a good brush lasts decades), but ACV doesn't care — the formula applies anyway. Paints, paper, and frames at RC get replaced at today's retail; under ACV you may recover less than you paid for the same items last year.

The general pattern: ACV penalizes you for owning things you actually use. RC rewards it.

COVERAGE TRADEOFFS for your specific items

Work equipment (laptop, monitor, possibly camera/lighting, peripherals):
- Electronics depreciate fastest under ACV, so this is the largest single line-item difference between the two quotes.
- Worth checking on both quotes: most renter's policies carry a "business property" sublimit (often $2,500) for items used for work. If Riley's laptop is employer-issued, it may be covered under the employer's policy, not yours. If Sam brings high-end chef knives or specialty equipment home, those may sit under the same sublimit rather than personal property.

Bikes:
- Theft away from home (rack-locked, on transit, at a friend's place) is usually covered but often with a sublimit — commonly 10% of personal property, or a flat $1,000-$2,000 cap per bike. This matters more than the deductible for bikes. Verify on both quotes.
- Crash damage is generally NOT covered by renter's insurance; that's an auto/homeowner or a separate bike rider.

Art supplies:
- Standard personal-property coverage handles working supplies (paints, brushes, paper, palettes, easel) cleanly. The replacement-cost version means you're made whole at current retail; the ACV version calculates depreciation on items that, in practice, don't wear out.
- If either of you has finished work on the walls — Riley's watercolors, prints either of you care about — those count as personal property under the same limit. Expensive original art often has a per-item sublimit (e.g., $2,500/item). Anything above that needs to be scheduled separately on either quote.

Other things Quote B buys you that Quote A doesn't:

Water-backup coverage: standard renter's policies exclude damage from sewer backup, sump-pump failure, and drain overflow. The endorsement covers belongings damaged by these specific causes. For a ground-floor unit or anything with finished space below, this is the most-used endorsement on a renter's policy and pays for itself in a single event. Worth knowing which floor/unit you're in.

Liability $100K -> $300K: most personal umbrella policies require underlying limits of $300K, so Quote B positions you for an umbrella later if neither employer provides one. Practical: chef's kitchen + water media + a dog in the home = a higher-than-average chance of someone getting hurt on-premises. $300K is the more conservative floor.

Deductible $1,000 -> $500: with a $1,000 deductible you'll sit on small claims (under ~$1,500-$2,000) rather than file, because the recovery after deductible isn't worth the premium impact. With $500, more claims are worth filing.

THREE FOCUSED QUESTIONS FOR THE INSURER

1. What are the personal-property sublimits — specifically for bikes (theft away from home), jewelry/fine art per-item, business property, and any per-category caps? A policy with a $30K personal-property limit and a $1,500 bike cap leaves you exposed on the bike regardless of which quote you pick. Get the actual numbers in writing.

2. How is depreciation calculated under ACV on Quote A — straight-line by age, condition-based, or category-specific? "Actual cash value" is not a defined term in most states; the formula is whatever the policy language says. If they can't or won't give you the formula in writing, that's a signal about how they'll handle a claim.

3. On Quote B, what does the water-backup endorsement actually cover, and at what limit? Specifically: does it cover sump-pump failure, sewer backup, and drain overflow from any source? Is the limit per occurrence or aggregate over the policy term? Does it cover the cost of access and remediation (tearing out wet flooring, drying the space) or only damaged belongings?

Two additional things to confirm on both quotes regardless of which you pick: that BOTH Sam and Riley are listed as named insureds (not just one of you — partner of a named insured has weaker claim standing in some states), and that Cherrywood's role is "certificate holder / interested party" only — not "additional insured." Those are different things on a renter's policy and they change who can file or be named on a claim.

To finish the dollar side, send me the two annual premiums and I'll work through the multi-year cost, including the expected-value cost of the RC-vs-ACV gap on your specific inventory (work gear + bikes + art supplies) over a typical claim horizon.

Recommendation: Option B.

  The $6.80/month delta (~$82/year) buys materially more protection on every
  dimension. The load-bearing differences:

  1. Replacement cost vs ACV is the biggest one. ACV pays the depreciated
     value of your stuff; replacement cost pays to buy new equivalents. On a
     $20-30K contents inventory that gap is usually worth the upgrade alone.

  2. $500 deductible vs $1,000: any claim, you pay half as much out of pocket.

  3. Water backup ($5K, B only) covers sump-pump failure and sewer backup —
     common rental losses and often excluded from base policies.

  4. Option A only clears Cherrywood's $100K liability floor by exactly $0.
     Option B has real cushion if something goes sideways.

  5. If a dog is in the household, dog-bite claims routinely clear $100K.
     Option B's $300K liability is the safer pick for that risk.

  Option A is defensible only if monthly cash flow is the dominant constraint
  AND the contents inventory is genuinely under ~$5K. Even then the deductible
  gap and missing water backup leave it thin.


One thing worth confirming before binding either quote: ask the carrier
explicitly about any dog on the premises — breed/restriction exclusions can
be buried in the policy and would void liability coverage mid-claim.

Practical effect of the four answers

- Computers, bicycles, and art supplies are personal property under both quotes — covered, not excluded. The "business inventory" carve-out only matters if you were storing stock for resale, which doesn't apply to either of you.
- Theft away from the residence is covered like any other theft claim, just subject to the policy's terms and deductible. No surprise gap; the away-from-home exclusion you might have worried about isn't there.
- No item you currently own is above the $2,500 scheduling threshold, so nothing has to be scheduled now. The rule is one to remember if either of you later buys something individually worth more than that.
- The two quotes are otherwise equivalent on coverage scope. The only price gap is $84/year for the replacement-cost endorsement.

What this narrows the choice to

The remaining decision is just whether to pay $84/year for the replacement-cost (RC) endorsement over the actual-cash-value (ACV) quote.

How the RC vs ACV difference plays out in a claim

- ACV pays the depreciated value of the item — what a used version is worth today. A bike insured for $1,500 that is two years old might pay out roughly $900–$1,100 depending on the depreciation schedule; whatever the replacement cost is above that comes out of your pocket.
- RC does not pay replacement cost up front. The insurer pays ACV first, then pays the recoverable depreciation separately — and only after you actually replace the item and submit receipts.
  - If you don't replace it (some losses are total and you don't want the same thing back), you only ever receive ACV.
  - You have to be willing and able to front the replacement cost briefly, or buy first and wait for reimbursement.

When the $84/year tends to be worth it
  - The items most at risk (your work computer, Sam's bike, anything you'd realistically buy again at full price) are the kind you'd actually replace after a loss.
  - The gap between ACV and a new replacement on a likely target item is bigger than $84.
  - You expect at least one meaningful claim over the policy lifetime, or want the peace of mind for low-frequency/high-impact loss.

When ACV is the more sensible pick
  - You'd be content with depreciated-value payout, or you'd replace with a used or cheaper item anyway.
  - Your exposure is genuinely low — secure building, indoor bike storage, light away-from-home theft risk.
  - You prefer to keep the $84/year and absorb the gap on a rare claim.

Two things to keep in mind whichever quote you pick
  - The deductible still applies; losses under the deductible aren't worth filing.
  - If you later acquire any single item over $2,500, it must be added as a scheduled endorsement — that's a separate step, not automatic under either quote.

Net: the only real choice is the $84/year RC endorsement, and it earns its premium only on claims where you actually go on to replace the lost item at today's price. If that's a realistic path for you, the RC quote is the better deal; if ACV payouts would still leave you close enough to whole, the savings aren't worth chasing.

Here is the comparison you asked for. Per your instruction, I'm not recommending an option.

THE MATH

With base + bonus only (everything else equal), total compensation as a function of the payout multiplier m (0% to 100% of target) is:

    A(m) = 128,000 + 0.10 * 128,000 * m  = 128,000 + 12,800 * m
    B(m) = 121,000 + 0.18 * 121,000 * m  = 121,000 + 21,780 * m

Solve B(m) = A(m):

    121,000 + 21,780m  =  128,000 + 12,800m
    8,980m             =  7,000
    m                  =  7,000 / 8,980  =  350/449  ~=  0.7795

Breakeven payout multiplier: about 77.95% of target (call it ~78%).

  Below ~78% of target paid out -> Option A pays more (because of the $7,000 higher base).
  Above ~78% of target paid out -> Option B pays more (because of the larger bonus).

SAMPLE PAYOUTS

  payout  |   A total   |   B total   |  who wins, by how much
  --------|-------------|-------------|------------------------
    0%    |  $128,000   |  $121,000   |  A +$7,000
   50%    |  $134,400   |  $131,890   |  A +$2,510
   70%    |  $136,960   |  $136,246   |  A +$714
   78%    |  $137,984   |  $137,988   |  tie (~+-$4)
   80%    |  $138,240   |  $138,424   |  B +$184
   90%    |  $139,520   |  $140,602   |  B +$1,082
  100%    |  $140,800   |  $142,780   |  B +$1,980

A useful shortcut: A is $7,000 ahead on base; B's bonus-per-1% of payout beats A's by $89.80. B needs about 78% payout to recover the $7,000 base gap.

If the plan ever pays above 100% (some do), B's lead widens every percentage point past 100.

WHAT MARCUS SHOULD BRING BEFORE DECIDING

The whole choice hinges on one question: in this role, at this company, what does the bonus actually pay out, and how predictable is it? He'll want:

1. Multi-year payout history for comparable roles.
   - Last 3-5 years of actual payouts, expressed as % of target, for people in the same org/level.
   - Median, mean, and the year-by-year spread (not just an average). A 5-year average of 90% can hide three 60% years and two 120% years; that distribution matters more than the mean.
   - Was there ever a year payouts were 0, or below 50%? If down years are plausible, A's higher base is real protection.

2. Plan mechanics, in writing.
   - Is the target a guaranteed target, or a "guideline"? Many plans say "target" but pay at manager discretion.
   - Cap: can payout exceed 100% of target? If yes, by how much (e.g., 150%, 200%)? If hard-capped at 100%, that bounds B's upside.
   - Threshold: is there a minimum performance level below which payout is 0?
   - Formulaic vs. discretionary: is the multiplier set by a formula tied to company financials/OKRs, or is it a management pool? Formulaic = backtest the formula on prior years. Discretionary = look at track record of his direct manager and skip-level.
   - What metrics drive it: company-wide, business-unit, team, or individual? His level of control over those metrics changes how much his own performance can shift the multiplier.
   - Payment timing and form: lump sum vs. spread; any deferral, clawback, or pro-ration if he joins mid-year.

3. Base-relative volatility.
   - A's base is $7,000 higher (about 5.8%). In a year B pays out at 50% of target, A is ahead by $2,510; at 0% A is ahead by $7,000. Marcus should weigh how much cash-flow predictability matters against how much upside matters.

4. Equity confirmation.
   - You said equity is the same. Worth confirming: same grant size, same vesting schedule (cliff + monthly/annual), same strike, same refresh cadence. A single difference here can swamp the base+bonus comparison.

5. Tax treatment of the bonus.
   - Lump-sum bonuses are usually taxed at the supplemental wage rate, which can differ from his marginal rate. If one option pays a bigger bonus, the marginal tax on the marginal dollars matters for net take-home.

6. Time horizon.
   - If he's likely in the seat for 1-2 years, his own performance this year matters most. If 4+ years, the company's payout distribution over a cycle matters more.

7. Manager / team track record (often the most underweighted input).
   - "What % of target did your team actually pay out the last five years?" from the hiring manager, in writing or at least on the record, is usually more predictive than the plan document.

Once he has 1, 2, and 6 in hand, the 78% breakeven turns from an abstract number into a question he can answer: is this team's realistic payout distribution centered above or below ~78% of target, and how wide is it? That comparison is what points to an option, not the headline base or the headline bonus percentage.

Plain calculation then.

Runtime vs. commute
  Weekly commute ceiling: 70 min round-trip × 3 days = 210 min (3.5 hrs).
  Stated single-charge runtime: 4 hrs = 240 min.
  Buffer above your heaviest week: 240 − 210 = 30 min, ~12.5% headroom.
  Round-trips per charge: 240 / 70 ≈ 3.4 — so a weekly charge (Sunday, say) easily covers Mon/Tue/Wed rides and almost a fourth.

Charging cadence check
  You said you can charge weekly. The 4-hr spec is runtime per charge, not charge time — what matters is that one charge outlives your busiest week, which it does. Worst case: 3 long commute days and you still have ~30 min in the tank; on a 2-day week you'd be charging with ~100 min unused, which is harmless.

Cost vs. what's actually being fixed
  $28 fixes only the cracked bracket; the corroded wired connector stays. Corrosion at a power connector tends to spread and intermittently kills the light — exactly the kind of failure you don't want mid-commute. The $45 option replaces the whole unit (new bracket + new connector + new battery), so it actually resolves both findings from the shop, not just one.
  Net premium: $17.

The judgment
  Rechargeable replacement is the sounder call:
    - It fixes both problems the shop flagged (bracket and connector), not just the visible one.
    - 4-hr runtime clears your 3.5-hr worst-week usage with margin, on a weekly charging habit you already have.
    - The $17 premium buys a sealed, non-corroding connector path — the part most likely to strand you on a dark road if you cheap out.

Only reason to hesitate: if your "up to three days a week" is really 1–2 days with margin to spare, the $28 bracket is fine for now and you'd just be replacing a corroded connector later. But given the shop already found corrosion today, deferring it doesn't save money — it just moves the same $45 (bracket + connector) onto a future, possibly roadside, appointment.

Three FAQ entries (boundaries unchanged; no paid-acquisition language):

  1. Company size and Helio Start eligibility

      Q: We're under the stated size. Doesn't that make us eligible for Helio Start?

      A: Size under the threshold is one input to Helio Start, but the application form also asks about your first step — the supported first integration, an import or migration, an ownership or permission question, or agency/consultant status. The form choices are routing decisions, not onboarding questions, and size alone doesn't determine where the application lands. After size is checked, your first-step choice is what sends the workspace to self-serve Start, assisted setup, pending (awaiting admin proof), or out of Start. If size were sufficient on its own, the form wouldn't ask.

  2. Direct-admin evidence

      Q: I can prove I administer our account. Does that settle our eligibility?

      A: Direct-admin evidence — proof that you own or administer the company account — moves an application from pending into a routing decision. Two cases where it interacts with eligibility:

        - If a consultant or agency owns setup on your behalf, the workspace routes out of Start regardless of admin status. Start is for direct admins of the company account, not for third-party owners.

        - If your first step is an import/migration or an ownership/permission question, verified admin status alone doesn't put you in Start self-serve; those choices route to assisted setup.

      Admin evidence is what unblocks ordinary setup (verified admin plus a supported first integration) and what gets a pending application off hold. It is not, on its own, a Start ticket.

  3. Import or migration routing

      Q: We need a CSV import (or a migration) before our supported integration is set up. Does the integration still qualify us for Start?

      A: No. Helio Start covers workspaces whose first step is a supported first integration. If the first step is an import or migration — even one that's followed by a supported integration — that step itself routes the application to assisted setup, not Start self-serve. The integration is still supported once the migration completes; the routing decision is made on the first step, not on the eventual destination. The same applies to workspaces that chose import/migration expecting to graduate into Start after the data loads: Start and assisted setup stay separated by that first-step choice.

   - Cluster B (1 Helio Start): the nested integrations field needs array iteration / length checks, not string interpolation. Re-test with empty array, single-item array, and multi-item array in synthetic.

Here is the breakdown check.

Category and total rates (d7 / admitted)

  API connector        23 / 28 = 82.1%
  CSV sync             11 / 17 = 64.7%
  Warehouse connector  10 / 13 = 76.9%
  Total                44 / 58 = 75.9%

Strongest descriptive difference

The biggest spread is API connector (82.1%) vs CSV sync (64.7%) — a 17.4 percentage-point gap. Warehouse sits between them, closer to API than to CSV. So descriptively the ranking reads API > Warehouse > CSV, with CSV the clear laggard and API the clear leader.

Why this does NOT establish that integration type caused the activation gap

The category is assigned by the first integration the account actually attempted, not by random assignment. Two confounds make that comparison un-causal:

1. Customer choice / self-selection. Admins pick the path they think they can finish. An account that already has clean, well-modeled data and a developer who can wire an API will disproportionately land in the API bucket; an account that is "admitted" only on paper and doesn't yet know where its source data lives will disproportionately fall into CSV sync. The category is a proxy for "how ready was this account on day 0," not an independent treatment.

2. Account complexity. Complexity shapes both the first attempt and the day-7 outcome. A simple stack activates fast via API; a messy stack that chose CSV partly because it had to clean data first will still be cleaning on day 7. Integration type and account complexity are tangled, so the 17.4 pp gap conflates "API is easier" with "the accounts that picked API were easier to start with."

For the same reason, the 5.2 pp gap between API and Warehouse is too thin to read as a real integration-type effect — it almost certainly reflects that warehouse accounts in this cohort happened to be slightly more mature than the API accounts, not that warehouse is a meaningfully worse surface.

Net read: the table is a useful descriptive segmentation of the second mature cohort (especially the CSV lag, which is worth a qualitative look), but it is not evidence that nudging admitted accounts toward API would raise the 75.9% overall activation rate. To make a causal claim you'd need random assignment of integration path, or an instrument that shifts path choice without shifting account complexity.

Short answer: yes, the scrap test is worth it, but the odds are against you. Eighteen months opened with visible phase separation that won't recombine is the textbook sign that the latex emulsion has broken — the "rubbery layer" is coagulated polymer and the thin liquid is the water/ammonia phase with most of the stabilizers gone. Rolling won't reverse coagulation the way it reverses simple settling. What you have left may still paint on, but it's behaving outside spec.

Why the test is still worth doing: the failure modes are predictable and the cost of finding out on a Sunday painting is one torn sheet or one yellowed reserve. A controlled test on the same paper stock takes maybe 20 minutes of active time over a couple of hours and tells you definitively whether to throw it out, demote it to sketchbook work, or trust it on the real painting.

Run this on a scrap of the actual paper you plan to use, not a different stock:

  1. Stir (don't shake — shaking introduces air bubbles that pop and leave halos) with a toothpick or small stick. Note whether it recombines into a smooth milky liquid, or stays stringy/chunky. Chunky = discard now, skip the rest.
  2. Apply in three zones: a thin wash, a medium stroke, a thicker line. Let it dry fully — masking fluid should be touch-dry in 20–40 minutes depending on humidity. If it's still tacky after an hour, the solvent balance is off and it will misbehave later. Discard.
  3. Paint a modest wash over the dried mask (the color doesn't matter; use something you'd realistically use). Let the wash dry completely before removing the mask — pulling while the wash is wet is a separate failure mode and not what you're testing.
  4. Remove with the method you actually use (rubber cement pick-up, clean eraser, or just fingers). Watch how it comes off and inspect what's left.

Discard criteria — any one of these is enough, you don't need all:

  - Tears the paper surface or pulls up fibers visibly, especially on cotton. The polymer has lost elasticity and will grab the paper instead of releasing it.
  - Leaves a yellowish stain or ghost on the white. Old ammonia-stabilized masking fluid oxidizes and can permanently tint, particularly on bright white paper.
  - Crumbles into dry rubber bits instead of lifting as a continuous film. Means the polymer has cross-linked beyond use.
  - Bleed-under: the wash seeped past the edge of the mask line during step 3. The mask lost its seal.
  - Residue that won't lift with a kneaded eraser or gentle rub. Anything that needs scrubbing to come off has already damaged the paper surface.

If it passes all five, it's safe for the painting — but write the batch age on the jar with a paint pen so next time you don't repeat the gamble. If it fails any one, it's still fine for sketchbook experiments and color studies, just not for a piece you care about.

Backup for Sunday if it fails: a wax-based resist (a white candle or a litho crayon drawn lightly) covers most of what masking fluid does for watercolor — preserving whites and soft edges — without the removal risk. Less convenient for fine lines, but it won't eat the paper.

One last thing worth saving to memory: do you want me to note the masking fluid age-tracking habit somewhere durable so it surfaces again before the next Sunday block?

**Inputs from your count (with Sam, 4/13)**
- Packed medium boxes: **42**
- Estimated remaining (unpacked) volume: **14** medium-box equivalents
- Total household volume: **42 + 14 = 56** medium-box equivalents
- Mover's included boxes: **50** (all-medium plan treats "boxes" as medium)
- Surcharge: **$8** per box over the included 50
- Large boxes on hand: **6**, each holding **1.5** medium volumes, capped at **35 lb** each

---

**Plan A — All medium**

Total boxes needed = **56**
Included = 50 → extras = **6**
Surcharge = 6 × $8 = **$48**
Box count: 56 medium, 0 large

---

**Plan B — Mixed: all 6 large + enough medium**

Volume after 6 large = 56 − (6 × 1.5) = 56 − 9 = **47** medium-equivalents
So Plan B needs **47 medium + 6 large**.
Medium included: 47 ≤ 50 → extras = **0** → surcharge = **$0**
Box count: 47 medium, 6 large

(If the mover counts large boxes against the same 50-box included allowance the way many do, even better — you're at 47 + 6 = 53 total, and surcharge is still $0 since you don't exceed 50 of *one* type and the contract as stated reads "each additional box" past 50. I read this conservatively: medium overage only.)

---

**Plan B cost summary**
- Surcharge: **$0** (saves $48 vs Plan A)
- Trade-off: 6 boxes must be packed light (≤35 lb each), and you need to fit 9 medium-volumes' worth into 6 large boxes — exactly the 1.5× ratio, so it's a clean fit volume-wise, but only if weight works.

---

**Recommended packing split**

The 35 lb cap on large boxes is the binding constraint, not volume. Volume is fine (6 × 1.5 = 9 vs. 9 needed). The plan:

**Put in the 6 large boxes (target ≤32 lb each, leaving a 3 lb buffer under the 35 lb cap):**
- Bedding, pillows, linens, blankets
- Clothing (especially coats, sweaters, anything bulky but light)
- Towels
- Lamps (shades separated), picture frames padded with linens
- Kitchen items that are bulky + light: plastic serving pieces, cutting boards, colanders, Tupperware stacks, pot lids, the roasting pan rack
- Soft toys, throw pillows, cushions, the dog bed / Kibo's bed, the yoga mat
- Vinyl, soft luggage, stuffed duffels
- Holiday decor that's mostly cardboard and tissue (NOT heavy ornaments — those go medium)

**Keep OUT of large boxes (medium only):**
- Books (paperback ≈ 1.5 lb each; hardcovers 3–5 lb; a large box of books lands 40–60 lb fast)
- Vinyl records / heavy media
- Small kitchen appliances (stand mixer body, food processor, blender base)
- Cast iron, stoneware, Le Creuset, ceramic mixing bowls
- Liquor, wine, oils, canned goods, bagged rice/beans, the stand-mixer attachments
- Tools, hardware, the toolbox
- Anything with "feels heavy for its size" in your hand — trust the lift test

**Weight rule of thumb for the large boxes:**
- Books: ~30 books per medium box → ~5 books per large max (or just don't)
- Cast iron: 1 Dutch oven + a skillet = a large box by itself; medium only
- Bedding: a queen comforter + 2 pillows + a sheet set easily fits one large well under 35 lb
- A full large box of t-shirts is fine; a full large box of jeans is right at the limit

**Why this split works**
The 1.5× volume ratio means each large box is doing the work of 1.5 medium boxes, but you're buying that capacity by giving up medium's higher weight tolerance. Routing bulky-but-light stuff into the large boxes is a near-perfect match — that category is also the category most likely to leave medium boxes half-empty under an all-medium plan, which is wasted capacity you'd pay surcharge on. The dense stuff stays in medium where it belongs.

**Bottom line:** Plan B saves **$48** and is the right call, provided you honor the weight split above. If you don't have enough bulky-but-light volume to fill all 6 large boxes (some apartments don't — bookshelves full of books is the usual culprit), then pack 4–5 large with what qualifies and convert the rest of the volume back to medium. In that fallback: each large box you skip adds 1.5 medium-box-equivalents, still inside the 50-box allowance until you convert more than 7 boxes' worth, which you won't with only 6 large. So even partial use of the large boxes stays surcharge-free.

Comparison of the two options for May 1:

Mom (7:30am-1:30pm at Holly, ~6 hrs)
  - Familiar person, lowest stress for Kibo
  - Fully contains the mover window (8am-noon)
  - No trial, no booking deadline, no financial commitment
  - Fixed return at 1:30pm — no buffer if movers run long
  - Stretches Mom beyond her usual short-drop-in pattern (~25 min)

Veterinary day boarding (7:00am-6:00pm, 11 hrs)
  - Supervised, structured, professional
  - 6-hour buffer after movers leave — covers any overrun plus settling time
  - Novel environment; longer separation
  - Requires Apr 16 booking commitment AND Apr 24 half-day trial
  - Trial and booking are decoupled (you commit Apr 16 before you have Apr 24 data)

Coverage of the mover disruption: both options fully contain it. The real differentiator is post-noon — boarding buys you the afternoon; Mom returns Kibo into whatever the house looks like at 1:30pm.

Stress differential: for a dog whose routine is being broken by open doors and truck activity, a familiar person almost always beats a novel kennel environment, regardless of how well-run the kennel is. The boarding option's main value isn't quality-of-care, it's time buffer.

Decision factors for whether the half-day trial is worthwhile:

1. Reusability beyond May 1. The trial is sunk cost if May 1 is the only foreseeable need. It's high-value optionality if you'll face future moves, vet stays, or travel where Mom won't be available. Most moves, in my experience, eventually recur — that's the strongest argument for doing the trial.

2. Booking-before-trial asymmetry. The Apr 16 booking deadline is 8 days before the Apr 24 trial. You cannot condition the booking on trial results. So the trial cannot reduce May 1 risk — it can only inform future bookings. Frame it that way: the trial pays for itself on the *second* use, not the first.

3. Kibo's kennel-tolerance is unknown. If you've never boarded Kibo, the trial is the cheapest discovery path — half a day, one morning of your time. If you already know he handles it or melts down, the trial is confirmation, not information.

4. Mom's 1:30pm return is a real risk. If movers reliably run to noon and the afternoon is just light organizing, Mom's window is fine. If movers overrun or you want a quiet reset afternoon, Mom's option forces you back into the chaos with a dog who's been crated/traveling. Boarding's 6pm return is the buffer; the trial is what makes that buffer trustworthy.

5. Trial cost is low but not zero. Half a day Apr 24, three weeks before May 1. Manageable. The bigger cost is the booking commitment on Apr 16 if you later decide not to use it — check the cancellation terms.

Worthwhile threshold — do the trial if any one of these is true:
  - You anticipate a second future need (move, trip, vet stay)
  - Kibo's kennel-tolerance is genuinely unknown to you
  - Mom's 1:30pm return feels tight given mover uncertainty

Skip the trial if all of these are true:
  - May 1 is a one-off and Mom's pattern is reliable
  - You already know how Kibo handles (or doesn't handle) novel environments
  - Mom is genuinely flexible on pickup time

Recommended sequence:
  Apr 16 — book if trial passes the threshold above (decision is about future optionality, not May 1, since Mom covers May 1 regardless)
  Apr 24 — complete trial; results feed future decisions, not May 1
  May 1 — Mom covers; boarding sits as unused insurance unless you discover Apr 24 that the kennel is clearly preferable for Kibo

The framing that makes this clean: the trial isn't about May 1. It's about whether you want a tested-OK backup option in your back pocket for the next time Mom isn't available.

Assessment of Daniela's 4/15 patch for narrow production rollout, with minimum monitoring and rollback criteria. Eligibility treatment is held fixed throughout (the 9 stay classified as they are, the 2 pendings stay pending until they retry on their own).

================================================================
WHAT THE CHECKS COVER
================================================================

  Root cause reproduced on mobile Safari.
  Symptom fixed: filename retained while empty blob submitted after camera-chooser cancel/background.
  Defect scope: empty blob now rejected client-side.
  Applicant state: other answers preserved across the failed attempt.
  UX: clean retry instead of stalled spinner.
  Coverage tested: camera path AND photo-library path.
  OS coverage tested: iOS 16 AND iOS 17.

================================================================
GAPS FOR NARROW PRODUCTION ROLLOUT
================================================================

  The patch is sound on the specific defect. For a narrow production rollout, these gaps need to be closed first; otherwise the rollout is going live with unverified tail behavior:

  1. The two 4/12 pendings are still the only real-world evidence the fix works on the originally broken devices. Until they retry, the patch has not been validated on the exact population it was written for. Recommend a one-touch nudge (lifecycle-owned, CS-routed) inviting them to retry once the patch is in production — not a reclassification, not an auto-route to assisted, just a retry touch. Their outcome is the rollout's ground truth.

  2. The patch logic is described generically (rejects empty blob, preserves answers). Confirm it is not Safari-specific. If it is generic to any browser that submits an empty blob, Android Chrome, desktop Safari, and Chrome-on-iOS (which uses WebKit) inherit the fix for free — that materially widens the covered surface without changing eligibility. If it is Safari-only, narrow the rollout to mobile Safari only and document the rest as out-of-scope for this change.

  3. Server-side defense in depth: confirm the server also rejects empty blobs. The client guard is necessary but not sufficient — a regression, a JS-disabled request, or a curl-equivalent could still submit an empty blob with a filename. This is instrumentation, not eligibility, so it does not change treatment.

  4. Network-failure path is not described. The defect is camera-chooser cancel/background. What happens when an upload itself times out on a flaky mobile network and the client retries? Is the same empty-blob or partial-blob failure mode possible? If yes, the patch should be tested on a simulated timeout, not just a cancel.

  5. File-input state on retry: "preserves the applicant's other answers" is stated. Confirm the file-input itself is fully reset between attempts (filename cleared, blob cleared, picker reopened cleanly) so the retry is not contaminated by stale state.

  6. iOS 18 was in beta on 4/15 (iOS 17.5 shipped in May). Not strictly required for narrow rollout, but worth a 30-minute smoke pass before declaring coverage complete.

  7. Telemetry: the rejection event should emit a structured signal so we can measure how often the underlying bug is being triggered versus how often the patch is saving us. Without it, the monitoring section below is built on proxies.

  Verdict: checks are sufficient for narrow production rollout once gaps 2, 3, and 5 are confirmed in writing. Gaps 1, 4, 6, 7 can run in parallel during the first 48 hours of production without blocking go.

================================================================
MINIMUM PRODUCTION MONITORING
================================================================

  All of these run on Daniela's existing instrumentation spine (raw events preserved, derived row per submission, exceptions view for missing/contradictory transitions, mutually-exclusive admitted/assisted/ineligible denominator, provisionals excluded from admitted count). No new taxonomy.

  A. Empty-blob rejection rate by client surface (mobile Safari / mobile-other / desktop). Expect zero successful empty submissions reaching the server. Non-zero server-side rate = defense-in-depth failure.

  B. Filename-without-blob incident rate. The pre-patch symptom. Should drop to effectively zero on iOS Safari within 24h of rollout.

  C. Ownership-proof completion rate by device class. The rollout's success signal: pre-patch mobile Safari was depressed by the defect; post-patch it should converge toward mobile-other and desktop. Compare against the 4/10–4/12 baseline.

  D. Exceptions view delta. Any new "missing/contradictory transition" entries referencing ownership-proof upload. Existing view catches this; no new work.

  E. The two pendings. Explicit daily check: retry attempted yes/no, and outcome if yes. They are the canary.

  F. Support contact volume referencing the upload flow, including stalled-spinner reports. Pre-patch had a clear uptick 4/10–4/12; post-patch should return to baseline within a week.

================================================================
MINIMUM ROLLBACK CRITERIA
================================================================

  Rollback scope is the client-side patch and/or the server-side empty-blob guard. Eligibility treatment is preserved across any of these triggers:

  1. Any successful server-side acceptance of an empty blob. Means client and server guards both failed. Full rollback, immediate.

  2. Sustained spike in stalled-spinner or upload-failure reports on mobile Safari within 48h of rollout. Client regression — client rollback only, server guard stays.

  3. Mobile Safari completion rate still depressed relative to desktop after 48h, at the same gap as pre-patch. Patch is not fixing the underlying issue. Client rollback.

  4. Empty-blob rejection rate substantially above the underlying bug-trigger rate (i.e., the patch is rejecting valid uploads as false positives). Client rollback.

  5. New exceptions-view entries that contradict existing routing on the same submission — i.e., the patch broke the event sequence. Full rollback plus Daniela investigation. This is a 4/4 routing-instrumentation rule, not an eligibility change.

  6. The two pendings retry and hit a new failure mode not seen in QA. Investigate, do not auto-rollback, but escalate within 24h.

  None of these triggers reclassifies the 9 incident applicants, auto-routes the 2 pendings to assisted, or changes any existing routing destination. They are operational rollbacks of the defect fix only.

================================================================
ELIGIBILITY-TREATMENT GUARDRAILS TO STATE EXPLICITLY
================================================================

  The 5 admitted applicants remain admitted; they are not reclassified as mobile-fixed.
  The 2 assisted applicants remain assisted; the upload defect is not a routing event.
  The 2 pendings remain pending; no auto-timeout is introduced by this rollout. They stay pending until they retry on their own, and when they do, they go through the same admin-proof evaluation as every other applicant.
  Mobile Safari completion post-rollout is reported under the same admitted/assisted/pending/ineligible outcomes as every other device — no separate mobile flag.
  Routing options and destinations from the 3/28 form revision are unchanged.
  This is a defect fix, not a beta expansion. No pricing-page, paid-acquisition, GA, or revenue-credit framing.

================================================================
RECOMMENDED PATH
================================================================

  Go to narrow production once gaps 2 (generic-vs-Safari-specific), 3 (server guard), and 5 (file-input reset on retry) are confirmed in writing. Run gaps 1, 4, 6, 7 in parallel through the first 48h. Hold off on any rollout that widens beyond the ownership-proof step — different forms have different file-input semantics and would need their own assessment.

Here is a 20-minute run sheet. It is structured so each thread earns the next, and so you can compress or drop thread 3 without losing the spine of the block.

  OPEN — about 90 seconds
    Reframe the three threads as one question: how does the novel handle what it does not say, what it withholds, and what it tries to put back together.
    House rule for your block: short reflections, no rush to consensus. You tee, others pull.

  THREAD 1 — narrator's omissions: protective or manipulative? (6-7 min)
    Tee-up: when did you first notice what was missing, and did you read that gap as the narrator protecting themselves, or protecting you?
    Sub-prompts to drop if it stalls:
      - Are there places the narrator seems to know more than they let on? What tipped you off?
      - Is the omission in service of a later reveal, or does it stay ambiguous?
      - If protective — of whom? If manipulative — toward whom?
    Listen for: whether the group reads the narrator as sympathetic despite the gaps, or whether the gaps become the central grievance.

  TRANSITION — ~30 sec
    "These omissions set up the architecture — which brings us to the train scene."

  THREAD 2 — how the final train scene changes the opening chapter (6-7 min)
    Tee-up: reread the opening with the ending in mind. What shifts, and what didn't shift but now feels different?
    Sub-prompts:
      - Is the train scene a literal return or an emotional one?
      - What does the narrator know at the end they didn't know at the start — and does the novel let them know it, or only let us?
      - Does the reframing redeem the opening, indict it, or just complicate it?
    Listen for: whether the group thinks the circular structure is earned or convenient.

  TRANSITION — ~30 sec
    "That reframing lands hardest on the relationships — the sibling thread."

  THREAD 3 — is the sibling relationship actually repaired? (5-6 min)
    Tee-up: the novel seems to offer a moment of repair. Did you trust it?
    Sub-prompts:
      - What does repair look like in this book versus what we'd call repair in real life?
      - Is the repair mutual, or is one sibling doing most of the work?
      - Does the ending confirm the repair, or quietly let it go?
    Listen for: whether anyone defends the repair, or whether the group is mostly skeptical. If it goes one way unanimously, push the other.

  HANDOFF — about 60 seconds
    "I'm going to stop here and open it up — anything on these threads, or anything the three of them didn't touch?"

  WHILE YOU LEAD
    - Don't resolve the threads. Tee, prompt, listen, tee the next.
    - If one thread catches, let it breathe; you can compress thread 3 (it is the most skippable of the three — the organizer opened the floor to all, so a thinner sibling beat is recoverable; threads 1 and 2 are the structural ones).
    - If someone goes long, name the moment not the person: "I want to make sure we get to the train thread — let me jump in there."
    - If silence lands after a tee-up, sit in it for ten seconds before rephrasing.

Two things that would let me sharpen the prompts:
  - The book (so I can pin a specific passage or scene for each tee-up, which is usually stronger than the general question).
  - How the group has been reading together so far — has it skewed formal/literary or personal/reflective? That changes whether I lean toward close-reading prompts or "what did you feel" prompts.

How the clause applies

The mover agreement language (logged April 20, 2024): the carrier will not transport "compressed-gas cylinders, fuel canisters, flammable aerosols, gasoline, solvents, and other hazardous liquids," and the customer must remove these items before loading and may not conceal them in cartons. Both items fall squarely inside that list:

- Partially used aerosol art fixative. A flammable aerosol. The hydrocarbon propellant (typically butane, propane, or dimethyl ether) is what makes it a prohibited item, not the resin itself. Even half-full, the can is still pressurized and still flammable.
- Two partially used butane cooking-fuel canisters. They sit in the prohibited list twice over — as compressed-gas cylinders and as fuel canisters. Residual liquid butane plus vapor pressure is the issue, not just whether the flame still lights.

Two consequences you should not blur:

1. These items cannot ride on the mover's truck under any circumstance, even if Sam carries them in his pocket. "Concealed in cartons" includes a box packed by you and handed to the crew, not only something the crew sneaks in.
2. The clause governs the carrier, not your own car. You may legally transport these items yourselves if you choose to keep using them at Cherrywood, but only with the safety conditions below. The clause is silent on that path; the safety rules are not.

Pre-move handling and disposal plan

For each item, decide one of three paths before May 1, and act on it during the April 20–30 window you're still living at Holly:

Path A — Use it up at Holly.
- Fixative: finish current pieces, run the can until it only mists, then treat the empty can as recyclable scrap metal if your locality accepts empty steel aerosols. Empty means truly empty; if it still hisses or sprays, it is not empty.
- Butane canisters: do a planned burn-through on a butane torch or burner (Sam's kitchen, a crème-brûlée task, or a controlled outdoor torch use). After the flame dies and you cannot relight, the canister is empty for disposal purposes; if even a short hiss remains, it is not empty.

Path B — Keep for use at Cherrywood, self-transported.
- Mark both items with your "do not pack" tape color (your system already has DIY/MOVER/do-not-pack tape — put these in the DIY bin or a dedicated red marker). They go in your car, not in any box.
- Safety conditions for in-cabin transport on May 1:
  - Cabin only, not trunk, and never inside a closed moving box or bag.
  - Upright and wedged so they cannot roll or tip; a small plastic bin with a lid works.
  - Out of direct sun; do not leave the car closed-up at Cherrywood while you direct movers — crack windows or pull them out with you.
  - Away from Kibo, food, paint, and any heat source. Aerosols + a panting dog in a warm car is the worst combination.
  - One trip, point to point, not a multi-stop shuttle. Fuel in, fuel out.
- If either item has only a small amount left, a fresh replacement at the destination is almost always cheaper and safer than transporting a half-pressurized can in late-April Texas heat.

Path C — Neither using up nor transporting; take to HHW.
- Do not put these in the Holly trash cart, the dumpster, or a recycling bin. A pressurized flammable can in a garbage truck or transfer station is a documented fire and injury risk, and Austin-area transfer stations reject them at the curb.
- Do not discharge indoors to "empty" them. Puncturing a butane canister indoors is the canonical mistake; spraying a fixative to empty it indoors fills the room with flammable vapor and overspray, which is worse than leaving it half full.
- Take to a household hazardous waste (HHW) drop-off. Both items are universally accepted there. Austin/Travis County runs an HHW program with a permanent facility and periodic collection events; verify the current drop-off location, hours, and any appointment requirement the week of, since the program has changed formats over the years. Bring them in their original form — don't tape over valves or puncture anything. There is no fee for residential HHW.

Distinguishing lawful HHW from safe self-transport

The line is intent and timing, not the items themselves.

- Lawful HHW disposal = you are done with the item. You drive it, in your own car, to the HHW facility during operating hours, hand it over, and keep the receipt. That receipt is worth saving with your move-out paperwork because the walkthrough on April 30 may ask what happened to leftover flammable materials, and "disposed of at [facility] on [date]" closes the question without argument.
- Safe self-transport = you still need the item at Cherrywood and you are transporting it in your own vehicle on May 1 with the cabin conditions above. The mover agreement does not prohibit this; the clause is about the carrier. The risk envelope is real (heat, vapor, rollover, Kibo, kids of neighbors who might be helping unload) but manageable if you treat the canisters like a small pressurized fuel can deserves.

Practical sequence for the next ten days

1. Today (April 20): segregate the three items from packing stock. Move them to a clearly labeled box that is marked NOT FOR PACKING — both of you will otherwise forget during the April 21 packing session.
2. This week: decide for each item — use up, transport, or HHW. The decision is per-item, not all-or-nothing.
3. If "transport": buy replacements now or plan to use the existing stock within the first week at Cherrywood, then HHW whatever is left. Don't ship a half-used butane canister across town in May heat just to have it.
4. If "HHW": take them once, before April 30, so they are not in the unit during the final clean on April 29 when Kibo is being boarded out. Don't leave flammable aerosols in a half-packed apartment while the dog is being shuffled.
5. On April 29 final-clean day, the three items should already be gone from Holly — either used up, at Cherrywood, or at the HHW facility. They should not be a "remember to grab" item on May 1 morning.

One small documentation note: in the move-out folder you've been keeping (signed agreement, walkthrough notes, photos), add a one-line entry for each item: "art fixative — used up at Holly" / "butane canisters — HHW on [date], receipt #___" / "fixative — self-transported to Cherrywood in cabin, May 1." That is exactly the kind of line that turns a walkthrough question into a one-sentence answer.

Recommendation: randomized 15-treatment / 15-holdout parallel split, with the treatment arm ramping five accounts per week to respect the CS handling limit. Holdout is a true concurrent control throughout the pilot — no live prompts at any point — and serves as the comparator in a defined post-ramp comparison window. This is the cleanest design that honors both the capacity constraint and the requirement for an explicit causal comparator.

Design mechanics

- Pre-randomization (before Jul 8). Draw the 30 accounts from documented eligibility and randomize 1:1 into treatment and holdout. Stratify on the few covariates that predict baseline expansion variance (account size band, tenure band, prior expansion history). Lock the assignment list and do not touch it again.
- Ramp inside treatment (weeks of Jul 8 / Jul 15 / Jul 22). Five treatment accounts begin receiving live prompts each week until all 15 are active. CS sees 5 newly exposed per week — at the limit, not above it. Holdout accounts receive nothing.
- Pre-period baseline. Pull the same five metrics for all 30 accounts for the 4–6 weeks before Jul 8 so every account has its own baseline. This is what makes the comparison usable at n=15 per arm.
- Comparison window. Opens once all 15 treatment accounts have been exposed for at least four weeks (≈ Aug 19 onward) and runs for a fixed pre-specified length (e.g., 8 weeks). The ramp weeks are run-in, not analysis.
- Primary estimator. Regression-adjusted comparison of cumulative net expansion in the comparison window, treatment vs. holdout, with pre-period baseline as a covariate. Net expansion is the only metric of record; the other four (prompt delivery, qualified expansion conversations, expansion $-amount, opt-outs, CS handling load) are descriptive process metrics and never substitute for the comparator.
- Stopping rule. Pre-specify an opt-out or handling-load threshold (suggest ≥15–20% opt-outs within the first two ramp weeks) that pauses the ramp and triggers a design review before continuing.

Why this beats the two alternatives the brief lays out

- vs. a clean 15/15 with no ramp. Same comparison structure, but now feasible under the 5/week limit. The only cost is that the first three weeks are ramp, not analysis.
- vs. randomized stagger with "temporary comparisons." That design contaminates the comparator over time — accounts that started as comparisons later become treated, and treated-cohort-1 is observed under different calendar conditions than treated-cohort-6. Here, holdout is holdout for the entire pilot and all 30 are concurrent, so calendar effects are differenced out rather than modeled.

What to lock into the brief before any prompts go out

1. Eligibility criteria and the exact 30-account list (or the sampling frame if not yet drawn).
2. Randomization procedure, stratification variables, and the locked assignment.
3. Ramp schedule (5/5/5 across the three weeks of July) and the CS capacity confirmation in writing.
4. Comparison window start date, length, and primary outcome definition.
5. Estimator (regression-adjusted) and the MDE the design can actually detect at n=15/15 — frame expectations honestly; this design can rule in or out large effects, not moderate ones.
6. Stopping rule for opt-out / handling overload.
7. Crossover plan: at the end of the comparison window, offer Expansion Assist to the 15 holdout accounts. Preserves the relationship and gives a within-account durability read, but the crossover is not part of the primary comparison.

Language note, consistent with the design-phase framing: until the comparator above is approved and locked, anything written about expansion outcomes stays descriptive (pre/post, observed changes). Causal language waits for the approved comparison plan — Owen owns that reporting line, CS owns the live handling line, and the brief should say so explicitly so neither side drifts into claims the design hasn't earned.

Skipping only on the two smallest cogs (highest gear ratios), with crisp shifting elsewhere and no visible damage, almost always means chain/cassette wear mismatch — the smallest cogs have the thinnest, most precisely-shaped teeth and they wear first. Damp grit without lube accelerates it and can cause intermittent skipping on its own, but the localization to the small cogs is the tell. Cheap causes (stiff link, derailleur hanger, cable tension) usually show up across more gears, so we'll deal with them in order while checking for wear.

Tonight, in this order
Do not skip steps. Clean first so you can actually see what you're looking at, and inspect before you lube so lube doesn't hide a stiff link.

1. Clean
   - Wipe the chain with a dry rag while backpedaling to remove surface grime.
   - Degreaser (or dish soap + warm water on a rag) on chain, cassette, derailleur pulleys. Don't soak the hub or bottom bracket.
   - Scrub between every cog with a brush or rag; spin the cassette slowly so you hit each gap.
   - Wipe pulleys — a seized pulley makes chain feed inconsistent and reads like skipping under load.
   - Dry thoroughly before inspection.

2. Inspect (do this before lubing)
   - Chain wear: if you have a go/no-go gauge, check at 0.5% and 0.75%. Without one, pull the chain straight at the front of the chainring and lift — if you can see daylight under most of a tooth, the chain is past useful life.
   - Stiff link: flex the chain in a zigzag along its length. Any link that won't fully articulate is a stiff link — flex it laterally several times; if it doesn't free up, it's a problem.
   - Cassette — focus on the smallest two cogs, viewed from the side AND looking down the line of the cog. Healthy teeth are symmetrical and slightly rounded. Worn teeth look like shark fins: the tip is hooked or leans (usually in the direction of chain engagement). Compare to the larger cogs — if only the small ones are asymmetric, the cassette is the issue.
   - Derailleur: push the body by hand, should move freely and spring back firmly. Look at the hanger from behind the cassette — visual check only catches gross bends.

3. Lube (after inspection)
   - One drop per roller, slowly backpedaling a full chain length.
   - Wait ~5 min for the carrier to penetrate.
   - Wipe the outside of the chain thoroughly. Lube belongs inside the rollers; outside lube just collects grit.

4. Low-load test (quiet street or parking lot, low traffic)
   - Middle cogs first, light pedaling, then moderate. Confirm smooth running there.
   - Then the second-smallest cog, light then moderate. Do NOT sprint.
   - Then the smallest cog, light then moderate. Do NOT sprint.
   - If any skip returns, abort. Don't work around it by avoiding the cog.

Do not ride it to work if any of these are true
   - Chain wear gauge reads 0.75% or higher, OR the visual lift test shows clear daylight under chainring teeth.
   - Any tooth on the smallest two cogs is shark-finned, hooked, or visibly leaning to one side.
   - A stiff link exists that flexing didn't free.
   - Skipping returns after cleaning and lube, even at moderate load.
   - Skipping shows up on cogs other than the smallest two — that points to derailleur/hanger/cable, which you can't safely rule out at home.
   - Any new noise (clicking, popping, clunking) under load that wasn't there before.
   - Visible rust pitting on the chain or any link that looks distorted from the side.

If everything looks clean after inspection
You can ride gently to work, but: avoid the smallest two cogs entirely (stay on cogs 3 and up), no sprints, no out-of-the-saddle climbs, no standing starts in those gears. Book a shop check at your next convenience and tell them exactly what you observed — they'll measure chain wear and cassette tooth profile properly. A worn chain on a still-healthy cassette is the cheap fix; a worn cassette is the expensive one. The fact that this appeared after damp commutes without lube means the wear is probably progressing, so don't defer the shop visit long.

One sequencing note if the chain is the problem
If your chain measures at 0.75%+ and the cassette still looks ok, replace the chain. But: if you put a new chain on a worn cassette, the new chain will skip on the old small cogs — confirming the cassette is shot. So if you're about to commute on a clearly worn chain, plan to replace both, or have the shop do it together. Don't commute on a chain you already know is at its limit.

That three-color kit is a near-classic limited palette — each pigment leans toward a different quadrant (ultramarine cool blue, burnt sienna warm orange, quin rose cool magenta-red), so most of what you need is two-color mixes. Three-color mixes go muddy fast; save them for one or two accents and never put all three on the same brushstroke.

Mixes for each element:

  - Warm brick wall: burnt sienna straight, or with a touch of quin rose for the warmer bricks; a tiny pull of dilute ultramarine cools the grout lines and the side facing shadow.
  - Muted green-gray door: ultramarine + burnt sienna, ranging from 3:1 (cooler green-gray) to 1:1 (neutral gray with a violet lean). Do NOT add quin rose — that pushes the door brown.
  - Cool blue-violet shadows: ultramarine + quin rose, 2:1 for the bluer cast, 1:1 for true violet. Shadows against the brick want more ultramarine than rose so the cool edge reads cleanly.
  - Terracotta pot: burnt sienna + quin rose, 1:1 to 2:1 sienna; a tip of ultramarine in the deepest cast shadow if you want it to sink.
  - The workhorse for porch-floor shadow: ultramarine + burnt sienna at roughly 2:1. Granulating gray you'll lean on hard.

Layering sequence — let each wash dry before the next; postcard paper dries fast:

  1. Light wash. Brick in dilute burnt sienna, door in dilute ultramarine+sienna 3:1, pot in dilute burnt sienna+rose. Lay brick and door in the same pass — they share the warm/cool axis.
  2. Mid-tones on dry paper. Vary the brick (some bricks warmer with rose, some cooler with ultramarine); bring the door to its full green-gray; deepen the pot.
  3. Cast shadows and the deepest shapes. Ultramarine+rose 2:1 along the door frame and under the eaves; ultramarine+sienna 2:1 in the porch-floor shadow.
  4. Final accents, last and quickest:
       - one clean stroke of pure ultramarine in the deepest cool shadow (no sienna, no rose)
       - one clean stroke of pure burnt sienna on the sun-struck brick edge
       - a small spot of quin rose on the brightest terracotta highlight
       - reserve untouched white of the postcard for the highest light on the door frame

Two rules to keep the neutrals from muddying:

  - Never stir all three into the same puddle. If a mix feels flat, add one pigment, not two.
  - If a wash starts to look chalky as it dries, you've overworked it — stop, let it dry, and glaze a second clean wash over it instead of fighting it on the page.

A video call dropping while the front room stays solid, plus a second drop on heavy traffic, is the textbook "5 GHz through one solid wall + closed door" failure pattern — not capacity, not a line problem. Below is a stepwise plan that treats relocation as a 30-minute experiment and treats the access point as a decision, not a default.

TODAY'S WORKAROUND FOR REMAINING CALLS
  Situate the laptop in the workroom doorway (you already saw this works) and use a phone or headset on a long USB-C cable so you can still face the desk. Don't move the modem yet — capture data first.

DIAGNOSTIC CAPTURE (15 MIN, BEFORE ANY MOVE)
  Run all of this from the laptop at the desk and a phone in the front room at the same time:
  - Time-stamp each existing drop. Note what was running and the laptop's battery/charge state (low-power Wi-Fi is a thing).
  - On the laptop, hold Option and click the Wi-Fi icon (macOS) or run `netsh wlan show interfaces` (Windows) to read RSSI in dBm at the desk. Repeat at the doorway. Negative number closer to zero = stronger.
  - Run a speedtest from the desk and the front room back-to-back (same server). Record down/up in Mbps.
  - On the router's status page (browser), note the WAN IP and DNS servers. If both are real ISP values, the line is fine and this is purely local Wi-Fi — that lets you rule out the upstream.
  - Don't touch any router settings yet. This is read-only, per the rule we set after the January 28 outage.

STEP 1 — MODEM + ROUTER PLACEMENT (TODAY, 30 MIN)
  Treat this as one experiment with two moves, not a permanent decision:
  a) Baseline. Router in current location; laptop at the desk running a continuous speedtest or `ping 1.1.1.1` for 10 minutes while a video call is active on another device.
  b) Move 1. Same wall outlet, but shelf at ~5 ft height and on the interior side of the wall nearest the workroom doorway. Repeat the 10-minute test at the desk.
  c) Move 2. If you have a long ethernet patch cord, temporarily put the router in the workroom doorway itself (power from a hallway outlet if needed). Repeat the test.
  Record RSSI and drop count at the desk for each move. If Move 2 is dramatically better than Move 1, the issue is wall + door attenuation; if Move 1 is already fine, you can leave the router in its new home and stop here.

STEP 2 — BAND CHOICE AT THE DESK
  While you're testing placement, force the laptop to 5 GHz at the desk and note RSSI. Then force it to 2.4 GHz and note RSSI. If 5 GHz is below about -70 dBm at the desk but 2.4 GHz is above -65 dBm, you have your answer for the work session: stay on 2.4 GHz for calls, 5 GHz for dashboard loads when signal is acceptable. This is a per-device setting, not a router change.

DECISION GATE — DO YOU NEED THE ACCESS POINT?
  Run the desk through a 60-minute work simulation: one 30-minute video call plus one dashboard load (or large file sync) for the remaining 30 minutes. Then check:

  AP is needed if ANY of these is true:
    - 5 GHz RSSI at the desk stays below -70 dBm after the best placement move
    - Speedtest at the desk is below ~25 Mbps down while the front room gets above ~100 Mbps
    - You see one or more drops during the 60-minute simulation
    - The only stable spot in the workroom is the doorway itself (i.e., you can't sit at the desk reliably)

  AP is NOT needed if ALL of these hold:
    - 5 GHz RSSI at the desk is -65 dBm or stronger
    - 2.4 GHz RSSI at the desk is -60 dBm or stronger
    - Speedtest at the desk is at least ~50 Mbps down
    - Zero drops in the 60-minute simulation, with the door closed

  The thresholds are conservative on purpose — they assume you want the room to be reliable, not just "usually fine."

STEP 3 — IF THE AP IS NEEDED (WEEKEND PLAN)
  Goal: a wired access point at or just inside the workroom doorway, same SSID and password as the existing network so devices roam.

  Hardware (one weekend, modest cost):
    - One tri-band or dual-band AP — UniFi U6 Lite, TP-Link EAP245, or eero (with ethernet backhaul). Skip "mesh" kits that pair wirelessly; you want wired backhaul.
    - One Cat6 ethernet cable, ~50 ft (round up, never up-and-back).
    - Cable clips or a low-profile surface raceway for the run along the baseboard.
    - If you want it tidy long-term, a keystone jack + wall plate at each end. Optional for this weekend.

  Placement: at the workroom doorway, mounted high on the door frame or on a small shelf, line-of-sight to the desk. Power from the east or west wall outlet in the workroom; ethernet back to the router along the baseboard of the interior wall, through the door frame.

  Configuration:
    - Same SSID and password as the existing router; security mode the same (WPA2 or WPA3). This is what lets the laptop roam without you touching it.
    - If the AP and router both broadcast 5 GHz, set the AP to a non-overlapping channel (e.g., 36 or 149) to avoid co-channel interference.
    - Don't disable the existing router's Wi-Fi. Let the laptop pick; it'll choose the stronger signal at the desk.

  Weekend timing: Saturday morning is fine; the workroom is unusable for about an hour during cable run and AP mounting. Sunday morning is the backup if Saturday fills up.

STEP 4 — VALIDATION AFTER THE AP IS UP
  Repeat the 60-minute simulation from Step 3 at the desk, door closed. The bar to clear is the same: zero drops, ≥50 Mbps down at the desk, 5 GHz RSSI ≥ -65 dBm. If those hold, the workroom is reliably usable and you can move on.

ESCALATION RULE (IF BOTH MOVES AND THE AP FAIL)
  If the AP-installed desk still shows drops, the problem is no longer coverage — it's line quality or a faulty device. At that point:
  - Capture the same RSSI/speedtest data
  - Contact the ISP and ask for a signal-level check at the tap; per our standing rule, do not accept a factory reset unless you want one
  - The modem+router restart is still the first thing they will ask you to do; do it once, with the router checked only after the modem's online light has been solid for at least 60 seconds

SUMMARY OF WHAT TO DO TODAY
  1. Workaround: laptop in the doorway for remaining calls.
  2. Capture the diagnostic data from the desk and front room.
  3. Run the placement experiment (baseline → Move 1 → Move 2), ~30 minutes total.
  4. Apply the decision gate. If AP is needed, buy the hardware today so the weekend install is unblocked.
  5. If AP is not needed, document the placement that worked and stop.

Arithmetic check
    9 + 12 + 5 = 26 active    ✓
    6 + 8 = 14 inactive       ✓
    26 + 14 = 40 contracted   ✓
    40 − 8 = 32 right-sized   ✓ (preserves 26 active + 6 planned)
    Numbers reconcile cleanly; the only thing the math tells you is that the two proposed endpoints are internally consistent. It does not tell you whether 32 or 40 is correct.

What the inventory actually shows
    The 14 inactive seats are not one population. They are three:
      - 6 with a stated next-quarter use case  → planned, low decision risk either way
      - 8 with no stated near-term use          → uncharacterized, this is the real decision surface
      - (the 26 active are a closed question — both proposals preserve them)
    "Weekly activity" is a single-window signal. It does not distinguish between: a seat held for a hire who has not started, a seasonal or exec-role user, a workflow being rebuilt, a license kept for an upcoming audit/review cycle, or genuinely orphaned access. The eight uncharacterized seats could be any of those. The proposal treats the eight as a homogeneous block; the framing should not.

Decision framing for CS
    Reframe the choice as a per-seat activation question, not a headcount question. For each of the 8 uncharacterized seats, CS needs a one-line answer to: "Is there a plausible activation path in the next 1–2 quarters, and what is it?" Until that exists, weekly inactivity is not evidence of non-need — it is just an unanswered question.
    Concretely, the review should produce, per inactive seat:
      - activation likelihood: planned / probable / possible / none
      - owner (who can move it to active)
      - expected activation quarter (if any)
      - cost of carrying it one more quarter vs. cost of re-provisioning if it activates later
    "Quarterly assignment review" is the right cadence and the right shape, but only if it produces per-seat answers, not a roll-up of "how many were active this week."

Risks of each option
    Retain 40
      - Carries the cost of seats we cannot currently justify by activity. Cheap if seats are a small share of Acme's contract; material if they are not.
      - Preserves headroom for activation, avoids re-procurement friction if any of the 8 activate, and avoids signaling "inactive = expendable," which can suppress legitimate low-frequency use.
      - Main risk is undisciplined: if the quarterly review is not real, the 8 silently grow.
    Right-size to 32
      - Recovers cost on the 8 uncharacterized seats immediately.
      - Two failure modes: (1) re-buying seats later at higher unit cost plus onboarding friction when one of the 8 turns out to have a real use case, (2) creating a signal that seat utilization is being monitored at weekly granularity, which can cause operators to manufacture activity rather than use the tool appropriately.
      - Only safe if the 8 have been individually classified and the 6 planned-users coverage is confirmed (i.e., we are not also accidentally trimming a planned seat because the activity snapshot missed it).

What to ask CS before the decision is made
    1. Per-seat activation path for the 8 uncharacterized seats — not a count, a name-and-reason for each.
    2. Cost of the 8 seats per quarter, so the savings of right-sizing are sized against the re-procurement risk.
    3. Whether any of the 6 "planned" users have a confirmed start date inside the next quarter; if not, they belong in the same classification exercise, not assumed away.
    4. What "quarterly assignment review" will actually produce — a checkbox, or a per-seat decision with an owner.

Bottom line for the framing
    The choice between 40 and 32 is downstream of a classification question CS has not yet done. Recommend CS run the per-seat activation review first; the 40-vs-32 question becomes much easier (and may resolve to a third number) once each of the 14 inactive seats has an owner and an expected activation quarter. Until then, weekly inactivity is not a basis for cutting — it is a basis for asking.

The pattern you're describing is the classic signature of a worn chain on a worn cassette, and the diagnosis drives what to ask the shop.

What's actually happening
  The chain has stretched past its service life (rollers no longer match the
  original pitch). On the smallest cogs, every chain link sees the highest
  torque and the most engagements per mile, so those teeth wear fastest into
  a "shark fin" / hooked profile. A new chain sits correctly on un-worn teeth
  but rides up over the hooked ones and skips. Because only the tooth
  profile is wrong (not the derailleur indexing), shifting stays crisp. The
  wear is hard to see with the naked eye — you have to compare the leading
  edge of each tooth against the trailing edge, or against a new cog. That's
  why everything looks fine but isn't.

Should you ride Monday
  Rideable for a short, relatively flat commute if you can avoid the two
  smallest cogs (stay on the 3rd-smallest or larger, shift before you load
  the pedals, no out-of-saddle sprints, no starting from a stop in a high
  gear). Not safe to ride hard in those gears — a hard skip while you're
  standing or accelerating into traffic is a real crash risk. If your
  commute has any hill where you instinctively reach for the small cogs, or
  if you start in traffic at an intersection, get it serviced before
  Monday or take a different bike / transit that day.

What to ask the shop (use roughly these words)
  1. Chain wear measurement with a chain-checker tool. Replace at 0.5%
     stretch for 11/12-speed (Shimano spec) or 0.75% for 10-speed and
     older. This is the root cause — start here.
  2. Inspect the two smallest cassette cogs specifically for shark-fin
     tooth wear. If they show it, replace the cassette at the same time as
     the chain. Replacing only the chain will leave you with a new chain
     that still skips on the worn cogs.
  3. While it's on the stand: check the rear derailleur hanger for

Diagnosis matches symptom. Chain stretch at 0.75% is past the usual 0.5% replacement threshold, and wear concentrated on the two smallest cogs is the classic signature of chain-induced cassette wear — the smallest cogs see the most chain links per pedal revolution and bend the chain at the tightest radius, so they go first. The skip under load on those cogs is exactly what worn shark-fin teeth + a stretched chain produce.

Chain-only at $68
Technically a valid chain replacement in isolation. The mechanic's warning is correct, not a sales tactic: a new chain has tighter pin-to-pin pitch than your current 0.75%-stretched chain, and the worn cogs' tooth profile is already missing the material that catches a new chain's rollers. Result is the skip returning specifically on the cogs you said you depend on. Two practical problems with this option:
- False economy is very likely. Realistic path: pay $68, skip returns on the small cogs, pay $214 for the cassette job anyway. Total $282, two shop trips, and a window where the bike is unreliable again.
- A new chain on a worn cassette also accelerates wear on the chainring and the still-good middle cassette cogs, because they're now meshing with a chain that's tighter than what they were running with. So you may be trading a near-term skip for a near-term chainring replacement.

Chain-and-cassette at $214
Replaces the matched-wear set together, which is the right way to do it. The adjustment matters — derailleur indexing and limit screws shift slightly with new cable tension and chain length — and the loaded test is the relevant test for your symptom. An unloaded spin won't reproduce what you're feeling; pedaling force is what makes the chain climb the worn tooth face. The mechanic's plan tests the fix the way you actually use the bike.

Riding before the work
Neither finding says "don't ride," but neither supports riding normally either. Three things to weigh:
- The skip is under load. That's a sudden loss of drive at the worst possible moments — pulling into an intersection, starting on a grade, merging across traffic. For a daily commuter that's a real safety consideration, not just an annoyance.
- Small but nonzero chance of the chain walking off a severely worn cog entirely under hard pedaling. Uncommon at this wear level, but not the kind of failure mode you want to discover in traffic.
- Every skip event chews the cassette and chainring a little more, so riding in this state is making the eventual repair slightly more expensive.

If the trip is essential, riding in the middle cogs only (the ones that aren't worn) is reasonable — just avoid the smallest cogs entirely, expect a much lower top speed, and treat every acceleration as if it might stutter. For routine commuting, getting the chain-and-cassette job done first is the cleaner call.

Bottom line: the chain-only option is the textbook false economy in this configuration, and the chain-and-cassette option is what the diagnosis actually calls for. Riding is possible but not advisable as a commuter until the work is done.
