A reasonable read on what happened this morning: Kibo's reaction was within the band of normal noise reactivity for a dog with a stable baseline elsewhere. Eight minutes of barking and pacing is meaningful but not alarming, and the fact that he settled in five minutes inside the workroom, without you having to physically manage him through it, is the strongest signal you have. The plan below is built around that fact: don't try to extinguish the reaction, just make sure it can't gather momentum.

LOW-STRESS PLAN FOR FUTURE TRUCK MORNINGS

1. Pin the schedule. Recycling pickup is on a fixed route. Note the time today and tomorrow; most municipalities stick to within about 30 minutes week to week. Once you have a one-week pattern, you have a clock.

2. Pre-position, don't react. Aim to have Kibo in the workroom about 5 minutes before the predicted truck window. Once he's already in, the workroom door closes, the white noise is already on, and the trigger is buffered by all three: closed door, familiar scent on the blanket, acoustic masking. Ten minutes after the truck typically passes, the door opens. This is the change with the highest expected payoff relative to effort.

3. Pair the room with a long-lasting oral activity. A frozen toppl, a Kong with wet food frozen inside, or a lick mat with peanut butter or wet food, dropped in the workroom when you pre-position him. Licking and chewing self-soothe; they downregulate arousal without you having to manage the behavior. This is the second-highest-payoff change.

4. Morning movement before the window, if schedule allows. A 10 to 15 minute sniff walk or yard time before the truck arrives drops baseline arousal. Hard to do on the walk mornings (the Wed AM walk is 8:15 to 8:50 — depends on when the truck actually comes), but on other mornings it costs little.

5. Don't add verbal reassurance during the barking. "It's OK, buddy" from you during the reaction can inadvertently reinforce the loop. The workroom plus activity is the intervention. Your voice at full calm before he enters the room is fine; your voice during the barking is not the lever.

6. Skip the recordings-and-treats desensitization for now. Desensitization to truck sounds is a 4 to 8 week project with its own failure modes (pushing volume too fast is the common one). It is worth doing only if the management plan above isn't keeping things calm; don't pre-emptively start it.

A note on what you're already doing well: putting him in the workroom with blanket, water, and white noise, and then leaving him to settle, is essentially the right intervention. The upgrade is mostly about timing (before, not after) and adding the oral activity.

SIGNS THAT WARRANT A VET OR BEHAVIORIST INSTEAD

These are the ones I'd actually act on. Anything on this list is enough to call:

- Escalation despite the plan. Duration lengthens, frequency rises (other sounds now trigger him), or settling time stops shrinking over 2 to 3 weeks of consistent pre-positioning. The management isn't sufficient.

- New behaviors outside the trigger window. Panting, pacing, or restlessness at times that have nothing to do with the truck. This is the signal that anxiety is generalizing.

- Destructive behavior or escape attempts. Crate or door scratching that damages things, or any attempt to break out. That is a different severity than barking at a window.

- Refusal to enter the workroom. If he starts avoiding the room or showing stress when you lead him there, he's forming a negative association with the room itself, and you need professional input before the protocol breaks down.

- Any aggression. Lip lift, growl, snap, or air-snap toward people during or after an episode. This is a hard stop on self-management.

- Appetite, sleep, or baseline behavior changes. Eating less, sleeping more or less, less interest in walks or play, that persists for more than a few days. Could be medical, could be anxiety, either way a vet visit is the right first move.

- Anything that could be physical rather than behavioral. Head shaking, ear scratching, head tilt, sudden hearing changes (he stops responding to cues he used to know), or any sign of pain on handling. These route to the vet first, not a behaviorist.

FIRST STEP IF ANY OF THE ABOVE FIRES: vet first. A general-practice vet can rule out pain, hearing loss, endocrine issues, and cognitive changes, and can refer to a DACVB (Diplomate of the American College of Veterinary Behaviorists) or a CAAB (Certified Applied Animal Behaviorist) if needed. Behaviorists generally want medical clearance before they start a behavior plan, so the vet visit saves a step either way.

Given what you described this morning — single trigger, clear window of duration, full resolution with a simple protocol, no residual symptoms — you are in the ordinary settling-in support lane, not the escalation lane. The plan above is the right next move.

I have it. The passage is the Goodhart-framed sentence you wrote down at 5:42pm on May 10, 2024:

"A measure begins as a window and ends as a target; once people are rewarded for moving it, the organization sees the number more clearly than the work."

And the connection you're drawing is real — Helio's habit of putting denominators and effect sizes before conclusions is the same instinct expressed as a procedural rule (a guardrail around the slide from window to target). Below are three angles sized for a book-club discussion, not a work deck.

1. Incentives — who is being paid to move the number, and what does the work underneath look like?
The sentence's claim isn't really about metrics; it's about who gets rewarded. The slide happens when the reward structure points at the number, not at the underlying work. So the interesting question in book club isn't "are our metrics bad?" but "in this passage, who are the 'people' the author has in mind?" Are they individual contributors optimizing for their own review, teams competing for budget, leaders defending a board narrative? Each of those produces a different flavor of distortion, and the book gets sharper once you name which one the author means. For Helio specifically — and this is where I'd let the parallel breathe rather than lean on it — the reason BRIEF-2024-04 named net expansion vs. holdout as the measure of record, and kept the five secondary metrics (prompt delivery, qualified conversations, expansion $, opt-outs, CS handling load) explicitly as signals not substitutes, is that the people being rewarded here are CS, and the visible secondary ("expansion $ booked") is the one most likely to bend the work underneath it. The metric-of-record rule is an incentive design, not a measurement preference.

2. What numbers hide — the work is still there, it just isn't legible.
This is the line I'd push hardest on in a discussion: "the organization sees the number more clearly than the work." The work doesn't go away when you stop measuring it; it just stops traveling upward. So the question is what gets lost in the gap between the work and the number — and whether the lost thing is actually the thing that matters. A book-club version: ask people to describe a moment where a metric their org reported looked fine but the work underneath was quietly degrading. The interesting move is noticing what you couldn't see until you stopped trusting the number. Helio-adjacent version, without making it a work talk: when a setup-call gate judges on completed calls + connection outcomes rather than bookings, what's being hidden from leadership's view is booking velocity — and that's a deliberate trade. Some signal has to die so a truer one can be read.

3. Using a metric without letting it replace judgment — the metric as a witness, not a verdict.
The healthy posture the sentence gestures at is treating a measure as a witness you can cross-examine, not a verdict you have to obey. That means three habits: the denominator stays visible (what population is this number actually about, and what would change your read), the effect size travels with the number (a movement of two points on a base of a thousand is not the same movement as two points on a base of ten), and the conclusion waits until the stabilization cohort confirms the first signal — Owen's sequencing for the expansion-nudge read, where prior-cohort differences of +0.7, +0.2, and +0.4 across n=2,446 were held as descriptive rather than shipped, is exactly this habit. The discipline isn't "trust the metric less"; it's "let the metric argue its case in the right order." That's the angle I'd offer if someone in book club asks the practical question — and it's where the Helio parallel is cleanest, because the rule is procedural, not philosophical, and that makes it portable to any group.

One framing note if it helps: the three angles aren't three separate claims about the passage. What this most likely is
  Gradual onset, lateral-ankle location, mild intensity (2/10 stairs), normal weight-bearing, and no swelling, bruising, pop, or twist point away from an acute ligament tear, fracture, or anything that needs urgent imaging. The final-mile timing during an otherwise uneventful 4-miler is a classic cumulative-load pattern. The most likely explanations are:
  - Early peroneal tendon irritation or a low-grade peroneal strain (peroneus longus/brevis run along the outside of the ankle and eccentric-load on stairs, especially going down).
  - Sinus tarsi irritation or a minor lateral-structural strain from a cambered surface, new shoes, or a small uptick in load.
  - A low-grade ATFL/CFL stretch you didn't notice as a "twist" (less likely without any mechanism, but possible).

  You don't need to settle on a label today. The plan below is the same either way.

Self-care for today and the next 48-72 hours
  - Stop running for now. You already did, which was the right call.
  - Ice the lateral ankle 15-20 minutes every 2-3 hours while awake for the first 48 hours. Thin cloth barrier; check the skin.
  - Light compression with a thin ankle sleeve or a soft wrap is fine if it feels supportive. Remove it if you feel numbness, tingling, or increased pain.
  - Elevate the ankle above heart level when sitting.
  - Walking is fine as tolerated; aim for a normal, non-favoring gait. Take stairs slowly and use the handrail — 2/10 on descent is expected to fade in 1-3 days.
  - OTC pain: acetaminophen is preferred. Avoid ibuprofen/naproxen for the first 48-72 hours if this is tendinous, since NSAIDs can blunt early healing; a short NSAID course is reasonable if pain disrupts sleep or clearly worsens.
  - Avoid: heat, deep massage, aggressive stretching, lacrosse-ball rolling the lateral ankle, KT tape "correcting" anything, and pushing through pain.
  - Hydration and normal meals; nothing else special.

Should you skip your next run?
  Yes. Plan on at least 4-7 fully off running days, and don't run again until ALL of these are true:
    1. Walking is fully pain-free at your normal pace.
    2. Descending stairs is 0/10 (not 2/10).
    3. Single-leg stand on the right foot for 30 seconds is pain-free and stable — no catching, no sense of giving way, no lateral-ankle awareness.
    4. Single-leg calf raise on the right is pain-free.
    5. A few minutes of brisk walking on uneven ground (grass, cracked sidewalk) is comfortable.

Return-to-running progression (only after the gate above is met)
  - Run 1: 15-20 min easy walk-jog on a flat, soft surface (track, grass, crushed gravel). Roughly 1-2 min jog / 2-3 min walk. No pace pressure.
  - Run 2 (2-3 days later, only if Run 1 was symptom-free during and after): 20-25 min continuous easy jog, same flat/soft surface.
  - Run 3 (2-3 days later, still symptom-free): 25-30 min easy jog.
  - Then every-other-day easy for a week before reintroducing hills, speed, and longer distances — one new stressor at a time, with 3-4 days between additions.
  - Skip cambered roads and uneven trail for the first week back; both load the lateral side.
  - If discomfort returns during or after a run, stop, repeat the gate, and retry the prior step after a day off. If discomfort recurs on two attempts, get evaluated rather than grinding through.

Signs that warrant prompt (same-day or next-day) medical evaluation
  - A pop, snap, or tearing sensation at any point — suggests peroneal tendon subluxation/dislocation or retinacular injury.
  - Rapidly increasing pain, swelling, or bruising around the lateral malleolus over 24-48 hours.
  - Pain at rest, or pain that wakes you from sleep.
  - New numbness, tingling, or burning in the foot (sural nerve involvement).
  - A cold, pale, or persistently discolored foot.
  - Calf or leg swelling, especially one-sided, with warmth, redness, a tender cord, or cramping — DVT concern.
  - Difficulty or inability to bear weight that develops over the next 1-2 days.
  - A new feeling of the ankle giving way, locking, or catching during motion.
  - Fever, chills, or feeling systemically unwell.
  - An open wound over the lateral ankle.
  - Symptoms that don't clearly improve after 5-7 days of rest, or that come back during the return-to-running progression above.

Brief recurrence note
  Once you're back to baseline, a few minutes of peroneal strengthening (banded eversions, calf raises, single-leg balance work) 2-3x/week lowers lateral-ankle re-injury risk.
  You've now had a left-calf tightness episode (Dec '23), a left-heel hot spot from new shoes (Feb '24), a right-calf tightness episode (Mar '24), and this right-lateral-ankle complaint. Each has been minor and resolved conservatively, but four different sites in six months is a pattern. If a fifth shows up — or this one lingers past the return-to-run gate — a one-time gait/cadence/shoe review with a running-savvy PT is worth it. Small form or shoe changes usually fix repeat minor overuse complaints of this shape.

What you're looking at: the insurer adjudicated the $185 follow-up as bundled into another service from the same day. The N20 remark code means "service not payable with another service rendered on the same date" — in their view, the post-procedure visit was never a separately billable item, which is why they allowed $0, paid $0, and assigned $0 to you.

What the provider did: ignored the EOB and balance-billed you the full $185. That move is generally improper in three common situations, and the EOB points to one of them:

  1.  The provider is in-network and the follow-up falls inside a global-procedure / global-surgery window. The post-op visit is part of the procedure's contracted package; they agreed to that when they joined the network.
  2.  Same-day E/M visit subsumed into a procedure on the same date for the same condition (the insurer is reading it as "procedure subsumes the visit," not the other way around).
  3.  The "follow-up" was a routine post-op check that the contract covers without separate billing.

What to do before May 23:

  1.  Call the provider's billing office, not the clinic line. Ask two specific questions: "What CPT code is on the $185 charge?" and "What was the other service on the same date?" You want the code and the bundling partner.
  2.  If in-network: cite the EOB and ask them to write it off per their contract. They cannot bill you for a service the insurer has adjudicated as $0 patient responsibility while they're bound by the network agreement.
  3.  Ask whether an ABN (Advance Beneficiary Notice) was signed before the visit. If no ABN was signed and the service wasn't formally non-covered at the time, they usually cannot bill you.
  4.  If they hold the line: open a formal dispute with the insurer (member services, number on the card). The N20 is their own determination — they'll defend it, and a successful dispute forces the provider to write off the charge.
  5.  After every call, note date, name, and what was said. Written follow-up email summarizing the call is the strongest evidence if it escalates.

Do not pay the $185 on May 23 if the EOB stands. Paying it can be read as accepting the charge, which weakens the dispute. If the deadline arrives unpaid, the next move is a formal complaint to your state insurance department — that's a slower lever but it's free and effective against contracted providers who ignore bundling determinations.

FAQ: Connector Access Confirmation

Q: Who needs to confirm connector access?
A qualified admin or someone with authority to authenticate the supported connector can confirm — not necessarily the connector owner. This is separate from Helio admin proof.

Q: What if SSO or security approval blocks confirmation?
If the applicant can sign in but can't approve the integration, or security still needs to sign off on OAuth, the answer stays pending. Customer Success resolves the case before admission rather than treating uncertainty as a yes.

Q: Can an applicant return after confirmation?
Yes. A definite confirmation lets them resume the ordinary eligibility path, but it does not bypass the other admission conditions.

Q: Should the applicant send credentials?
No. Don't send passwords, tokens, secrets, or another person's credentials. Helio needs confirmation of supported access, not copied authentication material.

A few notes up front: I'm not a clinician, and I don't have your injury history, what Saturday's intervals actually were, or the original diagnosis. Treat this as a conservative framework, not a prescription. If anything below contradicts what your PT/physician told you, follow them.

You're 48 hours out with a clean baseline and no overnight symptoms. That's a reasonable green light for the plan you described — gentle normal activity through the week, then Saturday test #2.

────────────────────────────────────────
THE WEEK (Mon–Fri)
────────────────────────────────────────

Goal: confirm that walking and easy cycling don't reintroduce any symptoms, and give you a buffer day or two before Saturday so you go in fresh.

Mon (today)   — easy 20–30 min walk if it feels good; no cycling yet. You're still
                inside the 48-hour symptom window, so keep it boring on purpose.
Tue           — 30–40 min walk + 20–30 min easy spin (low resistance, smooth
                cadence). This is your first real "loading" day — it matters.
Wed           — same shape as Tue, OR a touch longer walk. No intensity.
Thu           — easy walk + easy spin. Add a single-leg calf raise set (3x10,
                slow) and one set of heel raises off a step if pain-free — these
                are good return-to-run prehab markers and shouldn't flare
                anything if the ankle is truly at baseline.
Fri           — rest, or a short flat walk only. No spin. You want Saturday to
                start from a clean 24-hour window.

Walking and cycling are fine to do "normally" as long as comfort stays your gate. If anything during or after a session feels off, that day becomes the new floor — repeat it, don't advance.

────────────────────────────────────────
SATURDAY — repeat vs. one small progression
────────────────────────────────────────

Both are defensible. My recommendation is below.

Option A (REPEAT — most conservative)
  - Identical total duration, identical walk/jog intervals, identical paces.
  - Purpose: confirm Saturday #1 wasn't a fluke. Two clean sessions at the
    same dose before you add any load.

Option B (ONE SMALL PROGRESSION — what I'd actually pick)
  - Hold everything constant EXCEPT one of these single changes:
    (a) add exactly one interval at the end (e.g., +4 min of the same
        walk/jog pattern), OR
    (b) extend the last jog segment by ~60 sec before the cool-down walk.
  - Keep walk pace, jog pace, walk:jog ratio, and surface identical.
  - Reasoning: extending duration at the same pace is a more predictable
    load change than nudging pace. Your minute-16 ache suggests duration
    was the relevant variable, so test duration again, slightly more of it.

Recommendation: Option B with change (a) — one extra interval — IF the whole week goes by with zero symptoms AND your single-leg calf raises on Thursday are pain-free and symmetric. If Thursday or Friday surfaces anything, default to Option A without hesitation.

────────────────────────────────────────
STOP CRITERIA (during any session — walk, spin, or jog)
────────────────────────────────────────

Stop the session immediately if any of these appear:
  - Any ankle pain that isn't already present at the start (i.e., new pain).
  - Pain that persists past ~5 min of easy warm-up, or that gets worse
    instead of better during the session.
  - A feeling of "giving way," catching, clicking with pain, or loss of
    smooth motion.
  - Any limp forming, even subtle. If you notice yourself favoring it,
    you're done.
  - Sharp or focal tenderness, or pain that localizes to one spot you can
    point to with one finger.

For cycling specifically: stop if you feel anything at the bottom of the
pedal stroke or during high-torque efforts, even if the rest is fine.

────────────────────────────────────────
EVALUATION CRITERIA (next-morning check, every day)
────────────────────────────────────────

Before you progress the plan, the next morning has to be clean on all of these:
  - Pain at rest: 0/10.
  - Stiffness that resolves within ~5–10 min of normal walking: fine.
    Stiffness that lingers >15 min or forces a limp: red flag.
  - Swelling, bruising, or warmth compared to the other ankle: any of
    these = hold the plan, repeat the prior day's dose at most.
  - Focal tenderness on palpation around the malleoli, ATFL/CFL, or
    Achilles insertion: any of these = hold.
  - Stairs (especially down) feel identical to the other side: required.
  - No new nighttime aching or awareness of the ankle while trying to sleep.

Scoring rule of thumb: zero across all of these → proceed as planned.
One category "off" but mild and gone by midday → repeat today's dose, don't
advance. Anything sharp or persistent → rest 48 hours and reassess; if it
recurs, that's a "get it looked at" signal.

────────────────────────────────────────
SEE-SOMEONE RED FLAGS (don't keep self-managing)
────────────────────────────────────────

  - Swelling that appears or worsens the day after a session that felt fine
    during the session.
  - Pain that localizes sharply to bone or tendon rather than "the area."
  - Any true giving-way episode or feeling of instability on uneven ground.
  - Symptoms that don't fully return to baseline within 48 hours after a
    session, or that trend worse session-to-session instead of stable.
  - Pain at rest, or pain that wakes you up.

────────────────────────────────────────

Net summary: Mon easy walk → Tue/Wed walk + easy spin → Thu walk + spin + prehab → Fri short walk or rest → Saturday, one extra interval at the same paces — gated on a fully clean week and clean Thursday calf raises. Hold Saturday to a repeat if any day in between is even slightly off.

  $477.20 - $84.00 = $393.20                                    matches

All three reconcile.

Post-labor contribution
  At actual 3 hrs: $393.20
  vs. $450 threshold: short by $56.80

Max incremental labor the same $722 sales / $244.80 food cost can carry
  Dollars left for labor at threshold: $477.20 - $450 = $27.20
  At $28/hr: $27.20 / $28 = 0.97 hrs (about 58 min)
  Actual run used 3 hrs; that's $56.80 of labor above the max (84 - 27.20). The miss is exactly the labor overshoot.

Verdict on an unchanged repeat
  No. Three ways to see it:
  1. Post-labor contribution is $56.80 below the bar.
  2. Even at $0 incremental labor, $477.20 only clears $450 by $27.20 - thin headroom for any other variance.
  3. To clear $450 holding the 3 hrs of labor and the $244.80 food cost, sales would need to be $778.80, i.e. +$56.80 (+7.9%) on the same 44 plates - about a $1.50 ASP lift or one more cover at the current ~$19 plate.

Six unsold portions in view
  38 of 44 plates sold (86.4% sell-through).
  Per-plate food cost: $244.80 / 44 = $5.56
  6 unsold portions = $33.38 of food cost that earned no revenue.
  Hypothetical 38-portion build would have been food cost $211.42, contribution $510.58, post-labor $426.58 - still misses $450 by $23.42. So portion control alone does not rescue the special; the price/volume mix is the binding constraint.

Reminder
  $393.20 is contribution after food + incremental labor only, not profit. Base wages, overhead, utilities, etc. still apply on top.

Practical path that clears the threshold on this menu math
  38 portions + ~1 hr incremental labor: $510.58 - $28 = $482.58 contribution (clears $450).
  Or hold 44 portions and 3 hrs only if the next run can reliably hit ~$779 in sales.

Bottom line: do not repeat unchanged. The lever is labor time (closer to ~1 hr) or a sales/price lift; the 6 unsold plates are a yellow flag on demand, but they're not the dominant cause of the miss - the 3 hours of labor at $28/hr is.

Target temp: 175°F (80°C) for thigh meat, measured in the thickest part, just past the bone — dark-meat collagen needs higher heat than the 165°F floor to break down and stay tender. If you're using boneless thighs, 175°F at the geometric center is the same rule.

Probe placement for bone-in thighs:
- Slide the tip into the meatiest portion of the inner thigh, past (not touching) the femur bone.
- Bone conducts heat, so a reading taken against bone will lie high; touching the bone can give you a falsely "safe" number if the probe tip slips. Aim for meat-only contact about 1/2 inch in.
- Take it in two spots — front and back of the thigh — because thighs cook unevenly when seared.

The reserved marinade is already safe by the recipe's design. You set aside 2 Tbsp before the chicken went in, so that 2 Tbsp never touched raw poultry. Just keep it in a separate small bowl, brush from that bowl only, and never dip a brush back into the marinating dish. A clean spoon or silicone brush dedicated to the reserved bowl is the cleanest way to handle it.

If you want belt-and-suspenders (e.g., you're worried the reserved portion got contaminated somehow), boil the reserved 2 Tbsp in a small saucepan for a full rolling minute before brushing. The marinade is ginger-soy — it'll survive a boil fine, you'll just lose a touch of raw-ginger brightness.

To keep the rest of the dish clean during cooking:
- Don't reuse the bowl the chicken marinated in for anything that touches the cooked thighs.
- Wash the brush between the raw-marinate bowl and the reserved bowl if you ever do dip into the wrong one — or grab a fresh brush.
- Plate the cooked thighs on a clean dish, not the plate that held them raw.

Good checkpoint. Pain-free during the session and at the 8-hour mark, with no swelling, focal tenderness, limp, or instability — that's a clean green light, not a clearance to jump back to four continuous miles. Here's a cautious next-week plan plus the rules you asked for.

NEXT WEEK — 4 walk-jog sessions, flat surface, same shoes, conversational effort, with at least one rest day between sessions. Never stack two sessions into one day.

DAY 1 — anchor the new floor
  24 min. Same as today: 2:1 (walk:jog) for the first 12 min, then 1:1 for the last 12 min.
  This is your reference session. You must clear it cleanly before anything else in the week progresses.

DAY 3 — keep duration, shift the ratio
  24 min. 1:1 throughout (12 cycles of 1-min walk, 1-min jog).
  Same time on feet, but the work tilts toward more jogging minutes.

DAY 5 — first duration bump
  26 min. 1:1 throughout (13 cycles).

DAY 7 — second duration bump
  28 min. 1:1 throughout (14 cycles).

If the week only holds 3 sessions, run Day 1 / Day 3 / Day 7 and skip Day 5 — do not combine sessions.

Jog minutes per session: 10 → 12 → 13 → 14. Weekly total ~49 min of jogging, spread across four sessions. That's a real load bump from today's single 10-min jog block, but it's distributed and each step is small.

REPEATING A LEVEL
  - A session "passes" only if you're symptom-free during it AND for 24 hours after. Use a 0–10 pain scale; any reading >0 during the session, immediately after, at 2 hours, or at 24 hours is a fail.
  - If a session fails, repeat the SAME session next time. Do not progress.
  - If two consecutive repeats at the same level still fail, step back one full level (e.g., from a 26-min 1:1 back to a 24-min 1:1, holding the ratio before shortening further).
  - Two clean passes in a row at a level = clear to attempt the next level on the following session.
  - Pain that lingers past 24 hours counts as a fail even if the next session feels fine — treat it as a real signal, not noise.
  - The first session of the week is the gate. If Day 1 fails to clear, the whole week's plan slides back one slot and you repeat until it does.

STOPPING A SESSION (mid-walk-jog)
  Stop and walk home if any of these appear:
  - Pain ≥3/10, or any sharp or localized pain (versus general muscular effort).
  - Pain that worsens as the session progresses instead of warming up and staying stable or improving.
  - Pain that doesn't settle within 1–2 minutes of slowing to a walk.
  - A new limp, catch, click, feeling of giving way, or any sense of instability.
  - New swelling, hot spot, or focal tenderness during the session.
  - Anything outside the musculoskeletal system — lightheadedness, chest symptoms, etc.

Pre-session gate (don't start if any of these are present):
  - New resting pain, swelling, or focal tenderness that wasn't there the prior day.
  - A visible limp on your normal walk to the start point.
  - Poor sleep, illness, fever, or a generally rundown feeling — defer 24 hours and reassess.

SEEKING EVALUATION
  Contact a clinician (and pause the progression) if you notice any of the following:
  - Pain during a session that doesn't resolve within 2–3 minutes of walking.
  - Pain that recurs or intensifies over the 24–48 hours after a session, or pain still present at rest the next morning.
  - New or persistent swelling, warmth, or focal bony tenderness.
  - A limp during or after any session.
  - A sense of instability, catching, locking, or the joint "giving way."
  - Night pain that wakes you, or pain worse first thing in the morning before any loading.
  - You get "stuck" — two repeat cycles at the same level still produce symptoms and you're not trending back to clean.
  - Any focal pain that localizes to bone rather than muscle/tendon, or pain with a clearly different quality from general training effort.

OPERATIONAL NOTES
  - Change one variable at a time: same surface, same shoes, same time of day, easy conversational pace. Don't introduce a new surface or new footwear mid-progression.
  - 5–10 min easy walk warm-up before each session; 5-min walk cool-down after.
  - Skip a session rather than cram. The cost of an extra rest day is small; the cost of pushing through a symptom and re-injuring is weeks.
  - Log each session: date, total minutes, ratios, pain during / 2h / 24h, any swelling or limp. The log is what tells you whether the trend is clean — don't trust memory across four sessions in a week.

If the full week goes clean, the next natural step is 30 min of 1:1, then introducing 4:1 blocks (4-min jog / 1-min walk) at the front of sessions, then continuous easy running. That's next week's decision, not this one's.

One caveat worth stating plainly: this is a cautious return-to-loading framework, not a diagnosis. If anything in your history suggests a specific injury (stress fracture, tendonopathy, post-op, etc.), the gating thresholds and progression rate should come from the clinician managing that — these rules are the floor, not a substitute for their ceiling.

Cannot be guaranteed by removing the garnish

The garnish is the smallest of the problems. Sesame exposure on this plate still comes from:
- Sesame oil in the soy-ginger glaze (the ingredient, not a finishing touch)
- Cross-contact on any wok, pan, or sheet used earlier for sesame-crusted or sesame-oiled items
- Cross-contact on prep surfaces, ladles, tongs, sauce pots, garnishing tweezers
- Hand or glove transfer during plating
- Steam or aerosol in a shared hood from sesame toasting earlier in service
- Other menu items that quietly contain sesame (some soy sauces, miso, chili oils, dumpling sauces, finishing oils on vegetables, certain dessert components)

Removing the seed on a sesame-oil glaze is cosmetic, not protective. A guest with a real sesame allergy should not be served this dish in modified form.

Recommended framing

Build a separate, fully sesame-free entrée from scratch, not a modification of the standard. Hold it to the same plating standard. Identify it on the kitchen pass and on the server's ticket. Have the server quietly verify with the guest at drop-off. Don't announce it as "the allergy plate" to the table.

Reconfirm with the guest (via the event host, not the guest directly)

- Severity: anaphylaxis, anaphylactoid, OAS? Carries an EpiPen or equivalent?
- Trigger history: oil vs. seed vs. both? Airborne exposure or ingestion only?
- Their preference: a fully separate entrée, or a modified standard with self-managed risk? (Most operations won't offer the second option for sesame in a private-dining context.)
- They will have medication with them; host and server know where it is.
- Other allergies or restrictions. Sesame often travels with mustard and tree nuts; worth asking while you're at it.

Reconfirm with the chef-owner

- Whether the alternative entrée is built into the menu plan or Sam is proposing one, and who owns the recipe
- Dedicated equipment for the night: identified wok/pan, sheet pan, ladle, tongs, sauce pot, garnish tools, plateware — labeled, pulled from clean storage, not the line
- Sequencing: allergen meal cooked and plated before any standard sesame work, or run on a physically separated station with a clean hood if temporal separation isn't possible
- Plating pass: chef-owner (or Sam) does the final verification on the allergen ticket — colored ticket, sticker under the rim, whatever the existing system is
- Service hand-off: server knows the guest name and seat; allergen plate is identified at every transfer; server confirms with guest at drop-off
- Who runs the allergen plate at service — Sam, chef-owner, or a designated cook briefed separately on the workflow
- Menu sweep: every other dish for the 20 covers checked for hidden sesame
- 911 and escalation path: what server does, what kitchen does, who calls

Prep and service sequence

Pre-event
1. Confirm the alternative entrée with chef-owner; finalize the recipe; verify every ingredient (including soy sauce brand) is sesame-free
2. Pull and label dedicated equipment; deep clean and stage in a clean area
3. Update the menu sweep for hidden sesame across all 20 covers

48–72 hours out
4. Guest reconfirmation via host
5. Brief BOH and FOH: which guest, seat if known, severity, alternative dish, plating and identification system, escalation if symptoms appear

Day-of prep
6. Sanitize station, equipment, plateware. Lay out single-use gloves and a clean mise for the allergen meal
7. Prep allergen-entrée ingredients from sealed containers, not bulk bins
8. Cook the allergen entrée first, before any sesame work. Cover and hold at temp
9. Run standard dishes after, with sesame work last in the sequence

Service
10. Plating: Sam or chef-owner only, fresh gloves, plated from the dedicated pan, plate marked
11. Pass/expo verification: chef-owner signs off — correct ticket, correct dish, correct guest
12. Runner hand-off: server briefed on guest name and seat; verbal confirmation at pick-up
13. Drop-off: server quietly verifies with the guest that this is the meal prepared for them; doesn't announce "allergy plate" to the table
14. Server stays aware through the first few bites; host knows the escalation path

Contingency
15. Guest's medication location known to host and on-shift manager
16. Clear escalation: symptoms → server alerts chef-owner and host → 911 called immediately, medication administered by guest or trained responder. Kitchen does not improvise.

# Route decision

The applicant is an **agency identity, not an ownership mismatch**. The correct route is **out of self-serve setup and onto `assisted_setup`**. Customer Success owns the reply language and the handoff; the workspace is not created on the self-serve path, and no refusal-boundary, pricing-page, waitlist, sales/CSM, or launch-timing language is used. # Explanation draft (for CS to send, protective tone, no "bad fit")

Subject: Helio Start — next steps for [Agency Name]

Thanks for the application and for the authorization letter from [Client A]. Two things are worth separating, because they sound similar but route differently under Helio Start:

1. **A connector-access answer of "Yes."** That step is separate from workspace eligibility. It tells us your side can authenticate the integration; it does not, by itself, qualify a workspace for the self-serve setup path. A "Yes" here would not change the route below, because the gate that fires is admin ownership, not connector authentication.

2. **Who administers the Helio workspace day-to-day.** Helio's self-serve setup path is built for one named workspace owner who controls integration, settings, and billing for the client company. The applicant on the invite is that owner. An agency administering Helio on behalf of one or more client companies — even with administrator access to its own systems and a connector that authenticates cleanly — does not become the client's workspace owner through a letter of authorization. The letter is the right thing to send and we will keep it on file, but it identifies the client's administrator for the assisted handoff; it does not substitute for that person completing the setup step themselves.

That second point is why this is an **assisted_setup** case rather than a self-serve path case, and it is the same rule that handled the first live agency-boundary case on March 18 and the shared-agency OAuth case in the November cohort — neither of those changed the public rule.

To move this forward we need:

- The **client-side workspace owner's name and email** for each of the three client companies you intend to manage through this workspace, and
- A short note on which client each deployment is for, so the assisted setup team can scope one workspace per client rather than one shared workspace.

Once we have the client owner contact, the assisted setup team will reach out within **one to two business days** to walk each client's administrator through their own setup. That keeps integration administration, settings, and billing decisions with the people who actually own them on the client side, which is what protects each client's workspace from a setup that would otherwise get stuck at the first-integration step.

A note on what this **is not**: this is not a judgment about your agency's fit, not a waitlist, and not a sales conversation. It is the path that keeps each client's workspace from getting stuck. If the three client companies each have their own named administrator and want to run Helio themselves, they can apply directly and complete the self-serve setup path on their own workspaces.

# Distinguishing evidence: ownership mismatch vs agency identity

The same evidence does different work in the two cases. The boundary that matters is **who will be the named workspace owner operating the Helio workspace**, not whether someone can prove access to a third-party system.

Evidence that resolves an ownership mismatch (corroborating admin ownership, same case class as the 9 of 30 January dry-run non-agency cases):
- Exact OAuth email-domain match against the workspace-owner domain.
- Parent-company ownership where the applicant's email domain is a parent of the workspace-owner domain and the applicant confirms admin responsibility for the child entity.
- IT-managed SSO where the applicant authenticates through the customer's identity provider and is confirmed by that customer as the day-to-day administrator.
- A corroborating statement from the named workspace owner (the customer themselves, not a third party) that the applicant is their administrator.

In each of these, the **client-side administrator is being identified**; the applicant is that administrator, or is being confirmed as that administrator by the customer. That is why these are corroborating admin evidence rather than a route-out.

Evidence that does **not** resolve an agency identity (this case):
- The applicant's own administrator access to its own systems.
- A supported connector that the applicant can authenticate.
- A letter of authorization from one client naming the agency as administrator.
- Corroborating evidence from the agency about its own administrators' access.

The structural difference: in a mismatch, the question is *"is this person the customer's administrator?"* and the answer can be **yes** with the right corroboration. In an agency identity, the question is *"is an agency the customer's administrator?"* and the answer under the self-serve path is **no by design** — Helio's setup path requires the client's own workspace owner to complete the first-integration step, because integration, settings, and billing decisions need to stay with the people who own them on the client side. Written authorization from the client names the client's administrator for the assisted handoff; it does not retitle the agency employee as that administrator, and it does not move the case onto the self-serve path.

That is why the agency exclusion is unchanged by additional corroborating evidence, while a parent-company or IT-managed SSO mismatch is resolved by it. The first changes **who the applicant is**; the second only confirms **who the applicant already is**.

- The connector-access answer does not change the route and is not the gate that fires here; record it but route on admin ownership.

Q1 — What outcomes did I materially influence in H1?

The clearest outcome is the May 24 Helio Start scope settlement: organic pricing-page continues through Q3, refusal rules and the connector-access check remain intact, and the continuation gate is first-paid + day-90 retention evidence — not a pipeline number or a paid-acquisition read. I didn't run the dry-run or build the funnel; I worked on what the team was allowed to conclude from it.

Four specific contributions to that decision:

  - Evidence boundaries. I argued that the load-bearing facts were the dry-run baseline (six cohorts, 256/334) and the connector-access check (92 → 68 admitted → 59 activated, 15 connector-authority cases still pending/assisted), not durable retention or a forecastable-revenue claim. That kept the conclusion testable and the next decision made on inputs that would actually move when the channel moved.

  - Routing and support kept distinct. Support contacts (11 across 8 admitted) and routing outcomes are diagnostics, not a single signal. Treating them as separate streams kept the team from declaring "activation is fine" when what we had was "activation is fine, but support is absorbing friction we haven't named."

  - Connector-access check. Of 9 nonactivators, 3 hit credential/connector issues, versus 18/147 in the prior baseline. Without that check, the activation number was uninterpretable: low activation could mean a channel problem or a connector-authority problem, and the remedies are different. The check is what made the cohort story readable.

  - Decision structure. I held the Q3 continuation call apart from Marcus's paid-acquisition test and the Q3 pipeline target. Same time window, different motions — reading them off the same numbers would have collapsed two experiments into one.

What I did not do: build the reporting (Owen), instrument the funnel (Daniela), run the lifecycle QA on the pause-gate fixtures (Ines), or handle the live support load (CS). I asked the questions and held the boundaries; others built and ran the systems that answered them.


Q2 — Where did my judgment change the team's direction?

Three cases, each a reframe of what the evidence could support.

  1. The connector-access check itself. The dry-run was being read as an activation rate. The reframing question was: do we know whether admitted users had the authority to connect a workspace? Without that, low activation is uninterpretable, and high activation can hide the same problem in the cohort that didn't get past the gate. That moved the work from "is the channel producing activated users" to "is the channel producing users who can become activated, and what does the gap look like" — and surfaced 15 cases that needed assisted setup rather than a channel fix.

Short answer: REPEAT this 30-min session once before deciding. The data is consistent with acceptable tissue loading, not a red flag — but the repeat session is the test. Below is the decision rule and the thresholds that should stop progression and trigger evaluation.

WHY THE CURRENT SIGNAL IS NOT A RED FLAG
  - No pain during the session (pain-under-load is the most sensitive intolerance signal)
  - Delayed onset (~2 hr post) is typical of a mechanical loading response
  - Intensity 1/10, duration <1 hr, provoked only on stairs (loaded dorsiflexion — a known sensitive position for the lateral ankle)
  - No red-flag features: no swelling, limp, instability, bruising, focal tenderness, night pain

RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP
  1. Repeat the exact 30-min session in 2–3 days (no back-to-back running days)
  2. Track the same parameters: time-to-onset, intensity (0–10), duration, location, what provokes it
  3. If the repeat reproduces the identical pattern → progress by ~10% next week (e.g., 33 min, or extend one jog interval)
  4. If the repeat is same OR better on every axis → proceed

STEP-BACK TRIGGERS (return to the prior 24-min walk-jog level for ≥1 week)
Any ONE on the repeat session:
  - Pain during the session (even mild)
  - Delayed pain ≥2/10, or lasting >2 hours
  - Pain appearing on flat walking rather than only on stairs
  - Pain appearing earlier than 2 hr post-session
  - Any ache present the next morning that wasn't present before this progression

EVALUATION TRIGGERS — stop progressing and arrange a clinical assessment
Red flags (any one, ever):
  - Pain at rest or pain at night (wakes you, or present without activity)
  - Post-session pain lasting >24–48 hr
  - Visible or persistent swelling
  - Instability / giving way, especially on uneven ground
  - Inability to bear weight, or a limp persisting >24 hr
  - Mechanical symptoms: catching, locking, or painful clicking
  - Focal bony tenderness over the lateral malleolus, talus, sinus tarsi, or fifth-metatarsal base
  - Numbness, tingling, or pins-and-needles
  - Calf pain, swelling, or tenderness (separate rule-out: DVT/soleus)

Recurrence / trend thresholds (any one, across two consecutive sessions at the same load):
  - Intensity trending up (1/10 → 2/10 → 3/10)
  - Duration trending longer (1 hr → 4 hr → next-day)
  - Onset trending earlier (during session, or within 30 min vs 2 hr)
  - New anatomical distribution (medial ankle, Achilles, sinus tarsi, midfoot)
  - Pain that interferes with sleep

DECISION-RULE FRAMING (the form you'd want in a brief)
  - Hypothesis: 30-min flat is within tissue tolerance; the 1/10 delayed ache is an acceptable loading response
  - Test: one repeat session under identical conditions (same surface, footwear, time of day)
  - Decision rule: same-or-better on every axis → progress; worse on any axis → step back; red flag → evaluate
  - Window: a single session is not a trend. The signal you trust is the pattern across 2–3 sessions
  - Confounders to keep constant across the test: surface, footwear, sleep, prior-day activity. If any of these differ, the comparison is weaker

ONE HONEST CAVEAT
I'm reasoning from your description, not assessing you. If anything in that description undersells what's actually happening — a swelling you're dismissing, a limp you're compensating around, a focal tenderness you didn't palpate — the threshold for evaluation is lower, not higher. The list above is the floor, not the ceiling, for what should send you to a clinician.

If you'd like, after the repeat session I can help you structure a 4–6 week progression from 30 min flat to longer continuous running, with the same kind of decision gates baked in.

For the corner right now, in order of least invasive:

1. Don't touch it wet. The wash is intact; adding water will lift and shift pigment and turn a small fiber problem into a bloom. Leave it alone.

2. Press under weight. Set the painting face-up on a clean sheet of copy paper, lay a piece of glassine, baking parchment, or plain printer paper over it as a release, and weight it under heavy flat books for 24-48 hours. Many raised fibers settle back into the tooth on their own once the sheet reaches humidity equilibrium. Reassess after that — and don't fix it this morning; let it rest and decide with fresh eyes.

3. If a fiber tuft still stands up, groom rather than wet. Hold the painting at a low angle in raking window light and clip the longest protruding fibers flush with a fresh snap-blade or #11 scalpel. Cut in the direction the fiber lies. Never pull.

4. True last resort for a stubborn tuft inside the mat opening: a pinpoint of archival PVA or methylcellulose on a 000 brush, only on the lifted fibers, then re-press. It's the only wet step worth considering, and only because the paint film there is intact.

For framing: if the corner still reads after pressing, a mat with a 1/8" wider reveal, or non-glare glass, will usually hide what's left. Cold press already invites texture, so a slight difference is generally less visible matted and behind glass than it looks naked on the table.

Better tape method next time:

Cause diagnosis — fiber lift on 300 gsm cold press almost always means one of: the tape stayed on past full humidity equilibration, the paper was lightly sized, the pull angle was too vertical, or the adhesive was grippier than artist-grade paper wants.

What actually works:
  - Use artist tape (3M Scotch Artist Tape #2090, Yasutomo, or similar paper-backed drafting tape), not generic masking tape or most washi. Test on a scrap corner of the actual sheet before you commit.
  - If you taped the sheet down before painting, remove the tape while the paper is still slightly damp, not bone dry. The classic wet-stretch / dry-paint / damp-remove cycle is what keeps fibers down.
  - If you're taping a border for a clean white edge after painting, apply to fully dry paper but pull the tape within an hour or two — long enough for the wash to set, short enough that a humidity swing hasn't locked the adhesive into the fibers.
  - Pull angle matters most: low and parallel to the surface, with your other hand trailing behind pressing the paper flat. Straight-up pulls shear fibers off cold press.
  - A two-second pass with a hair dryer on low, held ~30 cm away, warms the adhesive slightly and gives a cleaner release. Don't overheat.

Two alternatives worth knowing:
  - A watercolor block (Arches 1000 H, Fluid, etc.) — paper pre-glued on all four edges. No tape, no fiber lift, no buckling. A palette knife separates the sheet after painting.

For a 9x12 study that's already painted, the press-under-weight step alone will probably resolve the corner. If not, the trimmed-fiber groom almost always does.

The arithmetic here is small enough that I'll just walk through it step by step rather than invoking a calculator — but I want to flag that I don't actually have a terminal/exec tool available in this session (only the app/integration tools and Hindsight), so I'm doing the math by hand rather than running it. If you want me to put numbers into a sheet or doc, I can do that.

Step 1 — DC wattage drawn by each device
- Modem: 12 V × 1.5 A = 18.00 W
- Access point (PoE injector): 48 V × 0.32 A = 15.36 W
- Combined DC load: 18.00 + 15.36 = 33.36 W

Step 2 — Add overhead
A small UPS converts battery DC → AC → device DC again (or, for the AP's injector, AC → 48 V DC). Each conversion costs ~5–10%, plus you want headroom so the unit isn't running at 90%+ of its rating. A reasonable overhead band is 20–30%.

- +20% overhead → 33.36 × 1.20 ≈ 40.0 W
- +25% overhead → 33.36 × 1.25 ≈ 41.7 W
- +30% overhead → 33.36 × 1.30 ≈ 43.4 W

Plan around ~40–43 W on the AC side of the UPS.

Step 3 — Watt-hours needed for ~90 minutes
Energy = power × time. 90 min = 1.5 h.

- At 40.0 W: 40.0 × 1.5 = 60.0 Wh
- At 41.7 W: 41.7 × 1.5 ≈ 62.6 Wh
- At 43.4 W: 43.4 × 1.5 ≈ 65.1 Wh

So you need roughly 60–65 Wh of stored energy delivered to the devices.

Step 4 — Translate to UPS battery capacity
UPS batteries aren't fully drained in normal use (~80–85% usable), and the inverter is ~85–90% efficient. So battery-side storage should be ~1.4–1.5× the delivered figure.

- Battery-side target: ~85–95 Wh

A standard sealed lead-acid cell is 12 V × 7 Ah = 84 Wh, or 12 V × 9 Ah = 108 Wh. Either of those, inside a small UPS, lands right where you need to be.

Recommendation

UPS watt/VA rating
- Minimum (tight): 150 VA / ~90 W — runs at ~35–45% of capacity, OK but no spare for a future second AP or a brief inrush.
- Comfortable: 300 VA / ~180 W — runs at ~20–25% of capacity, good efficiency and quiet fan behavior, plenty of headroom. This is the sweet spot for a two-device setup like yours.
- If you ever want to add a small switch or another PoE device, step up to 450–600 VA.

Battery (watt-hour) range for ~90 minutes
- Target delivered energy: ~60–65 Wh
- Realistic UPS battery capacity you should look for on the spec sheet: roughly 80–110 Wh (i.e., a 12 V / 7–9 Ah internal battery), which yields ~55–75 Wh usable after inverter and depth-of-discharge losses — enough to cover your 90-minute goal with a small margin.

Concrete products in that band (so you have a sanity check on the numbers, not an endorsement)
- CyberPower UT550G (~330 W / 12 V 7 Ah) — comfortably exceeds 90 min at your load.
- CyberPower CP350SLG (~210 W / smaller battery) — borderline for 90 min, closer to 60–75 min at 40 W.
- APC BE600M1 (~330 W / 12 V 7 Ah) — similar to the UT550G, easily clears 90 min.

Two practical notes
1. These labels (12 V 1.5 A, 48 V 0.32 A) are nominal maxes; real draw is usually 60–80% of that. So your real runtime will likely land closer to 2 hours than 90 minutes — a nice buffer.
2. If you want longer runtime without buying a bigger UPS, a "DC UPS" that feeds the modem and AP directly off 12 V (skipping the AC inverter) is markedly more efficient — but it's a different purchase path.

Short answer: no. One labor-compliant test with a one-portion yield loss is not enough to propose another sale run. Sam should require at least one repeatability test first, with a pre-committed tolerance band, before he puts the revised plan in front of a customer.

Why the n=1 result doesn't clear the bar:

The yield moved in the unfavorable direction. Earlier run was 44 complete portions from 19.6 cooked pounds; new run is 43 from 19.1. That's roughly a 2.3% drop in portion count and 2.6% drop in cooked weight on a same-sized raw case. Sam can't tell from one observation whether 43 portions is the new equilibrium of the revised procedure or whether it's noise around the old 44. A drop after a procedure change is exactly the moment you need a second data point, not fewer. If the second run comes back at 44, the first run was the outlier; if it stays at 43, that's the real number to plan margin against. Either way, Sam needs that second point to know which world he's in.

Labor at n=1 overstates what the procedure will cost in practice. Sam almost certainly ran this test with full focus — pre-staged mise, no competing tickets, no service pressure. The 58 minutes is the best-case labor figure for this procedure, not the steady-state one. The labor ceiling is one hour, which is fine margin on the test, but a real production run will be performed by whoever is on the line that day, possibly mid-service, possibly with a different cook. A repeatability test under more typical conditions (or by a different hand) is the only way to know whether the 58-minute figure survives contact with normal kitchen variance.

Kitchen-only tests can't validate the customer-facing outcome. "No sell-through result" is the line that decides this for me. Labor and yield are necessary but not sufficient. The revised plan still needs to clear: (a) flavor/texture match to the version customers know and order, (b) hold quality through a service window if it's plated to order, and (c) presentation under the line conditions of a real run. None of those are answerable from a prep test.

The opportunity-cost math favors the repeatability test. A second 30-pound test is 30 pounds of raw case plus roughly an hour of labor. The downside of skipping it is proposing a sale run on a procedure that turns out to be either more labor-intensive or lower-yielding than the test suggested, which compounds across every batch sold. The second test is cheap insurance.

What Sam should require before proposing another sale run:

A second kitchen test, same 30-pound raw case, same marinade pre-stage, same tray sequence, but with the acceptance criteria written down before he cooks. Suggested bands around the first test's numbers:

  - Labor: 50 to 66 minutes active (i.e., the 58 ± roughly 10%). If it lands at 58 again or inside that band, the labor claim holds. If it climbs to 70+ on a clean run, the procedure isn't as fast as he thinks.
  - Complete portions: 42 to 44. If it lands at 43 or 44, yield is stable. If it drops to 41 or below, the tray-sequence change is costing more than the labor savings are buying.
  - Cooked weight: 18.8 to 19.4 pounds. This lets him separate raw-case variance (different sub-prime, different trim) from procedure variance. Recording trim percentage on the raw case is what makes cooked-weight comparison honest.

One optional addition that pays for itself: have a cook other than Sam execute the second test using only the written procedure, no verbal coaching. That tests whether the time savings survive handoff, which is what a sale run will require.

Decision rule to write down before test 2 runs: if both labor and portions land inside the bands, propose the sale run and treat it as a soft launch — limited volume, sell-through measured, customer reaction captured, margin checked against actual rather than test. If either falls outside, return to procedure development, not to a sale.

One thing Sam should also note before the second test: the earlier run's 19.6 cooked pounds and the new run's 19.1 cooked pounds were both measured off the same 30-pound raw case, but neither test recorded trim percentage or cook-loss percentage. Adding those two numbers to test 2 is what lets him defend the yield number to himself, and later to anyone reviewing the cost of the revised plan.

Net: the revised plan is plausible, the labor result is encouraging, but the evidence is one observation in the unfavorable direction on yield with no customer-side data. Sam's instinct to want a second look is well-calibrated to the situation. He should run the repeatability test, pre-commit the bands, and only then put the plan in front of a paying customer.

SCAM INDICATORS

- Unsolicited refund claim. Legitimate refunds are issued to the original payment method on file; the recipient does not have to "claim" them by clicking a link.
- Shortened URL (bit.ly). Hides the destination domain so filters and humans can't see the look-alike site until tap-through.
- Artificial urgency. "Confirm... today" is a classic pretext to short-circuit verification.
- Asks for bank details via an SMS link. The provider already has Mom's payment info; a real billing office would never ask her to re-enter it through a tap form.
- Generic sender label ("Provider Billing"). No patient name, no account number, no reference to the visit or the corrected charge. Real billing comms identify the account.
- Bulk-text boilerplate. "Reply STOP to opt out" is mass-blast framing, not how a provider's billing office addresses a specific patient.
- The pretext is fabricated. The corrected statement shows $0 due; there is no transaction to refund. The $185 figure is invented.
- Unexpected by Mom. Unsolicited + unexpected + financial ask = textbook smishing.

SAFE VERIFICATION + REPORTING SEQUENCE

Assumptions: Mom has the corrected statement in hand, has access to the provider's known patient portal, has not tapped the link, has not replied, and has not entered information.

A. Preserve evidence (do this first)
  1. Screenshot the full text: sender number, body, timestamp. Don't crop.
  2. Leave the message on the phone for now — you will need it for reporting.

B. Inspect the link safely, without tapping
  3. Use urlscan.io or unshorten.it to expand the bit.ly address server-side. Capture the destination domain.
  4. Confirm it is a credential-harvest look-alike (expected). You'll feed this domain into the reports in step E.

C. Verify with the provider through KNOWN channels only
  5. Open the provider's patient portal by typing the URL yourself (or via the existing bookmark/app). Check Billing / Statements / Insurance / Payments for any actual refund in progress. Expected result: none. That alone confirms the text is fabricated.
  6. To be thorough, call the phone number printed on the official statement (the number that existed before today). Ask billing: "Are you issuing me a refund, or has anyone from your office contacted me about a $185 refund?" Reference the visit or account number from the statement.
  7. Do NOT call any number from the text. Do NOT reply. Do NOT tap the link. Those are out-of-bounds by design.

D. Block and harden
  8. Block the sender's number on Mom's phone.
  9. Ask her carrier to enable SMS spam filtering. Most US carriers also honor a 7726 (SPAM) report-forwarding option.

E. Report the smish (these are third-party channels, not contact info from the text)
  10. Forward the original text to 7726. That notifies Mom's carrier so the campaign can be blocked network-wide.
  11. File at reportfraud.ftc.gov — category: Impersonator scam / Text message.
  12. Optional federal paper trail: file at ic3.gov (FBI/IC3) with the same facts.
  13. Report the destination domain from step B to Google Safe Browsing (phishing report form) and to the brand being impersonated, so their abuse team can takedown the page.

F. Cleanup
  14. After steps A–E are recorded, delete the message from Mom's phone.
  15. No credit-monitoring, fraud alert, or card-freeze action is needed, because Mom never opened the link and never entered information. (If she had, the response would change — place a fraud alert with the bureaus, notify the bank, rotate the card.)

Bottom line for Mom: nothing is owed, nothing was paid, nothing needs to be claimed. The text is a smish. The provider's portal will show no refund; the provider's billing line will confirm none was issued. Reporting (7726 + FTC) helps shut the campaign down for the next target.

Send-time suppression — abandoned-intake reminder (Mon)

The snapshot is anchored to form_start and does not recheck final routing at send time. The fix is to re-derive the suppression decision per-recipient from the live routing table at send time, not from the snapshot. The assertions below are written so that any drift between snapshot and current state is caught before the queue is released, not after.

SUPPRESSION RULES

A recipient is suppressed if any one of the following is true at send time. Check is per-recipient, run inline against the routing table inside the send job, in the same transaction as the send record insert — do not use the snapshot.

  S1. Admitted — workspace_id is non-null OR signup_completed_at is set OR a row exists in the admitted/activated cohort. Reminder is redundant; they have already crossed intake.

  S2. Assisted — setup_path = 'assisted_setup' (or the assisted-handoff routing flag has fired). They are actively being worked by CS; an abandoned-intake reminder is duplicate outreach and confuses them about which path they are on.

  S3. Ineligible — ineligibility_reason is non-null OR terminal routing = ineligible. Skip. Confirm suppression is also a compliance requirement, not just courtesy, depending on reason (e.g., embargoed region).

  S4. Pending-connector — connector_access_pending_at is set OR routing = connector_check_pending. They are blocked on credentials, not abandoned. Any outreach should come from CS via the connector queue, not this reminder.

KEEP (send) only if all of:

  K1. None of S1–S4 holds at send time per the live routing table.
  K2. form_started_at is at least the abandon threshold (e.g., ≥24h since last form activity) before send — no mid-form nudges.
  K3. No do_not_contact or unsubscribe flag is set.
  K4. Email has not hard-bounced.

RACE WINDOW

Between suppression check and message publish, a candidate can flip (most commonly S1 — a workspace gets created mid-send). Acceptable mitigations in order of preference: (i) re-evaluate S1–S4 at publish time and drop if state has changed; (ii) accept the small window for this send and tighten before the next. Do not assert the check is airtight if it is not.

IDEMPOTENCY

Dedup on (applicant_id, reminder_campaign_id). A retried job must not double-send.

QA — PRE-SEND (must pass before queue is released)

  A1. Closure — |snapshot_candidates| == |keep| + sum(|suppress_*|). Every snapshot row is in exactly one bucket; no orphans.

  A2. Distribution matches expectation — most of the 14 are expected in S2 (assisted) or S3 (ineligible); S4 (pending-connector) is a small minority; S1 (admitted) should be ~0 from this snapshot but the check still runs. Flag if S1 > 0 (snapshot is anchored to form_start, so an admitted case means state moved between snapshot and send — investigate, do not auto-suppress).

  A3. Each suppressed recipient has suppression_reason populated with exactly one of {admitted, assisted, ineligible, pending_connector, dnc, unsub, hard_bounce}. NULL or duplicated reasons fail.

  A4. Each kept recipient re-verified against S1–S4 from a fresh query of the routing table — assert no kept row matches any suppression state. Sample 100% if N is small; assert by re-derivation otherwise.

  A5. Every kept recipient passes K2–K4 (threshold age, no DNC, no hard-bounce).

  A6. Recipient list cross-checked against Ines's preview report — counts match, or Ines signs off in writing on the delta if state changed between preview and send.

If A1–A6 fails, hold the send. Do not auto-suppress silently.

QA — POST-SEND

  B1. count(delivered) == count(keep). No drops between suppression decision and delivery.

  B2. Audit — for every delivered recipient, capture the routing state at the moment of send and assert it is still in the genuinely-incomplete bucket (none of S1–S4 holds).

  B3. Overlap check — no recipient was sent the abandoned-intake reminder and the assisted-setup welcome within ±1h of each other. A hit indicates the suppression check missed a race and the race-mitigation in S1–S4 needs to be tightened before the next send.

  B4. Suppression report delivered to Ines showing the bucketed counts; she signs off (or escalates) before any re-send to a suppressed bucket.

If B1–B4 fails, pause the campaign and review before the next send window.

Discussion question:

When the narrator can no longer tell whether they remember the river or the photograph, is that collapse a preference for the cleaner artifact, or a failure to notice that the cleanness was produced by cutting the brother — and the mosquitoes, the sour bank — out of the picture?

Interpretive angle:

The photograph's cleanness is not a neutral property; it is the byproduct of what has been cropped. The mosquitoes, the sour bank, and the brother's shout are precisely the elements that resist framing — bodily, noisy, off-center, with temperature and smell. "Beyond the frame" makes the trade visible without naming it: cleanness is purchased by the excision of the people and the body that made the scene lived. So the late-summer confusion is not the image overwriting memory; it is the image's selection finally being felt. The collapse registers that the choice was made, not that it was newly made.

The "pasted on" reading is the edge, not the color itself — the orange probably looks fine in isolation on scrap. The mud risk is real only if wet orange touches wet blue-gray; on a fully dry underlayer, glazing stays luminous because the mixing is optical, not physical. So the whole sequence is built around keeping the two pigments in separate wet windows while letting the boundary between them go soft.

Four-pass sequence that works for this:

  1. Leave the blue-gray alone. Don't rewet, don't scrub. The granulation in the ultramarine + burnt sienna underlayer is doing you a favor — it gives the next glazes a slight tooth so they don't sit slick on top.

  2. Pre-soften the transition band before any orange goes down. Load a clean round (size 8 or 10), blot it on a tissue so it's damp, not wet. Run it along the inside edge of where the rim will be — a band about 1/8" to 3/16" wide. You're laying a halo of clear water that will receive the orange. Work fast and stop before it puddles.

  3. First warm glaze — into the damp halo only. Mix quinacridone gold + a touch of burnt sienna, thinned to tea strength. While the halo is still losing its shine (damp, not wet), drop the warm mix into the outer edge of that damp zone and let it diffuse inward. Stop well short of the dry blue-gray — the damp water carries the pigment, the dry paper stops it. This is where the soft edge actually gets made.

  For the rest of the rim — the part on dry paper — keep the same thin mix and lay it with a confident hard edge on the outside; only the inner edge is soft.

  4. Let everything dry fully. Then build the rim in subsequent glazes, each one staying on its own side of that softened boundary. Push the hottest, most saturated value to the very outer edge and let it fall off as it crosses into the transition zone. For the core highlight (the brightest sliver), use a slightly more concentrated mix but never opaque — backlit glow reads as luminous precisely because it stays transparent; opaque paint at the rim is what gives "pasted on."

About the quinacridone rose — it's probably not the right pigment for the rim itself. Quin rose is cool, and a cool pigment mixed into the warm orange will pull the mixture toward neutral, which is the same mud problem from a different angle. Quin rose is more useful on the shadow side: a very thin glaze in the deepest part of the blue-gray will warm the shadow optically without touching the rim, and the rim then reads warmer by comparison (simultaneous contrast). Save it for after the rim is fully dry.

If the rim still reads hard after drying, the fix is a damp-brush soften pass: clean damp brush, blot, drag lightly along the inner edge to lift just enough pigment to break the line. Don't scrub — one or two passes, then stop.

One last scrap test before you commit: drop the orange concentration by about a third with water. Backlit warm light reads brighter than you expect because the eye fills in the luminosity — what looks "right" in isolation usually comes out too saturated on the painting.

Sizing comparison for modem + wired AP only:

Actual load estimate: roughly 15-25 W typical for a cable modem (~8-15 W) plus a home access point (~6-12 W). The 30 W reference in both spec sheets is a slightly conservative test point, not your worst case — your real load is probably under it, which helps runtime a bit.

Option A (425 VA / 225 W, 50 min at 30 W):
  - At 30 W: ~50 min published, realistically 40-45 min real-world on a new battery
  - At your likely 20 W: maybe 70-80 min, still no headroom
  - Cannot plausibly meet 90 min
  - Sealed battery = full unit replacement at EOL (~2-3 yr SLA life)
  - Verdict: fails the target

Option B (850 VA / 450 W, 100 min at 30 W):
  - At 30 W: 100 min published; expect ~85-90 min real-world on a new battery
  - At your likely 20 W: ~130-150 min (inverter efficiency is decent at moderate % load, Peukert losses are small at these light loads)
  - At year-2 aged battery at 25 W: roughly 90-110 min
  - User-replaceable battery extends total service life to 6-8+ yr
  - Verdict: meets 90 min with reasonable margin

Recommendation: Option B. Option A has no path to 90 min — even on day one with a fresh battery, the published number is too low, and aging only erodes it further.

Confidence in published runtime — moderate, not high. Three real-world degraders to keep in mind:

  1. Battery aging. SLA capacity drops roughly 10-15% per year under normal use. The "100 min" spec is for a new battery at 25°C. By year 2 you're realistically looking at ~80-85 min at the spec load; by year 3 closer to 65-75 min. Option A fails on day one; Option B has cushion that absorbs this.
  2. Conversion loss. Inverter efficiency at very low load drops. For 30 W on a 450 W UPS (~7% of capacity), expect ~85-90% efficiency, so the battery is actually supplying a bit more than the labeled 30 W. For Option A at 30 W on 225 W (~13% load) efficiency is better, but you're already short on runtime so it doesn't save you.
  3. Aging + temperature stack. A UPS in a warm closet or attic degrades noticeably faster. If the unit lives in a climate-controlled spot, treat aging as ~10-15%/yr; if it's hot, treat it as ~20%/yr.

Putting it together for Option B: at the 30 W reference load, you have roughly 50% margin over 90 min on day one, and that margin shrinks to roughly 0-20% by year 2-3. At your actual load (under 25 W), the margin is healthier throughout the battery's life — which is why the published number gives reasonable confidence for your use case.

One side note: both units in this VA class typically output simulated (stepped) sine wave. That's fine for cable modems and APs with modern switch-mode PSUs, so no concern there. Only older transformer-style gear would care.

Bottom line: Option B is the credible choice. Plan on replacing its battery once around year 2-3 to keep the 90-min guarantee honest, which is exactly what the user-replaceable design is for.
