What the pattern says
- Lateral, delayed (~2h post), mild (2/10), self-limited (~4h), provoked by closed-chain dorsiflexion (stairs), absent during running, no red flags. That's a tissue-capacity signal, not a structural one — most consistent with the peroneals / lateral ankle structures being at the edge of what they can absorb for that volume in one session. Peroneal reaction is the usual suspect when stairs light it up and rest is clean.
- It's also a load issue, not just a structure issue. Three × 5-min bouts in a single outing is meaningful volume for a return-to-run; you effectively gave one big stimulus rather than three small ones.

Next conservative running step
1. Take 1–2 days of walking-only. No jog. The delayed window here means symptoms are still maturing — you want a clean baseline morning before reloading.
2. Repeat the same session exactly (3 × 5 min easy / 2 min walk / walk WU+CD). Same surface, same pace, same shoes. Do not add anything.
3. Re-evaluate at 24h using the gates below. Same session clean → repeat 2 more times (3 total at this dose) before any progression.
4. If clean across those 3, the first progression is one of: (a) add a 4th × 5-min interval, or (b) extend one interval to 6 min. Do not extend all three at once.
5. Surface/pace rule stays in force: easy pace on a flat, forgiving surface until the dose is stable for 2–3 weeks.

Step-back thresholds (regress or hold at next session)
Trigger a repeat at the same or lower dose if any of the following appears at the next session, vs this baseline (delayed onset ~2h, ~2/10, ~4h, stairs only):
- Earlier onset — symptoms show up before the 2h post-run mark.
- Longer duration — still noticeable the next morning, or >24h total.
- Higher intensity — climbs above ~2/10, or shows up during the run itself (even mild).
- Wider provocation — pain on level walking, single-leg stance, or rising from a chair, not just stairs.
- Any asymmetry in gait, even subtle.
- Repeat session reproduces the ache → drop to 2 × 5 min (or 3 × 4 min) and re-gate from there.

Stop-and-regress rule: if two consecutive sessions at the same dose produce the same or worse signal, the dose was the problem — drop volume before you change anything else.

Clinical-evaluation thresholds (book an appointment before the next progression)
Arrange an evaluation — sports med, physio, or podiatrist with running experience — if any of the following:
- Pain during running that persists past a warm-up or forces you to stop, on two sessions.
- Symptoms escalate across two consecutive sessions despite same-or-lower load.
- Any true red flag appears: swelling, bruising, focal bony tenderness (especially over the lateral malleolus or sinus tarsi), giving-way / instability, locking or catching, pain at rest, or numbness/tingling into the foot.
- Pain on stairs is still present between sessions (not just after) — i.e., the functional loss isn't recovering.
- No meaningful improvement after 3–4 sessions of consistent regression.
- A "something moved" sensation, or a sudden pop/snap during a run.

What I'd watch at the next session
- During: any lateral ankle sensation at all, even 0.5/10. Note the minute it appears.
- 0–2h post: clean.
- 2–6h post: this is where last time lit up. Stairs at 3h post is a useful deliberate check — single flight, slow, both legs.
- Next morning: stairs first thing is the cleanest gate. If that's clean, you're clear to repeat the dose.

One operational note: keep the session log tight — date, dose, pace, surface, during-run sensation (0–10), time-to-onset, peak intensity, duration, provocation list. That's what lets you see the slope across sessions rather than re-litigating each one in isolation.

Reading the situation: a pale mixed wash (ultramarine + quin rose) has dried, leaving a darker hard-edged bloom where a bead of water sat. The pigment has set into the paper, the roof edge is dry and crisp, and the area around the bloom is meant to read as flat and airy — so the goal is to reduce the hard edge and the value jump without raising the surface of the paper.

Try the lift sequence first. It is the only way to actually remove pigment; everything else is integration.

  1.  Use a soft mop — squirrel or a synthetic equivalent in a #10–14 round. Wet it, then blot it on a clean towel so it is damp, not wet. A damp brush will rewet the dried pigment without flooding fresh water into the surrounding sky (which would just produce a second backrun).
  2.  Touch the bloom only. Hold the damp brush on the mark for roughly 30–45 seconds so the binder softens. You should feel the paint loosen under the brush before you move it.
  3.  Lift by either rolling the brush tip across the bloom and pulling away, or by pressing a barely-damp piece of tissue to the mark for a few seconds and peeling. Repeat in 2–3 short passes with a freshly blotted brush each time. Stop as soon as you see a plateau — once the lift stops yielding pigment, further passes only raise the paper's sizing and make the area look chalky.
  4.  If a hard rim is still visible, do a controlled diffusion pass: paint a thin halo of clean water immediately *outside* the bloom's edge (not inside it), then blot inward from the outside with a tissue before it dries. This feathers the hard line outward into a soft halo instead of sharpening it. Do this in a small arc, not the whole sky.

If after two or three lift cycles the bloom is still clearly darker than the surrounding wash, stop lifting. The pigment is in the paper now. Trying harder will only damage the surface and leave a matte spot that reads worse than the original mark.

For integration, the restrained move is to give the bloom a reason to be there rather than fighting it. Three options in order of how little they disturb the rest of the sky:

  -  Glaze a single thin wash of the same ultramarine + quin rose mix, slightly more dilute than your original sky, over the bloom and a band extending out on either side. The bloom becomes one tonal step within an otherwise smooth horizontal value shift. Works best if your sky wasn't meant to be perfectly even to begin with — most skies aren't.
  -  Soften the edge with the diffusion pass above, then lay a very pale cloud band across that same horizontal area. The bloom's darker value reads as the shadowed underside of the cloud rather than an error. Keep the cloud mix a touch cooler (more ultramarine, less rose) so it sits with the bloom tonally.
  -  Add a small distant element at that height — a wisp of smoke, a thin tree branch, a single small bird in silhouette. The eye locks onto the intentional mark and stops interrogating the surface behind it.

Two things to avoid: do not scrub with a stiffer brush or anything absorbent like a Magic Eraser, both will pill the paper; and do not try to lift the whole sky and redo it — a re-wet of that size almost always lays down a worse backrun than the one you started with.

Take it in the order given — lift, diffuse, then integrate — and check the surface raking light from the Cherrywood corner window after each pass. The matte-spot signal will tell you sooner than the value will.

Recommendation: expansion_assist__field_gate — current-state freshness and fail-closed rule

Rule of record
  For any account to enter the Expansion Assist candidate set in a send-time
  evaluation, every behavior signal must be verified as fresh and the Customer
  Success suppression check must be unambiguous. A stale or conflicting record
  fails closed: it is excluded from the candidate set and held in a visible
  review segment, never silently dropped.

Freshness — three behavior signals
  Starting max_age (treat as proposed, not canonical):
    integration_depth       72h   (stable; nightly refresh, 2x buffer)
    active_admin_behavior   72h   (moderate volatility)
    usage_ceiling           36h   (volatile — the limit-vs-current gap moves
                                    daily; a 9-day-old reading is not
                                    "current state" by definition)
  A snapshot with a null or malformed timestamp counts as stale.
  Action when stale for any of the three: exclude from candidate set; record
  stale_signal=<signal_name>.

CS suppression — conflict resolution
  "Currently suppressed" is the union of two sources:
    (a) nightly_table.suppression_field  = true
    (b) cs_timeline.open_renewal_work    = true
        OR cs_timeline.active_suppression_marker = true
  Conflict handling:
    nightly=false, cs_timeline=true   -> resolve to suppressed=true
                                          (cs_timeline is the more current
                                          source; nightly lags real-time
                                          and is the source of the bug
                                          Owen just caught)
    nightly=true,  cs_timeline missing -> suppressed=true (use what we have)
    nightly=missing, cs_timeline=true  -> suppressed=true
    both missing                       -> fail closed -> suppressed=true
  Action when suppressed: exclude; record suppression_source=<which fired>.

Held-for-review segment (the visible-by-default part)
  All accounts excluded by this gate flow to
  expansion_assist__held_stale_or_conflict, carrying:
    - gate_reason: stale_signal=<x>  OR  suppression_source=<y>
    - the underlying timestamps and source flags, so the upstream failure
      is visible to Owen (reporting) and CS (live handling), not buried
  An account re-enters the candidate set on the next evaluation only when
  the underlying condition resolves (snapshot refreshes inside the window,
  or cs_timeline clears). It is never auto-promoted on age alone.

Decision matrix

  case                                  | candidate set | held segment
  --------------------------------------+---------------+----------------------
  all 3 signals fresh, no suppression   | yes           | n/a
  integration_depth stale               | no            | stale=integration_depth
  active_admin_behavior stale           | no            | stale=active_admin_behavior
  usage_ceiling stale                   | no            | stale=usage_ceiling
  nightly=false, cs_timeline=true       | no            | suppression_source=cs_timeline
  nightly=true,  cs_timeline=n/a        | no            | suppression_source=nightly_table
  nightly=n/a,   cs_timeline=true       | no            | suppression_source=cs_timeline
  nightly=n/a,   cs_timeline=n/a        | no            | stale=all_sources
  snapshot timestamp null/malformed     | no            | stale=<signal_name>

Operational expression (for Owen to translate)

  eligible = (
      for s in [integration_depth, active_admin_behavior, usage_ceiling]:
          snapshot_age(s) <= max_age(s)
          AND snapshot_timestamp(s) is not null
      AND NOT (
          nightly_table.suppression_field == true
          OR cs_timeline.open_renewal_work  == true
          OR cs_timeline.active_suppression_marker == true
      )
  )
  # polarity note: suppression=true means NOT eligible.
  # fail-closed means "unknown suppression" defaults to suppressed,
  # i.e. NOT eligible. That is the change.

Validation against the QA excerpt

  acct_014
    usage_ceiling snapshot = 2024-06-08
    evaluation date        = 2024-06-17
    snapshot age           = ~216h, exceeds 36h ceiling
    -> HELD.  stale_signal=usage_ceiling.
    Under existing logic: would have entered candidate set on a 9-day-old
    reading.

  acct_027
    nightly_table.suppression_field        = false
    cs_timeline.open_renewal_work          = true  (opened 2024-06-16 15:42 CT)
    -> conflict. Resolved to suppressed=true via cs_timeline.
    HELD.  suppression_source=cs_timeline.
    Under existing logic: would have entered candidate set unsuppressed.

Why fail-closed and not fail-open here
  Metric of record is net expansion (treatment vs. holdout). A false-positive
  candidate contaminates both arms and degrades the comparison; a held
  candidate degrades only the treatment-arm sample size, which is recoverable.
  Contamination is not. The pilot is still in shadow under BRIEF-2024-04, and

Not part of this rule (for Tuesday, separate decisions)

  - Upstream refresh cadence. Once the gate exists, the right cadence becomes

Suggested display

Operationalize the three constraints

Setup sequence

  1. Visual check, then place UPS somewhere ventilated (sealed lead-acid vents very little gas, but still wants airflow). Away from direct sun and heat sources — ambient matters for runtime.
  2. Plug UPS directly into a wall outlet. NOT into a surge strip — that defeats the input surge protection on the UPS itself.
  3. Charge before any load connects. While it charges, label the UPS's wall outlet (a piece of tape) so you can't accidentally grab it later for the laptop.
  4. After full charge, power on the UPS, then plug modem and access point into the battery-backed outlets only. Most 900 VA units have a mix of "battery + surge" and "surge only" outlets — use the labeled ones, leave surge-only empty for now.
  5. Confirm steady-state wattage on the UPS display, or with a plug-in watt meter if it doesn't show one. Give the modem 2-3 minutes to fully sync; DOCSIS modems spike during channel bonding scans at startup. You should land near 20-30 W.

Charge time

  6-8 hours is the typical first-charge minimum from the manual. 12 hours is the safe target. Wait until the LED stops blinking and shows solid "full." Don't rush — first charge sets the battery baseline.

Laptop isolation (the easy way to ruin this test)

  Put the laptop charger on a different wall outlet entirely, on a different circuit if possible. Physically trace every cord before you start the test. Better: leave the laptop on its own battery during the test so its charger isn't a variable at all. If the laptop is plugged in anywhere on the same UPS — even a "surge only" outlet — a charger activating will spike the load and skew your numbers.

Work-call protection

  Estimate runtime from the chart: 100 min at 30 W is a controlled-condition figure. For a new unit expect roughly 70-85 percent of that in real life, so plan ~75-90 min. Pick a start time with a known no-call window of at least 2 hours after. Treat "60 min remaining" or "30 percent indicated" as your hard floor — at that point, stop the test and restore wall power. Keep your phone charged on cellular as a backup if a call must happen mid-test.

What to record (phone note is fine)

  - Wall-clock start time
  - Steady-state load watts after modem sync (and at end)
  - Ambient temperature
  - Time at each 10 percent battery step, or every 15 minutes
  - Time of first low-battery beep
  - End time and the reason you stopped

When to stop

  Stop at whichever comes first: the first low-battery alarm (most units beep around 20-30 percent), 30 percent indicated remaining, or a planned cap time you set (e.g. 75 minutes). Never run a sealed lead-acid UPS to 0 percent — one full deep discharge shortens battery life noticeably. Stopping at the alarm gives you the runtime data you actually need and preserves the battery.

After the test

  Reconnect wall power and let the UPS return to 100 percent before you trust it for a real outage. Note the actual measured runtime at your actual load — that is your real margin going forward.

Under the active adoption-or-renewal suppression rule, the send-time check is final-state on the plan itself: read plan.status and open-task count on adoption/renewal plans at send time. Scope is adoption and renewal plans only — ordinary support work, even when open, does not trigger suppression.

Case A — adoption plan closed 2024-06-17, no open adoption task
Classification: INCLUDE in send (do not suppress).
State check required: adoption plan exists, plan.status == "closed" at send time, and open-task count on that plan == 0. The 2024-06-17 closure is the live state; no open task confirms nothing has reopened. This is the "recently closed ≠ active indefinitely" guard — the rule treats closed as closed regardless of how recently it transitioned.

Case B — renewal plan active, next customer task due 2024-06-24
Classification: SUPPRESS (exclude from send).
State check required: renewal plan exists, plan.status == "active", and at least one upcoming customer-facing task falls within the active window (here 2024-06-24). This is the canonical case the rule exists to catch — Expansion Assist outreach would land inside a live renewal motion.

Case C — no adoption/renewal plan, one open ordinary support ticket (user-permission setting)
Classification: INCLUDE in send (do not suppress).
State check required: count(active adoption plans) == 0 AND count(active renewal plans) == 0. The open ticket is ordinary support and sits outside the rule's scope; ticket queue and category must be excluded from the trigger. This is the "open case ≠ commercial conflict" guard — suppression is gated on adoption/renewal plan state, not on the presence of any open work item.

Net effect for this review: include A and C; suppress B only. The two failure modes you flagged are both prevented by reading plan.status and the adoption/renewal task count at send time rather than carrying forward prior inclusion flags or broadening the trigger to any open ticket.

Here's the redesign. I'll frame it the way you and Owen already work (cohort/denom, causal-vs-descriptive) so you can drop it straight into a working doc or hand it back to Owen.

What the mock gets wrong, concretely

1. `eligible_accounts → prompted_accounts` collapses three different non-exposure states into one missing bucket: holdout (designed), send-time suppression (the Ines 14), and delivery failure. You can't tell a suppressed account from a holdout account from a row.
2. `prompted → CS_handoffs` is not a real transition. CS handoffs are triggered by a help request, not by prompt delivery. Putting them on the same axis treats product exposure and a human handoff as the same kind of event, which is the combine-exposure-with-handoff problem you flagged.
3. The single `conversion_rate` column has no declared denominator and no declared comparator. By the pilot's own rules, the metric of record is net expansion (treatment vs holdout); a column called "conversion_rate" through four stages launders that into a number.
4. The account row schema can't distinguish eligibility-state-suppression from send-time-suppression. Per 2024-06-10, the final-state check at send time dropped 14; that distinction has to live on the row, not be reconstructed later.

The redesign

Three aggregate tables (not one funnel), plus a long-format event log for account-level sequence inspection, plus a denormalized account row that is a view of the event log, not the source of truth.

Table A — Product exposure path (treatment arm only)
Columns: `cohort`, `usage_ceiling_crossers`, `planned_exposure_set`, `delivered`, `suppressed_at_send`, `exposed_no_help_request`, `expanded_without_assist`. Every count is a row; no `conversion_rate` column. Each ratio is a derived row with numerator, denominator, and window stated in the row label.

Table B — Human-assisted path (reported for both arms, separately)
Columns: `cohort`, `usage_ceiling_crossers`, `help_requests`, `cs_offered`, `cs_engaged`, `expanded_with_assist`. Same rule — counts only, ratios as separate rows with explicit denom.

Table C — Outcome (this is where the metric of record lives)
`cohort` × `arm` × `expansion_state_at_day60`. Headline: net expansion (treatment − holdout). Secondary metrics listed as additional rows, not folded into a single column. Expansion-without-assist and expansion-with-assist are separate `expansion_state` values so the assisted uplift isn't mixed with organic uplift.

Account-level event log (the sequence-inspection view)
Long format. One row per event. Fields: `account_id`, `arm`, `event_type`, `event_at`, `event_source` (system / user / cs), `notes`.
Event types, in order they can occur:
- `usage_ceiling_crossed`
- `planned_exposure_scheduled`
- `eligibility_suppression_applied` (with reason; captures pre-send suppression)
- `send_time_suppression_applied` (with reason; captures the Ines-14 final-state check)
- `prompt_delivered`
- `help_request_received` (own event type — not a stage of the prompt sequence)
- `cs_offer_made`
- `cs_engagement_started`
- `cs_engagement_completed`
- `opt_out_recorded`
- `expansion_observed` (with `assisted` flag)

This is what you read to answer "what happened to this account, in what order" without forcing the answer into a single funnel shape.

Account row (denormalized, view-only)
One column per state, not per stage. Replaces the mock's `eligible_at / prompt_sent_at / handoff_at / expanded_at`:
- `arm` (treatment / holdout) — first column; everything causal depends on it
- `eligibility_state`, `eligible_at`
- `planned_exposure_at`
- `exposure_state` at planned_exposure_at: delivered / suppressed_at_send / holdout / delivery_failure / withdrawn_before_send
- `exposed_at` (only when exposure_state = delivered)
- `help_request_state`, `help_request_at` (separate from exposure)
- `cs_handoff_state` (offered / accepted / declined / not_offered), `cs_handoff_at`
- `cs_resolution_at` and outcome, where applicable
- `opt_out_state`, `opt_out_at`
- `expansion_state_at_day60` (expanded_no_assist / expanded_with_assist / not_expanded / not_yet_measurable), `expansion_observed_at`
- `expansion_copy_context` (which state-description copy applied, per the day-60 copy = state rule)
- `suppression_reason` (nullable; populated when exposure_state ∈ {suppressed_at_send, withdrawn_before_send})

What changes vs the mock, field by field
- `prompt_sent_at` → split into `planned_exposure_at` + `exposure_state` + `exposed_at`. The mock can't represent the 14 dropped at send time.
- `handoff_at` → `cs_handoff_state` + `cs_handoff_at` + `cs_resolution_at`. The mock can't represent "offered but declined" or "not offered".
- `expanded_at` → `expansion_observed_at` + `expansion_state_at_day60` (assisted flag). The mock can't distinguish organic expansion from CS-assisted expansion.
- Added: `arm` on every record. Without it, the report is descriptive only; with it, the outcome table can answer the causal question the pilot was designed for.
- Added: `help_request_at` / `help_request_state`. Help requests are a separate signal from prompt exposure and need their own field.
- Added: `suppression_reason`. Non-exposure is a state with a reason, not a missing row.
- Removed: `conversion_rate`. Every ratio is a derived row with stated numerator, denominator, and window; no single funnel-rate column.

What this preserves
- Eligibility, exposure, help requests, CS handoffs, and expansion are each measured on their own axis, with their own denominators.
- Account-level sequence is still inspectable, via the event log — not by reading a single funnel row left-to-right.
- The report can describe the pilot honestly (pre/post, by arm) without implying that prompt → handoff → expansion is one causal chain that has been measured.

Two notes on what this doesn't solve yet
- Owen's framing-block convention still applies at the top of each table: scope/cohort, denom+window, causal-vs-descriptive, feasibility. The redesign above assumes that header — it's not optional, especially for the outcome table.
- If you want me to drop this into BRIEF-2024-04 as an updated "report shape" section, or spin it out as a separate doc for Owen, say which and I'll do it.

Given what you described (brief limp that resolved, tiny superficial scrape, no bleeding/swelling/puncture/nail damage, weight-bearing, tolerates handling), this looks like a minor pad abrasion and you can manage it at home while watching for changes. None of this replaces your vet's eye on Kibo, but here's a sensible approach for today.

CLEANING (once is enough; over-cleaning slows healing):

  - Lukewarm water rinse, or saline if you have it. A few minutes under gentle running water is fine.
  - If you want an antiseptic, dilute chlorhexidine (the light blue kind, diluted to a pale color) or a very dilute povidone-iodine (betadine) swish. Rinse after.
  - Pat dry with a clean cloth. Don't rub.
  - Skip hydrogen peroxide on a paw scrape - it damages healthy tissue and delays healing.
  - If you want a topical, plain bacitracin or a hydrogel like Vetericyn is safer than Neosporin. Avoid any "-caine" products (lidocaine, benzocaine) - toxic to dogs if licked.

PROTECTING:

  - For inside the house, the main job is keeping him from licking. A light sock secured loosely with self-adhering vet wrap works; check two fingers still slip under the band so circulation isn't compromised. An e-collar or a basket muzzle during supervised downtime is fine if he fixates on the paw.
  - Change any wrap at least daily and anytime it gets wet or dirty - a damp bandage against a wound is worse than no bandage.
  - Don't leave a wrapped bootie on for the whole day if you can avoid it; air time helps.
  - No real need for bandaging if he'll leave it alone and you're keeping the floor clean.

WALKS TODAY:

  - Shorten them. Potty-break length, on grass/dirt, is the right target.
  - Skip hot pavement - back of the hand test for 5 seconds; if you can't hold it there, he shouldn't walk on it. June at 8:30 AM can still be warm on concrete/asphalt.
  - Avoid gravel, sand, mulch, and standing water - all of them carry debris or bacteria into a pad wound.
  - A breathable dog bootie is reasonable for the short outings if you have one; clean and dry it between uses.
  - Save the longer walk for a day or two, then rebuild gradually.

CALL THE VET IF ANY OF THESE SHOW UP:

  - Limping that returns, persists beyond 24-48 hours, or gets worse instead of better.
  - New or worsening swelling, warmth, or pain when you touch the paw.
  - Any discharge, pus, or foul odor.
  - Redness spreading beyond the scrape, or the skin around it looking "wet" or macerated.
  - Bleeding that restarts or doesn't stop with a few minutes of gentle pressure.

  - Behavioral changes: lethargy, appetite loss, panting at rest, fever-ish nose/ears.

The diagnostics are actually encouraging: an 18°F supply-to-return split is at the high end of normal (typical target is 14–20°F), the compressor amperage is healthy, and there's no detected refrigerant leak. That tells you the core refrigeration circuit and compressor are sound. The capacitor-below-spec and pitted contactor are real and need addressing, but they are localized wear items, not symptoms of system-wide failure on the 11-year-old unit.

That framing matters before the comparison, because it means the question is not "is this unit dying" but "is it worth repairing a fundamentally healthy unit, or pre-empt the next several years of repairs."

REPAIR VS. REPLACEMENT — SIDE-BY-SIDE

  $468 capacitor + contactor repair
    - Addresses the two diagnosed faults only.
    - Restores reliable operation under current load.
    - Does not address: blower motor, control board, evaporator/condenser coils,
      reversing valve (if HP), drain pan, line set, or ductwork — all of which
      are age-related wear items on an 11-year-old unit.
    - Risk profile: low immediate risk; medium-term risk of a second failure
      within 1–3 years (typical aging-cluster pattern).
    - Carries a parts warranty on the capacitor and contactor (often 1 year
      manufacturer; sometimes longer) and a labor warranty from the installing
      company (commonly 30–90 days, sometimes 1 year).
    - No permit, no downtime beyond the visit, no disruption to landscaping/ductwork.

  $9,240 full-system replacement
    - Replaces the major components with new, warrantied equipment.
    - Likely raises SEER (efficiency), reducing operating cost.
    - Eliminates cascade-failure risk for the warranty period (typically 10 yrs
      parts, 10 yrs compressor on registered equipment).
    - High upfront cost (~20x the repair).
    - Scope variability is the main hidden risk — quotes at this price can differ
      enormously on what's actually included.
    - Permits required in most jurisdictions; should be pulled by the installer.

  Cost-per-remaining-year math worth doing mentally:
    If the existing unit has 4–6 more years of useful life with maybe $1,000–$2,000
    in additional repairs over that span, the replacement is paying ~20x to
    pre-empt those repairs plus buy efficiency. That's defensible but not automatic.

QUESTIONS TO RESOLVE BEFORE COMMITTING — grouped as you asked.

WARRANTY

  1. On the $468 repair: what is the labor warranty from this company (30/60/90 days,
     1 year?), and what is the parts warranty on the specific capacitor and contactor
     being installed? Get it in writing on the invoice.
  2. On the $9,240 replacement: is the manufacturer parts warranty 10 years on all
     parts and 10 years on the compressor, or is it a base warranty with a
     "registered" tier that extends it? Who handles registration — you or the installer?
  3. Is the installer's workmanship warranty separate from the manufacturer warranty?
     What does it cover (leaks at connections, ductwork transitions, electrical),
     and for how long?
  4. If the new compressor fails in year 8, who pays labor — is labor included in the
     manufacturer warranty or only parts?
  5. Does the existing 11-year-old unit have any remaining manufacturer warranty that
     survives? (Unlikely but worth one phone call to the original installer with the
     model/serial.)

FAILURE RISK

  6. What is the technician's confidence that the capacitor + contactor are the *only*
     cause of the intermittent afternoon shutdowns? Are there other plausible causes
     — high-head-pressure trip from dirty condenser coil, low voltage at the disconnect
     during peak demand, weak compressor start winding, thermostat/anticipator issue,
     low charge that didn't show today? Ask specifically: "what else did you rule out,
     and how?"
  7. What is the failure mode if the capacitor/contactor fix is incomplete and the
     shutdown recurs — could it damage the compressor (hard locked-rotor starts), or
     is the worst case just no-cool until the next visit?
  8. On an 11-year-old unit, what are the next-most-likely components to fail, and at
     what typical cost? (Blower motor $400–$900, control board $300–$700, evaporator
     coil leak $1,500–$3,000 if accessible, condenser coil $1,500–$2,500.) Knowing
     this lets her size the risk of the "repair now, replace in 2 years" path.
  9. Has the technician checked static pressure in the ducts and the condition of the
     evaporator coil? Both are common silent contributors to compressor overload and
     would change the calculus toward replacement if either is degraded.
 10. Are the pitting on the contactor and the capacitor drop consistent with each other
     (suggesting voltage irregularity at the disconnect), or independent wear? If
     voltage-related, has line voltage been measured at the disconnect under load?

REPLACEMENT SCOPE — the questions that protect her from a $9,240 quote with hidden gaps

 11. Exactly what is included: condenser only, or condenser + matching evaporator coil,
     line set, disconnect, pad, condensate line, thermostat? Get each line item.
 12. Is the new equipment properly sized via a Manual J load calculation, or is the
     installer quoting the same tonnage as the existing unit? Same-tonnage replacement
     without a Manual J is a red flag.
 13. What SEER rating is being quoted, and is the indoor coil being upgraded to match?
     (Mismatched indoor/outdoor coils void efficiency claims and sometimes warranty.)
 14. Are permits included in the price, and is the company pulling them? (Required in
     most jurisdictions; protects her on resale and insurance.)
 15. What brand and model specifically — and is it the company's mid-tier or entry tier?
     Get the full model number to look up the actual warranty terms yourself rather
     than trusting the verbal pitch.
 16. Is ductwork modification anticipated? If so, is that included or an add-on?
 17. Is the electrical service adequate (breaker, disconnect, whip), or will there be an
     extra charge for electrical work? Older homes often need a disconnect upgrade.
 18. Is old equipment removal, haul-away, and refrigerant recovery included?
 19. What is the payment schedule, and what is the warranty start date — installation
     date or commissioning date?
 20. Timeline: how long will the system be down, and what is the company's recourse if
     they miss the promised install window during a heat wave?

PRACTICAL APPROACH FOR MOM

  The reasonable path is: authorize the $468 repair, ask questions 6, 8, 9, and 10 in
  writing on the invoice before they leave, and treat the replacement quote as
  informational for now. If the unit runs cleanly through the rest of this summer and
  the technician's confidence on ruling out other causes is high, the repair buys
  multiple more years of useful life at ~5% the cost. If the shutdowns recur or the
  technician hedges on ruling out deeper causes, the replacement decision gets easier
  with real-world evidence rather than a single diagnostic visit.

  One thing worth flagging directly: an 18°F split on a hot afternoon is not a unit
  that is "failing" — it is a unit with two known worn parts. The replacement quote
  is essentially an insurance policy against the next 5–10 years of repairs, priced
  at ~20x the current known repair. That's a legitimate choice, but it should be made
  with eyes open on the scope questions above, not under the pressure of the next
  afternoon shutdown.

Yes — a sports-medicine or PT evaluation before running again is reasonable, and a same-week appointment (not urgent care, not the ER) is the right level of urgency.

What the presentation is consistent with:
    Localized lateral-ankle pain provoked by single-leg loading (hop, stair descent), absent at rest and during walking, with no swelling, bruising, limp, or instability — fits a low-grade lateral-ligament sprain (anterior talofibular / calcaneofibular), peroneal tendon irritation, or sinus-tarsi irritation. None of those are emergencies, but they're hard to distinguish without an exam, and the return-to-run plan differs for each.

Why an evaluation before running is warranted:
    - Hop and stair descent both load the lateral ankle under eccentric / impact control — exactly the pattern that fails first when something is irritated.
    - "Pain-free walking" plus no instability means the Ottawa Ankle Rules are negative for imaging, so you don't need an X-ray today, but bedside rules don't localize the structure.
    - A sports-medicine physician or PT can do a 10-minute differential: anterior drawer, talar tilt, peroneal tenderness, syndesmotic squeeze — and decide whether MRI / ultrasound adds anything.
    - Self-referral to PT is fine in most US states if you want to start sooner; sports-medicine is the right door if you want imaging or a same-day diagnosis.

Reasonable interim activity limits (until evaluated):
    Allowed / encouraged:
        - Walking as tolerated, normal gait.
        - Stationary cycling, low resistance — keeps cardio without ankle loading.
        - Swimming or pool running with a pull-buoy (avoid push-off if it pinches).
        - Upper-body and hip / core strength work.
        - Stair ascent is fine; stair descent is your test — slow it down, use the railing, and treat any > 2/10 pain as a stop signal.

    Avoid for now:
        - Running, including easy runs and the treadmill.
        - Jumping, hopping, bounding, cutting, lateral agility drills.
        - Hill running, especially downhill.
        - Deep dorsiflexion under load (deep squat, deep lunge).
        - Barefoot walking on hard floors if it reproduces the ache.
        - Foam-rolling or aggressive stretching of the lateral ankle — at this stage it usually irritates rather than helps.

Symptom thresholds to stay under:
    - During any activity: <= 2/10 pain, familiar and localized, gone within 1–2 minutes of stopping.
    - After activity: pain should return to the 24-hour baseline by the next morning. If it's higher the next day, you overdid it.
    - No new swelling, no bruising, no giving-way, no locking or catching.
    - Walking gait should stay symmetric — if you start avoiding the outside of the foot, that's a signal.

Mild self-care that does not replace an exam:
    - Ice 15–20 min after any provocative activity, with a cloth barrier.
    - A shoe with a slightly raised heel (a few mm) reduces lateral-ankle load while you wait.
    - Gentle eversion isometrics (push the foot outward against your hand, no movement, 5 x 30 sec) are usually tolerated even now and maintain peroneal tone — stop if they reproduce the ache.

Return-to-run criteria — do not restart until all of these are true and ideally a clinician has signed off:
    - Pain-free single-leg hop on the involved side, repeated, symmetric with the other side.
    - Pain-free stair descent, full weight, no railing compensation.
    - Pain-free brisk walking.
    - Able to do 15–20 minutes of fast walking or easy cycling without a flare the next day.

Red flags that should send you in sooner (urgent care or ER):
    - Sudden rapid swelling or bruising on either side of the malleolus.
    - Inability to bear weight, or a new giving-way episode.
    - Numbness, color change, or coldness in the foot.
    - Locking, catching, or a feeling that something is moving inside the joint.
    - Rest pain that wakes you or is unrelieved by position.

Plainly: this is not "run through it" territory, but it is also not "stop everything" territory. A sports-medicine or PT appointment within the next week, paired with the limits above, is the sensible middle path.

New sealed lead-acid UPS batteries commonly deliver only 70-85% of rated capacity on the first discharge after the initial charge, and full capacity typically develops over 3-5 full charge-discharge cycles. Your 12-hour charge sits at the low end of the typical 12-24 hour initial-charge window, which can amplify first-run underperformance.

Recommendation: one conditioning-and-retest cycle, with a hard decision rule baked in.

- Retest at or above 90 min: keep it.

FIRST-RESPONSE PLAN — OLD WATER-DAMAGED PHOTOGRAPHS

You already did the right thing by not pulling or brushing. Here's how to keep from making things worse while you sort, and how to tell what needs a pro.

BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANYTHING — SETUP
- Pick a dry, well-ventilated room. Crack a window but no direct draft across the photos.
- Nitrile gloves (not cotton — lint transfers to the gelatin emulsion). If the fuzzy spots look fluffy, damp, or the box smells musty, also wear an N95 mask.
- Lay clean white paper or a clean cotton sheet on the table. Avoid carpeted rooms — spores drop into carpet and recirculate.

ISOLATE FIRST — SORT INTO THREE PILES
  Pile A — Clean (~34 prints): dry, loose, no visible staining or spots. Move onto clean paper. NOT a plastic bag — plastic traps residual moisture and feeds future mold.
  Pile B — Stuck cluster (6 glossy prints, one corner): keep them exactly as they are. Do not slide paper, a card, or a knife between them. Set the whole stack on a clean sheet in a dry spot with airflow.
  Pile C — Suspect mold (2 prints with fuzzy edge spots): keep on their own sheet of paper, well separated from Pile A. Handle these LAST so you're not transferring anything to the clean pile.

If the box itself feels damp or smells musty, leave it in a garage or porch — don't bring it into living space until sorting is done.

WHAT THE FUZZY SPOTS LIKELY ARE
On old water-damaged photos, fuzzy edge growth is almost always mold — either still active or dormant. Quick read:
  - Active: fluffy, sometimes damp, earthy/musty smell, often whitish-greenish.
  - Dormant/dried: powdery, no smell, grayish or brownish.

Either way the rule is the same: do NOT brush, do NOT vacuum, do NOT use bleach, vinegar, alcohol, or any household cleaner. Brushing sends spores into the air and into the rest of the box.

WHEN YOU NEED A CONSERVATOR — NOT A DIY JOB
Send to a professional (American Institute for Conservation "Find a Conservator" directory — conservation-us.org — filter for "photographs" or "paper") if ANY of these apply:
  1. The 2 fuzzy-spot prints — send these. Paper photos with biological growth should be assessed at a HEPA-filtered workstation. Cost is usually modest for two prints.

CUCUMBER-HERB SALAD — 30 SERVINGS (scaled from Sam's 24-serving sheet)

Whole/whole-container amounts:
- 15 English cucumbers (whole, count is exact)
- 1 quart plain yogurt (the 3.75 cups you need; a standard quart container is 4 cups, so one quart leaves a 1/4 cup buffer for the cook's taste — practical since yogurt is a "dress to taste" ingredient)
- 1 cup chopped herbs + 3/4 cup chopped herbs + 2 tbsp (the 1.875 cups; if you're buying pre-chopped clamshells, that's one 1-pt container + a small top-up, or roughly 2 of the small 8-oz clamshells)
- 3/4 cup + 3 tbsp lemon juice (the 0.9375 cups; ~2 lemons of juice if you're juicing fresh, or one of the standard 1-cup bottles + a small pour)
- 1/2 cup + 2 tbsp olive oil (the 0.625 cups)
- 2 tbsp + 1 tsp kosher salt

The 3.75 cups of yogurt and 1.875 cups of herbs aren't clean numbers — that's where this recipe scales awkwardly. I've rounded yogurt to "1 quart container" because that's how it actually gets bought.

MIXING SEQUENCE (hold-back built in)

1. PREP (unchanged from sheet): Halve, seed, and thinly slice the 15 cucumbers. Chop the herbs. Juice the lemons.

2. BASE DRESSING — whisk in a small bowl or measuring cup:
   - 3/4 cup (12 tbsp) lemon juice — this is the BASE, not all of it
   - 1/2 cup (8 tbsp) olive oil — BASE
   - 2 tbsp + 1/2 tsp kosher salt — BASE
   - 3 cups of the yogurt (reserve ~3/4 cup yogurt to loosen later if needed)
   Whisk until smooth and emulsified.

3. TOSS: Pour the base dressing over the cucumbers and herbs. Toss gently but thoroughly so every cucumber gets coated. Taste a cucumber slice, not just the dressing — cucumbers carry dressing differently than the liquid reads.

4. HOLD-BACK PORTION — keep these on the pass, NOT in the bowl:
   - 3 tbsp lemon juice
   - 2 tbsp olive oil
   - 1 tsp kosher salt
   Plus the reserved ~3/4 cup plain yogurt (in case the batch needs loosening after chilling).

5. CHILL AND REST: Refrigerate at least 20–30 min. Cucumbers weep more liquid at 30 servings than at 24, so the salad will loosen in the bowl. After 20 min, drain off any obvious pooled liquid if it's sitting deep, then re-evaluate.

6. FINAL ADJUSTMENT (right before plating, not before):
   - If the salad looks tight or the yogurt has seized from the cold: loosen with a spoonful of the reserved yogurt, not extra dressing.
   - If it tastes flat: add lemon juice 1 tsp at a time from the held-back portion. Acid lifts more reliably than salt at the end.
   - If it tastes flat AND acid isn't fixing it: salt 1/4 tsp at a time.
   - If it tastes sharp or oily: don't add more yogurt yet — that dulls flavor. Drain a little liquid first.
   - If it's still oily after draining: a touch more lemon, then re-taste.

WHY HOLD BACK THIS MUCH (the rationale, since you asked)
At 24 → 30, you're not just scaling — you're scaling into a bowl where 25% more cucumbers are about to release 25% more water into the same volume of dressing. If you put the full 1.25× of acid, oil, and salt in now, the salad will taste over-dressed after 20 minutes of chilling because the dressing hasn't been diluted by cucumber water yet, but it will be an hour from now. The hold-back fixes the timing problem: acid and salt go in at the end when you can actually taste the dressed, rested salad.

EXPECTED LEFTPVERS / WASTE
You will almost certainly use:
- All 15 cucumbers
- Most of the yogurt (probably all of it — the 1-quart container)
- All the herbs
- Most of the lemon and oil (90%+ of base gets used, plus some of held-back)
- Most of the salt (use your judgment — with 6 more guests and no reported sodium concerns, you'll likely end up closer to the full 2.5 tbsp than the 2 tbsp + 1/2 tsp base)

You probably won't need the full 3 tbsp of held-back lemon — that's insurance, not a prediction. If you use all of it, the salad will be sharp; back off with a spoon of yogurt if so.

Short answer: yes, the repair is reasonable to try first. The current measurements (18°F ΔT, normal compressor amps, no leak) describe a system that is functionally healthy today, and the two components the contractor flagged — capacitor and contactor — are among the most common and plausible causes of intermittent shutdown in an otherwise-normal system. The cost asymmetry (~$468 vs $9,240) and the 30-day credit on the same symptom make this a low-regret trial if the credit terms are real and documented.

What still matters, in order of weight:

1. System age and overall condition. The measurements are a snapshot; they don't tell you whether the compressor, indoor coil, blower, and control board have 2 years or 8 years left. Ask the contractor directly: how old is the system (indoor and outdoor), and what is the expected remaining service life if the repair holds? If the system is past ~15 years or the indoor unit is original, the repair is buying time, not restoring life — and that changes the math.

2. The 30-day credit is narrowly worded. "Same intermittent shutdown" is the trigger. If the capacitor swap eliminates the shutdown but a different symptom appears in week 3 (weak cooling from a slow refrigerant loss, blower noise, thermostat dropout), the credit may not apply. Get the contractor to put the credit in writing and broaden the trigger to "any covered cooling failure attributable to the original diagnosis" or similar — or at minimum confirm in writing what counts.

3. Why these two components failed. Pitted contactors and weak capacitors fail from age, but contactor pitting can also be caused by low supply voltage, a loose disconnect, or short cycling. If the underlying cause isn't addressed, the new contactor can pit again — outside the 90-day labor warranty. Ask whether they checked supply voltage at the disconnect and inspected the wiring.

4. Refrigerant charge vs. leak. "No detected leak" is a static reading. Ask whether they weighed in the charge and confirmed it's at the nameplate spec, not just "no obvious leak." An undercharge mimics capacitor/contactor symptoms (high amp draw, poor ΔT under load, intermittent thermal cutoff).

5. Labor warranty length. 90 days is short. If the repair holds 4 months and then fails, you're back to square one with no warranty coverage. That's still acceptable given the cost, but worth knowing.

6. Timing. Late June is early for peak load in most climates; you have a margin if the repair doesn't hold and you need to schedule replacement. That margin shrinks in July–August. If the forecast is mild for the next two weeks, the trial is well-timed.

Practical questions to put to the contractor before approving the repair, in writing where possible:

- System age (both units), and expected remaining life if repair holds
- Supply voltage reading at the outdoor disconnect
- Refrigerant charge: nameplate spec vs. actual weighed-in amount
- Confirmation in writing that the $468 credit applies if any covered cooling failure recurs within 30 days, not only the exact "intermittent shutdown" symptom
- Whether any other concerning findings were noted but not included in the quote (coil condition, blower amp draw, thermostat behavior)

If the contractor answers those cleanly, the repair-first path is the right call. If they hedge on system age or refuse to broaden the credit language, that is information too — and pushes toward replacement.

Short answer: yes, but only under narrow conditions, and none of them align with your stated goal of a reliable 90-minute target. The manufacturer has, in effect, already answered your question by telling you the exchange is not guaranteed to fix the problem.

The defensible reasons to take the exchange are real but orthogonal to runtime:

  1. Continuity. You have a working-but-underperforming unit on the network today. A refund plus a new purchase leaves you uncovered for the shipping and setup window. If "reliable" matters more than "90-minute," an exchange shrinks the unprotected gap.
  2. Free retry. Same-model exchanges sometimes ship from a different production batch. Cost to you is zero if the retailer will honor a second return; you might draw a better unit.
  3. Form-factor lock-in. If this specific model is the only one that fits the rack, outlets, or management card, an exchange is faster than re-shopping and re-cabling.
  4. Price or model drift. If the SKU has been discontinued or repriced since you bought it, "refund and buy the same thing again" is harder than it sounds.

None of those reasons, however, address the 90-minute shortfall. For that goal specifically, the manufacturer's statement is the deciding evidence: they are explicitly disclaiming that a replacement will perform to spec. An exchange on those terms is, at best, a coin flip with no recourse if it lands the same way.

Before you treat the exchange as defensible, you need three things in writing:

  - The manufacturer's published runtime-versus-load curve for your exact model at 31 W, plus the published tolerance. If the curve shows ~95 min at 31 W with a +/-5% band, your unit is genuinely out of spec and an exchange should fix it. If the curve shows ~75 min at 31 W with a +/-10% band, the spec is the problem, not the unit, and no exchange of the same model will give you 90.
  - Confirmation from the retailer that a second return of the exchange unit will be accepted at no cost within the original return window (or an explicitly extended one). Without this, the exchange is a one-way bet.
  - Verification that your 31 W measurement matches the manufacturer's reference load conditions. If they spec runtime at, say, 25 W and you tested at 31 W, some shortfall is expected and an exchange is more likely to land closer to spec at your actual load.

Recommendation: take the refund unless you have a concrete non-runtime reason to keep this exact model on the network, you have the manufacturer's runtime curve in hand and it shows your unit is genuinely out of spec, and the retailer has confirmed in writing that the exchange unit is itself returnable. The exchange only makes sense as a path to the refund you should have taken first, with the retailer carrying the risk in between.

A few things to untangle here, because the criterion has two parts and you're clearing one but not the other.

How this fits the "48-hour pain-free" criterion

The requirement is "repeated hops AND stairs be pain-free for 48 hours" — it's a compound gate, not either/or. Right now:

  Stairs: cleared. Pain-free for 3 days, well past the 48-hour window.
  Repeated hops: not cleared. Today you reproduced 1/10 lateral ankle pain on hop 3, which is precisely what "repeated" is testing. The 48-hour clock for the hop component has not started, because the test produced symptoms today. You can't start a symptom-free clock on a test that wasn't symptom-free.

The hop-3-but-not-1-or-2 pattern is a classic load-tolerance finding: the tissue tolerates a few reps but not yet accumulated reps. That's useful information, not a setback, but it does mean you're in the "stairs cleared, hops pending" zone, not "fully cleared for impact." The absence of swelling, bruising, instability, limp, and rest pain is reassuring — those are the red-flag negatives, and you have none of them — but the criterion is about achieved load tolerance, not about resolution of acute inflammation. So the bar is the bar.

Is easy cycling still reasonable

Yes, with the usual caveat. The 25-minute ride was pain-free during and the morning after — that's a real data point, and cycling is sub-impact (no landing phase, controlled motion). It's reasonable to keep easy cycling as a maintenance activity as long as it stays symptom-free.

What I'd hold off on without PT input: out-of-saddle efforts, hills, intervals — anything that loads the ankle more aggressively or asymmetrically. And stop cycling if you feel the lateral ankle during or after.

Should running wait for the July 2 PT intake

Yes — and not just "wait." Don't self-test running before then. Single-leg hops are a single-leg plyometric event; running is higher-volume, multi-planar impact. If a third hop reproduced symptoms, running is premature, and self-testing it risks re-irritating whatever's still healing rather than giving you clearer information.

Bring this exact finding to the PT on Tuesday: "Single-leg hops pain-free x2, faint 1/10 lateral right ankle pain reproducibly on hop 3; no swelling, bruising, instability, limp, or rest pain; stairs and walking pain-free for 3 days; one 25-minute easy bike ride pain-free during and next morning." The dose-response pattern (fine for 2, symptomatic on 3) is the kind of detail a PT uses to grade you back into a walk-jog progression, and the bike data tells them your sub-impact baseline is solid.

One thing worth holding to between now and July 2: don't keep re-testing hops to "check again." Repeated loading on tissue that just reproduced symptoms mostly just re-irritates without sharpening the picture. Let the PT do the next test. And note that the bike ride doesn't appear to be the cause of today's finding (it was earlier, and the next-morning check was clean) — treat the hop test as the more sensitive probe, not cycling.

Bottom line

  Stairs: cleared. Hops: not yet — the 48-hour clock hasn't started for the hop component. Easy cycling: reasonable, stay easy, stop on symptoms. Running: hold until July 2, and don't self-test before then.

I'm reasoning against the criterion you were given, not substituting for the clinician who set it. If anything changes between now and Tuesday — rest pain, swelling, instability, limp, anything that worsens instead of plateaus — that's worth contacting them sooner rather than waiting for the intake.

Reversible comparison

The cleanest test is to scan or photograph the painting flat at high resolution (no flash, color-correct), then make an 8x10 print from the scan. Lay the print on top of the original sheet and step back four or five feet — at that distance your eye reads composition rather than surface detail. If a print isn't convenient, the next-best option is a paper mask: cut an 8x10 window in a sheet of mat board or card stock and lay it over the painting. The mask is faster than a print because your eye reads both versions at once instead of trying to hold two separate images in memory. Either way, the original sheet stays untouched.

Which tradeoff to favor

Favor the full 9x12 sheet. The painting is doing two related things at once, and the 8x10 crop weakens both of them.

First, the plant sits on the left third, which is a classic rule-of-thirds anchor. An 8x10 crop slides it toward center and onto the weakest zone of the picture plane — the middle is where compositions usually go slack, not where they tighten.

Second, that 1.25 inches of pale wash on the right isn't empty space; it's the runway the diagonal shadows need in order to read as movement across the picture rather than as marks crowding the plant. Truncate it and the shadows stop mid-trajectory, which tends to make them look like accidental smudges at the edge instead of a deliberate vector. Asymmetry is doing real work here precisely because the pale side gives the active side somewhere to go.

The framing convenience is real but it's a downstream concern, not a compositional one. A 9x12 fits a standard 11x14 readymade frame with a 1-inch mat border, or a frame shop can float-mount it in a few minutes — small one-time cost compared to keeping the painting's actual structure intact. Test with the mask first, and don't let the frame catalog make the decision for you.

Short answer: hold the commute this week. Use the indoor bike for your cycling dose, and add the commute only after a clean week of loading exercises plus indoor riding tells you the ankle tolerates the combination.

Why this week isn't the week to test the commute

1. The therapist's cycling allowance is 20–30 minutes per session, up to three times weekly, only if the ride and the next day are both pain-free. Your round-trip commute is roughly 50 minutes in one day, which exceeds the per-session cap even though the calendar fits three days.
2. The new loading program started this week. You have not yet confirmed that loading plus cycling on the same day is symptom-free. Stacking a brand-new exercise variable on a brand-new commute variable violates the "easy cycling only" guardrail — and the guardrail exists precisely because the peroneal tendon is the tissue at risk.
3. "Easy" on the indoor bike means controlled cadence and resistance. On the commute you have less control: two short rises, traffic starts from lights, headwind segments, and the temptation to stand on the rises. Out-of-saddle effort, hills, and high-torque starts are explicitly on the avoid list. That is exactly what a commute asks you to do.
4. Your own framing is the right one. A commute has a fixed arrival time and a fixed route, which converts "easy if pain-free" into "must complete." Indoor riding preserves the option to stop at minute 12 if anything feels off, which is what you actually want this week.

The during-session rule, applied to a bike

Stop the ride immediately for any of these, and don't resume that session:
- New or worsening lateral-ankle pain, including pain at the bottom of the pedal stroke
- Pain that persists past about five minutes of easy warm-up
- Pain above roughly 2 out of 10
- Instability, painful clicking, loss of smooth pedaling, limping, sharp focal tenderness, point pain
- Any urge to stand and mash the pedals on a rise — that's high-torque effort, which is on the avoid list

If nothing fires during the ride, the ride is provisionally clean. It is not yet a clean ride.

The next-day rule, applied to a bike

A ride counts only if the next morning is also clean. That means:
- No ankle pain at rest before you get out of bed
- No pain on stairs, especially descent
- No pain or new soreness during that day's loading exercises, especially the calf raises if it happens to be a calf-raise day
- No swelling, focal tenderness, limp, or instability

If any of those appear, the ride was a flare, not a clean ride. Do not repeat the same dose. Drop back to a shorter, easier indoor ride and re-confirm a clean next day before you try the dose again. Two consecutive flares or any pain at rest, swelling, or instability means you should call the PT clinic before the July 16 reassessment rather than push through.

Path to the commute, if you want it

Next week, if loading exercises alone have been clean for a full week and indoor rides have been clean, you can trial the commute on a Friday, with three conditions:
- Friday is not a calf-raise day, or the calf raises that morning were completely clean before you left
- You commit to seated climbing on both rises and walking the bike up if a rise starts to hurt
- You are willing to abort mid-route and walk the bike home or to a transit stop, which preserves the rule that easy cycling is only easy if it's optional

If that commute produces a clean next day, you have earned Tuesday and Thursday of the week after. If it produces any next-day symptom, the commute stays off the table until after the July 16 reassessment.

Here is a plain-text plan you can act on now. The structure is: keep doing what is working, layer in small things, plan the break deliberately, and know the red flags.

KEEP DOING WHAT YOU ARE DOING
- Interior room, blinds closed, low light. Stay in there with him; he has chosen proximity to you and that is the right answer.
- Your energy should be calm and normal — not effusive reassurance, not scolding. Quiet talking, slow movements, business-as-usual body language.
- If he wants to lean against you or put his head in your lap, let him. If he retreats to a corner, let him.
- Block the hallway if it leads toward an exterior door or any exit he could reach. His pattern (you, then hallway) could be route-seeking, not just reassurance. A baby gate or closed door removes the bolt risk if a loud burst sends him running.

LAYER IN THESE NOW (cheap and fast)
- White noise. A box fan, a podcast at low volume, soft classical, or a TV on a low, even tone — anything that masks the cracks and booms without becoming its own stressor.
- Water available in the room, but do not force him to drink.
- A worn t-shirt or small blanket with your scent in the spot he is choosing — den effect.
- Skip a Thundershirt or compression wrap unless you already own one and know the fit. July 4 humidity plus panting plus a tight wrap is a heat-stress risk; a familiar item is safer.
- Skip the Adaptil diffuser unless it is already plugged in and he has tolerated it before. Now is not the night to test a new product.
- No food treats used as "bribery to calm down" — that can reward the panic. Save high-value treats for AFTER a successful bathroom return.

BATHROOM BREAK PROTOCOL
- Timing: wait for the longest lull you can find. Neighborhood fireworks run in clusters; the gap between clusters is your window. Do not force a deadline.
- Pre-flight check: collar snug, ID tags current, leash in hand. Even in a fenced yard, leash him. A panicked dog clears a 4-foot fence faster than you can react.
- Route: shortest, quietest path. Avoid open sky if possible — under eaves, along a garage wall, the side yard over the front.
- Duration: under 2 minutes. Walk out, stand still in a quiet corner, let him circle and sniff. If he goes, mark and treat. If he does not, that is fine — bring him straight back inside. Healthy adult dogs can skip an evening break without harm; do not push it.
- Watch him, not your phone. If the bursts restart while you are out and he locks up, end the break immediately and return.
- Cool water on the paw pads and a quick feel of his inner thigh/groin on return — if those areas are hot to the touch, he is overheating on top of being stressed.

THROUGH THE PEAK (roughly the next 3 to 5 hours)
- Stay in the interior room with him. Do not move around the house trying to "settle" him in different spots — that just re-arouses him.
- Keep white noise running through midnight; fireworks often have a second peak at 12:00 to 12:30.
- Low ambient light, no flashing screens.
- If he finally settles and sleeps, do not wake him to check on him.
- If he has a crate and uses it voluntarily, that is the best den. Cover it loosely with a blanket on three sides. Do not crate him if he does not already love the crate.

RED FLAGS — CALL AN EMERGENCY VET NOW (not tomorrow, not in the morning)
- Gums, tongue, or inner eyelids turn blue, purple, gray, or very pale/white. Normal dog gums are bubblegum pink. Lift his lip and actually look.
- Collapse, sudden weakness in the legs, inability to stand, or loss of consciousness.
- Breathing that does not return to normal between bursts — open-mouth, deep, rapid, or with elbows flared out and neck extended. "Breathing normally between bursts" is your current baseline; if that changes, it changes.
- Heat stress: thick or ropey drool, bright red gums, vomiting, wobbling when he tries to walk, or panting that gets louder and more labored instead of better over time.
- Seizure activity — paddling, loss of bowel/bladder, loss of awareness, even briefly.
- Self-injury: broken or bleeding toenails from clawing, cut or bleeding paw pads, broken tooth or bleeding mouth from biting a crate/door, any laceration that is still bleeding after 5 minutes of direct pressure.
- A hard, distended, or obviously painful belly, especially with retching that produces nothing — that is bloat, unrelated to fireworks but a coincidence you do not want to miss.
- Repeated vomiting or bloody diarrhea — acute stress colitis can be severe in a few hours.

WATCH THROUGH TOMORROW MORNING
- Continued refusal of water past 12 hours, or refusal of food past 24 hours.
- Hiding that does not ease up by midday July 5.
- Any limping, licking one paw obsessively, or favoring a leg — could be a hidden injury from the night.
- Any of the red-flag signs above, delayed.

ONE SMALL THING WORTH REMEMBERING FOR NEXT YEAR
A dog who paces, pants, and refuses a walk during fireworks is noise-phobic at a clinically meaningful level, not just "spooked." If this pattern repeats on July 4, the December 31 run, thunderstorms, or any construction blasting, it is worth a conversation with your vet about a pre-event pharmaceutical plan (trazodone or a similar agent given 60 to 90 minutes before the trigger) plus a behavior plan. Tonight is not the night to start that — tonight is the night to be a quiet, boring, safe presence in a closed room.

You are already doing the right things. Stay in the room with him, be boring, and have his leash ready for the next lull.

The pattern you're describing — a 2/10 ache confined to the final set, settling within an hour, with a faint 1/10 next-morning twinge on first loaded ankle motion that resolves before walking, and no swelling, bruising, limp, instability, or rest pain — fits the model of approaching tissue tolerance rather than exceeding it. The cleanest way to read this is the 24-hour rule: symptoms returned essentially to baseline (walking pain-free, no resting pain), so the dose was on the high edge of what the lateral ankle structures currently tolerate, not a flare.

For the next resisted-eversion session, treat it as a step-back rather than a repeat. Two practical ways to do that:

  Hold the same resistance but drop the final set (for example, 3 sets instead of 4), or
  Keep the same set count but drop the resistance roughly 10 to 15 percent (one band color lighter, or about 5 lb on a machine).

Either keeps the stimulus inside the tolerated zone. Plan to hold the new dose for two sessions before any progression. If session 3 is asymptomatic during and after, you can return to the prior dose for one session as a recheck. If symptoms recur at the lower dose, regress further or pause eversion work entirely and reassess — that's a signal the tissues need a different stimulus (isometrics, slower tempo) or a clinical recheck. Avoiding load the day after a non-flare response usually isn't necessary; the deciding factor is whether symptoms settle to baseline within about 24 hours, which yours did.

For cycling, you can reintroduce it now, since the ankle under a seated pedal stroke stays well within mid-range and the lateral structures aren't pushed toward inversion/eversion end range under load. Start with:

  Low resistance, comfortable cadence, seated only
  About 10 to 15 minutes the first session, scaling up by 5-minute increments if tolerated
  No out-of-saddle efforts, no heavy gear, no maximal cadence

If you feel any lateral ankle ache during or after the ride, treat it the same way as the eversion session — that's information, and the next ride should be shorter and/or lighter. Out-of-saddle sprinting and standing climbs are the last cycling variables to reintroduce, not the first.

Hop testing stays where you have it. Single-leg hop is a high-load tolerance test, not a warm-up, and the decision to introduce it should come after pain-free single-leg calf raise endurance (roughly 25 or more reps), symmetric single-leg balance, and ideally Y-balance symmetry within about 4 cm — and ideally first performed under PT supervision so landing mechanics and any apprehension can be observed. Don't self-clear for it.

Running remains paused until: resisted eversion returns to the prior dose without symptoms across two consecutive sessions, low-resistance cycling is fully tolerated, and you can complete a pain-free set of single-leg calf raises and a controlled single-leg balance task. The hop test is the bridge back to running, not a substitute for it.

The patterns that would change this plan: any swelling, bruising, limp, rest pain, instability, or symptoms that don't return to baseline within 24 hours, or any lateral ankle symptom during or after cycling. Any of those is a reason to pause loading and get the ankle looked at rather than adjust around it.

The 1/8" overlap per edge is on the lean side of acceptable, but it's adequate — that's the standard configuration a custom framer would spec for a 12x16 frame opening on a 9x12 sheet, and it's symmetric on all four edges (no weak side). The mat has enough bite to hold a flat watercolor sheet behind the opening under normal conditions. It would be a concern only if the paper has heavy cockling or texture; for a typical study, it's fine.

Recommendation: Option 1, the archival full-sheet mount. Don't crop.

Three reasons, in order of weight:

1. Compositional intent. The right-side wash is part of the picture you painted. Stock frames are sized for stock art; the frame should accommodate the work, not the other way around. Losing the wash to save $46 inverts the priority.

2. Archival principle. Cutting down an original watercolor to fit a frame is a destructive, irreversible alteration of the sheet. The standard practice is to size the mat and frame to the existing artwork, not the reverse. A conservator would side-eye a cropped original.

3. Adequacy of the overlap. The 1/8" spec from your framer is at the minimum of conventional practice but is functionally sufficient — you've already verified the math (0.25" total per dimension = 1/8" per edge). If you want more grip without going to a larger frame, ask the framer to drop the mat opening to roughly 8.5x11.5 (3/16" overlap per edge) — still a clean fit, a touch more hold, no cropping needed.

The only situation where Option 2 would make sense is if the painting is a throwaway study and $46 matters more than the composition. From the way you've described it — "the wash I was trying to preserve" — it's not.

Yes, that fits the progression your rule is designed to gate, and the specific response windows to watch are well-defined.

Why it fits as a next step
- Your current green-lit base is: ADL pain-free for 48h + a loaded strengthening trial (resisted eversion, 2x8) that was clean during, immediately after, and the next morning. That's three time-points, which is the meaningful bar — a strength session only proves tolerance at the moment, not the next day.
- Cycling sits cleanly between loaded strength and return-to-run on a graded-reload curve: closed-chain, low ground-reaction force, controllable ROM and cadence, no impact spikes, and no balance perturbations from terrain. That makes it a useful bridge before you reintroduce running or hops.
- A 20-minute easy ride is a reasonable first exposure — long enough to actually test the tissue under sustained low load (a 5-minute trial tells you almost nothing), short enough that a bad response is recoverable. "Easy" and "indoor" matter: you want a fixed load, fixed cadence, and the ability to clip out immediately.

The pain-free rule already governs the decision; the operational conditions I'd hold to during the ride:
- Seated, easy resistance, moderate cadence. No out-of-saddle surges, no standing climbs, no sprints.
- Stay within your current pain-free ankle ROM arc — if dorsiflexion at the bottom of the stroke is irritable, raise the saddle slightly rather than pushing through.
- Treat any sensation during the ride as data, not something to warm through. Mild awareness is a yellow; true pain is a stop.

Immediate / same-day response that means stop or defer cycling
- Pain during the ride (even low-level — your rule is pain-free, not "tolerable")
- Clicking, catching, giving way, or any feeling of instability
- Pain or new stiffness that appears within an hour post-ride and doesn't resolve
- Visible or palpable new swelling
- A limp or guarded gait when you get off the bike and walk
- Tingling, numbness, or any sensation you don't recognize from your baseline

Next-morning response that means stop or defer the next session (and probably ping your therapist)
- Morning stiffness or soreness that exceeds the baseline you established after the resisted-eversion session (that one was clean the next morning — that's your comparator)
- Pain on first steps out of bed, or pain on stairs that's new or worse than the 48-hour pain-free baseline
- Increased tenderness on palpation of the injured structures
- Loss of ROM you previously had
- A fatigue or "heaviness" through the ankle that wasn't there the day before

If the ride and the next morning are both clean — comparable to or better than your post-eversion baseline across those same checks — cycling is unblocked and you can repeat at the same dose before considering any progression in duration or resistance. Running, hops, and full-dose loading are still gated separately and shouldn't piggyback on a clean ride.

  - Keep the house cool. AC stays on, or a fan pointed across his resting spot. Aim for ~68–72°F if you can.
  - Water available, fresh and cool. Don't force it; let him drink as he wants. Small frequent sips are fine.
  - Skip dinner if his appetite is off, or offer a light meal (some of his normal kibble, maybe a little plain canned pumpkin or a tablespoon of plain yogurt). Nothing rich, fatty, or new.
  - No more walks, no training, no excitement, no roughhousing. Quiet evening only.
  - Let him choose where to rest; don't move him. A cool tile floor or a damp towel over his bed helps.
  - Glance at him every hour or two tonight: gum color (stays pink and moist), breathing (calm and unlabored at rest), and whether he seems like himself.
  - He can sleep normally. Just keep the bedroom cool.

OUTDOOR BREAKS IN HOT / HUMID WEATHER

  Timing
    - Walk only when pavement is safe: pre-dawn (before ~6 AM) and late dusk (after ~9 PM, or whenever the back of your hand on asphalt for 5 seconds isn't hot).
    - In sustained heat/humidity, bathroom breaks only — short, purposeful, in-and-out. No exercise walks.

  Route and surfaces
    - Stay on grass, dirt, shaded concrete, or shaded sidewalk. Blacktop in summer can hit 140°F+ and burn paw pads.
    - Backyard is ideal if it's shady and untreated. Avoid mowed strips next to roads if anything's been sprayed.

  On the walk
    - Carry a collapsible bowl and water; offer a few laps before you go and again on return. Don't pour water on him unless he clearly wants it.
    - Never use a muzzle in heat — panting is his only cooling route.
    - Use a harness, not a tight collar, so throat/larynx aren't compressed if he pants hard.
    - Keep the leash short and the pace easy. If he slows down, sniffs a lot, or stops, that's him telling you it's too much — turn around.

  When to skip outings entirely
    - Heat index above ~90°F, OR humidity above ~70% even at moderate temps. Humidity blocks evaporative cooling, so 78°F + high humidity is worse for him than 90°F + dry air.
    - Days with poor air quality (smoke, ozone alerts) — skip and use indoor enrichment instead.

  Indoor alternatives
    - Frozen Kong, toppl, or lick mat with wet food; scent games; a few "find it" rounds with kibble in the yard. Tires a dog out without raising core temp.

SIGNS THAT MEAN URGENT VETERINARY CARE (not home monitoring)

  Go to an ER vet immediately if any of these appear — they can progress within minutes:

    - Collapse, sudden weakness, or inability to stand
    - Stumbling, wobbly gait, head tilt, loss of coordination
    - Mental change: confusion, staring, "not himself," dullness that doesn't lift, agitation that escalates, or any seizure
    - Gums that change from pink to bright red, then to pale, white, gray, or blue, or become sticky/tacky instead of moist
    - Thick, ropey drool, or sudden hypersalivation
    - Vomiting (especially repeated) or any bloody diarrhea
    - Respiratory rate still elevated after 15–20 minutes of cool rest, OR breathing becomes noisy, gaggy, or labored (heaving flanks, flared nostrils, open-mouth breathing at rest indoors)
    - Heart rate very fast or weak/thready
    - Body temperature above 104°F (if you have a rectal thermometer and can safely take it — don't force it if he's stressed)
    - Restlessness that escalates rather than fades over the first hour home
    - Any bleeding from nose, mouth, or in urine/stool (a late sign of clotting problems)

  Call your primary vet (not necessarily ER) within the day if:
    - He's "off" but not in the urgent list — quieter than usual, eating less, a little lethargic, or any mild cough/gag that wasn't there before. Heat stress can occasionally trigger issues that surface hours later.

A reasonable rule of thumb for tonight: if you have to ask "is this normal?" about any single sign in the urgent list, treat it as not normal and go. Heat stroke has a survival window that's much better when treated early — ERs would much rather see a dog that's fine than a dog that's been seizing at home for 20 minutes.

Hold 2x8 for the next one or two sessions, then restore 3x10 if those sessions stay clean. Don't fold this into a run decision.

Reasoning on the dose call:
  - One pain-free session at the reduced dose, plus a pain-free easy ride, is "below irritability threshold" evidence, not "tolerates the target dose" evidence. Symptoms in tendon/soft-tissue loading often lag a session or two, so a single clean data point is thin.
  - 3x10 is roughly double the current volume (30 vs 16 reps). That's a real step, even if the load per rep is unchanged.
  - The cost of holding 2x8 for one or two more sessions is small. The cost of stepping up, flaring, and having to step back down is a week or more. The asymmetry favors patience.
  - Reasonable gate to move from 2x8 to 3x10: same dose tolerated across 2-3 separate sessions, with no symptoms during the session and none the next morning. You're at one session plus the ride; you want one or two more clean data points before adding volume.

Reasoning on the run question, since you flagged it explicitly:
  - Pain-free ride + 2x8 eversions + walking + stairs tells you the irritated structure handles sub-threshold cycling, the current strength dose, and ADL loading. Useful, but it's not a load-tolerance test.
  - Run clearance lives behind hopping, not behind eversion strength. Typical gate: ~10 single-leg hops pain-free, no next-day flare, before any jog. Then a graded walk-run progression (e.g., 1:1 or 2:1 walk:run, building volume over 2-3 weeks), with the same "no symptoms during or the morning after" rule.
  - So keep two questions separate: (a) strength dose, (b) energy-storage / run-readiness. Answering (a) does not answer (b), and a clean (a) is not a green light for (b).

Practical shape for the next week or so:
  - Next 1-2 sessions: 2x8 resisted eversion. Same ride cadence if you have one. Log symptoms same day and next morning.
  - If both sessions clean: step to 3x10. Treat 3x10 itself as a new dose — confirm it across another 2 sessions before assuming it's home.
  - Hop test (single-leg, ~10 reps, compare sides): only after 3x10 has been tolerated for several sessions and the easy ride is consistently clean. Hop is the gate to any run work, not the dose step.
  - Run work, if/when it comes, is its own graded progression with its own session-by-session check, independent of where the eversion dose sits.

If the sheet itself specifies a different progression rule (e.g., "if pain-free for 3 consecutive days, advance"), follow the sheet — your PT wrote it for your specific case and I haven't.
