What your test already tells you. Clean water plus a drip that stops when you close the dishwasher's local shutoff = supply side, not drain. A drain leak has nothing to do with the supply shutoff and would continue regardless. So the only real question left is *where* on the supply side: the angle-stop under the sink, the supply line itself, or the dishwasher's inlet fitting. The most common cause of a small clean-water leak at the supply connection is a loose compression ring nut at one of those joints — often fixable with a quarter turn, no plumber needed.

Overnight precautions

1. Leave the dishwasher's local shutoff CLOSED. The rest of the house can run normally.
2. Dry the cabinet thoroughly with towels. Lay a fresh dry paper towel under the supply connection as a telltale — it will localize the leak by morning.
3. Put a shallow pan or baking sheet under the connection as a backup catch.
4. Leave the cabinet door open overnight for airflow, so any residual moisture evaporates instead of sitting.
5. Verify the dishwasher plug and the outlet in the cabinet stayed dry. You already checked; recheck before bed.
6. Optional belt-and-suspenders: flip the dishwasher's circuit breaker off. The supply is already isolated, so this is just extra margin against any electrical concern.
7. Confirm you know where the whole-house main shutoff is, so it's not a scavenger hunt at 2 a.m.
8. One quick check before bed and one during the night: telltale still dry, pan dry, cabinet floor dry, outlet dry.

Distinguishing a loose fitting from a line/inlet problem without dismantling

The differential is essentially: nut at the angle-stop end, nut at the dishwasher end, or a split in the supply line itself. Without pulling the unit, you can usually localize it:

1. Dry the entire visible run of the supply line and both fittings with a paper towel.
2. Crack the supply shutoff open about 1/8 turn so a small amount of pressure is in the line.
3. Watch for 2–3 minutes with a flashlight. The first joint that beads water is the leak.
   - Wet at the angle-stop end: loose compression nut or worn ferrule there. Fix by hand-tight + 1/4 to 1/2 turn with a wrench, holding the valve body steady with a second wrench so you don't twist the pipe in the wall.
   - Wet along the run of the line: split or cracked supply line. Replace the line — braided stainless lines are $10–15 and a 10-minute swap.
   - Wet only where the line disappears into the dishwasher: the inlet valve on the unit. That one needs the dishwasher pulled out and is usually a plumber or appliance-repair job.
4. The overnight paper-towel telltale will confirm the same thing in the morning, no active watching required.

When to make an urgent call vs. schedule a routine visit

Call tonight or first thing tomorrow (same-day):
- Active drip or running water you can't stop with the local shutoff.
- The local shutoff won't fully close, or it leaks from the valve body when closed.
- Water has reached or is creeping toward an electrical outlet, the dishwasher's plug, or any junction box.
- Cabinet floor is swelling, sagging, or showing water damage.
- Water is on the floor outside the cabinet base.
- The water meter is still spinning with every fixture in the house off (means the leak is bigger than the dishwasher).
- You hear water moving in the wall when nothing is running.

Schedule a normal appointment (next day or two, or DIY):
- Drip stopped when you closed the shutoff, cabinet is dry, no water near electrics, no swelling. That's where you are. A small supply-side drip at a fitting is a 30–60 minute fix for any plumber, or 10 minutes for you with two adjustable wrenches and a $12 braided line if the line itself is the culprit.

1. Rates on the 52-workspace denominator

2. What changed moving from partial to fully mature
--------------------------------------------------

The same four categories have been visible since the first partial cut on 6/14. What changed is the denominator and the unobserved tail, not the labels.

Internal-subset rates (paid-active / mature-windows-only) at each prior audit pass were:

  6/14: 14 / 18 = 77.8%   (18 mature; 34 immature)
  6/17: 18 / 24 = 75.0%   (24 mature; 28 immature)

  7/19: 39 / 52 = 75.0%   (52 mature;  0 immature)

So as more windows matured, the internal paid-active rate wobbled between 75.0% and 77.8% — essentially flat within sampling noise — and landed at 75.0% on the full 52. Three things happened mechanically:

  (a) The denominator grew from 18 → 52. Internal-subset rates stopped being defined (and were already correctly flagged as not-cohort rates); only the 52-denominator rate is reportable going forward.
  (b) The unresolved statuses — past due and billing hold — grew in absolute terms as expected (4 and 2 now vs. 1 and 2 at 6/17) and were re-classified by Finance on 6/21.   (c) Post-day-90 churn stops being silent. A workspace that paid at d30 and then cancels on, say, d92 still reads paid-active at the d90 timestamp; any later cancellation is reported separately, never rolled back into the 39.

Honest framing first: a fully dried bloom on cotton paper can't be removed — only softened or absorbed into the composition. The eye and nose being intact is the important constraint, so work stays on the bloom's lighter (muzzle) edge, never toward the cheek.

Sequence, least destructive first:

1. Live with it for a few minutes. Step back, look at the whole head, not the spot. Cotton paper loves a little atmospheric variation, and a bloom in the cheek-to-muzzle transition often reads as fur texture once your eyes adjust. If the answer becomes "it's fine," stop here.

2. If it still bothers you, single-pass lift:
   - Small round brush, size 2 or 4, damp — not wet. Load it, then blot on a paper towel until the belly of the brush just barely holds moisture.
   - Touch only the lighter, outer lip of the bloom where it bites into the pale muzzle. Do not cross into the shadowed cheek — that value is doing work for the form.
   - Hold for 10–15 seconds so the damp brush reactivates just that pigment ring.
   - Press a clean folded tissue or paper towel, lift straight up. Don't drag.
   - Inspect the eye and nose edges immediately. Any creep toward them and you're done for the day.

3. If the hard ring is still there after it dries: glaze, don't scrub.
   - Mix a very dilute wash of the muzzle tone — more water than pigment, the consistency of weak tea.
   - Lay it across the bloom zone with the same small brush, feathering into clean muzzle on either side. One pass.
   - Let it dry fully before judging. Cotton dries slow; give it 15+ minutes.

Stopping point: after one lift and at most one glaze. The rule you already named is the right one — a painting with a faint bloom is healthier than one with a scrubbed patch and fuzzy paper. If a second pass tempts you, that's the signal to stop and accept the texture.

One thing not to do: don't reach for a clean water wash across the whole area. That will bleed into the cheek shadow and lift pigment you actually want, and is how the eye/nose get soft.

The numbers tell a story in three parts: 204 eligible - 201 triggered = 3 missing at generation; 201 triggered - 160 accepted = 41 missing at provider acceptance. Each layer needs its own check, in order, with no blanket action until we know which layer is responsible.

-------------------------------------------------------

Walk the 3 eligible-but-not-triggered IDs through the suppression stack in order: global unsubscribe table, hard-bounce history, active workspace-level pause (admin_email_pause__ops_hold or cohort_deferred class), CS adoption/renewal open-task suppression, recent support contact (14-day window), duplicate-admin rule (same user_id across slots on one account, or identical role and scope), and merge-alias check.

Layer 2 — Worker submission: prove every trigger became a submit attempt
------------------------------------------------------------------------

Goal: confirm all 201 trigger records reached the worker, not just 160.

4. For each of the 201 trigger records, confirm there is a corresponding submit-attempt log row tied to the eligibility-submission ID (or whatever the durable key is — not the message-attempt ID; the March 20 duplicate-send incident established that message-attempt keys allow retries to duplicate).

5. Bucket the 41 missing-message-ID records by what actually happened to them in the worker: enqueued but never submitted; submitted but no provider response yet (still in flight); submitted and provider rejected with a non-retryable error; submitted and provider accepted but the response write-back failed.

6. The bucketing determines everything that follows. A "still in flight" bucket means the 41 are not lost and a retry would create duplicates. A "rejected" bucket means they are unsendable as-is. A "response write-back failed" bucket means the provider may have sent them — exactly the population you flagged as unsafe to blanket replay.

Layer 3 — Provider acceptance: distinguish delivered-but-unacknowledged from rejected
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Goal: separate the "might already be in someone's inbox" population from the "definitely didn't go" population before anyone proposes a replay.

7. Pull the 41 trigger records and cross-reference each against the provider's delivery/webhook log, not just the send API response. The handoff decision and the program-attribution decision are different questions with different answers.

1. Handoff — CS may begin ordinary commercial follow-up.

The customer has explicitly asked for pricing and effective dates. That qualifies as a help request under the rule you set (CS handoff only on help request or usage-ceiling crossing), so the commercial conversation transfers to CS now. Pricing for the two options is on the published schedule (organic pricing-page channel through Q3 under Helio Start), and effective-date questions are normal commercial clarifications — neither requires new program authority. CS should answer factually and run the opportunity as it would any other. If it closes, the revenue is real and books normally; Expansion Assist suppresses nothing.

2. Reporting — Expansion Assist receives no automatic pipeline or forecast credit for this engagement.

The pilot is in shadow by design (BRIEF-2024-04, approved 2024-06-20): outside pipeline, outside forecast, outside revenue. Marcus's request to count engagement immediately as Expansion Assist pipeline was declined for the same reason — engagement is not the metric, and an engagement credit would corrupt the measurement.

The metric is net expansion (treatment vs. holdout). Until the holdout comparator runs, no individual touchpoint can be attributed as program-caused lift. The mechanic on display here — Owen's prompt, the customer's pricing request, CS closing — is exactly the conversion pattern the pilot is designed to measure, but the measurement is comparative across the cohort, not per-engagement. Counting this one as pipeline would (a) double-count the same revenue in normal commercial reporting and in pilot credit, and (b) break the holdout logic that makes the causal claim valid.

3. What gets reported, and by whom.

CS: a normal commercial opportunity, logged through standard pipeline. If it closes, it closes on its merits.

Owen: per the established protocol — eligibility, prompt, handoff, and expansion as separate fields. The pricing request is a handoff event, not a pipeline credit. The pilot's eventual read is "of the ~30 retained mid in treatment, how many expanded net of the holdout comparator," not "count the deals that started from a prompt." The 5-secondaries rule (from the Helio Start settlement) and the BRIEF-2024-04 framing both point the same way: this is the kind of signal that gets measured, not monetized in flight.

4. The principle.

Customer-initiated commercial motion is always allowed and never suppressed by a shadow pilot. Program attribution is a causal claim that requires the comparator. Letting CS sell while refusing Marcus's credit is the only consistent position: the customer gets the right answer, the pilot stays clean, and the causal read at the end of the window is what actually decides whether Expansion Assist earned anything.

TASK SEQUENCE (Friday, 30-lb case, target ≥44 portions)

  Pre-trial (before T0)
    - Sheet pans counted, lining station set
    - Oven preheat on
    - Birds weighed, broken to target portion count
    - Seasoning mix portioned

  T0 onward (sequencing depends on rhythm; goal is no idle gaps)
    1. Sam — seasoning application, one continuous block
    2. Line cook — pan stage, in short blocks between existing
       duties (roughly 4-6 min each, several blocks). Target: all
       pans lined and racked before seasoning ends.
    3. Sam — oven staging + load (rack position, load pans)
    4. Roast (timer-driven; no labor)
    5. Sam — mid-roast check/baste (~3 min)
    6. Pull and rest (Sam)
    7. Sam + line check — yield count and portion
    8. Line cook (interstitial) — pan clear during/after rest

  Parallelism note
    Sam's oven staging will overlap with the tail of the line cook's
    pan-stage blocks. That overlap is the reason the line cook's
    work is broken up; it is expected, not a problem.

LABOR-LOGGING METHOD

  Format — one row per contiguous block of work (shared note,
  clipboard, or paper tally — whatever the kitchen will actually
  use):

    Person     | Start  | Stop   | Activity        | Trial (Y/N)
    Sam        | 14:05  | 14:32  | seasoning       | Y
    Sam        | 14:32  | 14:48  | oven staging    | Y
    Line cook  | 14:10  | 14:15  | pan stage       | Y
    Line cook  | 14:15  | 14:38  | normal line     | N
    Line cook  | 14:38  | 14:44  | pan stage       | Y
    ...

  Rules
    - One row per block. A block is a contiguous span on one task.
    - Within a single person, intervals must not overlap.
    - Trial = Y only for work that is part of the run. The line
      cook's normal-line rows are logged N so the gaps are visible
      (proves trial work did not displace normal duties) but they
      do not enter the labor total.

  Computation
    person_minutes(p)     = sum of (Stop - Start) for person p
                            where Trial = Y
    total_trial_labor     = sum over persons of person_minutes(p)
    yield_per_labor_hour  = portions / (total_trial_labor / 60)

  Why this satisfies the four constraints

    Counts added trial minutes.
      Only Trial = Y intervals enter the sum. Anything else is
      filtered out before totaling.

    Does not count full scheduled shift.
      Every block requires a Stop time. Unworked minutes are simply
      absent from the log — there is no shift envelope being
      subtracted from, so there is nothing to subtract incorrectly.

    Avoids double-counting overlapping clock time.
      Each person has non-overlapping intervals with themselves, so
      one person's minute cannot be logged twice. When Sam and the
      line cook both work on trial during the same wall-clock
      window (e.g., 14:32-14:44), each minute is one person-minute
      for Sam and one person-minute for the line cook. The sum is
      two person-minutes per wall-clock minute, which is the correct
      measure of labor, not double-counting. The trap to avoid is
      logging the same person's minute twice (e.g., a row for
      "seasoning 14:05-14:32" and another for "oven 14:05-14:32"
      that overlap) — the one-row-per-block rule prevents that.

      Note on units: total_trial_labor is person-minutes. It can
      exceed wall-clock minutes; that is correct, and it is also
      what the 60-minute ceiling should be read against (the
      ceiling is on labor, not elapsed time). If the June 28
      baseline was read against elapsed time, that is a separate

      before drawing conclusions. The numbers that compare across
      runs are total_trial_labor and yield_per_labor_hour; the
      ceiling check is total_trial_labor ≤ 60.

  H2 — Real signup decline:        Safari users genuinely started fewer signups; predict a parallel drop in server-accepted signup starts or completions, with sessions flat only because top-of-funnel traffic held.

Sequence (run in this order; each step either rules H1/H2 in or rules one out)

Split 7/24 into hourly buckets and overlay three series: pricing-page sessions, front-end `signup_start` (analytics), backend application-session creation. The discriminating shape is a single-step gap (analytics only) vs a co-moving gap (analytics + backend). A co-moving gap means real decline; analytics-only means tracking. If hourly overlay is noisy, fall back to 4-hour buckets before going daily.

  4. Check the conversion gap, not just the event count. Compute pricing-page-session → `signup_start` and pricing-page-session → backend application-session for 7/24 and the prior 6 Wed medians, by browser. A widened front-end rate with a flat or improved backend rate is the cleanest signature of an analytics-only failure; a widened rate on both sides points to real decline.

The gate is the plan's own instrument for separating "stay" from "step." It was written to clear on the exact signals you described — two consecutive sessions, pain-free during, after, on stairs, and the following morning, with no added distance, speed, or continuous running. You cleared every one of those, on both sessions, with the dose held exactly. Refusing the step at this point isn't following the plan more conservatively; it's substituting a stricter rule (effectively "three clean sessions, not two") that the printed plan doesn't contain.

The real load change at 6 × 3 min vs 7 × 2 min isn't distance — total distance is essentially unchanged on the same flat route. It's two things:
  - walk-to-jog ratio drops from 1:1 to 2:3, so each jog block has proportionally less recovery behind it
  - the continuous jog block goes from 2 min to 3 min, which is the first interval length where sustained cyclic tendon load starts to feel qualitatively different

You're in a good position: fine-tipped tweezers, no counterproductive home remedies applied, and Kibo acting normally. Act now — transmission risk rises meaningfully after ~24 hours of attachment.

REMOVAL (in order)

1. Steady his head — a second pair of hands makes behind-the-ear work much easier. If he's wiggly, a calm scruff-and-steady hold works; don't restrain so hard he shakes his head mid-pull.
2. Part the fur so you can see the mouthparts meeting the skin.
3. Grasp with the tweezers as close to the skin as possible. You want the tips on the head/mouthparts, not on the engorged body. Squeezing the body can push saliva and pathogens into the bite.
4. Pull straight up with steady, even pressure. No twisting, no jerking, no rocking. Slow and constant.
5. Inspect the site. A small dark fragment (broken mouthpart) left behind is common; leave it. Digging causes more trauma than the fragment itself.
6. Clean the site with chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine. Soap and water is fine if those aren't at hand. Then wash your hands and the tweezers.

AFTERCARE FOR KIBO

- A small red bump or scab for 2–3 days is a normal local reaction and not a problem.
- No topical antibiotic unless the site becomes weepy or clearly infected.
- Note today (2024-07-27) and that the exposure was the Cherrywood yard. That timestamp matters if symptoms show up later.

WHAT TO DO WITH THE TICK

- Don't flush or bin it yet.
- Drop it into a small sealed bag or jar with isopropyl rubbing alcohol — that kills and preserves it.
- Label with: date, location, host (Kibo). A photo next to a ruler is a useful backup for ID.
- Reason: if Kibo develops symptoms in the next 2–4 weeks, your vet can ID the species or send it for pathogen testing, which changes what they treat for.

In central Austin, the likely culprits are Lone Star tick (aggressive biter, very common, transmits ehrlichiosis, tularemia, STARI) and American dog tick (RMSF vector). Lone Star is the bigger worry here.

LOCAL SIGNS — same-day vet call, not urgent

- Expanding redness or rash around the site over several days
- A bull's-eye or target lesion
- Persistent swelling, discharge, or crusting past 3–5 days
- Retained mouthparts that look infected rather than just inflamed

SYSTEMIC SIGNS — urgent care or ER, call before you go

These can appear from a few days to ~4 weeks post-bite. Big ones for Texas tick-borne disease:

- Lethargy or "just off" — sleeping more, not greeting you, skipping walks
- Skipping a full meal, or any real appetite drop
- Fever (rectal temp over ~102.5°F is suspicious, over 103°F is definitive; warm ears alone aren't reliable)
- Lameness, stiffness, or shifting-leg lameness — the classic ehrlichiosis presentation
- Vomiting or diarrhea
- Unusual bruising, pinpoint red spots on gums or belly, or pale gums
- Yellow tinge to gums, inner eyelids, or whites of eyes
- Enlarged lymph nodes (feel under the jaw and behind the knees)
- Breathing changes — fast, shallow, or labored
- Any neurological change: head tilt, wobbly gait, sudden confusion, seizure

Anything in that second list is "call now, don't wait a day." Ehrlichiosis and RMSF respond well to treatment but escalate quickly once symptoms start.

ONE FOR YOU AND SAM

Same yard, same exposure. Check yourselves tonight — pay attention to the scalp, behind the ears, waistband, and socks. Lone Star ticks carry pathogens that affect humans too, and symptoms (rash, fever, flu-like feeling, joint pain) are easy to dismiss for a week. If either of you finds an attached tick on yourselves, use the same removal method.

A restrained sequence for a dry single-glaze warm bank with the horizon light intact:

1. Lifting — one pass, targeted, not chasing full removal
   - Soft round (sable/squirrel), damp with clean water, not flooded
   - Work only the lower two-thirds of the warm bank; keep a dry margin of roughly 5 mm around the horizon opening
   - Short strokes following the cloud forms; blot with tissue or a dry sponge after each sweep
   - Let it dry completely before judging — wet lifting always looks more dramatic than the dried result
   - If the warmest, most solid patches still read too warm after drying, repeat once on those spots only

2. Cool glaze — after the lifting is fully dry
   - Mix a thin wash of ultramarine blue with a small touch of dioxazine violet (ties to the violet sky already working). Payne's grey works if you want it more neutral, less violet
   - Consistency: tea-stained, not milky. Transparency is what modulates the warm without burying granulation
   - Load the brush, lay it in, let it pool where the bank is heaviest, and keep it off the horizon opening — a dry-brush shield (scrap of paper or your hand edge) at the horizon gives you margin if you're nervous about creep
   - Avoid phthalo here — it stains too aggressively and flattens texture

3. Reassess as it dries
   - Granulation should reassert as the glaze settles; if it looks flat, the wash was either too wet or over-worked
   - If the bank still reads warmer than the sky once dry, a second thin cool pass only on the offending areas, not over the whole shape

4. Stop point
   - One lifting pass plus one cool glaze is usually enough. Further work risks the chalky lift patch that a single-glaze condition is already warning you away from

Leave alone: the violet sky (working), the horizon light (don't glaze into it), and any granulation still visible in the warm bank — a transparent cool glaze modulates it without erasing the texture.

One note worth flagging: if the original warm was something like burnt sienna or a quinacridone gold, the lifted area will still lean slightly warm even after pigment is removed, because the stain sits in the paper. That's another reason the cool glaze does real work here, not just finishing — plan the second pass as a likely step, not a contingency.

PROCEDURE: Controlled Rescan for P007 Front and P014 Back

PRE-RESCAN

  1. Confirm scope out loud and in writing: only P007 front and P014 back are in
     scope. The eight treated photographs stay outside the session. The other
     thirty dry photographs and their Saturday passes are untouched.
  2. Pull the original capture files for P007 front and P014 back plus their
     Saturday session metadata (exposure, lighting notes, framing notes) from
     the runbook / session log.
  3. Re-inspect the two physical prints: confirm they are still dry, undamaged,
     and that their temporary IDs (P007, P014) are intact and legible. If either
     has degraded since Saturday, stop and flag — do not rescan a compromised
     object.
  4. Set up the same capture station, camera body, lens, color/white-balance
     target, and capture profile that Saturday used. Same color target in frame.
  5. Mark only the two prints with a "RESCAN" tag so they cannot be confused
     with the untouched set during handling. Do not mark the other 30.

RESCAN — P007 FRONT (glare)

  1. Diagnose from the original TIFF: locate the hot spot and infer the key-
     light angle that caused it. Note the affected region only; do not
     characterize the whole image.
  2. Make the smallest lighting change that resolves it. Typical first move:
     reposition the key light off-axis (around 45 degrees from the camera-to-
     subject axis) and/or add diffusion. Keep framing, focal length, subject
     distance, and registration identical to Saturday.
  3. Do not introduce a polarizer unless the Saturday runbook already used one
     on this surface. Adding new optics is a setup change, not a fix; it would
     change the comparison baseline against the other 30 fronts.
  4. Capture a single frame at the same aperture and depth as Saturday. Do not
     bracket. Confirm on the live histogram that the previously obscured region
     now sits within the dynamic range (no clipped highlights where detail
     should live, no crushed shadows). If not, iterate with a smaller light
     adjustment — not a post-processing adjustment.

RESCAN — P014 BACK (handwriting too faint)

  1. Diagnose the medium from the original: graphite pencil, ballpoint, or
     faded fountain-pen ink. The medium dictates the fix.
       - Graphite / pencil: the fix is lighting, not exposure. Switch to raking
         light from one side at a low angle (roughly 15–30 degrees) so the
         strokes catch texture. Do not lengthen exposure to compensate — that
         washes graphite out.
       - Faded ink: lengthen exposure (or raise ISO) by 1–2 stops. Verify the
         histogram peak stays below clipping and surrounding paper does not
         blow out.
  2. Keep framing, registration, color depth, and resolution identical to
     Saturday. Only the light position and/or exposure change.
  3. Confirm at 1:1 pixel view on the capture preview that the previously
     unreadable handwriting is legible without any post-processing — i.e., the
     capture itself solved it.

FILE HANDLING (preserves IDs, avoids destructive enhancement)

  1. Do not overwrite or delete the original TIFFs. They stay as the audit
     record of Saturday's pass.
  2. Save the rescans under versioned names that keep the original IDs:
       P007_front_rescan_v1.tif
       P014_back_rescan_v1.tif
  3. If your pipeline uses sidecar metadata (XMP, JSON), add a "rescan" event
     to each new file capturing: reason, date, operator, lighting change vs.
     Saturday, exposure change vs. Saturday, and a checksum. Do not modify
     the original's sidecar.
  4. Post-processing on the rescans is limited to whatever the Saturday runbook
     allowed for the originals (typically: white balance from the in-frame
     target, crop to registered edges, nothing else). Explicitly DO NOT apply:
     sharpening, noise reduction, dehaze, content-aware fill, contrast curves
     that clip, or any local retouch on the previously problematic region.

VERIFICATION (same two-person check Mom + Marcus ran Saturday)

  1. Review the two rescans side-by-side with the originals on the same
     display used Saturday, at the same zoom levels used Saturday.
  2. P007 front: confirm the previously glare-obscured area is now readable
     and that no new hotspot was introduced elsewhere; confirm edge
     registration matches the Saturday batch within tolerance; confirm no
     sharpening halos.
  3. P014 back: confirm the handwriting is readable at 1:1 without zoom tricks;
     confirm surrounding context (other annotations, deckle/edges) is not
     blown out; confirm registration matches.
  4. For both: confirm color and tonal balance are consistent with the other
     30 dry files, so the rescan does not become a visual outlier in the set.
  5. Sign-off: each reviewer initials the rescan sidecar (or your equivalent
     log). Only after both initials is the rescan treated as canonical. The
     original remains archived, not deleted.

POST-PROCEDURE

  1. Update the session manifest so P007 front and P014 back are flagged
     "rescanned, verified, canonical = rescan_v1; original retained for audit."
  2. Leave the eight treated photographs and the other thirty dry photographs
     with no status change.
  3. Add one short line each to the runbook for future sessions: the
     controlled fix for glare is key-light repositioning only (polarizer
     requires a runbook amendment first); the controlled fix for faint
     handwriting is medium-dependent — raking light for graphite, +1–2 stops
     exposure for faded ink, with histogram check. That keeps next time
     equally controlled and equally least-disruptive.

Yes — what you're describing fits a minor local reaction to a tick bite well. Five days is a typical window for the small, raised, pink bump (sometimes called a "tick bite granuloma" or simply residual inflammation) that develops as the skin reacts to leftover saliva proteins or minor trauma from the bite itself. A dry center suggests the surface is scabbing over rather than staying moist or draining, and the lack of enlargement, heat, drainage, marked tenderness, or systemic signs argues against infection or an acute tick-borne illness at this moment.

Care without irritating the site

- Leave it alone as much as possible. Don't pick, squeeze, scratch the scab, or rub it.
- If Kibo scratches or rubs at it (behind the ear is a common spot to be bothered), a short course of an Elizabethan collar or a soft e-collar prevents self-trauma, which is the most common cause of a simple bite site turning into a true wound.
- Cleaning, if needed: once daily (or every other day) you can gently wipe with a cloth or cotton ball dampened with dilute chlorhexidine (the blue veterinary kind, diluted to a pale color) or mild saline. Pat dry — don't soak or scrub.
- Avoid hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol, essential oils, Neosporin without vet approval, and any "drawing" salves. These delay healing and can irritate.
- Don't bandage the ear. It will hold moisture and trap debris.
- Bathe normally but rinse the area clean of shampoo and dry it well.

Local changes that should prompt a routine (non-emergency) vet call

- Bump enlarges beyond ~6–8 mm, becomes more raised, or develops a ring of redness around it
- New or increasing drainage (pus, crusting that doesn't dry, oozing)
- A bullseye or expanding red ring (EM-like) — in dogs this is uncommon but warrants a vet look
- The site stays pink/raised beyond 2–3 weeks without trending down, or a firm nodule persists
- Itching becomes intense enough that Kibo is scratching even with a collar on
- Hair loss spreading from the site

Whole-body changes that should prompt a routine vet call (within a day or two)

- Mild lethargy or a drop in appetite lasting more than 24 hours
- Low-grade "off" behavior — quieter than usual, slow on walks, hesitant to jump
- A new, intermittent limp that shifts between legs or favors one leg for more than a day
- Slight feverish feel (warm ears, panting at rest when not hot)
- Mild GI upset that resolves but recurs

These are the early, low-grade signs of tick-borne illness (Lyme, anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, RMSF), which typically show up 2–6 weeks after a bite but can vary. A routine vet call lets them decide on a baseline blood test or a watch-and-wait plan.

Whole-body changes that should prompt urgent or emergency care

- Facial swelling, hives, or sudden swelling anywhere (possible anaphylaxis)
- Difficulty breathing, rapid breathing at rest, pale or bluish gums
- Sudden collapse, severe weakness, or wobbly/stumbling gait that comes on over hours to a couple of days (tick paralysis progresses ascending — back legs first)
- Repeated vomiting, bloody diarrhea, or vomiting + lethargy together
- Dark urine, yellow gums, or unexplained bruising/pinpoint red spots on the belly/gums (signs of immune-mediated complications from some tick diseases)
- Any sudden change that worries you — gut feeling is a valid reason to call

A practical note on follow-up

Because tick-borne diseases have a delayed window, the bigger risk isn't this bump today — it's a low-grade illness 3–8 weeks from now. If you know what kind of tick it was and where you are (Lyme-risk region, RMSF region, etc.), your vet can give you a more specific watch plan. Many practices will run a 4Dx/Accuplex snap test at the 4–6 week mark as a routine screen even in asymptomatic dogs after a known tick bite; that's worth asking about at Kibo's next wellness visit or scheduling a quick nurse-visit blood draw if you'd rather not wait.

One last thing: save the tick in a sealed bag or vial in the freezer if you still have it (or a photo of it). Species identification can sharpen the watch list substantially, and your vet can use that information.

The hallway wall is the safest of the three. The reasoning, and what to actually do once it's hung:

Why the hallway wins on conservation

  Living-room (direct west, ~3–5pm): West-facing afternoon sun is the most aggressive light a residential interior gets — high intensity, low angle, often hot. UV-filtering acrylic blocks roughly the UV band, but it does NOT block the visible-light and near-IR energy that drive fading and thermal stress in paper and pigment. Two hours of daily direct sun on an unprotected float-mounted sheet (where the paper is exposed through the mat opening, not sealed behind an airtight barrier) will produce visible fading and possible cockling long before any other location shows damage. UV-filtering acrylic is a partial mitigation, not a substitute for avoiding direct sun.

  Kitchen (no direct sun, cooking humidity): Humidity is the bigger long-term threat to a float-mounted watercolor than light is. Steam, grease aerosols, and rapid RH swings cause paper to expand and contract, which on a float mount shows up as ripple, cockling, and eventually foxing or mildew at the sheet edges where air meets the paper. Cooking also deposits organic film on the acrylic that is hard to clean without micro-scratching the UV coating. UV-filtering acrylic does nothing for any of this.

  Hallway (indirect light, steadier humidity): Lower total light dose, stable RH away from the cooking plume, and no direct-beam heating through the glazing. The "viewed from farther away" tradeoff is real but small for a 9×12 — at normal hallway viewing distance the float-mount and signature still read cleanly. Conservation-wise this is clearly the right call.

Practical placement precautions for the hallway

  - Position it on a wall segment that never receives a direct beam, even seasonally. In the Northern Hemisphere, summer sun angles are higher and winter sun rakes farther into interior spaces — a spot that's shaded in August can get a sliver of direct light in January. Watch the spot across a full day before you commit the hanger holes.
  - Offset the frame from the wall. Use D-rings plus picture-h wire and small felt or rubber bumpers on the back corners so there's a ~1 cm air gap behind the frame. This lets the back of the sheet breathe and prevents moisture from being trapped between the frame and the wall — important because drywall and especially exterior hallway walls can off-gas moisture during temperature swings.
  - Keep it off any exterior wall that backs the outside of the building if the hallway runs along an outside wall. Exterior walls have higher diurnal temperature swing, which drives humidity cycling right at the paper.
  - Stay clear of HVAC supply registers, return grilles, and bathroom-adjacent walls. A supply register pointed at the frame is the same problem as direct sun on a smaller scale: forced dry air plus particulates.
  - Maintain whole-home RH in the 40–55% range. A basic hygrometer is worth it; archival float mounts assume a stable environment and quietly degrade when the room swings from 30% in winter to 70%+ in summer.
  - Hang it at eye level in a spot where it won't be routinely bumped — the float mount has no glazing pressure holding the sheet, so a hard nudge can shift the paper against the mat opening and abrade the deckled edge or the signature corner.
  - Clean the acrylic with a soft microfiber and distilled water only; no ammonia, no Windex, no paper towels. UV-filtering coatings scratch easily and once scratched the UV protection is locally compromised.
  - Once a year, lift it off the wall and inspect the sheet edges and the signature corner for any ripple, tide line, or pigment shift. Catching a humidity problem early is the difference between a stable piece and a restoration job.

Short version: hallway for stability, offset from the wall, away from any exterior wall or register, and treat the UV-filtering acrylic as one layer of protection rather than the protection.

Here is the recommended neutral inventory convention. It preserves both attributions for P023 as first-class data, leaves P028 open, and uses the physical album or envelope as the verification gate.

Summary

The core principle is to record what each witness says, when they said it, and how confident they were — without promoting either memory to "the answer." The original family album (or any paper envelope/caption) is the only thing allowed to upgrade an attribution from "tentative" to "confirmed," and only when the album side is itself unambiguous.

1. Inventory row schema (one row per print, unchanged otherwise)

For the 32 dry/loose prints P001–P032, every row already has: temporary ID, estimated date, people/location, condition, open questions, future scan filename. Add three new explicit fields per row to carry the new convention:

  attribution_status     one of: confirmed | tentative | conflicting | unknown
  attribution_sources    list of named witnesses and the artifact (album, envelope, caption), with the
                         exact statement or quote and the date it was given
  verification_artifact  the physical object (album page, envelope, paper caption) that would
                         resolve the row, named explicitly; blank if none known

The eight treated photographs remain outside this schema until they return from the conservator with condition notes. They are not silently merged in.

2. Status definitions (tight, no judgment)

  confirmed     – a named source (album page, envelope caption, written note) directly states it
  tentative     – one named witness recognizes it but no artifact exists yet
  conflicting   – two or more named witnesses disagree (city, year, occasion, or people)
  unknown       – no witness recognition above the no-guess threshold

Status changes only upward: unknown → tentative → confirmed. A row can move from tentative to conflicting if a second witness later disagrees. A row cannot move from conflicting to confirmed without an artifact.

3. P023 specifically — preserve both, do not pick

Current state, in plain language:

  P023  attribution_status:     conflicting
        attribution_sources:
          - Mom (2024-08-03 reply): "Austin family gathering, around 2002" — tentative, her wording
          - Marcus (2024-08-03 reply): "San Antonio, around 2004" — tentative, his wording
        verification_artifact:    original family album page or paper envelope/caption that places
                                  the photo's location and date; the check is whether the album side
                                  is itself unambiguous, not which witness sounds more confident

Do not write "Austin, 2002" or "San Antonio, 2004" into the date or location columns. Leave both as the witness values inside attribution_sources, and keep the headline date/location columns at their current "tentative / TBD" level until the album check resolves it. The two memories are recorded as evidence, not adjudicated.

4. P028 specifically — leave unknown

Current state:

  P028  attribution_status:     unknown
        attribution_sources:    (none — neither witness supplied a date or occasion they would
                                stand behind)
        verification_artifact:  blank for now; if either witness later offers even a tentative
                                lead, capture it as a tentative row, not a confirmed one

The "13 unknown photographs must not be guessed" rule (P020–P032 range) continues to govern. P028 staying unknown is the correct state, not a failure to fill the row.

5. Verification step — the album or envelope, not memory

When the family album (or any paper envelope, sleeve caption, or written back) is in hand, the row is upgraded only when the artifact is unambiguous:

  - If the album page or envelope clearly places the photo (city + year, or named event + year),
    the row moves conflicting → confirmed with the artifact named in attribution_sources.
  - If the artifact is itself ambiguous or silent on the disputed point (city or year), the row
    stays conflicting; the artifact is added to attribution_sources as a third data point, not
    a tiebreaker.
  - Memory arbitration between Mom and Marcus is explicitly not a verification step. Neither
    witness is treated as more reliable a priori, and confidence of phrasing is not a signal.
  - If the two witnesses later agree on rechecking the album together, that joint recheck is
    recorded as a single attribution_sources entry with both names and the date; their agreement
    on an unambiguous artifact can move the row to confirmed.

This keeps the gate physical and reviewable, which is what the original "original family album or envelopes as the verification step" rule calls for.

6. Other rows this turn

The reply from Mom and Marcus also confirmed several tentative IDs. Those move tentative → confirmed only if a witness's recognition is paired with a named artifact, and stay tentative otherwise. The exact per-row edits are below; nothing about P023, P028, or the eight excluded prints is changed by these updates.

  Tentative-only rows (one witness, no artifact; status stays tentative):

7. What stays excluded

  - The eight prints with the conservator are not in this update. They are not merged into the
    32-row inventory, not assigned IDs in P001–P032, and not scanned. They enter only after the
    conservator returns them with final condition notes, at which point they get their own IDs

  - P020–P032 no-guess rule remains in force. P028 is governed by it.
  - The 32 dry/loose prints are otherwise unchanged: filenames stay P001.jpg–P032.jpg, no writing
    on prints, two-person file check before re-sleeving, original TIFFs archived and not overwritten.

Why this is the right shape

It records disagreement as a first-class state instead of forcing a winner, it uses the physical album or envelope as the only upgrade path from tentative to confirmed, and it explicitly refuses to use the more confident-sounding memory as evidence. P023 keeps both attributions with named sources and dates. P028 stays unknown. The eight treated photographs stay out. Nothing in the existing workflow — IDs, filenames, two-person check, re-sleeving — changes.

The trade doesn't come close to favoring the higher deductible. Math first:

  Annual premium savings (B over A): $36/yr ($3.00/mo)
  Extra out-of-pocket if a claim hits the $1,000-$2,500 band: $1,500
  Break-even on a single such claim: ~41.7 years of premium savings
  EV breakeven: B wins only if your annual probability of a band-claim is below ~2.4%

That 2.4% threshold is the whole question, and it isn't low. For a renters policy covering $40k of personal property over a year — a single-room theft, a kitchen fire that doesn't reach dwelling-severity, a burst pipe that wrecks electronics and furniture, a liability claim — 2–5% annual probability of a claim landing somewhere in that band is a reasonable working estimate, not a worst case. At 3% you'd be paying an expected $9/yr in extra exposure to save $36 in premium, which still favors B by $27. At 5% it flips and A wins by $39. We genuinely don't know which side of 2.4% we're on.

But that's the expected-value framing. The actual decision is better made on three other grounds, and they all point the same direction:

  1. Risk-aversion pricing. $3/month to cap your worst-case out-of-pocket at $1,000 instead of $2,500 is among the cheapest hedges you'll ever buy. A reasonable risk-aversion coefficient on a $1,500 loss is worth far more than $36/yr in expected premium. The "lower premium" framing only works if you treat $36 and $1,500 as the same kind of dollar — they aren't.

  2. Cash-flow and friction at claim time. A deductible is paid out of pocket at the worst possible moment, often right after a stressful event. Going from $1,000 to $2,500 raises the chance that a real claim becomes "annoying enough that we don't bother filing," which silently reduces the value of the policy you're paying for. That's a real cost, not a theoretical one.

  3. The framing itself is the warning sign. The renewal went up $48/yr ($264 → $312, +18%). The deductible "choice" softens that by $36 — barely three-quarters of the increase. The insurer is using a small, lopsided trade to make the renewal feel like it has an upside. That's the moment to slow down, not speed up.

Recommendation: keep the $1,000 deductible at $312/yr. If the renewal increase itself is the real problem, the better move is to shop the same $40k/$300k/$1,000 limits with two or three competitors this week — not to trade $1,500 of downside for $3/month. Friday afternoon deadline is fine for that comparison; carrier switches usually bind within a day or two.

If you do want to capture something from the deductible lever, the symmetric question to ask the insurer is the opposite: at $1,000 deductible, what's the premium? That's the anchor. Then see whether $500 deductible buys anything meaningful, which is the direction most people under-rate.

1. Leave the scab alone. Don't pick, peel, or scrub it off. The skin underneath is still re-epithelializing, and lifting the scab pulls that new layer with it, restarts the clock, and reopens a bacterial entry point. If Kibo paws at it with his hind paw, a brief e-collar or a snug t-shirt/sock cover during unsupervised time is reasonable.

2. Cleaning is optional at this stage. If you want to clear flaky debris from the surrounding fur, a soft cloth dampened with warm water, or a dilute chlorhexidine wipe (0.05%), is fine. Avoid hydrogen peroxide (damages healing cells) and avoid alcohol. Don't soak the scab itself — moisture softens it and can lift it before the skin underneath is ready.

3. Routine vet-call triggers despite the current improvement:
- Scab unchanged past week 3-4, or pink/red ring reappears around it after fading
- Patch of hair loss or persistent scaling around the site
- A small, firm pea-sized nodule still palpable under the skin once the scab drops — usually a benign reaction to retained mouthparts, but worth confirming
- Kibo starts scratching the spot repeatedly
- Mild intermittent lameness, joint stiffness, low energy, or appetite drop in the next 2-4 weeks (tick-borne disease window for Lyme/anaplasma/ehrlichia — worth a heads-up to the clinic even if subtle)

For contrast, same-day (not routine) signs: rapid swelling, heat, pain, pus discharge, a quickly enlarging lump, fever, marked lethargy, or sudden lameness.

A neutral shadow against rust fur reads as a decal because it has no temperature relationship with the figure. Interior cast shadows pick up cool ambient bounce (gray-blue from walls and window light), and that temperature contrast is what makes a shadow look like it shares a room with the dog. Cool fixes that. The rim of light has to stay bone dry and untouched — every pass stops short of it.

Sequence, all on dry paper:

1. Glaze 1 — establish the cool field. Mix French ultramarine (PB29) thin, roughly 2:1 water to pigment. PB29 leans slightly violet and granulates softly on cold-press, which gives the floor texture instead of a flat stain. Avoid Payne's gray here — it leans neutral and reads as dirt against warm fur. Paint the cast shadow as a single shape, leaving 1–2mm of dry paper between your brush and Kibo's silhouette all the way around. Outer edge soft (penumbra); inner edge can sit slightly harder (umbra). Dry fully.

2. Glaze 2 — anchor the umbra. Same ultramarine, slightly stronger (about 1.5:1), still cool. If you want more depth without losing the cool, add a tiny amount of dioxazine violet rather than more blue — violet deepens without going neutral. Paint only the band directly adjacent to Kibo's body, the darkest 20–30% of the shadow. Feather it so there's no internal hard edge; it should grade into glaze 1.

3. Optional glaze 3 — unify. Only if the shadow still reads pasted. A very dilute cool wash (4:1 or weaker), brushed lightly from under Kibo outward. Or, less commonly, a whisper of dilute burnt sienna along the very outer edge of the cast shadow — the place where light bounces back off the floor — reads as reflected warmth and locks the shadow to the surface.

Restrained defaults:
  - Two thin passes is almost always enough. A third is for rescue, not routine.
  - Stop the brush a hair before the rim every time. The rim is doing the work; don't risk it.
  - Don't mix blue with yellow to neutralize — goes muddy against the warm fur.
  - Don't glaze before the paper is bone dry between passes — a damp underlayer lifts the fur wash.

One distinction worth holding: the cast shadow is the pool on the floor behind and under Kibo. The contact points (paws, low belly where fur actually meets floor) are usually a tiny warmer-darker mark — a small touch of burnt umber or raw umber — done before the cool cast shadow, so the figure has a true anchor to the surface. With that single warm whisper in place, the cool cast shadow reads as environment rather than as outline.

Hold the dark facial details until the shadow is dry and resolved. Eyes and nose marks next to a fresh cool wash will read too sharp and pull focus from the soft fur.

Conservative temporary plan for the 40 stabilized photographs after ~6 hours at 67% RH:

First, a calibration: 67% RH for six hours with no condensation, odor, tackiness, or visible change is meaningful exposure but not catastrophic. Mold typically needs 48+ hours at sustained high humidity to establish, and dry sleeves/boxes means no ferrotyping occurred. You have room to be deliberate — not room to be casual.

  1. Relocation of the closed boxes

  Move them out of the closet to a stable interior room on the main living floor. In order of preference:
    - A room you're actually comfortable in right now (window AC, central air, or dehumidifier running).
    - Avoid: kitchen, bathroom, laundry room, basement (often 60%+ year-round), attic, garage, exterior-wall closets.
    - Avoid any room where cooking, showering, or drying clothes is happening today — those activities spike RH by 10-20 points for an hour or more.
    - Keep boxes out of direct sunlight. UV + ambient heat is bad for chromogenic dyes and for dimensional stability.

  Do not seal the boxes in plastic bags or bins. The closed archival boxes already buffer adequately; trapping 67%-RH air inside an airtight container risks localized condensation when AC surfaces cool later. Slow equilibration through the box walls is what you want.

  Move them level, ideally as a single stacked unit, no tilting, no jostling. One careful move is better than leaving them in marginal conditions for another 6-12 hours.

  2. Monitoring without opening

  - Place a digital hygrometer/thermometer with min-max memory ON TOP of or BESIDE the boxes — not inside. Check it once a day. The min-max tells you whether conditions swung while you weren't looking. Target: stable 40-55% RH and 65-72°F.
  - If the room RH is consistently above 60%, run a dehumidifier in that room (not pointed directly at the boxes).
  - Do not open any box to "peek." Opening introduces fresh humid air and disrupts the slightly-buffered microclimate inside the closed box. One inspection later is fine — only after conditions have been stable for at least 24 hours post-repair.
  - Non-invasive signals you can use now:
      * Sniff near (not at) a closed box seam — musty or sour smell = trouble.
      * Look at the outside of each lid — fog, droplets, or visible moisture = trouble.
      * If you have a small kitchen/luggage scale, weigh each box now and again in 3-4 days. Paper absorbs moisture; a measurable weight gain means humidity is still migrating in.

  3. Conservator triggers — call a professional if you see any of these

  - Visible mold anywhere — white, green, gray, or black spots, fuzz, or web-like growth on prints, sleeves, or interior box surfaces. Even one small spot.
  - Musty or sour smell from inside a closed box.
  - Tackiness, slipperiness, or stickiness on print surfaces during the eventual inspection.
  - Ferrotyping — a glossy print face fused to its sleeve/envelope, leaving a shiny patch when separated.
  - Cockling, warping, curling, or waviness in any print.
  - Whitish haze, new silver mirroring, or any image-quality change beyond the pre-existing condition.
  - Condensation inside a box (fog on the lid interior, droplets on the print surface).
  - Sustained RH above 65% in the storage room for more than 24 hours despite dehumidification.
  - Any direct water contact, even brief.

  Even without these signs, given a collection of 40 stabilized prints and a documented humidity event, a phone consultation with a paper/photograph conservator in the next 1-2 weeks is reasonable and proportionate. The AIC Find-a-Conservator directory (culturalheritage.org) lists one near you; most will do a brief free phone consult.

  After the AC is restored

  Let the closet run with the door open for 24-48 hours before moving the boxes back, so its climate re-equilibrates. When you do move them back, do it when the destination RH is within ~5 points of the room RH they've been sitting in — otherwise they get a second humidity swing. The original closet is actually a fine long-term storage location once AC is functional; small enclosed spaces buffer well against daily RH swings, which is what you want for photo storage.

  When you eventually open the boxes for inspection, do it one at a time in stable conditions, on a clean dry surface, and photograph anything that looks off before touching it.

Short answer: an 8 mm sidewall cut with visible casing means the tire is done for commuting duty. A boot is a "get home / get to the shop" patch, not ongoing safety equipment.

Why, in plain terms:

  The casing is the structural fabric that holds the tire together under inflation and your weight. Once the outer rubber is cut through and you can see threads, those threads are severed. The tire still holds pressure because enough casing is still intact — and the absence of a bulge is a good sign that nothing has started to delaminate yet. But the sidewall flexes every revolution, and on a loaded commute (your weight, rack/pannier load, road buzz, the occasional pothole or curb) the cut is the highest-stress point. Failure modes are a sudden blowout under load, the casing zipper-tearing further, or a frayed thread working through into the tube.

  A boot (Park Tool boot patch, a cut piece of old tire, tough nylon, even a folded bill in a pinch) goes between the tube and the tire. Its job is just to keep the tube from herniating through the cut and to give the damaged area a little extra support. It does not restore casing strength. Mechanics generally treat boots as a one-ride emergency repair to limp home or to the bike shop, not as something you keep commuting on.

  So:
    - If you're already out and need to get back: boot it, ride cautiously (lower pressure a bit if you can, avoid big hits), get home or to a shop.
    - Before riding to work again: replace the tire. At ~8 mm with visible casing on a sidewall that will be loaded, riding on it is choosing a noticeably elevated blowout risk against the cost of one new tire.

  One nuance worth flagging since I can't see the tire: if the cut is very close to the bead (the wire ring that seats on the rim), it's even more urgent than a mid-sidewall cut, because bead-area damage compromises the tire's seal under load. Mid-sidewall at 8 mm is already a replace; bead-adjacent is "don't even boot it for the ride home if you can avoid it."

Not a mechanic — this is the consensus view across the usual sources (Park Tool repair help, Sheldon Brown's site, bike-shop guidance), and it's the answer I'd give my own commuter bike.

Here is the distinction, written so it can stand on its own or be adapted into a Slack/email reply to Marcus.

What $18,960 / 52 actually describes
- Refund-adjusted cash collected across the mature Helio Start cohort, divided by admitted workspace count.
- It is observed average organic cash per admitted workspace in a matched cohort.
- It is a revenue-side, descriptive figure: cash yield per workspace in the organic pricing-page channel.
- It is not an acquisition cost. There is no acquisition cost in the numerator.

Why it is not a paid CAC
A paid CAC needs three things this evidence does not contain:
- Paid-media spend in the numerator. CAC = paid acquisition spend / net new paid-acquired workspaces. The mature Helio Start cohort has no paid spend attributable to it.
- Channel attribution and acquisition mix. A paid CAC is channel-specific; you have to know which workspaces came in through the paid channel versus organic, repeat, or other paid channels. The 52-workspace cohort is by construction an organic cohort — there is no paid-channel breakdown to divide by.
- Incrementality. A CAC is supposed to measure the marginal cost of acquiring one more workspace through paid. Establishing that requires a paid-vs-not-paid comparison (holdout, matched-pair, geo test, or a matched intent-to-treatment design). The mature Helio Start evidence is descriptive of an organic cohort, not causal for a paid treatment.

The category error
The two figures have different units and opposite business meaning:
- CAC numerator = paid cost (what you spend to acquire)
- $18,960 numerator = organic cash collected (what those workspaces have paid you)

Calling the quotient an "allowable paid CAC" inverts the formula and reassigns the sign. A $/workspace figure derived from cash collected describes yield per workspace, not cost per acquisition. Yield supports a "is this worth paying for" question; it does not answer "what did it cost to acquire."

What the $364.62 is and is not usable for
- Usable as: a per-workspace cash-yield reference point for the mature organic Helio Start cohort, alongside its retention and refund profile.
- Not usable as: an allowable CAC, a ceiling for paid-media bids, the basis for a paid-channel test design, or a justification for a paid-acquisition proposal on its own.

Where the mature Helio Start evidence fits in the revisit gate
The revisit gate is the combination of three things evaluated together, not any one of them in isolation:
- mature retention,
- refund-adjusted cash,
- account-level support effort (Owen + CS).

That combination is the precondition for revisiting paid acquisition. It is not the design of a paid test. A paid-acq proposal still needs its own design — paid spend level, channel(s), attribution, an incrementality design with a holdout or matched comparator, and an a-priori decision rule. The mature Helio Start cohort does not supply any of those, and the cohort evidence is necessary context for a future proposal, not a substitute for one.

Note on pattern
This is the third attempt to fold mature Helio Start evidence into a paid-acq justification (after the original paid-acq test and the Q3 pipeline target). The consistent answer has been: the cohort is necessary evidence for any later paid proposal, but it does not, by itself, constitute, justify, or bound a paid test. Recommendation: the puncture-protected 700x32 at $58 installed.

The reason isn't the price gap — it's that your stated priorities line up with what that tire buys you.

What the $58 tire actually gives you that the $44 one doesn't:

- A puncture belt (usually an aramid/Kevlar layer, sometimes a thicker casing) under the tread that resists penetration from glass, wire, thorns, and the rough-pavement debris that caused today's 8mm sidewall cut. Your existing failure mode is the evidence here — a casing-visible cut is exactly the kind of event this layer is designed to prevent or at least contain.
- More predictable wet behavior. Puncture-protected commuter tires typically pair the belt with a more aggressive tread compound and better casing stability, which improves cornering grip and reduces the chance of a sudden deflation on a painted line, manhole cover, or wet tram track — all common wet-commute hazards.
- Longer service life on rough pavement, since the belt slows tread wear and casing fatigue.

The tradeoff you're accepting with the heavier tire:

- Rotational weight. You'll feel a small sluggishness off the line and a slightly less eager spin-up compared to the lighter casing. On a flat commute this is mostly cosmetic; you'll notice it more on climbs or if you sprint from lights.
- Slightly harsher ride feel at the same pressure, because the stiffer casing transmits more vibration. You can partially offset this by running a few PSI lower than the sidewall max — a 700x32 at ~55–65 psi on rough pavement rides noticeably more comfortably than at 80+ without meaningful rolling-resistance penalty.
- Marginal top-speed cost on a sustained effort. For commuting, this is irrelevant.

Why this matches your stated priorities:

- "Predictable commuting matters more than saving rotational weight" — that sentence alone settles it. The whole point of the $44 tire is lower rotational weight. You're paying for the opposite of what you said you value.
- Rough city pavement + wet conditions is the textbook use case for a puncture-protected commuter tire. The lighter tire is the right pick for someone prioritizing efficiency on smoother roads in dry weather — that's not your situation.

One practical note: since the cut is on the rear sidewall with casing visible, make sure the shop inspects the rim and rim tape before mounting the new tire. A sidewall cut that deep often means debris worked its way around the rim, and a fresh tire on a damaged rim tape will give you a slow leak that looks like the new tire's fault.

# Containment and diagnostic sequence — 11 delivered trial-ending rows

## Frame (what we know vs. what's open)

  Known (locked):
  - Friday: QuickBits.io is an active paid Starter customer (sub_helio_starter_sentinel_001, starter_25_seats, $440 MRR since 2025-09-30). Receipt of a "trial-ending" template is a known defect signature.
  - 11 delivered rows from the unpaid-trial campaign share one template.
  - Every delivered row has a populated `trial_end_at` in the lifecycle export.

  Open (the three hypotheses you named):
  - H1 — Audience-state failure: the campaign's eligibility query pulled rows whose actual billing state is paid/active or otherwise ineligible, but `trial_end_at` was non-null because the lifecycle export doesn't drop the trial-clock on conversion. The template is correct for true unpaid trials.
  - H2 — Billing-state lag: lifecycle export reflects a pre-conversion snapshot; the billing-state column or related event hasn't propagated yet, and at send time the customer was actually paid. The audience query was correct in principle; the export is stale.
  - H3 — Template defect: the template itself is wrong — copy, subject, or render condition misfires regardless of audience state (e.g., fires when `trial_end_at IS NOT NULL` rather than when billing state is unpaid). If so, even a correct audience would still leak.

  These are not mutually exclusive, and the sequence must let us distinguish them on the same evidence.

## Principles this sequence enforces (consistent with the runbook pattern)

  1. State snapshot at query execution, not pre-computed export. Re-derive audience state from the source-of-truth tables the moment we rerun, and record the as_of timestamp.
  2. Account-level eligibility base, then attach admins. Never drive the suppression decision off the admin row.
  3. Independent rerun reproduces recipient IDs and exclusions — Ines reruns, you (or a second person) rerun, results match.
  4. Send log and lifecycle export are immutable evidence rows from this point. No retroactive edits. Post-snapshot changes are recorded as subsequent events.
  5. Nothing queued or sent during the hold; unrelated campaigns untouched.
  6. Pre-send QA gate stays the same one Ines owns: duplicate parity, zero active-suppression matches, no global unsubscribes, no hard bounces, test-send render OK.

## Phase 0 — Freeze and preserve evidence (do this first, in order)

  Goal: stop further sends of the defective template, and lock the 11 rows so nothing in the export or send log gets overwritten by a normal lifecycle update.

  0.1  Pause the unpaid-trial campaign workflow in Customer.io. Pause, not delete — we need it intact for diagnostics. Confirm no scheduled send is in the next send window. Record the pause event with timestamp and actor in the campaign record.

  0.2  Snapshot the Customer.io send log for the unpaid-trial campaign: the 11 delivered rows plus any held/queued/suppressed siblings from the same run. Export and store as `unpaid_trial_sendlog_2024-08-26.csv`. This is the delivery evidence — it must not change.

  0.3  Snapshot the lifecycle export as it stood at the moment the campaign queried it: `lifecycle_at_query_ts.csv`, with the `as_of` value the audience query used. This is the state-of-truth-as-the-campaign-saw-it. Do not let a re-export replace it; later refreshes become a separate file (`lifecycle_post_snapshot.csv`) for the lag hypothesis.

  0.4  Snapshot the audience query itself — the SQL or Customer.io segment definition, the suppression list in effect, and the resulting 11 recipient IDs and admin emails. Save the query text verbatim, not a paraphrase.

  0.5  Confirm unrelated campaigns (day-7, setup reminder, day-14 check-in, abandoned-intake reminder, etc.) are not paused and not affected by the same predicate. The defect should be scoped to this one campaign until evidence says otherwise.

  0.6  Open a campaign record / preflight doc with: campaign name, pause time, the three evidence files, the as_of timestamp, the 11 recipient IDs, and a hypothesis table with H1/H2/H3 and a status column (open / partial / closed). Ines owns lifecycle pre-send; the record lives with her.

  You should now be able to answer: "How many messages went out, to whom, on what template, against what audience state, with what suppressions, and can we reproduce that exactly?" If any of those is a no, Phase 0 isn't done.

## Phase 1 — Disambiguate H1 (audience-state failure) vs. H2 (billing-state lag) vs. H3 (template defect)

  These run in parallel as far as the data is concerned, but Phase 1.1 should happen before 1.2 and 1.3 because it determines whether 1.2 and 1.3 are even the right next questions.

  1.1  Billing state of the 11 recipients, at the *current* moment (not at the original query's as_of).
        For each of the 11:
          - Pull the customer's subscription store row (status, plan, MRR, started_at).
          - Pull the most recent successful invoice and any open invoices.
          - Pull the customer's most recent billing-state event from the source event stream.
        Classification per recipient:
          a. Active paid subscription now → audience-state failure (H1) confirmed for this row. They were never eligible for a trial-ending template.
          b. Active paid at query time but lapsed/canceled since → still H1 for the original send (the send was wrong), but log the state change as a subsequent event.
          c. Active paid at query time and still active → same as (a).
          d. Trial-now → H2 candidate: they may have been unpaid at send time; the question is whether the lifecycle export correctly reflected that.
          e. Canceled/expired trial with no paid conversion → they were correctly eligible, which means H3 (template) is implicated or the message was acceptable but the customer's lifecycle expectation was miscalibrated.

        Expected shape for an unpaid-trial defect: most or all 11 land in (a) — QuickBits is the canary, and the audience query is letting paid customers through. If a meaningful share lands in (d), H2 is real and the export is the failure surface. If a meaningful share lands in (e), H3 is real.

  1.2  Lifecycle export join audit (H1 vs. H2 distinguisher).
        Take `lifecycle_at_query_ts.csv` and join to:
          - The current subscription store (status at query time, recoverable from billing event history).
          - The audit log of billing-state events between query-as_of and now.
        For each of the 11, classify:
          - State in lifecycle export at query time: trial / paid / lapsed / unknown.
          - State in billing source-of-truth at query time: same.
          - State in billing source-of-truth now: same.
        Outcomes:
          - Lifecycle said "trial," billing said "paid" at query time → H1 (the export is wrong, or the join dropped billing state).
          - Lifecycle said "paid," but the template's eligibility predicate ignored billing state and only used `trial_end_at IS NOT NULL` → H3 (template).
          - Lifecycle and billing both said "trial" at query time, and the customer is still on trial → H1 unlikely; H3 or a new H4 ("trial-ending template shouldn't have been sent to a healthy trial") is the candidate.
          - Lifecycle said "trial," billing said "paid" now but said "trial" at query time → H2 confirmed: lag. (This is the row class that argues for send-time final-state suppression.)

  1.3  Template render audit (H3 specific).
        Pull the trial-ending template source. For each of the 11, render the template against the row's lifecycle data exactly as the send would have. Compare to the message actually delivered (Customer.io render log or archive).
        Specifically check:
          - Eligibility predicate. If it's `trial_end_at IS NOT NULL` without an AND on billing_state IN ('trial','unpaid','past_due'), H3 is confirmed for every row the export classified as paid. This is the most common failure shape for this campaign class and is exactly the kind of defect a state-snapshot fix alone won't cure.
          - Liquid render exceptions, missing-attribute warnings, and whether the workspace/admin context was the right one. A Customer.io profile-sync delay can cause the wrong workspace's render to fire (we've seen this before — six workspaces connected their integrations 20–47 minutes before export, profiles still showed incomplete, send held, profiles synced, no send). Render the 11 against current profiles; if a different workspace would now resolve, that's a profile-sync class problem, distinct from H1/H2/H3 but worth flagging.
          - Subject and body wording. If the template says anything implying "trial is ending, set up billing to continue," that copy is unsafe to send to a paid Starter customer regardless of how the audience got there.

  1.4  Independent rerun (the audit gate).
        Ines reruns the original audience query against the same as_of snapshot and reproduces every recipient ID and exclusion. A second person (or the contractor) reruns independently and confirms the same 11. If the rerun reproduces 11 eligible recipients under the original query, the audience-query logic is what let them through — H1 confirmed by reproduction. If the rerun excludes them once the corrected predicate is applied, the fix path is clear; if the rerun still includes them, the predicate itself is wrong and H3 is implicated.

## Phase 2 — Containment actions keyed to the classification

  These are the actions, not just findings. Each is gated on Phase 1 evidence.

  2.1  H1 confirmed (audience predicate wrong):
        - Apply the corrected eligibility predicate: billing_state IN (trial-unpaid classes) AND trial_end_at IS NOT NULL AND no active paid subscription AND not unsubscribed AND not on a CS-open or recent-support-contact list.
        - Re-run audience preview; require the 11 to drop to 0 before any send is unpaused.
        - Decide whether the corrected audience still has any eligible recipients. If it does, queue only after Ines's full pre-send QA (duplicate parity, suppression matches, render test).
        - If the corrected audience is empty, the campaign may be paused indefinitely pending a re-scope with the campaign owner. Don't ship a campaign to zero.

  2.2  H2 confirmed (billing-state lag in the export):
        - Treat the lifecycle export as unfit as a direct audience source. Replace with send-time final-state suppression: at send, pull current billing state and suppress if the customer has reached a paid, canceled, or assisted state. This is the pattern that's already shipped elsewhere and works.
        - Re-run audience preview against the new pipeline; require 0 paid customers in the result.

  2.3  H3 confirmed (template defect):

Recommended method: primary-driver + secondary-tag (zero minutes).

Schema for each of the 23 mixed contacts

  primary_issue     = the single issue that owns the full contact minutes
  secondary_issues  = zero or more issues that also came up, carrying 0 minutes
  minutes           = stays attached to the contact as a whole, not split

Total minutes across the 66 contacts stays at 684 by construction: every contact contributes its minutes exactly once, to its primary.

Picking the primary — commit the rule before reading the notes

  1. If CS already tagged a "main topic" on the contact, use it.
  2. Else use first-mentioned-in-notes (the issue that opens the contact record).
  3. Else use the resolution-critical issue (the one whose unblock let the
     contact end). Use this only when 1 and 2 don't apply, and flag it.

The rule is decided once and applied uniformly. Document it in the brief so the read is reproducible and so you can't be accused of rationalising after the fact.

How the issue-level operating read works (this is the part most analyses get wrong)

Report two metrics per issue, never one:

  minutes_primary      = sum of contact minutes where primary = issue
  contacts_touched     = count of contacts where issue is in primary OR secondary

minutes_primary is the time-attribution read (no double-count, no fabricated splits).
contacts_touched is the multi-issue signal — it tells you which issues show up in conversations even when they aren't the main reason for the contact.

Example for permissions:
  minutes_primary_permissions = sum over contacts whose primary is permissions
  contacts_touched_permissions = contacts where permissions is primary OR secondary

Reporting only minutes_primary undercounts the true permissions footprint; reporting only contacts_touched loses the time weight. The pair is the read.

Worked example

A 12-minute mixed contact: "Permissions — locked out of dashboard. Then automation — needs help designing the welcome workflow."

  primary_issue     = permissions
  secondary_issues  = [automation_design]
  minutes           = 12 (all attributed to permissions)

  minutes_primary_permissions       += 12
  contacts_touched_automation        += 1   (secondary, no minutes)

If you had split 6/6, you'd be asserting the operator spent equal time on a 2-minute unlock and a 10-minute design session — that precision is not in the notes. If you had tagged both at 12, automation would carry 12 phantom minutes. Primary-driver + secondary-tag keeps the minutes honest and the multi-topic signal visible.

What to avoid

  - Winner-take-all on the 43 clean contacts is fine; applying it to the 23
    mixed contacts erases the secondary signal entirely. Don't.
  - Equal-split minutes ("allocate proportionally to issue count") invents a
    precision the notes don't support. Don't.
  - Counting each tag at full minutes breaks the 684 total. Don't.
  - Letting the primary rule vary contact-by-contact based on what "feels
    right" — that destroys reproducibility. Pick the rule, apply it.

What to add to the brief alongside the numbers

  - The primary-driver rule (one sentence).
  - minutes_primary and contacts_touched, per issue, side by side.
  - One aggregate: share of the 66 contacts that carry at least one secondary
    tag (i.e. multi-issue share). For the 23 mixed contacts this is 23/66 ≈
    35%. That's the headline operating signal that pure single-tag would hide:
    more than a third of post-admission contacts span more than one topic,
    which has direct implications for how CS scripts the queue.

Bottom line

Primary-driver + secondary-tag preserves all 684 minutes, attributes each contact's minutes to exactly one issue (no double-count), carries the multi-issue signal at zero-minute cost, and supports a paired-metric issue read that doesn't lie about either time weight or topic breadth. Apply the rule pre-committed, document it once, and report minutes_primary and contacts_touched together.
