Likely cause (educated guess, not diagnosis): a partial clog downstream of where the dishwasher drain line ties into the sink drain. When you ran the dishwasher, its discharge hit the clog and the only place for the water to go was back up into the sink. No sewage smell and no supply-side leak both point to a localized drain-side blockage (grease, food buildup, or a clogged disposal) rather than a main-line or supply-line problem. Good news: usually fixable without wall-opening.

CONTAINMENT (do these now)
  1. Leave the dishwasher off. Its drain hose ties into the sink's drain system; running it will keep pumping water into the same clog, which can overflow onto the floor or siphon dirty water back into the dishwasher tub.
  2. Bail the standing water out of the sink into a bucket and dump it down a different drain (bathtub, shower, or toilet). Less water sitting on top of the clog = less chance of an overflow if someone accidentally runs the tap, and it makes any later snaking easier.
  3. Lay a dry towel or a shallow pan under the sink cabinet to catch any seepage at the P-trap while you wait. Even a slow drain can weep at the trap joints.
  4. Stop using the sink until maintenance clears it. If you must use it (e.g., to fill a pot for cooking), use the smallest amount possible, have someone standing by with a bucket, and do not run the faucet unattended.
  5. If you have a double-bowl sink, plug the working bowl's drain with a wet rag before any minimal use so the clog can't push water up through the shared trap.

SAFE TROUBLESHOOTING YOU CAN TRY (only if you want to; you can also just wait for maintenance)
  - Garbage disposal (if you have one): the overload reset is a small red button on the bottom of the unit. Press it once. Then, with the dishwasher NOT running and the sink empty or nearly so, run water and flip the disposal switch for a few seconds. If it hums without grinding or doesn't turn on, that's the problem — but don't put hands or tools inside.
  - Air gap (if installed): the small chrome cylinder on the countertop next to the faucet. Unscrew the cap, look inside with a flashlight. If it's full of gunk, clean it out — a blocked air gap is a common cause of dishwasher-back-up-into-sink.
  - Dishwasher filter: many dishwashers have a small basket/filter at the bottom. If it's clogged, the dishwasher won't drain properly and can backfeed. Quick to check; twist or pull per the manual.

WHAT NOT TO POUR DOWN THE DRAIN
  - No chemical drain cleaners (Drano, Liquid-Plumr, sulfuric or caustic products). Reasons: (a) they sit in the standing water and release fumes in your kitchen, (b) they're hazardous to the person who comes to snake the line and can splash into eyes/skin, (c) they can damage older metal or PVC pipes and garbage-disposal seals, (d) they often don't fully clear a real clog anyway.
  - No boiling water. Can crack a porcelain or enameled sink, and can soften or loosen joints in PVC drain piping.
  - No grease, oil, or coffee grounds, even as a "flush" — these are common culprits and will worsen a partial clog.
  - No baking-soda-and-vinegar "miracle" mixes for this situation. Mostly cosmetic on real clogs; the fizz doesn't reach the blockage.
  - In short: pour nothing into that sink until it's draining normally.

WHILE YOU WAIT FOR MAINTENANCE — QUICK RULES
  - Dishwasher: stay off. Non-negotiable until the drain clears.
  - Sink: ideally unused. If you absolutely need a few cups of water, bail as you go and plug the other bowl.
  - Run no other water-using appliances (washing machine is usually fine on a separate line, but if it's on the same branch it can also push toward the clog — listen/look if you're unsure).
  - Keep the cabinet door open a crack for airflow; if any moisture appears under the sink, switch to towels and note the time for maintenance.

ESCALATE SOONER IF
  - Water starts coming up into the dishwasher tub or the other sink bowl.
  - Multiple drains elsewhere in the home slow at the same time (suggests a main-line issue, not just the kitchen branch).
  - You notice any wetness under the cabinet, a sewage smell, or gurgling in a nearby tub/floor drain when the sink is used — those change the picture and should go back to maintenance as an update.

You've already done the right things (stopped the dishwasher, filed the request). The above is just to keep things from getting worse and to give you safe things to try if you want to before maintenance arrives.

  - The page relies on JavaScript to render its content, and Safari blocked or stalled it
  - The page is "cloaked" — it serves different content to first-time mobile visitors than to Google's crawlers, which is why Apple's Fraudulent Website Warning didn't fire
  - A redirect or geo-check failed and returned an empty body

None of that means the phone is compromised. On a current iPhone, a single Safari page load with no input cannot install an app, install a profile, capture your Apple ID, or run code on the device.

WHAT (LIKELY) GOT COLLECTED
  - Your IP address (rough city), your browser and device info, sent to whoever runs that domain
  - That's it. No credentials, no card, no codes, no profile, no app, no password.

DEVICE STEPS (iPhone)

1. Settings -> Safari -> scroll down -> "Clear History and Website Data." Drops any cookies or local storage the page set.
2. In the same Safari settings screen, confirm "Fraudulent Website Warning," "Block Pop-ups," and "Prevent Cross-Site Tracking" are all on. They are on by default on a current iOS, but worth confirming.
3. Settings -> General -> VPN & Device Management. It should say "No Device Management" or only show a profile you recognize (for example, a work profile). If anything new is there that you didn't install, that's the one real red flag — tell Riley.
4. Restart the iPhone once. Optional, just clears any in-memory state.
5. Do not install any "security" or "antivirus" app. On iOS they cannot meaningfully scan a Safari visit, and most are themselves scams.

ACCOUNT STEPS

1. Apple ID is the one that matters most. Settings -> [your name] -> Sign-In & Security. Confirm two-factor authentication is on. Scroll the trusted-devices list and sign out anything you don't recognize.
2. Email: turn on two-factor authentication if it isn't already (Gmail, iCloud, Outlook, Yahoo all support it). The same crew sometimes follows up by trying to log into your email.
3. USPS Informed Delivery: if you have an account, sign in via the official USPS app or by typing usps.com yourself — never via a link. Change the password as a precaution.
4. Passwords: if you reuse the same password anywhere that the phishing page might have asked about (email, bank, shopping), rotate those. Since nothing was entered, this is low risk — just a quick pass.
5. Never change a password by following a link from a text or email. Type the address yourself or use a saved bookmark.

REPORTING

1. Forward the text to 7726 (that spells SPAM on a phone keypad). In Messages: long-press the bubble -> "More..." -> tap the forward arrow at the bottom right -> send to 7726. AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon all participate; you'll get an auto-reply.
2. Email a screenshot of the text to spam@uspis.gov — the USPS Inspection Service is the actual law-enforcement arm that investigates these.
3. File a short report at reportfraud.ftc.gov — about 5 minutes, helps federal tracking.
4. After forwarding, delete the message and block the sender (Messages -> tap the number at the top -> scroll down -> "Block this Caller").

MONITORING (NEXT 30 DAYS)

1. Expect a possible second wave: a follow-up text, an email, or a phone call claiming to be from USPS, "Apple Security," your bank, or even the FTC — using your real name or the same "package held" pretext. One tap on a phishing link confirms your number is live, so it often gets sold onward. The rule: any unsolicited call asking you to install something, share a code, or visit a site — hang up and call the company back at the number on its official website.
2. Bank and credit-card statements: scan weekly for anything odd. No card was entered, so baseline risk is low, but a glance costs nothing.
3. Place a free one-year fraud alert through any one of the three credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, or TransUnion). They are required to notify the other two. It makes it harder for anyone to open new credit in your name. Even with nothing entered, this is good baseline hygiene.
4. If anything unexpected shows up over the next month — a charge, an email saying your Apple ID was used on a new device, or a USPS text asking for money to release a real package — tell Riley right away and we'll handle it together.

BOTTOM LINE

Because nothing was typed, the risk drops from "real" to "minimal." Everything above is reasonable hygiene, not panic-mode. You're in good shape.

ASSESSMENT

Load-dependent skip in specific gears, light pedaling clean, no brake rub, wheels seated — this is the textbook signature of drivetrain wear, most likely a stretched chain engaging worn cassette teeth (and possibly a worn chainring). The overnight rain didn't cause the wear; it likely washed residual lube out of the chain joints, which made a marginal drivetrain suddenly noticeable. This is a wear condition, not a progressive failure — the chain isn't about to throw or break, and the skip only occurs under heavy pedal force.

Easy ride home is reasonable if you ride conservatively. Take the bus if any of these apply: your route has steep climbs; the two affected gears include your easiest climbing cog; traffic requires hard acceleration or out-of-saddle efforts; you don't feel confident on it; or the weather is wet (skip plus wet rims plus braking force is a worse combination than skip alone).

If you ride home:
  - Avoid the two affected middle gears. Downshift to easier cogs and keep cadence moderate.
  - Stay seated; don't stand on the pedals.
  - Keep force moderate — smooth pedaling at a normal load should be clean.
  - Expect one lurch per revolution if you hit a bad gear under load. It's startling, not a loss of control, but it can upset balance in a tight maneuver, so avoid those.

SAFE INSPECTION SEQUENCE (at home)

  1. Position the bike so the drivetrain is at chest height against a wall or on a hook. Good light matters — a headlamp or phone flashlight is worth the trouble.

  2. Cassette visual check. With gloves, slowly back-pedal and look at each cog from the side. Healthy teeth are symmetric with squared-off tops. Worn teeth look like shark fins — symmetrically pointed and leaning outward. Check every cog, not just the middle two; middle cogs usually show wear first because that's where most riding happens.

  3. Chain wear check. Two methods:
     a. Chain checker tool — 0.5% means replace the chain; 0.75% means replace chain AND cassette (a new chain on a worn cassette will skip immediately).
     b. Without a tool: measure 12 full links pin-to-pin. Twelve links should measure exactly 304.8 mm. 305.6 mm (about 1/16") = past 0.5%. 307 mm (about 1/8") = past 0.75%.

  4. Chainring check. Look at the drive-side face of the front chainring under the same light. Healthy teeth are symmetric trapezoids; worn teeth are hooked, with the leading edge curving outward. A worn chainring typically affects ALL rear gears because the chainring is shared across the cassette, so if the skip is gear-specific (only middle cogs), the chainring is probably secondary, not the primary culprit.

  5. Stiff link check. Shift to the small ring + biggest cog so the chain is slack. Flex each link side-to-side with clean hands. A stiff link won't articulate freely. If you find one, don't ride it — flex it laterally with the chain on each side of the joint, drop of lube on the pin helps. A stiff link usually skips in a single specific gear pattern, so if you're skipping in two different middle cogs, stiff link is less likely — but it's free to rule out.

  6. Derailleur hanger alignment. Sight down the rear derailleur from behind the bike. The two jockey pulleys should line up directly under the cassette cogs. A bent hanger shifts poorly across the whole range; if shifting otherwise feels normal, this is probably fine, but it's a ten-second check.

SHOP-REPORTING SEQUENCE

The goal is to make clear this is a system-wear issue, not a tensioning issue. A shop that just throws a new chain on a worn cassette will hand the bike back skipping under load and you'll be back within a week.

Report content (write it down or put it in the work order):

  - Symptom: chain skips once per crank revolution under heavy pedaling force; absent under light load. Clean under casual pedaling.
  - Affected gears: name the two cogs (e.g., "4th and 5th of 11-speed cassette"). Clean shifting and clean pedaling under load in all other gears.
  - Brakes: not rubbing. Wheels: seated, no play.
  - Recent history: bike sat overnight under a covered office rack in rain; symptom appeared on next ride. The rain likely washed lube and revealed pre-existing wear rather than causing it.
  - Inspection at home: cassette teeth condition (describe what you saw); chain wear measurement if you took one; chainring condition; stiff link test result.
  - Request:
    - Replace chain and cassette as a system. If the chainring shows wear, replace it at the same time — riding a new chain on a worn chainring will skip and accelerate wear on the new cassette.
    - Check derailleur hanger alignment.
    - Check cable tension and B-screw with the new drivetrain installed.
    - Lube and load-test across the full gear range before pickup.

If the shop pushes back on replacing the cassette ("let's just try a new chain first"), the right answer is: visibly hooked cassette teeth will skip on a new chain. Measure, don't guess — and ask them to show you the cassette teeth before authorizing work.

ASSESSMENT OF THE ENZYME SUGGESTION

Sensible, with one expectation to calibrate. Enzymatic cleaners (live bacterial cultures + enzymes like protease, lipase, amylase) are built for partial organic blockages — grease, food residue, soap scum in the trap or branch line. Your symptom picture fits that:

  - Slow drain alone = restricted flow but not fully blocked
  - Backup only when the dishwasher discharges = a partial blockage downstream of the trap, overwhelmed by the DW's slug (5–8 gal pumped out in a short cycle)
  - No sewage smell = trap is holding water and venting is intact (rules out dry trap or venting failure)
  - No supply leak = rules out pressurized-side issues

So enzymes are a reasonable interim measure for the slow-sink-alone symptom. One important caveat: an enzyme dose poured down the sink sits mostly in the P-trap. It may not reach far enough down the branch line to clear the partial blockage that the DW discharge exposes. The enzyme is more likely to help sink-alone flow than to eliminate the DW backup. Keep your expectations anchored there.

ENZYME LABEL — CONDITIONS THAT ACTUALLY MATTER

When you pick a product, the things worth checking:

  1. Disclosed cultures and enzymes. Look for named strains (Bacillus, Pseudomonas) and specific enzymes (protease, lipase, amylase). "Secret blend" or unspecified cultures are usually weak.
  2. Viable culture / CFU. Better products state colony-forming units or "viable through [date]." Old stock on a shelf may be inert.
  3. pH range. Most work near neutral (6.5–8.5). You haven't used any chemicals, so the line is fine.
  4. Temperature. Room-temp to hot tap water is OK. Do NOT pour boiling water — it kills the bacteria and can crack porcelain or cast iron.
  5. Contact time. The label will say something like 6–8 hours or "overnight." This is the most important number. Short contact = almost no effect. Dose at bedtime, don't run that drain until morning.
  6. Dosage. Follow the label — over-dosing doesn't help. Typical is a capful or scoop per drain.
  7. Septic safety. Should be marked safe. Almost all enzymatic products are.
  8. Garbage-disposal compatibility. If you have a disposal, many labels say to run it briefly with water after dosing so the product moves past the grind chamber into the trap.
  9. Compatibility warning. Should explicitly say "do not mix with bleach, ammonia, or caustic drain openers." This is critical — do not combine.

INTERIM GUIDANCE, NOW THROUGH TUE OCT 15 09:00

Sink-use rules starting today:

  - Scrape plates into trash/compost before rinsing. Sink strainer in place at all times.
  - No fats down the drain: no frying oil, no bacon/pan grease, no butter, no dairy. Fats re-solidify in the line and are exactly what you're trying to clear.
  - If you use the disposal, run it only with a strong stream of COLD water. Cold keeps fats solid so the grinder can break them up; hot water melts fats, which then re-congeal downstream.
  - After each sink use, run hot tap water for 10–15 seconds to flush the line.
  - Pour one enzyme dose per the label at bedtime the night before the visit (Mon Oct 14). Let it sit untouched overnight. Run only the sink briefly in the morning; do not run hot water for long, and do not pour boiling water.

Dishwasher-use rules starting today:

  - Preferred: do not run the DW until after the visit. Two days is a small cost to avoid a backup. This is the cleanest path.
  - If you must run it: pick the late evening after a fresh enzyme dose, and pre-stage a manual flush. Fill the sink partway with hot tap water right before the DW's drain phase. As the DW pumps out, manually dump the sink water into the drain at the same time — your bucket/flow adds volume that helps push the partial blockage through. Stay near the sink for that minute or two.
  - Do not run the DW overnight unattended. If it backs up while you're asleep, you'll know about it only when you step in water.

THINGS TO AVOID UNTIL AFTER THE VISIT

  - No chemical drain openers (Drano, Liquid-Plumr, lye, sulfuric-acid products). Reasons: damage plumbing over time, dangerous to the maintenance tech working the line Tuesday, and they interact badly with any enzyme residue.
  - No boiling water down the drain.
  - No aggressive plunging — you can blow out trap seals or push the blockage deeper.
  - No mechanical snake unless you're experienced with kitchen lines; the trap configuration makes this easy to get wrong.

WHAT TO TELL THE TECH ON TUESDAY

Briefly: enzyme used, no chemical opener, symptoms (slow sink alone, DW causes backup, no smell, no leak), and when each started. The tech will likely snake the branch line past the trap; knowing the upstream state helps them read what's coming back.

ESCALATE BEFORE TUESDAY IF YOU SEE

The $60 gap between the EOB and the portal balance is almost certainly a timing-and-adjustment issue, not a billing error or an indication you owe $95. Here's how to think about it, what to compare, and what to ask before paying anything.

The reconciliation principle
- An EOB is not a bill. It is your insurer's explanation of how they adjudicated the claim: what they allowed, what they paid, and what they assigned to you. The clinic's portal balance is what the clinic's system currently shows you owe, based on charges and payments it has actually posted.
- The portal status "insurance pending" is the key clue. It means the clinic has submitted the claim but has not yet received and posted the ERA (Electronic Remittance Advice) from your insurer. Your EOB is the patient-facing version of that ERA. Insurance processed 10/09; the clinic's posting typically lags by days to a few weeks.

Why the numbers don't match yet
The accounting identity for any claim is:
  billed amount
  - contractual adjustment (billed minus allowed)
  - insurance payment
  - patient payments already made
  = remaining patient balance

Your EOB shows: allowed $145, plan paid $110, patient responsibility $35. It does NOT show the original billed amount. The most common scenario that produces a $95 portal balance alongside a $35 EOB patient share is:
  - Clinic billed gross charge, e.g. $205
  - Insurer allowed $145 → contractual write-off of $60
  - Insurer paid $110
  - Patient owes $35
  - Until the $60 write-off posts, portal shows: $205 - $110 = $95 remaining
  - Once the write-off posts, balance drops to $35

Secondary possibilities to rule out: the $95 includes a different visit or a prior balance; or the clinic billed exactly $145 and there is a separate non-covered line item. The questions below are designed to surface which one it is.

Identifiers and records to compare and retain
For the 10/02/2024 visit, line these up side by side and keep copies:
1. Date of service — both sides show 10/02/2024, so the visit matches.
2. Provider name and NPI on the EOB — compare to the clinic's superbill/visit summary.
3. CPT procedure code(s) on the EOB — compare to the superbill. The codes drive the allowed amount; any mismatch changes everything.
4. ICD-10 diagnosis code(s) on the EOB — compare to visit notes. A mismatched diagnosis can trigger a different allowed amount or denial.
5. Original billed amount on the claim the clinic sent to insurance — not on the EOB; you have to request it from billing (CMS-1500 or 837 file).
6. Allowed amount — EOB $145.
7. Insurance payment — EOB $110, plus check/EFT trace number if listed.
8. Patient responsibility — EOB $35.
9. Contractual adjustment — derived as billed minus allowed; ask billing to confirm in dollars.
10. Claim number — EOB (top right area, often called Claim # or Reference #).
11. Member ID and group number — EOB header.
12. Date processed — EOB 10/09/2024 (sets the expected posting window).
13. Any denial codes, remark codes, or CO-x codes on the EOB — usually on the back or in small print; they explain why the patient share is what it is.
14. The clinic's original superbill or visit summary for 10/02.
15. The EOB itself (PDF or paper) — retain at least 12 months; longer if you anticipate any appeal.

Retain all of these in one place. If anything goes to dispute, the EOB plus the clinic's claim submission is the document pair that resolves almost everything.

Specific questions to ask billing before paying anything
Ask in this order; the early ones establish facts, the later ones pin down what you'll actually owe.

1. What was the original billed amount you submitted to insurance for the 10/02/2024 visit, and what CPT and ICD-10 codes were on it?
   (Establishes the basis; lets you compute the contractual adjustment yourself.)

2. Has the insurance payment of $110 for this claim been posted to my account yet?
   (Confirms whether the portal balance is pre- or post-payment.)

3. What is the current status of claim [claim # from EOB] in your system — submitted, paid, adjusted, or pending?
   (Sanity check against the portal's "insurance pending" label.)

4. Once the insurance payment posts, will a contractual adjustment be applied? If so, in what amount, and what will my remaining patient balance be?
   (The reconciliation question; the answer should be $35.)

5. Will you email me an updated itemized statement after insurance processes, so I can verify the balance matches the EOB's $35 patient responsibility for 10/02?

6. Is the $95 balance solely for the 10/02 visit, or does it include any other service, prior balance, or self-pay item?
   (Rules out bundling or a stale prior balance.)

7. If after posting the patient balance on my portal exceeds $35 for this date of service, what is your dispute or appeal process and timeline, and who is the supervisor I escalate to?

8. Can you email me a copy of the claim (CMS-1500 or 837) you submitted to insurance for this date of service?
   (Gives you the billed amount and codes on record, in writing.)

9. If I were to pay the $95 today and the correct patient share turns out to be $35, how long does a refund take and is it automatic?
   (Frames the risk of paying prematurely — usually not worth it.)

The action rule for right now
- Do not pay the $95 today. The EOB documents your patient responsibility for 10/02 as $35. Paying $95 before the clinic posts the insurance payment and applies the contractual adjustment risks an overpayment that can take 30–60 days to refund, and creates an awkward dispute if the refund is slow.
- Reasonable wait: 30 days from the EOB processing date (10/09/2024). If by then the portal still shows $95 or more, escalate using questions 6 and 7, in writing (email is fine; ask for a written response).

If the numbers still won't reconcile after adjustment
- If billed ≠ allowed on the claim: missing contractual write-off is the most common cause. The $60 write-off is owed by the clinic under their in-network contract; they should not be billing you for it.
- If billed = allowed ($145): then $145 - $110 = $35, so a $95 portal balance means something else is in there — a different visit, a prior balance, or a non-covered service. Ask billing to itemize the $95 by date of service and CPT.
- If there are multiple CPT lines: each has its own allowed/paid/patient portion. The EOB shows the breakdown; the sum of the patient lines must equal the $35 total. If it doesn't, the discrepancy is usually a code-level contractual adjustment that didn't propagate.

Yes — the paired replacement matches the diagnosis. Chain at 0.75% is past the standard replace threshold on its own (a Park-style chain checker reads .5 as "replace soon" and .75 as "replace now"), and once a chain has stretched that far the cassette has almost always worn enough that a fresh chain will skip on it — the visible hooking on the middle sprockets is exactly that symptom. Because the shop ruled out the other usual suspects (rear derailleur aligned, hanger straight, wheels seated, brakes clear), the skip is isolated to drivetrain wear, so chain + cassette together is the targeted fix. Trying chain-only would be a false economy — the skip would reappear within days and you'd be back for the cassette anyway. $148 is the right scope; nothing on that estimate looks like padding.

For the pickup test, do it before you leave the shop parking lot or on a short block loop, carrying whatever load you normally commute with (backpack, panniers, laptop bag — same thing). Two passes:

    1. No-load sweep. Prop the bike or put it on a stand, spin the cranks,
       and shift through every gear both directions. Each click should
       land immediately and quietly — no chatter, hesitation, or clunk.

    2. Loaded shifts (this is where the original skip surfaced). About
       5 minutes of riding:

         a. Mid-cassette pedal-mash. Pedal hard in each of the middle
            3–4 cogs at a moderate cadence. Must be silent and solid —
            this is the zone that was visibly hooked.

         b. Full-range upshift under load. In a moderate gear, shift up
            one click at a time all the way to the smallest cog while
            pedaling firmly. Each click should drop crisply.

         c. Hardest-gear stress test. Drop into your top gear (big ring,
            smallest cog) and pedal hard standing. This is the worst
            case — if anything is still off, it'll show here.

         d. Downshift under load. While pedaling moderately hard, drop
            to an easier gear. The chain should move quickly and
            smoothly without delay.

         e. Slow-cadence shift drill. At low rpm, shift up and down
            through the middle cogs several times. Surfaces lazy limit
            screws or sloppy cable tension.

If all five are clean, you're good for the commute. If anything skips, chirps, hesitates, or refuses a shift under load, go back in before you head out — the adjustment and road test are already on the estimate, so it's covered.

Quick read on Kibo's situation:

The two-finger fit and clasp integrity are good. No redness is good. But consistent one-directional rotation toward the left armpit during a calm 10-minute test is a real signal, not noise. Kibo is at 25.5" inside a 24-32" range — that puts him at the lower end, and most chest panels in that size band are cut for dogs closer to the upper end. The plate may simply be wider than his sternum, which is why it migrates sideways under motion rather than sitting centered. Tightening won't fix a too-wide plate; it'll just pull it harder into the armpit.

Verdict before you test again: adjustment is reasonable to attempt one more time with a structured protocol, but if the rotation behaves the same way after a clean re-fit, the shape is the problem and you should return it without an outdoor walk. Don't do a real walk to "test harder" — outdoor pulling, sniffing pauses, and uneven footing will amplify the same flaw and risk armpit chafing.

Five-step indoor fit test that distinguishes adjustable from return-grade:

  1. Reset and refit (cold start)
     - Loosen all straps fully, then put the harness on flat — no twists.
     - Y-front or T-front should sit on the sternum, not slide toward the throat.
     - Back panel flat between the shoulder blades, not riding on them.
     - Adjust neck first to two fingers, then chest to two fingers, then back/belly strap. Chest last is important — the back strap sets the balance point.

  2. Static check, 60 seconds standing still
     - Pass criteria: harness sits symmetrically when viewed from the front; chest piece centered on sternum; you can slide a finger under the back strap over the shoulder blade.
     - Fail signal: it already sits crooked while Kibo stands still — that's a shape problem, not a motion problem.

  3. Slow walking, 3-5 minutes on leash
     - Watch from the side and front.
     - Note: does the chest piece drift, and in which direction each time? Drift to one armpit consistently = shape issue. Drift randomly that self-corrects = adjustment issue.
     - Stop every minute and look — is the chest piece still on the sternum, or has it slid toward the armpit during motion and stayed there?

  4. Transition set: sit, down, stand, shake, two slow turns (3 minutes)
     - Transitions expose whether the harness catches on his anatomy during real movement.
     - Sit: chest piece should not slide up toward the throat.
     - Stand from sit: back panel should not slide back onto the shoulders.
     - Turns: this is where one-sided rotation either shows up clearly or doesn't.

  5. "Settle" test, 2 minutes standing still after the walk
     - Stop, leash slack, let Kibo stand relaxed.
     - Drift back to centered on its own = the harness shifts during motion but isn't structurally wrong. Adjustable.
     - Stays pinned off-center even at rest = the balance is wrong for his shape. Return.

  6. Removal and skin/fur check (immediate and 30 minutes later)
     - Immediate: any redness, raised skin, or damp/hot spots, especially in both armpits and behind the elbows. Redness = stop, return.
     - 30 minutes later: compressed fur lines should spring back. If the same spot under the chest strap is still flat and Kibo is scratching at it, the harness is rubbing the same patch every wear — return regardless of rotation result.

Decision rule:

  Adjust and keep if: rotation only happens during motion, harness settles back to center when Kibo stops, fur recovers within ~30 minutes, no redness, no scratching. Likely fix: shorten the back/belly strap one notch to pull the chest piece more firmly onto the sternum, and make sure the back panel is sitting forward of the shoulder blades rather than behind them.

  Return before any outdoor walk if: rotation persists in the same direction across two clean refits, the chest plate sits off-sternum even at rest, fur compression lines don't recover within 30 minutes, any redness appears, or Kibo tries to scratch the harness off after wearing it. These are shape-mismatch signals, and an outdoor walk will convert "flattened fur" into a chafe or hot spot on the armpit.

One more practical note: if you do decide to return, a Y-front style harness (the one with a center chest strap that drops between the front legs in a Y shape rather than a T across the chest) tends to fit narrow-sternum dogs in wide chest ranges better than a T-front. Worth trying as the replacement rather than another T-front in the same size band.

Verified by hand:

Summed human agent-minutes (literal sum across the three segments)
- Agent A, first touch:  09:18–09:38 = 20 min
- Agent B:                09:30–09:45 = 15 min
- Agent A, resumed:       09:48–10:02 = 14 min
- Literal sum: 20 + 15 + 14 = 49 min

Wall-clock minutes any human agent was actively working (overlap merged)
- A and B overlap on 09:30–09:38 = 8 min
- Merged total: 49 − 8 = 41 min

Elapsed customer-blocked-time
- Total blocked window:                09:10 → 10:02 = 52 min
  - Pre-engagement wait:               09:10 → 09:18 =  8 min
  - During-engagement (still blocked): 09:18 → 10:02 = 44 min

How the overlap is treated
The 09:30–09:38 window is the only point where two agents are simultaneously on the case. The two metrics answer different questions and should both be reported:

- "Summed agent-minutes" is a labor-input figure — how much total human effort was spent. It adds the three segments as written and therefore counts the 8 min twice, which is correct for that purpose (two agents really were working those 8 min, and the cost of that labor was real).
- "Elapsed blocked time" is a customer-experience figure — how long the customer was actually stuck. The 8 min of overlap is not added twice here; it is counted once. The 41-min merged-work figure is the labor-side equivalent of that single counting and is the right number to pair with the 44-min during-engagement blocked figure when you want a labor-efficiency ratio.

The overlap is not "lost" or hidden — it is reported once per metric it belongs to, twice across the two metrics, which is the standard pattern in support diagnostics.

Why the automated acknowledgement contributes nothing
The ack at 09:10 is an instantaneous system event, not an interval of work. It has no duration, no agent time, and it does not advance the customer's blocked state — the case is still blocked at 09:10, still blocked at 09:11, and still blocked at 09:18 when the first human picks it up. Its only role in the log is a timestamp marking the system's response to the report; including it would inflate the blocked-time total and create a phantom labor entry with no underlying work. So it is intentionally excluded from both the summed agent-minutes and the blocked-time fields.

The notice is the 2025 Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) for a Medicare Part D prescription-drug plan. It's plan-level only — it changes three things on paper and tells you nothing about how those changes land on Mom's specific drugs.

WHAT THE NOTICE CONFIRMS
- Premium is roughly doubling: $14.20/mo (2024) → $28.90/mo (2025). That's +$176.40/yr on premium alone, before any cost-sharing changes.
- Deductible is going up: $545 → $590 (+$45/yr).
- The preferred-pharmacy network is being re-set for 2025. The notice does not say whether her current pharmacy stays preferred, gets demoted to standard, or drops out.

WHAT THE NOTICE DOES NOT ESTABLISH
- Her actual 2025 out-of-pocket. The notice itself disclaims this in the last line you quoted — and it has to, because total cost depends on:
  - which drugs she takes (formulary placement, tier)
  - whether any of her drugs move tiers year-over-year
  - whether prior authorization, step therapy, or quantity limits attach to any of them
  - whether she uses preferred retail, standard retail, or mail order
  - whether her spend crosses the initial coverage threshold and reaches catastrophic
- Whether her current pharmacy is still preferred in 2025 (separate document).
- Whether this plan is still her best option versus other plans in her zip code for her specific drug list.

RELEVANT 2025 PART D CHANGES THE NOTICE DOESN'T MENTION
These are real and decision-relevant, so flag them before she does anything:
- New $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap on Part D drugs (IRA). Once her spending reaches $2,000, she pays $0 for the rest of the year. If her spend is low enough, the cap is irrelevant; if it's high enough, it's the most important number on the page.
- The coverage gap ("donut hole") is restructured — a manufacturer discount applies in the initial coverage phase instead of after a gap. Don't model 2024 donut-hole math onto 2025.
- Medicare Prescription Payment Plan (M3P) is new and opt-in: she can spread monthly drug costs across the year instead of paying large bills in one month. Worth considering if she expects to hit the cap or have one expensive drug early in the year.
- $35/mo insulin cap and $0 Part D adult vaccines continue.

DOCUMENTS TO PULL BEFORE SHE COMPARES PLANS
- 2025 Summary of Benefits (SOB) — tier structure and cost-sharing amounts by tier in the initial coverage phase.
- 2025 Formulary (drug list) — confirms each of her drugs is covered and at which tier; check for PA / ST / QL flags.
- 2025 Pharmacy Directory — preferred vs standard network for her zip code; flag her current pharmacy specifically.
- 2025 Evidence of Coverage (EOC) — full rules, including catastrophic-phase cost-sharing and any specialty-drug rules.
- Her 2024 Explanation of Benefits or year-end pharmacy printout — gives her real 2024 total spend as a baseline to project against.
- Her complete current medication list with exact dosages and frequencies.
- LIS / Extra Help screening (ssa.gov/extrahelp or her State Health Insurance Assistance Program / SHIP) — if she qualifies, the premium increase, deductible, and most cost-sharing go away or shrink sharply.

VERIFICATION QUESTIONS BEFORE SHE COMPARES OR SELECTS
- For each drug she takes: covered in 2025 formulary? Same tier as 2024? Any new PA/ST/QL?
- Is her current pharmacy preferred, standard, or out-of-network in 2025? If preferred, what is the standard-network copay penalty? Is the nearest alternative preferred pharmacy far enough to matter?
- What are the 2025 copays/coinsurance by tier at a preferred pharmacy vs standard vs mail order?
- At her expected 2025 spend, does she cross the $2,000 cap? If yes, the cap is the binding constraint and plan choice matters less than pharmacy choice.
- Does the deductible ($590) apply to any of her drugs, or are they on tiers that bypass the deductible? (Many plans put low-tier generics outside the deductible.)
- Should she opt into the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan to smooth costs?
- Does she qualify for Extra Help / LIS? If yes, the premium-doubling is largely moot.
- Run the Medicare Plan Finder (medicare.gov/plan-compare) with her actual drug list, dosages, and preferred pharmacy for 2025. Don't reuse 2024 rankings — preferred networks and tiers have already shifted.

Decision frame for her: the notice tells her the plan is getting more expensive on premium and deductible and is reshaping its pharmacy network. It does not tell her whether the plan is still the right one. The actual comparison has to be done against her drug list and her pharmacy, with the 2025 documents above and the Plan Finder output, ideally before the December 7 end of the Annual Election Period.

Verdict: mixed.

Component 1 — external access or authority
Supporting event: "Workspace waited two business days for its Okta owner to approve the application assignment."
The blocker is not the customer's understanding of Helio; it is an authority outside the customer's direct control (the customer's own Okta/IT owner) gatekeeping the application assignment to the workspace. Setup could not proceed until that external party acted. That is the access/authority signature: the customer is willing and (per the pre-admission admin proof) capable, but is waiting on someone else's permission. The connector authentication check passing in pre-admission is consistent with this — the customer passed the gates Helio controls, then hit a gate Helio does not control.

Component 2 — product guidance
Supporting event: "After approval, the customer could not map lifecycle stages and completed setup after a 35-minute guided product session."
The blocker here is the customer's own configuration skill on a specific feature (lifecycle stage mapping). The 35-minute guided session is the fingerprint of a product-guidance case — a CS hand-hold through a step the customer could not complete unaided. It is not authority (the Okta gate is already cleared) and it is not an admission check (admin proof already passed pre-admission). It is a guided-setup gap on a configuration task.

Why mixed rather than one or the other
Both events independently delayed setup, and neither subsumes the other. Removing the Okta wait would still leave the lifecycle-mapping gap; removing the guided session would still leave the two-day authority wait. Sequencing (authority first, then guidance) does not collapse them into a single cause — they are two distinct setup frictions stacked on the same workspace.

Three constraints are passing right now — two-finger fit under the neck and chest straps, clasp holds under firm hand pressure, no rotation over the ten-minute walk. The belly-strap shortfall (one finger-width behind the front legs vs. the card's two inches) can't be fixed in the direction that would help. Loosening the neck/chest straps would buy clearance but break the two-finger rule and reintroduce the rotation problem that retired the previous harness. Tightening the belly strap would push it forward into the front-leg crease, the opposite of what you want — and on this style the belly strap is fixed-length, so there's no adjuster to turn anyway. The 1.5-inch shortfall reads as a body-length or shape mismatch (the harness's chest plate is shorter than Kibo's torso), not a strap-length problem. Going one size up in the same model is likely to be too loose in the neck at a 25.5" chest; a different model with a longer chest plate is the more probable fix.

Indoor test before any outdoor use:

  1. Leashed figure-eight walk, 3-4 minutes on a flat non-slip surface, with light steady leash contact (not pulling). Have a second person watch from above and behind. Pass: the Y-junction stays centered between the shoulder blades the whole time. Fail: the Y-junction drifts toward either armpit at any point, or the belly strap rides forward into the front-leg crease.

  2. Sit-to-stand cycles, 10 reps, watched from the side. Pass: the belly strap returns to the same behind-the-front-legs position on every stand-up. Fail: the belly strap visibly walks forward into the front-leg crease on stand-up, or the neck strap presses into the throat when he rises.

  3. Two sharp leash redirects from a sit — call him to you left, then right, twice each. Pass: the harness re-centers within one step of the redirect. Fail: the harness stays offset after the redirect.

Any single fail → return before outdoor use. Outdoor terrain (uneven ground, scent-pulling, another dog) amplifies the exact forces that ended the previous harness. If all three pass, the shape is usable — recheck at the 30-minute mark of the first outdoor walk for the same hair and skin signs you already cleared (redness, abrasion along the front-leg crease and behind the elbows), and treat the one-finger shortfall in belly-strap clearance as a tolerable compromise rather than a deal-breaker.

---

**Study 3 — Lower-bead removal frequency at 35° wash angle**
*Isolates only how often you wick the lower bead; everything else is locked.*

**Independent variable**
Wick frequency = how often you touch the pooled lower edge with the corner of a clean, dry, soft tissue or a squeezed-dry brush to remove the forming bead.

**Held constant (from prior studies + 10/20 instructor note)**
- Paper: 140 lb cold-press quarter sheet, taped, pre-wet stretch and dry to flat
- Brush: #8 round, loaded with the same pigment mix used on 10/20 (same two-wash sky palette)
- Brush moisture: one firm blot only — no half-blot, no second blot
- Wash angle: 35° (steeper; the failure condition from 10/20)
- Bead pickup method: single touch, held ~20 s, lifted once — no return
- One-touch rule on the upper wash edge — no return stroke after the sheen dulls
- Hands-off rule once sheen disappears
- Same palette, water jars, room, and lighting as the 10/20 sheet
- Forward-only; no corrections, no scrubbing, no glazing over blooms

**Layout — single sheet, four horizontal bands, separated by ~1 cm dry gaps**

Band A — Wick every 10 s while the bead is visible
Band B — Wick every 20 s (control; matches your 20-second touch cadence)
Band C — Wick only when the bead clearly ponds (variable, "as needed")
Band D — No wicking (control for what the 10/20 sheet showed)

For each band:
1. Lay the wash at 35° using the same stroke rhythm as band B of the 10/20 sheet.
2. Watch the lower edge. Wick with one clean dry tissue touch at the prescribed interval, holding ~20 s per touch, one touch only.
3. After the sheen dulls, stop. Mark band label and actual wick times in pencil in the margin.

**Predictions (calibrated to what 10/20 produced and your diagnosis)**
- Band B (20 s) reproduces the two cauliflower edges — confirms the diagnosis.
- Band A (10 s) shows the cleanest band: bead never accumulates enough to feed back.
- Band C (as needed) is the test of whether *judging* bead weight beats *timing* it.
- Band D (no wicking) blooms hardest — replicates the 10/20 failure cleanly.

**What a clean answer looks like**
If A reads cleanest, the wick frequency is the lever and 20 s is simply too slow for this angle + this brush load. If C reads as clean as A, you switch from timed wicking to bead-judging and drop one whole layer of clock-watching. If both A and C are visibly worse than B, the problem is not wick frequency — it is the bead forming *between* touches, and the next study moves to a smaller bead to begin with (drier brush or lighter load at 35°), not to a different wick rhythm.

**Stop conditions (unchanged from your clinic studies)**
- Any band that blooms: leave it, label it, move on. No lift, no glaze, no rework.
- One sheet only. If results are ambiguous, repeat the whole sheet once before changing anything.

**Materials to stage before you start**
- Two clean dry tissues per band (eight total) so a used tissue is never reused
- A small phone timer with 10-second audible cues (so 10 s and 20 s bands stay honest)
- Pencil for margin notes — actual wick times per band, not just the plan

Estimated time: 12–18 minutes of painting, plus 10 minutes of margin notes while the bands dry. Falls inside a Sunday block without becoming a finished piece.

CORE SAFETY RULE
Do not delete anything until step 1 confirms a restorable backup. If verification fails, stop and fix the backup before freeing space — running an OS update against an unverified backup is the actual risk, not the 8 GB shortfall.

PHASE 0 — STOP CONDITIONS
If any of these are true, pause the whole plan:
- Oct 19 backup is not the most recent *successful* (a scheduled run that crashed doesn't count).
- Backup target is a personal cloud account, an external drive that isn't currently attached, or unknown.
- You can't identify which Helio export each Desktop file came from.

PHASE 1 — VERIFY BACKUP (no destructive ops)
1. Open the backup tool (Time Machine, OneDrive, File History, or whatever your IT-mandated tool is). Confirm the most recent backup timestamp is Oct 19 and the status is "Completed" / green — not "Pending," "Failed," or "In progress."
2. If your tool supports it, run a verify/restore-check (e.g., Time Machine → "Verify Backup"). This catches silent corruption.
3. Note: the backup is 7 days old. Any work since Oct 19 is not in it. Either (a) accept rolling back to Oct 19 state if something goes wrong, or (b) do an incremental backup of just the working folders before continuing. Option (b) is the safer choice given an OS update is imminent.
4. Confirm the backup destination is company-managed (work OneDrive, corporate endpoint backup, work laptop's managed Time Machine volume, etc.). If it routes through a personal Apple ID / personal Google account / personal Dropbox, the company-data boundary is already broken — flag it to IT before proceeding.

PHASE 2 — CLEAR VIDEO-CALL CACHE (lowest risk, ~6 GB)
Cached video files are regenerable and not source-of-truth. Common locations:
- macOS Zoom: ~/Library/Application Support/zoom.us/data/
- Teams: ~/Library/Application Support/Microsoft/Teams/*/Cache and ~/Library/Caches/com.microsoft.teams/
- Webex, Meet: similar paths under ~/Library/Caches/ and ~/Library/Application Support/
- Windows: %AppData%\Zoom\data\, %AppData%\Microsoft\Teams\Cache, %LocalAppData%\<app>\Cache

Process: quit the app fully first (so files aren't locked), then delete the cache contents, not the folder itself. Reopen the app and confirm it still signs in and joins a test call.
Expected free after Phase 2: 19 + 6 = 25 GB. Still 2 GB short.

PHASE 3 — TRIAGE DOWNLOADS (~4 GB, mostly safe)
Downloads is usually the cleanest win. Sort by size, then for each item ask:
- Installer for an app already installed and updated? Delete.
- One-off export already moved into a project folder? Delete.
- An archive (zip/dmg) whose contents you already extracted and saved? Delete.
- Anything you don't recognize? Don't delete — park it in a `_review_2024-10-26` subfolder for 30 days, then re-decide.
- Anything that looks like Helio raw data or a customer export: stop, treat like Phase 4 (don't delete, archive to work-managed storage only).
Expected free after Phase 3: 25 + ~3-4 = 28-29 GB. You may already be done.

PHASE 4 — DESKTOP EXPORTS (Helio analyses, ~9 GB, treat carefully)
The Desktop files are derivatives — Helio is the system of record, so these are reproducible as long as the underlying analyses still exist. Don't trust the filename alone; cross-reference before archiving.

For each Desktop export:
1. Open the corresponding analysis in Helio. Confirm it still exists and the export date in Helio matches or is older than the file's modified date. If it doesn't exist in Helio anymore, or the file is newer than what's in Helio (you edited the CSV locally), park it in a `hold_DO_NOT_DELETE/` folder and skip it.
2. If it matches: zip the file (preserves the export as a single dated artifact), name it `YYYY-MM-DD_<analysis-name>_<export-type>.zip`, and move it to a company-managed location — typically your work OneDrive/SharePoint synced folder, or a project archive folder on the work laptop outside Desktop. Do not move to personal iCloud, personal Dropbox, personal Google Drive, a personal email, or a USB stick that leaves the building.
3. After the move, confirm the file opens correctly from the new location, then delete the Desktop original.
4. Repeat. Order: largest files first to hit the 27 GB threshold quickly, smallest and most-recently-modified last so you can stop early if you change your mind.

Expected free after Phase 4: 29 + (variable, often 3-6 GB) = 32+ GB. Comfortable margin for the OS update and any post-update caches it generates.

PHASE 5 — PRE-UPDATE CHECKS
- Empty Trash / Recycle Bin. Deleted files don't free space until this step.
- On macOS, also run `sudo purge` or reboot once so the OS drops any still-mapped cache. On Windows, Disk Cleanup → "Clean up system files" can add a few hundred MB to a couple GB by removing the previous Windows.old and update caches.
- Re-check the storage view and confirm ≥27 GB free before kicking off the OS update.

WHAT TO COME BACK TO ME WITH
After you run this, tell me:
- Which backup tool and whether the Oct 19 backup verified clean.
- Free space after each phase (so we can see where the 27 GB actually came from).
- Any Desktop export you couldn't cross-reference in Helio — those are the only files I'd flag for a second look.

Two things I'd want on your radar going forward, not today: (1) a scheduled export pipeline so Helio analyses land in the work archive folder directly instead of accumulating on Desktop, and (2) a backup cadence tighter than once a week given the OS-update pattern — a backup older than the last meaningful change is the real risk here, not the disk-space gap.

Day-30 retention, Q3 mature activator cohort (n=96)

Deeper integration sub-segment:    45 retained / 54 mature activators = 83.33%
Lighter integration sub-segment:   27 retained / 42 mature activators = 64.29%
Total cohort:                      72 retained / 96 mature activators = 75.00%

Composition: deeper = 54/96 (56.25%), lighter = 42/96 (43.75%). Split is exhaustive: 54+42 = 96 and 45+27 = 72, so these are the only two sub-segments in the cohort as given.

Gap: 83.33% - 64.29% = 19.05 percentage points absolute. As a ratio of rates, deeper is ~1.30x the lighter rate. In raw retained counts, the deeper sub-segment yields 18 additional retained customers out of 12 additional mature activators at that level.

Descriptive read

Within the Q3 mature activator cohort, the deeper-integration sub-segment shows a higher day-30 retention rate than the lighter-integration sub-segment. The direction is clear and consistent with what you'd expect from an integration-depth read; the size is non-trivial. That is the whole claim — it is a within-cohort observation, not a causal one.

The 75.00% cohort rate sits between the two sub-segment rates and skews toward the deeper rate simply because deeper is the larger share (56.25%) of the cohort. That is arithmetic, not a finding.

What this does not say

  Integration depth is not being treated here as a proven mechanism driving retention. The split is descriptive stratification of an already-mature cohort.
  Activation is not being redefined. "Mature activator" remains the cohort boundary (Q3 settled 5/24, day-90 mature reaffirmed 8/2). Integration depth is a characteristic observed within that boundary, not a new activation criterion.
  This is not a forecast, not a paid-acquisition or pricing-page lever, and not a basis for changing the Helio Start revisit gate (mature retention + refund-adjusted cash + account-level support effort, Owen + CS).

Caveats worth carrying alongside the numbers

  Selection. Customers who integrated more deeply may differ on intent, use case, team size, contract structure, or pre-existing product fit in ways the integration-depth label does not capture. The descriptive gap is consistent with several stories, not just one.
  Timing of integration. The depth label does not tell us when in the maturity window the integration happened. Customers who integrated earlier have more mature-state time on the platform, which is itself retention-correlated.
  Sample size. 54 and 42 are modest. The direction of the gap is stable in this snapshot; whether 19 pp is a stable effect size on the next settled quarter is a separate question, and I would not put it behind this number as an estimate of true effect.
  No third bucket. The two sub-segments as given sum to the full cohort, so the rates describe exactly the 54 and 42 named and nothing outside them.

  "Within Q3 mature activators, deeper integration use is associated with higher day-30 retention." Associated, not drove / caused / led to.

Here's a low-stress Halloween setup for Kibo using only what you have, plus a clear line for "call the ER vet tonight."

**The setup (5:30–9:30 pm window)**

1. **Pre-window leashed potty walk, ~5:15 pm.** Brief, on leash, before foot traffic builds. Carry high-value treats; reward easy check-ins so he associates the early walk with calm, not a cue that something scary is coming.
2. **Move to the rear bedroom before the first knock (ideally by 5:30).** The goal is he's already settled in his safe spot before the doorbell starts. Bring his normal bed, a worn shirt or blanket that smells like you, fresh water, and one long-lasting food toy (Kong, Toppl, lick mat) pre-loaded.
3. **Layer the sound masking.** Close the bedroom door, run white noise louder than usual — enough that individual knocks and doorbells blur into a steady hum rather than sharp transients. Curtains drawn so he can't see flashes of costumes passing windows.
4. **Porch-side: take yourself off the equation.** Put the candy bowl and a "take one" sign on the porch with painter's tape so you're not opening the door at all. Zero doorbell rings inside the house = the biggest single win you can engineer tonight.
5. **Cue him that you're nearby, not hovering.** Sit on the floor in the room with him for the first 15–20 minutes so he settles, then drift to the hallway or adjacent space. Present but not watchful — dogs read anxious hovering as "yes, something is wrong."
6. **Treats = reinforcement, not bribery.** A few high-value rewards for any calm moment (settling, soft eyes, choosing his bed). Don't use treats to pull him away from shaking — let him be shaky, reward when he resettles.
7. **No late walks during the window.** If he absolutely needs to go out after 7 pm, leash him, stay in the driveway/side yard away from the street, and come back inside.
8. **Wrap is on standby, not on by default.** Only deploy the calming wrap if he escalates past what the room + white noise + treats are handling. Putting it on a mildly worried dog can sometimes backfire by adding a new sensation.

**What's expected vs. what's a problem (his baseline matters)**

Kibo's established storm/fireworks pattern is: panting, pacing, occasionally settling beside you, taking treats. That's tonight's baseline — uncomfortable but not a crisis, and he's done this before without a vet visit. If he stays inside that envelope (responsive, treat-taking, breathing hard but not labored, no drool/vomit/escape attempts), you're managing, not failing.

**Call an emergency veterinarian tonight if you see any of these:**

- Collapse, stumbling, or sudden weakness/disorientation
- Pale, gray, blue, or tacky gums (check while he's calm — now is the baseline)
- Thick ropey drool he can't swallow, or vomiting
- Repeated unproductive retching or a hard, distended, painful belly
- Labored breathing, persistent panting that doesn't ease when the room is quiet, or any blue tinge to tongue/gums
- Seizure, or any episode where he loses awareness
- A rectal temp above ~104°F if you can safely take it (don't struggle with him to do it)
- Self-injury — breaking through the door, lacerated nails, broken tooth from crate-biting, bleeding you can't stop in a few minutes
- Sudden escape through a door you didn't expect him to bolt from (treat as a lost-dog situation immediately: ask neighbors, post, call the microchip company — and check him over for injury/heat stress once found)

Two of those signs together = call without waiting for a third. One alone, especially breathing or gum color, = call.

**After the window, ~9:30 pm**

Open the bedroom door slowly, keep white noise on for a few more minutes, then transition. A short leashed yard potty if he needs it, water, and his normal evening routine. Expect him to be a little flat or clingy tomorrow — that's normal post-event recovery, not a vet issue unless it stretches past 24–48 hours or he's refusing food and water.

You're set up well for this. The porch bowl is the move — the less the doorbell rings inside, the less there is for him to react to.

Bottom line: the two plans are essentially tied ($48/year apart), and the deciding factor is the pharmacy channel, not the dollar gap.

The numbers, broken out:

  Hill Country Rx Value
    Premium:  $28.90 x 12 = $346.80
    Deduct:   $590
    Drug cost: $1,284 - $346.80 - $590 = $347.20  (using preferred mail order)

  Lone Star Saver Rx
    Premium:  $36.40 x 12 = $436.80
    Deduct:   $545
    Drug cost: $1,236 - $436.80 - $545 = $254.20  (at her neighborhood preferred pharmacy)

Lone Star is cheaper by $48/year, but charges $90 more in premiums and $93 less at the drug counter -- the savings come almost entirely from cheaper drug pricing at her preferred pharmacy. Hill Country's $347.20 figure assumes mail order; filling the same scripts at her neighborhood pharmacy, which Hill Country classifies as standard rather than preferred, would push the total higher than $1,284.

The pharmacy tradeoff:
  - Hill Country only makes sense if she's comfortable with preferred mail order for ongoing meds. Mail order typically requires 90-day fills, so refills are batched and delivery-driven. Good for stable meds, less good for new prescriptions or anything she wants same-day.
  - Lone Star rewards her existing local pharmacy relationship -- short trips, real-time pharmacist questions, easier to drop off a new prescription mid-cycle.

For someone who values the local pharmacy and may have as-needed meds added during the year, Lone Star is the lower-friction default and the cheaper plan. For someone already set up with mail order and happy with it, $48 is essentially noise either way.

Before enrolling, she should verify on Plan Finder:

  1.  Vaccines. Part D covers Shingrix, Tdap, RSV, and others; the estimate almost certainly excludes vaccine costs. For each vaccine she might get this year, check tier and copay/coinsurance at a preferred pharmacy (or preferred mail order under Hill Country).
  2.  As-needed medications. If Plan Finder doesn't include them, add realistic quantities (albuterol ~1-2 inhalers/yr, prednisone bursts, nitroglycerin, antihistamines, sleep/anxiety meds, etc.) and re-run. The current $48 gap can flip.
  3.  Mail order specifics for Hill Country. Are 90-day fills required? How do refrigerated or controlled substances work? Holiday delivery delays?
  4.  Preferred pharmacy network under Hill Country. Her local is standard; are other nearby pharmacies (Costco, Walmart, CVS, grocery) preferred? Sometimes a 10-minute drive saves the spread.
  5.  Formulary tier check on every current med. Confirm each drug sits at the expected tier with no prior authorization or step therapy that would change the math.
  6.  Coverage gap. The Part D out-of-pocket cap is $2,000. If her drug spend is high enough, both plans hit the cap and the comparison becomes a wash on drug spend.
  7.  Refill synchronization. If she's switching pharmacies in January, can the new plan align refills so she's not making multiple trips in February?
  8.  Mid-year formulary risk. Plans can move tiers or remove drugs mid-year with notice. Small but real risk on any med where she doesn't have a stable substitute.
  9.  Star ratings and PA friction. Lower-rated plans tend to have more prior authorization and slower turnaround. Worth a glance.
  10. Mail-order reliability, if relevant. A friend or pharmacist who's actually used either plan's mail-order service is the most useful single data point.

Highest-leverage single check: add the as-needed meds and planned vaccines to Plan Finder and re-run. Everything else is small relative to that.

Longer-wash consistency study — design

Purpose
Test whether the 20-second bead-wicking interval, as calibrated on the shorter 10/20 strips, holds across a single longer passage at the same steep angle. One variable in, one number out.

Variables
  Fixed (held from the 10/20 ladder):
    - brush + size
    - paper (same sheet or matched batch)
    - pigment + dilution
    - steep angle (the one used for the three reference strips)
    - one firm blot to set brush moisture
    - 20-second edge touch hold
    - one-touch boundary, no return after dull
  Tested:
    - passage length (longer than the 10/20 reference strips)
  Measured at each observation point:
    - actual wick interval (seconds)
    - edge character: clean line / skip / bloom
    - any dulling of the bead

Setup
  - Same materials as 10/20.
  - Stopwatch in hand; do not estimate wick intervals.
  - Pre-paint: one firm blot only, per the ladder rule.

Procedure
  - Lay one continuous wash longer than the 10/20 reference strips.
    Proposed length: 1.5x the reference strip. Conservative step — doubles
    the observation surface without doubling the failure risk. If you want
    a sharper test, 2x works but raises the chance the wash breaks before
    you reach the late segment (which is itself useful information, but
    means no late-segment data).
  - Divide the wash mentally into three equal observation segments:
        A: early third
        B: middle third
        C: late third
  - Per segment, log three things:
        (a) measured wick interval, seconds
        (b) edge character: clean line / skip / bloom
        (c) any dulling observed in that segment
  - Rule: target 20s at every segment, but if the interval drifts, LOG IT
    and do not correct mid-passage. A drift is the finding, not a fault.
    Correcting would hide the question you came to ask.

Pre-registered outcomes (define "consistent" before you paint)
  PASS       wick interval within ±3s of 20s at A, B, and C; edge stays
             a clean line at all three segments; no dulling before the
             passage ends.
  DRIFT      interval trends one direction across A → B → C, even if it
             stays inside the ±3s band. Direction matters:
               interval lengthening late → paper is saturating; the 20s
                                          rule is an early-passage artifact
               interval shortening late → paint is loading up on the brush;
                                          the 20s rule is masking buildup
  FAIL       any segment shows skip (over-wick) or bloom-back (under-wick
             or edge instability), regardless of interval timing.

Why this shape
  - One wash = matches the instructor's "one longer wash" and isolates
    passage length as the only thing that changed.
  - Three internal segments = three data points from one execution, which
    is what makes it a study rather than a single observation.
  - Pre-registered ±3s band + edge criteria = "stays consistent" defined
    before you see the result, so you cannot rationalize the outcome after.
  - "Do not correct mid-passage" rule = preserves the signal. The most
    informative result is the one you would otherwise talk yourself out of.

One thing to confirm before you start
  The length multiplier. 1.5x is my default. Tell me if you want 2x and I
  will revise; otherwise I would start at 1.5x and only step to 2x if the
  first longer wash produces a clean PASS across all three segments.

Goal: never overwrite the Desktop (newer) copy, never delete anything before the managed copy is proven equal-or-better, never run the OS update until reconciliation is fully verified.

The 4-minute-later Desktop mtime is the only signal you have that the sync client captured an older snapshot of that one file. Treat that as a hypothesis, not a fact, until you compare content — editors routinely rewrite the same bytes and bump mtime, and sync clients sometimes preserve or reset mtimes unpredictably. Hash both, then act.

Sequence (do steps 1–4 in order, without opening the CSV in an editor that auto-saves):

1.  Capture state before touching anything. Write down, in one place you won't lose:
    -   filename
    -   Desktop path and mtime
    -   managed path (Helio Secure Analysis/Riley/Q4 exports/...) and mtime
    -   file sizes (bytes) on both sides
    Do not edit either copy. Do not let the sync client run a "force resync" or "restore from server" — that would pull the older server version down on top of your newer Desktop file.

2.  Hash both copies (the truth test, mtimes can lie):
    -   macOS:  shasum -a 256 "<Desktop path>"  and  shasum -a 256 "<managed path>"
    -   Windows (PowerShell):  Get-FileHash "<path>" -Algorithm SHA256
    Record both hashes.

3.  Decide direction from the hashes:
    -   Hashes match → the "newer" Desktop mtime is a touch/rewrite of identical bytes. Nothing real to preserve content-wise. You can either leave both alone or copy Desktop → managed to refresh the managed copy's mtime. No content is at risk either way.
    -   Hashes differ → Desktop has real newer content. The Desktop copy is the one to keep. Copy Desktop → managed (never the reverse — the server side has the older snapshot by definition, since the sync captured before your later save).

4.  If you copied in step 3, verify the copy landed correctly:
    -   Re-hash the managed copy. It must equal the Desktop hash (the one you're preserving).
    -   Re-check file size on both sides — must match exactly.
    -   Open the managed copy in the actual app (not the sync client's preview) and skim the rows/columns you know you edited in that final save. A byte-identical copy can still be silently truncated if the sync was mid-write; an open-and-skim catches that a hash cannot.
    -   Re-check the sync client's status on the folder. The hash test on this one CSV is a leading indicator; you want a fresh full-folder verification (re-scan / verify / "check folder" depending on the client) before trusting the rest of the 6.8 GB.

5.  Quarantine, don't yet delete, the Desktop originals. Rename to *.pre-reconciliation.bak or move them to a holding folder outside both Desktop and the managed tree. Leave them there for at least one sync cycle (and ideally until after the OS update is done and the managed folder is rescanned clean). Only after that cycle shows the managed folder intact do you delete the quarantined originals. This is the asymmetry: a copy is recoverable; a premature `rm` is not.

6.  Only then run the OS update. The OS update is the last step, not because it's risky in itself, but because updates can remount volumes, reset sync-client state, or interrupt half-written files mid-run. You want reconciliation fully proven before introducing that variable. After the update, re-run the sync client's folder verification once more before deleting the quarantined Desktop copies.

What not to do:
-   Don't trust "6.8 GB synchronized" as proof of THIS file. Your own observation already contradicts it for one file.
-   Don't delete Desktop first "to free space" and then copy from managed — if the direction was wrong, the newer work is gone.
-   Don't open the CSV in an editor that auto-saves while you're inspecting; a stray save will touch mtimes and possibly content and invalidate the comparison.
-   Don't use the sync client's "restore from server" / "force download" on this folder without checking — it will overwrite the newer Desktop content with the older server snapshot.
-   Don't run the OS update mid-reconciliation; finish step 5 first.

The one-sentence version: hash both copies first, copy Desktop → managed only if hashes differ, re-hash and open-and-skim the managed copy to prove it landed whole, quarantine the Desktop originals for one full sync cycle, and put the OS update strictly after all of that.

Salvage for the lifted edge

The strip is fiber still attached, not torn free, so it can usually be re-set without touching the wash:

1. Lightly dampen only the lifted strip with a small brush (size 0 or 1), water only, contact just the raised fiber. The wash zone stays untouched.
2. Wait roughly 30 seconds for the moisture to soften the fiber bond; the strip should relax visibly.
3. Press it back with a bone folder through silicone release paper (or wax paper), working from the attached end toward the loose end so you push fiber down, not lift more.
4. Blot firmly under a clean blotter with light weight (a few books) overnight.

Trade-off: you are introducing a small amount of water adjacent to (not inside) the wash. With the 20s interval and one-touch edge rule held, a single controlled pass on the strip should not bloom anything. If the lift is below your final trim line, the lower-risk move is to leave it and trim past it later.

Tape-removal test, single variable held

Hold all of these constant: 20s bead-wicking interval, one firm blot, one-touch edge boundary, sheet fully dry before removal.

Change only the peel mechanics. The failure today — ~90 degree pull on a fully dried sheet — concentrates force perpendicular to the paper plane and is the classic cause of fiber pick. The standard fix:

- Peel the tape back on itself at a low angle (~180 degrees, folded back along its own length, pulling parallel to the sheet rather than up off it).
- Direction: along the paper grain if you can identify it.
- Speed: slow and steady, no jerk. If resistance builds, pause rather than pull through it.

To keep the variable clean, run both pulls on scrap of the same paper with the same wash and same dry time: first strip at ~90 degrees (replicates today's failure), second strip at ~180 back-on-itself, low and slow. If the second comes up clean with no fiber lift, peel mechanics is confirmed as the independent variable and you can adopt the new technique on the real sheet. If 180 still lifts fiber on a fully dried sheet, the next isolated step is adhesive choice (low-tack artist tape vs. standard masking tape) — that is a second test, not this one.

LOWEST-RISK FEEDING BRIDGE FOR KIBO
Sunday Nov 10 → Tuesday afternoon Nov 12

Recommendation in one line: try to buy a small bag of Kibo's exact current formula locally today; if that's not available, fall back to a controlled bland bridge.

Why the local purchase is best
The bridge is only 4 meals long (Monday lunch, Monday dinner, Tuesday breakfast, Tuesday lunch), and a small bag of the same formula keeps the GI tract on the exact same protein/fat/fiber profile it's adapted to. There's no transition risk. Most pet stores stock the common lines; an independent store is more likely to carry boutique or veterinary formulas than a big-box chain. A 2-4 lb bag is plenty to bridge and finish out the week.

Order of preference if the exact formula isn't available

  1. Same brand, different flavor within the same product line (e.g., another primary protein in the same kibble line Kibo currently eats). Same general profile, just a different primary protein.
  2. Bland bridge: plain poached chicken breast (boneless, skinless, no salt, oil, or seasoning), shredded very fine or pulsed in a food processor. Mix roughly 70% current food / 30% chicken for Monday lunch to ease in; if well-tolerated, move toward 50/50 for Monday dinner and lean mostly chicken (still small portions) for Tuesday breakfast and lunch.
  3. Avoid during the bridge: canned tuna in oil, deli meats, baby food (often contains onion or garlic powder), milk or cream, butter or oils, raw fish or eggs, ground beef, any seasoned or rich protein — these are common vomiting triggers.

Portion and pacing
Keep each bridge meal roughly the same size as a normal meal of his current food. If Kibo tends to eat fast, split each meal into two smaller servings ten minutes apart. Fresh water should be available at all times — bridges with novel protein often shift stool firmness slightly, and hydration helps.

Resume transition once the shipment arrives
When you open the new bag, mix about 25% new shipment with 75% of whatever he's been eating for one meal, then move to full new shipment by Wednesday. Before opening, check the bag: if it smells off, looks greasy, has clumped or discolored kibble, or the seal looks compromised, don't feed it — call the vendor.

SIGNS THAT PROMPT A VETERINARIAN CALL
Call your regular vet (or the nearest emergency clinic if after hours) if you see any of these during the bridge:

  - Repeated vomiting (more than once) or vomiting with blood.
  - Diarrhea with blood, mucus, or very watery stool that persists beyond a couple of movements.
  - Refusal to eat for more than about 24 hours total. This is the most important one and is specifically a cat concern: cats who stop eating entirely for over a day are at real risk for hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver disease), which becomes harder to reverse the longer it goes on. Don't wait this out.
  - Lethargy beyond a single off afternoon — not greeting you, not moving to his food area, hiding.
  - Straining in the litter box without producing urine, or producing only drops. This is a separate emergency (possible urinary obstruction, especially in male cats) and is time-critical regardless of food.
  - Hunched posture, vocalizing when touched or picked up, or guarding the abdomen.
  - Gums that look pale, tacky, or yellowish.
  - Any breathing change — fast, labored, or open-mouth.

For any of these, call rather than email — and if your regular vet isn't reachable, use the nearest emergency clinic. The 24-hour food-refusal threshold is the one most people underestimate; if Kibo snubs the bridge food, try warming it slightly, adding a teaspoon of warm water, or offering a different protein before assuming he's just being picky.
