The cloudy-then-bubbly pattern with normal pressure, no odor, no sediment, and no boil notice is the typical post-valve-work signature: disturbed sediment that flushed out fast and entrained air (dissolved gases coming out of solution as the tap opens). Air-driven cloudiness clears bottom-up in a glass and bubbles rise; sediment hangs in suspension or settles. What you saw after five minutes sounds like air, not sediment — good sign. Your stored water is the right move in the meantime.

SAFE FLUSHING SEQUENCE

  1. Before opening any tap, unscrew the aerators from the cold taps you plan to flush — kitchen cold tap and any bathroom cold taps. Sediment gets caught in the fine screens and keeps a tap sputtering or cloudy even after the main lines are clear. Drop the aerators in a cup; you'll rinse and reinstall them at the end.

  2. Flush cold lines only, working from the tap nearest the water entry point outward to the farthest cold tap. For each tap:
       - Open fully, COLD only (handle fully to the cold side).
       - Run 3–5 minutes, or until the water has been clear and bubble-free for at least 1–2 minutes straight.
       - Start nearest the entry, end at the farthest (often a bathroom or outdoor hose bib). The farthest tap usually holds the last air pocket.

  3. After the cold lines are clear, briefly flush the hot branch lines. Do NOT aggressively run the water heater yet:
       - At each hot tap, run cold for a few seconds, then flip to HOT for 1–2 minutes. This clears the hot branch piping without pushing a slug of sediment through the heater.
       - The heater itself clears over its next normal use cycle. If yours has a bottom drain valve and you're comfortable with it, you can open it into a bucket for a minute or two to flush tank sediment before drawing hot water.
       - If the heater rumbles or pops loudly on the first hot draws, that's sediment shifting in the tank. Not dangerous, just noisy — let it settle.

  4. Reinstall aerators only after the taps have run clear. If a faucet keeps sputtering or streaming sideways after reinstalling, the aerator is still partially clogged — remove and rinse it again.

  5. Final sanity check on the kitchen cold tap: fill a clear glass against a white background. Truly clear and bubble-free for a minute = ready for drinking and cooking.

WHAT NOT TO RUN OR USE YET

Hold off on these until cold lines are clear AND hot branches have been flushed:

  - Dishwasher — sediment can clog inlet valves and the pump. Wait one full cycle after flushing before running.
  - Washing machine — same; inlet screens are a pain to clean.
  - Ice maker — the first 2–3 batches of cubes will be cloudy and taste off from trapped air and sediment. Either turn the ice maker off until things settle, or discard the first few batches.
  - Humidifier (if plumbed-in) — sediment clogs the unit. Use stored or bottled water.
  - Coffee maker, kettle, espresso machine — sediment clogs valves and ruins the taste of the first several pots. Use stored water.
  - Under-sink reverse-osmosis or any fine filter — bypass it during the post-flush period; its membrane will clog with disturbed sediment. Run cold unfiltered until things settle, then follow the filter's flush or replacement procedure.
  - Tankless water heater (if you have one) — do NOT run hot water through it until cold lines are fully flushed. Sediment can damage the heat exchanger.
  - Drinking or cooking with hot tap water in general. This is standard advice regardless of shutoff: hot lines leach more metals, and your heater hasn't been flushed.
  - For Kibo — keep using the stored water until you've done the clear-glass check. Tap water is normally fine for dogs, but no reason to switch mid-event.

CHANGES THAT MEAN STOP USING AND CALL MAINTENANCE

Call the property manager (and stop drinking or cooking with the water) if any of these appear:

  - Persistent cloudiness that does NOT clear after 15–20 minutes of running, or any visible particles settling out in a glass.
  - Discoloration: yellow, brown, orange, red, or black water. Brown or orange is often just rust that resolves with flushing, but still report it. Black, yellow, or green tints = call immediately.
  - Any odor beyond a mild chlorine smell. Utilities often boost chlorine after main work, and a faint chlorine smell is normal and benign. Anything else:
       - Rotten egg or sulfur = possible bacterial activity or heater issue. Don't drink.
       - Fuel, solvent, or chemical smell = report immediately, don't use.
       - Sewage smell = report immediately, don't use.
       - Earthy or musty = usually benign but worth reporting.

SHORT ANSWER
Do not ride the bike. The cut exposes the casing and opens under hand squeeze, which means the sidewall's structural ply is severed. Any riding risks a blowout and crash, and the tube is only holding because the casing hasn't fully separated yet. A sidewall cut that reaches the casing is not a conventional repair — replacement is the answer.

WHY (briefly)
- The casing (fabric/aramid/nylon ply under the rubber) is what carries load and resists flex. Once it's cut and visible, the tire cannot safely hold pressure or rider weight.
- A hand squeeze is mild compared to real ride loads (your weight, bumps, pedaling force on the rear). The gap will work open and shut under riding and propagate.
- A flex-opening cut adjacent to the tube is a high tube-damage risk even if pressure holds now.
- If you were truly stranded with no other option, an inside-the-tire boot (Park Tool boot patch or similar) at reduced pressure would let you limp a short distance slowly on smooth pavement. You are not stranded — use transit/rideshare.

DEFLATE + TRANSPORT SEQUENCE

1. Move the bike out of the street to where you'll leave it (office, lobby, bike room).
2. Deflate fully with the wheel still on the bike. Easier and safer than wrestling a soft tire off the frame:
   - Presta: cap off, unscrew the small knurled nut at the top, press the valve. For a fast full release, unscrew the whole valve core with your fingers.
   - Schrader: cap off, depress the center pin with a small tool or key.
   - Press the stem a second time after air stops hissing to confirm it's empty.
3. Remove the rear wheel:
   - Rim brakes: open the quick-release or unhook the noodle so the brake opens.
   - Quick-release axle: open the lever, loosen the non-lever side a few turns.
   - Thru-axle: unscrew it fully. Note orientation if it's asymmetric (most are not, but some frames only fit one way).
   - Shift to the smallest cog before removing (easier chain slack). Disengage the chain from the sprocket and lift the wheel out of the dropouts.
   - Disc-brake bikes: do NOT squeeze the brake lever with the wheel out — the pads will close and you'll need a spreader or ride to the shop to reset them. Wrap the rotor in a clean rag or paper towel so it can't get greased or cut anything.
4. Transport — flat rear wheel on the bike is fine for short carries; you do NOT need to dismount the tire from the rim:
   - Rideshare SUV/truck: bike fits as-is, flat tire, rear wheel stays on.
   - Rideshare sedan: remove rear wheel (and often front). The remaining triangle fits diagonally in a trunk.
   - Transit (bus/train): most allow bikes; a flat rear wheel is much easier to manage than inflated. Fold if it's a folder.

WHAT TO SEND THE SHOP
Send 4–6 photos plus a short written note.

Photos:
1. The cut with the tire still mounted on the rim, taken from a few inches back — shows position on the sidewall (near bead, mid-sidewall, near tread shoulder). Location matters for the diagnosis.
2. A close-up of the cut with a coin or your fingernail next to it for visual scale, confirming the ~8 mm size.
3. The tire's size marking on the sidewall — e.g. "700x28c", "27.5x2.2", "650bx35". They need this to spec a replacement if they don't stock your exact model.
4. The tread from above — shows overall wear. If the tire is bald or close to it, the answer is "replace anyway" regardless of the cut.
5. The cut photographed from the inside of the tire after dismount — tells them whether the casing is cut clean through. (Shop does this when they dismount; you can do it yourself with two plastic tire levers if you want to include it.)
6. The rim under where the cut sits — look for dents, cracks, or spoke-nipple bulge. Sidewall cuts near the bead frequently pair with rim damage.

Note to include:
- How and when it happened (pothole strike, curb impact, debris, noticed on arrival — whatever is true). Cause matters: impact damage to a sidewall often implies a rim strike as well.
- Rider + typical cargo weight, and where you ride (urban with curb hops vs. smooth greenway). Helps them recommend a more sidewall-resistant replacement if you want an upgrade — Schwalbe Marathon Plus, Continental Contact Urban, Panaracer FlatAway, or similar.
- Tire brand/model if readable from the sidewall.
- That the tube is still holding and whether you rode on it at all (likely no).
- Whether you want the same tire back, an upgrade with better sidewall protection, or whatever they recommend given availability.

Expect the shop to recommend a new tire rather than a patch. A boot is a "get you home today" fix, not a real repair, and most reputable shops won't sell it as permanent.

SUPERFICIAL PAW SCRAPE — AT-HOME CARE (KIBO)

INSPECT FIRST (one more pass)
  In good light, run a finger gently along the pad and between toes.
  Confirm: no remaining grit, no flap of skin, nail still intact and seated.
  If you find anything embedded or a flap, stop home care and call the vet.

CLEANING (once today, then once daily for 2-3 days)
  1. Lukewarm water rinse over the paw for 30-60 seconds to flush any

     works; no high-pressure sprayer.
  2. If you have it: dilute chlorhexidine (0.05%) or povidone-iodine
     (betadine) until it's the color of weak tea — dab, don't soak,
     20-30 seconds, then rinse with plain water.
  3. Pat dry with a clean towel. Do not rub.
  4. Thin smear of plain triple-antibiotic ointment (bacitracin/polysporin)
     or a pet antiseptic gel. No Neosporin with pain relief ("-caine"),
     no hydrogen peroxide, no alcohol — they damage healing tissue.

ACTIVITY / ENVIRONMENT (next 48-72 hours)
  Short, leashed potty walks only. No off-leash, no running, no jumping.
  Avoid: hot pavement, sand, gravel, mud, de-icer, wet grass with debris.
  Keep the paw clean and dry between outings — wipe with a damp cloth
  after each walk, re-ointment once a day.
  If he licks: an e-collar or a snug sock secured above the wrist with
  a bit of cohesive wrap. Supervise with a sock — some dogs chew them
  off and can ingest fabric.

CALL THE VET IF YOU SEE ANY OF THESE
  - Bleeding that doesn't stop with gentle, steady pressure in 5-10 min
  - New or spreading redness, warmth, or swelling around the scrape
  - Any discharge (pus, cloudy fluid, foul smell)
  - Limping that worsens after 24 hours or doesn't improve in 48 hours

  - Lethargy, refusing food, fever-ish (warm ears, shivering)

RECHECK WINDOW
  Expect the scrape to look smaller and pinker each day; a faint scab
  is normal. If it looks the same or worse at the 48-hour mark, that

Short interpretation:

Observed activation rates (descriptive)
- Partner: 73.3% (33/45)
- Organic: 65.0% (78/120)
- Paid social: 46.7% (42/90)

What the cut shows vs. what it does not
The ranking Partner > Organic > Paid social is what the numbers say, full stop. These are activation rates among users who were already deemed "eligible" through each channel — they are not a measure of channel quality, channel contribution, or incremental lift.

A causal "Partner produces better users" or "Paid social underperforms" reading does not follow, because:
1. **Unequal and non-random denominators.** The eligible counts differ by ~2.7x (120 vs 45), and eligibility itself is upstream of channel. "Eligible" almost certainly means different things per channel — e.g. who completed signup, who matched a targeting rule, who passed a fraud/quality filter. If Paid social's bar is lower, its lower rate is partly a denominator artifact, not a channel weakness.
2. **Selection into channel.** Users self-select (or are targeted) into channels before eligibility is even defined. The composition — intent, ICP fit, device, geography, time-of-day — differs across channels by construction. The rate differences reflect that composition as much as they reflect anything the channel "did."
3. **No counterfactual.** Without a randomized exposure or a clean holdout, we can't separate "the channel caused the activation" from "the kind of user the channel attracts activates more."

What the cut is good for
- A descriptive snapshot of who's activating within each channel's current funnel.
- A flag that Paid social's 46.7% is meaningfully lower than the other two and worth a follow-up cut (eligibility definition, audience composition, funnel step before activation).
- Volume context: 78 of 153 activations came from Organic (~51%), so even a higher-rate channel like Partner is contributing fewer activations in absolute terms.

What it is not good for
- Ranking channels on quality, ROI, or incremental value.
- Reallocation decisions without the denominators being made comparable and the selection effect being addressed.

Recommended next cuts before any causal claim
- Define "eligible" identically across channels, or split the funnel at a common step (e.g. "reached the activation surface") and re-rate from there.
- Break out activation rate by an ICP/intent proxy within each channel — if the gap shrinks, it's selection; if it holds, it's worth a controlled test.
- Pair rate with volume and downstream retention/paid conversion before reallocation talk.

The echo is real, and your member is right that it pulls in the direction of an invitation. Mara's hiding place was never framed as a secret from intimates — it was an inheritance of access, a standing offer to anyone who knew the narrator. When the ending returns the key to that same spot, the narrator is reaching for a gesture whose meaning was always shared. So the repeated location carries forward the offer, and the reading the member is proposing has real traction.

But I keep stalling on the sentence order. The key goes back *after* the gate is locked, and the lock is a deliberate, completed act — simple past, declarative, no hedging ("I locked," not "I was locking," not "I thought about locking"). The narrator does not bury the key first and then walk away. Does not leave the gate ajar. Does not frame the lock as provisional. The lock is the operative verb. Only then does the key go home.

And the key going home is not quite the same gesture Mara taught. Mara's protocol was open — leave the key where anyone who knew you would look. The narrator is doing something adjacent but distinct: returning the key to a known location *while the gate is locked*. The hiding place still means what it meant; the narrator has simply added a new condition that Mara's teaching never contained. Access now requires not only knowing the spot but also choosing to unlock — a step the earlier passage did not include.

So I think the ending holds both acts at once and refuses to let us rank them. The invitation survives in the key, in the location, in the echo of Mara's words. The boundary survives in the lock, in the deliberate completed gesture, in the new condition the narrator has quietly introduced. Either reading can be made coherent; neither cancels the other. A pure invitation would not need the lock. A pure boundary would not bother returning the key to the place anyone who knew the narrator would look. The book ends in the middle, and that middle feels intentional — the kind of ending that asks us to sit with the doubleness rather than collapse it.

REVISED SCHEDULE — SINGLE COUNTERTOP OVEN, 2:00 PM THURSDAY

THE TIGHT CONSTRAINT
The mac needs 60 min of oven time (two 30-min pans, sequential), and the casserole rule says a completed casserole can sit covered no more than 45 min before serving. With one oven you can't cook the mac and stuff the stuffing after without bumping one of those limits, so the only workable plan treats the mac as ONE casserole that completes when pan 2 comes out, and runs the stuffing AFTER the mac. That's the schedule below.

COUNTDOWN FROM 2:00 PM (backward)
  2:00 PM   Serve.
  1:50 PM   Pull stuffing AND rolls. Cover both.
  1:40 PM   Slide rolls into the oven (last 10 min, alongside stuffing, still 350°F).
  1:15 PM   Pull mac pan 2. The mac casserole is now complete; cover and hold.
 12:45 PM   Pull mac pan 1, slide mac pan 2 in (oven stays at 375°F).
 12:15 PM   Slide mac pan 1 into a preheated 375°F oven.

OVEN TIMELINE (forward)
 12:15–12:45 PM   Mac pan 1          375°F
 12:45– 1:15 PM   Mac pan 2          375°F   (no temp change — same dish)
  1:15– 1:50 PM   Stuffing (9x13)    350°F   (drop oven from 375 → 350; ~5 min cool-down)
  1:40– 1:50 PM   Rolls              350°F   (added for the final 10 min with stuffing)

HOLD TIMES (out of oven → 2:00 PM, covered)
  Mac casserole (complete at 1:15 PM):  45 min  ← exactly at the limit
  Mac pan 1 alone (12:45 → 1:15):      30 min covered wait before the dish is "complete"
  Stuffing (out 1:50):                  10 min
  Rolls (out 1:50):                     10 min

WHAT TO WATCH
  - Mac pan 1 sits covered on the counter for 30 min before pan 2 joins it. Keep the foil tight; it's still very hot out of a 375°F oven, but it's the soft spot in the plan. Don't unwrap or stir it during that wait.
  - The 375 → 350 transition eats ~5 min. If your oven is slow to drop, pull mac pan 2 at 1:10 PM and start the cool-down earlier; the stuffing will still get its 35 min at 350°F if you slide it in around 1:15–1:20 PM.
  - If you'd rather not have pan 1 sitting 30 min alone, the only alternative is to run the rolls as their own batch 1:50–2:00 PM at 350°F instead of riding along with the stuffing. That uses 10 more oven minutes but gives you a clean "stuffing out, rolls in" handoff at 1:50.

WHY NOT THE OTHER ORDERINGS
  - Stuffing first, then mac: stuffing would finish no later than ~12:45 PM to leave 60 min of mac time, which means the stuffing sits 75 min covered — over the 45-min rule.
  - Mac first, then stuffing, but starting mac earlier than 12:15 PM: the completed mac casserole would sit more than 45 min before 2:00 PM.
  - Interleaving mac and stuffing: different temperatures (375 vs 350), so they can't share the oven at the same time.

Bottom line first: based on Kibo's size (~42 lb / ~19 kg) and the amount you described (<1 tsp gravy with cooked allium, asymptomatic now), this is well below the threshold where most published sources predict clinical Heinz-body anemia. An emergency vet visit right now is not warranted on the information you've given. A call to ASPCA Animal Poison Control (888-426-4435) or Pet Poison Helpline (855-764-7661) for documentation is reasonable but not strictly required at this dose.

Why (so you can sanity-check the call I'm making)

  Onion and garlic damage is oxidative: organosulfur compounds bind hemoglobin, form Heinz bodies, and over time cause hemolytic anemia. The dose that produces clinical illness in dogs is typically cited around ~5 g/kg of onion, with garlic roughly 5x more potent by weight. For Kibo at ~19 kg, that's on the order of 95 g of onion before clinical anemia is expected, and a teaspoon of gravy carries a fraction of a gram of actual allium solids. So you're looking at one to two orders of magnitude below the symptomatic threshold.

  The other key feature of this toxicity is that it is delayed: Heinz bodies take time to form and to cause enough red-cell loss for clinical signs. That is what makes the monitoring timeline below actually matter even when the acute call is "watch and wait."

Immediate contact

  ER now: no, based on your description. Indications that WOULD change this: any symptom at all (vomit, drooling, lethargy, pale/tacky gums, dark or red urine, fast breathing, jaundice); a substantially larger dose (grams of raw allium or multiple tablespoons); a small/mediterranean/japanese-type breed; or known G6PD deficiency or prior anemia.

  Poison control: optional but defensible. The case number and the consult are cheap insurance if you'd like it logged. Skip it if you'd rather just monitor.

Delayed signs and timing

  0-24 hours (acute GI): vomiting, diarrhea, appetite loss, abdominal discomfort, drooling, lethargy. Possible but uncommon at this dose.

  1-3 days (early hematologic, often subclinical): subtle drop in energy or exercise tolerance. Gums may start to look a little pale.

  3-7 days (peak anemia window - the one that actually matters):
    - pale or white gums (normal = pink, like yours)
    - jaundice - yellow tint on gums, inner eyelids, or sclera
    - dark, red, brown, or orange urine (hemoglobinuria - the most specific late indicator)
    - weakness, ataxia, reluctance to move
    - rapid breathing or panting at rest, fast heart rate

Daily checks for the next 7 days

  Gums: pink and moist. Capillary refill <2 sec on a finger press.
  Urine color: any darkening, red, brown, or orange tint.
  Energy and eating: a meaningful drop from baseline.

Repeated low-dose allium exposures (e.g., regular table scraps) accumulate; an isolated one-off small lick is the easier case.

The turkey is safely out of the danger zone right now (165°F breast, 173°F thigh), but it can't stay in a 200°F roaster for three hours without the breast drying out, and it can't sit on the counter until 2:00 — that's almost three hours in the danger zone, past the 2-hour rule for cooked poultry.

The cleanest answer is an insulated hold in a clean cooler. Caterers and BBQ cooks use this routinely for 3–4 hour holds of large hot proteins. The thermal mass of a hot bird plus good insulation keeps it above 140°F the whole time without the dry heat of a 200°F oven.

Steps starting now (it's about 11:10):

  1. Pull the turkey from the roaster. Let it rest on the counter 10–15 minutes so juices redistribute and surface steam drops (otherwise the foil traps condensation and softens the skin).

  2. Wrap tightly in heavy-duty aluminum foil — two or three full sheets, sealed at every seam. The foil is the vapor barrier; if steam escapes, the bird dries.

  3. Wrap the foil-wrapped turkey in two or three clean kitchen towels, or set it on a folded towel in the cooler with another towel draped over the top. Towels are the insulation.

  4. Place in a clean, empty cooler (no ice, no water). Close the lid. Don't open it again until you're ready to carve.

  5. If you have a leave-in probe thermometer, tuck it into the thickest part of the thigh before closing up — that's the only way to actually verify hold temp. Otherwise, trust the method: a foil- and towel-wrapped hot turkey in a closed cooler will still be 150°F+ at 2:00.

At 2:00, unwrap, set on a cutting board, and rest 10 minutes before carving. If you want to refresh the skin, run it under the broiler for 3–5 minutes while you carve the dark meat — optional, and don't put it back in the 200°F roaster to "warm up" or you'll undo the whole plan.

If you don't have a cooler that's clean, big enough, and ready, the backup is the carve-cool-reheat method:

  - Carve now (whole or in large pieces), spread in a shallow pan in a single layer.
  - Cool fast: set the pan over a larger pan of ice water in the sink, stirring gently, until the meat drops to around 70°F (roughly 20–30 minutes for sliced meat).
  - Cover and refrigerate.
  - At about 1:15, pull it out, splash a little warm broth or pan drippings over the slices, cover tightly with foil, and warm in a 275–300°F oven for 20–25 minutes until the meat hits 165°F internal. Carryover will hold it there through plating.
  - More work and slightly more risk of drying at the reheat step, but it's the standard safe path if the cooler isn't available.

What not to do:

  - Leave it on the counter or in the roaster with the lid off — past the 2-hour mark by service.
  - Hold at 200°F for three hours — safe but the breast will be overcooked and dry.
  - Put a whole hot turkey straight into the fridge — the center cools too slowly, it spends hours in the danger zone, and it warms everything else in the fridge.

The cooler hold is the right call here: safe, hands-off for the next three hours, and the meat comes out at serving temperature without the dry-edge problem the 200°F roaster would have caused.

No shell/terminal access in this environment, so I worked the scaling by hand (factor = 14/8 = 1.75). Here's the scaled recipe with the awkward bits flagged honestly.

SCALED INGREDIENTS (8 → 14 servings, factor 1.75)

  Cornmeal         1 1/2 c  →  2 5/8 c  (2.625)
  All-purpose flour  1/2 c   →   7/8 c  (0.875)
  Sugar            2 Tbsp   →  3 1/2 Tbsp
  Baking powder    2 tsp    →  3 1/2 tsp
  Salt             3/4 tsp  →  1 5/16 tsp  (1.3125)
  Buttermilk       1 1/4 c  →  2 3/16 c  (2.1875)
  Eggs             2 large  →  3 1/2 large   ← awkward
  Melted butter    4 Tbsp   →  7 Tbsp

  Oven stays at 400°F.

AWKWARD THINGS I DIDN'T HIDE

  Eggs at 3.5: you can't buy half an egg. Three options, pick one — don't just round to 3 or 4 in silence.

    1. Whisk one egg in a small bowl (a beaten large egg ≈ 3 Tbsp), then measure out 3 Tbsp of it and discard the remaining ~1 Tbsp. Cleanest.
    2. Use 3 whole eggs + 1 yolk. Slightly richer, fine in cornbread.
    3. Use 4 whole eggs and pull ~3 Tbsp of buttermilk to compensate (drop buttermilk from 2 3/16 c to 2 c). Easiest if you're not in the mood to fiddle with a partial egg.

    Don't round to 3 eggs — 25% less binder than the recipe calls for, cornbread will be drier and more crumbly.

  Salt at 1 5/16 tsp: also awkward but small. Round freely to 1 1/4 tsp; nobody will notice the difference and it keeps the measuring spoons clean.

  Baking powder at 3 1/2 tsp: this is a real number (cornbread uses a generous leavening amount), measure it. Don't "round down to 3 tsp" — that's a real loss of rise.

PAN CHOICE

  The original 8×8 = 64 sq in. 14 servings at the same batter depth needs 64 × 1.75 = 112 sq in.

    9×13 pan = 117 sq in. Closest match. Batter depth comes out almost exactly the same as the original — center will set about as reliably as the 8×8 does. This is the right choice.

    Two 8×8 pans = 128 sq in. Total area is right, but each pan is only half-full, so you'll get two thin, extra-crusty slabs and the bake time drops noticeably. Fine if you want to serve one and gift one; not a clean equivalent for one family lunch.

    Don't use a 9×9 (81 sq in). It holds 75% of what you need — batter will overflow or mound in the middle and bake unevenly.

BAKE-TIME CHECK

  Because a 9×13 is bigger in every dimension than an 8×8, the thermal path to the center is longer even though the depth is similar. Plan on the high end of the original range, possibly slightly past it.

    1. Start checking at 22 min (low end of the original window).
    2. Toothpick in the center should come out with moist crumbs, not wet batter.
    3. Expect 25–30 min total. Pull at 25 and recheck every 3 min if needed.
    4. If the top is browning faster than the center sets, lay a loose sheet of foil over the top and give it another 5 min — classic move, not a failure.

SUMMARY FOR MOM

  Use a 9×13. Do the partial-egg trick (whisk one, measure 3 Tbsp) or 3 eggs + 1 yolk — don't round the eggs down. Round the salt up to 1 1/4 tsp and call it good. Everything else measures cleanly. Start the toothpick check at 22 min, expect to go to about 28.

What the result shows

- One clean edge at 45° back-over-self, one lifted at 90°. Consistent with standard watercolor guidance (low-angle peel along the edge, not straight up).
- A single pair shows a difference but cannot isolate which variable produced it. Direction is one candidate. Any edge-level difference you didn't notice is another.

The most likely silent confound

- Paper grain. Tape removal against the grain lifts fibers far more readily than with it. If the two edges sat at different orientations to the grain — even by accident — that alone accounts for the result. Moisture at removal is a smaller concern given your wash controls were held constant.

Recommendation

- Adopt 45° as your working rule on the next painting. It costs nothing, it matches the result, and it matches established practice. Treat it as provisional.
- Run the minimum confirmation before you generalize. One small sheet is cheap; committing a confound-driven rule across many paintings is not.

The confirmation that separates direction from edge differences

- One new sheet. Same wash controls, same tape, same dwell time. Reverse the assignment: the position that was clean before is now removed at 90°; the position that was damaged is now removed at 45°. Position changes; direction does not.
- Lift follows direction (new 90° edge lifts, new 45° edge is clean) → direction is doing the work.
- Lift follows position (same physical spot lifts again, opposite spot is clean at 90°) → an edge confound, almost certainly grain, drove the first result.
- Both clean → the first lift was an anomaly; 45° is reliable.
- Both lift → something other than direction is wrong (paper batch, seal, technique).

A shortcut worth checking first

- On the current sheet, identify the grain (deckle edge, or the smoother direction by feel). If the lifted edge ran against the grain, the rule is "remove with the grain at a low angle," not just "45°." That settles the question without a second sheet. If grain doesn't align with the damage, run the reversal test above.

Math check (sanity):

- October: 790 kWh ÷ 29 days = **27.24 kWh/day**
- November: 1284 kWh ÷ 31 days = **41.42 kWh/day**
- Change: **+14.18 kWh/day, +52.1%** (November vs October)
- Effective rate: Oct ≈ $0.1418/kWh, Nov ≈ $0.1386/kWh — very close, so the rate lines really did hold; this is a usage jump, not a billing artifact.
- Days in period differ by 2, but 1284 vs 790 is a 62.5% jump in total kWh, which is well outside what the extra 2 days can explain.

Practical sequence before contacting the utility or maintenance:

1. **Pin the meter window.** Confirm the bill's "service period" dates and the actual read dates on each line — November should be Oct X → Dec Y. If the period is longer than 31 days, the jump partly dissolves; if it's a different number of days than the calendar month, normalize (kWh ÷ days) and recheck the percentage.

2. **Thermostat history.** Pull the runtime log for both months from the thermostat app (setpoint changes, aux-heat / heat-strip runtimes, average indoor temp, outdoor temp if shown). Look specifically for: heat-strip activation hours (a bad balance, a stuck relay, or a recent cold snap will show here even if the setpoint didn't move) and whether the schedule matches what you actually lived on in November.

3. **Water-heater behavior.** This is the usual silent 30–50 kWh/day culprit. Check: (a) is it electric resistance vs. heat-pump (look at the nameplate or the breaker — a heat-pump unit pulling 4–5 kW in resistance mode looks like a new dryer); (b) recent error/fault codes in the app if it's a communicating unit; (c) is the cold-water inlet on the recirculation loop actually cold — a stuck recirc pump or failed mixing valve can run the element near-continuously. Run it 24 hours with the heater breaker off and compare meter disc / smart-meter kWh against a normal day.

4. **Other plug loads and the fridge.** Unplug or breaker-test anything new since late September — window AC stored then plugged back in, space heaters, a dehumidifier, an EV charger on a 120V outlet, a treadmill in a cold room. Check the fridge/freezer: door gaskets, condenser-coil dust, and listen for a compressor that now runs almost continuously. A failing fridge can quietly add 20–40 kWh/day.

5. **Cold-snap normalization.** Pull NWS or utility-website HDD (heating-degree-days) for your zip, Oct vs Nov. If Nov had ~50% more HDD than Oct, a 50% jump in kWh is largely weather-driven and you may not need a service call at all — just thermostat tuning.

6. **Self-read the meter.** If you have a smart-meter portal, compare portal kWh to billed kWh for both periods. A mismatch means the utility estimated one of the bills — and "estimated" can look exactly like a usage spike when the next actual read catches up.

7. **Then decide who to call.** If thermostat/heat-strip runtimes explain it → HVAC contractor. If recirc or element behavior explains it → plumber or water-heater tech. If everything looks normal except the meter numbers → utility first, ask them to re-read or pull interval data (most smart meters log 15-minute or hourly kWh, which will localize the spike to a specific day or a specific appliance signature).

Quick read on what you've described: a GFCI that trips only under hair-dryer load and accepts a small lamp afterward is behaving normally for its job — it just means the dryer is leaking a few milliamps to ground (or the GFCI is on the sensitive side). No heat, smell, discoloration, or buzzing is reassuring: there is no active fire or shock hazard right now. The most likely cause is the dryer, not the outlet, but the lamp test alone does not close the case either way.

Safe isolation sequence (do these in order)

  1. Stop using the dryer on that outlet. (Already done — good.)
  2. Unplug the dryer and let it sit unused for a few hours in a dry room. Any internal condensation from bathroom humidity will partially dry out, which matters for the next test.
  3. Inspect the dryer itself with the plug UNPLUGGED:
     - cord: any nicks, kinks, crush marks, exposed copper, or a bend that stays bent
     - plug: discoloration, looseness, bent or pitted prongs, melted plastic
     - air intake (rear screen): clogged with lint/hair? heavy clog makes the element run hotter
     - housing: any cracks near the handle or barrel, any melted or warped plastic
     - age: if it's 5+ years old and used heavily, heating-element degradation is common
  4. Test the dryer in a DIFFERENT GFCI-protected outlet — another bathroom, kitchen counter outlet, or garage GFCI. Use it for a full 1–2 minute cycle on high heat. Note whether it trips that other GFCI.
  5. Test this outlet with a DIFFERENT high-draw appliance — a vacuum cleaner or space heater is fine, on for 30–60 seconds. Note whether it trips.
  6. Press the GFCI TEST button on the outlet itself. It should trip and the lamp should go off. Press RESET. The lamp should come back on. If RESET doesn't hold, or the button feels loose or stuck, the outlet is suspect regardless of the dryer.
  7. Leave the dryer unplugged and the outlet unused until you've completed the tests and know what you're dealing with. Do not "try it one more time" to see if it still trips.

How to read the results — appliance vs. outlet vs. both

  Dryer trips THIS outlet but works in another GFCI  →  this outlet is the problem (likely a marginal or aging GFCI, or a wiring issue). Appliance is probably fine.
  Dryer trips THIS outlet AND also trips another GFCI  →  appliance is the primary fault. Outlet may still be a secondary contributor; get it inspected if it's old.
  A vacuum or space heater also trips THIS outlet  →  outlet/wiring is the problem. Stop using this outlet for any high-draw appliance and report it.
  Only the hair dryer trips, in multiple outlets  →  retire the dryer. Do not donate or sell it; the heating element or cord is faulting.
  GFCI TEST/RESET buttons feel loose, won't hold reset, or trip instantly with nothing plugged in  →  outlet itself is faulty. Don't keep using it for anything until it's replaced.

Reporting sequence

  If you rent or live in managed housing (which the "report to maintenance" phrasing suggests):
   - Notify maintenance today with a short, factual message: which outlet (bathroom, which side of vanity, etc.), what was plugged in, how many trips, what you have and have not observed (no smell, no heat, lamp works after reset, dryer stopped in use). Attach the inspection findings from step 3 and the test results from steps 4–6.
   - Ask them to send a licensed electrician, not just a handyman, because repeated GFCI trips can indicate either an aging GFCI device or a developing wiring issue that warrants a proper look. GFCIs older than ~10 years are a routine replacement item anyway.
   - Do not move back to using the outlet on your own until they clear it.

  If you own the unit:
   - The dryer should be retired and replaced; a hair dryer that trips GFCIs repeatedly is no longer safe to keep using even if it "works" elsewhere — the fault can progress.
   - Schedule an electrician to swap the GFCI if it's old, and to inspect the bathroom circuit while they're there. Cost is usually modest; this is a one-trip fix.

Urgent escalation — these change the situation from "annoying, handle this week" to "stop using the area and act now"

  - Any burning smell, even faint, even momentary, from the outlet, plug, dryer, or wall
  - Discoloration, brown/yellow marks, or melting on the outlet face, the wall plate, or the dryer plug
  - The outlet face, wall plate, or plug feels warm or hot to the touch at any time — not just during use
  - Buzzing, crackling, sizzling, or popping sounds from the outlet or appliance
  - Visible sparking when plugging in or unplugging
  - A physical tingle or shock when touching the dryer, the outlet, the faucet, or any metal fixture while the dryer is running
  - The GFCI trips immediately with nothing plugged in, or the RESET button will not latch
  - Water intrusion near the outlet: a leak, a splash zone you didn't notice, steam damage, or a wet wall
  - The dryer trips a GFCI in a DIFFERENT outlet too — and on a third use, anything in the urgent list above appears
  - The trip frequency is increasing: if it trips a third time even with shorter use, or starts tripping other appliances in the same bathroom

  If any of those appear: stop using the bathroom outlet, leave the breaker off if you know which one serves the bathroom, and call a licensed electrician same-day rather than waiting for routine maintenance.

Two things worth saying out loud because they are common misreads of this exact situation:

  - "The lamp works, so the outlet is fine" is only partly true. A lamp draws maybe 10–60 watts; a hair dryer draws 1,500–1,875. The lamp test rules out a dead outlet; it does not rule out a marginal outlet, an aging GFCI with shifted sensitivity, or a wiring issue that only shows up under high load.
  - "It's just a hair dryer" can mislead. Hair dryers combine a heating element, a motor, and high current in a wet-room environment, which is exactly the failure pattern that GFCIs exist to catch. A dryer that repeatedly trips GFCIs is telling you something about itself; the right move is to listen to it, not to retry it.

If after steps 4 and 5 the dryer is the confirmed culprit and there are zero items on the urgent list, you do not need to panic — you need to replace the dryer and give maintenance a heads-up so they can note the GFCI's age and condition. If you want, tell me the results of the cross-outlet test and the high-draw test and I'll read them with you.

Opening observation:

The two sentences run on different clocks. The first — "not tonight" — refuses a specific hour. The second — sliding the letter beneath papers she'll have to find every April — sets a calendar. She isn't choosing between temporary deferral and lasting avoidance; she's doing both at once. The question for the room is whether she knows the two clocks are running simultaneously, and what that awareness does to the meaning of either one.

Three questions:

1. Why the tax papers specifically? Tax documents are read out of obligation, not want — private, recurring, tied to the calendar. Is she filing the letter as one more annual duty she'll have to perform, or is she giving it the most private, recurring shelf she has? Does the container she chose tell us what kind of encounter she expects — or has she deferred that decision too?

2. What distinguishes this hour? The simile makes the hour the asking party: she's not refusing the letter, she's refusing the moment. Is the refusal about her capacity (too tired, too raw, too late) or about the letter's timing (some messages shouldn't be opened at this hour)? If the hour changes, does her refusal change with it — or has she already made a decision the night can't undo?

3. What does the key do that the refusal doesn't? She doesn't just decline; she seals. Turning a key closes more than a door, and the simile suggests she's sealing against the hour itself. Is the lock a temporary measure she'll undo tomorrow, or is the gesture of sealing the more honest act — the one that tells us what she actually wants? And if she has to "find" the letter again every April, how often does she expect to look?

FRAME FOR YOU (not the group)
You came with an opening observation. As facilitator now, your read is one of four, not the spine. Bracket it for the first round; if it hasn't surfaced by the closing, you can name it there.

THE TWO TEXTUAL ANCHORS — load-bearing throughout
  1. The storage: she puts the letter with documents she returns to annually. This implies preservation, future revisiting, ritual.

OPENING (3 min)
  - One-sentence acknowledgment of the shift (host lost her voice, you're stepping in).
  - State the question plainly: temporary boundary or lasting avoidance?
  - Name the asymmetry: "The book gives evidence for both. Disagreement tonight isn't failure — it's two legitimate ways of holding the same text."
  - Invite each person to bring their own read; don't ask them to converge.

GROUNDING (5 min)
  Anchor everyone in the same facts before anyone argues a reading.
  - Ask one member to paraphrase the storage scene, or read it yourself.
  - Ask another to paraphrase the refusal, or read it yourself.
  - Check: "Is that the moment we're all holding?" If anyone remembers it differently, surface that now. This prevents 20 minutes of talking past each other.

ROUND 1 — FOUR READS, ONE ENTRY ANGLE EACH (12 min, ~3 min per person)
  Offer these angles; let people self-select or assign one. Each gives a different reader a clean way in.

  Angle A — Inside the body: What does the refusal feel like from her side? What would it cost to open it that night?
  Angle B — The container: What does storing it with annual-return documents do — preservation, postponement, or the performance of return?
  Angle C — The arc: How does the scene land in the larger shape? Does the letter come back later, or is this the last we see of it?
  Angle D — The "and": Can the same gesture be a boundary AND avoidance? What would that even look like?

  Operational moves:
  - Each person speaks uninterrupted.
  - After each, do a 20-second "what I heard you say" paraphrase before moving on. This equalizes airtime and surfaces where two people actually agree without realizing it.

PRESSURE-TEST EXCHANGE (12 min)
  Two options — pick whichever fits the room:

  Option A — Steelmanning pair (works if the split is clean):
    "Take 2 minutes each: steelman the reading you don't hold. What does the other side see that you might be missing?"
    Then 6 minutes of open exchange.

  Option B — Paired exchange (works if you want to slow a dominant voice):
    Pair the two members who read differently on the storage detail for 5 minutes.
    Pair the two who read differently on the refusal for 5 minutes.
    Reconvene for 2 minutes: "Anything from your partner that surprised you?"

  Your moves during this block:
  - When someone argues abstractly, ask: "Where in the text?"
  - When someone shifts ground, name it: "Earlier you said X — now you're saying Y. Both can be true; I want to follow you."
  - Do not resolve the "and." Let it sit.
  - If silence opens, count to 10. Don't fill.

CLOSING (8 min) — no consensus
  Do not ask "so which is it?" Pick one of these three closings:

  (a) Sit-with: "What's one sentence from the book you want to hold after tonight?"
  (b) Movement: "Did anyone's read shift in the room? What moved?"
  (c) Counterfactual: "What would have to be true — in the text, or in her life — for your reading to be the right one?"

  End by naming the disagreement itself as the product of the evening: "We didn't land on one answer, and I don't think the book wants us to. What we did was hold both readings carefully, and that's the work."

TIMING
  Opening 3 / Grounding 5 / Round 1 12 / Exchange 12 / Closing 8 / Buffer 5 = 45.

RISKS TO WATCH
  - The strong reader pulls the room. Round structure slows them down.
  - The quiet reader needs a specific prompt, not "what do you think?" Hand them an angle directly: "Want to come in on the container question?"
  - The conversation drifts from the two anchors. Reset by re-reading the storage detail or the refusal aloud.
  - You have your own read. Don't lead with it. Save it for the closing if it hasn't surfaced.
  - If the room converges too fast, ask: "What's the strongest case for the other side?" If it stays split — that's the success condition.

7-DAY POST-REPLACEMENT MONITORING PLAN
Start date: 2024-12-19 (Day 0 = replacement day)

DAILY LOG — 5 FIELDS, ONE ROW PER DAY
Record each evening, same time if possible.

  Date       | Ambient low (°F) | T-stat sensor (°F) | Aux-heat runtime (min or hr) | Setpoint changes | Daily kWh
  ---------- | ---------------- | ------------------ | --------------------------- | ---------------- | ---------
  Day 1 (12/19) |              |                    |                             |                  |
  Day 2 (12/20) |              |                    |                             |                  |
  ...        |                  |                    |                             |                  |
  Day 7 (12/25) |              |                    |                             |                  |

Where to pull each field:
  - Ambient low: a separate calibrated source (nearby weather station, second
    thermometer, or utility-app "outdoor temp" if independent of thermostat).
    Do not use the thermostat's outdoor reading — that's what we're validating.
  - T-stat sensor reading: the thermostat's reported outdoor temp at the same
    hour each day (e.g. 7am).
  - Aux-heat runtime: thermostat's auxiliary / emergency-heat run-time counter
    for the day. If it shows cumulative hours, log the reading and subtract
    yesterday's to get the daily delta.
  - Setpoint changes: note only if changed. Default = "no change, 68°F."
  - Daily kWh: utility bill portal, smart-meter app, or meter manual read at
    same time daily. If daily kWh is not available, mark "N/A" and use weekly
    instead — do not skip the other fields.

EVIDENCE-SAFE COMPARISON BOUNDARY
What this 7-day log CAN support:
  - Whether the new sensor's readings track the calibrated ambient within ~2°F.
  - Whether aux-heat runtime looks proportionate to the actual outdoor lows.
  - Whether the system behavior changed in a sensible direction after repair.

What this 7-day log CANNOT support, and you should not claim:
  - That the full November electricity increase was caused by the old sensor.
  - A percent attribution of the November spike to the faulty sensor.
  - A clean before/after kWh delta attributed to the sensor alone.

Reasons the naive before/after is unsafe:
  1. The 7-day window after replacement will almost certainly have a different
     average outdoor temperature than November. Colder post-period → more kWh
     from real heating load, masking any improvement. Warmer post-period →
     looks like a big saving that is really just weather.
  2. November's kWh includes non-heating loads that also rise seasonally
     (shorter days = more lighting, more hot-water use, holiday cooking, etc.).
     None of those are affected by the sensor.
  3. The old sensor read ~32°F low. The thermostat may have responded with
     longer compressor cycles, more aux-heat staging, OR both. Total kWh
     conflates these. Aux-heat runtime is the cleaner signal of the sensor's
     effect, but only if normalized by actual outdoor temperature.
  4. A 7-day sample is too short to average out day-to-day usage variance
     (occupancy, defrost cycles, setpoint overrides, overnight setbacks).

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY QUANTIFY THE SENSOR'S SHARE
Pick at least one of the following before drawing a numeric conclusion:
  - Normalize aux-heat runtime per Heating Degree Day (HDD) for each day, then
     compare Nov daily values vs. post-replacement daily values at similar
     actual outdoor lows. A persistent gap is signal; a one-week gap is noise.
  - Pull the same address's electricity usage for the same calendar weeks in
     one or two prior winters (pre-fault) as a weather-matched baseline.
  - If the old sensor is still available, have it bench-tested at a known
     temperature alongside the new one. A controlled lab delta + measured
     aux-heat response curve gives a defensible estimate without relying on
     the field before/after.

REPORTING RULE
When you summarize the 7 days, state the comparison as:
  "Aux-heat runtime per degree-day after replacement vs. the same ratio during
   the November period, with the caveat that a 7-day window is descriptive
   only and does not establish attribution of the November total."
Do not state a percentage of November's increase that came from the sensor
unless supported by one of the methods above.

PHISHING INDICATORS

  - Unsolicited, with artificial urgency ("within 30 minutes") - classic pressure tactic.
  - Oddly precise micro-amount ($2.14) - chosen to look like a real, small charge.
  - Sender is a plain 10-digit phone number. Real airline bag alerts come from a short code (e.g., 4-6 digits) tied to the carrier's SMS gateway, or from the airline's own app, never a vanilla mobile number.
  - Link domain is a hyphenated .co ("airline-baghelp.co/release") - real airlines use their own .com. The hyphen + unusual TLD is a lookalike pattern.
  - "Release fee" is a fabricated concept. Airlines do not charge a fee to release a bag you've already paid to check; if a bag is held for, say, a customs or oversized issue, the airline contacts you in-app or at the carousel - never via an SMS payment link.
  - The pretext is false on its face: mom has no checked bag, so the trigger condition can't exist.
  - No corresponding alert in the airline app = verifiable absence of the legitimate notice a real hold would produce.

SAFE VERIFICATION (app + ticket number only)

  1. Open the airline app the normal way (home screen icon, not the link). Sign in.
  2. Go to the trip for that day and open the bag/checked-items section. A genuinely held bag surfaces there as a status banner.
  3. Open in-app messages / notifications. Real bag issues post a card inside the app; SMS is at most a duplicate pointer, never the only channel.
  4. If still uncertain, call the airline using the phone number printed on the paper ticket or boarding pass. If the paper copy isn't handy, type the airline's main URL into a browser manually and use the "Contact us" number from there. Do not call any number from the text.
  5. Ask the agent to confirm by name and record locator whether any bag is associated with mom's itinerary. Answer is no - because there is no bag - which independently invalidates the text.

SAFE DELETION

  - Do not tap the link, do not reply STOP, do not call the sender's number, do not forward to anyone else for "help."
  - iPhone: long-press the message, tap Delete. If iOS offers "Delete Link," accept it so the URL is also removed from caches. Optionally tap "Report Junk" before deleting - Apple then strips sender info and forwards the content.
  - Android (Messages app): long-press the message, choose Delete. If a "Report spam" toggle appears, turn it on before deleting.
  - On either platform, after deletion, open Settings -> Messages and confirm "Filter Unknown Senders" is on, so future smishes route to a separate list.

SAFE REPORTING

  1. Forward the original text (unchanged, including the sender number) to 7726 (SPAM). This is the GSMA short code the major US carriers use; forwarding is free and the carriers use it to track scam campaigns.
  2. File at reportfraud.ftc.gov - the FTC routes SMS scams to its Consumer Sentinel database.
  3. File at ic3.gov (FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center) if mom clicked the link or entered anything on the linked page; skip this step if she never touched it.
  4. Optionally forward a screenshot to the airline's published fraud / phishing address (most US carriers publish one on their security page). This helps the real brand get the lookalike domain taken down.

NET

  The text is a smish impersonating a bag-fee notice, with no real bag behind it. Mom is safe as long as the link was never opened and no info was entered. Verification via the app and the ticket's printed number will confirm within a minute that there is nothing to pay.

Good news: a foil + insulated cooler hold is exactly the right tool for this — that's a standard catering holding method. You can keep the chicken safely above 140°F for an hour-plus without further cooking, and the oven sequence still fits a 1:30pm service.

CHICKEN HOLD
- 12:35 — chicken hits 165°F. Pull it, leave it uncovered on a board to rest.
- 12:35 to 12:45 (10 min rest) — this is the key step you were asking about. Letting the surface steam off before wrapping is what stops the foil from trapping moisture and continuing to cook the chicken dry. Don't skip it.
- 12:45 — wrap tightly in 2–3 layers of heavy foil, no air gaps.
- Pre-warm the cooler first if you haven't: boil water in it for 5 minutes, dump, then add the foil-wrapped chicken. Close the lid. Don't open it again until service. With a 165°F start and a pre-warmed cooler, you'll lose roughly 15–20°F over 45 min — it lands at about 145–155°F, well above the 140°F hot-holding floor.

OVEN SEQUENCE
- 12:50 — macaroni in at 350°F.
- 1:20 — macaroni done (30 min). Cover with foil and set aside, or drop it into the cooler with the chicken. Either way it holds fine for 10 min.
- 1:20 — turn the oven down to 325°F; crack the door for 30 seconds if it doesn't drop fast enough.
- 1:18 — rolls in at 325°F. (A minute of overlap is fine; the oven hits 325 quickly once you turn it down.)
- 1:30 — rolls done. Plate everything.

SANITY CHECK AT 1:30
- Stick an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part of the chicken. Anything 140°F or higher is safe; you'll almost certainly see 145–155°F. If for any reason it's under 140°F, slip it into the (now-empty, hot) oven for a few minutes to bring it back up before plating.

WHY THIS WORKS
- Foil + pre-warmed cooler is a true hold, not a continuation of cooking. After the 10-min rest the chicken is just losing heat slowly, not gaining it.
- Mac and rolls each get their proper oven temp without either being rushed or held so long it dries out.
- Total hands-on time during the hold is essentially zero.

Slow drain in BOTH basins of a double-basin kitchen tells you the blockage is downstream of the basin tee — usually the P-trap (grease + food sediment after holiday cooking) or the wall stub-out. Below is a lowest-risk-first sequence. Stop at any point you hit a stop sign.

PREP BEFORE YOU START
  - Clear under-sink cabinet. Bucket, old towel, flashlight, tongs, slip-joint pliers (not a wrench — plastic nuts crack).
  - Find the disposer switch and the breaker for it. You will turn the disposer OFF. For any step where a hand goes near the disposer chamber, flip the breaker OFF.
  - Bail standing water out of both basins into the bucket (don't pour it down another drain).
  - Have a wet rag ready to seal the second basin during any plunging.

STEP 1 — VISUAL + DISPOSER CHAMBER (zero hazard)
  - Pull both basket strainers/stoppers. With the disposer breaker OFF, shine a flashlight into the chamber. Use tongs to remove visible debris. Never a hand, never a wooden spoon while energized.
  - Run the disposer briefly with water to confirm it spins freely (breaker on, cold water running).
  - If you find a compacted mat of debris at the bottom of the chamber, that's a partial cause — clear and retest both basins with 2 inches of water.

STEP 2 — PLUNGE THE NON-DISPOSAL BASIN (low hazard if done right)
  - Use a flat-bottom sink plunger. Never plunge the disposal basin itself — the seal can blow back.
  - Seal the OTHER basin (wet rag pressed into the drain or a weighted strainer).
  - 6 to 10 firm vertical strokes. Pull the plunger off on the last stroke to break the vacuum.
  - Retest. If one basin clears but the other doesn't, the clog is upstream of the tee in that tailpiece — proceed to step 3 for that side.

STEP 3 — CLEAN THE P-TRAP (this is the most likely holiday fix)
  - Bucket under the U-bend. Hand-loosen the two slip nuts on the trap. Pull the U down slowly; water will fall into the bucket.
  - Clear the U-bend of grease and food solids. Run a brush or bottle brush through the trap arm toward the wall.
  - Reassemble hand-tight. Hand-tight only on plastic. Run water and inspect for leaks for a full minute before walking away.
  - If the slip nuts are metal and corroded, don't force them — stop and call maintenance.

STEP 4 — HAND-CRANK SNAKE INTO THE WALL OPENING (only if trap was clean)
  - Use a 1/4-inch hand-crank drain auger, not a powered machine. Feed gently.
  - If you meet solid resistance that doesn't give to gentle cranking, stop. Don't keep cranking.
  - Retest both basins.

STOP AND CALL MAINTENANCE IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR
  - Water backs up into the bathtub, washing machine, or other sink when you run the kitchen sink. That's a main-line issue, not a trap issue.
  - A wet floor appears under the cabinet at any point — especially after reassembly.
  - The trap nuts won't budge or the metal is corroded; don't apply force.
  - The snake meets hard resistance you can't identify or clear in 30 seconds of gentle cranking.
  - Gurgling sounds from other drains in the house while the kitchen is running.
  - Sewer gas smell (rotten egg) after you open the trap — the trap was dry, suggesting a venting problem rather than a clog.
  - Disposer hums but does not spin, or trips its breaker during the test — that's a separate fault; stop and call.
  - Drainage does not improve after trap cleaning and gentle snaking — the blockage is past what a hand snake reaches.

UNTIL IT'S FIXED
  - Keep using the sink minimally. Scrape plates into the trash before rinsing. Don't run the dishwasher if its drain is tied into the disposer or sink tailpiece while the line is slow — it can siphon or back up. If you must use the dishwasher, watch the sink while it drains.

The most likely outcome is step 3 (trap cleaning) resolving it — holiday cooking loads grease into the cool trap and it solidifies within a day or two. If steps 1 to 3 don't fix both basins, the problem is past the trap arm and that's reasonable territory to hand off.

Here is a practical workflow for the two-hour session. It reuses conventions already established in your prior photo-archive work (the K/E/U labeling scheme, the no-writing-on-originals rule, the front-only-unless-back-carries-info scan rule, and the two-person verify-before-re-sleeve check).

PRE-SESSION SETUP (15 min before Mom arrives)

  Scanner: TIFF archival profile, auto-correction / auto-contrast / auto-exposure DISABLED. Reason: the August 25 treated-photo session lost faint pencil writing on a back because auto-contrast was on. Run one test scan and open the TIFF to verify before production.

  Two folders ready:
    Photos/M-batch/M_tif/      masters
    Photos/M-batch/M_jpg/      access copies (~2500px long edge)

  Inventory open: a sheet or text file with columns
    M-ID | Status | People | Approx Year | Notes/Sources | Filename(s) | Sleeve

  Sleeve labels, blank cards for in-sleeve IDs, sticky notes for DEFER and DUP-candidate piles, phone camera for any back-text too faint to scan, timer visible.

ROLES (consistent with prior sessions)

  Mom   - identification authority. Names, approximate years, occasion, place. Her memory is the bottleneck; never let her wait on the scanner.
  Marcus - scanner operator and mechanical filer. Captures, labels sleeves, places files.
  Riley - orchestrator. Metadata capture, duplicate calls, defer/keep decisions, timekeeper, inventory writer.

TIME BUDGET (120 min)

  - Phase 1 (40 min): count, ID, inventory all 240. No scanning unless something is at risk.
  - Phase 2 (60 min): scan keepers, front-only unless the back carries information.
  - Phase 3 (20 min): two-person verify, three backups, defer-list handoff.

  Capture-as-you-go is the rule. If scanning slips behind, slow Mom down rather than letting unverified scans pile up.

PHASE 1 - FIRST SWEEP, ALL THREE BOXES (40 min)

  For each box, working together:

    1. Lift photos in stacks of ~10. Look at fronts only.
    2. Assign the next M-ID by writing it on a small card and slipping it beside the photo. IDs go on sleeves/cards, NEVER on the print.
    3. For each photo, ask Mom: "Who is this, and when?" Capture her answer in one short line. If she pauses, mark U (unidentified people/date) or E (estimated year). Do not prompt guesses.
    4. If a photo looks like a duplicate of an earlier M-ID, set it in a DUP-candidate pile with a sticky note linking it to the keeper's M-ID. Do not scan it now and do not discard it.
    5. Photos with writing on the back stay paired front/back. The back gets scanned even if blank-looking.
    6. Photos with uncertain dates: mark E with the range Mom gives ("maybe 1985-88"). If she says "no idea," mark U for date but capture any names she does know.

  End of Phase 1: every photo has an M-ID card, a one-line inventory row, and a placement (keep / DUP-link / DEFER). Roughly 240 inventory rows.

  Soft stop check at 40 min: if Box 1 alone took longer, day's capture is whatever fits the next 80 min - do not push to scan everything.

PHASE 2 - SCAN THE KEEPERS (60 min)

  Marcus scans in M-ID order, in stacks of ~10:

    M###_front.tif     master, scanner-output, no enhancement
    M###_front.jpg     access, ~2500px long edge
    M###_back.tif      only if the back carries information
    M###_back.jpg      only if the back carries information

  Convention: front-only unless the back has writing, a caption, or where Mom's identification came from something on the back. This matches the P-batch rule where only annotated backs were captured separately.

  Two-person verify before re-sleeve: Riley confirms the file on disk matches the inventory row before Marcus puts the original back. Same protocol used for P001-P032.

  Pause condition: at 60 min, stop scanning even if more remain. Unfinished photos stay in their sleeves with M-ID cards. Nothing is lost.

  Duplicate handling during scan: if a scanned photo turns out to be a duplicate of an earlier M-ID, keep the second scan's files but mark the inventory row "DUP of M###." Decide later whether to drop the access JPG; never delete the master until you've verified the keeper.

PHASE 3 - CLOSEOUT (20 min)

    1. Two-person sleeve verification. Riley reads inventory rows; Marcus confirms each photo is back in its labeled sleeve in the correct box.
    2. Three backups before anyone leaves:
         - Master TIFFs to laptop
         - Access JPGs to phone or second drive
         - Inventory file to cloud email or shared doc
    3. Defer list: anything not scanned gets an X row with date and reason ("ran out of time," "back annotation needs transcription help"). This is the handoff doc for the next session.
    4. End-of-session notes on the inventory's first page: scanned count, deferred count, open identification questions, any physical-condition flags (stuck glossy corner, fuzzy edge, etc.).

NAMING CONVENTION (the card by the scanner for Marcus)

    M = the new mixed-box cohort, distinct from P (dry/loose 32) and T (treated 8). M is a natural fit for "mixed boxes" but the prefix is your call.

    M###_front.tif / M###_front.jpg      always when scanned
    M###_back.tif  / M###_back.jpg       only when back carries information
    M###_dup_ofM###                       not a filename - this is an inventory note linking two M-IDs

    Filenames never change once written. Re-scans use a suffix: M###_front_rescan_v1.tif with a sidecar noting reason, date, operator, and SHA-256 checksum.

UNCERTAINTY FLAGS (carry over from the box-labeling convention; single-letter codes in the Status column)

    K   known - names + occasion + year confirmed by Mom, or by caption / album match
    E   estimated - year is a range or "around"; names may be partial
    U   unidentified - people, date, or both unknown. Do not guess.
    D   duplicate of another M-ID (also write the keeper ID: D -> M###)
    X   defer - not scanned today; reason in Notes

    A photo can carry more than one flag, e.g., K + D (you know who it is, but it's a copy), or U + X (unknown and deferred).

THINGS NOT TO DO TODAY

    - Do not write on the front or back of any photo. IDs go on the sleeve or the card beside it. Established rule.
    - Do not discard a photo just because it looks like a duplicate. DUP-link it in the inventory and decide later.
    - Do not promote a tentative ID to K on Mom's "probably" alone. E stays E until verified by album, envelope, or transcribed caption.
    - Do not run scanner auto-correction. See Aug 25 incident above.
    - Do not start Box 2 if Box 1's metadata isn't fully captured. Mom's knowledge is the rate-limiter.

WHAT "DONE FOR TODAY" LOOKS LIKE

    - All 240 photos have an M-ID, a sleeve label, and a one-line inventory row.
    - A subset (likely 80-120, depending on how many backs need separate capture) are scanned with verified front/back files on disk.
    - Deferred photos are flagged X with a reason, ready for next session.
    - Two backups of master TIFFs exist on separate media.
    - Mom's tentative identifications are captured as E or U, never silently promoted to K.

The full archive is multi-session by design. Today's win is: Mom's memory is captured while she's here, the cohort is counted and labeled, a verified subset is on disk, and there is a clean handoff for next time.

One thing to flag for your call: the M prefix is my suggestion based on "mixed boxes." If you'd rather use a different letter (B for box, or something tied to where the boxes came from), say so before the session and Marcus's scanner card updates accordingly.

Event ID: evt_1789344213146

DEC vs NOV — kWh and bill

  Nov  1,284 kWh over 31 days → 41.42 kWh/day,  bill $178 → ~$0.1386/kWh
  Dec    972 kWh over 30 days → 32.40 kWh/day,  bill $146 → ~$0.1502/kWh

  Total kWh change:   −24.3%   (1,284 → 972)
  Daily kWh change:   −21.8%   (41.42 → 32.40)
  Bill change:        −18.0%   ($178 → $146)
  Implied rate:       ~+8%    ($0.1386 → $0.1502 per kWh)

  The bill fell less than kWh did because the per-kWh rate actually
  crept up; the savings is entirely on the consumption side.

What the numbers say (cautious, observational only)

  December's electricity use is materially lower than November's on
  every measure we can form from two month totals — total kWh, daily
  kWh, and the bill itself. That is a real observation.

  The 12/30 diagnostic confirms the system was operating normally at
  year-end: outdoor sensor within 1°F, defrost and heat-strip
  behavior OK, no fault identified, and short auxiliary-heat runs
  during humid above-freezing defrost were characterized as normal
  rather than as excess. The reopen triggers (aux >2 hr/night with
  outdoor low >45°F, or indoor overshoot of 68°F by >2°F) were not
  met.

What the numbers do NOT say

  They do not establish that the outdoor-sensor replacement caused
  the December decline, and they do not establish that a faulty
  sensor caused the November increase. Reasons to hold that line:

    1. Two months is one observation pair, not a trend. There is no
       counterfactual December without the sensor repair to compare
       against.

    2. The diagnostic was explicitly not designed to assign a causal
       share to November's increase — the contractor warned of this
       on the visit, and the closing line of record is "Visit did NOT
       pin Nov elec increase." That warning is part of what we know.

    3. A passing diagnostic at the end of December does not retro-
       actively prove a sensor was running hot in November. "Normal
       now" is consistent with both "sensor was always fine" and
       "sensor was repaired and is now fine." The data do not
       distinguish those stories.

    4. Several confounders move with the period and could explain
       part or all of a ~22% daily-kWh swing on their own:

         - Weather. HDD/CDD differences between Nov and Dec in
           Austin can move residential kWh significantly; mild
           stretches in December suppress auxiliary heat use.

         - Billing-cycle length. 30 vs 31 days is about −3% on
           total kWh. It is small relative to the 22–24% drop but
           it is real and in the same direction.

         - Occupancy and routine. Holiday travel, work-from-home
           patterns, cooking/lighting/water-heater behavior all
           shift between Nov and Dec and aren't visible in the
           monthly total.

         - Rate-class/pricing. The ~8% increase in $/kWh shows up
           in the bill but not in kWh; it doesn't explain the kWh
           decline, but it does mean we can't read a price effect
           off the bill.

         - Random month-to-month noise on a single residence.

    5. The November spike itself isn't pinned to any cause in the
       record, so a "sensor was the cause of Nov, repair fixed it"
       narrative is unsupported on both ends.

What would actually let us attribute the change to the sensor

  Any of the following would strengthen or weaken that claim; we
  don't have any of them today:

    - Sub-metering on the air handler before and after the swap.
    - Thermostat runtime logs of compressor/aux stages paired with
      outdoor temperature.
    - A weather-normalized baseline (e.g., a comparable neighbor-
      hood or a multi-year Riley baseline at this address).
    - A longer series showing November was an outlier above trend
      rather than the trend.

  Without one of those, the cleanest reading is: December use is
  down, the system is operating normally as of the 12/30 diagnostic,
  and the cause of the Nov→Dec move is unassigned.

Bottom line

  Treat December as "system OK at year-end, kWh down ~22%/day, bill
  down ~18%." Do not treat the sensor repair as the demonstrated
  cause of either the prior increase or the current decline. Keep
  the reopen triggers from the 12/30 note in mind for the next
  month; if those trip, the work order is the right path back to
  the contractor, not a re-litigation of the Nov→Dec comparison.

Owen's revised specification vs. the complete standing Expansion Assist eligibility and suppression rules

Standing rules of record (Dec 27, 2024 canonical statement, plus the earlier fuller version used as the implementation baseline):

1. Monthly refresh
2. Deeper integration use
3. Product-visible usage ceiling crossed within the prior 14 days (anchored to each check date)

8. Suppress if Customer Success has active renewal work

Mapping to Owen's revised spec:

- refresh_cadence = monthly → matches rule 1
- deeper_integration_use → matches rule 2
- usage_ceiling_crossed_at >= eligibility_check_at - 14 days → matches rule 3
- qualifying_human_admin_recent_activity = true AND qualifying_human_admin_status = 'active' → matches rules 4 and 5 together
- source_state = 'fresh' AND state_conflict = false → matches the stale/conflict half of rule 6
- "Rows with stale source state, conflicting state, or a deactivated qualifying admin fail closed" → matches rule 6 (deactivated-admin half)
- customer_success_renewal_work_active = false → matches rule 8

What's missing or not unambiguously present:

- Rule 7 (active CS adoption work) is NOT in the spec as written. Owen's suppression clause names only customer_success_renewal_work_active. The standing rule requires both adoption AND renewal work to suppress, evaluated against the authoritative CS system of record near exposure time. Owen's current text fails to suppress on active CS adoption work, which is the distinct stream the standing rule requires.

- Rule 6 fail-closed semantics: Owen states the conditions correctly but does not pin down what happens to a previously-eligible account whose record has since gone stale, conflicting, or whose qualifying admin has been deactivated. The standing rule explicitly requires no carry-forward of prior eligibility for that cycle, and any unavailable input makes the account ineligible. Owen's narrative is consistent ("fail closed") but the spec is silent on the no-carry-forward behavior and on how unknown/missing CS suppression data is treated. The canonical rule requires unknown or malformed CS suppression data to fail closed and default to not eligible; the spec needs to make that explicit rather than leaving it to interpretation.

  - The active-CS-suppression check is forward-only on already-completed exposures; later CS involvement does not retroactively invalidate, but no further EA prompt may be sent while the CS task is open. Owen's spec is silent on this forward-only rule.

Bottom line:

Owen's revised specification covers 7 of the 8 standing requirements cleanly and is consistent with the fail-closed posture. It does not match the complete standing rules because it omits the active Customer Success adoption work suppression clause. Before implementation, Owen needs to:

PRE-FREEZE — confirm with property management (Sat/Sun, before Mon evening)

1. Drip protocol. Ask whether the lease or their house rules require dripping during freezes, and whether they want a heads-up when you do it. Get any documented procedure in email, not just verbal.

2. Thermostat and HVAC controls — the things you'd actually be changing:
   - Minimum overnight temp they require (often 60–65°F)
   - Whether a smart thermostat or setback timer is in play that you shouldn't override
   - Whether the HVAC fan "on/auto" switch is your call
   - Anything else on the equipment (zoning panel, breaker-labeled HVAC, etc.) you shouldn't touch

3. Hose bib isolation. Do either bibs have an interior shutoff you're supposed to close during freezes? Austin rentals often don't, but if they do, that's the more reliable protection than a foam cover.

4. Water heater location. If it's in a garage or attic, ask whether there's anything you should do (keep garage door closed, open attic hatch, etc.). If it's in the conditioned envelope, no action.

5. Known weak spots. Ask directly: prior freeze claims on this property, and any exterior-wall plumbing beyond the two sinks (toilets, laundry, etc.).

6. Emergency contact for a burst pipe — after-hours number, preferred plumber, and whether the lease holds you responsible for damage if you followed (or didn't follow) their written prep steps.

Also do this yourself, now: locate the main water shutoff and verify it turns (quarter turn and back). If a pipe bursts at 3am, knowing the shutoff is the difference between a mop and a claim.

---

MONDAY EVENING — sequence, in order, before temps drop

1. Disconnect any hoses from the two exterior hose bibs. A frost-free bib with a hose attached can't drain back — that's the single most common burst-pipe scenario in this kind of cold.
2. Put the insulated covers on both exterior bibs.
3. Open the cabinet doors under the kitchen sink and guest bath sink. Do this before bed, not after.
4. Confirm the thermostat holds a consistent temp overnight — no setback. At 27°F exterior with normal heat, 68°F interior is the usual safe target; below ~60°F and the exterior-wall pipes are at real risk.
5. If you got the OK from management on the fan setting, switch HVAC fan from "auto" to "on" so warm air keeps moving across the exterior walls all night.
6. Drip both the hot and cold supplies at the kitchen and guest bath sinks — pencil-lead stream on each side. A washcloth in each basin keeps it quiet.
7. Drop a towel under each drip and leave a flashlight by the shutoff, just in case.

---

OVERNIGHT

At least one of you check once. If you hear water running when nothing's on, see water where it shouldn't be, or the heat stops — shut off at the main and call the emergency line.

---

TUESDAY MORNING (once temps have been above freezing for an hour or two)

Close up: stop the drips, shut the cabinets, fan back to "auto" if you changed it. Leave the hose bib covers on and the hoses disconnected until you're confident the cold snap is past — single-digit overnight forecasts can still come in the second half of the week.

---

IF YOU CAN'T REACH PROPERTY MANAGEMENT BEFORE MONDAY EVENING

Proceed with steps 1, 2, 3, 6, and 7 above — those don't touch equipment. Hold the thermostat at whatever it's currently set to and leave the fan on "auto" until you've confirmed there isn't a smart-thermostat or building control you're overriding. Disconnecting hoses, opening cabinets, and dripping two faucets are standard tenant-level freeze prep and won't conflict with any reasonable lease.
