ARCHIVAL PHOTO NAMING + METADATA CONVENTION
============================================

Goals this convention has to satisfy, restated so the design is auditable:
  - 6 colliding base filenames across boxes must become globally unique
    while still pointing back to the original box + handwritten sequence.
  - 4 tentative years must be visible from the filename itself (Mom browses
    folders visually, not just by clicking into metadata).
  - 2 suspected duplicate prints stay as two distinct source objects; the
    suspicion is recorded, but the records are not collapsed.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. FILENAME PATTERN
----------------------------------------------------------------------

    {BOX}-{SEQ:02d}__{DATE}_{SLUG}__{INSTANCE}.{ext}
    {BOX}-{SEQ:02d}__{DATE}_{SLUG}__{INSTANCE}.json   (sidecar)

Component rules:

  BOX      short label for the physical box, e.g. B1, B2, B3.
           This is the disambiguator that fixes the collision problem
           when two boxes both used "1, 2, 3..." as handwritten seqs.

  SEQ      the ORIGINAL handwritten sequence number inside that box,
           zero-padded to two digits so the field sorts correctly.
           If the number is illegible, use "XX" and flag in metadata.
           The composite BOX-SEQ is the durable archival identifier;
           it never changes, even if the date guess gets refined.

  DATE     one of five tokens (see section 2). Tentative dates are
           spelled out in the filename, never silent.

  SLUG     kebab-case, letters/digits/hyphens, <= 40 chars. Short
           human description of the scene (who/where/what). Mom's
           identifications go here. If unidentified, use "unidentified".

  INSTANCE always present. "p1" for a unique print or the first
           physical print of a scene; "p2", "p3"... for additional
           prints of the same scene. Two prints of the same image
           are NEVER merged — each gets its own file and sidecar.

  ext      .jpg for delivered scans; .tif if you keep the master.

Why this shape:
  - Filename alone tells you: which box, which sequence in that box,
    how confident we are about the date, what it shows, and which
    physical print of the scene this is.
  - Sorting the folder alphabetically groups by box first, then by
    original sequence number inside the box — i.e. it preserves the
    physical order Mom and the original archivist used.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
2. DATE TOKEN VOCABULARY (exactly five allowed values)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

    1972              confirmed year
    1972-08           confirmed year + month
    circa-1972        tentative year only
    circa-1972-08     tentative year + month
    undated           no date clue at all

  - "circa-" prefix is reserved for tentative dates. No other token
    uses it. A filename without "circa-" and without "undated" is
    declaring the date as confirmed (subject to Mom's review).
  - "circa-" must never be silently upgraded to a plain year. If Mom
    later settles on 1972, the filename becomes 1972 and the sidecar
    records the prior "circa-1972" value in date.history.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
3. METADATA SIDECAR (.json, one per scan)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

Same basename as the image, .json extension. Fields:

  id                  BOX-SEQ_DATE_SLUG_INSTANCE (mirrors filename)
  box_id              "B1"
  sequence_original   "12"           the handwritten number as written
  sequence_unique     "B1-12"        composite, globally stable
  date.value          "1972" | "1972-08" | null
  date.precision      "year" | "month" | null
  date.status         "confirmed" | "tentative_year_only" |
                      "tentative_month" | "undated"
  date.notes          free text, e.g. "Mom: could be 1971 or 1972"
  date.history        array of prior {value,status,changed_on} records
  subject.description short scene description (matches SLUG semantically)
  subject.people      ["Mom", "Marcus", "Grandma"]   as identified
  subject.certainty   "confirmed" | "tentative" | "unidentified"
  instance.role       "unique" | "duplicate_print_a" | "duplicate_print_b"
  instance.duplicate_of          null | id of the other print
  instance.duplicate_status      "confirmed" | "suspected" | "ruled_out"
  physical.medium     "print" | "negative" | "slide" | "polaroid"
  physical.condition   "good" | "fair" | "poor" + free text
  scan.operator       "Marcus"
  scan.date           ISO date the scan was made
  scan.source_file    original scanner filename before rename
  scan.sha256         content hash; lets you detect true file-level
                      duplicate scans (different problem from duplicate
                      physical prints) without merging the records.

Key invariants enforced by the sidecar:
  - date.status = "tentative_*" is the only way to record uncertainty.
    Tentative state lives in BOTH the filename (visible) and the
    sidecar (queryable); they cannot drift.
  - instance.duplicate_status = "suspected" on the two prints Mom
    flagged. They remain separate source objects, each with its own
    physical.medium / physical.condition / scan.sha256. Only the
    suspicion is recorded, not the conclusion.
  - sequence_original preserves the handwritten number exactly, even
    if Mom reorders prints mentally. You can always recover the
    physical-archive reference.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
4. AGGREGATE MANIFEST (for Mom's review)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

One CSV per scan session, alongside the renamed files:

    manifest_2025-01-04.csv

Columns: id, box_id, sequence_original, date_value, date_status,
subject_certainty, instance_role, duplicate_status, notes

This is what Mom opens in Numbers/Excel to:
  - sort by box, then by original sequence;
  - filter date_status = "tentative_*" to revisit the 4 she's unsure of;
  - filter duplicate_status = "suspected" to decide on the 2 prints.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
5. WORKED EXAMPLES
----------------------------------------------------------------------

Collision case (two boxes, both had handwritten "01"):
  Box 1, seq 1, 1972, Mom on porch:
    B1-01__1972_mom-on-porch__p1.jpg
    B1-01__1972_mom-on-porch__p1.json
  Box 2, seq 1, 1983, Dad with new car:
    B2-01__1983_dad-with-car__p1.jpg
    B2-01__1983_dad-with-car__p1.json
  These no longer collide. The composite B1-01 vs B2-01 is the durable
  reference back to each original artifact.

Tentative year (one of the 4 Mom is unsure about):
    B3-04__circa-1968_family-picnic__p1.jpg
    B3-04__circa-1968_family-picnic__p1.json
  date.value = "1968", date.status = "tentative_year_only",
  date.notes = "Mom: probably 1968, possibly 1967 or 1969".
  The "circa-" prefix is what makes this visible in the folder listing.

Undated (no clue at all):
    B2-07__undated_kids-by-tree__p1.jpg

Suspected duplicate prints (two physical prints of the same scene):
    B1-12__1975_christmas-tree__p1.jpg  + .json
    B1-12__1975_christmas-tree__p2.jpg  + .json
  Same scene, two source objects. Each sidecar has:
    instance.role = "duplicate_print_a" / "duplicate_print_b"
    instance.duplicate_of = the other file's id
    instance.duplicate_status = "suspected"
  If Mom later confirms they are prints of the same negative, status
  flips to "confirmed" — but the two files stay separate. If she
  decides they are actually different scenes, status flips to
  "ruled_out" and duplicate_of is nulled. The records carry the
  judgment history either way.

Illegible sequence (edge case worth deciding up front):
    B2-XX__circa-1979_unidentified__p1.jpg
  sequence_original = "XX", plus a metadata flag
  sequence_legible = false so it can be filtered out of any
  "rename by original number" pass later.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
6. ORDER OF OPERATIONS WHEN MARCUS PROCESSES A SCAN
----------------------------------------------------------------------

  1. Scan to a temp folder using the scanner's default name.
  2. Open it, ask Mom (or use her notes) for: people, scene, year.
  3. Pick the DATE token from section 2 (do not skip the prefix on
     tentative dates).
  4. Build SLUG from Mom's description. If she can't identify the
     scene, use "unidentified" and set subject.certainty accordingly.
  5. Pick INSTANCE — "p1" by default; bump to "p2" only when there is
     a known second physical print of the same scene.
  6. Rename the file and write the sidecar.
  7. Append a row to manifest_YYYY-MM-DD.csv.
  8. Compute sha256 and store in scan.sha256. This catches true
     file-level duplicates (the scanner rescanning the same print)
     independently from physical duplicate prints.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
7. WHAT THIS CONVENTION EXPLICITLY DOES NOT DO
----------------------------------------------------------------------

  - Does not silently rename tentative dates to confirmed ones.
    Promotions require touching both filename and sidecar.
  - Does not merge suspected duplicate prints into one record.
    The judgment is recorded; the artifacts stay separate.
  - Does not use generic counters (scan_001, scan_002) as the durable
    identifier. BOX-SEQ is durable; scan counters are session-scoped
    and live in scan.source_file.
  - Does not rely on EXIF alone for date. EXIF is convenient for
    viewers but is overwritten by some tools; the filename and
    sidecar are the source of truth.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
SHORT VERSION (for a README card)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

  File:   {BOX}-{SEQ}__{DATE}_{SLUG}__{INSTANCE}.{ext}
  Date:   YYYY | YYYY-MM | circa-YYYY | circa-YYYY-MM | undated
  Inst:   p1, p2, p3 — never merged across prints
  Sidecar: same basename .json with date.status, instance.duplicate_*
  Review: one CSV manifest per session, filter on date_status and
          duplicate_status to revisit the 4 tentative years and the
          2 suspected duplicate prints.

If you want, I can also produce: (a) an empty sidecar JSON template
file you can copy per scan, (b) a CSV manifest template with the
first row pre-filled as a worked example, or (c) a short checklist
Marcus can run through one scan at a time.

What you're seeing is the standard restaurant authorization pattern, not a duplicate charge.

What happened at the restaurant
    Most card terminals place a pre-authorization hold when the card is first presented
    (here, $86.40 against your available credit). When the server closes the check and
    the final total is captured, that creates a separate posted transaction. If the
    final amount happens to equal the hold, you end up with two entries showing the
    same dollar amount and the same merchant descriptor: one pending (the original
    hold) and one posted (the settled charge).

How to handle them
    Do nothing active right now. The pending $86.40 is an authorization hold, not a
    charge. It has reduced your available credit temporarily but has not debited
    anything a second time. Pending holds fall off on their own once the merchant's
    authorization window expires.

    Typical release timing for restaurant MCCs:
        - Common: 1 to 7 business days
        - Worst case still normal: up to 30 days
        - The release does not require any action from you, the merchant, or the issuer

    The posted $86.40 is the real charge and matches your receipt, so do not dispute
    it. Disputing the posted entry is what would actually cause a problem, since the
    charge is valid.

Evidence to preserve before you forget the details
    Keep these in one place (a folder, a note, an email to yourself with attachments):
        - The paper or emailed receipt showing $86.40, date, and merchant name
        - A screenshot of the posted charge entry (amount, date posted, descriptor,
          last 4 of card if shown)
        - A screenshot of the pending entry showing the same amount and descriptor
        - A one-line written note: "Dec 29 dinner at [merchant], receipt $86.40;
          posted [date], pending hold still showing as of [today's date]"
        - Optional but useful: the authorization date/time if your issuer's app or
          statement shows it (the pending hold usually carries an earlier timestamp
          than the posted charge, which proves it is the original pre-auth)

    The point of preserving both sides is so that if the pending entry later turns
    into a second posted charge, you can show that one of them is the duplicate
    rather than the merchant being able to argue you were double-charged at the
    table.

When to actually contact someone

    Wait it out, with one light check:
        - Glance at the pending entry every few days. Once it disappears, you are
          done and can delete the screenshots once the statement cycle closes
          cleanly.

    Contact the merchant only if the pending entry converts into a second posted
    charge (i.e., you now have two posted $86.40 transactions instead of one posted
    and one pending). At that point it is a true duplicate and the merchant can
    usually void or refund the second one the same day, which is faster and cleaner
    than a chargeback.

    Contact the card issuer instead of (or after) the merchant if:
        - The pending hold has not dropped off after roughly 30 days. That is
          abnormal for a restaurant MCC and the issuer can force a release on the
          auth.
        - A second charge actually posts and the merchant is unreachable or refuses
          to refund. The issuer's dispute process is the formal path; preserve
          everything from step 2 first.
        - Anything else looks wrong: a different amount posts, a second charge
          posts under a descriptor that does not match the restaurant, or you see
          other unfamiliar merchants in the same window. Those move from "wait and
          watch" to issuer contact, since the pattern would suggest the card
          number was exposed somewhere beyond this one visit.

    Do not contact the merchant or issuer now. Nothing in your situation
    (posted amount matches receipt, pending amount matches posted, same descriptor)
    indicates a problem that requires their involvement yet.

Impact: none on the tax figures. The IRS keys off TIN for matching; the mailing address on the 1099-R is informational, and the return's mailing address is what the IRS actually uses. So this is a recordkeeping item, not a filing blocker.

Two ways to close it, if you want it tidy:
1. Request a corrected 1099-R from the plan administrator (cite current address; typical turnaround a few weeks, may arrive after filing — file now with what you have, then amend if a corrected form materially changes anything)

Want me to draft the correction request, or log this on a tax-prep doc / brief?

The old address on a 1099-R is usually one of two issues (sometimes both at once):

  1. The plan administrator printed an old address on the form itself.
  2. The administrator mailed the form to an old address that was on file.

The handling is similar, but worth separating because the fixes aren't identical.

What to verify first

  Confirm the high-stakes fields on the 1099-R are correct: SSN, account number, distribution amount, tax year, distribution code, and (if applicable) the rollover/exchange indicator. These are what the IRS actually uses for matching. The address is essentially decorative from the IRS's perspective.

  Confirm your mom's current address and what address appears on her most recently filed Form 1040. If they don't match each other, the address problem is bigger than just the 1099-R.

  Check where the actual distribution went. An old mailing address on the form doesn't mean the money went to the wrong place — verify direct deposit or check destination separately. If a check was mailed to the old address and may not have been received or forwarded, that's a separate issue from the form's address.

What to request from the plan administrator

  A corrected 1099-R with the current address. Note: most administrators will only reissue a corrected form if something financial on it changed. An address-only "correction" is often declined, because the IRS doesn't key off the form's address — they match by SSN and amounts. So this request may be refused, and that's not a red flag.

  Confirmation that the current address is now on file for all future tax forms and account correspondence. This is the part that actually matters going forward.

  If the original 1099-R went to the old address and was never received, request a duplicate. Most administrators can re-print or re-mail within a few business days, often without fee. That's usually the more productive request than asking for a "correction."

What to do on the IRS side

  File her return using the current address, regardless of what the 1099-R says. The IRS matches 1099-R data by SSN and taxable amount, not by address, so address mismatches on the form do not delay processing or generate notices.

  If the IRS still has the old address on file (from a prior return), the cleanest fix is to put the current address on the current 1040 — IRS updates its records when it processes the return. Form 8822 is only needed if she isn't filing a return that year.

  Don't amend prior returns for an address change — that's not how address changes work.

  If an IRS notice ever does arrive about this 1099-R, call the number on the notice and confirm the address on file. The address printed on the 1099-R is not what's in the IRS's records; their records come from filed returns.

What NOT to do

  Don't cross out the old address and handwrite a new one on the form. The IRS doesn't see the form, and a manually altered 1099-R creates more problems than it solves (it also doesn't fix anything, because nothing is "fixed" by it).

  Don't omit the income from her return because the address is wrong. The distribution has to be reported regardless.

  Don't assume the IRS will "match" addresses and reject or flag the return. They don't, and address anxiety around 1099-Rs is one of the more common unnecessary tax panics.

Net of all that: the IRS does not care about the address printed on the 1099-R. The two fixes worth making are (a) get the current address on file with the plan administrator for future forms, and (b) make sure her filed return uses the current address. A reissued form is nice-to-have, not necessary.

If the situation is anything beyond a simple address mismatch (e.g., the distribution amount looks wrong, the SSN doesn't match, or there's an unsolicited 1099-R for an account she doesn't recognize), that's worth a quick call to a tax professional before filing.

The three readings aren't really competing — character is a question about whether it acts, archive is about what it holds, frame is about how it organizes. They can all be true at once, which is probably why the group converged on the shared point: the recurring physical details are doing the connective work, not the house as a whole.

On the unresolved point, "agency" might be the wrong frame for this novel. If agency means intention or volition, the house doesn't have it. But Danielewski seems more interested in something like accumulation or conditioning — the house doesn't act, but it persists across everyone who passes through, and the recurring details (fruit, the wooden bones, the music, the rooms as they get subdivided and rewired) carry meaning forward whether or not anyone notices. The structure of the book is the argument: the house outlasts every inhabitant, and the pattern only becomes legible from outside any single life.

So the sharper version of the unresolved question might be whether the house generates meaning independent of witness. The novel's answer looks like yes — which is also what's unsettling about it, and probably what the two "character" readers are reaching for when they resist the cleaner archive or frame answers. "It's a character" is a way of saying "it does something to us and we can't fully account for how."

DAYLIGHT TROUBLESHOOT SEQUENCE (light off the bike, on a stable surface):

  1. Battery as a variable — swap in a known-good, fully charged battery of the correct type. If you have a multimeter, measure the suspect battery's resting voltage against its spec.
       Works on known-good → battery was the problem; charge or replace it.
       Still no light → go to step 2.

       Works now → contact/seating issue; you're done.
       Still nothing → go to step 3.

  3. Light-on-the-table test (isolates the LED/switch from the mount) — with the working battery installed, power the light in your hand on a flat surface, no vibration.
       Lights up → the light unit is fine; the fault is in the mount, cable, or under-vibration connection. Go to step 4.
       Does not light → light-unit failure. Skip to step 5.

  4. Mount/connector check — reinstall on the bike; test stationary first, then walk the bike off a curb to simulate road buzz. If the mount is a quick-release with electrical contacts, clean them and check spring tension. Wiggle the light in the clamp — a cut-out when wiggled points to a worn clamp or interface, not the battery. If the light is wired to an external pack, check strain relief for a broken conductor.

  5. Light-unit failure — look for water ingress (condensation under the lens, damp seal) and a stuck or mushy switch. If wet, dry thoroughly with silica gel for 24–48 h before declaring it dead. Otherwise the switch or LED driver has failed — replace or warranty.

The sequence isolates the battery first (steps 1–2), then the light body (step 3), then the mount/cable (step 4); if 1–3 all fail, you have a light-unit failure, not a battery problem.

The conservative first move is humidification and pressure, not paste. What you have is a "pick" — surface fibers raised from the sheet, with the substrate intact — and those almost always relax back down with moisture and weight alone. Wheat-starch paste is for tears and losses; using it on a lift locks in something that may not need adhesive at all and removes your options.

  Why not paste first
  - Paste is reversible in theory but consolidates the fibers permanently and changes the local surface.
  - Your current goal is to see whether the fibers will settle on their own.
  - If humidification-and-weight fails, every option (including paste) is still available.

  Stabilization sequence
  1. Humidify from the back only. Place the sheet face-up on a clean dry blotter. Lay a second blotter, lightly moistened (cool-damp, not dripping), across the back in the area of the lift. Cover with a sheet of plastic to slow evaporation. Leave 30 to 60 minutes — check by feel; the back should be cool-damp, not wet. Do not get the front wet; watercolor pigment sits on the surface.
  2. Remove the damp blotter and plastic. Turn the sheet face-down on a dry blotter so the lift contacts the blotter. Stack another dry blotter on top of the back, then a light, even weight — clean glass with a few books is plenty. You want gentle pressure, not a press.
  3. Leave it 24 to 48 hours under weight. The fibers will relax toward the sheet and dry set in that position.

  Assessment after drying
  Lift and inspect under raking light (light from the side, so any surface irregularity casts a shadow). Three outcomes:
    a. Lift is essentially flat, not visible at oblique angles. Proceed to mat with the lower mat border positioned ABOVE the lift zone, fully covering it. This is the likely outcome for a fresh tape pick on dry paper.
    b. Lift is partially settled — a faint ridge or fuzzy line visible only at raking angles. Still usually mat-able: widen the lower mat border, float-mount the sheet, or recess the bottom edge slightly. No adhesive needed.
    c. Lift remains raised and conspicuous. Now paste is the right tool — applied very thinly under the fibers with a fine brush, repositioned, blotter-and-weight again, dried.

  Two details worth flagging
  - Do not press on the lift with fingers, tweezers, or a bone folder before humidifying. That tends to rough up the fibers or detach them.
  - Keep the offcut flat and dry as your matching-paper reserve for any later repair. Do not consume it now.

  Decision rule
  Try the mat option first. A 1.5-inch pick along the lower edge, outside the image, is well within what a deeper lower mat border or a slightly recessed bottom edge can conceal. You only need adhesive if the lift stays conspicuous after humidification-and-weight, which is uncommon for fresh picks on dry paper.

Scope: this is a decision-framework comparison, not a return prep. Nothing below is offered as a deduction or as eligibility advice.

The shape of the decision

Her profile — one 1099-R, one SSA-1099, one 1099-INT, health-insurance records, no wages/Schedule C/rental/crypto, no interstate move, standard deduction expected — is one of the cleaner Form 1040 shapes. The relevant differences between the two options:

- Cost gap is $236. Small relative to her likely income, so the choice turns on her time and comfort more than the dollar amount.

- Software at $89 is usually federal-only; state return typically $30-60 extra per state. The EA at $325 normally bundles federal + state. If she lives in a state with income tax, the real gap is closer to $170-200.

- Both routes e-file. Both produce a signed return with audit support; the EA's added value is that someone reviewed the inputs and asked follow-ups, and their signature is on the return.

- Audit-risk profile on her inputs is low. Three information returns, standard deduction, no unusual items.

- The work the IRS requires (SSA taxable-amount worksheet, 1099-R box-code handling, 1099-INT) is mechanical and software does it reliably. The work software can't do is decide whether her return is actually as simple as it looks — that's what the questions below are for.

Questions for Mom before she picks

About her documents:

1. State return: does she need one, and in which state was she a resident all year? Software charges separately for state; an EA bundles it.
2. 1099-R — what is Box 7 (distribution code), and does Box 2a equal Box 1? Blank or unknown Box 2a is a signal for a preparer — the codes (pension vs. IRA vs. disability vs. Roth) determine how the distribution is taxed.
3. SSA-1099 — is she comfortable running (or letting the software run) the IRS taxable-Social-Security worksheet, or would she rather someone else run it and explain the result?
4. "Ordinary health-insurance records" — which is it?
   - 1095-A (ACA marketplace) — changes the return materially; premium tax credit must be reconciled.
   - 1095-B or 1095-C — informational only, no effect on 1040.
   - Medicare Part B/D premiums — not deductible, but may affect her IRMAA (Medicare premium surcharge) two years out based on this year's MAGI.
   - Private premiums — generally not deductible without self-employment income.
   - HSA contributions or distributions — opens Form 8889.
5. Did she also get a 1099-DIV (mutual-fund dividends / capital-gain distributions)? Brokerage and bank products often issue 1099-INT and 1099-DIV together.

About her situation:

6. RMD: was she required to take a Required Minimum Distribution from a traditional IRA or 401(k), and did she take it? Missing an RMD is a 25% excise on the shortfall.
7. Filing status: anything other than single (or MFJ if married all year)? Spouse died during the year, divorced, married on Dec 31?
8. Dependents: anyone she supports who could be a qualifying relative, or a child for whom she'd claim a credit?
9. Withholding or estimates on the 1099-R: is tax being withheld via Form W-4R, or did she pay quarterly estimates? Either way software handles it; she just needs the numbers.
10. Items easy to forget: stock sales, HSA activity, state refund from a prior year, unemployment, inheritance, gift over the reporting threshold, jury-duty pay.

About her preferences:

11. Time: how many hours is she willing to spend entering data and reading screens? First-time DIY often runs 3-5 hours.
12. Goal: does she want it done, or does she want to learn the form? Either is fine — the answer points to one option.
13. If the software raises something she doesn't understand, would she rather call support or hand the return to a preparer mid-stream?
14. If a notice arrives later: the EA represents her as a client; software audit support is real but narrower (typically limited to errors on the return they prepared).

Worth a one-line sanity check:

15. "Doesn't expect to itemize" — if her medical premiums + out-of-pocket exceed roughly 7.5% of AGI, or she made large charitable gifts, itemizing could matter. Software has a click-through comparison; a preparer runs it.
16. Some 1099-Rs carry a one-time election (e.g., 10-year averaging on a qualifying lump sum). Software generally doesn't surface this; a preparer would.

A short way to weigh it

If her answers to (1)-(10) come back clean — single state, no 1099-DIV, 1095-B only or nothing, RMD already taken, no surprises — software at $89 (plus state if applicable) is the rational pick and saves roughly $170-200.

If any of (1)-(10) turns into "I'm not sure," the $325 is paying for the preparer to find out and handle it correctly, which is worth more than the price gap.

The worksheet's $260 food+labor figure checks out, but it does NOT clear the 42% target. Here is the math, line by line.

COST BUILD
- Ingredients: 20 × $8.10 = $162.00
- Direct labor: 3.5 hr × $28 = $98.00
- Food + labor (pre-overhead): $260.00

TARGET TEST AT $26
- Revenue: 20 × $26 = $520.00
- Food+labor as % of menu revenue: $260 / $520 = 50.0%
- 42% ceiling on this revenue: $218.40
- Gap: $260.00 − $218.40 = $41.60 over target (8.0 pts above ceiling)

Verdict: the dish fails the target as priced. Overhead isn't even in the picture yet — at 50% pre-overhead, prime cost alone is already above the band.

TWO LEVERS TO CLOSE THE $41.60 GAP

A. Reprice upward
- Needed revenue for 42%: $260 / 0.42 = $619.05
- Per-portion: $619.05 / 20 = $30.95
- Required lift: $26.00 → ~$30.95 (+$4.95, +19.0%)

B. Redesign (hold price at $26)
- Combined cost ceiling: $218.40 → must cut $41.60
- Ingredient-only path: $2.08 less per portion ($8.10 → $6.02)
- Labor-only path: cut 1.49 hr ($41.60 / $28), i.e., 3.50 → 2.01 hr
- Most realistic: split the cut — e.g., ~$1.10 off ingredients and ~0.75 hr off labor

RECOMMENDATION FRAME FOR THE CHEF-OWNER
The reprice alone (+19%) is large for a single test dish and likely to suppress volume on a Saturday test. The redesign path is smaller per move but touches the recipe and the prep flow. A blended move (modest price lift to ~$28–$29 plus a modest ingredient or labor trim) usually lands the dish inside the band with less demand risk than a straight reprice. Worth deciding which lever the chef-owner wants to pull before re-costing the test.

The lift is stable under blotter because compression has set it in position — that's positional memory, not a bond. Once the sheet goes into a mat it's no longer under compression, and a humidity cycle can bring the lift back. Mat overlap protects visually; it does not substitute for re-adhering the fiber.

Your observations all read green for paste:

  - pigment unaffected — no risk of tidelineing or pigment lift under a damp brush
  - no tear-through — substrate is continuous, so paste bonds paper-to-paper, not paper-to-air
  - 1.5" along the edge — small, controlled field
  - one week flat — the area is clean and relaxed; good working surface

Wheat-starch is the right adhesive here: reversible, archival, standard for paper-to-paper on a watermedia sheet. Your moisture ladder is exactly the paste-under-a-watercolor sequence — paste on damp-not-wet, single controlled touch, 20s hold, no return after the surface dulls. You don't want to rewet the pigment layer, and you don't need to: the bond is mechanical, between paper fibers, not through the paint film.

Two practical notes for the application: dampen the lifted fiber and a hair of the surrounding sheet (not the painted area); work the paste into the fiber with the tip, not a flood; press under blotter with light weight for 24h before matting. The mat then covers the overlap and the repair is invisible.

Apply the paste. The blotter week bought you a clean, stable field — paste turns that into a permanent fix.

Bottom line: a single, stable lifted fiber that's pinned flat under a mat and not progressing can generally be left alone, but only if a few conditions hold. Most "lifts" that look stable turn out to be early-stage snags, seam failures, or backing delamination — and the mat hides all three until they aren't subtle anymore.

WHEN LEAVING IT IS REASONABLE

  - The lift is a single tuft or small cluster, not a run, ripple, or seam gap.
  - It lies flat under the mat with no curl, no catch on socks, no further pull when the mat is lifted and replaced.
  - The backing underneath looks intact — no crusty latex, no powdery degradation, no exposed secondary backing.
  - The surrounding pile still rebounds when you press it; no crush or compaction radiating outward.
  - No odor when the mat is lifted (mustiness = moisture under the mat, separate problem).
  - It has been stable across at least 2–3 weeks of normal mat use.

SIGNS THAT JUSTIFY PROFESSIONAL REPAIR (NOT JUST "WATCH IT")

  1. Growth. The lifted zone is wider or longer than when you first noticed it. A snag that walks itself across the backing is a backing failure, not a fiber issue.
  2. Mat no longer lies flat. If the mat edges curl or the mat rocks, the carpet underneath has lost dimensional stability — the mat is masking a depression or a bubble, not a fiber.
  3. Multiple lift points appearing, especially along a line. That's a seam coming apart or a backing delamination running under the field.
  4. Visible discoloration around the spot (yellowing, browning, darkening). Latex degradation or adhesive bleed; both spread.
  5. Crushing/texture loss in a halo around the spot that doesn't recover after vacuuming. The carpet is failing locally, not just snagged.
  6. Any moisture signal: smell, dampness under the mat, darkening that doesn't vacuum off, white powdery residue (alkaline salt from wet backing).
  7. The lift is near a transition, threshold, or pad seam — those are the usual early failure points.
  8. Carpet is warrantied. Lifting the mat to "fix it yourself" with adhesive can void the warranty; a documented pro visit protects it.

PRACTICAL MONITORING IF YOU LEAVE IT

  - Lift the mat monthly. Photograph the spot from the same angle. Compare.
  - Run your fingers flat across the area with the mat removed. Anything you can feel is already past "cosmetic."
  - Vacuum with the beater bar off over that spot; a powered bar will grab a marginal fiber and convert a stable lift into a run.
  - Don't stretch the mat tighter over it. Tension makes backing failures propagate.

If any of items 1–8 above show up, stop monitoring and get a carpet tech to look — at that point a $150–250 repair beats replacing a room later, and the mat has already been hiding the problem long enough.

Pipeline-stale only fires when source has advanced and consumer has not.
- This preserves the standing rule that missing or unknown state routes back to engineering rather than becoming an Ines lifecycle decision, and it stops the alarm from blaming the export job for an upstream warehouse pause.

Auto-resolution and acknowledgment
- The alarm auto-clears only on a verified fresh refresh: a new consumer load with consumer_as_of within the current hour, or with consumer_as_of matching source_as_of within tolerance. Manual acknowledgement by an operator does not clear the alarm.
- Auto-resolution must not infer freshness from a prior export. The Oct 18, 2024 warehouse-backfill precedent (release_metadata_age nulled on 41 rows without rewriting values) is the canonical pattern to guard against.

Stability and stand-down
- If Daniela signals timestamp plumbing is unstable (e.g., during a source rewrite, scheduled backfill path, or known incident), the alarm is moved to staging behind existing work. While staged, it is informational only and does not replace hold-and-investigate or fail-closed row handling.
- The alarm does not auto-page during planned maintenance windows Daniela's team has declared in advance; unplanned degradation still fires.

Audit linkage
- Each warning and critical event is logged with source_as_of, consumer_as_of, evaluation timestamp, and the on-call ack timestamp (if any). Logs are append-only and immutable for the alarm's own audit period.
- Ines's 24h send audit does not depend on the alarm. The alarm is an operator aid, not a freshness proof for any governed send. If a send-time preflight and the alarm disagree, the preflight's row-level checks govern and the alarm is treated as a separate observation.

Operational metadata the alarm must surface
- Both timestamps in a single operator view, with timezone (warehouse local + UTC) and the evaluation clock.
- A "mismatch flag" plus a numeric age in hours/minutes.
- The last successful consumer load's job run ID for traceability into Daniela's release/incident log.
- A clearly labeled state ("fresh," "warning," "critical," "source stale," "unknown") and the path that produced it.

What the alarm is NOT, and what AC should say so explicitly
- It is not a freshness SLA on entitlement_state, support_state, integration_depth, active_admin_behavior, usage_ceiling, or any other field. Those limits remain field-by-field and surface-by-surface, with Owen as the freshness SLA owner for the surfaces that have one written down.
- It is not an override path. Warning and critical do not justify treating a stale or conflicting row as fresh, releasing a held row, or skipping a preflight. The standing "stale fails closed" rule still governs every row.
- It is not a shared state contract. The cross-surface state contract work remains a governance proposal under the existing operating model with distributed owners; the alarm does not move it to "live."

Bottom line on the thresholds: 2h warning / 4h critical are appropriate for the pipeline-level alarm as scoped, and they should be accepted. The risk is not the numbers; the risk is the alarm being read as evidence that field-level shared-state freshness is settled. The acceptance criteria above pin the alarm to pipeline-level observability, preserve row-level fail-closed behavior, and leave the field-level rules where they actually are — Expansion Assist only, and unresolved everywhere else.

Pension or annuity.

Three signals all point the same direction:

- Distribution Code 7 = "normal distribution." That's the code used for qualified-plan payouts (pensions, annuities, 401(k), 403(b), etc.) made under the plan's regular terms. IRAs typically carry code 1 (early) or 7 with the IRA box *checked* — code 7 on its own is a plan-side marker.
- IRA/SEP/SIMPLE box is blank. If the payer had sent this from an IRA, that box would be checked. Blank = not an IRA.
- Gross = taxable. Nothing exotic here, but it confirms there's no basis recovery layered in (which can complicate IRA reporting via Form 8606). Consistent with a plain pension payout.

Practical effect: this goes on Form 1040 line 5a / 5b (pensions and annuities), not 4a / 4b (IRAs). Pick "pension or annuity" in the prompt.

The prior-year AGI field and the IRA-vs-pension prompt are independent questions — don't let the AGI you just confirmed bleed into the 1099-R answer. The AGI goes into IRS e-file identity verification only. The IRA-vs-pension choice controls how each distribution flows through her 2024 return (line 4a/4b for IRA, line 5a/5b for pension/annuity) and which supporting forms apply (Form 8606 for nondeductible IRA basis; simplified-method worksheet for pensions).

How the visible 1099-R fields answer IRA-vs-pension:

  Box 7 (Distribution Code) is the primary signal.
    - IRA family (traditional, Roth, SEP, SIMPLE): payer is a bank, brokerage, or mutual-fund company acting as custodian, and Box 7 begins with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, A, B, C, G, H, J, P, Q, R, S, T, U, or W.
    - Qualified plan, 401(k), 403(b), pension, annuity: payer is an employer, plan trust, or insurance company, or Box 7 begins with D, E, F, K, L, or M.

  Supporting clues.
    - Payer name (header / Box 14): contains "IRA," "Roth," "SEP," or "SIMPLE" → IRA. Names like "Teachers Insurance," "Prudential," "Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp.," or "[Employer] Retirement Plan" → pension side.
    - Box 6 (nondeductible contributions) is an IRA-only concept; non-zero means Form 8606 is needed.
    - Box 9a / 9b (total employee contributions) is pension-side.
    - Box 2a (taxable amount): often populated by IRA custodians; pension payers frequently leave it blank and the software computes taxable amount via the simplified method.

  Note: a "G," "H," "P," "Q," or "K" code means a direct rollover was reported on the 1099-R even though no check came to her — the IRA-vs-pension question still has to be answered correctly so the receiving-side reporting is right.

Facts to verify before answering the prompt:

  1. Was the source account ever in her name as an IRA, or was it an employer-sponsored plan she never owned personally? If she can't reconstruct this from memory, the payer's name is usually decisive.
  2. The exact Box 7 code. Read it as a two-character field — "7" and "7" (with letters as second character) are different.
  3. That the payer is who she expects. A 1099-R from an unfamiliar name is a red flag; do not enter it.
  4. Whether any portion was rolled over. 60-day and direct-rollover rules depend on plan type.
  5. Whether Box 1 differs from Box 2a by more than withholding. A gap usually means basis (nondeductible contributions for an IRA, after-tax contributions for a pension).
  6. That the prior-year AGI in the e-file field is from her 2023 Form 1040 line 11 — NOT a 1099-R amount. If she can't locate the exact 2023 AGI, use IRS Get Transcript (online account) or last year's filed return rather than estimating; an estimate causes e-file reject.

Stop and ask the plan administrator (the phone number on the 1099-R) or a tax professional when:

  - Box 7 has a code she cannot interpret, especially G, H, J, K, P, Q, R, S, or T — these carry rollover / Roth-classification rules that are easy to misapply.
  - The payer name doesn't match any account she recognizes.
  - Box 2a is blank or $0 and the distribution isn't purely a return of basis — wrong application of the simplified method (pension) or pro-rata rule (IRA with nondeductible contributions) cascades into state returns too.
  - She received more than one 1099-R for the same plan in the same year; the plan administrator can tell her whether one is a corrected version.
  - The distribution came from a deceased spouse's or parent's account — survivor treatment on Form 1099-R is specific.
  - She isn't sure whether the event was a loan, hardship withdrawal, or corrective distribution (codes L, M, W, or C).
  - Box 10–14 shows state tax withheld she didn't see deducted from a check.
  - Her 2023 AGI number isn't findable. Guessing produces a reject that's harder to unwind than pulling the transcript first.

Practical sequence for her:

  1. Pull the 2023 AGI exactly (filed return line 11 or IRS transcript). That answer goes into the e-file verification field — nothing else.
  2. For each 1099-R, identify the payer and Box 7 code first. That pair answers IRA-vs-pension for that specific 1099-R.
  3. If the 1099-R is clearly an IRA and Box 7 is straightforward (1, 2, 7, or B), select IRA; Form 8606 is only required if Box 6 is non-zero.
  4. If any element of the 1099-R is unclear, call the number on the form before answering the prompt. The plan administrator can confirm plan type and explain the distribution in writing, which protects her if the return is later questioned.

That reject means the AGI you typed in does not match what IRS has on file for the prior tax year. The number on the filed return is usually right, but several things can throw it off. Before re-submitting, verify against IRS records — not just against the paper return.

What to check first

- Pull up last year's filed return and use line 11 of the 1040 (AGI). Not the refund amount, not taxable income, not W-2 box 1. Software sometimes auto-fills from the wrong place; type it in yourself from the return.
- If anyone amended that return (1040-X), the AGI to enter is the AMENDED AGI, not the original.
- If filing status changed this year vs. last year (joint vs. separate), the rule is: enter the AGI IRS has on file for the primary SSN on this year's return, whatever last year's status was. Don't combine or split it manually.
- If Mom has (or was issued) an Identity Protection PIN, it must be entered in its own field. Missing IP PIN is a separate reject but worth checking while you're in there.

Authoritative source

The IRS Tax Account Transcript shows exactly what they have on file, including any AGI adjustments from corrections or amended returns. Two ways to get it:

  - Online: irs.gov → "View your tax account" / "Get Transcript" (identity verification required; the tool has been intermittent, so if it errors out, fall back to mail).
  - Mail: Form 4506-T, check "Account Transcript" — about 5-10 days. Most reliable path.

The AGI shown on the transcript is the number to type into the software. Do not pad, round, or guess — IRS compares it character-for-character as a whole-dollar amount.

Fallback

If the deadline is tight and you can't reconcile the AGI, paper-filing the return bypasses the e-file match entirely. Slower, but guaranteed acceptance. Most guided software will print a PDF return you can mail.

If you want, I can draft a short plain-language note to Mom with these steps, or walk through the transcript line item once you have it in hand.

IND-031-04 means the prior-year AGI your mom entered does not match what IRS has on file. Here is a stepwise resolution that avoids blind guessing:

1. STOP re-submitting e-files with variations. Each failed e-file attempt can eventually lock the return or trigger additional identity checks. Two attempts is reasonable; beyond that, switch paths.

2. Determine what happened with last year's return.
   - Was it e-filed or paper-filed?
   - Was it PROCESSED (not just mailed or accepted)?
   - Paper returns can take 8-12+ weeks to process; e-file typically settles within 21 days but has been slower in recent years.
   - If last year's return is still unprocessed, that is the most likely cause of the mismatch. Wait for it to finish, then retry the current e-file.

3. If last year is processed, get the exact AGI IRS has on file and use that figure:
   - IRS "Get Transcript" online tool at irs.gov
   - IRS2Go mobile app
   - Form 4506-T by mail
   - Or the IRS automated phone line
   - Pull an Account Transcript for the prior tax year. The "AGI" line is the value to use.
   - Use that EXACT number on the current e-file. Do not adjust, round, or "correct" it.

4. Common reasons the figure differs even when she typed what she thought was correct:
   - Math error correction IRS made on last year's return
   - Amended return (1040-X) changed the AGI
   - Software pulled "total income" or "taxable income" instead of AGI
   - Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) needed but not entered (this usually produces a different code, but worth checking)
   - Filing status change between years - the prior-year AGI is still her AGI, but the e-file match logic can still flag it
   - A parent or ex-spouse claimed her as a dependent, shifting how AGI was reported

5. Enter ZERO only if your mom did NOT file a federal return last year. The $0 rule is for first-time filers and non-filers. Because you said she entered "the prior-year AGI from her filed return," $0 is almost certainly NOT applicable here, and submitting $0 when a prior return exists is itself a mismatch that will reject.

6. If after the transcript you still cannot reconcile, paper-file as a fallback:
   - Mail Form 1040 to the address in the instructions for her state
   - Include any payment due by the deadline
   - Paper filing has no AGI-match requirement
   - Expect a longer refund timeline if a refund is owed
   - Attach a brief explanation of the e-file rejection if desired

Suggested order of operations:
  a. Check "Where's My Refund" or her IRS online account for prior-year status
  b. If processed, pull the Account Transcript and use that exact AGI
  c. If not processed, wait for processing, then re-transmit
  d. If truly unresolvable, paper file before the deadline

This should resolve the rejection without further guessing.

Generic progression language for stationary cycling rehab usually reads something like:
  - "As tolerated, increase duration by 5 min OR add light resistance"
  - "Advance one variable at a time after 3 symptom-free sessions"
  - "Progress when you can complete 3 sessions without setbacks"

On its face that language is permissive — it sounds like either axis is open once you've cleared 3 sessions, and it doesn't cap how aggressively you advance.

Your specific restrictions are tighter and they govern:
  - After 3 clean sessions: +5 min OR +light resistance. NOT both.
  - One ride is not clearance to run or advance further.
  - STOP and contact therapist on any symptom increase — during the ride, after, or next morning.
  - Feb 28 reassessment is the gate, not a suggestion.

Where they diverge, the specific wins. The generic "as tolerated / one variable at a time" is overridden by the explicit "not both" rule and by the Feb 28 hold.

Safest next step before Feb 28:
  Advance ONE variable only — duration, not resistance.
  Next ride: 25 minutes at your current resistance level. Same warm-up, same cadence, same bike.

Why duration over resistance:
  Resistance loads the joint more directly per pedal stroke and is harder to titrate; a flare mid-ride is less recoverable in the moment. Duration extends time under the same low load, is easier to monitor for symptoms, and is trivially reversible (stop at 20 if 25 feels off). For an ankle on a 6-week strengthening block with reassessment pending, duration-first is the lower-regret choice.

Guardrails to keep in place until Feb 28:
  - One increment only. Do not stack +5 min AND resistance in the same week.
  - 25 min becomes the new baseline. Don't quietly slide back to 20, don't push past 25 on a "good" day.
  - Any new ache during the ride, after, or next morning → stop the bike progression and message your therapist. That's the "any increase" trigger, not a "wait and see."
  - Run, 4:1 run-walk, and loaded calf stay on HOLD regardless of how the bike feels.
  - Feb 28 reassessment is the only next decision point. Between now and then the bike moves exactly one step: 20 → 25 min at current resistance.

If you want an extra layer of safety against the "no self-test" rule, I can draft a short message to your therapist asking them to confirm the 25-min step before you take it. That makes the next ride a clinician-acknowledged increment rather than a self-advanced one.

Below is the staging-acceptance spec. Constraints are named first because they govern every criterion.

Fail-closed preservation (cross-cutting)
- The alarm is pipeline-level observability only. It does not change routing, eligibility, hold behavior, source semantics, or row state.
- During any alarm state (warn, crit, unknown) and during the post-repair window until auto-clear fires, the candidate set, hold list, and suppression list must remain byte-identical to their pre-alarm state. Test: replay an alarm cycle against the last closed send fixture; assert zero row-state diffs.
- Held rows are released only by Ines's fresh current-state preflight, never by alarm state. Alarm clearing is a pipeline fact, not a release event.

Automatic-clear criteria
A repaired lag is not treated as active only when ALL of the following are observed, not before:
- A new consumer load has completed successfully after the lag repair. Success is proven by a recorded job run ID on the consumer side, not by the absence of a banner.
- consumer_as_of is within the current evaluation clock and within the freshness tolerance of source_as_of (default: ≤ the 2h threshold; no grace beyond it). Divergence computed against source_as_of, not against the prior consumer_as_of.
- source_as_of itself is not stale or unknown. If source_as_of is null/malformed or older than its own SLA, the alarm transitions to "unknown" rather than auto-clearing to fresh. Unknown does not auto-clear on its own.
- Null or malformed watermarks on either side keep the alarm out of fresh. They are reported as unknown until engineering supplies both timestamps in a valid load.
- Manual page refresh, manual acknowledgment, or operator "looks fine now" never clears the alarm. The 2/12 stale-banner failure mode is closed by data, not by display.
- Transition from crit → fresh is logged with both timestamps and the job run ID that satisfied it; transition from warn → fresh follows the same rule. Transitions out of unknown require the same evidence as transitions out of crit.
- An auto-clear that fires inside an active send window (between preflight and release) does not retroactively reopen or close any prior hold. In-flight decisions stand on the preflight they were made under; the alarm re-evaluates only on the next evaluation tick.
- Recovery test (must be runnable in staging before sign-off): inject the 1/27-style 11h lag, observe warn → crit → unknown as appropriate, run a verified catch-up load, observe auto-clear to fresh with both timestamps and job run ID recorded, then assert zero row-state changes across the full cycle against the held-row fixture.

Audit-history criteria
Every state transition is operator-reconstructible from the log alone, with these fields per event:
- Event ID, evaluation clock timestamp (and UTC), source_as_of, consumer_as_of, consumer job run ID, prior state, new state, transition cause (data / manual-refresh-display-only / engineering-side repair / scheduled re-evaluation), and operator actor if any.
- State labels are from a closed set: fresh, warning, critical, source_stale, unknown, cleared_by_display (visual-only, distinct from cleared_by_data). Cleared_by_display is logged so the 2/12 failure mode is detectable after the fact, but it is not a real clear.
- Transitions to log: nominal → warning, warning → critical, any → source_stale, any → unknown, warning → fresh, critical → fresh, source_stale → fresh, unknown → fresh, plus all cleared_by_display events. Manual-refresh clicks on the operator UI log a cleared_by_display event without changing real state.
- Retention and cross-reference: alarm history is retained for at least the duration of Ines's 24-hour send audit window and is queryable by date range, by send-window ID, and by incident ID. It is cross-referenced from Daniela's incident log for export-refresh incidents and from Ines's 24-hour send audit so an auditor can see the alarm timeline alongside the row-level disposition for the same window.
- Held-row interaction audit: for any send window in which the alarm was in warning, critical, source_stale, or unknown at any time during preflight or release, the audit must show (a) the alarm state timeline for that window and (b) zero held-row releases attributable to alarm state. A window with any alarm non-fresh state and any held-row release is a control failure and blocks sign-off.
- Threshold-change audit: any change to the 2h / 4h thresholds is logged with Daniela approval, old/new values, effective time, and reason; threshold changes never retroactively reclassify historical events.
- Replay: given an event ID, an operator can reconstruct the alarm state at that evaluation tick and the timestamps that produced it without reference to the live UI.

Held-row constraint (explicit, not implicit)
- The alarm has no release authority. A held row stays held across warn / crit / auto-clear / unknown transitions and is reconsidered only by Ines's fresh current-state preflight under the existing fail-closed rule. Stale fails closed governs the row; alarm state does not.
- Test: hold 5 rows in staging under a crit alarm, run a verified auto-clear, assert all 5 remain held with the same hold reason and timestamp, then run a fresh preflight and observe normal held/released disposition driven by current state, not by alarm state.

Open items still owed before ship (not closed by this spec)
- Alert surfaces, response ownership and on-call expectations, hours of operation, and precise source_as_of / consumer_as_of definitions remain with Daniela's five-detail list. Auto-clear and audit-history are now specified; the other three still need sign-off before the alarm leaves staging.

TL;DR: It is reasonable to drive this tire to a nearby shop at low speed for a short trip, after airing it up to the door-jamb spec if you can. Leave the screw where it is. None of your current facts (27 psi, center-tread screw, no hiss, no sidewall damage) meet the stop-driving criteria, but several conditions would change that — listed below.

PRESSURE (27 vs 35)
- 27 psi is about 23% under the door-jamb cold spec. For a normal passenger tire, TPMS warning lights usually fire around 25% under spec, so you are sitting right at the warning threshold, not below it.
- 8 psi lost overnight is a definite leak (a healthy tire loses ~1 psi per month from natural permeation). At a roughly constant rate that is on the order of 0.5–1 psi per hour, so pressure will keep dropping until repaired.
- 27 psi is drivable for short, low-speed, lightly-loaded trips. It is NOT safe at highway speed for an extended drive because underinflation builds heat in the sidewall and shoulder, which is the failure mode that ends in a blowout.
- Recheck cold pressure right before you leave. If it has fallen to roughly 22 psi or below, do not drive — call for a flatbed or have the shop come to you. (Below ~20 psi the tire can damage the rim and the bead can unseat over a bump.)

SCREW
- Leave it in place. Three reasons:
  1. It is currently acting as its own plug and is the main reason the leak is slow rather than fast.
  2. Pulling it out usually increases the leak rate immediately and you lose the visual reference of where the puncture is.
  3. The shop will want to see exactly where the injury is; they remove it themselves during dismount.
- Center-tread location is the repairable zone of the tire (industry repairability standard). Sidewall and shoulder punctures are not repairable; yours is, which is good news.
- Do not smear it with anything, do not try to "seal" around it with a sticky repair, and do not run a rope-style external plug yourself. The proper fix is an internal patch-plug from the inside of the tire, done by the shop.

STOP-DRIVING CONDITIONS
None of these are present now, but stop and arrange a tow if any of them appear:
- Visible sidewall damage, cut, or bulge.
- Audible hiss that is getting louder, or pressure dropping faster than ~1 psi in 15 minutes of driving.
- Vibration, thumping, or the car pulling to one side.
- Tire visibly deforming or squishing hard at the contact patch when you look at it.
- Pressure at or below ~22 psi cold.
- Lightning, ice, or a long grades-only highway route to the shop — anything that pushes speed, load, or duration up.

ADDING AIR FOR THE TRIP
- Yes, this is reasonable, and it is the safer move. Top up to 35 psi cold before you leave so you start the trip at spec, not at 27. The leak continues, so this only buys you margin; it does not fix anything.
- If you have a portable compressor or a gas-station air hose nearby, do it. Drive immediately after airing up — pressure rises while driving from heat, which masks how much air you actually have.
- If you cannot air up, 27 psi is still acceptable for a short, slow, light-load drive to a close shop. It is just less margin than starting at 35.

RECOMMENDED TRIP PROTOCOL
1. Cold pressure check. Airing to 35 if possible.
2. Shortest route, surface streets, under about 50 mph.
3. Light load only — no passengers or cargo you do not need.
4. Visual glance at the tire when you first move and at any stop; listen for hiss or thump.
5. If anything in the stop-driving list above appears, pull over and stop.

WHAT THE SHOP WILL DO
Expect dismount, internal inspection, a water-dunk or soap test to confirm the leak path, an internal patch-plug (not an outside-only plug, which is not considered a permanent repair), then balance and remount. Ask them to confirm the injury is fully inside the repairable tread zone and to check the inside for any internal damage from running briefly underinflated.

Sources for the underlying guidance, if you want to read them yourself: Rubber Manufacturers Association (RMA) tire repairability guidelines; Tire Industry Association (TIA) basic tire repair protocol; NHTSA underinflation/heat-buildup guidance.

STORM-EVENING RUN-OF-SHOW
Kibo — Thursday 2025-02-13
Storm ETA: ~9:00 PM, East Austin
Dose: 50 mg @ ~7:30 PM (T-90)
Solo operator: Riley (Sam in service)

Expected baseline tonight — this is the bar for "the dose is doing its job":
same as this morning's quiet-day observation — mildly sleepy, coordinated,
responsive, no vomiting, no agitation, no inability to stand, no excessive
sedation. Anything beyond that baseline is the escalation bar, not "the dose
failed."

If the storm shifts earlier or later, slide the 7:30 PM dose to stay 90 min
ahead of the new ETA. The 50 mg + 90-minute rule is the only hard number from
the vet.


PRE-STORM PREP — by 6:00 PM
- Draw/cut the 50 mg dose, leave it in one spot so you're not searching later
- Pick safe spot: interior room with no exterior windows (interior closet,
  hallway crate zone, bathroom). Familiar bedding. Door latchable but not
  locked. Low light
- Pre-position the calming wrap on a chair so it's body-temp at apply time
- Two water bowls — one in safe spot, one in usual spot. Shallow, won't slosh
- Charge phone. Write the nearest 24-hr vet ER + address and leave on counter
- Confirm leash by the door for the post-storm walk


LIGHT DINNER — ~6:00 PM
- Normal-evening portion, not heavy, not skipped
- Goal: food in him but not stuffed — settles the stomach for the dose and
  avoids hunger-stimming
- Water available; pick the bowl up ~15 min before dose so he doesn't
  drink a lot right at T-90


LAST POTTY — ~7:00-7:15 PM
- Quick leash walk or backyard
- Stay close to home; weather still calm
- Back inside before the wind/pressure shift


DOSE — ~7:30 PM (T-90)
- Give 50 mg with a small treat or lick of wet food
- Note exact time on the bottle or a sticky note — for vet reference
- Do NOT give a second dose tonight, regardless of behavior. The Rx was
  a single pre-storm dose; any further dose is a vet call, not a judgment call


SETTLING — 7:30-8:45 PM
- Apply the calming wrap NOW, before peak arousal. Snug, not tight —
  two fingers under the straps
- Move Kibo to safe spot with water. Dim lights. White noise or soft
  music if he settles to it
- Stay in the same room, low voice, hands-off unless he seeks contact
- This is the dose-onset window. He should look like the morning:
  mildly sleepy, able to stand and walk, responsive


STORM ARRIVAL — ~8:45 PM onward
- First thunder / wind shift / pressure drop
- He may whine, press into you, pace, or tremble — that's the fear
  response, not medication failure. Wrap + safe spot + your presence
  is the plan
- If he's pacing, leash him in the safe spot — prevents a bolt if a
  door opens during a crash
- Do NOT latch the door if he's panicking; that's when injuries happen.
  Door open is fine
- Do NOT punish vocalizing; it's noise, not behavior


MONITORING — through storm end
Every 30-45 min, quick check:
- Respiration steady, not labored
- Gums pink, not pale/gray/blue
- Able to stand and walk a few steps without falling
- Rouses and responds when you speak

Mild sedation matches this morning's baseline — that's OK, not a flag.
Offer small water sips if he gets up; don't force.


POST-STORM — wait for lightning to clear, not just thunder to fade
- Slow, on-leash walk — 10 min, sniff-led, your pace matches his
- This is decompression, not exercise. Stop if he balks
- Brief bathroom break, then back inside


RE-CHECK — back inside
- Coordinated walk, pink gums, responsive when spoken to
- Refill water; leave wrap on another 30 min if he's still settling,
  then remove


NO-REDOSE SEQUENCE — rule for the rest of tonight
1. The Rx was a single 50 mg dose before the anticipated storm. That
   instruction has been carried out at 7:30 PM. There is no standing
   order to repeat.
2. Do NOT redose for any of: continued shaking, whining, panting,
   pacing, hiding, or refusal to settle. Those are fear behaviors the
   dose is taking the edge off of, not signs the dose failed.
3. The bar for "the dose worked" tonight is the morning baseline —
   mildly sleepy, coordinated, responsive — NOT silence, NOT sleeping
   through the storm.
4. Continued restlessness during thunder is the storm, not the
   medication. Adding a second dose won't fix it and wasn't authorized.
5. Any further dose requires the vet, not a judgment call tonight.
   If you're tempted to redose, that's the moment to call the clinic
   or ER line first.


ESCALATION — call vet/ER if you see
- Vomiting that doesn't stop, or any blood in vomit
- Inability to stand, OR severe ataxia — knuckling, falling,
  head-pressing, leaning to one side
- Excessive sedation — hard to rouse, breathing slow/shallow, blue
  or gray gums
- Severe agitation that risks injury to him or you and isn't
  redirected by wrap + safe spot + your presence
- Any seizure, collapse, or pale/white gums
- Anything NEW that wasn't part of this morning's observation
  (sudden stiffness, drooling, disorientation, vocal change)


BEDTIME — after the post-storm walk + re-check
- Wrap off
- Water in safe spot, lights low
- Sleep within earshot; staying in the same room is a judgment call,
  not required


THINGS NOT TO DO TONIGHT
- Add a second dose
- Walk during lightning — wait it out
- Latch him in if he's panicking
- Skip the post-storm walk — it closes the loop
- Treat continued vocalizing as a dosing problem
