Got it. Cherrywood requires meter photos immediately before and after a continuous 8-hour window with zero water use in the unit. Anything that draws water kills the window — toilet flush, dishwasher, washing machine, fridge dispenser.

Eight hours without a flush is effectively "nobody home." Cleanest setup is a block where you and Sam are both out — a work day with photos at departure and on return, or a weekend outing that clears 8 hours.

Want me to pull your calendar and propose a specific day, or do you already have a window in mind?

================================================================
8-HOUR NO-USE METER TEST — PLAN
================================================================

GOAL
Detect unauthorized water movement between the meter and the
building (service-line / pressurized-side leak) by holding every
fixture and appliance idle for 8 contiguous hours and observing
whether the meter advances.

WINDOW
Daytime, 8h 0m ± a few minutes. Long enough to catch slow leaks
that 1-2 hour tests miss; daytime avoids restricting Kibo
overnight and lets you react in real time if a fixture is
accidentally used.

================================================================
1. PRE-TEST (1-3 DAYS BEFORE)
================================================================

- Locate the meter; confirm access. Note the serial number, the
  units (gallons or cubic feet), and whether the register is
  mechanical (odometer + sweep hand) or electronic.
- Identify the leak indicator: small red triangle, silver disc,
  or star that spins with very low flow. Locate it on YOUR
  specific meter.
- Pick the day. Avoid freezing forecast, scheduled irrigation
  runs, and the day your water softener is set to regenerate.
- Baseline check. Run every fixture briefly, then watch the
  leak indicator for 2-3 minutes. If it ALREADY spins at rest,
  there is an active leak — record it; the 8-hour test will
  still quantify it.
- Pre-stage supplies:
    - phone (camera + timer + notepad)
    - small flashlight if the meter vault is dark
    - 3x5 card or painter's tape + marker for date/time caption
    - watch as backup timer
    - optional: smart leak sensor or recording camera at meter

================================================================
2. JUST-BEFORE-START (LAST 60 MIN)
================================================================

- Run any appliance you must finish before the window
  (dishwasher, washing machine, ice-maker harvest). Once they
  end, leave them off.
- Pre-fill every container you'll want during the window:
    - drinking water, water bottles, coffee thermos, ice
    - cooking water (fill a kettle/pot before start; do not
      draw mid-window)
    - Kibo's bowl (see section 4)
- Toilets: plan around flushing. Go before the window; end
  the window before you need to flush. If a flush is
  unavoidable, mark the time, mark the meter reading, and
  exclude that interval from the result.
- Disable the ice maker (raise the arm, flip the switch, or
  set to OFF). Verify it will not harvest mid-window.
- Disable the irrigation controller (OFF or RAIN DELAY for
  at least 12 hours — cover the window plus margin). If you
  cannot reach the controller, close the irrigation shut-off
  valve at the backflow preventer.
- Water softener: if the next regen falls inside the window,
  force a manual regen NOW so the next one is 24+ hours out,
  or temporarily bypass the softener.
- Reverse osmosis / instant hot / hot-water recirculation
  pump: any of these with timed auto-flush or auto-run —
  set to "away" or "sleep," or shut off at the unit's plug
  or supply valve.
- Whole-house or plumbed humidifier: unplug it or close its
  supply valve.
- Outdoor hose bibs: confirm nothing is connected and
  dripping. Disconnect any hose.
- Pool/hot tub auto-fill: turn off at the equipment.
- Notify everyone in the home (and any house-sitter, cleaner,
  or guest) that ALL water is OFF-LIMITS for the next 8 hours.

================================================================
3. PROHIBITED USES — COMPLETE LIST & MANAGEMENT
================================================================

INSIDE — fixtures
- Kitchen sink, prep sink, pot filler
- All bathroom sinks
- Utility / laundry sink
- Shower, bathtub, hand-held sprayer
- Toilet (no flushing — every flush = ~1.6-3 gal)
- Bar sink, wet-bar tap
- Bidet
- Hot/cold filtered water tap at sink
- Instant hot / boiling-water tap

INSIDE — appliances and equipment
- Dishwasher
- Washing machine
- Refrigerator ice maker and water dispenser
- Plumbed coffee maker / espresso machine
- Tankless water heater (some have auto-purges)
- Water softener (regen cycle)
- Reverse-osmosis drinking system (periodic flush)
- Hot-water recirculation pump (timer-controlled)
- Whole-house humidifier on a water line
- Evaporative cooler (swamp cooler)
- Whole-house filter (some auto-flush)
- Any appliance with a direct water line

OUTSIDE
- Outdoor hose bibs (hose, watering, car washing)
- Irrigation / sprinkler system (any zone)
- Drip irrigation / soaker hoses on a timer
- Pool auto-fill / leveler
- Hot tub auto-fill
- Decorative fountain / water feature on a pump
- Garden hose for Kibo's outdoor water (if any)
- Snow-melt system (if applicable)

MANAGEMENT FOR EACH
- Confirm OFF / don't run (humans)
- Disable timers and set delays (appliances)
- Lock out controllers (irrigation, softener, RO flush)
- Close supply valves where practical (humidifier, RO,
  recirculation pump, fridge supply)
- Physically disconnect or close at the fixture (outdoor
  hose bibs, hose on Kibo's outdoor bowl)

================================================================
4. KIBO WATER PLAN
================================================================

Key insight: the meter only sees water that passes through it.
Water already inside the home, poured into a bowl, does not
register on the meter when Kibo drinks from it.

Procedure:
1. Right before the test starts, fill Kibo's bowl from a tap.
   This draw is the LAST one before start. Let the meter
   settle (10-30 sec), take the BEFORE photos, then begin
   timing.
2. Leave the bowl in place for the full window. Kibo can
   drink freely — drinking does NOT move the meter.
3. Do NOT refill, top off, or rinse the bowl during the
   window. If the bowl is at risk of running dry (large dog,
   hot day, full 8h), pre-fill a second bowl and place it
   out of reach until needed; any swap is from pre-filled
   stock only.
4. After the window ends, refill normally — that draw is the
   first post-test draw and is NOT part of the reading.

If Kibo normally has access to multiple water sources (kitchen
bowl, outdoor bowl, auto-waterer, dog-door fountain), consolidate
to ONE pre-filled bowl inside, and remove or shut off the others
before the window starts.

If Kibo goes outside during the window (yard, dog door), confirm:
- no outdoor hose bib reachable
- no irrigation zones overlapping the yard
- no auto-waterer active

================================================================
5. BEFORE PHOTO EVIDENCE
================================================================

On the 3x5 card, write: date, start time (to the minute),
your initials, and the word "BEFORE" (or "T0").

Capture three frames:
  Frame 1 — WIDE. Meter box open, card at the edge, full
            meter face in view, surrounding area visible
            (so location is unambiguous).
  Frame 2 — CLOSE-UP, full register. All digits readable,
            including the smallest fractional sweep hand
            (usually 1/10 or 1/100 of a unit). Use flash
            if the box is dark; take a second shot without
            flash.
  Frame 3 — LEAK INDICATOR. Zoom/macro on the small red
            triangle or silver disc. Frame should show it
            stationary.

Confirm the serial number is visible in one frame (usually
stamped on the register housing). Confirm the photo's EXIF
timestamp matches the time you wrote on the card.

================================================================
6. STARTING THE TEST
================================================================

1. Take and review the BEFORE photos. Reshoot if any are
   blurry, dark, or unreadable.
2. Read the meter directly: write down every digit
   left-to-right, plus the position of the small sweep hand
   (treat as 0/10 or 0/100 of the smallest unit). If the
   meter is in cubic feet, 1 unit = 7.48 gallons.
3. Note the leak indicator state: still, or moving.
4. Record start time.
5. Close the meter lid/box. Do NOT lock it — you must
   reopen at end.

================================================================
7. DURING THE TEST
================================================================

- Stay out of the meter box. Do not tap it, pour water on
  it, or leave a flashlight pointed at the register (heat
  can shift it slightly).
- The leak indicator is sensitive. Glance at it from inside
  occasionally if you can see it without a special trip —
  it should NOT move.
- No water use in the home. Period.

================================================================
8. END-OF-TEST PHOTO EVIDENCE
================================================================

Same three frames, same framing, same camera angle as BEFORE.

On the new card, write: date, end time, your initials, and
"AFTER" (or "T+8h").

Re-read the meter: every digit plus the sweep hand position.
Note the leak indicator state: still, moved (and how far),
or moved N spins.

================================================================
9. STOP / INVALIDATE CONDITIONS
================================================================

Stop the test and start over (do NOT interpret the result)
if ANY of these happen:

- Any fixture was used mid-window (flushed a toilet, opened
  a tap, ran a cycle, started a shower).
- An appliance cycled automatically: ice-maker harvest,
  water-softener regen, RO flush, recirculation pump,
  irrigation zone, humidifier. These register on the meter
  even though no one "used" anything.
- Someone entered the home and used water without your
  knowledge.
- Freezing temperatures occurred in or near the meter vault
  (ice can stall or unstick the register).
- The meter register was unreadable in the BEFORE photo
  (glare, dirt, condensation, low light).
- You forgot to disable a system and it ran during the
  window — restart the test after correcting.

Do NOT stop the test for any of these:

- The leak indicator already moving at start. That is a
  FINDING, not an error. Record it and continue; the test
  will quantify the leak.
- Kibo drinking from the pre-filled bowl. Drinking does not
  move the meter.
- A neighbor's irrigation running. Their meter, not yours.
- The dog walking past the meter box. No effect.

================================================================
10. WHAT TO RECORD (single log entry)
================================================================

- Test date
- Start time, end time, total elapsed (target: 8h 0m ± a few
  minutes)
- Meter serial number
- Meter units (gal or ft³)
- Start reading: odometer digits + sweep-hand position
- End reading: odometer digits + sweep-hand position
- Delta = end − start (in meter units)
- Delta converted to gallons if meter is ft³ (× 7.48)
- Leak indicator: still / moved / moved N positions
- Temperature at start and end, indoor and outdoor
- Weather (sunny / cloudy / rain / freeze risk)
- Appliance overrides applied: ice maker (Y/N), irrigation
  (Y/N), softener regen deferred (Y/N), RO/hot/recirc off
  (Y/N), humidifier off (Y/N)
- Kibo plan executed: pre-fill done (Y/N), secondary sources
  removed (Y/N), walk planned before/after (Y/N)
- Notifications sent: to whom
- Photo file names: BEFORE wide / BEFORE register / BEFORE
  leak indicator / AFTER wide / AFTER register / AFTER
  leak indicator
- Any anomaly during window (note time, what happened, what
  you did)
- Result interpretation (next section)

================================================================
11. INTERPRETATION (after recording, not before)
================================================================

- Delta = 0 and leak indicator stayed still: no detectable
  leak through the meter during the window. Strong negative.
- Leak indicator moved but odometer did NOT: very small leak,
  typically under ~0.1 gal/hr. Often a running toilet flapper,
  a slow faucet drip, or a tiny service-side seep. The 8-hour
  test will NOT give you a precise rate — isolate fixtures
  next.
- Odometer advanced: leak rate = (delta in gallons) / 8 h.
  Examples:
    1 gal in 8 h ≈ 0.125 gph ≈ 90 gal/day
    8 gal in 8 h ≈ 1 gph   ≈ 720 gal/day
- Odometer advancing with leak indicator STILL = a substantial
  leak, large enough that the low-flow detector is bypassed.

================================================================
12. ISOLATION IF POSITIVE (one extra step)
================================================================

Shut off the house-side valve (at the meter or at the house)
and re-run the 8-hour test.

- Meter still advances → leak is between the meter and the
  house-side valve: service line, the meter itself, or curb-
  side plumbing. Call the water utility; service-side leaks
  are often their responsibility.
- Meter stops → leak is on the house side. Then isolate by
  branch (hot vs. cold, fixture-by-fixture) using the same
  method.

Common culprits in rough order: running toilet flapper,
dripping faucet, water-heater relief-valve seep, irrigation
lateral leak, service-line crack, water-heater drain-valve
seep, icemaker supply line leak.

================================================================
END OF PLAN
================================================================

The gap is real and Daniela's framing understates it. Three independent restores means three independent failure windows — during any of them the consumers are producing from different authorities, and anything that joins across them (cohort deltas, eligible counts, audit packets) gets computed over mixed populations. That's worse than what the kill switch was added to contain.

Two things worth pinning before the next review:

1. What "rollback complete" means. The runbook shouldn't call it done on the kill-switch flip. It should call it done on a post-revert assertion that all three selectors match their pre-incident pinned values, with a timeout that escalates instead of declaring success on the flip alone.

2. Whether the restores stay independent. If yes, the runbook needs a sequenced order, a check after each, and a final aggregate check. If they get unified under one revert mechanism, that's a structural change and worth surfacing now so the assertions aren't papering over it.

Want me to draft a reply to Daniela in her register (operator-facing, concrete), or do you want to handle that yourself and have me tee up the next-review agenda?

VERDICT

Yes — the non-atomic rollback is itself a release blocker. Not a "fix before next rehearsal." A blocker.

WHY IT IS A BLOCKER, NOT A DEFECT

The kill switch as currently specified does not contain a coordinated revert; it only stops new transport. The three consumers (Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, lifecycle preflight) each restore their prior selectors through independent mechanisms. During the window between kill-switch flip and final restore, any one of those consumers can be reading from a different authority than the others. That is the failure mode, not the kill switch's purpose.

Concrete consequences during the mixed-authority window:

  - Mixed-population outputs. A query hitting Helio Start reporting sees one authority; the same query hitting Expansion Assist sees another; lifecycle preflight sees a third. Includes/excludes diverge silently.
  - Corrupted cohort deltas. The Helio Start operational setup-path totals, Expansion Assist selection counts, and lifecycle eligible counts all become non-comparable for any minute inside that window.
  - Corrupted audit packets. Anything written during the window uses values that cannot be reconciled to a single source-of-truth. Replay against those packets fails the dual-read parity check.
  - Held-row leak risk. If lifecycle preflight restores early and the others lag, preflight may momentarily treat held-but-stale rows as fresh and write a release-basis event the other two consumers would not have authorized. This is exactly the failure class the stale-fails-closed rule exists to prevent.
  - Mid-window consumer reconciliation is undefined. Nothing in the current runbook asserts all three are at the same authority at the same instant. There is no sampling, no timeout-with-escalate, no completion check.

The mixed-authority state is worse than the condition the kill switch was meant to contain. A kill switch that creates a worse failure mode than the incident it stops is not a kill switch; it is a new incident source. That is the blocker.

COORDINATED ROLLBACK BEHAVIOR — WHAT THE NEXT REHEARSAL MUST DEMONSTRATE

1. Atomicity requirement. "Atomic" here means: either all three consumers revert to their pinned pre-incident selectors within one verified step, or restores are sequenced with a per-step selector-match assertion and an aggregate check before completion is declared. Either form is acceptable; the current form (three independent restores with no assertion) is not.

2. Pre-incident pinned values. For Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, and lifecycle preflight, the exact pre-incident selector values must be captured to a rollback-pinned-values artifact before any flip, and that artifact must be referenced by name in the runbook. The artifact itself is immutable for the duration of the release window.

3. Post-revert assertion. Rollback is not complete until a single check returns: all three consumers' current selectors equal their pinned values. Kill-switch flip alone is not completion. Restore-script exit-zero is not completion.

4. Timeout with escalation. Per-step and aggregate timeouts must be defined. On timeout, the runbook escalates rather than treating partial state as success. No implicit completion. No "looks fine, moving on."

5. Held state preserved, not re-eligible. Any row held at the moment of kill-switch flip stays held through and after rollback. No held row acquires new eligibility from the rollback. Held-but-stale rows remain held until fresh current-state checks; the rollback does not constitute fresh evidence.

6. In-flight row decision documented and exercised. A row mid-evaluation at kill-switch time must have an explicit disposition in the runbook: abort-and-discard, complete-under-prior-authority, or quarantine-for-audit. The rehearsal must demonstrate the chosen disposition against a synthetic in-flight fixture.

7. Mid-window reconciliation monitoring. During the revert window, the rehearsal must show that sampled queries against all three consumers return values consistent with a single authority at each sampled timestamp. Any sample showing divergence is a rehearsal failure, not a partial pass.

8. Authority and trigger per section. Each rollback step in the runbook must specify exact pull trigger, the authority who can invoke it, and the execution time, per the standing rule. Vague language treated as no rollback.

REHEARSAL EVIDENCE THE NEXT REHEARSAL MUST ATTACH

  - Rollback-pinned-values artifact: pre-incident selector values for all three consumers, timestamped, immutable reference.
  - Shadow replay artifact covering the revert path: input window, timestamps, freshness snapshot, identical-input outputs from all three consumers at each step of the revert.
  - Atomic-restore demonstration: either a single-step coordinated restore, or a sequenced restore with per-step selector-match assertions logged, ending in an aggregate check that all three selectors match pinned values.
  - Held-state preservation evidence: held row IDs at kill-switch flip; same IDs still held post-rollback; no held row written to a release-basis event during the revert window; no held row acquired new eligibility.
  - In-flight fixture run: a synthetic in-flight row demonstrating the documented disposition; outcome logged.
  - Mid-window sampling log: timestamps and three-consumer selector values sampled across the revert window; divergence count = 0.
  - Timeout-and-escalate run: at least one forced timeout scenario (e.g., one consumer's restore delayed past the per-step timeout) showing escalation, not implicit completion.
  - Old-transform counterfactual: pre-incident selectors, run against the same input window, producing expected outputs (the values the system returned before the change). This is the "did we actually go back" check.
  - Freshness alarm behavior during revert: 2-hour warning and 4-hour critical thresholds verified; banner visible during mixed state if any sampling exposes it; auto-recovery after verified catch-up; audit view retains warning interval and recovery time. (Alarm is staging-only as of last record; rehearsal runs in staging.)
  - Audit-trail integrity check: no packet written during the revert window is silently mutated; any reconciliation is logged with before/after.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE

  - Sign-off authority is unchanged. Owen is standard approver; Riley signs off on exceptions including held-row gating, eligibility logic changes, or production releases involving held rows. Approval, if and when granted, applies only to this release and does not blanket-approve future shadow-to-production moves.
  - Stale-fails-closed is unchanged. Warning or critical pipeline status does not justify treating state as fresh, releasing a held row, or skipping preflight.
  - No production release, cutover sign-off, held-row override, or source-semantics change is authorized by this assessment. The system remains non-live.
  - The Feb 14, 2025 nonproduction replay finding (Lifecycle preflight parsing entitlement source timestamps as Central local time; Helio Start and Expansion Assist in UTC) remains an open precondition, separate from this rollback question, and must be cleared before the release gate can be reconsidered.

NEXT STEP

Take the eight coordinated-behavior requirements and the ten evidence items above to Daniela's next production runbook review. The next rehearsal's pass/fail is judged against that list, not against the existing runbook. If the rehearsal cannot produce the atomic-restore demonstration plus the held-state preservation evidence plus the mid-window divergence-zero sampling, the release gate stays closed.

Short answer: everything you listed is safe. Nothing crossed into the 40-140°F danger zone, and USDA FSIS guidance is that food still containing ice crystals, or still at 40°F or below, can be cooked or refrozen without a safety concern.

Per-item:

  Sealed chicken portions (hard, ice crystals): safe to cook now or refreeze. Once fully thawed, smell-check before cooking as usual; if anything seems off, discard.

  Frozen vegetables (hard, ice crystals): safe to cook or refreeze. No quality concern worth flagging.

  Bread (still frozen): safe to refreeze as-is.

  Ice cream (soft at edges, cold, partly frozen): safe to refreeze. Expect some ice-crystal/texture loss — not a safety issue, just quality. Eat sooner rather than later if texture matters.

Caveats worth flagging:

  Your freezer reading 24°F is the one real finding here. 0°F is the standard; 24°F means the seal, gasket, or thermostat needs a look. Three hours of a slightly ajar door wouldn't normally raise the temp that much on its own — warm air infiltration through a compromised gasket, or a compressor that's struggling, is more likely. Worth checking the door seal (paper-test: close on a dollar bill, should resist a tug) and the condenser coils before restocking.

  No leaking package and no cross-contact noted, so nothing to discard on that basis.

Nothing in your description meets a "throw it out" threshold.

Conservative food-by-food assessment (2025-02-22, ~3h door ajar, freezer 24°F)

Decision rules I'm applying (no smell/taste):
  - Keep iff the item still shows ice crystals or is rock-hard AND the package is intact AND no raw-fluid cross-contact occurred.
  - Refreeze-with-quality-loss iff food thawed enough to lose ice crystals but never entered the danger zone above 40°F AND package integrity is intact.
  - Discard iff the item is fully thawed and warm to a probe, OR the package is compromised/leaking, OR cross-contact with raw juices is possible.

Food-by-food:
  - Sealed chicken (rock-hard, visible ice crystals, intact package, no leak)
      Action: KEEP. Safe to refreeze as-is or cook tonight. Cook-first is the most conservative path; if you do cook it, refrigerate the cooked portion and use within 3-4 days.
  - Frozen vegetables (firm, ice crystals present, intact bag)
      Action: KEEP. Refreeze or cook. Blanched vegetables tolerate refreeze well; no quality concern worth mentioning.
  - Bread (cold, no ice crystals described — soft freeze state)
      Action: KEEP, but do NOT refreeze. Treat as refrigerated bread. Use within ~1-2 weeks. Refreezing degrades crumb and can introduce mold risk over storage.
  - Ice cream (cold, partly frozen, soft at edges, container intact)
      Action: KEEP and refreeze. Texture will suffer (icier, grainier), but refreezing is a quality issue, not a safety one. If you don't want to eat degraded ice cream, discard it on quality grounds — not safety grounds.
  - Anything you didn't mention: probe it. If still 32°F or below with ice crystals, keep. If 33-39°F and slushy with no crystals, cook tonight or move to a working freezer within hours. If 40°F or above, discard.

Underlying issue to address before restocking:
  24°F after ~3 hours of a *slightly* ajar door is not normal. A healthy full freezer should have stayed within a few degrees of 0°F in that window. Don't relist the freezer as "fine" until you've checked the four things below — otherwise the next event will look the same and you'll be guessing again.

Restore the freezer (do these in order, all temperature-based, no smell/taste):
  1. Close the door fully. Confirm latch seat by trying to slip a piece of paper into the gasket seam at top, both sides, and bottom; a properly sealed gasket will resist the paper.
  2. Move food into a cooler with ice or gel packs while the freezer recovers, so the load isn't slowing the pull-down.
  3. Check the condenser coils (usually back or underneath) — if they're visibly dusty/pet-hair loaded, vacuum or brush them.
  4. Listen for compressor start within 2-3 minutes of door closure. Confirm the condenser fan is spinning.
  5. Do not restock until the freezer reaches 0°F or below on the probe.

Monitor the freezer (probe in a central spot, not against a wall or package — a cup of water or a block of butter works as a thermal buffer; readings without a buffer swing fast and mislead you):

  - At 1 hour: temperature should be falling. If it's still 24°F or rising, the seal or compressor is failing — move food now.
  - At 4 hours: temperature should be clearly trending downward (target mid-single-digits °F or below). If it's stalled in the teens or above, this is an appliance problem, not a door-ajar problem.
  - At 12 hours: target is 0°F or below. If you're still above 10°F here, escalate to service and keep food in the cooler.
  - At 24 hours: must be at 0°F or below. If it's still at 24°F at the 24-hour mark, treat it as a failed freezer — service call and don't restock.

What to log so you don't have to relitigate this:
  - Time door was found, time door was closed
  - Freezer temp at discovery
  - Probe readings at 1, 4, 12, 24 hours
  - Items removed for cooler, items discarded (and the reason — temp, crystals, package, cross-contact)
  - Compressor/fan behavior at minute 3
  - Gasket paper-slip test result

Two things worth flagging separately from food safety:
  1. The 24°F reading after only 3 hours is the kind of reading that points to a compromised gasket or a struggling compressor. The recovery checkpoints above are designed to tell you which one — if it pulls down on schedule, it's a gasket/lid-seating problem; if it doesn't, it's the sealed system.
  2. After this resolves, a standalone freezer thermometer (not the built-in dial) and a recurring paper-slip gasket check every few months are the cheapest insurance against repeating the same three-hour window.

I have the context — this is the Kibo veterinary claim from Feb 6, 2025. The $78 consultation line was excluded as "behavioral services excluded" while the $50 medication line was allowed and applied to the $250 deductible. The memory note flags that the policy summary covers behavioral treatment after the deductible but doesn't define consultation vs. treatment or provide the diagnosis code.

Let me give you the reconciliation analysis and the question list.

Possible reconciliation between disposition and policy wording

The insurer's stated rationale — "behavioral services excluded" — and the policy summary you have — behavioral treatment covered after the $250 annual deductible — can be reconciled in only a few ways, and each one points to a different fix.

1. Definitional gap in your policy document. The summary says "behavioral treatment" is covered. The exclusion reason treats "consultation" as a distinct, non-covered service category. If the policy's full text defines covered behavioral services as "treatment" but excludes "evaluation, consultation, or assessment" line items, the disposition is internally consistent with the policy — and your leverage is whether the vet's submission is coded as evaluation vs. treatment. This is the most likely reconciliation, given that vet invoices typically bill an exam/consult separately from a procedure.

2. Coding mismatch on the submitted claim. The vet may have submitted a behavioral consultation under a general "office visit / exam" CPT code rather than a behavioral-health-specific code. The insurer's adjudication system then routed the line through a behavioral-services exclusion filter rather than the standard office-visit benefit. The policy would allow it under a different code path; the disposition is a coding artifact, not a policy exclusion.

3. Misapplied exclusion flag. The insurer tagged the line as behavioral because of the diagnosis code (likely an ICD code starting with F or in a behavioral range), even though the service rendered was a standard exam for a behavioral complaint. Some policies cover office visits regardless of presenting complaint; others exclude any visit tied to a behavioral diagnosis. The disposition is consistent only if your policy falls in the second group.

4. Policy actually excludes behavioral consultations but covers behavioral treatment. This is internally consistent and your leverage is narrower — you'd be arguing medical necessity of a consultation as part of treatment, or asking whether the consultation was separately billed when bundled treatment was already provided.

What I do not want you to assume: that the disposition is wrong. It's reconcilable with the policy as written in scenarios 1 and 4, which means appealing without the items below would be a weak appeal.

Questions to ask before accepting or appealing

Policy questions (to your insurer, in writing — ask for the cite, not a verbal "yes"):

P1. Where in the full policy document (section, page, and exact wording) is "behavioral services excluded" defined, and does that definition include or exclude consultations, exams, evaluations, and assessments specifically?

P2. Does the policy distinguish between "behavioral consultation / evaluation" and "behavioral treatment"? If yes, request the verbatim definitions of each.

P3. Is the behavioral exclusion a flat exclusion (never covered) or a conditional exclusion (covered only when bundled with active treatment, or only after a specific waiting period, or only when performed by a credentialed behaviorist)?

P4. Does the policy cover office visits / consultations generally, and is there any carve-out that the carve-out applies when the presenting complaint is behavioral? If yes, request the exact carve-out language.

P5. Does the $250 annual deductible apply to covered behavioral services, and is the $50 medication line's application to the deductible consistent with that?

P6. Is there an internal claims-processing guideline, FAQ, or clinical edit that triggered the behavioral exclusion on this specific line? Insurers are not required to share internal manuals, but you can ask.

Coding questions (to the vet's office — ask for the actual claim record, not a summary):

C1. What was the submitted ICD diagnosis code on the $78 consultation line? (You need the actual code, not "behavioral.")

C2. What was the submitted CPT / service code on the $78 consultation line? Was it billed as a behavioral consultation code or a general office-visit / exam code?

C3. Was the $78 line billed as a stand-alone consultation, or was a treatment or procedure performed at the same visit? If a procedure was performed, why was it billed as a separate line rather than bundled?

C4. Did the vet's office note or claim record indicate the visit was a recheck / follow-up for an existing treatment plan, or a new consultation?

C5. Was the visit performed by the primary vet or by a credentialed behaviorist / veterinary behaviorist? (If the policy ties coverage to provider credentialing, this matters.)

C6. Is the vet willing to resubmit the claim with a corrected CPT code (e.g., a general office-visit code rather than a behavioral-consultation code) if the original submission was coded in a way that triggered the exclusion? Most vets will do this without arguing the diagnosis.

Claim-record questions (to the insurer):

Q1. On what date was the claim received, and what is the claim number? (Needed for any appeal letter.)

Q2. What specific diagnosis code and service code did the insurer's adjudication system use to assign the "behavioral services excluded" reason? Insurers will sometimes release this on request, especially for a pet policy.

Q3. Was the $78 line adjudicated under a behavioral-services exclusion rider, a behavioral carve-out clause, or a general office-visit exclusion? The reason code on the EOB is usually a short label; the underlying logic may differ.

Q4. Was the $50 medication line's application to the $250 deductible done before or after the $78 exclusion? If the $50 applied to the deductible even though it's allowed, the policy is working as designed; if not, that's a separate error worth flagging.

Q5. Is there an appeal right, what is the deadline from the EOB date, and what documentation does the appeal require (vet records, letter of medical necessity, signed statement from the attending vet)? Pet-policy appeal windows are often shorter than human-medical appeal windows — confirm the date.

Q6. Has the insurer seen this exact configuration before (behavioral consultation submitted, medication line allowed) and do they have a standard resolution path? Frontline reps often answer this honestly.

Suggested sequence

1. Pull the vet's submitted claim record first (C1, C2, C4). This is the cheapest step and tells you whether the issue is a coding mismatch or a policy-definition gap.
2. Pull the full policy document and find the behavioral-exclusion language verbatim (P1, P2, P4).
3. If the vet's CPT code is a general office-visit code, ask the insurer in writing (Q3, Q6) why it was routed to a behavioral exclusion. This is your strongest appeal angle.
4. If the CPT code is a behavioral-consultation code, ask the vet to resubmit under a general exam code only if the original visit was a standard exam (C6). Do not ask the vet to misrepresent what happened.
5. If the policy unambiguously excludes behavioral consultations regardless of coding, decide whether the $78 is worth an appeal based on principle versus the time cost, and pay the $78 under protest in writing if you want to preserve future challenge rights on a similar line.

---

**Subject: Why four suppression checks are labeled `reconstructed` and two remain an unresolved historical evidence gap**

The six historical suppression-check records split cleanly into two groups, and the split is evidentiary, not procedural. Engagement completion (the contractor's cataloging pass, the audit matrix entry, the archived-manifest pointer) does not establish evidentiary completion (contemporaneous proof that the check actually ran against that release). The four records that have a release manifest plus a timestamped audit on file can be reconstructed from preserved artifacts. The two that do not cannot be reconstructed from anything currently available, and current template configuration does not tell us what ran in those older releases — it only tells us what the template would do today.

**The four reconstructable records.** For each, we have a contemporaneous release manifest and a timestamped audit tied to that release. That is the minimum proof we accept for a suppression check at send time: a manifest showing the release existed and an audit showing the check ran against it. We label these `reconstructed__archived_manifest_and_timestamped_audit` rather than `complete` because the artifacts were assembled from archive after the fact, but they are sufficient to document that the check occurred. The labels carry provenance, the source archive path, SHA-256, the original date, the reconstruction date, and the contractor/Ines verification trail. They document historical evidence; they are not retroactive approval, do not authorize a customer-facing correction, and do not change current owner assignments.

**The two unresolved records.** For these, no contemporaneous manifest and no timestamped audit are on file. The contractor cataloged the gap; the engagement was completed. The evidence, however, is not present in any archive we can reach, and the current template configuration does not establish what ran in the historical release. We are not saying the check did not occur — we are saying we cannot prove that it did from preserved material. These rows are labeled `[check_name]__evidence_gap__no_contemporaneous_proof` and fail closed. They are not `complete`, not `failed`, and not reclassifiable from current state. They stay unresolved until either contemporaneous proof surfaces or the historical window is formally retired with explicit owner signoff.

**Why engagement completion does not move the two to `reconstructed`.** The contractor engagement closing means the cataloging and repeatability work is done; it does not manufacture proof that did not exist. Treating closure as evidentiary completion would convert a preparation step into an approval — which it is not, and which prior decisions (the 10/29 backfill closure on 10/31, full closure on 11/6, last-exception closure on 11/20) explicitly do not support. The same rule applied to the January 2025 template validation: forward-looking, not retroactive.

**What the labels do and do not authorize.** The four reconstructed labels let us cite those checks as documented historical evidence; they do not let us treat the corresponding sends as approved, the recipients as re-confirmable, or the records as basis for a current customer-facing action. The two evidence-gap labels carry no approval, no authorization, and no implication of good standing. The historical window remains open for those two rows. No current send decision, owner reassignment, or customer correction follows from either set of labels.

============================================================
2. How Mom reconciles $12.01 to $11.84
============================================================

The reconciliation is a matching exercise, not a refiling trigger. Run this three-way match before concluding anything:

  - Bank 1099-INT box 1 (interest income): $12.01
  - Mom's filed Form 1040 line 2b (taxable interest): $11.84
  - Bank's own records: usually the online interest ledger for January through December 2024, summed.

Likely causes for a $0.17 gap on a small bank interest account:

  a. Accrual cut-off: the dashboard typically shows interest through December 31, but a few days of year-end accrual post in early January and land on the 1099-INT. Most common explanation and benign.
  b. A small interest adjustment, fee reversal credit, or a Reissue of the form: uncommon for $0.17, but possible. Confirm the form is not marked "CORRECTED" in the box at the top.
  c. Different interest categories: the dashboard may net a small credit while the 1099-INT reports a slightly higher gross interest figure, or vice versa.
  d. Payer error: possible but rare for this size.

What the IRS sees: the bank reports $12.01 to the IRS on the same 1099-INT. The IRS computer-matching system does compare information-return totals to the return, but a small difference does not automatically create an automatic underreport notice. The IRS weighs whether the difference is material and whether the return's interest line is consistent with the rest of the return.

============================================================
3. What Mom should verify before deciding any follow-up
============================================================

Run each check below, and only decide on a Form 1040-X amendment after every box is checked.

Identity and form integrity
  - The form is addressed to Mom and shows her correct SSN.
  - The bank's name and EIN are correct.
  - Tax year is 2024.
  - The "CORRECTED" box is empty.
  - Box 1 (interest income) is $12.01 and the rest of the form is consistent.

Reconciliation math
  - Sum of monthly interest from the bank statement matches one of: $12.01, $11.84, or a third figure, with a clear explanation of the small gap (year-end cut-off, posting date, small adjustment).

Filed-return line items
  - Form 1040 line 2b shows $11.84.
  - Schedule B Part I lists the bank with the figure actually entered.
  - The total on Schedule B Part I matches Form 1040 line 2b.

Filing status
  - The federal e-file was accepted on February 16, 2025 (not rejected, not pending).
  - The state filing, if any, also accepted and uses consistent figures.

Pending IRS correspondence
  - No IRS letter, notice, or account-transaction entry has arrived since the acceptance.
  - Her IRS online account does not show a new issue, adjustment, or balance due tied to 2024 interest.

============================================================
4. Whether the 17-cent gap requires refiling
============================================================

No. The 17-cent gap does not, on its own, require refiling. The right posture is "filed return stands; 1099-INT retained; only respond if the IRS writes." Reasons not to amend:

  - The IRS does not require an amended return solely because an information return (1099-INT) differs by a few cents from the return's reported figure, especially when the amount is small and the rest of the return is otherwise consistent.
  - Filing Form 1040-X is appropriate when there is a real error on the return, an omitted income, a deduction or credit that should have been claimed, a status change, or an IRS instruction to amend. None of those apply here on the current facts.
  - An amended return can itself be reviewed and can create additional IRS correspondence; it should not be filed speculatively.

When an amendment would actually be required
  - The IRS sends a notice (CP2000, CP2501, or similar) proposing a change to tax owed based on the $12.01.
  - Mom actually understated interest by a meaningful amount (not the case; $0.17 is below the rounding noise for Schedule B).
  - The 1099-INT is later reissued as a corrected form with a substantially different figure, or her personal information on the form is wrong.

============================================================
5. Action plan for Mom
============================================================

  1. File the 1099-INT, dated note, dashboard screenshot, filed 1040 PDF, federal acceptance confirmation, prior-year transcript, and IND-031-04 rejection notice together in a single 2024 tax folder.
  2. Do not file Form 1040-X now. The 17-cent gap is not, by itself, a basis for amendment.
  3. Check the IRS online account roughly once a month through the end of 2025 for any 2024 notice. If a CP2000 arrives, the response package should include the reconciliation note and copies of the 1099-INT and the bank interest ledger, with a short written explanation that the difference is a year-end cut-off effect.
  4. If the bank issues a corrected 1099-INT with a materially different figure, revisit only then.
  5. For the 2025 return: in late December 2025 or early January 2026, check the year-to-date interest from the bank and wait until the official 1099-INT is downloadable before filing, so the prior-year gap pattern does not repeat.

============================================================
Bottom line
============================================================

Retain the official 1099-INT in her 2024 tax file with a dated reconciliation note; reconcile $12.01 against the $11.84 on the filed return and the bank ledger; verify that no corrected form was issued, that the e-file is accepted, and that no IRS notice has arrived. On those verifications, the filed return stands; the 17-cent gap does not require a refile; respond only if the IRS writes.

Practical-risk comparison

  The premium gap is $42/year — small in absolute terms, but the right
  framing isn't "spend $42 for $42 more coverage." The two coverages B
  adds are very different in shape:

  1. Lower deductible ($500 vs $1,000). This only matters at the moment

     the deductible alone" the first time you have a single claimable
     personal-property loss under $2,000. Frequency is the question, not
     severity.

  2. Higher water-backup limit ($5,000 vs $2,500). Water backup is the
     asymmetric, tail-risk coverage in this package. A sump/sewer backup
     can easily produce $3,000–$8,000 of damage in a single event (finished
     flooring, lower-level drywall, contents). A is capped at $2,500; B
     is capped at $5,000. The $42/yr premium buys you $2,500 of
     additional ceiling on the worst-case-loss category you actually
     face. This is the dominant reason to pick B in plain risk terms.

  Net practical risk: A is "fine for normal years, exposed on a bad
  water-backup year." B is "pay $42 to roughly double the cap on the
  one loss type that can run four figures."

  neighborhood drainage, and claim history?"

       If 3+: B earns its $42.

  the extra $500 of deductible savings change our month in any
  meaningful way?"

Mom should put these side by side and walk through them with the provider field by field. A dollar-for-dollar match in Box 1 does not mean the correction was cosmetic — banks reissue for TIN, address, entity-name, or payer-EIN changes that the IRS uses to match returns to payers.

  1. The bank's CORRECTED Form 1099-INT (received 3/14). This is the authoritative document; the IRS treats it as superseding any prior 1099-INT from this payer. If a "VOID" original is enclosed, that earlier form is null. If no original exists, that's itself a fact to tell the provider.
  2. Mom's filed Form 1040 / 1040-SR. Confirm Box 2b (taxable interest) and whether Schedule B, Part I was required. $12.01 alone wouldn't trigger Schedule B (the threshold is $1,500), but if other interest put her over, Schedule B matters.
  3. The "official form" Mom saw March 1 — same fields as the corrected form. Compare Box 1, Box 2 (early-withdrawal penalty), Box 3, payer EIN, payer name/address, and Mom's TIN. Identical dollar amounts with other field changes are still a "correction" in IRS terms.
  4. Bank statements covering the period the interest accrued, to confirm $12.01 was actually paid and not a placeholder.
  5. State return for the same tax year. Some states (CA, NY, MN, a few others) require a state-level amendment for any 1099 difference, even when federal doesn't.

Records to retain

  - All of the above for at least 7 years from the original filing date. The IRS has a 3-year assessment window, 6 years if more than 25% of gross income is omitted (the $12.01 itself doesn't trigger that, but the broader return might), and indefinitely for fraud.
  - The envelope or email showing when the corrected form arrived. Timing establishes that the form was unavailable at filing — that's material to the amendment decision.
  - Any bank correspondence explaining why the form was reissued.
  - A written record of the guided-filing consultation: date, advisor name, exact advice, and any disclaimer language.
  - If she amends: Form 1040-X, proof of e-file or mailing, IRS acceptance ("Return Acknowledgement"), and any refund check or direct-deposit record.
  - If she doesn't amend: the advisor's written rationale, including any IRS citation they relied on. Informal de minimis is not codified, so a citation matters if the IRS later questions the omission.

The exact question to ask the guided-filing provider

  "Given that my filed return omitted the $12.01 in Box 1 interest income because the 1099-INT was unavailable at filing, and the bank's corrected form now reports the same $12.01 I would have reported had it arrived in time, am I required under Form 1040-X instructions and current IRS guidance to file an amended return — and does the informal de minimis practice commonly cited for sub-$50 corrections with no tax impact apply to adding previously unreported interest income, or only to correcting an overstated amount?"

  Why that wording matters — it does three things the provider needs to resolve:

  a. Anchors the corrected form as authoritative, so they're not tempted to treat the corrected label as an automatic amendment trigger in itself.
  b. Frames the omission as a timing failure (the bank's, not Mom's), which is the cleanest basis for either amending or not amending.
  c. Tests the de minimis boundary in its specific application: practitioners handle it inconsistently — some amend any unreported income no matter how small, others skip when additional federal tax is under roughly $1. The provider should give you a straight answer on which side they fall on and why.

Working assumption: "sealed" means a film finish (polyurethane, lacquer, conversion varnish) unless you know otherwise. Wax-oil and shellac need different handling — flagged where it matters.

Why a shadow persists after a water blot: pigment particles have lodged in micro-defects in the seal, or under it (more likely if the surface is a wax-oil rather than a film). Water only moves unbound pigment.

Sequence — run each stage once, then evaluate before escalating.

Stage 0 — re-blot with clean water
- Damp (not wet) microfiber, fresh section each pass.
- Press, don't rub. Lift straight up.
- Dry the area immediately with a second dry microfiber.
- Stop if: no pigment transfer after 4 passes, OR any change in sheen.

Stage 1 — dilute soap
- 2-3 drops of plain dish soap (non-ionic, no lotions or additives) in ~250 ml water.
- Damp cloth, single pass over the mark, immediately rinse-blot with clean water, then dry.
- Stop if: pigment is unchanged AND finish is unchanged → accept or escalate.
- Stop if: any dulling, hazing, or tackiness — soap has lifted the finish; stop, dry thoroughly, do not continue.

Stage 2 (optional, gentle) — low heat
- Hair dryer on low, 30+ cm away, short passes. Warmth can wick residual pigment out of micro-defects without solvent risk. If the shadow lightens, repeat Stage 0.

Stage 3 — 70% isopropyl alcohol, cotton swab
- Patch-test first on an inconspicuous spot (under the desk, back edge): 1 swab, 10 seconds, wait 5 minutes, check for sheen change.
- If the patch test is clean: lightly touch the swab to the shadow, single pass, rotate to fresh cotton. Do not flood the area.
- Stop if: pigment stops transferring OR any finish softening, dulling, whitening at edges.
- Stop immediately if the swab picks up any clear or amber liquid — that is the finish dissolving.
- Do not use this stage if the finish is wax-oil or shellac: IPA will strip wax and dissolve shellac. For wax-oil, skip to a refresher coat of the same product on a soft cloth, worked into the spot only.

Stage 4 — do not pursue unless you plan to refinish
- Oxalic acid, wood bleach, magic eraser, acetone, lacquer thinner, mineral spirits, scrubbing compounds — all will damage or remove the seal. A shadow that survives Stage 3 with no finish change is best left alone, or accepted until the next refinish of that surface.

Hard stop criteria (any one → stop, dry, do not continue)
- Sheen change at the spot or in the surrounding area.
- Tackiness, softening, wrinkling, or whitening of the finish.
- Color on your applicator that is not blue: amber means the finish is dissolving; white haze means the finish is clouding.
- Pigment transfer has plateaued with no further progress.

Realistic outcome: a true staining blue (phthalo, indigo, some quinacridones) that has reached micro-defects in a film finish often leaves a permanent faint shadow. If Stage 3 produces no transfer and no finish change, the mark is likely permanent without refinishing the spot — and a spot refinish on sealed wood is more disruptive than living with a pale blue ghost next to the painting corner.

One adjacent note: a small duster brush kept at the painting corner catches pigment dust before it becomes a splash. Cheap insurance for next session.

Procedure below. It is grounded in the conventions already in use (the three provenance categories established 2025-03-22, the reconstruction-folder pattern from the P014/P015/P016 work, the non-canonical-until-two-person rule, and the audit-log field set used by preflight and the lifecycle send audit). Nothing here invents metadata; every field is tagged to a source or marked unavailable.

══════════════════════════════════════════════
Sidecar Reconstruction & Audit-Log Procedure
Provenance-preserving; no fabricated metadata
══════════════════════════════════════════════

1. SCOPE AND TRIGGERS
   Use this procedure when an image has no on-disk sidecar but at least
   one authoritative off-disk source exists. Triggers:
     - Sidecar absent from current export AND backup
     - Sidecar present but provenance unrecorded (treat as absent)
     - Hash mismatch between image and recorded sidecar metadata
   Reconstruction is NEVER recovery. Every reconstruction is labeled as
   such and held non-canonical until two-person verification completes.

2. PRECONDITIONS (any one missing blocks reconstruction)
   - At least one authoritative source for the affected image ID exists
     (paper log page, prior export row, or external backup entry).
   - The image file itself is present and its current SHA-256 is computed.
   - The reconstruction operator and a second verifier are named.
   - A reconstruction folder is created at
     catalog/reconstructed_<YYYY-MM-DD>/ with a dated manifest.
   If a paper-log transcription appears erroneous, STOP and record the
   discrepancy; do not silently correct.

3. PROVENANCE CATEGORIES (applied per field, not per record)
   Exactly one tag per populated field:
     paper_log          Verbatim handwritten value transcribed by Marcus
                        from the paper log; quoted as written.
     verified_file      File property re-pulled from the current image
                        (dimensions, format, SHA-256, mtime) and noted
                        with the verification timestamp.
     paper_log_inferred Schema field conservatively derived from paper-log
                        content by Riley; the inference rule is stated
                        in the field note.
   Unpopulated fields are marked unavailable and given a reason in the
   field note (no source, contradictory source, source degraded, etc.).
   No field is left empty without an explicit unavailable tag.

4. SIDECAR RECONSTRUCTION STEPS
   4.1 Open the reconstruction folder; record reconstruction_id, date,
       operator, second verifier, and reconstruction version.
   4.2 Compute SHA-256 of the current image; store under verified_file.
       If the hash differs from any backup hash, STOP and open an
       incident; reconstruction proceeds only after disposition.
   4.3 Transcribe paper-log values verbatim into paper_log fields.
       Do not normalize, modernize, or correct obvious errors.
   4.4 For schema fields not on the paper log, derive conservatively
       under paper_log_inferred; write the inference rule in the note.
   4.5 For any field without a defensible source, mark unavailable
       with the reason; do not invent a value.
   4.6 Write the sidecar with canonical = false; reconstruction = true;
       reconstruction_id; reconstruction_date; sources_consulted list;
       per-field provenance tag; and a link to the paper-log entry.
   4.7 Write a pointer file (or CSV row) naming the sidecar, image ID,
       image SHA-256, paper-log entry ID, and reconstruction_id.
   4.8 Append a manifest row to the reconstruction folder manifest:
       image_id, sidecar path, image SHA-256, reconstruction_id,
       operator, verifier, date, canonical = false.
   4.9 Do NOT delete, overwrite, or rename the original image file.
       Originals remain on disk for audit; reconstruction lives in the
       dated reconstruction folder only.

5. AUDIT-LOG ENTRY (one entry per reconstruction event)
   Each reconstruction writes a single audit-log record containing:
     - reconstruction_id
     - reconstruction_date (UTC) and timezone
     - affected_image_id(s)
     - reconstruction_version (schema version of the procedure used)
     - sources_consulted (paper-log page ID, backup path, prior export)
     - operator name, role, timestamp
     - second_verifier name, role, timestamp (pending until signed)
     - image_sha256 (verified_file)
     - hash_comparison_result vs backup (match / mismatch / no backup)
     - per-field provenance counts:
         paper_log_count, verified_file_count,
         paper_log_inferred_count, unavailable_count
     - unavailable_fields list with reasons
     - inferred_fields list with inference rules
     - paper_log_errors list (transcribed verbatim; not corrected)
     - reconstruction_folder path
     - manifest_pointer path
     - canonical_status: false
     - two_person_verification_status: pending
     - retention_window (named, e.g., "lifecycle audit + 24 months")
     - transformation_version (reconstruction-procedure version)
   Audit-log writes are append-only. No field in a prior entry is edited
   to reflect later verification; the verification result is a separate
   append referencing the same reconstruction_id.

6. TWO-PERSON VERIFICATION GATE
   - The operator and a second verifier (Mom and Marcus, or designated
     substitutes) review the sidecar against the paper log and image
     side-by-side.
   - The verifier initials the sidecar or signs the audit-log entry;
     either is acceptable, but the choice is recorded.
   - Discrepancies are logged as separate audit entries with the
     reconstruction_id; the sidecar is amended only by writing a new
     versioned sidecar, not by in-place edit.
   - Two-person verification is the ONLY path that promotes a
     reconstruction to canonical. Reconstruction alone does not
     satisfy the requirement.

7. CANONICAL PROMOTION (separate step, after verification)
   - Promotion writes a new audit-log entry referencing the same
     reconstruction_id with canonical_status: true and the verifier's
     identifier.
   - The promoted sidecar is moved to the canonical catalog location.
   - The reconstruction folder is archived; its contents are retained
     for the named retention window and not deleted.
   - Originals and any rescans remain on disk; canonical promotion does
     not touch image files.

8. RETENTION AND ARCHIVAL
   - Reconstruction folder, manifest, pointer files, and audit-log
     entries are retained for the named retention window.
   - Two backups (non-adjacent locations) hold the reconstruction
     artifacts; each backup is verified by opening two non-adjacent
     files and confirming SHA-256.
   - Audit-log records are queryable by reconstruction_id, image_id,
     operator, verifier, and date range.

9. EXPLICIT PROHIBITIONS
   - Never overwrite an existing sidecar in place; write a new version.
   - Never correct a paper-log error silently; record it as-is.
   - Never promote a reconstruction to canonical on operator authority
     alone; two-person verification is required.
   - Never treat inferred values as confirmed; the tag stays
     paper_log_inferred, and inferred-only fields cannot make a record
     field-complete.
   - Never reuse a prior reconstruction's window or pointer when a new
     request arrives; re-pull and write a fresh reconstruction event.
   - Never delete originals, backups, or reconstruction folders to
     "clean up"; archival only, with retention recorded.
   - Never log a reconstruction as recovery; the audit entry must use
     reconstruction, not recovery or restore.

10. FAILURE MODES (open an incident, do not proceed)
   - SHA-256 of image differs from any backup hash.
   - Paper log and backup disagree on a field.
   - No authoritative source exists for a required field.
   - Two-person verifier is unavailable and a substitute is not named.
   Any of these blocks canonical promotion and may block the
   reconstruction itself; the incident is logged before any further
   action.

══════════════════════════════════════════════

Notes on alignment with prior decisions:
- The provenance tags (paper_log / verified_file / paper_log_inferred)
  match the 2025-03-22 catalog convention.
- The reconstruction-folder path pattern
  (catalog/reconstructed_<YYYY-MM-DD>/) matches the P014/P015/P016
  layout.
- canonical = false until two-person verification matches the standing
  rule from the rescan and reconstruction work; canonical promotion is
  always a separate step.
- Audit-log fields (operator role, timestamp, transformation version,
  retention window) match the lifecycle preflight operator-view and
  send-audit field sets, so reconstruction events are queryable
  through the same audit surface.
- The reconstruction-procedure version field is logged on every event,
  matching the preflight transformation-version logging rule.

  Pale or white gums
  Unproductive retching or distended painful belly
  No urine for 12+ hours or painful urination
  Severe weakness or inability to stand

Salmonella can also sicken people — kids, elderly, immunocompromised household members especially. Hand-washing after any contact with the dog, food area, or stool through the 72-hour window.

Two parts here: (1) what the issuer will likely do on a refund, and (2) the math on staying vs. downgrading.

ON THE REFUND QUESTION

A silent notice is the norm — most US issuers don't publish refund terms for product changes. Typical default behavior:

  Chase: does not refund the annual fee on mid-year downgrades once it has posted. Refund window is short (often 30 days from the statement close on which the fee posted); after that the fee is treated as earned for the year in which benefits were accessible.

  Amex: same pattern — short statement-tied window, then no refund.

  Capital One / Citi: similar.

So the default expectation if you downgrade after April 15: the $150 fee posts and is forfeited. Some reps will refund as a one-time courtesy, but it's not a published right. The clean way to avoid that risk is to downgrade before April 15 — no fee posts, no refund question, but you also lose immediate access to the $75 credit and lounge passes for whatever's left of the current cardmember year.

BREAK-EVEN MATH

Sticker increase: $150 - $95 = $55/yr.

Your actual usage (last 12 months):
  - $75 travel credit used in full — only realized if you stay
  - 2 lounge visits used — Priority Pass visits retail ~$30-35 each, so ~$60-70 of value, only if you stay
  - $218 in points redeemed — unaffected on the existing balance either way

Net annual cost of staying on the new $150 fee:
  $150 fee - $75 credit - ~$65 lounge value ≈ +$10/yr
  (vs. the $95 era: $95 - $75 - ~$65 ≈ -$45/yr — the old card was paying you to keep it)

The $55 hike effectively cancels the benefit value you'd been extracting. You're now roughly break-even on the card instead of net-positive.

Net annual cost of the downgrade path:
  - $0 fee
  - lose $75 credit
  - lose ~$65 lounge value
  - earn drops to 1.5x on travel/dining — 25% cut if you currently earn 2x, 50% cut if 3x

The earn cut is the hidden cost and scales with category spend. If you put $X/year on travel+dining, you lose 0.5X points at 2x→1.5x, or 1.5X points at 3x→1.5x. (At 1cpp baseline value, that's $0.005X or $0.015X in cash-equivalent.)

Given your usage, the two paths are roughly a wash — the $55 fee increase eats the credit + lounge value you were getting, and the earn-rate cut on the downgrade path recoups whatever travel/dining points you'd otherwise leave on the table.

THREE REASONABLE PATHS

  1. Stay, accept the $55 hike. Net cost ~$10/yr. Worth it if (a) you actually want ongoing lounge access, (b) you spend enough on travel/dining that the earn cut on the downgrade path would hurt, or (c) you value the card's higher earn rate enough that paying ~$10/yr to keep it is fine.

  2. Downgrade before April 15. Saves the $150 with no refund-question risk. Costs you ~$140 in benefits for the year. Net positive ~$10/yr on a pure dollars basis, more if the earn-rate cut on your actual spend is meaningful.

  3. Use the rest of this cardmember year's benefits (credit + any remaining lounge visits), then downgrade before the next annual fee posts. Captures full near-term benefit value but you pay $150 and almost certainly don't get it back — and you should expect to forfeit any un-used-after-downgrade portion of the credit.

CONCRETE NEXT STEPS

  - Call the issuer before April 15. Ask two specific questions:
      (a) "If I downgrade on [date], will the April 15 fee have posted, and if so is it refundable or waivable?"
      (b) "If I downgrade today, when does access to the $75 credit and lounge visits end?"
  - Get the rep's name and a reference number. If they commit to a refund or waiver on (a), it's documented; if they say no refund, you've confirmed you need to act before April 15.
  - Don't use the app's "product change" flow as a shortcut — it typically posts the fee and treats it as non-refundable regardless of timing.

Plan for Kibo — single loose stool 1 week post-recall exposure:

Background framing first, then the plan. Single loose stool after grass-chewing in an otherwise alert, eating, drinking dog is most consistent with benign grass-induced GI irritation. Salmonella incubation in dogs is typically 6-72 hours; a single episode a full week later without any systemic signs is unlikely but not zero. Your instinct to monitor conservatively given the recall is appropriate.

Home monitoring plan:

Hydration
  Fresh water available at all times; do not restrict.
  Goal is roughly normal intake (~50 mL/kg/day). Note if he drinks noticeably less or noticeably more than usual.
  Dehydration check, twice daily: lift lip — gums pink and moist; tent skin over shoulder blades — snaps back in under 2 seconds; eyes bright, not sunken.

Feeding
  Skip the next regular meal and give the gut a short rest, about 6-12 hours, with continued water access.
  Reintroduce bland diet for 2-3 days: skinless boiled chicken (no salt, no oil, no bones) plus plain white rice, roughly 1 part chicken to 2-3 parts rice.
  Feed small frequent meals, 3-4 per day, about half his normal total volume split that way.
  Transition back to regular food over 2-3 days once stools are consistently formed.
  Optional but reasonable: a canine probiotic (FortiFlora, Proviable) once daily during the bland period.

Hygiene — Salmonella is zoonotic, so handle this like a confirmed-shedder protocol until told otherwise
  Wash hands with soap after handling Kibo, picking up stool, or touching bowls and bedding.
  Pick up stool promptly, bag and trash. Do not compost.
  Wash bedding and bowls in hot water.
  No face-licking for any household member; extra caution around young children, elderly, pregnant, or immunocompromised people.
  Recall lot is already out of the home per your note, so no further dietary exposure.

Monitoring log — twice daily, brief
  Stool: count, consistency, color, any blood or mucus.
  Vomiting: count and contents.
  Appetite and water intake.
  Energy level and attitude.
  Gums and hydration check.
  Temperature if you have a rectal thermometer — normal 101.0-102.5°F (38.3-39.2°C).

Thresholds:

Call regular vet within 24 hours (non-emergency)
  Second loose stool, or stool stays soft more than 48 hours.
  Any vomiting, even one episode.
  Mild appetite drop lasting more than 24 hours.
  Mild lethargy — still responsive, just lower energy than his baseline.
  Any mucus or streaking in stool.

Go to urgent care or ER now
  Repeated diarrhea — 3 or more episodes in 12 hours, or persistent watery stool.
  Any blood in stool — red fresh blood or black/tarry melena.
  Repeated vomiting, or vomiting that will not stop.
  Refusal to drink for more than 12 hours, or dehydration signs that do not correct.
  Temperature above 103°F (39.4°C) or below 99°F (37.2°C).
  Severe lethargy, weakness, wobbliness, or collapse.
  Abdominal pain or distension — hard or bloated belly, "prayer posture" (front down, rear up, reluctant to move).
  Pale, white, yellow, or brick-red gums.
  Tremors, seizures, or sudden behavior change.

Two additional notes worth flagging:

Even if Kibo stays entirely well, a fecal Salmonella PCR at the regular vet is a reasonable next step given the confirmed recall exposure — Salmonella can shed asymptomatically for weeks, and a negative result lets you relax the hygiene protocol and stop second-guessing every grass incident. A quick call to ask whether they want a fresh stool sample submitted is enough.

Keep the recall notice and lot number on file in case the vet needs it, or in case any household member develops GI symptoms in the next 2-3 weeks — Salmonella is a real zoonotic concern and the recall lot is the cleanest link between pet and human cases.

If anything in the "call regular vet" list happens tonight or tomorrow, that is still well within normal-clinic timing. Nothing in your current picture points to needing urgent care tonight.

Study: value separation, cool window / warm counter edge. Isolating lift-only (no added pigment).

Held constant across all panels
- Paper: four 4x4" blocks on one quarter-sheet, same side, same pre-wet timing (single brush-pass + 20s hold before painting each block)
- Pigment: two pre-mixed wells — cool (e.g., ultramarine + burnt sienna gray) and warm (e.g., burnt sienna or quin gold). Same paint:water ratio, same volume in the well, every block
- Brush: one brush per pigment, same dip-and-load cycle, same puddle size
- Wash timing: window wash first, counter wash 3–5s later, identical in every block
- Drying env: same position on board, fan off, same room

Variable: degree of controlled lift on the counter edge while still wet.

Four blocks, painted left-to-right in one sitting

A. Control — no lift. Counter goes on at the same value as the window. (Reproduces Sunday's failure.)

B. Slight lift — at the wet-touch window (~20s after the counter wash): one damp-brush blot across the counter edge, no transition. Target: counter ~1 value lighter than window at the wet stage.

C. Moderate lift — same timing, the 10/20 refine protocol: 1 firm blot → controlled transition (light→broad, 2×→seam), 20s touch hold, 1 touch only. Target: counter ~2 values lighter than window at the wet stage.

D. Near-reserve — same timing, lift continued until the counter edge approaches paper white; warmth survives only as a thin halo at the seam.

No-return rule applies inside every block: one touch, hold 20s, no return after dull.

Observation rubric — record per block at three stages
- Wet (right after lift): is the gap where you intended it?
- 50% dry (back-of-hand test): does counter still read lighter than window?
- Bone dry: has the gap held, narrowed, or closed?

What the result decides
- Gap survives dry in B → minimal lift is sufficient; no glaze needed. Default going forward.
- Gap closes in B, holds in C → wet-stage target ≈ 2 values lighter. Calibration point.
- Gap closes in B and C, holds in D → counter edge needs to be reserved, not painted at full strength. That's a compositional call, not a finish move — flag it for the unresolved-boundary decision.
- Gap closes in all lifted blocks → value separation isn't the operative variable; suspect pigment choice or paper interaction. Re-design before another study.

The two readings diverge most clearly on what the third scene is doing, not on what's happening in the first two. The flooded underpass and the rerouting are the same facts under either interpretation — what's at stake is what it means when the planner labels that rerouting "resilience."

If genuine adaptation: the novel is showing a community developing a workable response to a condition the institution hasn't resolved, and the planner's word is the name catching up to a practice. The repetition of repair matters less than the emergence of the workaround; "resilience" is descriptive.

If institutional renaming: the planner character is using a vocabulary that converts the community's labor into a flattering property of the system. The repetition of repair is then load-bearing — same fix, same place, recurring failure — and the workaround gets named as if it were the system absorbing the shock rather than residents absorbing the institution's gap.

What might help hold both: the residents' practice and the planner's vocabulary aren't the same object. You can read the rerouting as genuinely adaptive — skillful, situated, real work — and still read "resilience" as the word doing institutional work over the top of it. The two readings collapse each other only if you treat them as competing claims about the same thing. They're more like claims about different layers of the same scene.

The narrower question the structure seems built to keep open is what the planner's language accomplishes, and for whom. Whether the novel ultimately indicts or endorses the move may turn on cues you haven't listed — whose interiority we get in scene three, what other characters do with the word afterward, whether the planner's framing gets tested against the residents' own self-understanding or left uncontested.

One thing the three-scene setup is already doing, whether you lean one way or the other: scene one's repetition establishes that the institution's response has a ceiling. If the underpass were repaired successfully and the flooding ended, the rerouting would read as caution. Because it recurs, the rerouting becomes load-bearing for daily life — which is what makes the planner's vocabulary either praise or euphemism rather than neutral description. That ceiling is where the interpretive pressure lives.

Two-sided interpretation

Reading A — adaptation. The character reads rooms fast and reshapes themselves to fit: practical, perceptive, fluent in what a given moment requires. Survival looks like getting good at the surface, not fighting it.

Reading B — institutional avoidance. The same moves keep them just outside any structure that would actually hold them — the temporary arrangement is accepted, the permanent offer is declined, the record is left unsigned. What looks like adaptation is also a steady refusal to be pinned.

Why they stay in tension. Every adaptive gesture in the book is also a way of not committing to the institution it serves, and the text never forces the question — the same scenes support both readings cleanly. A facilitator who pushes one side usually loses the other; the interesting move is to let both sit and watch which one each reader reaches for first.

When [character] does [specific gesture — the one you'd flag], are we watching someone get better at the room, or someone making sure they never have to belong to it — and what's in the scene that makes that hard to settle?
