Yes — this fits trapped air, and the signature you described is textbook for it.

WHY IT'S AIR, NOT SOMETHING ELSE
    After a planned common-line shutoff, the building's risers refill under pressure and dissolved/supplied air gets pushed into unit supply lines. At the tap, that air emulsifies into microscopic bubbles that scatter light and make the water look milky-white. In a glass, the bubbles migrate upward and burst at the surface, so the column clears from the bottom up — exactly what you saw. Air has no color, no sediment, and no odor. Thirty seconds is on the fast end of normal for a unit on a small branch; longer holds are also consistent. The "no leak in the unit" point is the other confirming signal: a pressure surge that broke something would usually show itself as a drip, a spinning meter, or a wet cabinet, not clear water.

CONSERVATIVE COLD-WATER FLUSHING SEQUENCE
    Cold only, throughout. Do not run any hot tap until cold is fully clear. Mixing in hot while air is still in the lines can pull air into the water heater and give you sputtering hot water for hours.

    1.  Start at the cold tap closest to where water enters the unit — kitchen cold is usually it, and it already shows the pattern. Open it fully (no aerator restriction). It will look milky at first. Run it until a glass held under the stream looks fully clear and bubble-free, then keep it running another 1–2 minutes past that point to confirm stability.
    2.  Walk outward through the unit in order of distance from the entry point: kitchen cold, then bathroom cold, then any other cold taps (utility sink, laundry cold). Flush each one the same way — until clear, plus a minute more.
    3.  Flush every toilet once. Each flush pulls a slug through the cold branch and helps move pockets along.
    4.  If the unit has an outdoor spigot or a balcony hose bib on the cold side, run that last and let it run a few minutes — it often vents the largest air pocket.
    5.  Only after all cold taps are running consistently clear, briefly test the hot side starting at the kitchen: run hot until it's clear, then move to other hot taps. If hot milks at any point, that tap isn't fully cleared yet — keep flushing.
    6.  Aerator check: if a tap sputters or "rains" after the line is clear, unscrew the aerator, rinse the screen and housing, and refit. Aerators trap residual air bubbles and will keep producing cloudy bursts even when the supply is fine.
    7.  Appliances: empty the ice maker and run a cycle; if the dishwasher or washing machine ran during the milky period, run a short rinse cycle on each. They pull air into their supply hoses and will re-aerate the next draw otherwise.

    Building-side note: in a multi-unit building, the booster pumps and risers can release additional air pockets intermittently over the next several hours. A brief return of milky water at one tap later in the day is not a problem — repeat the flush at that tap. If it recurs across multiple taps over more than a day, that's a building-system signal worth reporting.

SIGNS TO STOP USING THE TAP AND CONTACT MANAGEMENT
    Each of these is a stop signal, not an air signature. The rule is simple: air is colorless, odorless, sediment-free, and clears bottom-up in under a couple of minutes. Anything else needs a report.

    -  Discoloration. Yellow, brown, rust, reddish, or any tint that does not clear from the bottom of the glass within a minute or two of full-flow flushing. Suggests disturbed sediment from the city main, mobilized corrosion scale from building risers, or — less commonly — a cross-connection. A faint yellow tint that disappears after a few minutes can be stirred sediment from the mains and is sometimes seen right after a shutoff, but anything persistent or reddish/brown should be reported rather than flushed through.
    -  Persistent particles. Anything that settles rather than rises — sand, grit, black specks, gray flakes, jelly-like material. Indicates pipe scale, biofilm, or main sediment. Air bubbles rise; particles sink. The distinction is visible in a single glass.
    -  Odor. Air has none. A rotten-egg smell points to hydrogen sulfide, often from a water-heater anode reaction that the shutoff stirred up, or from biofilm in the building main. A petroleum or solvent smell is a contamination signal and is urgent. A metallic smell suggests iron corrosion. Any odor at all means it's not just air.
    -  Pressure loss. Pressure that drops while a tap is running, pressure that stays noticeably lower than usual after the flush, sudden pressure swings between fixtures, or any fixture that will not deliver a steady stream. Can indicate a partially closed building valve, a leak in the riser, or an air pocket stuck in a vertical run that is restricting flow rather than passing through it.
    -  Leakage. Any new drip, damp cabinet base, water staining on a wall or ceiling, a floor drain that runs when no fixture is in use, or a meter that keeps moving with every tap closed. After a repressurization event, weak joints, old shutoff valves, and braided supply lines are the typical failure points. Check under every sink, behind the toilet, around the water heater, and at the main shutoff. If you find any of these, close the unit's main shutoff and report it — don't keep running water into a leak you can't see the end of.

    Practical use rule while flushing: don't drink or cook with the milky water. Use bottled or the pre-shutoff filled supply until a cold tap has run clear with no bubbles for a full minute. Once it does, that tap is fine.

1. Keep the bike out of commute use until you've found the cause.

Chain skip under load is a safety issue, not just a wear issue:
- The lurch is unpredictable and happens most often when you're already working hard (climbing, sprinting, accelerating into traffic) — exactly when balance is hardest to recover.
- A skipping chain under load means the drivetrain is compromised; continuing to ride accelerates damage to the cassette and chainrings. A stretched chain can destroy a fresh cassette in a few dozen miles.
- Your walk-home call was the right one.

If you need to physically move the bike, rolling it or pedaling it gently on flat ground in an easy gear with light effort is fine. No climbs, no sprints, no firm pedal pressure until you know what's wrong.

2. Conservative stationary inspection sequence.

Each step is non-destructive. A workstand is ideal; leaning the bike against a wall with the drivetrain side out and someone stabilizing the front also works. Go in order — the cheap/obvious checks first.

a. Confirm the symptom before touching anything.
   - With the rear wheel free, spin the cranks by hand in a mid-range gear while applying firm pressure.
   - Watch the chain through the rear derailleur. Does it visibly jump a tooth or more on the cassette? On a chainring? Does the wheel momentarily freewheel while you push? Each points to a different cause.
   - Note any "clunk" once per crank revolution that doesn't correspond to a chain jump — that's freehub pawl engagement, not chain skip, and is usually benign. Worth distinguishing because the shop will ask.

b. Chain — stiff links.
   - Slowly backpedal and watch each link as it passes through the upper and lower derailleur pulleys. A stiff link visibly binds instead of flexing smoothly.
   - If you find one, flex it side-to-side to free it. If it won't free, that link needs replacement.

c. Chain — wear/stretch.
   - Best: a chain-checker tool (Park Tool CC-3.2 or similar). Drop the chain into the tool; 0.5% = replace soon, 0.75% = cassette is almost certainly worn too.
   - Without a tool: the 12-inch ruler method. 12 full links (24 half-links, including the pin) on a new chain measure exactly 12 inches. At 12 1/16" replace; at 12 1/8" the cassette is shot. For 11- and 12-speed chains, replace earlier (0.5% threshold) because the cassettes are expensive and don't tolerate stretched chains.

d. Cassette tooth profile.
   - Drop the chain off the front ring, or just look at the cassette from the side in the smallest cog.
   - Inspect under good light with the wheel at eye level. New teeth are symmetric and squared; worn teeth are hooked/shark-fin, leaning in the direction of chain travel.
   - Wear concentrates on your most-used cogs (often mid-range if you climb). If one or two cogs look bad you've localized it; if all look bad, the whole cassette is suspect.

e. Chainring tooth profile.
   - Lift the chain off the front ring and look at the teeth. Same hooked/shark-fin test. Wear is most common on the inner/small ring; the big ring often looks fine even when the small one is shot.

f. Rear derailleur hanger alignment.
   - Stand behind the bike and sight along the cassette toward the derailleur pulleys. The two pulleys should sit parallel to the cassette cogs — not visibly tilted in or out.
   - Eyeballing this is unreliable. Without a hanger alignment tool (Park Tool DAG-2.2 or equivalent), this is one to flag for the shop.

g. Rear derailleur function.
   - Shift through every gear, both directions, with the wheel free. Hesitation, clunks, or delay = indexing problem (cable tension, hanger, or B-tension).
   - In the largest cog, check the B-tension gap: roughly 5–6 mm between the top of the cassette teeth and the bottom of the upper jockey wheel. Too far = skipping; too close = noise.

h. Cable and housing.
   - In the smallest cog, push the derailleur body inward by hand and release. It should snap back crisply. Slow/sticky return = cable friction.
   - Look for frayed cable, missing end caps, housing that's bottomed out into a frame stop (it should have a small gap so it can flex). Housing that takes a long curve under the bottom bracket is a frequent friction point.

i. Pulleys.
   - Spin the derailleur pulleys by hand. They should spin freely and quietly for several seconds. Stiff, gritty, or ones that stop in under two seconds should be replaced.

j. Wheel seating and axles.
   - Confirm the rear wheel is fully seated in the dropouts and the QR or thru-axle is tight. A wheel that has crept forward in the dropouts shifts the chainline and can cause skip events.
   - Spin the wheel and check for true; confirm the tire is properly seated with no bulges or cuts. (You said these felt normal — sanity check, not the prime suspect.)

3. What to tell the shop.

Concrete facts make diagnosis faster:
- Chain skipped twice under firm pedal pressure while climbing. They need to know it was under torque, not at low effort.
- Approximate age/mileage of the chain and cassette, and when each was last replaced (if known).
- Recent shifting behavior: any hesitation, slow shifts, clunks, or unusual noise in the last weeks or months, even if you didn't think it was a problem at the time.
- Recent conditions: wet rides, mud, pressure-washing, recent cleaning/lubing (especially the wrong lube — anything solvent-based or wet-style lube that has dried and gunked up the chain).
- Whether the rear wheel has been removed recently (e.g., for a flat). Reinstalling a wheel slightly off in the dropouts is a common cause of one-off skip events.
- Anything you found in the inspection above (stiff link, shark-fin teeth, hanger that looked off, sticky pulleys, sluggish cable return, etc.).
- Confirm that you have not done a loaded road test since. They'll likely want to do that themselves, on a stand with a load simulator, rather than have you ride it.

If everything above looks clean and you can't find an obvious cause, still take it in. The most common cause — chain past service limit — is invisible without a checker tool, and replacing just the chain before it eats the cassette is much cheaper than replacing both.

---

Findings — Expansion Assist wording comprehension signal (n = 3)

Scope. Three de-identified administrator interviews conducted by Ines with mid-segment Expansion Assist accounts, focused on draft notification and action-surface wording. These findings describe patterns of comprehension and preference across the three interviews. They are not evidence of efficacy, behavior change, or rollout readiness, and they are not generalizable beyond these three accounts.

Finding 1 — "Recent workspace activity" was understood more quickly and more confidently than "approaching a limit."
All three administrators read "recent workspace activity" as a descriptive statement about their own account's near-term state. "Approaching a limit" was read by Admins 1 and 2 as a warning or threshold framing, and Admin 1 explicitly noted a mismatch between the warning framing and the explanation that usage had already crossed a line. This is a comprehension finding, not a preference claim: the descriptive frame produced a cleaner read in all three cases. It does not imply the descriptive frame would change downstream behavior.

Finding 2 — Urgency framing was rejected across all three administrators, but for different reasons.
Admin 1 rejected urgency because it conflicted with the actual state being described. Admin 2 rejected urgency as a general matter of tone. Admin 3's objection was closest to "don't dress up a description as an alert," but the rejection was consistent. Treating these as three different reasons matters: the shared signal is the rejection; the underlying rationales should not be collapsed when designing variants.

Finding 3 — Tying the trigger to actual usage rather than a forecast was a precondition for trust, not a stylistic preference.
All three administrators accepted the wording as legitimate only after the trigger was anchored to observed recent activity. Admin 2 stated this most directly ("recent usage is why I'm seeing it"); Admins 1 and 3 treated it as an unstated requirement and didn't accept the surface until that anchor was present. The signal is that observed-usage grounding is what makes the surface legible at all, independent of which CTA follows.

Finding 4 — The CTA split between Admins 1 & 2 and Admin 3 is a surface-design question, not a wording question.
Admins 1 and 2 landed comfortably on a review-options path as the next step. Admin 3 wanted concrete add-capacity options surfaced directly, without the review-options intermediary. The three administrators all agreed on the lead-in and trigger framing; they diverged on what should follow it. This split should be resolved as a product call about which surface the wording lives on (notification surface vs. action surface), with copy variants produced to match the chosen surface. It is not a signal about which words to use.

What this set does not establish. Three interviews are sufficient to identify comprehension and preference patterns, and not sufficient to claim any wording change will reduce confusion, increase engagement, or perform better than the current default. Findings here should be used to inform copy direction and the surface-choice conversation with Ines, and should be paired with a behavioral read (funnel, activation, or activation-adjacent step) before any rollout decision.

  - Surface decision (notification vs. action) is the call she needs to make.
  - Once surface is chosen, produce the matching copy variant; the divergence is resolved by routing, not by picking words.

Here is a conservative sequence. It moves from items that cost nothing if you change your mind, to a verification gate, then to the heavier items. Stop at any phase and you'll still have only touched reversible stuff.

PHASE 1 — REVERSIBLE / LOW-RISK (typical yield: 1–2 GB)

  1. Reboot the phone. On its own this often frees 200–600 MB by clearing the "Other / System" cache and consolidating temp files.

  2. Offload unused apps.
       iOS: Settings → General → iPhone Storage → enable "Offload Unused Apps." The app icon disappears but its data stays in iCloud; reinstalling restores it.
       Android: Settings → Apps → sort by "Last used" or "Storage" — only uninstall apps you know you can redownload and whose data is cloud-synced.

  3. Clear browser caches only (not history if you want autocomplete, but cache alone is safe).
       Safari: Settings → Safari → Clear History and Website Data.
       Chrome: ⋯ → History → Clear Browsing Data → uncheck everything except "Cached images and files."

  4. Delete offline map areas you won't use on the trip.
       Google Maps → profile → Offline maps → Delete.
       Apple Maps → search the area → swipe up → "Delete map."

  5. Clear downloaded episodes you've already finished in podcast / music apps. Re-download takes a minute.

  6. Clear app caches for messaging apps, not chat history.
       WhatsApp: Settings → Storage and data → Manage storage → clear cache and large media you've already saved.
       Telegram: Settings → Data and storage → Storage usage → Clear cache.
       Signal: Settings → Storage → Clear message history cache.
       iMessage / Messages: clear "Keep Messages" to a shorter window if you're comfortable; otherwise leave alone.

  7. Empty the "Recently Deleted" / Trash album in Photos after a quick spot check that nothing important is there.

VERIFICATION GATE — DO NOT START PHASE 2 UNTIL ALL OF THESE ARE GREEN.

  A. Photos: open Photos, confirm iCloud Photos (iOS) or Backup & Sync (Android) is on and the most recent sync timestamp is today with no "uploading N items" pending. Open one older family photo and confirm it shows as synced / backed up. If a single important photo isn't in the cloud, stop and back it up first.

  B. Authenticator apps (the ones you said NOT to delete):
       - Google Authenticator: Settings → "Transfer accounts / Cloud backup" — confirm backup is on, or that you have exported each account to a second device.
       - Authy: confirm "Backups" is on for your account.
       - Microsoft Authenticator: confirm "Cloud backup" is current.
       - For any 2FA app without cloud backup: confirm you have recovery codes or seed text stored outside the phone (password manager, paper in a safe place). If you do not, stop here — losing that app without a recovery path locks you out of accounts on the trip.

  C. Messaging history:
       - WhatsApp: Settings → Chats → Chat backup → confirm timestamp is recent (last 24 h, or back up now).
       - Signal: confirm you have your safety number recorded for any chats you might need to re-verify.
       - iMessage / SMS: covered by the overall iCloud / Google backup — confirm the device backup is recent.

  D. Travel confirmations: these usually live in Mail or Wallet. Search Mail for the airline, hotel, and any rental car; confirm the original confirmation emails are still there, or screenshot them into your cloud photo album. Anything not yet backed up: forward to yourself or save to Files / Drive before touching anything else.

PHASE 2 — DOWNLOADED MEDIA & APP DATA (only after the gate passes)

  8. Streaming downloads: Netflix / YouTube Premium / Disney+ / Prime Video → Downloads → delete the titles you won't rewatch offline. All re-downloadable from the service on demand.

  9. Mail attachment cache: iOS — Settings → Apps → Mail → clear cache if available (varies by provider); Android — Settings → Apps → Mail → Storage → Clear cache. Originals stay on the mail server.

  10. Voice memos and screen recordings older than the trip: export to cloud first if you want them, then delete the local copies.

  11. Per-app "Documents & Data" in iPhone Storage, in this order:
       - Delete for: streaming, social, casual games, old video editors. You can re-download and re-login.
       - Skip for: banking, auth, password manager, notes, health, mail, maps, calendar.
       On Android: Settings → Apps → sort by data size → same rule.

  12. Voicemail: Phone → Voicemail → delete old messages. Note: voicemail recovery depends on carrier; if any are sentimental, screenshot or export first.

  13. If still tight: Settings → General → iPhone Storage → "Show All" will list one-off large items — failed iOS update files, old IPSWs, downloaded PDFs, large ZIPs. These are safe to delete individually once you've verified they're not in active use.

EXPECTED YIELD
  Phase 1: usually 1–2 GB.
  Phase 2: another 1–3 GB depending on how much streaming you cache.
  A reboot between phases sometimes frees another 200–400 MB by letting the OS reclaim marked-free blocks.

PRE-TRIP SANITY CHECK (5 minutes, the day before you leave)
  - Generate a fresh authenticator code and use it once.
  - Open one travel confirmation offline (airplane mode on).
  - Send yourself a test message to confirm iMessage / WhatsApp / SMS still works.
  - Confirm Focus / Do Not Disturb modes aren't set to silence anyone you actually need during travel.
  - Confirm Maps has offline access to the area you're headed to, if relevant.

If you want, tell me roughly how the storage is split (Settings → Storage usually shows a breakdown like Photos X GB, Apps Y GB, Other Z GB) and I can tell you which phase to prioritize first.

Right now there's no visible damage, so the goal is preventive isolation and, ideally, replacing the non-archival cardboard before it can off-gas or transfer acidity. Two paths, lightest to heavier intervention:

  1. Interleave without disturbing the mount. Slide a full-sheet barrier between the watercolor and the cardboard. Cheapest, fully reversible, no contact with the painted surface.
  2. Lift the sheet and replace the backing with an archival board. Cleaner long-term solution; more handling risk, but proportionate if the cardboard is clearly acidic (gray chip board, newsboard, construction paper).

Safe materials. Look for "acid-free, lignin-free, pH-neutral" or "conservation grade":

  - Buffered acid-free tissue (calcium-carbonate-treated): appropriate for most watercolors on cotton or alpha-cellulose paper.
  - Unbuffered tissue: the safer default if you're unsure about pigment sensitivity (some early synthetic dyes and a few lake pigments are alkali-sensitive). When in doubt, unbuffered.
  - 100% cotton rag museum board (matboard), 4-ply for a 7x9: the standard replacement backing.
  - Polyester film (Mylar / Melinex), about 4 mil: inert and dimensionally stable; good as a folder separator, less ideal in long-term direct contact with friable media because of static.
  - Avoid as barrier or backing: ordinary cardboard, gray board, construction paper, newsprint, glassine in long-term direct contact (it can cloud and stick in humidity), masking tape, any self-stick product, plastic sleeves that off-gas.

Handling precautions.

  - Clean, dry hands or nitrile gloves; handle by edges or by the support, never the painted surface.
  - Work on a clean, flat surface; lay down a sheet of clean glassine or release paper as a working surface.
  - No talking or coughing directly over the work; no food or drink nearby.
  - Slide tissue in from one edge rather than lowering it across the surface; keep the sheet flat, do not flex it.
  - Stable environment: roughly 45-55% RH, ~65-70°F, no direct sun, no attic or garage swings.
  - If you re-mount: T-hinge or corner-mount with Japanese tissue and wheat starch paste (methylcellulose alone is also acceptable) on the top edge only. No tape, no glue-on-corners, no dry-mounting.

When to involve a professional.

  An archival framer: re-house and frame to museum standard, hinge properly, back with rag board, seal the package. Worth engaging if you'd rather not do the swap yourself or want the piece reframed cleanly.
  A paper/prints conservator: needed for actual treatment. Call one if any of the following appears, even faintly:
    - Foxing (small reddish-brown spots), tide lines, water staining, or a mildew / chemical odor
    - Yellowing or browning of the paper, or of the cardboard in contact with it
    - Cockling or buckling that doesn't relax at normal room humidity
    - Visible media lifting, chalking, pigment transfer, or surface tackiness
    - Tears, losses, creases, insect activity, frass
    - Adhesive residue from prior tape, labels, or hinges
    - The sheet is on wood-pulp (non-cotton) paper — these age faster and warrant professional advice before you intervene
    - The piece has real market or sentimental value and you'd like a written condition report (useful for insurance or future exhibition)

Triage decision for this piece. Since you see no staining, buckling, odor, or transfer, an interleaving barrier buys time and is reversible. But it only slows further acid migration; it doesn't undo any already underway. If the cardboard is plain gray chip board and has been in contact for any length of time, swapping it for rag board during a clean, flat-block session is the higher-value move.

One piece-specific note: when you do swap the backing, keep the original cardboard aside in a labeled envelope (artist, title, date, dimensions, contact material) rather than discarding it — provenance of the support matters if this work is ever exhibited, insured, or formally valued.

Package acceptance — short checklist

1. Document the package (before opening)
   - Photos of the sealed box from two angles with the shipping label visible
   - Note carrier, tracking number, ship date, delivery date, order/PO number
   - Flag visible damage: dents, crushed corners, water staining, broken seals
   - Keep all inner packaging, paperwork, and the shipping box until fully settled

2. Confirm the order details (before doing anything with the product)
   - Pull up the confirmation and match item/SKU, size, quantity, variant, personalization
   - Check the packing slip against what's actually in the box — every line item and sub-component
   - Read back any custom text, spelling, dates, or specified options from the physical item
   - If anything is off, stop here: photograph the discrepancy and message the retailer before use

3. Try the remake cautiously
   - Start with the smallest sensible test portion, not a full batch/use
   - Use the simplest, most-documented method first; add variables one at a time
   - Pause and note observations (look, smell, feel, reaction) at each step rather than pushing through
   - Have a neutral fallback (plain water, a discard plan, a way to abort) within the first few minutes

4. Stop and contact the retailer immediately if any of these show up
   - A strong or unexpected reaction (smell, skin, respiratory, GI)
   - Product looks, smells, or behaves clearly outside what the listing implied — mold, off-color, leaking, swelling, sharp chemical smell
   - Foreign object, contamination, broken seal on something that should be sealed, or a recalled batch/lot number
   - Order details don't match what arrived (wrong item, missing pieces, custom text wrong) and you'd rather not use it at all

When you reach out: include photos, order number, lot/batch number if visible, and a one-line description of what stopped you. Ask for next steps in writing.

Recommendation: one primary row per unique scheduled decision, with linked append-only audit history that preserves the initial hold and the later fresh-check disposition as a supersession pair (not duplicates).

Primary ledger (one row per scheduled decision)

  decision_id                  unique scheduled-decision identifier (primary key)
  scheduled_for                decision date / time
  lane / cohort                e.g., Expansion Assist Q4, CS auto-nudge week-of

  latest_evaluation_at         timestamp of most recent eval

  initial_disposition          first eval result: Proceed or field-specific Hold
  initial_hold_reason          field + reason text, or empty
  final_disposition            Proceed / Suppress / Hold, recorded only after a fresh check
  final_disposition_basis      "fresh check after [field] repair" / "original current state" / "still held, awaiting fresh check"
  audit_history_ref            pointer to the append-only event list

Audit history (linked from each primary row, append-only, never collapsed)

  evaluation_id                distinct per check event
  decision_id                  foreign key to primary row
  evaluation_timestamp
  transformation_version
  governed_fields_at_eval      F1-F5 as-of values
  preflight_result
  hold_reason                  if any
  recovery_event               e.g., "F5 refreshed 2025-05-22 09:14"
  disposition_at_this_eval     Proceed / Suppress / Hold (or "still held")
  notes

Reporting rules

  Primary denominator = unique decision_ids, counted once, even when paired evaluations exist.
  Current-state reporting uses the latest evaluation per decision_id.
  Audit exports retain both rows of a stale-to-fresh pair as supersession; the earlier hold is not double-counted.
  Paired rows sharing a decision_id with distinct evaluation_timestamps are labeled "stale-to-fresh supersession" - intentional, not duplicate-data.

Labels to use / avoid

  Use: Proceed, Suppress, Hold, fresh check, field-specific hold, stale-to-fresh supersession, recovery timestamp, governed field (F1-F5), latest evaluation.
  Avoid: "duplicate", "manual release", "approved after repair" (held rows auto-evaluate when fresh data arrives; repaired evidence does not grant retroactive approval).

Chart recommendation

  Primary view: stacked bars by week or checkpoint, one bar per unique-scheduled-decision count, segmented by final disposition (Proceed / Suppress / Hold). Y-axis is the evaluated-decision denominator (latest eval per decision_id).

  Linked audit panel: a secondary table or thin bar showing audit-event count for the same week. Where audit-event count exceeds unique-decision count, label the delta "stale-to-fresh supersession events" - not "duplicate decisions."

  Annotation pattern: for each checkpoint with holds, a callout block listing decision_id, initial hold field, recovery timestamp, final disposition - drawn from the audit history, not duplicated into the primary count.

  Framing block at the top of the chart: scope / cohort, denominator (unique decisions, latest eval), window, causal-vs-descriptive (descriptive operating record, not a launch or forecast claim), feasibility note (what "fresh check" requires).

What a typical adult portal would flag vs. not flag, using standard reference ranges (caveat: each lab sets its own cutoffs, so the actual UI may differ):

Likely flagged (above the usual reference range)
  - Fasting glucose 102 — most labs flag above 99 or 100
  - Calculated LDL 132 — most labs flag at 130 or above (borderline-high zone)

Likely not flagged (within range, or favorable direction)
  - A1c 5.4% — below the 5.7% cutoff
  - HDL 67 — above the 60 threshold; higher is generally considered favorable
  - Triglycerides 84 — well below 150
  - The rest of the metabolic panel — within range per your notes

Two things worth knowing before you talk to the clinician:
  - "Calculated" LDL uses the Friedewald formula, which is less reliable when triglycerides are elevated or LDL is low. 132 is in the borderline zone where the formula's accuracy matters more than at higher values.
  - The portal can only flag against a reference range — it can't tell you whether a single reading represents a new shift, a stable pattern, or expected variation for you.

Suggested questions for your clinician, kept neutral and descriptive:

Interpretation
  1. "Does this lab's reference range treat a fasting glucose of 102 as within normal variation or as impaired fasting glucose, and does the A1c of 5.4% change that read?"
  2. "The LDL is reported as calculated — does that change how you'd interpret 132, and would a directly measured LDL, non-HDL cholesterol, or apoB give a clearer picture at this level?"

Trend context
  3. "Could we pull my prior glucose and lipid results going back a few years so we're looking at trajectory rather than a single point? If there are no priors, what window would you want for a repeat to establish a baseline trend, and should the repeat be fasting?"

Follow-up
  4. "Given these numbers together, are there lifestyle factors (diet pattern, weight, activity, alcohol) worth discussing before any medication or further testing?"
  5. "Is there a role for additional risk markers at this point — for example Lp(a), apoB, or a coronary artery calcium score — based on my age, family history, and these values?"
  6. "When would you want the next set of labs, and is there anything you'd add to the order beyond the standard lipid and metabolic panels?"

At 480 miles with lateral heel tread nearly smooth and pronounced midsole creasing, two of the structural signals have clearly tripped. The midsole creasing is the more important one — once the foam is creased and compressed, cushioning and geometry are degraded even if the upper still looks fine. For a rehab cadence where predictable support matters, this is the relevant threshold, not mileage alone.

REPLACEMENT FRAMEWORK

Use these signals together, not in isolation:

  1. Mileage: 300-500 is the typical lifespan. At 480 you are at the upper edge.
  2. Outsole wear: lateral heel smoothness or any exposed midsole foam — traction and stability compromised.
  3. Midsole creasing: pronounced, clustered creases or compression lines — foam cells collapsing, geometry shifting.
  4. Symptom signal: new in-run fatigue, post-run ache, or "working harder than usual" feeling that wasn't there 50-100 miles ago.

Replace when any two of (2), (3), (4) are clearly present, even below 300 miles. At 480 with (2) and (3) both clearly present, the case is straightforward.

TRANSITION PLAN

Same cadence, same route, same effort. No added variable.

  - Start a fresh mileage log for the new pair (date and miles).
  - First run in new shoes on your next scheduled day (the nonconsecutive one from your last run).
  - Keep the first 2-3 outings on the lake trail so terrain is unchanged.
  - Stay at 30 minutes easy for at least 4 runs in the new shoes — roughly two weeks at your 2/wk cadence.
  - Do not raise duration or frequency during this window, even if the new shoes feel great.
  - If the new pair has a noticeably different drop, stack height, or cushion feel, do a 10-15 minute walk in them the day before the first run to confirm fit and break in the upper only — don't pre-run to "log miles."
  - One pair only during rehab. No rotation yet — single variable, simpler read on symptoms.

PRESERVED RULES (no change)

  - Symptom rule still governs: any in-run, post-run, or next-day focal inside-R-ankle ache = stop that session (or the next one), log it, and don't progress until you have two consecutive symptom-free sessions.
  - Clinical follow-up trigger still active: focal ankle pain that recurs — not a one-off — goes back to the clinician, regardless of the shoe change.
  - New shoes are a controlled variable swap, not a treatment. If your ankle changes, treat the shoes as suspect #1 but don't assume they are the cause.

WHEN TO CONSIDER PROGRESSION

Only after the 4-run transition window with zero symptoms, and only one lever at a time. Per your existing rule, never raise duration and frequency together. Natural next move if everything stays clean: add 5 minutes to one of the two weekly runs, hold the other, then reassess over the following two weeks.

The $72/year differential

Option A's extra $72/yr buys three things relative to B:
  • $500 lower comprehensive deductible ($500 vs $1,000)
  • $750 lower collision deductible ($750 vs $1,500)
  • Rental reimbursement coverage (removed in B; towing remains in both)

The three variables that actually decide this

1. Whether you have a backup vehicle
  This is the rental question. If the car is in the shop after a collision and B is in force, you're paying out of pocket for a rental (or going without). Typical rental reimbursement sublimits run $30–$50/day up to ~$900–$1,200 per loss. If Sam's car is the household backup and reliably available, rental coverage is low-value; if it isn't, one collision could easily cost more than years of the $72/yr difference.

2. Vehicle value vs. the collision deductible gap
  Collision coverage on a vehicle worth less than ~2–3× the deductible is generally weak economics — you're paying to insure against losses the insurer will mostly write off anyway. If the car's market value is, say, under ~$4–5K, the $750-vs-$1,500 deductible gap may not matter much because a total loss gets paid at ACV either way. If the car is meaningfully newer/higher-value, the gap is real money.

3. Your expected claim frequency
  The $72/yr roughly prices the insurer's expected extra payout under A plus the rental benefit. If you drive a lot, park on-street, or have had comp/collision claims in the last 5 years, A is more likely to pay for itself. If the car is low-mileage and garaged, B is more likely to be the rational bet.

What I'd need from you to land a recommendation

  • Vehicle year/make/model (or just ACV) — to size the collision question
  • Whether Sam's car is a real backup (i.e., you'd actually have wheels while yours is in the shop)
  • Whether either of your credit cards already provides primary rental coverage (many Visa/Mastercard products do, but usually secondary and time-limited)
  • Any comp or collision claims in the last ~5 years, and rough annual mileage

If you want to give me those, I'll pick one and tell you why. If you'd rather just decide against the framework, the quick rule of thumb is: A if no backup car or car is worth >~$5K; B otherwise.

Auto-renewal: A $684 vs B $612, six-month terms, same 100/300 + $100 PDSC, towing on both. The $72 = $12/month is buying three things in A that B removes or shrinks. Below is a quantified framework, not a "cheaper is better" answer.

  1. What the $72 actually buys in Option A

  - Comprehensive deductible: $500 (A) vs $1,000 (B) — +$500 of exposure removed
  - Collision deductible: $750 (A) vs $1,500 (B) — +$750 of exposure removed
  - Rental reimbursement: present in A, absent in B — value is conditional, see §3

  Total maximum deductible delta you accept by switching to B: $500 + $750 = $1,250 per claim. On a six-month policy that is a worst-case $1,250 of out-of-pocket exposure in exchange for $72 saved. Even one mid-size claim under B (e.g., a $2,800 deer-collision or hail claim) erases the savings and then some.

  2. Expected-value view (illustrative, plug in your own numbers)

  P(comp or collision claim in 6 months) × E(claim) is what you'd need to size the risk. If you assume:
    - 4% six-month claim probability, E(claim) $1,800 → expected loss under A = 4% × ($1,800 − $500) = $52; under B = 4% × ($1,800 − $1,000 deductible) = $32. The $20 expected-loss gap is well under the $72 premium, so on pure EV B wins.
    - But EV ignores two real-world frictions: liquidity and the 0/1 nature of a single bad claim.

  3. Liquidity test (the part that matters more than EV)

  Ask: if a covered event happened tomorrow, could you write a check for the B deductible within 30 days without disrupting other goals?
    - $1,500 cash readily accessible in checking/HYSA, no balance on a high-utilization card, no upcoming large outflows within the next month → B's deductible exposure is tolerable; the $72 is real money.
    - $1,500 would require moving money from a long-term bucket, opening a 0% APR card, or delaying another planned expense → A is the right answer; the lower deductibles are worth $72 because the claim is a cash-flow event, not just a math event.
    - The collision case is the binding one: a $1,500 hit during a month with rent, Kibo's vet visit, and a household move is a different animal than the same hit in a quiet month.

  This is the test that should override the EV calculation, not a generic "cheaper premium wins."

  4. Rental-coverage value (the part you've been asked to price)

  Rental coverage only matters if your car is undriveable after a covered claim. Quantify it as:
    - Typical repair time after a not-total collision: 2–4 weeks
    - Daily rental cost in Austin for a comparable class: $45–$70/day
    - Rental reimbursement sublimit on these policies is usually $30–$50/day up to a max number of days (often 30). Confirm the exact cap on your dec page.
    - Out-of-pocket rental cost if you paid cash for 14 days at $55/day = $770.

  So the rental-reimbursement value to A is up to ~$770 of avoided expense, but only if:
    a. You don't have a reliable same-day backup car (Sam's car counts if it's actually available most days), AND
    b. You'd otherwise rent rather than skip driving for 2+ weeks

  If Sam's car is the de facto backup and you can absorb 2–4 weeks of one-car logistics without renting, rental coverage has near-zero realized value to you, and A is paying $72 purely for the deductible delta. If you genuinely have no backup or the repair will leave you stranded for work commutes, A's rental endorsement is doing real work and the $72 looks cheap.

  5. The decision rule

  Choose B if all three are true:
    - You can write $1,500 from liquid savings within 30 days without strain
    - Sam's car (or another household car) is a reliable same-day backup
    - You can absorb 2–4 weeks of one-car logistics without paying for a rental out of pocket

  Choose A if any one of these fails:
    - Liquidity is tight enough that a $1,500 surprise would force trade-offs
    - No reliable backup car, or one-car logistics would require renting
    - You want a single bad claim to be a $500 or $750 problem rather than a $1,500 one

  If you're between those poles, the tiebreaker is vehicle value: if the car is worth materially more than $5,000 and you'd repair rather than total-loss it, A's lower collision deductible is worth more than $72. If it's worth less than ~$3,500, the higher collision deductible barely matters because the insurer will total it either way and pay ACV; in that case B is fine on the collision line and the whole question reduces to liquidity + rental value.

  Bottom line: the right answer is conditional on (a) can you actually access $1,500 quickly, and (b) is rental coverage a redundant endorsement or a real one. The $72 premium difference is small relative to either of those two facts, so the framework — not the sticker — should drive the pick.

SAFEST ORDER (with lightning + hail as the deciding risks):

1. Wait out the warning — best option
   The office is a proper lightning shelter. The 4:15–6:30pm window is roughly 2h 15m; stay inside and ride home after the warning has expired and lightning has cleared. You'll still get some wind and rain on the ride, but no frequent lightning and no hail. Four miles on a bike in frequent lightning is the actual hazard here: you're elevated, exposed, often the tallest object in the bike lane, with metal handlebars — the classic cyclist-strike profile.

2. Rideshare now, collect the bike later — solid alternative
   If waiting isn't workable (pets, family, appointment, fatigue, etc.), take a car. A vehicle is a safe lightning shelter and gets you home promptly. Trade-off vs. waiting: you don't have the bike tonight and you have a brief exposure walking to/from the pickup. Still vastly safer than riding into the storm.

3. Leave immediately on the bike — don't do this
   Four exposed miles into frequent lightning plus possible hail is the high-risk option. Cyclists are killed this way; hail adds impact injury and near-zero visibility. No commute is worth it.

One contingency: if the storm is still active at 6:30 (warnings sometimes run long), give it another 20–30 minutes after the last observed lightning over your route before you roll out. Glance at radar (weather.gov or a reliable app) before you leave the building.

Securing the bike in office storage:
"Secured office storage" already covers the main protections — indoor, controlled access, weather-sheltered. What you mainly need is theft resistance and traceability:
  - Use your own U-lock or heavy chain in addition to whatever the facility provides. Lock the frame and at least one wheel to the rack.
  - If your wheels or saddle are quick-release, swap to locking skewers/bolts for the overnight, or take the quick-release-able parts with you — theft from shared indoor bike rooms is real.
  - Photograph the bike, the lock position, and the exact rack/location (floor, rack number, nearest wall marker). Makes tomorrow's retrieval faster and is your insurance record.
  - Note the building's access hours for retrieval so you don't show up before doors open.

Retrieving it:
  - Go during building access hours with your lock key/combination.
  - If you need the bike for tomorrow's commute home, the cleanest play is rideshare home tonight, then rideshare/transit in tomorrow morning and bike home from there. (Most transit buses have front racks if you'd rather not rideshare twice.)
  - Quick check before the ride home: confirm the warning has actually cleared on radar, not just hit 6:30 on the clock.

If the picture changes mid-window — warning expands, hard reason you can't stay, visible structural damage on your route — the rideshare option flips from fallback to default.

Holds aren't delivery failures because they sit at a different layer of the system. The single path being healthy answers one question — "when we attempt to send, does it get there?" — and holds aren't about that question at all.

A hold means "permission to attempt has not been granted," not "attempt failed." Different state, different remediation, different downstream behavior:

- **Failure** says: the path tried and was blocked. Retry, fix the path, escalate to engineering.
- **Hold** says: we've deliberately declined to try. Retry would be a permission violation, not a robustness signal.

Why holds still exist on a healthy path:

1. **Permission precedes delivery.** Even with one working path, we still gate on contact-level authorization (consent state, eligibility, suppression rules). Path-health ≠ send-permission.
2. **Freshness ≠ send perm.** A record being current tells us the connector can read it; it doesn't tell us we're cleared to write to that contact. Connector readiness is upstream of, not equivalent to, contact permission.
3. **Fail-closed needs a state.** When the underlying source is stale or conflicting, the only safe move is to stop — and "stop" has to be observable as its own state, not flattened into "the path failed." Otherwise you can't tell apart "we chose not to send" from "we tried and couldn't."
4. **Different owner, different action.** Failures route to path/engineering work. Holds route to permission/operational work (re-verify consent, wait on eligibility, resolve conflicting state). Merging them collapses two queues into one and breaks the routing.

Concretely: if a hold got retried as if it were a failure, you'd attempt to deliver to contacts we have no current permission to send to. That's the harm the hold state is there to prevent — not a path problem, a governance problem.

So the framing "single path is healthy → no holds needed" assumes holds are a symptom of path sickness. They're not. They're a symptom of permission not being settled, which is orthogonal to whether the path works.

Three distinctions worth keeping separate:

1.  Intermediate fail-closed check vs. unique evaluated decision.
    A fail-closed check is an early guard: when a prerequisite is missing, it stops the path without producing a customer-facing result. A unique decision is the single terminal outcome (send / suppress / hold) for a contact-field pair in a window. The check never decides; the decision does.

2.  A hold is the intended result when required state is stale, unresolved, or conflicting.
    Fail-closed on stale or conflicting state is by design. The hold is the system doing the right thing — not a defect to clear and not a queue to drain on autopilot.

3.  Holds are neither final outcomes nor delivery failures.
    A hold is an internal non-decision pending resolution: no message is attempted, so there is nothing to deliver and nothing to bounce. It is distinct from a settled suppression and distinct from a true send-time failure.

What a hold is not:
    Not harmless noise — each one is a contact we couldn't safely reach this cycle.
    Not a customer-facing send — customers never observe a hold.

Venue reminder

The fix is to work inside what is allowed: brushes, palettes, painter's tape, clips, personal rinse containers, paper, boards, and protective sleeves. Compact, low-mess substitutes

For soft dampening (the spray-bottle role on the rainy doorway):
1. Wide flat or mop brush pre-dampener. Load from your rinse jar, one firm blot on a paper towel, then sweep a single even pass across the area you want damp. Gives a uniform, controlled wet zone with no aerosol and no extra container.
2. Damp paper-towel pad. Fold a towel into a small pad, dip and wring hard so it is just barely moist, press onto the sheet for 5–10 seconds. Good for a localized wet-into-wet sky strip above the doorway.
3. Brush-flick droplets. Load a brush, hold it over the sheet, tap the ferrule with a finger to release a fine scatter. Useful for the speckled texture of rain on a step or pane, and stays inside the venue's allowed-supply list.

For reserved whites (the masking-fluid role on rain streaks, doorframe edges, hardware highlights):
1. Painter's tape strips torn to shape. Already allowed and already in your kit. Best for the doorway verticals and any straight rain lines; press down with a fingernail, paint up to the edge, lift while the wash is just damp to protect the paper.
2. White crayon or candle resist. Draw the rain streaks lightly first, then paint over them; the wax pushes the wash away. No bottle, no cleanup, no rubber pickup risk, and no fiber lift on the cotton sheet.
3. Negative painting. Leave rain streaks as paper white while you build the doorway and sky around them. Works whenever the paper's white is bright enough to read as rain on its own.
4. Lift-out with a thirsty brush. While the sky wash is still damp, drag a clean damp brush along the streak lines to pull pigment back up. Single touch, no return — matches your usual one-touch rule.
5. Final white accent. A white gel pen or a touch of white gouache applied last on the driest pass covers any streaks you forgot to reserve. No bottle, no drying wait, and stays sealed in a tin.

Critique of the default readout order, then the recommended sequence.

WHAT GOES WRONG WITH THE COMMON ORDERING

The typical readout opens with the question, walks through methodology, lands on a result, and only then names the denominator and decision surface. Three failure modes follow:

  1. The denominator arrives after the reader has already formed a take. "We saw a 17% lift" reads as evidence; "17% lift over a 7-decision denominator, 5 of which were governed holds" reads as a story. The framing block (Owen's 2/27 aid) catches this only when he remembers to use it; when it gets buried in section 2, Priya is debating the conclusion before she knows what the conclusion is allowed to mean.

  2. Evidence boundaries slip in next to results rather than preceding them. Window, causal-vs-descriptive, and feasibility show up in footnotes where they function as caveats instead of bounds. A result that is correctly labeled descriptive often sounds prescriptive because the boundary sat two paragraphs below it.

  3. Intermediate holds collapse into final outcomes. A governed hold, a stale-suppression hold, and an active-CS-suppression hold look like the same thing in a flat results table. Priya cannot tell which of these is an operating decision waiting on her, which is a system state that resolves itself, and which is a contested classification that needs her judgment. The decision path blurs.

  4. Disputed semantics and cross-surface consequences get absorbed into the routine narrative. "We treated the September window as separate from the November hypothesis" sounds like a methodology note; it is actually a release-boundary claim that should not be made in routine prose. Same for executive phrasing like "stabilized" or "validated" — these belong to Riley's lane, not Owen's.

RECOMMENDED SEQUENCE (OWEN-OWNED, PRIYA-DECISION-PATH)

Six blocks, in this order. Each block is a single-paragraph read except where noted. Owen owns 1–5; block 6 is the only one that names Riley as a routing target.

  1. Scope and unit of analysis (Owen, 1 short paragraph)
     Named cohort, named evidence window, named population. No result yet.

  2. Unique-decision denominator (Owen, 1 line + table)
     The count of decisions in the window, before any holds are applied. Sub-rows split:
       - active / in-window decisions
       - governed holds (field-specific reason + age + owner)
       - stale or conflicting inputs (fail-closed, not released)
       - excluded populations with reason
     The headline number is the unique-decision denominator. Everything downstream is denominated against it.

  3. Evidence boundaries (Owen, 1 short paragraph)
     Three explicit statements:
       - window boundaries (start, end, any post-cutoff corrections still pending)
       - causal vs descriptive (one sentence; default is descriptive unless a controlled comparison is named)
       - feasibility assumptions that, if false, would change the conclusion
     These are stated, not footnoted. If any of these changes, the conclusion is reconsidered — that contract is named here.

  4. Observed counts and effect size, denominated (Owen, table + 1 paragraph)
     Numbers expressed as fraction of the unique-decision denominator from block 2. Effect size stated before any directional language.

  5. Operating consequence and exception pattern, with holds separated (Owen, 2 short paragraphs)
     Two distinct sub-blocks:
       (a) What the supported result or exception pattern means for the existing operating boundary — phrased as "this leaves X unchanged," "this tightens Y," or "this does not change Z."
       (b) Intermediate holds vs final outcomes, kept in separate lines:
           - Intermediate holds: governed-field holds (named field), stale-input holds, active-CS-suppression holds. Each row has reason, age, owner, and resolution path. None of these are decisions waiting on Priya unless flagged.
           - Final outcomes: the only items in this list are decisions that change an operating boundary or commit to a release direction.
     If a final-outcome row touches disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, executive language, customer-correction, or incident-stop, Owen flags it here as "escalation candidate" and stops. He does not characterize the disputed part.

  6. Decision path (Owen → Priya)
     Three lines, exactly:
       (a) Decisions Owen is closing in routine lane (no action).
       (b) Decisions that need Priya's call, framed as a question with the bounded evidence in one sentence each.
       (c) Items routed to Riley: disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, executive claims, customer corrections, incident stops. Named, not paraphrased.

WHERE THIS PUTS EACH OWNER

  Owen: blocks 1–5, plus block 6(a) and 6(b). He states the question, the bounded evidence, and the operating consequence. He does not interpret disputed semantics, does not frame cross-surface effects, does not write executive claims.

  Priya: receives block 6(b) with the bounded evidence above it. Her job is the decision, not the interpretation. The denominator in block 2 and the boundaries in block 3 are the only things she needs to read before deciding.

  Riley: receives block 6(c) escalations and the full readout for context. Routes disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, customer-correction, incident-stop, and executive-language calls. Does not rewrite Owen's blocks.

  Ines (when messaging-state or lifecycle is in scope): her section sits inside block 5(a), before Owen's operating-consequence paragraph. Same rules — denominator and boundaries first, consequence second, no disputed-semantics interpretation.

WHAT TO REMOVE FROM THE ROUTINE READOUT

  - Methodology paragraphs that belong in a brief, not a readout.
  - Forecast or revenue language of any kind.
  - First-significance framed as ship-readiness.
  - Disputed-semantics interpretation in routine prose (move to Riley escalation block).
  - Cross-surface consequence claims ("this also affects X team's metric") outside of block 6(c).

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE

  - Owen still owns the readout shape and examples.
  - Ines still owns the messaging-state and lifecycle-risk section within block 5.
  - Priya still owns the governance / release-direction decision.
  - Daniela still owns engineering, schema, alarms, rollback.
  - Riley still owns disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, customer corrections, incident-stop, executive claims.

Kit (fits in a small zip pouch, ~6×9 in):
- 7 sheets acid-free, unbuffered archival tissue, cut ~1/4 in larger than the largest photo on every side
- 2 sheets acid-free card stock or rag board, same footprint as the tissue
- 6 thin tissue slips (~1 in wide × photo height), pre-numbered 1–6 in soft pencil (#2 or softer), kept face-down so the pencil only touches slips, never photos
- 1 soft pencil
- 1 large archival folder or acid-free envelope, big enough to hold the flat bundle

Pack procedure (one pass, photos stay face-down the whole time):
1. Clean, dry, flat surface. Lay down: bottom board, then one full tissue sheet.
2. Take the top photo from the box and lay it face-down on the tissue. Image touches tissue; back faces up.
3. Place slip "1" on the photo's back, near the top edge, away from any central area where writing would sit.
4. Lay a full tissue sheet over the photo's back — this is what covers any handwriting.
5. Lay photo 2 face-down on that tissue. Slip 2 on its back. Tissue. Photo 3 face-down. Continue until photo 6.
6. After photo 6: slip 6 on its back, one last full tissue sheet, then the top board.
7. Stack reads bottom-up: board / tissue / P1 / slip1 / tissue / P2 / slip2 / … / P6 / slip6 / tissue / board. The slips and the stack order together give you the original sequence; the photos themselves are unmarked.
8. Slide the bundle into the archival folder, flat. Tuck the folder in the carry-on between soft layers (folded sweater, etc.), away from liquids and the overhead vent's direct airflow.

Provenance without identifying content:
- The slips encode only sequence, not who or when.
- Mom can add one short provenance line on a small slip tucked at the front of the bundle before it goes into the folder, e.g., "From [box label]; single face-up stack; pulled top to bottom." Procedural only — no names, no dates, no reading of any back-of-photo writing.

Writing protection:
- The photo with handwriting sits face-down with a full tissue sheet directly over the back. No adjacent photo, board, or printed paper touches the writing surface. The numbered slip on that photo's back sits at the edge/margin, not over the written area.
- Don't reorient the bundle once built; the face-down side is now the protected side.

Don'ts:
- No pens, ballpoint, or hard pencil anywhere near the photo surfaces. Pencil lives on the slips only.
- No rubber bands, paper clips, staples, tape, or adhesive on or near the photos.
- No glassine for long storage (it can stick over time), and no PVC sleeves — polyethylene, polypropylene, or polyester/Mylar only.
- No checked baggage. Carry-on, with mom, the whole trip.
- At security: she can ask for a hand inspection if she wants to skip the conveyor x-ray; modern carry-on scanners are low-dose and generally fine for a single pass, but a hand check is allowed and removes the question entirely.

Open at home on a clean flat surface, lift the top board and each tissue/slip layer in the same order mom built it, and the sequence and provenance reconstruct without anyone having to read the photos before the visit.

Interpretation of the three mixes (from the July 12 rainy-doorway test):

  Blue + brown
    The doorway edge held its value separation all the way through drying. The
    brown carries warmth without the chroma push of a primary red, so the warm
    edge reads as a tonal step (half-step darker) rather than as a competing
    hue. This is the mix that lets the edge stay quiet.

  Blue + red
    Lively while wet because red is high-chroma, but the eye followed the warm
    into the street wash instead of stopping at the edge. The doorway became
    part of a larger warm-cool argument instead of being a single preserved
    boundary. Useful if you wanted the street to lead, not what you want here.

  Three-pigment mix (blue + red + brown)
    Gave the darkest, most dramatic rain interruption in the wet pass, but
    rewetting reactivated all three at once and the doorway value collapsed
    into the street. Three pigments in one wash means more granulation, more
    settling, and no clean place for the edge to hold its separation under
    any later damp pass.

Recommended setup for the next personal study:

  Hold constant
    Paper (140 lb cold press, one quarter sheet)
    Brush condition (one firm blot, per your standing rule)
    Brush load and pigment ratio (same blue + brown ratio that held on 7/12)
    Wash angle and board position
    Drying conditions (no fan, no rewetting during the pass)

  Composition rule
    The warm doorway edge is the one unresolved boundary. Everything else
    can finish; this edge stays as a value step only, not as added pigment.

  The one variable to isolate
    Wet-stage value gap. Lay the cool street wash first, then bring the warm
    edge in at four discrete test points along the same doorway line:
      A  one step darker than the dried street target
      B  half a step darker
      C  matched wet value (so it dries lighter, creating the gap by drying)
      D  one step lighter wet (control: should lose the edge)

  Read the sheet after full drying under the same light you will judge the
  finished study by. The strip that still shows a clear value step from the
  cool wash, without the warm edge reading as a color event, is your target
  wet-stage gap. That is the controlled answer the 7/12 test was pointing at:
  preserve the edge by how much darker you start, not by adding warmth later.

  One touch hold at 20 seconds on the warm edge, no return after dull, full
  dry before any later pass. If you want a second sheet later, vary only the
  blue + brown ratio; everything else stays fixed.

ONE-PAN FARRO SKILLET WITH EGGS
(~22 min hands-on, plenty of margin inside your 45)

PREP (do while the skillet warms):
  Halve a generous handful of cherry tomatoes
  Cut kernels off 1-2 ears of corn
  Slice 3-4 scallions, whites and greens in separate piles
  Chop a small handful of basil (or basil + chives — that's the July pairing for these tomatoes)
  Crack 4-6 eggs into a small bowl so they pour fast when the moment comes

COOK:
  0:00  Skillet over medium-high, 2 Tbsp olive oil
  0:03  Add scallion whites + corn. Sear 4-5 min until the corn picks up real char spots
  0:08  Add tomatoes + a big pinch of salt. Cook 2-3 min until they slump and release their juice
  0:11  Stir in ~2 cups cooked farro. Heat through 2-3 min. Taste and adjust salt
  0:14  Make 4-6 shallow wells in the farro. Slide an egg into each. Salt + pepper the eggs
  0:16  Cover (lid or a sheet of foil), drop heat to medium-low. Cook 4-6 min — whites set, yolks still soft
  0:22  Off heat. Hit it with scallion greens, basil, cracked pepper, chili flake. Done.

SERVE straight from the skillet. Bread on the side if you've got it; a squeeze of lemon at the end is the only thing that makes it better.

FOOD-SAFETY TRIAGE — POST-OUTAGE (4h 5min, noon–4:05pm)

GOVERNING FACTS

  - Fridge held closed, thermometer now 44°F (4°F above the 40°F safety floor)
  - Freezer items still feel solid — freezer held
  - No odor, no equipment fault
  - You are just past the USDA 4-hour boundary; thermometer reading lags actual food-peak temperature

CORE UNCERTAINTY TO WEIGHT

  Treat all perishable fridge food as if it spent the full window in the 40–140°F danger zone. Bacteria that cause foodborne illness (Salmonella, Listeria, Staph, Bacillus cereus from cooked starches) often produce no odor, no slime, no visible change. Do not taste or sniff as a decision method.

SEQUENCE (do in this order)

  1. Reset the clock. Don't open the fridge again to "think about it." Every extra open adds warm-air time and weakens the case for keeping anything borderline.
  2. Bag and remove the discard list now. Out of the house — not back into the fridge.
  3. Wipe any thawed-liquid spills with mild soap-water. Residual moisture is a faster bacterial growth surface than dry.
  4. Salvage the keep-list, mark it "use within 24 hours."
  5. Triage the freezer (see below).
  6. Verify the fridge returns below 40°F by ~7pm. If it doesn't, equipment fault from the outage — service call before restocking.

DISCARD (perishable, above 40°F for >4 hours)

  - Raw or cooked meat, poultry, fish, shellfish
  - Eggs (raw and hard-cooked), egg dishes, custards, puddings
  - Milk, cream, yogurt, soft cheeses (cream cheese, ricotta, fresh mozzarella, brie, queso fresco, cottage cheese)
  - Lunch meats, hot dogs, deli meats, pre-cooked sausages, pâté
  - Cooked leftovers, casseroles, soups, stews, gravies, broth
  - Salads with mayo/egg/dairy (potato, coleslaw, tuna, pasta, chicken)
  - Cut melons, cut leafy greens, pre-cut fruit/veg, opened juice
  - Hummus, salsa, opened jarred refrigerated sauces, opened mayo, ranch, creamy dressings
  - Cooked rice, cooked pasta, cooked grains, cooked potatoes held cold
  - Cream-filled pastries, cheesecake
  - Tofu, tempeh, plant-based meats (these behave like animal protein in the danger zone)

COOL PROMPTLY / KEEP (use within ~24 hours or freeze now)

  - Whole fruits (apples, oranges, bananas, whole berries, citrus)
  - Whole vegetables (potatoes, onions, carrots, cabbage, squash, garlic, intact cucumbers, peppers)
  - Hard/aged cheeses (cheddar, parmesan, romano, grana padano) — trim any softened surface; use within days
  - Butter — generally safe; if very soft, refrigerate and use soon
  - Whole uncut melons — fine
  - Acidic opened condiments (mustard, ketchup, jam, jelly, honey, vinegar-based hot sauce, soy sauce)
  - Pickles, olives in brine, sauerkraut — stable
  - Bread, crackers, tortillas, dry goods — never a refrigeration safety item
  - Unopened shelf-stable cans/jars/pouches — fine regardless
  - Whole spices, salt, sugar, properly stored oils — fine

FREEZER TRIAGE

  - Solid, icy, or visible crystals → safe to refreeze. Expect quality loss (freezer burn, texture change, dairy separation). For raw meat in this state, cook first, then freeze cooked portions if you want best results.
  - Thawed but still cold to touch (under 40°F) → cook immediately. Do not refreeze raw.
  - Thawed and at room temperature → apply the fridge discard list to whatever they were.

WHERE TO TREAT UNCERTAINTY CAUTIOUSLY

  1. Eggs in shell — borderline. USDA = discard after 4 hours above 40°F; you are just past it. Conservative call: discard. If you keep them, crack into a clean bowl, smell, and cook fully today — no undercooked runny yolks.
  2. Hard cheese with a softened rind — salvageable, but only if you'll actually use it within ~3 days. Otherwise treat as borderline.
  3. Anything pre-cut, pre-washed, or pre-cooked that has been opened — higher starting bacterial load than whole produce. Default discard.
  4. Cooked grains/rice/pasta — these are the silent failures. Bacillus cereus toxin is heat-stable; reheating kills the bacteria but not the toxin. If you cooked any Tue/Wed/Thu and they sat through the outage, discard without tasting.
  5. The "does this smell off" question — the fact that you're asking is the answer. Discard.
  6. Kibo — water available, cool interior room is fine. Note that cats don't self-regulate by drinking more when warm, so ambient temperature is the lever, not intake. Not a food-safety item but a separate welfare check; he should be OK through the evening.

RECOVERY CHECK (next 2–3 hours)

  - Fridge thermometer should drop back below 40°F by ~7pm
  - Don't load the doors with new warm items
  - Don't open repeatedly
  - A few clean water bottles placed inside now add thermal mass and help the empty space hold temp
  - If thermometer still >40°F by 7pm, assume compressor fault from the surge/outage → service call before restocking

This is the conservative USDA/FDA 4-hour-at-40°F template applied with extra margin for the boundary case and the thermometer-lag uncertainty. If you want a tighter interpretation on any specific category (e.g., willing to keep eggs in shell and test-cook them), tell me which and I'll recalibrate.

Here's the structure I'd recommend.

Goal: leadership view shows counts and conclusions; reviewers can independently verify that holds and reevaluations aren't double-counted; no customer-linked or record-level identifiers in the main view; raw evidence lives in a restricted appendix.

Three-layer structure

Layer 1 — Leadership deck (main view, ~6–8 slides)

Slide 1: Executive takeaway. One sentence, sign-off only. Cite the agreed metric, cohort window, and snapshot date.

Slide 2: Framing block (mandatory, before any numbers). Scope/cohort, denominator + window, causal-vs-descriptive, feasibility.

Slide 3: Decisions evaluated and coverage dates. Unique-decision denominator, broken down by cohort + evaluation window. No account IDs.

Slide 4: Decisions proceeding or suppressed under current state. Two stacks: proceed (Proceed decisions), suppressed (active-CS suppressions). Distinct rows; never summed into a single "non-held" bucket.

Slide 5: Field-specific holds and reasons. One row per governed field, with count and the freshness/transport reason. No account IDs, no source-table IDs.

Slide 6: Hold age, source owner, disposition. Min/median/max hold age; source owner label (CS, billing, admin-graph, etc.); pending-fresh-check vs reevaluated-and-still-held. Reevaluation history shown as a separate distribution, not folded into "held".

Slide 7: Cross-view agreement and customer-correction check. Whether governed-field stack matches Ines's messaging-state stack and the legacy nightly's view. Discrepancies named, not hidden. Customer corrections during the window listed by field, not by account.

Slide 8: Source-reliability patterns and escalations. Patterns Owen sees, items routed to you (Riley).

Layer 2 — Restricted appendix (linked from deck, separate doc, restricted access)

Appendix A: Raw ledger (Owen's authoring). One row per decision. This is the only place account/customer identifiers appear. Columns: decision_id, customer_id (restricted), cohort, evaluation_date, governed_field_states, source_owner, freshness_timestamp, decision (Proceed / Suppress / Hold), hold_reason, reevaluation_history (array of timestamps + source-check results), cross-surface linkage flag.

Appendix B: Hold and reevaluation audit log. For every held decision, the sequence: held_at → freshness re-check timestamps → source_owner check → reevaluation_outcome (released, still-held, escalated). This is what makes double-counting verifiable: a decision held on day 3, reevaluated on day 5, and still held on day 10 should appear once in the hold count and once per reevaluation event in the reevaluation log, with the two linked by decision_id.

Appendix C: Cross-view reconciliation. Governed-field ledger vs Ines's messaging-state ledger vs legacy nightly. Differences itemized with decision_id and reconciled disposition.

Appendix D: Customer-correction log. Customer ID + field + before/after, only here.

Layer 3 — Source ledger (Owen's owned artifact, the append-only original)

Double-counting protection — the four rules

1. Disjoint categories at the decision level. Every unique decision has exactly one final state at snapshot (Proceed, Suppress, or Held). Holds and reevaluations are not alternative states — reevaluations are events on a held decision. Leadership counts add the disjoint states; the audit log reconciles event counts.

3. Hold age is computed per unique decision. If a decision is held, reevaluated, still-held, and reevaluated again, it's one held decision with an age computed from initial hold timestamp, not a fresh hold each pass.

4. Cross-view reconciliation is an explicit pass, not a checkmark. Slide 7 names any disagreement between Owen's governed-field stack, Ines's messaging-state stack, and the legacy nightly. Silently agreeing is not allowed; explicit agreement is.

- Per-account narratives

Your read is right — this is a value problem, not a chroma problem, so the fix lives in moisture and edge, not in the palette. The warm edge is heading toward the same middle value as the cool wash beside it; if you add orange you'll just brighten a boundary that's already about to disappear into the wash.

Working window
Both areas need to be at the dull stage — sheen gone, paper cool to the touch, no puddling. That's your edit window. Wet = bloom and feather into the warm edge. Bone dry = no take, no lift, and any stroke sits on top as a stain rather than a value plane. Dull is the only stage where a 1-touch move actually integrates.

The controlled move (pick one, not both)

Path A — deepen the warm edge without changing its hue:
Reload the same warm mix from the swatch, but at a higher pigment-to-water ratio so it's a darker value of the same color, not a more saturated one. One stroke along the interior edge only. 20-second hold, no working. The chroma stays where it is; only the value drops, so when the cool side finishes drying to middle, the warm edge sits one step lower and reads as a distinct plane.

Path B — lift value on the cool side adjacent to the edge:
Damp clean brush, one firm blot, then a single light-to-broad pass along the doorway/street wash just inside the boundary. This raises the cool wash's value locally, so the warm edge wins the comparison without being touched. Useful if you want to keep the warm mix untouched for reference.

Edge handling
At the boundary, hold a hard edge, not a soft one. A soft edge at this stage is what blended the two values together in the first place — softening again will just re-flatten the separation you're trying to recover. Hard edge on the cool side, hard edge on the warm side, value gap between them. The edge itself doesn't need to be a finished line; it just needs to not be wetted back into a gradient.

Drying protocol
Lay the stroke, hold 20 seconds without going back in. One touch. If the paper has gone dull under your hand while you worked, stop — return after dull is what causes bloom and a muddy seam. Let the whole thing dry flat and undisturbed.

Stop condition for this study
Don't follow with a second pass yet. Let it dry fully, then read the value jump at bone-dry state, which is the only state that tells you whether the separation actually held. If the warm edge still flattens at full dry, the move needed was one value step deeper (Path A) or a broader lift (Path B), not another application — and you'll see that on the dried study, not while it's damp.

  Three swatches, blue+brown at increasing depth steps beside a small

Three pairings to pick from — all use descriptive language (no "launch/beta/holdout"), keep policy out of the headline, and put the bounded cadence in the subhead without making it sound like a gate:

Option 1 — most direct
Headline: Self-serve setup is open
Subhead: We onboard in small batches each week. Start when capacity allows — we'll confirm your spot and walk you through each step.

Option 2 — most inviting lead
Headline: Set up your account, at your pace
Subhead: Self-serve setup opens as space allows. We'll let you know when a spot is ready and guide you from there.

Option 3 — shortest, headline does less
Headline: Self-serve setup
Subhead: New spots open weekly as capacity allows. Start when you're ready — we'll confirm and guide you through.

Notes on the trade-offs:
- Option 1 leads with availability, which is the truest read of operational state and easiest to keep accurate week-to-week. Good if the page already has "Start setup" as the primary CTA.
- Option 2 is warmer but asks the visitor to do a beat of inference ("open as space allows") before the CTA click. Better if the page is aimed at people still deciding.
- Option 3 is the cleanest if a product surface already says "Setup" prominently above the fold — the subhead just qualifies what "setup" means here.

All three avoid implying automatic admission (the "we'll confirm" / "as space allows" framing does that work) and stop short of policy language (no waitlist mechanics, no SLAs, no cohort-window specifics).
