The support-effort distribution from the 52-workspace mature Helio Start cohort — 684 validated post-admission product-support minutes across 21 contacted workspaces, with 31 workspaces recording zero minutes and 8 workspaces driving 472 of those minutes — can be read in three layers. Here is each layer held apart.

WHAT THE DISTRIBUTION DEMONSTRATES (operational signal)

  Shape is heavy-tailed, not uniform.
    - 59.6% of the cohort (31/52) had zero post-admission contact. Typical
      customer-success load in this organic cohort is therefore low in the
      unconditional sense: 13.15 minutes per workspace across the full
      denominator.
    - 15.4% of the cohort (8/52) drove 69.0% of post-admission minutes
      (472/684), averaging ~59 minutes each.
    - The remaining 13 contacted workspaces averaged 16.31 minutes each
      and accounted for the residual 212 minutes.

  The heavy tail is mechanically separable, not monolithic.
    - 4 of the 8 were authority/access blockers (238 minutes, customer-side
      environment pole, ~4.0 business-day median resolution, 8 repeat
      contacts).
    - 3 were product-guidance cases (174 minutes, ~1.6-day median, 4 repeat
      contacts).
    - 1 was a mixed data-import case (60 minutes).
    The 4/3/1 split tells us the tail is not a single failure mode. It is a
    mix of customer-side environment delays and product-side guidance gaps,
    and these respond to different fixes (admin/IT routing vs. docs/UX).

  No manual-billing, import-help, or migration handoffs entered the
    admitted path. The excluded categories — 11 pre-admission connector-
    authority contacts and all billing contacts — were tracked separately
    and not folded into the 684 minutes. The number is therefore a clean
    post-admission product-support figure, not a mixed-channel total.

WHAT THE DISTRIBUTION DOES NOT DEMONSTRATE (its limitations)

  Magnitude claims about the 8-workspace breakdown are not reliable.
    - 4/3/1 is a direction statement; means and standard deviations across
      three observations are not. Per-workspace values and ranges are the
      honest reporting unit, not point estimates of "the" authority-burden.

  Day-90 statuses are point-in-time. The 39 paid-active / 7 canceled /
    4 past-due / 2 billing-hold partition is a separate measure, not a
    retension curve. Post-snapshot reactivations belong in exception
    review, not in revising the minutes.

  The distribution is for an organic cohort on a settled self-serve
    support channel. It measures what contacted workspaces cost in that
    channel; it does not measure what non-contacted workspaces would cost
    if acquisition velocity changed their mix, and it does not measure
    what a paid channel would generate by way of incremental contacts.

  The 684 minutes exclude pre-admission connector help and billing by
    design. That is correct for the revisit-gate definition, but it means
    this number cannot be lifted into a "total CS cost per workspace"
    line — the pre-admission and billing tracks are separate and not yet
    joined here.

WHAT THE DISTRIBUTION DOES NOT AUTHORIZE (paid-acquisition / unit-economics)

  Nothing here unlocks a paid-acquisition claim. The revisit gate that
  was settled on 2024-08-02 requires three measures presented together
  at the account level, with no combined denominator or arithmetic join:
    - mature day-90 retention classification
    - refund-adjusted cash joined to workspaces
    - post-admission support effort per admitted workspace
  First-paid, activation, and paid-active counts alone — and support
  minutes alone — are explicitly insufficient substitutes.

  No CAC, payback, LTV/CAC, or gross-margin figure can be derived from
  this distribution. The numerator has no paid-media spend, no
  comparator cohort, and no holdout. The 8-workspace concentration
  cannot be repurposed into a staffing recommendation, a paid-channel
  readiness statement, or a forecast input. The 2024-09-03 slide
  wording ("onboarding is broken, need staffing before scaling paid
  acquisition") was declined for exactly this reason: descriptive data
  turned into a conclusion the data does not support.

  The $364.62 per-workspace cash-yield figure (Marcus Vail's
  2024-08-19 proposal) is not established by this distribution either.
  It is a separate arithmetic that lives on the cash side, not the
  support side, and it does not become a CAC ceiling, a bid ceiling, or
  a paid-test basis even after the support minutes are read.

WHAT WE STILL CANNOT CONCLUDE WITHOUT REFUND-ADJUSTED CASH JOINED

  Until the support minutes are joined to refund-adjusted cash at the
  workspace_id level, the economic interpretation of this distribution
  remains gapped. Specifically, we cannot conclude:

    1. Whether the 8 heavy-tail workspaces are net-positive or net-
       negative on cash. They account for ~69% of support minutes but
       their individual cash contribution is not yet attributed. The
       tail could be subsidized, neutral, or upside-down — and we do
       not know which without the join.

    2. Whether the 31 zero-contact workspaces carry enough cash to
       absorb the average support cost across the cohort. The 13.15
       minutes/workspace average is meaningful only relative to a cash
       denominator, which is what the join supplies.

    3. Whether a structural per-customer support cost exists that is
       suitable as a fixed denominator in a future acquisition model.
       The revisit gate's stated purpose for measuring support-effort
       concentration was exactly this — to learn whether paid
       acquisition would amplify a burden concentrated in a few
       workspaces, or whether a per-customer cost could anchor a later
       model — and that question cannot be answered from minutes alone.

    4. Any per-workspace support-cost-as-share-of-cash ratio, and
       therefore any statement about whether the support burden is
       proportionate, concentrated-in-losers, or concentrated-in-winners.

    5. Any unit-economics output: no CAC, no payback period, no
       LTV/CAC, no gross margin, no allowable acquisition spend. The
       three later refunds are still pending workspace attribution
       (Owen was asked on 2026-09-13 for invoice ID, customer ID,
       refund date, refund amount, and original settled-payment date
       for each), and no paid-acquisition analysis is to be produced
       from the unmatched aggregate.

    6. Whether the revisit gate is satisfied. The support-effort
       measure is one of three; the other two (mature retention
       status and refund-adjusted cash with workspace attribution)
       have to land before the gate can be evaluated. Today's read
       is therefore partial-by-construction, and the economic read
       stays gated on Finance's refund-to-workspace mappings.

In short: the distribution is honest evidence of a low-burden, heavy-
tailed, mechanically separable support pattern in an organic cohort —
and that is all it is. Anything stronger, and especially anything that
binds support minutes to acquisition cost, payback, or forecast, has
to wait for the cash join.

The 7-minute result is the one worth anchoring on: continuous cool mass *plus* preserved warm edge is the condition you were actually after, and neither the wetter nor the drier condition hit it.

For the next study, the three open variables worth isolating one at a time:

1. **Re-entry wait as the only knob** — same cool wash, same stroke, but try 4 / 5 / 6 / 7 / 8 minutes and see if the transition from "breaks" to "preserves" is a sharp threshold or a gradient. If it's a threshold, you have a usable rule. If it's a gradient, the rule is going to be humidity-dependent and harder to pin.

2. **Rain mark timing only** — lock the cool wash at 7 minutes (your known-good), then vary only when the rain mark goes in: while still damp / tacky / fully dry. You're testing whether the "sits too sharply on top" failure was a wash-timing problem or a rain-timing problem, or both.

3. **Paper absorbency as a confound** — if you have a scrap of the same paper pre-wet and blotted flat, run one of the above against it. The 3-vs-7-minute gap may compress or widen depending on how much water the paper is actually holding, which would explain why verbal advice is unreliable.

Five minutes is a useful probe but not yet a settled working window. The continuity of the cool wash and the clarity of the warm doorway edge both held better than at three minutes, which means the timing is moving in the right direction: the wash is damp enough to take the dark mark as an interruption rather than a pasted-on shape, and the boundary is still being protected by value separation rather than pigment. The small bloom at the entry point is the signal that you haven't quite crossed the bloom threshold yet — it's a "small" bloom, which means the gradient is closing but not closed.

Recommended next study: six minutes. One variable changed, everything else held — same paper, same blue-plus-brown mix, same brush load, same cool-wash continuity goal, same warm-edge goal, dark rain interruption moved from five to six minutes.

Why six rather than four or five-and-a-half:

  Six sits on the existing 3 / 7 / fully-dry ladder as the half-step between your current test and the established seven-minute hold. It's the most informative single move because the five-minute result has already told you the bloom threshold sits somewhere between three and seven. Six is the discriminating point: if it works, you've bracketed the window; if it fails, you've learned that timing alone isn't the controlling variable and the next study has to move elsewhere (brush load or pigment ratio, not timing).

  Four minutes would mostly confirm the gradient direction you already suspect (more bloom) without narrowing the optimum, and a half-minute step at five would just refine a point you've already established isn't the answer.

What to look for at six minutes:

  Entry-point bloom — should be smaller or absent. "Small" at five means the threshold is close; six is the next step toward it.

  Cool-wash continuity — should still hold. Five was already continuous, and the absolute moisture difference between five and six is small.

  Warm doorway edge — should still be clear, because the edge is doing its own work via value separation. Watch specifically for whether the warm pigment starts to lift into the cool field as the wash dries past its working dampness; if it does, that's the edge telling you the window has closed.

  Dark mark character — the new read. At five it integrated as an interruption. At six you want to see whether it still reads as wet-edge or whether it starts to look pasted on, sitting on top of the wash rather than inside it.

How to read the result:

  No bloom, continuity held, edge clear, mark still integrates → six minutes is the new working window, and five was the late-wet edge of it.

  No bloom, but the mark looks pasted or stiff → the useful window is somewhere between five and six, and five is the practical answer if you can compose around a small bloom or budget it into the picture as a feature rather than a defect.

  Bloom still present at six → timing alone is not the controlling lever, and the next study should hold timing at six and revisit brush load or pigment concentration as a separate single-variable change.

One note on "useful working window" as a standard: five minutes gave you a result that's contingent on that morning's drying rate. Six minutes buys you a wider margin against humidity and paper-temperature drift, which is part of what makes a regime worth keeping rather than just a probe worth running.

Short answer: yes — ride in this morning, leave the bike locked at Helio, and don't ride home this afternoon. A 108°F heat index window from 3–7pm puts bike commuting firmly in NWS "Danger" territory for heat exhaustion and heat stroke, and there's no upside to riding through it when the bike can sit safely at the office overnight and come back tomorrow morning in much cooler air.

Here is the conservative breakdown:

Morning ride in
- Get going early. Aim to be on the bike before the temperature climbs — leaving at 6:30–7:00am is meaningfully easier than 8:30am even though the advisory doesn't start until 3pm. Austin pavement and ambient temps rise fast after sunrise in late August.
- Pre-hydrate starting the night before and again 60–90 minutes before you leave: roughly 16–20 oz of water with a pinch of salt or an electrolyte tab. Don't chug; steady sips.
- On the ride: aim for 20–28 oz across the trip, sipping every 10–15 minutes rather than at red lights. Plain water is fine for a sub-hour ride, but if you're sweating heavily, an electrolyte mix (sodium + potassium) is better than water alone — sweat losses at Austin humidity are saltier than people expect.
- Clothing: light color, loose weave, UPF if you have it. Avoid cotton — it holds sweat and stays hot. Light-colored helmet or a light cover under it. UV sunglasses. Sunscreen SPF 30+ on arms, neck, ears, and the back of your calves; reapply at lunch so the afternoon sun through office windows doesn't get you on the way to a rideshare.
- Bring a dry shirt and a small towel for the office. Don't sit in riding kit under AC all afternoon — you'll get chilled and your skin stays salt-crusted.
- At Helio: lock the bike to a secure rack inside the building or to a fixed, camera-visible rack outside. Take the lights, computer, and any quick-release bags with you. Note where it is so tomorrow's ride home is frictionless.

At the office through the afternoon
- Keep drinking on a schedule — 8–12 oz per hour is a reasonable target in AC. It's easy to under-drink indoors after the morning ride, and you'll be starting the day slightly behind.
- A small salty snack at lunch (pretzels, brothy soup, pickle, electrolyte tab in water) helps you replace what the morning ride cost.
- Watch for delayed heat-illness signs later in the day if you under-drank on the ride: headache, dizziness, nausea, sudden fatigue, or stopping sweating. If any of those show up, hydrate, get cool, and sit down — don't push through.

Return trip home
- Do not ride home in the 3–7pm window. 108°F heat index on a bike, even with shade and stops, is a real medical risk for heat exhaustion in under an hour.
- Use a rideshare (Lyft/Uber) from Helio, the company's commuter benefit if you have one, or coordinate with Sam if her route is conveniently close to the office — though given your low-noise cadence with her, I'd default to a rideshare and only ask if it's genuinely on her way.
- If a rideshare isn't workable and Helio is genuinely unreachable by transit either, ride only after 8pm when the index has dropped, and even then treat it as an emergency option — short it, hydrate heavily before and during, wear light colors, and stop at any shade break for 5–10 minutes.
- The cleanest move: ride the bike home tomorrow morning at the same time you'd ride in today. Overnight in the office rack is a non-issue.

Tomorrow morning
- Same hydration protocol as today. The bike comes home in cooler air, no advisory, no pressure.

One thing worth flagging: if you end up under-hydrated or overheated by this evening, take it as data — the morning protocol worked or it didn't, and you can tune the pre-ride fluid + electrolyte load for next time. None of this is a one-off; Tuesday rides in late August in Austin are going to keep producing these advisories through September, so locking in a "ride in early, leave bike, rideshare home on advisory days" pattern as a standing rule is reasonable if this week goes smoothly.

Conservative framing: you're testing one variable (duration on one slot), so hold everything else fixed — same shoes, same lake-trail surface, same warm-up, same easy pace ceiling, same ankle/calf strengthening. Don't add load on a second axis in the same week.

Which slot gets the 35 (spacing)
  Extend the session with the longer recovery runway before your second run. If your two days are e.g. Tue/Thu, extend Tue (1-day buffer → Thu). If Mon/Fri, extend Mon (3-day buffer → Fri). You want maximum buffer between the test and the recovery-confirmation slot. Keep the days nonconsecutive as they already are.

Effort and structure of the 35
  Easy means easy — conversational pace, the same effort the 30s have been at. Do not let the extra 5 minutes drift pace upward; if anything, hold pace slightly more conservatively than the 30s, since the new variable is duration, not intensity. Treat the 35 as 35 minutes of easy running total — don't bolt an extra warm-up on top.

The unchanged second run
  Keep it identical to baseline: 30 minutes, same easy effort, same shoes, same surface. Do not extend it, do not push it to "balance" the 35. This run is your recovery-confirmation slot — it is the second half of the test. A clean second 30 is part of what makes the 35 count as clean.

Stop / rollback conditions under your session-plus-following-day rule

  Session-time (during or within ~30 min after the 35):
    - focal ankle pain — sharp, pin-point, or different in quality from the diffuse muscular fatigue of a normal easy run
    - any new gait change — shortened stride, asymmetric foot strike, lateral drift, limping, involuntary compensation
    - calf tightness that doesn't feel like normal training soreness
    - ankle feeling unstable or "giving" on trail surface
    - sharp pain = stop the run, don't try to finish the 35
    - plain muscular fatigue at easy effort is not a trigger; note it, finish normally

  Following day (the 24h after):
    - focal ankle pain at rest or with daily activities (stairs, uneven ground)
    - next-morning stiffness localized to the ankle rather than general leg soreness
    - swelling, warmth, or visible change around the ankle
    - gait change noticed by you or someone else when you're not running
    - calf tightness that persists into the morning of Day 2
    - any of these = the next test slot rolls back to 30 minutes

Rollback, not escalation
  A clean session + clean following day does NOT mean next week is 40. This is one test. If clean, the next decision is separate — typically hold 35 at that single slot for another clean week before considering extending the second slot or stepping duration further. If either window fires, the next test goes back to 30, and you re-establish a clean two-30s week before another single-slot test.

Adjacency to strengthening
  Don't pile a harder calf/ankle session the day before the test, and don't skip the session after if it's normally scheduled — the strengthening is part of what supports the ankle's tolerance to the extra 5 minutes. Keep it at its usual dose on its usual days.

Operating interpretation — Expansion Assist: eligibility vs. exposure

Eligibility is a static filter: the account meets tier, usage, and stage criteria that qualify it for Expansion Assist outreach. Eligibility says nothing about whether outreach has occurred, what the account did in response, or whether expansion will follow.

Exposure is a recorded action: the account was actually contacted through Expansion Assist within the window in question. Only exposed accounts belong in conversion math, response rates, holdout comparisons, or forecast denominators.

Consequences for how eligible accounts are handled:

  - Not pipeline. An eligible account that has not been contacted contributes zero to current-quarter pipeline. Including it inflates coverage optics without grounding in action; reporting "X eligible" as if it were "X in motion" is the error this rule prevents.

  - Not causal evidence. Pre-treatment criteria cannot establish that Expansion Assist drives expansion. Any uplift claim must be conditioned on exposure, with a comparable control. Eligible-only comparisons describe who qualifies, not what the program caused.

  - Not forecast credit. Expansion forecasts book credit on converted exposed accounts, not on the eligible-but-untouched pool. Booking against eligibility double-counts intent the program has not yet earned and makes the forecast non-additive with actuals.

Stale eligible cohorts fail closed. If the exposure window lapses without contact, the account returns to the standard expansion path and is removed from Expansion Assist attribution until re-exposed. Eligibility does not persist as a standing claim on future quarters.

Quick fried-rice-style skillet. Cold rice is actually ideal here — it toasts instead of going mushy. Plan leaves ~20 min of active work and a clean kitchen (one pan, one board, one knife, one small bowl).

Mise (0–3 min)
  Chop scallions, whites and greens separate
  Tear spinach into ribbons
  Halve the lime
  Dice or shred chicken into bite-size pieces
  Beat the 2 eggs with a pinch of salt in a small bowl
  Fluff the cold rice with a fork (or wet fingers) so clumps break up easily

Cook
  3:00  Large skillet, medium-high, 1–2 tbsp oil. Add scallion whites + corn. Stir 90 sec until hot and fragrant.
  4:30  Add chicken. Spread in a layer, let it warm and pick up a little color, ~2 min.
  6:30  Pour eggs into one side of the pan. Let set 30 sec, scramble into small curds, then fold everything together.
  9:00  Add rice. Spread evenly, press flat with the spatula, then leave it alone for 3 min — this is where the texture comes from.
  12:00 Break it up, stir, press flat again, 2 more min. You're looking for some crispy edges.
  14:00 Fold in spinach. Stir just until wilted, ~60 sec. Kill the heat.
  15:30 Season: salt, pepper, then lime to taste (start with half). Taste — rice usually wants more salt than you'd guess.
  17:00 Plate your portion while it's hot.

Sam's portion (18:00–20:00)
  Portion hers into a container, press flat (reheats more evenly), lid on, fridge. Roughly half-and-half, skew slightly toward her — she's eating after service.
  Tell her: microwave covered with 1 tsp water for ~90 sec, OR a skillet with a little oil over medium heat. Finish with a fresh squeeze of lime when it's hot. Eggs in fried rice reheat fine.

Cleanup: the pan, the board, the knife, the egg bowl. Done well inside your 25.

5.5 min sits inside the break regime but close to the wet edge — narrow. The lower feathering tracks gravity pooling: the bottom of the wash is wetter than the top at any given moment, so the same interrupt time isn't uniform across the mark. If you want crisp top-to-bottom, either tilt the paper to even drainage or split the timing (5.5 at top, ~6 at bottom). If you want atmosphere, the feathering is the mark — depends on whether the rain reads as falling or pooling.

Short answer: timing is bounded only if you log the conditions that drive it. 5.5 min sits between your break (3) and hold (7) anchors — that's the transition band where moisture differences should be most legible, so it's a reasonable probe. The risk is that "5.5 min" drifts with humidity and sheet state, so the brush-moisture sweep inherits that drift unless you record temp/RH and a one-line note on sheet condition (sizing feel, any prior wettings that day).

Yes — keep 5.5 min fixed and change only brush moisture.

Design:

  Hold fixed: paper (same sheet if possible), pigment + dilution, brush, your touch sequence (1 firm blot → light → broad → 2× seam, 20s touch hold, 1 touch, no return), room.

  Vary: brush load only. Four levels — (a) blotted dry, (b) lightly moist, (c) loaded, (d) loaded + shaken once. Three is cleaner if you want less noise; five+ makes the touch itself the variable.

  Replicate: 2 trials per level on the same sheet, in a grid. Paper variance cancels that way; different sheets only if you also vary paper deliberately.

  Read one outcome: bloom character — your "no return after dull = no bloom" rule. Don't also score hue shift, edge hardness, or granulation in the same pass. That tips the study into illustrative territory.

  Log on the sheet: time, moisture code, temp/RH, one-line outcome (edge took color / edge only water / no merge).

Why not vary timing instead: the 3 / 7 / fully-dry triad already covers the timing axis. Moisture at fixed 5.5 is the missing leg — it tells you whether your touch sequence is robust to brush state, which is the variable you actually control at the moment of painting. Timing already has anchors; brush moisture does not yet.

One guardrail, given your boundary rule: this is technique calibration, not a vote on the unresolved compositional edge. Run it on practice sheets; don't read the results back into the quiet/boundary decision. That decision stays separate.

  1. Don't tap, click, copy, or paste the link. Treat it as inert.

  6. For "someone you know" messages on a new number or channel, reach the person through a channel you already trust before responding.

REPORTING
  - Email: forward as attachment to your provider's abuse desk (e.g., reportphishing@apple.com for iCloud, abuse@gmail.com for Gmail, phishing@irs.gov for tax scams). Then delete from inbox and trash.
  - SMS: forward to 7726 (SPAM) in the US/Canada — carriers use this to track and block. Delete after.

  - Work account: forward to your security team / abuse mailbox before deleting. Don't just delete a work phish — IT needs the headers.
  - Financial fraud attempt: report to the bank and to the FTC; if identity exposure is possible, to IdentityTheft.gov.

BLOCKING

CONSERVATIVE SHUTDOWN (do these first, in order)

1. Leave the cycle stopped. Don't try to restart.
   A low hum with standing water above the filter is most likely the drain pump running against a blockage. The main way a drain pump burns out in this situation is repeated restarts while the water won't clear.

2. Kill power at the breaker.
   Open the panel and find the circuit labeled DW, dishwasher, or kitchen. Flip it OFF. The hum should stop immediately. If it doesn't, the breaker may be mislabeled — kill any 15A/20A breakers that look kitchen-adjacent until the hum stops. Don't assume the hum will time out on its own.

3. Optional but prudent: shut the water supply.
   Under the sink, find the braided line to the dishwasher and close the hand valve (quarter turn clockwise). The cycle is already stopped, so this is defensive, not urgent.

4. Check the base pan.
   The toe / kick panel at the bottom front is usually held by 2 screws or clips. Pull it off and look at the pan with a flashlight. Many dishwashers have a leak sensor + float in the base. A dry pan is reassuring; standing water there means the leak sensor didn't trip (or doesn't exist) — flag it for the tech.

BASIC USER CHECKS THAT ARE SAFE (power OFF at the breaker throughout)

  Filter screen. The round cover at the bottom of the tub, under the lower rack, usually twists out or lifts. Pull it and look underneath. A clogged or mis-seated filter is the single most common cause of exactly this symptom. Rinse the screen under the tap and reseat it.

  Air gap (if installed). Small chrome cylinder on the back of the sink near the faucet, with a cap that pops straight up. Pop the cap and check for a gummy plug of food debris.

  Sink drain behavior. Run the kitchen sink for 30 seconds with the disposal off. If it drains slowly or gurgles, the clog is downstream of the dishwasher connection — not the dishwasher's fault, but worth telling the tech.

  Garbage disposal port. If you have a disposal installed or replaced recently, the dishwasher port sometimes still has the factory knockout plug in place. Look into the port with a flashlight; removing the plug is a disposal-level task, so just note whether the disposal is new.

  Drain hose under the sink. Visual only — look for a sharp kink or a U-bend that's holding water. Don't detach it.

WHAT NOT TO DISASSEMBLE

  The control panel, door latch, or any wiring.
  The pump impeller (under the filter, inside the sump). Even with power off, the pump housing and check valve are tech-level.
  The door seal / gasket around the tub edge.
  The unit itself. Don't pull the dishwasher out from the cabinet — it's heavy, the water line and drain hose can kink or detach, and there's always some residual water in the base.
  Don't pour drain opener, vinegar "flushes," or bleach into the sump. They're either ineffective on dishwasher drains or they damage seals and create a respiratory hazard the next time the tub is heated.
  And: don't restore power and run another cycle as a test. At most, one brief restart to listen and watch the water level, and only after the breaker has been off for a full minute.

WHEN TO FILE A MAINTENANCE REQUEST (this is your path right now)

  This is a maintenance request, not an emergency. When you submit it, include:
   - Standing water above the filter at end of cycle
   - Low hum on restart attempt
   - No leak, smoke, odor, breaker trip, or cabinet damage
   - Cycle stopped, breaker off, pet kept away from open door
   - Whether the base pan was wet or dry (step 4)
   - Whether the filter, air gap, and sink drain looked clear

WHEN TO TREAT IT AS EMERGENCY INSTEAD

  Stop and call emergency maintenance (or the building's emergency line) if any of these appear:
   - Burning smell, smoke, or visible arcing
   - Active water on the floor or a sudden increase of water in the base pan
   - Breaker that won't reset, or trips again immediately on reset
   - The hum turns into a louder mechanical grinding or high-pitched whine
   - Water near any energized outlet, the disposal, or under the sink cabinet

  Until any of those appear, you've already done the right things: stopped the cycle, cut the power, kept Kibo away from the open door, and not forced another run.

Good afternoon — I'm Sam, head chef at the restaurant in Hyde Park. PROMPT 1 — How advance counts preserve seasonal-menu quality
Advance counts are how we protect the seasonal menu. We size every private-event batch to a known guest count and run a tested pre-staging sequence — mise, tray, pan-staging — so a private dinner doesn't quietly pull from the seasonal menu's quality or labor budget. The clearest worked example is the single-run roasted chicken approval: it stayed an advance-count private-dinner option because we needed the 60-minute labor ceiling and the 44-portion threshold to hold before we even considered repeating it. That run met both, and the approval closed as a one-run, not a weekly special. Advance counts let us say yes to private events without absorbing the cost on the menu's seasonality or the team's hours.

PROMPT 2 — Keeping menu and production authority separate from service attendance
In our setup the handoff is clean: I approve the menu and own production, and service coverage runs through a separate intake. That separation matters because it lets a private event run inside the normal service rhythm instead of becoming a parallel job. We don't add a second close for a private dinner — it replaces an ordinary service assignment — and the Sunday prep absorbs the planning. So authority stays with the kitchen, attendance stays with service, and neither one quietly turns into the other's problem.

PROMPT 3 — When a private-dining team should decline customization
The honest test is operational margin: does the customization add time we haven't budgeted, source something outside our regular purveyors, or push past the brand fit of what we already do? A simple yes-with-parameters example: a protein we already buy, in a portion we don't normally plate — we can usually size it, that's parameters, not unlimited customization. A clear no: a dish that needs a separate shopping run, a technique the line hasn't run, or a per-guest labor cost that erodes the event margin. The point isn't to be difficult — it's that "we can do anything" quietly turns private dining into a second restaurant.

The black residue is almost certainly fragments of the original album page and adhesive the print was mounted to — friable, and any attempt to lift it risks pulling paper fibers or image layer with it. Your minimum-intervention instinct is the right call. Here is a conservative sequence.

  1. Document before any further handling.
     Photograph the print under raking light from both sides. Close-ups of the two corners, taken straight-on and from a low angle so the standing flake edges cast shadows, will let you later detect new flaking, lifting, or staining. Save these files under your pair-05 index. Use even, diffuse lighting; avoid harsh glare on the image.

  2. Move it to a clean, calm workspace.
     Clean, dry hands or nitrile/cotton gloves. Carry the print flat on a sheet of acid-free paper; do not carry it vertically with corners unsupported — gravity can lift a flake. Do not blow, tap, or brush the residue. If a flake falls free during handling, keep it in a small labeled archival envelope (label on the outside of the envelope, not on the flap touching the flake); it is part of the object's history.

  3. Isolate for today.
     Lay the print image-up on acid-free paper on a clean, flat surface. Do not sandwich it under another sheet where flakes could transfer to the facing paper. Move it away from HVAC vents, fans, or doorways while you work.

  4. Store it.
     Sleeve the print in a four-flap archival polyester (such as Mylar or Melinex) enclosure — the four flaps fold over each other so nothing adhesive touches the print, and the gentle pressure holds flakes in place. If you only have paper enclosures, fold an acid-free sheet around the print and place it flat in a rigid, acid-free, lignin-free archival box. Store flat, never upright. Cool, dry, stable conditions — roughly 18°C and 35–45% relative humidity. Avoid attics, basements, exterior walls, and any spot with direct sun or heat. Write the pair-05 index on the enclosure or on a card that travels with the print — never on the photograph or on the residue.

  5. Keep order and provenance intact.
     The residue belongs with the print. Do not bag it separately. Do not annotate the print, the residue, or the back, even lightly in pencil — pencil can indent. Record any condition note in your index entry, not on the object: e.g., "dry flaking album-paper residue at two corners; no treatment attempted, [date], [initials]."

  What to avoid

     - Pressure-sensitive tape of any kind (Scotch, masking, archival/filmoplast) — even on the back, even temporarily.
     - Paper clips, staples, rubber bands, binder clips, or any mechanical fastener.
     - Soft PVC ("vinyl") sleeves, ziploc bags, or other plastic that off-gases or traps moisture.
     - Water, breath, saliva, erasers, kneaded erasers, art gum, or any "home" cleaning method.
     - Solvents, gels, or any adhesive (wheat starch paste, methylcellulose, archival glue) — these are conservator materials.
     - Consolidants, sprays, or fixatives of any kind.
     - Heat sources (sunlight, hair dryers, warm lamps) used to "dry" anything.
     - Vacuum cleaners, soft brushes, or cotton swabs anywhere near the residue.
     - Annotating the back, the residue, or the print itself — even lightly in pencil.
     - Separating any flake from the print.

  When to involve a photograph conservator

     - New flakes appear, or any flake edge lifts higher than at documentation.
     - Glossy or pigmented image layer coming up with the residue (a sheen lifting with the flakes is a serious warning sign that the image layer is failing).
     - Discoloration spreading from the residue — yellowing, darkening, or haloing — which can indicate active adhesive degradation.
     - Any moisture event, condensation, mold, or insect activity near the print.
     - If the handwriting on the back is at risk of abrasion from the residue shifting.
     - If you want the print stable for decades rather than years, or if it is a unique image with no other copy.
     - For a referral: the American Institute for Conservation (conservation-us.org) maintains a Find-a-Conservator directory — look for specialty in photographic materials; a regional paper conservator can also refer.

TWO-WEEK PLAN
=============

Assumptions: same shoes, same lake-trail surface, easy effort. Spacing is a starting point — shift days, don't compress them.

WEEK A — Sept 22 to 28
  Promote the 35-min test from a one-off to the floor:

  - 3 sessions — Tue 35 / Thu or Fri 25 to 30 / Sat 35
    - Keep the new session shorter than the established ones
  - Ankle + calf strength: 2 to 3 sessions

Rule in action: Week A advances duration; Week B advances frequency. One variable per week, never both.

SYSPTOM CHECK — what to look at, when
  During run
    Focal ankle pain, calf tightness, a limp, any gait change (even subtle)
  0 to 2 hr after
    Walk, stairs, sit-to-stand — anything new?
  Following morning
    First steps out of bed, stairs, normal walking
  24 to 48 hr
    Confirm nothing lingers before the next session

ANKLE + CALF STRENGTHENING (pick what you have)
  Calf raises — straight-knee + bent-knee, 2 to 3 x 10 to 12, slow tempo
  Single-leg balance — 30 to 60 s; add eyes-closed once it's easy
  Band work — inversion / eversion / dorsiflexion, 2 x 15 each
  Optional: slow step-downs on trail stairs (eccentric focus)
  2x/wk minimum; 3x is fine if recovery feels clean

ROLLBACK CONDITIONS — apply the smallest change that fits
  Focal pain during a run ............... stop the session; do not push through
  New or recurring pain on follow-day .. hold frequency this week (no 3rd session)
                                          drop next session's duration 5 min and
                                          hold there the rest of the week
  Visible or felt gait change mid-run ... end early; repeat last week's plan

  Same symptom on 2 consecutive sessions pause progression; hold current load

  Sharp one-sided calf sensation ......... stop running until a full week of

PRACTICAL NOTES
  Same shoes on the same surface keeps the test clean — if you change either, treat the next session as another test, not a progression step.

Reading

Recording a problem is a document act — it freezes what happened so it can be looked at later. Responding is a relation act — it changes what happens next, between the people involved. The two get confused because both produce artifacts (a ticket, a write-up, a Slack thread, a one-on-one), but they answer different questions. A record asks "what was this?" A response asks "what will we do about it, and who is accountable?" Recording without responding turns into an archive of deferred decisions — neat, complete, and inert. Responding without recording leaves the organization with only the latest voice in the room, and no way to learn from itself.

A useful test: if the artifact disappeared tomorrow, would anyone change behavior this week? If no, you recorded. If yes, you responded.

  How to read it without jumping to a conclusion

The ANOC is one-sided. It tells you only what her current plan will look like next year — it says nothing about whether another plan would cost less, cover her meds better, or keep her pharmacy in network. A higher premium on this plan doesn't automatically mean switching saves money overall; it depends on what the alternatives price her meds at and whether her preferred pharmacy is in their networks. A fair review weighs this plan against at least one or two others on the same total-annual-cost basis, not on premium alone.

  Evidence-based checklist for the review with Mom

  1.  Pull the actual ANOC and circle the three concrete numbers: new premium, inhaler tier/copay, any pharmacy-network note.
  2.  Confirm her preferred pharmacy is still preferred for 2026 — that's what keeps the generics at $0 and the inhaler at $47. A drop to standard status changes those numbers.
  3.  Around October 1, when 2026 plan data lands in Medicare Plan Finder, enter her exact meds (two generics + inhaler), her ZIP, and her preferred pharmacy. Plan Finder does the side-by-side on total annual cost, not premium.
  4.  Run the comparison for at least one alternative plan — ideally two — even if she's leaning toward staying. The premium gap is one input, not the verdict.
  5.  Verify the inhaler specifically: is prior authorization or a quantity limit new for 2026? The ANOC may not flag that.
  6.  If she expects any vaccines in 2026 (flu, shingles, RSV, COVID), confirm $0 coverage under whichever plan she picks — this was an open item in past reviews.
  7.  Decide whether mail order makes sense for the generics (cheap, predictable) and whether it suits the inhaler (as-needed meds often don't).
  8.  Deadline: the Annual Election Period closes December 7. Any switch has to land by then for a January 1 start.
  9.  Don't enroll during the review call. Document the comparison, sleep on it, then decide.
  10. If an alternative plan looks meaningfully better, that's evidence worth pursuing. If not, the higher premium is just the price of staying with what works for her meds and pharmacy.

**Arithmetic verification (14.7¢/kWh).**

The September 25, 2025 Cherrywood bill had: 911 kWh used, with three line charges — $109.32 energy, $22.44 delivery, $2.11 taxes — and no base charge or plan fee. Stated total: $133.87. Sum of the three lines: 109.32 + 22.44 + 2.11 = $133.87. Reconciles exactly.

All-in effective rate = 133.87 / 911 = $0.14695…/kWh = **14.695¢/kWh ≈ 14.7¢/kWh**. Your arithmetic is correct, and so is the rounding. (If you did it as 14.695 → "14.7," that's the right one-decimal read.)

The same divisor also produces a clean breakdown:
- Energy: 109.32 / 911 = 12.000¢/kWh
- Delivery: 22.44 / 911 = 2.463¢/kWh
- Taxes: 2.11 / 911 = 0.232¢/kWh
- Sum: 14.695¢/kWh

So "about 14.7¢" is actually 14.70¢ rounded — the precise figure is 14.695¢.

**Comparing to the facts-label estimate (13.5¢/kWh at 1,000 kWh).**

The facts label on the 12-month fixed plan lists three usage points: 14.1¢ at 500 kWh, 13.5¢ at 1,000 kWh, and 13.3¢ at 2,000 kWh. To compare meaningfully, three things have to be true at the same time:

1. The 13.5¢ is **all-in** (energy + delivery + taxes/fees), not just an energy rate.
2. The curve between anchor points is reasonably smooth, so 911 kWh sits between 14.1¢ and 13.5¢ rather than somewhere unexpected.
3. The label was generated using the same fee/structure that the actual bill applies — i.e., the same delivery rate, the same tax treatment, and **no recurring base charge**, which the September bill confirms is the case here.

Assuming all three hold, the right way to compare is to ask what the label *predicts* at 911 kWh, not at 1,000 kWh. Linear interpolation between the 500 and 1,000 anchors:

rate(911) ≈ 14.1¢ + (13.5 − 14.1)¢ × (911 − 500) / (1000 − 500)
        ≈ 14.1 − 0.6 × 411/500
        ≈ 14.1 − 0.493
        ≈ **13.607¢/kWh**

Predicted bill at that interpolated rate: 911 × 0.13607 ≈ **$123.96**.
Actual bill: **$133.87**. Gap: about **+$9.91**, or roughly **+8%** over the label-predicted total.

The all-in 14.695¢ sits about **+1.09¢ above the 13.5¢ anchor** and about **+1.09¢ above the interpolated 13.61¢ you'd expect at 911 kWh**. So the bill is meaningfully above the facts label, not at it — but the gap is small and concentrated in cents-per-kWh terms.

**Is the gap plausibly explained by lower usage + statement components, or does it suggest the plan terms weren't applied?**

Two clean ways to read this.

**Reading A — gap is mostly explained, no evidence of plan misapplication.**

The September bill's own structure shows the confirmed plan terms *were* applied: the energy rate came in at exactly 12.000¢/kWh (energy-only), the delivery rate at 2.463¢/kWh, taxes at 0.232¢/kWh, and there is no base charge and no monthly recurring fee. That's consistent with the plan being live and the supplier not having layered on default variable-plan charges. The 14.695¢ all-in is therefore an artifact of *what the facts label is and how the bill is structured*, not of a wrong rate being applied. Specifically:

- The facts label is computed at rounded anchor usages (500, 1,000, 2,000) and almost certainly **excludes or rounds out small per-kWh riders** that the actual statement picks up — sales-tax reimbursement, a regulatory charge, a PUC fee, a fuel-adjustment line. On this bill, the 0.232¢ tax line alone is small, but in Texas fixed plans it's common for the all-in number on the label to omit line-item riders that show up on the actual statement. That rider component is on the order of a fraction of a cent to about a cent per kWh — easily enough to bridge a 1¢ gap.
- The label curve is downward-sloping with usage (14.1 → 13.5 → 13.3). At 911 kWh, you should already be paying **above** the 13.5¢ anchor simply because you're below 1,000 kWh. The interpolation above puts the expected rate at ~13.6¢. The remaining ~1.1¢ gap from there is the rider/statement-component piece.
- Net: plan terms look applied. The label is an estimate at rounded anchor usages; the statement reflects actual line items at actual usage. That mismatch is structural, not evidence of error.

**Reading B — gap is too large to be explained by usage + components alone, and merits a check.**

A 1.09¢/kWh gap is **not** trivially small. As a dollar figure on this bill it's only ~$9.91, which feels minor, but as a deviation from the advertised rate it's about **8%** — and the entire reason to choose the fixed plan over month-to-month was to land near 13.5¢ rather than the 14.8–15.2¢ variable rate. So an 8% miss matters for the value proposition of the plan.

The structural explanations above are plausible but not guaranteed. Specifically, they would *not* explain the gap if any of the following turned out to be true on closer inspection of the Electricity Facts Label (EFL) and the actual rate schedule:
- The 13.5¢ figure on the label is meant to be truly all-in inclusive of exactly the riders on the statement, and the EFL lists them at the same per-kWh values. In that case the gap is real, not structural.
- The plan's energy rate is supposed to be a flat per-kWh number (e.g., 10.5¢ or 11.0¢) with delivery and taxes layered on, and the label's 13.5¢ is just the **sum** of those components. The September bill's 12.000¢ energy rate would then be slightly above the contracted energy rate, which would be a real discrepancy.
- The fixed plan has tiered energy rates that step up at certain usage thresholds and 911 kWh lands in a higher-cost tier than 1,000 kWh. (Unlikely — the curve on the label is *decreasing* in usage, which is the opposite of what tiering would produce — but worth confirming.)

**Bottom line.**

Your 14.7¢ number is arithmetically right (precisely 14.695¢). It sits about 1.1¢ above the facts-label 13.5¢ anchor. The lower-usage point (911 vs. 1,000 kWh) accounts for roughly 0.4¢ of that gap via interpolation; the remainder is on the order of magnitude typical of small statement riders (sales tax reimbursement, regulatory fees, fuel adjustments) that the rounded-anchor label doesn't surface line by line. The bill structure — 12.000¢ energy, 2.463¢ delivery, 0.232¢ tax, no base charge, no monthly fee — looks consistent with the confirmed fixed plan being live and applied, not with the variable plan's 14.8¢ or a default rate leaking through.

That said, "plausibly explained" and "verified explained" are different things. To close the loop rather than just close the question, the two checks that would convert this from plausible to confirmed are: (1) pull the EFL and confirm the 13.5¢ is labeled all-in and which riders it includes, and (2) confirm the contracted energy rate in the plan's Terms of Service and that 12.000¢/kWh matches it exactly. Conservative read of the recall

The notice describes a defect, not an emergency. The fuel-pump impeller inside the tank can deform over time, which can reduce or cut fuel pressure. The manufacturer did not tell you to stop driving; it told you the remedy is still being prepared and a second letter will arrive when parts are ready. That's the only status claim you should treat as firm right now.

What it means in plain terms: until the second letter arrives, this is a monitor-and-document situation, not a "park the car" situation. A deformed impeller tends to produce recognizable symptoms before it strands you, but that isn't guaranteed — symptom-free driving does not mean the part is fine, and a single stall at the wrong moment (intersection, merge, highway speed) is the real safety concern, not the stall itself.

Records to retain (keep until the remedy is performed and the close-out invoice is in hand)
- The original recall notice, including the campaign/recall number, NHTSA ID, and VIN — the second letter will reference the same campaign number.
- The second "parts available" letter when it arrives.
- Every dealer service write-up, work order, and paid invoice tied to this recall.
- Current odometer reading at the time of each dealer visit.
- A short running log: date, what you felt, conditions (warm/cold engine, fuel level, speed), whether the engine stalled or only ran rough, and any warning lights. Symptoms before the remedy are useful if a future claim or warranty dispute arises.
- Any tow, roadside-assistance, or rental receipts if a stall occurs before the remedy.

Symptoms that should end a trip (pull over safely when you can)
- Engine actually stalls while driving — even once. Don't try to "babysit" it to a destination.
- Hard restart after a stall that takes multiple crank attempts, or the engine won't restart at all.
- Visible or strong fuel smell, or fuel leak under the car (the recall is fuel-pressure related; a deformed impeller can be accompanied by fuel-delivery anomalies).
- Loss of power on a highway merge, passing maneuver, or while entering traffic — get off the road.
- Any pulsing, surging, or hesitation severe enough that you'd describe it as "the car is fighting me."

Symptoms that should prompt urgent dealer service (don't wait for the routine second letter)
- Repeated hard starting when the engine is warm (this is the most characteristic early sign per the notice).
- Rough idle or rough running under load that recurs and is getting worse.
- Check-engine light or other fuel-system warning lights that appear in connection with the symptoms above.
- Any single stall event, even if the car restarts normally afterward.

Verification of future remedy availability — without relying on unsolicited links
- Manufacturer's second notice by mail is the authoritative signal. Use the campaign number from the first letter to match it.
- Manufacturer owner portal: type the brand's portal URL directly into the browser (or use a bookmark you've placed yourself), then enter the VIN yourself. Never follow a "check your recall status" link delivered by email, text, or social media — those are common phishing vectors that imitate recalls.
- NHTSA: nhtsa.gov/recalls — look up by VIN. NHTSA's recall database is the third-party cross-check.
- Dealer: call a dealer using a phone number you looked up yourself (dealer locator on the manufacturer site) and ask specifically whether parts for this campaign number are in stock before booking.
- For text/email alerts from the manufacturer: if the message contains a link, don't use it. Open the app or type the site yourself. Unsolicited outreach about recalls is one of the more common phishing patterns.

What I'm explicitly not doing here
- Not recommending any non-manufacturer "interim fix," additive, or aftermarket part — the only remedy that resolves a recall is the manufacturer's.
- Not telling you to stop driving; the notice doesn't say that, and I won't widen a regulator's instruction on your behalf.
- Not opening links on your behalf or fetching a third-party status page — the verification path above is the safe one.

Want me to set a single follow-up reminder (e.g., 60–90 days out) to recheck remedy status through the owner portal / NHTSA, or to log a symptom entry whenever one of the watch-for items above happens?

Three structural issues, all on the scorecard's framing rather than its numbers. None of these are tweaks — they're why the twelve top-line metrics can't be read together as one picture.

1. Helio Start activation + retained-mid activation as a single rate
   Different acquisition surfaces, almost certainly different activation definitions and time-to-value curves. A combined rate hides whether either cohort is moving on its own, hides tradeoffs (Start up + retained-mid down can net flat), and hides which surface deserves Q4 investment.
   Right shape: two rates, each with its own denominator and definition, side-by-side. A combined only if explicitly weighted — and that weighting is itself a decision to publish.

2. CS auto-nudge holds reported as a rate beside customer outcomes
   Holds is an operational counter. Outcomes are downstream effects. Putting them on the same row implies false equivalence. The direction is also ambiguous in isolation: a higher hold rate could mean better filtering (good) or over-blocking (bad).
   Right shape: holds live in a quality/operations section, paired with held-vs-sent nudge conversion so the policy can be evaluated, not just counted.

3. Expansion Assist expansions without denominators
   Raw expansion count answers nothing. At minimum it needs the eligibility denominator; ideally a funnel — eligible → exposed → engaged → expanded. Without that you can't tell whether a movement is an expansion-rate move, an exposure move, or a population-shift move.
   Right shape: expansion rate = expansions / eligible, and exposure rate = exposed / eligible. Both required before the count means anything.

Side note: (1) and (3) are exactly what Owen's framing block is supposed to catch at draft stage — denom + cohort + scope. (2) is a section-belonging question rather than a framing-block one, which is probably why it slipped through.

The math:

    Annual premium    A: $732      B: $576      diff: +$156 for A
    Deductible        A: $500      B: $750      diff: -$250 for A
    Reimb. per claim  80% of (bill - deductible), same 10k cap

Per claim, A's lower deductible is worth 0.8 x $250 = $200 in extra reimbursement. So A recoups its $156 premium premium only if Kibo has any single claim large enough to clear A's $500 deductible in a given year — and once a claim clears A's deductible, A finishes the year ~$44 ahead of B. With no claim at all, B is $156 ahead.

Break-even probability of "any claim above $500 this year" = $156 / $200 = 78%. For a healthy adult pet with no pending issue, that's well above typical observed rates, so B wins on expected cost.

The only feature A offers that B doesn't is behavioral-care eligibility after the deductible. Per memory Kibo is a calm greeter — that's a low-priority tail risk, not a near-term need. If that profile changes (new household, anxiety onset), A becomes worth the upgrade.

One-skillet potato hash with eggs and melted cheddar. Cooks in ~22 minutes; the rest of the 30 is buffer and cleanup.

Mise (min 0-3)
  - 3 cups cooked potatoes, cut into 1 cm / 1/2-inch cubes
  - 3 scallions: whites thinly sliced, greens sliced and kept separate
  - 3-4 handfuls baby spinach (rinsed if not pre-washed)
  - ~60 g / 1/2 cup sharp cheddar, shredded
  - 4 eggs, cracked into a small bowl (easier than cracking into wells)
  - 2 Tbsp oil, 1/2 tsp salt, black pepper

Cook (min 3-20)
  Min 3   Heat oil in a 10-12 inch nonstick (or well-seasoned cast iron) over medium-high. When shimmering, add potatoes in one even layer. Press flat with a spatula. Don't stir.
  Min 8   Lift an edge: when the underside is deeply golden, flip in sections. Add scallion whites and the salt. Toss 30 sec.
  Min 11  Push the hash to one side. Pile spinach into the empty half with 1 Tbsp water. Cover; wilt 2 min.
  Min 14  Stir the spinach into the hash. Make 4 shallow wells. Slide an egg into each. Cover; cook 3-4 min until whites are set, yolks still soft.
  Min 18  Scatter cheddar over the top, cover 30 sec to melt. Off heat: scallion greens and pepper.

Plate and reset (min 20-30)
  Serve straight from the skillet to two plates (or eat family-style at the table from the skillet — one fewer dish).
  While you eat:
    - rinse the cutting board and knife now, before scallion juice sets
    - rinse the small egg bowl and your spatula
    - wipe the stovetop and counter with a damp cloth
  Right after the skillet is empty, give it a quick rinse while it's still warm (prevents sticking), towel-dry, and put it away. If a dishwasher is running, drop the tools in; otherwise a short hand-wash finishes the job in under 2 min.

Two notes that earn the timing
  - Cold fridge potatoes cool the pan and won't crisp. 30 seconds in the microwave first brings them back to room temp so the press-and-don't-stir step actually browns.
  - Covering for the eggs traps steam. If Sam prefers firmer yolks, leave the lid on an extra minute; if you want runny yolks for dipping toast, pull at 3 min.

Salt and pepper cover the seasoning. If you want a warmer note without buying anything, a pinch of smoked paprika on the potatoes at min 8 is the only addition worth making.

Keep paper, pigment family, large cool wash, and the value-separated warm edge fixed. Change only the silhouette of the darkest doorway accent — let the warm counter edge cut INTO the dark shape at one point, so the accent has a single notch where warm shows through. Footprint, position, and pigment load stay identical to today's study.

**Quick check on the numbers**

LDL wasn't reported directly with the Friedewald inputs, so the lab likely gave you a direct LDL. The cross-check: with TG=72 and HDL=61, Friedewald would estimate LDL ≈ TC − HDL − TG/5 = 193 − 61 − 14.4 ≈ 118, which matches the reported 118 exactly — so the LDL is internally consistent, not a lab quirk. Non-HDL = 193 − 61 = 132, also matches the report.

**Reading the panel (asymptomatic, single draw)**

  Total chol    193        fine (<200)
  LDL-C         118        flagged; ref <100 — moderately above, not alarming
  HDL-C          61        good for any sex; excellent for a male
  Triglycerides  72         comfortably normal (<150)
  Non-HDL       132        flagged; ref <130 — just over the line, driven entirely by LDL

Nothing here is a red flag. No symptoms, no very-high LDL, no high TG, HDL is doing its job. The two flags are essentially the same finding from two angles: LDL is in the "borderline-high" range (100–129 is borderline; 130–159 is officially high), and non-HDL sits 2 mg/dL over its 130 threshold.

**What this does and doesn't tell you**

  - This is one fasting draw on Dec 12. Lipids drift day to day and seasonally (often ~5–10% higher in winter), so a single mildly-elevated LDL is not a diagnosis.
  - "Borderline-high" LDL is a risk *context* input, not a treatment threshold on its own. What matters next is your 10-year ASCVD risk estimate (age, BP, smoking, diabetes, HDL, total chol) — that's what a clinician uses to decide whether the conversation is "lifestyle" or "medication."
  - Symptoms aren't expected here regardless. Hyperlipidemia is silent by design; the "no new symptoms" part is reassuring but doesn't move the needle.

**What I'd actually do**

  1. Don't react to the portal flag in isolation. Send the panel to your clinician (or message through the portal) and ask for the 10-year ASCVD risk score. Anything under ~5% means borderline LDL is generally observed, not treated.
  2. Ask whether a repeat fasting lipid in 4–8 weeks is warranted. One repeat is standard before any lifestyle or medication decision on a borderline value, because of biological and seasonal variability.
  3. If you want one thing you can already act on while you wait: triglycerides of 72 with HDL of 61 already suggests your carb/alcohol/saturated-fat pattern is reasonable — the lever, if any, is usually LDL-specific (saturated fat, soluble fiber, weight), and that's a conversation for after the repeat, not tonight.
  4. No need to fast again before the repeat unless your lab specifically asks for fasting — non-HDL and direct LDL are robust to non-fasting state.

**Bottom line:** mildly elevated LDL with excellent HDL, normal TG, and no symptoms on a single draw is a "note it, repeat it, frame it with ASCVD risk" situation — not an urgent one and not a "something is wrong" one. The portal flagged a number, not a diagnosis.

Opening the frame (face-down on a clean blotter/cotton sheet)

1. Photograph the back before touching anything — orientation, hinge positions, any spacer.
2. Peel the dust cover slowly, parallel to the backing, no upward force toward the artwork. Keep the kraft paper; you'll reuse it with gummed (water-activated) tape.
3. Release the spring clips or framer's points and lift the backing board straight up. Keep it flat — no flex.
4. Lift the mat sandwich out as a unit. Don't separate layers yet.

Handling the sheet

- Clean cotton gloves, or freshly washed dry hands.
- A "newly matted" sheet is usually held one of two ways: (a) loose between back mat and window mat, retained only by mat pressure, or (b) hinged along the top edge with Japanese tissue + wheat starch paste to the back mat. Check before you touch.
- If hinged: lift by the hinge tab, never by the sheet edge.
- If loose: photograph current position, lift the window mat straight up (no sliding), move the sheet with a soft brush or a puff of breath, never with fingertips on the image area.

Reseating a 1/8" shift

- The sheet itself has probably not moved — a shifted back mat, window mat, or spacer is the usual cause.
- Reassemble in reverse: back mat → sheet (registered, all four edges clear of the window by a consistent border) → window mat → spacer if present → backing → clips → dust cover resealed with gummed tape.
- Confirm even pressure: the sheet should not bind anywhere in the window.

If the mount must be replaced

- 100% cotton rag board, 4-ply minimum (8-ply for depth), bevel-cut window at 45°.
- Rehinge only if the original is failing: Japanese kozo tissue + wheat starch paste, top edge only, ~1/4" overlap onto the sheet. Let paste dry under weights before closing the frame.
- Never use: archival film tape, gummed linen tape, masking tape, "magic" tape, self-adhesive hinging tissue, or any PSA — including "archival" brands. Wheat starch paste or methyl cellulose only.

Tools worth having on hand: cotton gloves, soft hake/sable brush, blotter paper, bone folder, gummed paper tape, mat cutter, rag board, optional Japanese tissue + wheat starch paste.

Stop handling the sheet at home and call a paper conservator if you see any of these:

- Foxing (small brown spots), tide lines, water staining, musty odor
- Flaking, lifting, or powdering pigment; cracked gouache or thick watercolor passages
- Old repairs, yellowed or brittle tape residue, glued-down corners, sheet stuck to glazing
- Insect frass, fresh holes, or paper tunneling
- Sheet stuck to the mat or glazing — do not pull
- Paper that crackles or resists the slightest flex
- Anything you can't immediately identify

A 1/8" shift on a clean, flat, unblemished sheet is a routine reseat. The moment the sheet shows damage history you didn't expect, the cost of pausing is much less than the cost of handling further.

The phone is doing two predictable things: auto-WB is fighting your balanced paint (it sees the cool wash and pushes warm/orange to compensate, then sees the warm edge and pushes cool/blue, exaggerating the separation), and auto-exposure is metering off whatever it thinks is brightest. A neutral reference in the same plane fixes both with almost no post work.

Light (≈90 sec)
- Use the corner's indirect natural light, but set up so the light rakes across the painting from one side, not head-on. Perpendicular to the window, painting flat on the table.
- Prop a white foam board or sheet of matte paper on the opposite side as a bounce. That single bounce is what makes a watercolor wash read flat in a photo instead of gradient.
- No direct sun on the painting. If the indirect light has a warm cast (late afternoon bouncing off a warm wall), block it with a sheet over the window or a curtain, or you will fight the WB all the way through post.

Camera alignment (≈90 sec)
- Phone on a stack of books or leaning mini-tripod, lens axis dead-perpendicular to the painting plane. Painting edges parallel to the frame edges. Any tilt produces keystoning that the phone "corrects" with extra processing you don't want.
- Distance: roughly 1 to 1.5× the painting's longest side. Avoid the ultra-wide — it darkens corners and shifts color toward blue at the edges, which is exactly the cast you're trying to kill.
- Frame so the painting fills about 75% and a gray card (or a swatch of neutral mat-board) sits in one corner of the same plane as the painting, in frame.

Reference and minimal correction (≈2 min)
- Use an 18% gray card, or a piece of uncoated neutral mat-board. Regular copy paper has optical brighteners that glow under daylight and will fool the WB; do not use it as the reference.
- Long-press on the gray card in your camera app to lock AE/AF, then nudge exposure down about a third of a stop if the app lets you. Recompose to include the painting with the lock still held.
- If your camera app has a manual or custom WB preset (Pro mode, Halide, Lightroom Mobile, even some stock apps now): point at the gray card, set the preset, then shoot. This single step is worth more than everything else combined.
- Shoot RAW/DNG if the phone supports it — gives you real headroom to nudge WB in post without banding.

In post (≈30 sec, only if needed)
- Drop the editor's WB eyedropper on the gray-card pixel. Done.
- If you forgot the card: pick the eyedropper on the cleanest white of the paper, away from any wash, and set that as the white point. Do not globally desaturate — that's what flattens a wash and pushes a warm edge into looking hotter by comparison.
- Skip sharpening and HDR/clarity. Both will re-introduce the cast separation you're trying to remove.

ONE-POT ORZO WITH CHICKPEAS, KALE & TOMATO
Serves 3 (dinner for 2 + 1 lunch leftover)

Quantities
- 1 cup dry orzo
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and rinsed
- 1 can (14 oz) crushed tomatoes
- 1 small bunch kale, stems out, chopped (~3-4 cups)
- 3-4 cloves garlic, minced
- 3.5 cups broth (chicken or veg), plus more if needed
- 1/2 cup grated Parmesan, plus extra to pass
- 3 tbsp olive oil, salt, pepper, optional red pepper flakes

Timing — start ~30 min before Sam walks in

 0:00  Large pot or deep skillet, medium heat, olive oil in.
 0:02  Garlic in. Stir 60-90 sec, don't brown.
 0:04  Orzo in. Toast 1-2 min, stirring, edges go translucent.
 0:06  Tomatoes, chickpeas, 3 cups broth, salt, pepper, red pepper flakes.
        Stir, bring to a steady simmer.
 0:08  Simmer uncovered, stir every couple minutes so orzo doesn't catch.
 0:18  Kale in, push it down, wilts in 2-3 min.
 0:22  Check orzo. If tight, add remaining 1/2 cup broth a splash at a time.
        You want loose and creamy, not pilaf-stiff.
 0:25  Off heat. Parmesan in. Lid on. Rest 3-4 min — this is when Sam arrives.
 0:29  Uncover, stir, taste salt, drizzle of olive oil, more Parmesan. Serve.

Cleanup: one pot, one spoon, one board, one knife. Done.

Notes
- Reheating the lunch portion: orzo soaks up sauce as it sits. Add a splash of broth or water and warm on the stove over low heat, stirring — don't microwave dry or it goes gluey.
- Lower-effort shortcut: skip the cutting board for the kale. Strip leaves, roll, snip straight into the pot at 0:18 with kitchen shears.

Adjustment: push the yellow-ochre table value (not the hue) down roughly a half-step in a tight zone around and behind the cup. Same pigment, just a heavier mix — this is a value move, and that's what separates the cup's warm counter edge from the warm tabletop without adding anything new to the palette. The ultramarine window and burnt-sienna shadow stay where they are.

Sequence (paper fully dry, cup fully dry):

1. Mix yellow ochre one notch heavier than what's already on the table — same hue, less water, more pigment in the puddle. Swatch on a scrap or paper towel: it should read visibly darker than the dry table but clearly lighter than the burnt-sienna shadow.
2. With a small round (size 4–6), lay a thin damp guard line 2–3 mm OUTSIDE the cup silhouette. Not flooded — just a moistened margin so pigment can't crawl onto the cup.
3. Pre-wet the table zone immediately around and behind the cup with clean water, stopping at that guard line. Even sheen, no puddles.
4. While the table sheen is still up, drop the heavier yellow-ochre mix into the damp zone with the same brush. Let edge tension pull the pigment outward — don't chase it.
5. Tilt the board a few degrees toward you so excess flows away from the cup, not into it.

Stop condition: stop the moment the table reads about a half-step darker than the cup's pale body AND you can see a clean value step between the cup's warm counter edge and the table surface — i.e. the cup sits on the table rather than floating in it. If the cup's edge starts to soften or feather, you've crossed the guard line; stop at once and let it dry, because any further work becomes repair, not refinement. One pass only. If after drying it's still not enough, you can judge a second pass — but make that call on the dry result, never while it's wet.

40-MINUTE STATIONARY BIKE SUBSTITUTE
Replaces one easy run. Does not count toward running-duration progression. If the trail closes again and you bike instead, it's still a substitution, not a third weekly session — do not stack two runs plus a bike in the same week from repeat closures.

WARMUP (5-8 min)
  - Resistance at lowest setting or 1-2/10. Cadence ~80 rpm, light pedal.
  - Goal: slightly elevated breathing, blood flowing, no perceived effort.
  - If you feel anything in the ankle during warmup, end the session — do not push into the main set to "see if it settles."

MAIN SET (about 30 min)
  - Cadence 85-90 rpm. Resistance 3-5/10 — enough to keep the pedal moving without grinding or rocking your foot to generate power.
  - Effort: 3-4/10. Conversational. Should feel noticeably easier than your easy run feels.
  - Foot on pedal: ball of foot or midfoot, heel slightly down. Keep the ankle near neutral — avoid long stretches of pointed toe under heavy load.
  - No standing climbs, no surges, no high-torque pushes. If you want to go harder, that's the cue to back off — easy is the assignment.

COOLDOWN (2-3 min)
  - Lowest resistance, let cadence drift down to ~70 rpm, breathing back to baseline.

STOP CONDITIONS — any one ends the session
  - Ankle: sharp pain, dull ache, stiffness, "awareness," or any sensation you don't have walking.
  - Knee, hip, or lower back discomfort.
  - Lightheadedness or sudden unusual fatigue.
  - Resistance so heavy you have to grind or your foot starts slipping on the pedal.
  - Note: muscle burn in the quads is expected. Joint or tendon sensation is not.

FOLLOWING-DAY SYMPTOM CHECK (before your other scheduled run)
  - First steps out of bed: any ankle stiffness compared to your normal baseline?
  - Walk one flight of stairs the way you normally would.
  - Seated ankle circles both directions — tightness, clicking, or asymmetry vs. the other side?
  - If any of those are different from baseline: hold the next run and reassess before adding running volume back. If they match baseline, run as planned at your normal easy effort.

NOTES
  - Duration is matched to your run on purpose — it preserves the time-on-feet habit without adding impact.
  - Easy on the bike should feel easy on the run. Mouth-breathing, can't hold a sentence = past easy.
  - This is conservative because the ankle is symptom-free at rest, not because it's been load-tested. Treat any during-session sensation as information, not something to push through.

The 30-minute fallback notes cover what to cover if the slot has to be shortened or the therapist is unavailable.

What the caps can and cannot tell us

What we can read off the caps directly:
  - Maximum total spend exposure: $15,000 (six-week shape) or $8,000 (fallback).
  - Maximum admission count exposure: 50 or 25 admitted workspaces.
  - Worst-case implied $/admit if both limits bind simultaneously: $300 (50-shape) and $320 (25-shape). These are pivot points, not ceilings or expected values.
  - If the admission cap binds first, the realized $/admit is below the pivot (channel delivered admits cheaper than the pivot).
  - If the spend cap binds first, the realized $/admit is above the pivot, but admission count comes in under the cap.

What the caps cannot tell us:
  - Expected $/admit, expected admission count, or which cap binds first. Both shapes are deliberately underdetermined on direction.
  - Anything about downstream behavior — day-7 first integration rate, paid-active conversion, refund-adjusted collected cash, or account-level support effort. The caps shape exposure to those outcomes; they don't predict them.
  - Anything about payback period or LTV/CAC. Refund-adjusted collected cash requires a complete collection window we don't yet have.

What the $300 and $320 ratios are not:
  - Not cost-per-acquisition. CPA requires an expected count and an expected spend.
  - Not a $/admit ceiling. The cap structure lets $/admit run above $300 if the spend cap is the binding constraint.
  - Not a forecast, target, or go/no-go threshold. The pivot is a mechanical artifact of paired caps.

Information value vs exposure: 50-shape vs 25-shape

The 50-shape has roughly 1.875x the spend exposure ($15K vs $8K) and 2x the admission exposure (50 vs 25) of the 25-shape. Per the cap pivots, it carries a slightly lower worst-case per-admit ($300 vs $320), but more absolute downside.

Information tradeoffs:
  - If the admit cap binds first on either shape, the 50-shape yields more admits to study downstream (50 vs 25), which directly improves precision on day-7 first-integration rate and any cohort cut. The 25-shape yields less.
  - If the spend cap binds first on either shape, we learn that the channel is admission-constrained at the realized rate, but we don't get a clean $/admit. The 50-shape admits a wider range of realized rates before binding the spend cap because the spend ceiling is higher.
  - Neither shape resolves channel efficiency. Both bind on whichever constraint is tighter; the cap ratio tells us which side binds, not the underlying admit rate.

Sample-size resolution (binary indicator, illustrative):
  - At N=25, standard error on a binary indicator near p=0.4 is roughly 9.8 percentage points — a 10-point move is hard to attribute to the channel vs noise.
  - At N=50, the same SE drops to about 6.9 percentage points — a 10-point move is still noisy but materially more readable.
  - This is the cleanest case for the 50-shape if admits come in. If the spend cap binds first, realized N will be smaller and that advantage shrinks.

Operating-indicator discipline

Day-7 first integration is the leading operating indicator we'll read during the test. It is observable inside the test window and tracks to paid-active and retention in the organic cohort, so it gives us an early read on whether paid admits look like organic admits or like a different population.

Defer mature claims until three windows are complete:
  - Paid-active status complete window. We can't claim "this channel produces paid workspaces" until we observe paid conversion through its full window.
  - Refund-adjusted collected cash complete window. Gross collected minus refunds requires refund cycles to close; calling LTV or payback before that is premature.
  - Account-level support effort complete window. Support load per admit needs its own observation window before any efficiency claim.

Three-value structure
  V1 light — floor strip only (warm)
  V2 mid   — wall + interior field around Kibo (cool, passive, recessive)
  V3 dark — Kibo's body mass (slightly warmer than V2, never lighter)

  Separation comes from V2 receding hard so V3 reads dark against it. Do not give Kibo a "warmer" mix than the background — give the background less chroma.

Mixes (three pigments, no others)
  Floor light       — yellow ochre + tiny burnt sienna (warm gold)
  Cool shadow field — ultramarine + a touch of burnt sienna. The burnt sienna neutralizes the blue into a chromatic gray. Pure ultramarine would compete with Kibo's mix (same pigment in both) and would not recede. This passive pair is what makes the background disappear.
  Kibo base         — ultramarine + burnt sienna, slightly burnt-sienna heavy. Dark neutral with hidden warmth.
  Kibo deepest      — same mix loaded thicker. One pass, no glaze.

  Same two pigments in different ratios do all the work. No fourth color needed.

Painting order
  1. Dampen just the floor-strip zone; drop the warm gold. Let it settle. This is the only warm note in the painting — anchor it first so every later pass can stay cool.
  2. While the paper is evenly damp (not pooling), lay the cool gray shadow around where Kibo will sit. Let the edge where cat meets shadow stay soft on the contact side — the curled silhouette into shadow stays unresolved.
  3. Define Kibo with the dark mix in one confident pass for the bulk of the body. One firm blot on the brush, light-to-broad strokes, no chasing the edge.
  4. One thicker touch for the deepest accent — the curve of his back, the tucked paw fold. Then stop.

Stopping point
  Stop the moment the surface dulls. Any return on the dark coat after dull lifts pigment into a chalky bloom and flattens exactly the depth you want. The unresolved boundary between Kibo and the shadow is not an unfinished passage — it is the separation. The value gap does the work; you do not need to draw the edge. If it feels like you left something out, the painting is probably right.
