TOMORROW MORNING (May 6) CHECKLIST

  - Eat a normal breakfast — the office said eat normally, so don't skip. Something filling is smart because you probably won't want a real meal again until numbness wears off later.
  - Take any regular medications on your normal schedule, unless the office told you otherwise.
  - Hydrate normally through the morning.
  - Brush and floss before you go. A clean mouth helps; the hygienist will likely do a quick rinse.
  - Bring: photo ID, insurance card, payment method, your phone.
  - If you have a medication list not already on file, bring a copy.
  - Plan to arrive by 8:20am (10 minutes before 8:30).
  - Wear comfortable clothes — you'll be reclined in the chair for a while.
  - Local anesthetic alone typically doesn't impair driving, so a ride isn't required. Bring one if it would make you more comfortable.

PRACTICAL PRECAUTIONS

  Before tomorrow:
    - Chew on the left side for tough or crunchy foods; the painless marginal crack on the lower-right is exactly the spot you don't want to load with hard bites.
    - Skip very hot or very cold drinks on that side if they trigger even a faint twinge.

  After the appointment, until numbness fully wears off (usually 2–4 hours, sometimes longer):
    - Do NOT eat or drink anything hot. You can't accurately feel temperature yet and can scald your lip, cheek, or tongue without noticing.
    - Do NOT chew on the treated side. It's very easy to bite the cheek or tongue and not realize until the feeling returns.
    - Be mindful when talking and smiling — the numb lip and tongue can catch themselves.

  For the next 24–48 hours after numbness resolves:
    - Some cold and pressure sensitivity on the new filling is normal (see below).
    - Chew on the opposite side if anything feels tender.
    - Skip very sticky or hard foods on that side (caramel, taffy, ice, hard nuts, crusty bread) for a day or two.

EASY FOODS WHILE NUMB

  Cool or room-temperature, soft, no real chewing needed:
    - Yogurt, applesauce, pudding
    - Smoothies or milkshakes
    - Lukewarm (not hot) oatmeal, mashed potatoes, scrambled eggs
    - Lukewarm soup — test temperature on your hand, not your still-numb mouth
    - Cool water between bites

  Avoid: hot coffee/tea, anything that requires real chewing, crunchy things, chewing gum.

ORDINARY SENSITIVITY vs. CALL THE DENTIST

  Normal — no need to worry:
    - Soreness at the injection site or in the jaw for a day or two
    - Cold sensitivity on the new filling that fades within seconds once the cold is gone
    - Mild tenderness when biting that improves day by day over 1–2 weeks
    - Brief twinges with very cold or very sweet for the first week or two
    - Gum tenderness where the clamp or band rested

  Call the dentist (next business day is fine):
    - Bite feels uneven or "high" — usually a quick adjustment solves it
    - Cold or pressure sensitivity that is clearly getting worse after the first 2–3 days instead of better
    - Sharp pain on biting that doesn't settle within a couple of weeks
    - Filling feels loose, rough at the edge, or comes out
    - Persistent dull ache that isn't gradually improving over 1–2 weeks

  Call sooner (same day):
    - Swelling of the gum, face, or jaw
    - Fever
    - Throbbing, spontaneous pain — especially pain that wakes you up at night
    - Numbness that has not resolved after roughly 6 hours

  Seek urgent or emergency care:
    - Swelling that makes swallowing or breathing difficult
    - Allergic-type reaction — rash, hives, swelling of the face/throat, or trouble breathing (call 911 or go to the ER)

Pan: one large skillet with a lid. Plan ~25 min; cleanup is the one skillet.

Approximate amounts (2 servings)
  Gnocchi: ~12 oz (about 2/3 of the 17.6 oz pkg)
  Cherry tomatoes: most of the pint, halved (~12 oz)
  Baby spinach: all 5 oz
  Garlic: 2–3 cloves, thinly sliced or minced
  Olive oil: 2 tbsp to start, small drizzle to finish
  Parmesan: 1/3–1/2 cup, finely grated
  Salt, black pepper; optional pinch of red pepper flakes

Sequence
  0:00  Mise en place — halve tomatoes, slice garlic, grate parm. (Saves the most time.)
  5:00  Skillet, medium heat, 2 tbsp olive oil. Garlic in; cook 30–60 sec until fragrant, not browned.
  6:00  Tomatoes in with a pinch of salt. Cook 5–7 min, stirring now and then, until they soften and start to burst.
 13:00  Add the gnocchi straight from the package (no boil needed). Stir to coat, then pour in ~1/4 cup water.
 14:00  Cover. Cook 6–8 min, lifting the lid once to stir, until gnocchi are tender and the liquid is mostly absorbed. Uncover for the last 1–2 min if you want light crisping on edges.
 21:00  Stir in the spinach; it wilts in ~1 min. Off heat.
 22:00  Add most of the parm, a few grinds of pepper, optional chili flakes. Toss; taste for salt.
 24:00  Plate, finish with the remaining parm and a small drizzle of olive oil.

Notes
  - Use only a splash of water — gnocchi release starch; too much makes it gluey.
  - If tomatoes are very juicy, skip the water or just use 1–2 tbsp.
  - Leftover gnocchi: keep dry in the bag, use tomorrow pan-fried with butter and sage, or in soup.

Three-value plan — mix these in three palette wells before touching paper:

  V1 Pale cool — ultramarine + a touch of burnt sienna (about 8:1), heavy water. The interior shadow field.
  V2 Mid neutral — ultramarine + burnt sienna (about 1:1), medium water. The bottle body mass.
  V3 Deep — ultramarine-heavy + burnt sienna (about 2:1), minimal water. Core shadow and deepest accents.

Yellow ochre is reserve pigment only — drop into V1 last if the interior shadow reads too cold, or use a hairline of pure ochre at the warm edge of the highlight to set it off. Never use it to "warm up" the bottle body.

Mixing order: pre-mix all three values first. Ultramarine into the well first, then burnt sienna in. Adding burnt sienna into ultramarine (not the reverse) keeps the granulation from going chalky.

Edge strategy:

  Hard edges — bottle silhouette, cast shadow line, the lit edge of the reflected highlight against the dark body. Dry paper, loaded brush, single stroke. Don't go back.

  Soft edges — bottle body falling into shadow, interior shadow gradient on the wall. Paint into a damp (not flooded) wash, or soften with a clean damp brush before the stroke dries.

  The reflected window highlight: hard on the side where the window frame cuts, soft where it curves off the glass.

Preserve the highlight:

  Reserve paper white from the pencil stage — sketch the highlight shape and never cross it.

  If the surrounding neutral drifts in, lift immediately with a damp brush while still wet; don't rewet the highlight zone later.

  The highlight pops by value separation (it's the only value 9–10 in the field), not by added white or rework. If it dims, the problem is V2/V3 around it being too pale — deepen those, don't repaint the highlight.

Stop condition:

  Squint test passes — three values read clearly at arm's length, highlight is the brightest thing on the page.

  "Quiet" edges stay quiet — soft transitions left as-is, not tidied up. Quiet is an unresolved boundary, not a finish to chase.

Both critiques land. Quick sharpening, plus a structural issue:

On the opening prompt — the problem isn't just the disclosure pressure. "Hardest thing you have overcome" forces a narrative arc (adversity → resolution) before students have any practice writing. It also front-loads vulnerability: in 5 minutes, students either go abstract/generic to protect themselves, or write something real and then have to read it aloud in front of peers 25 minutes later. Either outcome trains them wrong. A prompt that demands specificity without demanding hardship — e.g., a scene where something ordinary goes slightly wrong — gets the same craft work (concrete detail, stakes, voice) without the exposure tax.

On "interesting" — that's a feeling-judgment, not a craft criterion. Peer feedback under that frame collapses to "I liked it" / "it was cool." Worse, the feedback step happens before students have any shared model of what openings do, so they're improvising criteria. If you keep peer feedback at all, it needs structured prompts (e.g., "what's the first specific detail?" / "where did you slow down?") and ideally runs *after* they've seen one or two examples to anchor on.

The thing neither critique touches: there's zero explicit teaching in the 35 minutes. Draft → feedback → revise is a sound sequence, but with no model of what good openings are and what useful feedback looks like, students are guessing at all three stages. That's the design problem underneath the two prompts.

==============================================================
35-MINUTE WORKSHOP REDESIGN
Opening-Paragraph Workshop (Hardship Prompt)
For: Marcus's HS senior English class
==============================================================

Standing frame (carries over from prior session)
  - Don't pressure hardship disclosure. Give students a genuine choice between an ORDINARY moment and a DIFFICULT moment, and let either carry the scene.
  - Feedback has to be craft-specific. "Is it interesting?" is too vague — it produces feeling-based replies. Use the four criteria below.
  - The opening is the student's to write. The teacher models, peers practice; the student revises and keeps authorship.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
TIME BLOCKS (35 min total)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

[0:00 – 0:03]  OPEN + OPT-OUT (3 min)
  - Name the goal: by the end, every student has written one concrete
    scene and rewritten their opening paragraph using peer feedback.
  - Read the opt-out aloud:

      "You may choose an ORDINARY moment (a meal, a walk, a chore,
       a waiting room) or a DIFFICULT moment (a loss, a conflict,
       a failure). Both are valid. If you don't want to write about
       anything personal, write about a place you don't know well —
       a hotel lobby at 6 a.m., a laundromat at midnight, a bus
       stop in rain — and put a person you've never met in it.
       There is no obligation to disclose anything real."

  - Distribute the choice slip (see below).

[0:03 – 0:04]  CHOICE SLIP (1 min)
  Each student marks one:
    [ ] Ordinary moment
    [ ] Difficult moment
    [ ] Third-person place, unknown person (the off-ramp)

[0:04 – 0:14]  SCENE DEVELOPMENT (10 min)
  - Teacher models for 90 seconds on the board, thinking aloud:
      * one concrete sensory anchor (what you can touch/see/hear)
      * one small action that reveals character
      * the first line, written last
  - Students write one scene (8–10 sentences) in silence.
  - At 0:12, teacher says: "Two minutes left — land the last line
    in the middle of an action, not on a reflection."

[0:14 – 0:23]  STRUCTURED FEEDBACK EXCHANGE (9 min)
  Pairs. Partner A reads partner B's opening paragraph (first 3–5
  sentences) aloud once, silently. Then both fill the feedback card
  together. Swap at 0:18. Both partners get a completed card back.

  FEEDBACK CARD — four craft criteria, each scored 1–2:
    1. SENSORIAL ANCHOR — Is there at least one thing I can see,
       hear, touch, smell, or taste in the first three sentences?
    2. ACTION OVER ABSTRACTION — Does the opening show a person
       doing something, rather than telling me they felt something?
    3. SPECIFICITY — Could I picture this place and person, or is
       it generic ("a room," "a guy")?
    4. TRUST THE READER — Is anything explained that the scene
       already shows? (Circle the word or phrase, don't fix it.)

  After the score, each partner writes ONE sentence:
    "The strongest move in your opening is __________."
    "One thing to try in the rewrite is __________."

[0:23 – 0:32]  REWRITE THE OPENING (9 min)
  - Students rewrite ONLY the opening paragraph, using the
    feedback card. They may keep, cut, or change everything.
  - Mid-point check at 0:27: "If you got a 'trust the reader'
    note, that's usually a 3–5 word cut. If you got a low
    specificity score, that's a concrete noun."
  - At 0:30, soft close: "You have two minutes. Stop in the middle
    of a sentence if you have to — incomplete is fine."

[0:32 – 0:35]  CLOSE (3 min)
  - One sentence on the board, attributed to no one:
      "An opening is a promise about what the reader will see."
  - Collect choice slips (just to confirm the off-ramp was used;
    do not read them aloud or use them for grading).
  - Homework: finish the opening at home if unfinished; bring
    the full draft next class.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
WHAT'S DIFFERENT FROM THE ORIGINAL
----------------------------------------------------------------------
- Three real choices (ordinary / difficult / off-ramp) instead of
  a hardship-shaped default.
- One concrete scene gets developed in class, not a whole essay.
- Feedback uses four named craft criteria, not "is it interesting."
- Rewrite window is protected (9 min) and bounded (opening
  paragraph only).
- Volunteer read-alouds dropped — they were the main vehicle for
  pressuring disclosure.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
WHAT'S DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED
----------------------------------------------------------------------
- 35-minute total length.
- Pair work in the middle block.
- The opening paragraph is the unit of revision.
- Teacher models briefly, then students write in silence.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
NOTES FOR MARCUS
----------------------------------------------------------------------
- The off-ramp (third-person place, unknown person) is the
  explicit opt-out. It's not a punishment path — frame it as
  "a different kind of challenge."
- If a student picks "difficult" and the scene gets raw, the
  feedback card keeps the conversation on craft, not on whether
  the story is "sad enough."
- You don't need to read choice slips. Their only job is to let
  you know the off-ramp is being used so you can adjust next
  time's modeling examples.

Mild edge buckle on a fully dry 140-lb cold-press sheet with an intact paint film is the easy case. A slow dry press usually resolves it without ever touching the painted surface. Conservative sequence, no heat, no iron, no adhesive, no contact moisture.

Materials
  Smooth rigid surface: glass sheet or smooth melamine board (no grain transfer)
  Clean dry blotter or smooth cotton-rag paper
  Light even weight: 2–3 books, ~5–10 lb total, flat-distributed
  Clean hands; lift, never slide
  Optional, phase 2 only: a sealed plastic box or large zip bag, plus a small dish and a piece of blotter for an off-painting humidifier

Sequence

  1. Inspect under raking light now. Confirm no flaking, lifting, or pigment shift. Photograph the buckle — your before reference.

  2. Dry press, cycle 1:
       a. Painting face-up on the rigid surface.
       b. Dry blotter over the painting.
       c. Light even weight on top.
       d. 24–48 hours at normal room humidity (40–55%).

  3. Lift from the board, re-inspect under raking light. If flat or near-flat, store between clean sheets in the portfolio laid flat; don't stack weight on the closed portfolio.

  4. If still buckled, run a second identical 24–48 hour dry cycle before escalating.

  5. If still buckled, ambient-humidity relaxation only — no contact moisture:
       a. Painting face-up on its board inside the sealed box or bag.
       b. Lightly damp blotter on a dish at the floor of the box, well separated from the sheet — humidity transfers through air only.
       c. Close. 30–60 minutes.
       d. Remove immediately to a fresh dry blotter stack with light weight for 24–48 hours.

  6. Re-inspect under raking light. If still buckled or any new distortion appeared, stop and take it to a conservator.

Stop — go to a professional conservator if any of the following:
  Buckle does not improve after 2 dry cycles plus 1 humidity cycle (about 5–7 days total).
  Buckle worsens, or new cockling, ripple, or corner curl appears anywhere.
  Any pigment lift, tide line, color shift, bloom, or tackiness on the paint film.
  The sheet rocks on a flat table, or the paint film near the buckle looks stressed — that's no longer mild.
  The sheet is fragile (old, prior restoration, mixed media, wax or gouache resist) — start with a conservator instead of the home sequence.

Two cautions throughout: keep hands clean and dry, and lift the sheet — never slide it across any surface — to avoid a micro-tear along the buckle crest.

Smoky smashed chickpea tacos with cabbage slaw — dinner tonight + one lunch portion tomorrow. Cook all the chickpeas now; flavor improves overnight.

1. Drain the chickpeas. Smash in a bowl with a fork — about half mashed, half left whole for texture.
2. Warm a slick of oil in a skillet over medium-high. Add 1 minced garlic clove, stir 30 seconds, then 1 tsp smoked paprika and the chickpeas. Cook 7–8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the edges crisp and dry out a bit. Season with salt and pepper, squeeze in half the lime, off heat.
3. Slaw: thinly shred about half the cabbage, slice 1 scallion, toss with 2 tbsp yogurt, the other half-lime's juice, salt, pepper.
4. Split both the chickpea mix and the slaw in half. One half assembles tonight, the other half goes into a sealed container for tomorrow (holds 1 day easily).
5. Char 2 tortillas over a gas flame or in a dry hot pan. Fill with chickpea mix, slaw, an extra spoon of yogurt. Eat.
6. Tomorrow: char the other 2 tortillas, fill with the cold chickpea mix (or warm it 1 minute in a dry pan if you'd rather), top with reserved slaw and yogurt.

About 15 minutes, one pan, one bowl. The lime-yogurt-scallion slaw does the work a salsa would, and the chickpea mix stays good cold — so tomorrow's lunch is just reheating tortillas, no real cooking.

Serves 2. About 20 minutes. One skillet.

Ingredients (chickpeas + cabbage only, plus pantry basics):
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 1/2 small head green cabbage, shredded thin (~3 cups)
- 1.5 tbsp oil
- 1/2 tsp salt, several grinds of pepper
- 6 small tortillas (the "taco" vessel)
- Optional: lime, hot sauce

Sequence:

0-5 min  Prep: shred cabbage, drain chickpeas well, pat them dry with a towel (dry = crispy later).

5-12 min  Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add cabbage, salt, pepper. Cook 5-7 min, stirring now and then, until wilted with a few browned edges. Scoop into a bowl.

12-20 min Same skillet, add remaining 1/2 tbsp oil. Add chickpeas. Smash roughly half with a fork or potato masher so you get a ground-meat-like texture alongside whole ones. Cook 6-8 min, stirring occasionally, until some chickpeas are crisp and golden. Return cabbage to the pan, toss 1 min, adjust salt.

Meanwhile warm tortillas: 10-15 sec per side in the dry skillet (or directly over a gas flame). Fill, squeeze lime, hot sauce.

Minimal cleanup:
- One large skillet
- One cutting board + knife
- One mixing bowl
- A fork or masher
Towel-drying the chickpeas is the only "extra" step; skip it and they steam instead of crisp.

Notes: if you want the chickpeas + cabbage to actually taste like taco filling rather than just be chickpeas and cabbage, you need acid and heat — lime at the end plus a pinch of cumin or chili flakes is the smallest possible departure from "only those ingredients." Without it, expect pleasantly savory but quiet.

75-MINUTE STUDY SEQUENCE — KIBO, CURLED, WARM/COOL LIGHT

LIMITED PALETTE (pre-mix before timer starts):
  Burnt sienna, ultramarine, burnt umber. Water only — no white.
  Three wells, named so you stop thinking about color:
    A = warm light: burnt sienna + a touch of ultramarine (~8:1), thinned to tea
    B = cool mid: ultramarine + burnt sienna, roughly equal, thinned slightly heavier than A
    C = dark mass: burnt umber dominant + ultramarine to deepen, thinned to cream — two strengths on the palette (working C and concentrated C)

THREE-VALUE PLAN:
  Light  = warm reflected edge on coat + lit rug patches (A)
  Mid    = cool window-shadow side of coat + cast shadow on rug (B)
  Dark   = coat mass in TWO internal values — never one flat silhouette (C, both strengths)

MIXING ORDER ON PAPER (0–55 min):
  1. A first. Establish the warm reflected edge as a thin band along the lit contour and a few small rug warmth passages. Wet-on-dry. This band is doing most of the picture's work — paint it, then leave it. No glaze of extra orange later; that is the trap.
  2. B second. Cool shadow on the coat's window side and the rug cast shadow. Wet-on-dry, let it sit. Do not soften into A — the seam between them is value separation, which is what makes the warm edge read at all.
  3. C last, in two passes. First a broader working-C pass for the body shape while still damp-soft; second a smaller concentrated-C pass for the deepest pockets (under chin, ear interior, tail curl, eye sockets). Two values internally, not one.

EDGE STRATEGY:
  Body perimeter: lost/soft on the warm-lit side, slightly firmer on the shadow side. Apply your standing rule — 1 firm blot, light broad stroke, 20-second hold, one touch, no return after dull. If a seam wants to stay quiet, it stays quiet: per your rule, that is unresolved boundary (compositional), not underwork. Do not "finish" it with a second pass.
  Warm reflected edge: paint as a band, then stop. Value separation against the dark mass is the whole move — added saturation will read as costume, not light.
  Hard edges: only the eye-line, ear tip, and nose bridge. Everywhere else, soft.

FACE PRIORITIES (55–70 min, single short sitting):
  Eyes: two small concentrated-C dabs with a hard brush, leaving one pinpoint of paper-white as catchlight. One touch each. If a dab blooms, leave it — do not chase.
  Nose: one soft mid-value shape. No outline.
  Muzzle / whiskers: protect paper-white. If lost, stop and let dry — do not lift back in.
  Fur direction: one or two thin mid strokes near brow and cheek only. Do not stroke the whole face.
  Late-stage warning: if you find yourself "improving" the face, the face is already done. The danger window is the final ten minutes.

STOP CONDITION (75 min, hard):
  Walk away when ALL are true:
    - the warm reflected edge reads against the dark coat with no added warmth on top
    - the coat shows at least two internal values, not a single silhouette
    - eyes, nose, and one ear interior are placed, even if imperfect
    - you have not touched the face in the last 5 minutes
  If 75 hits with any unmet, that is the loss you accept. Do not extend. The unfinished read is the value separation working — quiet edges are composition, not incomplete work.

TIME MAP (for reference, not a leash):
  0–10  prep, pre-mix, light pencil placement of curl
  10–25 A and B passes
  25–55 C in two strengths, lost edges set
  55–70 face accents only, single sitting
  70–75 stop check + sign

- Only deductible + coinsurance on allowed medical are counted toward the OOP max (no separate copays modeled).
- Preventive care = $0 under both plans (per plan inputs).

```
PPO             $192         $1,000   20%     $4,500    $0

```

Annual premiums

- HDHP: 118 × 12 = $1,416/yr
- Premium gap: PPO costs $888/yr more in premium alone.

Effective fixed annual cost before care (premiums paid − employer HSA contribution):
- PPO: $2,304 − $0 = $2,304
- HDHP: $1,416 − $900 = $516
- HDHP advantage: $1,788/yr

Cost examples at allowed nonpreventive medical expense
Member total OOP = deductible + coinsurance on the amount above the deductible, capped at OOP max.

```
Allowed        PPO OOP   HDHP OOP   PPO all-in   HDHP all-in   HDHP−PPO
$1,000         $1,000    $1,000    $3,304      $1,516        −$1,788  (HDHP saves)
$2,500         $1,300    $2,050    $3,604      $2,566        −$1,038  (HDHP saves)
$5,000         $1,800    $2,300    $4,104      $2,816        −$1,288  (HDHP saves)
```

Where the crossover actually sits: solving HDHP total = PPO total in the region where both have hit their deductibles gives ≈ $5,880 of allowed nonpreventive medical. TIRE PRESSURE PLAN — Sat Oct 17, 2026

Frame: a 6 psi gap between FR and the other three is too wide to be pure weather — all four should drop similarly on a cool morning. Working hypothesis is "weather + a small slow leak in FR." The 2-3 day cold recheck is what tells you which. Until you know, treat FR as potentially underinflated and avoid highway driving on it.

PHASE 1 — Inflate tonight or first thing Sunday morning

  - Use a digital gauge if you have one; analog stick gauges vary 1-2 psi.
  - Inflate FR to 35 psi COLD. That is the door-placard spec, not the max on the sidewall.
  - "Cold" means the tire has been driven less than a mile in the past 3 hours, or has sat overnight.
  - If you inflate now and the tire is warm from today's driving, fill to about 38 psi; recheck cold in the morning and bleed back to 35 if it creeps above.
  - Top off the other three to 35 while you're at it (they're 34-35, optional, not urgent).

PHASE 2 — Same-day check (today)

  - Wait 2-3 hours after inflating. Recheck FR. It won't be true cold, but you want to confirm the valve isn't hissing air back out.
  - If FR is steady or only down 1 psi: good. Plan the morning recheck.
  - If FR has dropped 3+ psi in a few hours: go straight to the "Shop today" rules below.

PHASE 3 — Cold rechecks (the actual test)

  - Sunday 10/18 morning, before driving: gauge FR. Note the psi.
    33-35 psi cold: weather was the main factor. Continue to next morning.
    30-32 psi cold: small slow leak. Drive minimally; book a shop this week before the airport run.
    Below 28 psi cold: definite leak. See red flags below.
  - Repeat Monday morning before any driving. A drop of more than 1-2 psi/day across two mornings = slow leak confirmed. Get to a shop before pickup day.
  - Two consecutive mornings where FR reads 33-35 psi cold = you're fine, drive normally.

PHASE 4 — Local-driving limits until FR holds cold

  - Under 45 mph.
  - Under 5 miles per trip.
  - No highway, no long commute.
  - Avoid potholes, curbs, and hard cornering.
  - Recheck pressure every morning before driving.

PHASE 5 — Before Mom's airport pickup

  - Day before: cold gauge check on FR. Must read 33+ psi.
  - Morning of: cold gauge check again. If 33+ psi cold, fine to drive normally including highway.
  - If below 33 cold on either day: top off, then judge based on how much it dropped since the previous morning. Anything below 30 cold means drive directly to a shop rather than to the airport.
  - Don't drive to the airport on a tire you're topping off between cold checks — an underinflated highway tire is the failure mode that causes blowouts.

STOP DRIVING (put on the spare if you have one, otherwise call a tow) if any of these:

  - Visible bulge, crack, blister, or split in the sidewall or tread.
  - Hissing sound, or bubbles when you spray soapy water on the valve and the rim edge.
  - Pressure below 25 psi cold per the gauge, not the TPMS light.
  - New vibration, pull to one side, or thumping that wasn't there before.
  - The tire looks visibly flatter than the others when parked, or feels "squishy" when you push on it.

GO TO A SHOP TODAY (don't keep monitoring) if:

  - A nail, screw, or sharp object is visibly embedded. Do NOT pull it — it may be the only thing plugging the hole. Drive slowly to the shop with it in place.
  - FR drops 3+ psi between any two checks taken within a few hours.
  - FR is below 28 psi on a cold morning.
  - You can hear air leaking.
  - The rim is bent, deeply scratched, or the valve stem is wet or cracked.

DECISION RULES, ONE LINE EACH

  - Inflate FR to 35 cold tonight or by 9 AM Sunday.
  - Two consecutive mornings at 33-35 psi cold = safe, drive normally.
  - Any morning below 33 cold, or a drop of more than 1-2 psi/day between mornings = book a shop before the airport day.
  - No highway driving on FR until you have at least one stable cold recheck.
  - When in doubt, slow local driving only, and recheck.

Block layout
  1:30–1:45   Setup (still life, water, paper taped, brushes out)
  1:45–3:15   Paired exercise (90 min)
  3:15–4:00   Cleanup and unhurried conversation

Exercise (90 min, two passes around one pause)

1:45–2:10   Pass 1 — three-value study (25 min)
  Pick your three values silently before you start: lightest, middle, darkest. Don't name them aloud yet.
  Spend the first ~5 minutes on two or three tiny thumbnails to find your value map, then commit to the sheet.
  One wet pass of the whole composition in those three values. Light first, then mid, then dark. Hold 20 seconds, one touch. No return after dull.
  Each of you assigns the values differently — that's the point. Mom's pear might be her mid; yours might be your dark. Same setup, different maps.

2:10–2:25   Midpoint pause — compare, don't correct (15 min)
  Brushes down. Stand the two boards side by side in the window light.
  Talk about decisions, not fixes. "I went with…", "I noticed…", "the towel surprised me because…". No "you should…" or "try this instead."
  If a quiet edge shows up, leave it — it's compositional, not unfinished. If you're tempted to warm it up, counter with value separation, not added pigment.

2:25–2:55   Pass 2 — same three values, more deliberate (30 min)
  Same three values, applied with more intention: pear form, bowl curvature, the folds where the towel bunches.
  One pear, one bowl, one folded towel. Resist adding anything — a stem, a shadow cast, a second pear. The study is the constraint.
  Brush-moisture rule still in force. Blot once, then light-to-broad, or twice to seam. No bloom.

2:55–3:10   Quiet finish (15 min)
  Last ten minutes are for one or two value corrections only. No new shapes, no new colors.
  If either of you finishes earlier, stop — don't push into the next phase just to keep pace.

3:10–3:15   Wind down
  Boards flat, paper taped in place to dry. Brushes into rinse water. Step back once more.

3:15–4:00   Cleanup
  Rinse and blot brushes. Pull tape while damp or fully dry — your call. Wipe palettes, refill or empty water, move the still life back to the kitchen. Tea, conversation, the drying boards on the counter.

Notes
  Palette choices stay independent. Bring what each of you likes; don't try to match.
  The exercise is about seeing three values in shared light, not about getting the pear "right."
  If a moment needs more time, the midpoint pause is the one that can stretch. Pass 1 and Pass 2 should not.

0. Inventory before copying anything
   - List the scan folder and the mounted scanner card: counts, sizes, names.
   - Flag any files that exist on the card but not on the laptop — those are the ones most at risk if you clear the card too early.
   - Note front/back pairings (filename convention, or a tiny pairing log: e.g. IMG_0412_front.jpg ↔ IMG_0412_back.jpg). Keep this log alongside the scans.

1. Make the laptop the single source of truth
   - If the card has files missing from the laptop, copy them in with `cp -p` (preserves timestamps; does not touch image metadata).
   - Do not rename. Do not run any image tool, organizer, or `exiftool`.

2. Hash the source
   - In the scan folder: `sha256sum * > MANIFEST_2026-10-29.sha256`
   - Store the MANIFEST inside the scan folder and copy it forward with every backup so the receiver can re-verify.

3. Copy 1 — encrypted external SSD
   - Unlock and mount the SSD.
   - `rsync -avh --dry-run` first to preview, then the real run. `rsync -a` preserves filesystem metadata but never modifies image content or EXIF.
   - On the SSD, run `sha256sum -c MANIFEST_2026-10-29.sha256`. Every line must say OK. Any FAILED line means stop and re-copy that file before continuing.

4. Copy 2 — private cloud folder
   - Sync the scan folder into the cloud folder with your normal sync tool.
   - Verification here has to be byte-level, not just "sync finished":
     - List the remote: same file count and same total size as the laptop.
     - Download at least one full front/back pair and run `sha256sum -c` against the MANIFEST locally. Treat the sync tool's success message as necessary but not sufficient.
   - If your cloud tool does any on-the-fly processing/compression, replace "sync" with explicit upload + download + hash check so the copy is provably byte-identical.

5. Cross-check before touching the card
   - Counts match across laptop, SSD, and cloud.
   - SSD `sha256sum -c` is fully clean.
   - Cloud count/size match and the sampled pair's hashes match.
   - Front/back pairing visually re-confirmed for at least one pair (open both, confirm they belong together).

6. Clear the scanner card — only after step 5 is fully green
   - One last `sha256sum` of the card's contents compared to the MANIFEST (or to the laptop copies).
   - Then delete the card files (or reformat). Don't do this on a hunch; do it on a verified match.

Rules to hold throughout: no `exiftool`, no image editors, no "organize/rename" utilities; `cp -p` and `rsync -a` are safe — they preserve timestamps and permissions but never alter image metadata; original filenames and front/back pairings are preserved exactly as they are today.

Aim the beam at roughly 30–45° onto the paper, but offset it so the specular reflection off any wet wash is aimed past your opposite shoulder, not back at your eyes. That clears your line of sight and removes glare on glossy washes in one move.

2. Cut competing light. Drop the blind on the window side and kill the overhead room light for the rest of the block. Mixed color temperatures are what make values look "off" — a single dominant source is the only way to trust what you see. Make the switch once, at the start, not mid-wash.

3. Lock the lamp at neutral-daylight (~5000K). If your model shows a CRI rating, pick the higher one. Don't drop to warm for evening comfort; warm compresses value separation and shifts cools, which is exactly the confusion you're trying to avoid.

5. Calibration swatch. Tuck a small grayscale strip (or any printed neutral gray scale) at the edge of the work area. Glance at it before judging a value. If the grays read neutral, you're calibrated. If they look tinted, give your eyes another 30 seconds, or the lamp isn't where you think it is.

6. Diagnostic A/B when something looks wrong. Note what's off (too dark, muddy, cool?). Kill the lamp, look under ambient. If the problem persists, it's the painting. - Online: you pay $118 up front, then file an out-of-network claim with your vision carrier. The reimbursement rate is the missing number, and two consequences follow from it:
  - Cash flow: you carry the full $118 for 2-6 weeks until reimbursement clears.
  - Net cost depends on the rate. If the plan reimburses ~$80 of $118, online ends up ~$38 net, cheaper than in-network. If it reimburses ~$40, online ends up ~$78 net, more expensive than in-network.
- A separate-but-related question: is the online retailer actually in-network with your plan? If yes, the shop-style filing reappears and the comparison collapses back to a $7 gap. If no, you're in out-of-network territory regardless of the retailer's branding. This is the single biggest swing factor and is still unverified.
- Net: in-network is administratively free; online is administratively yours, and the dollar result is unknown until you check the out-of-network schedule and the retailer's network status.

DECEMBER 31 BENEFIT TIMING

- In-network: typical delivery is 5-10 business days. Ordered today (Nov 12), you'd land between Nov 19 and Nov 25. To protect a Dec 31 in-benefit delivery, ordering by ~Dec 15 is the safe cutoff — that gives the full 10 business days plus buffer. Comfortable margin.
- Online: AR coating is the long pole at 10-14 business days. Ordered Nov 12, you'd land between Nov 26 and Dec 2. To protect a Dec 31 in-benefit delivery, ordering by ~Dec 10-12 is the safe cutoff. Tighter margin; a single lab delay pushes you into January.
- Carrier rule varies: most vision plans key in-benefit on order date or service date, but some key on delivery date. If the rule is delivery-date and the AR lab slips, you lose the 2026 allowance entirely. Confirm before relying on a late-December online order.
- Waiting: pushes everything to the 2027 plan year.
  - You get a fresh frame allowance and new copays, but the 2027 design (allowance amount, covered lens tiers, online reimbursement rules, network retailer list, mid-year change window) hasn't been published yet. It could be more generous, less generous, or restructured around a different online-reimbursement model.
  - The current glasses remain adequate for distance with mild end-of-day blur, so a January order is operationally fine.
  - State prescription expiration: confirm how long a November 5, 2026 prescription is valid under Texas optometry law. If it expires before you're ready to order in 2027, you may need a new exam regardless of choice.

STILL UNVERIFIED (worth confirming before ordering either path)

- Online retailer's in-network vs out-of-network status with your specific plan
- Out-of-network reimbursement schedule (frame, lenses, AR coating each separately)
- Whether the online retailer's 30-day window covers prescription errors, coating defects, and fit issues — in writing
- Whether your plan keys benefit year on order date or delivery date
- 2027 plan design (allowance, online rules, network) — only relevant if you're leaning toward waiting

OPERATIONAL TAKE

The $7 is noise. The real question is whether you want the shop to carry the logistics (in-network) or whether the $7 saving plus any out-of-network reimbursement is worth 2-4 weeks of downtime, a self-filed claim, and self-managed fit (online). With the AR coating window tight against Dec 31, in-network has materially more timing slack. With your current glasses adequate and the prescription change optional, waiting remains a defensible third path if the 2027 plan design is announced before your current prescription expires.

Comparing the three options against the four dimensions, plus where each lands on your retained authorities and the 10 escalation triggers.

OPTION A — Rotating deep recheck of one evidence lane after closure

- Direct evidence-system contact: HIGH. You open records, replay the closure trail, verify source fields end-to-end.
- Duplicates Owen's source-completeness work: HEAVY. Closure is Owen's lane under the 4-condition gate. A second-seat recheck is the same work twice. The 11/17 calibration direction is the inverse — Owen strengthens cert + exact through-dates; this asks you to re-lift what he just lifted.
- Owner-role ambiguity: HIGH. Lane owner certifies closure; you redo the cert. Owners will read this as "Riley is the real closer," quietly relitigating whether they actually own the lane.
- Second approval queue risk: HIGHEST. By construction a second gate that fires after the first. Even framed as a spot recheck, owners will wait on you before shipping.

OPTION B — Targeted sample from that month's exceptions

- Direct evidence-system contact: MODERATE. Real contact, bounded population — exceptions are edge-of-population by definition.
- Duplicates Owen's source-completeness work: PARTIAL. Exceptions usually already passed closure with a flag, or already hit one of your triggers (customer correction, incident stop, lane-owner flag). The audit re-reads what already surfaced — useful for pattern, weak on unseen gaps.
- Owner-role ambiguity: MODERATE. Can read as a quiet competence check on whoever raised the exception, or as "flag more so Riley doesn't sample me."
- Second approval queue risk: MODERATE. Exceptions already have a path (trigger → Riley). A monthly sample of the same population is a second pass on already-known cases.

OPTION C — Small cross-lane trace of governed fields and claim treatment

- Direct evidence-system contact: MODERATE-HIGH, distributed across systems. You pull from two or more lanes simultaneously, trace how a governed field is sourced in one lane and treated in another, and follow a claim from source through board/exec language.
- Duplicates Owen's source-completeness work: LOW. Cross-lane is by definition outside a single source-closure exercise. Owen's seat is per-source; this seat is per-claim across sources.
- Owner-role ambiguity: LOW. This is the seat the current structure leaves open — board-readiness, exec language, final-claim, definition change. The 11/17 calibration has Ines's next move as "surface cross-surface ambiguity earlier"; a cross-lane trace formalizes exactly that.
- Second approval queue risk: LOW. Nothing in the trace asks owners to wait on you. Findings land in your retained-authority lanes, not as closure gates.

MAPPING TO RETAINED AUTHORITY + TRIGGERS

Retained authority:
- A touches source fields — overlaps Owen, not your retained set.
- B touches exception patterns — light overlap with final-claim/exec-language when exceptions are claim-shaped.
- C directly exercises board-readiness, final-claim, exec-language, definition-change; secondarily causal/rev/forecast when claims turn on those.

Escalation trigger counterpart (the audit is for what did NOT trigger):
- A maps to triggers 1 (missing fields) and 10 (cert gap) — but those already route to Owen's closure, not to your audit.
- B maps to triggers 4 (customer correction), 5 (incident stop), 8 (lane-owner flag) — but those already escalated, so you're re-reading what you already saw.
- C maps to triggers 3 (cross-surface), 6 (exec language), 7 (definition change) — the three the audit is uniquely positioned to catch when nothing escalated. This is the complement the structure actually needs.

RECOMMENDATION

Carry Option C as the primary audit design, with a light sampling logic borrowed from B for cadence — pick 2–3 traces per month anchored against one rotating lane, so each lane gets attention quarterly and the trace stays cross-lane in character. A workable shape:

- One trace of governed-field consistency. Pick a field with an active definition (cohort boundary, "paid," a revenue recognition point), trace how it's sourced in two lanes, check whether cross-lane treatment matches the definition. Lands in your definition-change authority.
- One trace of claim treatment. Take a board- or exec-bound claim, follow it from source through framing, check whether exec-language and final-claim standards hold. Lands in board-readiness / exec-language / final-claim.
- Optional third trace, time permitting, on a causal/revenue/forecast claim where cross-lane sourcing affects the number. Lands in causal / rev / forecast.

Reject Option A outright in the proposal. It creates the owner ambiguity and second-queue risk the design is meant to prevent, and it points Owen's development the wrong way (your audit pulling closure back rather than Owen lifting cert).

Treat Option B as a sampling principle inside C, not a standalone option. Exceptions are still useful evidence when they show up in a trace, but the audit shouldn't be built around them.

PROPOSAL FRAMING NOTES

- The audit rotates by anchor, not by exhaustive coverage — each quarter covers all four lanes; each month is one lane's slice seen cross-lane.
- Audit outputs land in your retained-authority lanes, not closure decisions in owner lanes. Phrase outputs as "claim / field / definition observations for Riley," not "lane recheck results."
- Preserve the 10 triggers exactly as drafted. The audit is for what did not trigger; if the audit starts triggering the same set, you've built a second queue.
- State explicitly that the audit does not block closure. Closure ships on owner cert under Owen's gate; the audit observes and feeds your retained-authority work.
- One open question for 12/4: does an audit finding write back into a lane (e.g., a cross-surface observation goes to Ines for earlier surfacing per the 11/17 calibration) or stay Riley-internal until threshold? Flag this as a sub-decision rather than resolving it pre-proposal.

This is proposal-stage design. Nothing takes effect pre-amendment, and the audit shape should be revisable on the first 90 days of operation if the cross-lane traces surface something the on-paper design didn't predict.

Quick framing: the second edge means the reflector has stopped acting as fill and started acting as a second key light. Fix the setup, not the painting. Sequence below.

1. Lamp first, no reflector on the cup
   - Aim lamp ~30–45 degrees off your viewing axis, opposite your painting hand so wet glare doesn't hit your eye.
   - Set height so the cup's cast shadow length matches ordinary room light. Too low = long shadow and foreshortened lit side; too high = short hard shadow and crushed form.
   - Goal: one clean terminator on the form shadow, lit side reads as one midtone family.

2. Reflector at distance, fill only
   - Start foam-board 3–4x the cup's diameter away on the dark side, angled to bounce lamp light back into the form shadow.
   - Bring it in slowly. Stop the instant the dark side shows a smooth gradient from terminator to reflected edge — no second terminator.
   - If a second edge appears, back the reflector off until it disappears. Do not soften or thin the terminator to mask it.

3. Neutral-value check without wet-wash glare
   - Squint at the still life, then squint at the painting. Match value maps, not edges. One terminator on the cup should equal one terminator on the paper.
   - Or hold a small gray card beside the cup, not over the painting, and read the dark side against it.
   - View the painting at a low rake angle so wet specular skims off instead of bouncing back to your eye — this is the cheapest glare fix.

Stop condition (the discipline line, write it on a scrap if it helps):
- Stop adjusting the moment the cup shows one primary shadow with one terminator and a smooth dark-side gradient.
- Do not add or soften a wash to match the second edge the reflector is creating. That edge is a setup artifact, not in the cup.
- If a second edge shows up on the paper, the fix is to move the reflector, not to repaint. The painting is of the cup, not of the lighting.

THANKSGIVING DAY — RILEY 2PM / SAM LATE PLATE

ONE COOK, TWO PLATES. Active cooking about 1 hour. Two vessels only: one pot for stuffing, one full sheet pan for everything else. Oven stays at 425°F the whole time.

THE SEQUENCE

1. STUFFING (stovetop, do first while oven preheats, ~10 min)
   - 3 to 4 Tbsp butter in a small pot over medium heat
   - 2 minced garlic cloves, saute 30 sec
   - Add stock per box (usually 1.5 cups), bring to a simmer
   - Stir in stuffing mix, cover, off heat, rest 5 min. Leave covered on the stove.

2. OVEN 425°F — one parchment or foil-lined full sheet pan, three phases

   PHASE A — sweet potato + chicken together, 40 to 45 min
   - Halve the sweet potato lengthwise, brush cut side with butter and salt, place cut-side down on one end of the sheet pan
   - Pat the 4 thighs dry, season with salt, pepper, garlic powder, a squeeze of lemon
   - Place skin-up on the other end of the same pan (skin can drip near, not onto, the potato)
   - Middle rack, 425°F

   PHASE B — pull chicken at 175°F internal (about 35 to 40 min in)
   - Move thighs to a plate, tent foil, rest 10 min on the stovetop (carryover to about 180°F)
   - Leave sweet potato in if not yet tender

   PHASE C — green beans in the drippings, 12 to 14 min
   - Toss 12 oz trimmed beans with 1 Tbsp melted butter, 1 minced garlic clove, salt, pepper
   - Spread on the same pan, return to upper rack
   - Pull sweet potato when a fork goes in easily (about 45 to 55 min total)
   - Pull beans, squeeze half a lemon over, toss

3. FINISH
   - Re-warm stuffing covered on the stovetop, low, 3 to 5 min
   - Re-warm the two sweet potato halves briefly if they finished early (5 min at 350°F, or split open and reheat on the plate)
   - Plate both meals: 2 thighs each, half the sweet potato, half the beans, half the stuffing

TIMELINE (Thanksgiving Day, rough)

12:00 — Chicken out of fridge; oven on 425°F
12:15 — Stuffing on stovetop, rest covered
12:25 — Sheet pan: sweet potato halves + chicken thighs, into oven
1:05 — Pull chicken to a plate, tent, rest on stovetop
1:10 — Beans on same pan, into oven
1:15 — Pull sweet potato
~1:22 — Pull beans, lemon, toss
1:25 — Reheat stuffing
1:35 to 1:45 — Plate both meals
~2:00 — Riley eats

MINIMAL CLEANUP NOTES

- Stuffing pot also reheats stuffing at the end. No extra pan.
- Sheet pan handles sweet potato, chicken, and green beans in sequence. Nothing else touches it.
- Parchment or foil on the sheet pan means a 30-second wipe at the end.
- Sweet potato halves can also go directly on the oven rack with the sheet pan underneath to catch drips — even less to wash.

SAM'S PLATE — COOLING AND REFRIGERATION

After Riley plates Sam's portion (2 thighs, rest of sweet potato, rest of beans, rest of stuffing):

- Spread the food in a SHALLOW container or on a wide plate. A dense pile cools slowly and is the usual leftover-safety problem. Shallow is the goal.
- Cool uncovered on the counter 10 to 15 min, just until steam stops rising. Do not leave uncovered past 30 min.
- Cover and refrigerate by about 2:45pm at the latest — well inside the 2-hour USDA window, with margin.
- If your fridge runs cold and the container is shallow, going straight into the fridge once the steam dies down is also fine.
- Keeps 3 to 4 days refrigerated.

SAM'S REHEATING — when he gets home ~10:30pm

MICROWAVE (about 5 min, easiest):
- Cover the plate with a damp paper towel
- 70% power, 3 to 4 min
- Check chicken at the thickest part — should read 165°F
- Add 30 to 60 sec if needed; rest 1 min before eating

OVEN (about 20 min, better texture):
- 350°F, plate covered with foil
- 15 to 20 min, until chicken hits 165°F internal

QUICK TIPS FOR SAM
- Splash of water on the sweet potato before covering helps it steam back soft
- A small pat of butter on top of the stuffing before microwaving keeps it from drying out

One-pan leftover hash, two people, ~15 min. Start at 1:50 so it's ready when Sam walks in at 2:00.

Pan: 10–12" heavy skillet (cast iron or thick nonstick), medium-high, 1 tbsp neutral oil. Heat the pan dry 60 sec before the oil goes in, oil 30 sec before food.

Sequence:

3.  Stuffing broken into rough chunks, pressed flat, 2 min undisturbed to crisp, then flip and another 1–2 min. Probe the center — stuffing is your highest-risk item, it must hit 165°F.

4.  Push everything to the edges. Pull the chicken off the bone into bite chunks into the cleared center. Add 1 tbsp water or stock to the pan and COVER for 90 sec. The steam brings the chicken to 165°F without drying the thigh out.

5.  Uncover, toss everything together, 30 sec to drive off extra moisture. Taste for salt.

Safety check: probe a chicken piece — 165°F confirms thorough reheating. If the stuffing center is still cool, recover 30 more seconds and recheck. Don't crowd the pan; if it's tight, do it in two batches — a packed pan steams instead of crisps and the chicken won't come up to temp cleanly.

Portal messages typically clear in 1-3 business days, so 10 days out from a fasting lipid with no result and no clinician interpretation is past the normal window — even with holiday slowdown. The fact that you already asked and got no reply is the bigger signal: someone on the clinical side needs to actively look at this.

A few practical options, in order of how I'd weigh them:

1. Call the clinic today, ask for the nurse triage line directly (front desk will route you back to messages). Frame it as: "I sent a portal message N days ago about a Dec 7 fasting lipid that has no posted result and no interpretation, and I haven't heard back." Ask (a) is the result in the system, (b) when interpretation will post, (c) should you continue current meds or wait. This gets you a real human and usually same-day resolution.

2. Send a sharper follow-up portal message flagging it's been ~10 days and asking for a callback. Lower yield if the queue isn't being worked, but creates a paper trail if the issue compounds.

3. Wait through the holiday and call Monday. Reasonable only if you genuinely don't expect a medication change pending this — and you want to confirm that explicitly with someone.

Worth pinning down before you act: was this a routine panel, or were you expecting a statin (or dose) change based on the result? That changes how aggressive I'd be. If a medication decision is hanging on it, option 1 is clearly the move.

A 60-minute sequence, in four ~15-minute phases. Anchored in your watercolor rules: 1 firm blot, 20s hold, 1 touch, no return to a dull wash. The whole study is built to fail gracefully — if you run out of time at minute 35, the 3-value structure still reads.

────────────────────────────────────────
PHASE 1 · 0–15 min · SETUP + VALUE MAP
────────────────────────────────────────
Two brushes (small round for body, larger mop for washes), palette with ultramarine, burnt sienna, raw umber, water jar, paper towel. Two mixing wells — one for the body mix, one for the deep mix later.

Pencil: locate only the major creases and the 3–5 brightest highlight reserves. Do not draw every fold.

Value map — read the ribbon as exactly three values:
  · HIGHLIGHT  : paper white (reserved, no paint)
  · MID        : cool silver body (your main wash)
  · DEEP       : cool dark in crease valleys (final pass only)

The kraft paper itself is your warm fourth value, working for free. Do not paint it.

────────────────────────────────────────
PHASE 2 · 15–30 min · COOL-NEUTRAL FIRST WASH
────────────────────────────────────────
Mixing order — restrained, prevents mud:
  1. Wet brush, pick up ultramarine, dilute until the puddle is weak tea with a blue cast.
  2. Touch the tip into burnt sienna — roughly 1/10 the volume of the blue — and stir once. Result should read as cool graphite: not sky, not chocolate.
  3. Test on scrap. If it leans brown, add blue. If it leans bright blue, add sienna.

Apply: 1 firm blot per shape (1 firm blot, no return). Light → broad for the largest body areas; 2× → seam where two folds meet. 20-second hold after each blot. If it dulls, leave it — returning to dull paint blooms it.

Edge policy on this pass: keep almost everything soft. Hard edges come later, only where the value jump demands them.

────────────────────────────────────────
PHASE 3 · 30–45 min · RESERVES + EDGE WORK
────────────────────────────────────────
While the wash dries, sharpen the highlights: lift any faint tint from the reserved whites with a damp brush and paper towel — single gentle touch, no scrubbing.

Hard edges: paint these next, only at abrupt value shifts — the ridge where a fold catches light, the edge of a highlight against a deep crease. Use the same cool-neutral mix slightly stronger, finer brush, one confident stroke. 1 touch, no return.

Lost edges: where a reflection blends into the kraft or into the next fold, leave the wash edge soft. Do not chase these. This is where "chasing every reflection" loses the painting.

If a passage reads quiet or flat, the fix is a value jump, not more paint and not warmer paint. The kraft is already your warm counter — silver does not need warmth added to it.

────────────────────────────────────────
PHASE 4 · 45–60 min · DEEP COOL DARKS + STOP
────────────────────────────────────────
Deep mix: same recipe, slightly more blue and a hair more sienna. Should read as deep graphite, never black. Test on scrap.

Place only in the deepest crevices — usually 4–7 small shapes total. Each is a single firm blot. No blending outward, no return.

Optional final accent: 1–3 pinpoints lifted back with a clean damp brush if the brightest highlights lost their snap. Stop there.

Stop condition — step back 6–8 feet, or arm's length + squint:
  · Does the three-value structure read instantly? Yes → stop.
  · Is there an edge you'd be tempted to "tighten"? No → stop.
  · Does any passage want warmth or another reflection? Yes → it is already done; do not add.
  · Is the paper still showing reserve white at the brightest points? No → stop right now, before the next stroke.

If 60 min arrives during phase 3, stop at the end of phase 3. A study with structure preserved beats a study with one more dark added.

COLLARD GREENS & BLACK-EYED PEAS OVER RICE
serves 2 generously, with leftover greens-and-peas for one more meal

PREP — about 10 minutes
- Strip the collard leaves from the thick stems; discard stems (or save for stock). Stack leaves, roll, and slice into 1/2-inch ribbons. Rinse and shake out — no need to dry fully.
- Mince 3 to 4 garlic cloves.
- Open both cans of black-eyed peas; drain and rinse.
- Slice the lemon into wedges.
- Fluff the rice and warm it: microwave covered with a splash of water for about 90 seconds, or warm in a covered pot on low with a tablespoon of water.

COOK — about 20 minutes
1. Warm 2 to 3 tablespoons olive oil in a wide pot or deep skillet over medium heat. Add the garlic and a small pinch of salt; stir 30 to 45 seconds until fragrant. Don't let it brown.
2. Pile in the collards with another pinch of salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Toss until wilted, 2 to 3 minutes.
3. Add the black-eyed peas, 3/4 cup vegetable broth, about 1 teaspoon smoked paprika, and more black pepper. Stir and bring to a low simmer.
4. Partially cover; simmer gently 12 to 15 minutes, until the collards are silky and the broth has thickened just enough to coat the beans. Taste and adjust salt, pepper, and paprika.

SERVE
- Divide the rice between two bowls.
- Spoon the greens and beans (with their broth) over the rice.
- Squeeze a lemon wedge over each bowl — the acid brightens the whole pot.
- Pass the remaining lemon.

NOTES
- The greens-and-peas mixture keeps 3 days in the fridge; the rice is best fresh. Reheat leftovers with a splash of broth.
- Make it richer whenever you have it: a small pat of butter stirred in at the end, or a poached egg on top if an egg turns up.
- Quiet New Year's nod: peas for coins, greens for dollars — tradition intact, no special trip required.

ONE-POT COCONUT-TURMERIC RICE WITH GREENS & CHICKPEAS (lunch for 2 + 1 leftover)

Ingredients (3 portions)
  1 cup basmati or jasmine rice (rinsed)
  1 tbsp olive or coconut oil
  1 small onion, diced (~1 cup)
  2 garlic cloves, minced
  1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
  1 tsp ground turmeric
  1/2 tsp ground cumin
  1/4 tsp red pepper flakes (optional)
  1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and rinsed
  1 can (13.5 oz) full-fat coconut milk
  1 cup broth or water
  1 tsp salt, plus more to taste
  4 oz baby spinach or chopped kale
  Juice of 1 lime
  Optional garnish: cilantro, toasted cashews or pumpkin seeds

Timing (~30 minutes)
  0–5 min   Heat oil in a wide pot over medium. Cook onion until soft.
  5–8 min   Stir in garlic, ginger, turmeric, cumin, and red pepper flakes; toast 30 seconds.
  8–10 min  Stir in rice to coat in the spice oil.
  10–22 min Add chickpeas, coconut milk, broth, and salt. Bring to a simmer, cover, reduce heat to low, cook 12 minutes undisturbed.
  22–25 min Remove lid, stir in greens until wilted, replace lid for 1 minute.
  25–30 min Off heat, squeeze in lime juice, taste for salt, fluff with a fork. Garnish.

Safe cooling for the leftover
  1. Serve the two portions you want now.
  2. Within 1 hour of cooking, transfer the leftover into a shallow container no deeper than 2 inches. A wide glass or metal container beats a deep bowl — it cools faster.
  3. Leave uncovered or loosely vented for ~20 minutes to release steam and stop the center staying hot.
  4. Lid on, move to the fridge. Aim to drop from ~140°F to 70°F within 1 hour, then 70°F to 40°F within another hour (a flat, shallow container usually does this in ~90 minutes total).
  5. Use within 3–4 days. Reheat to a steady simmer/165°F before eating.

Notes
  - One pot, one wooden spoon, one cutting board. Rinse the rice while the onion cooks to save time.
  - Swap spinach for chopped kale (stir in 2 min earlier, since kale needs longer to soften).
  - If you don't have coconut milk, use 1 cup broth + 1/3 cup canned tomato or a splash of cream; cook time is the same.

Do this in order, and stop at any step where the test goes wrong:

1. Don't rub. Blot — press a clean white cloth or paper towel against the spot to lift what you can. Rubbing drives tannin deeper and abrades the cotton.

2. Colorfast check first, since the label didn't vouch for it. Dampen a hidden area (inside the cuff fold or a seam allowance) with cold water, press a white cloth against it for 30 seconds, and see if dye transfers. If color comes off, treat more gently and don't add anything but cold water to the cuff itself.

3. Flush from the back. Hold the cuff with the stain facing down under cold running water so the coffee is pushed out of the fabric rather than through it. A minute of this usually gets most of a fresh, plain (no milk/sugar) coffee spill.

4. If a faint tan shadow remains, work a tiny drop of plain liquid dish soap or gentle laundry detergent into just that spot with your fingertip, then cold-rinse again from the back. Don't use vinegar, baking soda paste, or anything acidic/alkaline — both can shift dye on uncolorfasted cotton.

5. Air dry flat or on a hanger, away from direct sun. No tumble dry (label forbids it, and heat will set any residual tannin permanently). Only machine-wash once the spot is fully gone.

6. When you do machine-wash (label is your spec: cold, no bleach), run it alone or with other darks in case the dye bleeds. Skip the dryer entirely for this jacket.

If after step 3–4 you still see a shadow, repeat the soap + cold rinse once more before drying. Once it goes through the dryer, any leftover tannin is essentially permanent, so the air-dry discipline is the real safety net.

Conservative stain-removal sequence (fabric, unknown stain):

0. Read the care label FIRST. If it says "dry clean only," stop — take it to a cleaner and point out the stain. Do not wet-treat at home. If it gives a max wash temp or bleach restriction, that governs everything below.

1. Blot, never rub. Place a clean white cloth or paper towel under the stain (catches wicking) and press a second clean white cloth onto the stain from above. Lift, rotate to a clean area, press again. Work from the OUTSIDE of the stain inward so you don't spread the halo. No scrubbing — grinding pushes the stain deeper into fibers and spreads it.

2. Spot-test before any chemical. Pick a hidden spot (inside seam, hem allowance, under a collar). Apply the same water/solvent you plan to use, wait 10 minutes, blot dry, check for color loss, bleeding, or texture change. If anything shifts, switch to a milder approach (cold water only) or stop and take it to a cleaner.

3. Pre-treat gently. Apply a tiny amount of the chosen agent (plain cold water first; then a drop of mild liquid detergent; then a diluted solvent only if the label permits) to the OUTSIDE edge of the stain and work inward. Blot — don't rub. Let it sit 5–10 minutes; do not let it dry on the fabric.

4. Rinse cold, from the back. Hold the stained area face-down under cold running water so the water pushes the stain OUT of the fibers rather than through them. Cold only — warm or hot water can set protein (blood, sweat), tannin (coffee, wine, grass), and many oil-based stains permanently.

5. Wash per the care label, cold-water default. Use the gentlest cycle and the coolest temperature the label allows. If you have any doubt about heat-setting, stay cold. Use a detergent appropriate for the fabric; skip chlorine bleach unless the label explicitly permits it.

6. INSPECT before drying. This is the gate. Check the still-damp stain in good light. If any trace remains, repeat steps 1–5. Do not proceed to drying until the stain is fully gone.

7. Air-dry only. Hang or lay flat away from direct heat and sunlight. Do NOT machine-dry and do NOT iron a stained area — dryer heat and iron heat will set anything left behind permanently. Air-dry, then re-inspect; one more round of treatment is possible before heat ever touches the garment.

Three rules that override everything else: cold water, blot-don't-rub, outside-in. If you remember those, the rest is just sequencing.

Sheet-pan chickpea, sweet potato & broccoli + couscous + lemon-tahini
Serves 2 (1 dinner tonight, 1 lunch portion)

Setup (one counter-to-oven trip)
- Oven 425F. Line a sheet pan with parchment (no scrubbing later).
- Drain 1 can chickpeas; pat dry with a towel so they crisp.
- Cube 1 medium sweet potato ~3/4 inch. Cut broccoli into large florets, halve any thick stems so pieces match the potato in size.
- Pile it all on the pan. Add 2-3 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp smoked paprika, 1 minced garlic clove, 1/2 tsp salt, pepper. Toss with tongs right on the pan, spread in one layer.

Roast
- 25-30 min, stir once at the halfway point. Done when sweet potato is fork-tender and chickpeas are browning at the edges.

While it roasts (stay off your feet)
- Couscous: boil 3/4 cup water in a kettle (no pot to carry). Pour over 1/2 cup couscous in a bowl, plate on top, rest 5 min. Fluff with fork.
- Sauce: in one bowl, whisk 2 tbsp tahini, juice of 1/2 lemon, 1 small minced garlic clove, 2-3 tbsp water until drizzleable, pinch salt.

Plate only the dinner portion. Keep sauce and couscous amounts separate so the lunch keeps texture.

Safe cooling for the lunch portion
- Portion into a shallow container (spread flat, not mounded) within 30 min of plating — shallow = faster cooling = safer.
- Refrigerate promptly; do not let it sit at room temp more than 2 hr total (1 hr if your kitchen is warm).
- Sauce in a separate small jar so the veg doesn't get soggy.
- Reheat to steaming (165F) before eating. Keeps 3 days refrigerated, or 2 months frozen.

Ankle notes
- Sit on a stool for the chopping step; slide the pan onto the rack, don't lift high.
- Kettle = no pot to haul. One sheet pan, one bowl, one pot total.
- Single plating pass: portion lunch while dinner is on the plate, then sit down.

If you want even less standing: cube the sweet potato and cut the broccoli earlier in the day (or the night before), keep in a sealed container in the fridge, and the active work at dinner drops to drain-chickpeas + toss + roast.

Put the warm reflection down first as a light wash, then deepen the cool shadow last. Don't leave the mug white until the end.

Reasoning:

  Watercolor builds light-to-dark — you can't reliably lift once a passage is down, so save the deepest darks for the end. The warm bounce is the lower-stakes, higher-payoff passage: paint it while the brush is clean and your eye is still calibrated to the orange, so the chroma stays clear and the orange actually "reads" as the source of the reflection. The blue-gray form shadow is a darker, more controlled mix you can deepen at the end once you've seen how the cool needs to sit against the warm.

  The "keep it white until the end" instinct protects the highlights but costs integration. A warm note stamped on at the end tends to sit on top of the cool instead of melting into it. And per your own rule — quiet edge = unresolved boundary, warm as the counter via value separation — the orange's reflection on the mug is exactly the move that closes the form-shadow seam. Leaving it for last is the move that produces the unresolved boundary you're trying to avoid.

Practical: where the warm reflection meets the cool form shadow is the seam that defines the cylinder. Paint the warm first, let it dry, then drop the cool beside it — you'll get a clean edge. If you want a softer transition (say, where the warm wraps around the belly), touch that seam line with a clean damp brush for a few seconds before the cool goes in, then drop the gray right next to it.

Two things to watch while you work: keep the warm thinner than you think — ceramic bounce light is subtle, and a heavy warm will fight the cool. And reserve a true white passage on the lit side of the mug (not just unpainted paper, but paper you've actively protected from any wash creep) so the ceramic reads against the window light at the end.

After the deductible is met, the plan's preferred-pharmacy copay kicks in and the member pays the flat copay instead of the full price.

  2. So if on this fill the deductible hasn't been cleared, "plan paid $0" is correct by design — the copay doesn't apply yet because the post-deductible gate hasn't opened. The $49 would then be the discounted pharmacy price, not the copay.

  3. The "$49 preferred-pharmacy copay after deductible" only takes over on the fill where the running total of in-network, deductible-eligible pharmacy charges first reaches or crosses the deductible. From that fill forward, the plan's preferred-pharmacy copay replaces the full-price charge; on subsequent fills the plan pays the difference between the pharmacy price and the copay, so "plan paid $0" stops being the right shape and you'd instead see plan_paid = price − $49.

  4. The arithmetic check on a given fill is therefore: deductible_remaining_before_this_fill > 0  →  plan_paid = 0, member_paid = negotiated_price; deductible_remaining_before_this_fill ≤ 0  →  plan_paid = negotiated_price − copay, member_paid = copay. "Plan paid $0 with member_paid = $49" is consistent with the first branch only if $49 is the negotiated pharmacy price, not the copay. If $49 is in fact the post-deductible copay and the plan paid $0, that's an inconsistency — either the deductible gate fired when it shouldn't have, or the fill was mis-routed (non-preferred pharmacy, non-covered drug, HSA contribution not yet applied to deductible, etc.).

Sequence (24–48 hr total)

Immediate (first hour):
1. Remove insoles. Loosen laces, open tongue wide. Wipe uppers with a barely-damp microfiber cloth — no soaking, no detergent yet.
2. Stuff uppers with crumpled plain paper (paper towels or newsprint). Replace paper every 2–3 hr while damp; it wicks moisture out faster than letting the shoe sit closed.
3. Lay insoles flat on a dry towel, top surface up, somewhere with airflow.

Drying environment:
4. Room temp, 20–25°C, moving air (fan on low, or an open window across the room — not aimed directly at the shoes).
5. AVOID: radiators, baseboards, hair dryer, clothes dryer, oven, fireplace, car interior in sun, direct sunlight. Heat degrades EVA/TPU midsole foam and can delaminate glue lines you can't see yet.

Damage check before any rehab use:
6. Midsole integrity: press your thumb into the heel and forefoot foam of both shoes. Foam should rebound fully and feel identical left vs. right. Any permanent indent, soft spot, or asymmetry = retire for rehab.
7. Drop check (the 8 mm matters for rehab): with the insole out, rest each shoe on a flat surface and confirm the heel sits visibly higher than the forefoot by a consistent amount on both shoes. A collapsed heel wedge changes your biomechanics, which is the opposite of what you want in rehab.
8. Flex test: bend the shoe at its natural toe-break (under the ball, not the midfoot). Should flex smoothly, no cracking sound, no new stiff crease at the midfoot.
9. Upper + glue lines: look along overlays, toe cap, heel counter, and the midsole-to-upper seam for any lifting, glossiness, or fine gap. Press along the seam with a fingernail — it should feel bonded, not tacky.
10. Insole: lay on a flat surface. Should sit flat with no curling edges, delamination, or compressed foam that doesn't recover.
11. Tread: recheck grooves dry — dampness can hide grit.
12. Fit test: insole back in, usual sock, walk indoors 5–10 min. No new hot spot, heel lift, or lateral slip.

Reuse verdict:
- Rehab-ready only if steps 6–12 all pass and drop still reads ~8 mm on both shoes.
- If the midsole rebound is uneven or the wedge looks compressed on one side, swap them out for rehab even if they feel fine walking around — neutral shoes with a compromised drop are exactly the footwear that re-loads whatever you're rehabilitating.

Given the lightest area is adjacent and the bloom is contained, default to LIFT FIRST; glaze only if the lift under-delivers.

LIFT (one shot):
1. Confirm bone-dry — back of hand to the paper, no chill.
2. Damp (not wet) clean mop or sable. Paint the bloom only, feather 1–2 mm past its hard edge into the surrounding wash.
3. Hold ~20 s — surface goes shiny to matte-damp.
4. ONE firm blot with a dry, lint-free tissue; 5 s hold, lift straight up. No rub.
5. One light→broad feather to soften the seam. STOP.

GLAZE FALLBACK — only if the bloom still reads more than one value step off after the lift:
- Sheet fully dry again (no chill, back-of-hand test).
- Mix a thin glaze matching the surrounding wash hue and value, slightly cooler.
- Apply to the bloom only; 2× feather the seam. Dry untouched.

STOP CONDITION — gate before any abrasion or overwork:
At arm's length, the bloom reads within roughly one value step of the surrounding wash AND no fiber disturbance shows at raking light AND the paper is fully dry to the back of the hand. If any of those three fails, stop. Re-evaluate — one re-lift, one re-glaze, or accept and repaint that wash on a fresh sheet. Never scrub, scratch, or re-wet a dull area; that's how the next bloom gets made.

SEQUENCE

1. Photograph before moving the bag.
   The split itself, the lot code, the expiration date, the shipping box exterior, and any visible kibble near the split. Use a camera or phone that stamps the date, or write the date on a slip of paper and include it in one frame. This is the evidence the replacement claim needs; you can't recreate it after the bag has been moved or poured out.

2. Quarantine the bag, unopened, in a clean secondary container.
   Drop the whole bag into a clean plastic tote or a large zip bag. Label the outside: "DO NOT FEED — packaging split, awaiting claim." Store dry, room temp, away from the open-food bin and the feeding station. This contains any spillage from the split and prevents accidental cross-use if anyone else in the household helps with feeding.

3. Do not feed from it, even though it looks and smells fine.
   The seam is the safety barrier. Kibble can take on mold spores, bacteria, moisture, oxidation, or pests through a split with no visible or olfactory change in the early window. Once the maker's seal is broken pre-use, the maker can't stand behind the contents, and "looks and smells fine" is not evidence the barrier held. The cost asymmetry also points the same way: one bag is cheap relative to a GI or mycotoxin vet visit. This is the conservative default you asked for.

4. Quick sanity check on the rest of the supply.
   Confirm existing sealed bags are still sealed, the storage bin is clean, and the scoop is clean. The split bag didn't contaminate them — it was never opened near them — but this is a 30-second check worth doing while the issue is fresh.

5. Open the replacement claim today, while the photos are fresh.
   Contact the seller (or the maker, if you bought direct). Include: photo of the split, lot and expiration, order number, and date received. Stick to facts: "top seam split on arrival; shipping box intact; bag not opened and not fed from." Ask for a replacement bag of the same lot; refund if that's not in stock. Most sellers replace on photo evidence; delay risks a "when did you first notice?" dispute.

6. Hold the quarantined bag until the claim resolves.
   Don't discard until the seller tells you to — some want it returned or want a follow-up photo in place. If they do say toss, discard it sealed so the compromised kibble can't be poured into anything else later.

7. Plan the feeding gap now, before it becomes urgent.

Most likely identity: case-bearing clothes moth (or webbing clothes moth) — a dry empty casing + small holes in stored wool + untouched cotton is the textbook pattern. Carpet beetles are a secondary possibility with nearly identical handling. Treat one finding seriously because populations build slowly and damage is cumulative.

ISOLATION + INSPECTION (in this order)

  1. Close Kibo out of the room first. Pet out before any handling.
  2. Do not shake the throw. Fold it loosely where it sits and seal it inside a plastic bag (gallon zip or kitchen trash bag) right at the spot.
  3. Flashlight the storage spot: shelf seams, drawer corners, the fold of anything else stored there. Look for more casings, fine webbing on folds, tiny dark fecal specks, adult moths (~5–8 mm, buff-gold, flutter then rest on walls), or bristly cast skins (carpet-beetle variant).
  4. Audit every other natural-fiber animal-product item in the room — wool, cashmere, silk, wool rug under furniture, wool-upholstered chair, natural-bristle brush, feather/down, fur trim. Cotton, linen, and synthetics are not at risk.
  5. Move the sealed bag somewhere Kibo cannot reach (garage, car trunk, or a closed closet behind a door Kibo can't open). Off the floor.

WOOL-APPROPRIATE CLEANING (pick one)

  - Freezer kill: bag airtight, -18°C / 0°F for 72+ hours. Most reliable and pet-safe. Thaw, then brush and vacuum.
  - Heat kill: dryer on high or hot wash at 130°F+ for 30+ min — only if the care label allows. Wool felts easily with heat + agitation, so skip if unsure.
  - Dry cleaning: solvent bath kills all stages. Choose a cleaner who doesn't commingle unwashed goods (rare but documented moth vector).
  - Steam: handheld steamer on folds and seams kills surface stages; good follow-up, not sufficient alone.
  - Vacuum + brush after the kill step with a narrow nozzle; empty the vacuum canister or bag into an outdoor trash bin immediately — vacuums can keep live stages alive.

  Skip: mothballs (toxic to pets via off-gassing in closed closets), cedar or lavender alone (repellent at best, no kill), any spray or fogger.

MONITORING

  - Clothes-moth pheromone sticky traps: 1–2 in the closet and any other wool storage. Non-toxic, but place them where Kibo can't bat them or get adhesive on fur (behind stored items works). Catch counts map activity.
  - Weekly flashlight check of the same spots for 6 weeks (one full life cycle).
  - Vacuum closet floor, walls, and shelf seams weekly for the same period; empty vacuum outside each time.
  - Quarantine incoming wool/silk/fur items — freeze or heat-treat before they go into storage.

PROFESSIONAL PEST ADVICE IF

  - More than one item shows damage, or casings/webbing appear in multiple locations.
  - Traps keep catching adults over multiple weeks after cleaning.
  - You find a likely source (closet, dresser, rug pad, duct, an old bird nest in a chimney or eave) you can't fully clean yourself.
  - Kibo shows any unusual symptoms after exposure — vomiting, lethargy, drooling, respiratory changes. Clothes moths aren't a primary pet-toxicity issue, but unexplained symptoms in Kibo warrant a vet call regardless.
  - You're not confident it's moths vs. carpet beetles vs. something else; a licensed pro can ID a sample in minutes.
