Setup

  Block placement
    - Set the block on a non-slip surface: a rubber shelf liner, a slightly damp folded towel, or a cutting mat. The block must not slide when you push against it.
    - Orient it so the unglued gap is on the side away from your body, so every cut goes away from you.

  Tool (dull, thin, with a rounded tip)
    - Best: a dull palette knife (flexible metal blade, rounded corners, no sharp point).
    - Good substitutes: a butter knife, an old table knife, or a small flexible putty knife.
    - Avoid: fresh X-Acto / box-cutter blades, scissors, or anything with a sharp point. A sharp blade wants to dive into the sheet below; you want a blade that separates paper from glue rather than slicing it.

  Stabilizing hand
    - Place your non-dominant hand flat across the center of the block, palm down, fingers spread, and press down firmly. The block should not shift or lift when you push the blade through glue.

Removal sequence

  1. Find the gap
     - Inspect all four edges. You're looking for a section where the top sheet is not adhered to the layer beneath it. On most blocks this is a 1-2 inch break along the top edge, often next to the manufacturer's binding strip. On some blocks only two edges are glued; on others all four. The gap tells you where to start either way.

  2. Insert the blade
     - Hold the blade nearly parallel to the paper - about 10 to 15 degrees from horizontal, never vertical.
     - Slip the tip into the gap with a gentle wiggle. Do not force. If it won't go in, you're at the wrong spot or the angle is too steep. Re-check both before adding pressure.

  3. First cut: along the edge with the gap
     - Pull the blade away from your body along that edge.
     - Keep the blade FLAT against the layer below the top sheet. It should feel like it's gliding on a firm surface with mild tack from the glue.
     - Use a slow, smooth stroke. A slight back-and-forth sawing helps if the glue is tacky, but most of the motion is one steady pull.

  4. Work the perimeter
     - Once the first edge is free, the gap there widens. Rotate the block 90 degrees, reinsert the blade into the now-wider gap at the same shallow angle, and cut along the next edge.
     - Repeat for each glued edge. Usually three or four passes around the perimeter free the sheet.

  5. Lift
     - Lift the painting by a freed corner or edge. Support the sheet from below with your free hand as it comes up so it doesn't flop and crease the paint film.

When to stop and reconsider

  Stop immediately if any of these happen:
    - Resistance suddenly increases past the feel of tacky glue. You are probably catching paper, not slicing glue.
    - You hear a tearing sound (a quiet peel or slice is normal; a rip is not).
    - The top sheet starts to lift, wrinkle, or buckle ahead of the blade.
    - The blade wants to dive downward, or you feel it engaging a lower sheet.
    - The painted surface begins to deform or catch.

  What to do when you stop:
    - Back the blade out along its entry path. Do NOT reverse direction while it is engaged in glue - that almost always snags the paper above.
    - Re-check the angle (very shallow) and the position (in the gap, not pressed against glued paper).
    - Wipe glue residue off the blade with a damp cloth; a gummy blade grabs paper.
    - If a corner of the top sheet has lifted unintentionally, press it flat again before resuming.

After the sheet is free

  - If a small sliver of unglued paper remains at an edge, trim it with scissors only after the sheet is fully out and supported flat.
  - If any section still feels attached, do not tug - it is still glued. Find or create a new blade entry point and release that section rather than pulling on the painting.

The key principle: at 38 psi (12+ below the marked 50 psi minimum), the rear tire has lost meaningful air with no obvious visible cause. Treat it as a possible slow leak until proven otherwise — a small embedded object (thorn, wire, glass shard) can seal against the tube under pressure and stay nearly invisible. The goal of the steps below is to confirm whether the tire holds air, not to declare it road-ready.

A useful diagnostic note before you start: the front tire, presumably the same age and same exposure, is at 54 psi. That contrast (12+ psi gap between two tires sitting in the same air) makes a rear-specific cause — puncture, valve, bead, or rim interface on that wheel — more likely than ambient/aging pressure loss.

VISIBLE-DAMAGE SEQUENCE — DO THIS FIRST, BEFORE TOUCHING THE PUMP

1. Tread, full circumference. Run your fingers (gently) around the entire tread and across the centerline. Embedded thorns, wire, or glass can sit flush with the rubber and be palpable before they're visible. Flex the tire slightly side-to-side to expose the shoulders.
2. Both sidewalls, full circumference. Re-scan for cuts, scuffs exposing casing threads, blisters, raised bumps, bulges. Any of these = stop, no inflation, shop visit.
3. Both beads, full 360°. Feel for a section that lifts away from the rim or sits unevenly. Look for dried fluid tracks or sealant residue (if tubeless).
4. Rim. Spin and inspect the rim sidewalls for dents, cracks, hop. Check rim tape through the valve hole — if it's shifted, torn, or a spoke nipple is poking through, that alone can cause a slow leak.
5. Valve. Stem straight, not cracked at the base? Cap off briefly to confirm the core is seated and not weeping when you wiggle the stem side-to-side.

If anything in 1–5 looks wrong, skip inflation entirely.

CONSERVATIVE STATIONARY INFLATION

Goal: confirm the tire holds air, not put it into service.

- Inflate only to ~25–30 psi — enough to give the tire shape and seat the bead, far below the 50 psi minimum. This limits how much force goes through a potential puncture site.
- During inflation, pause around ~15 psi and listen at the tire on both sides and at the valve.
- At test pressure, brush soapy water (or a thin line of saliva) across the tread, both sidewalls, both beads, and the valve base. Bubbles pinpoint a leak.
- No bubbles, no hiss → tire passed the low-pressure leak test. Do NOT yet go to 50 psi.

SHORT-INTERVAL PRESSURE RECHECK

Treat this as a staged bring-up. A single check is not enough.

Stage A — at ~30 psi, wait 15–30 min, re-measure. A healthy tire should hold to within ~0.5 psi over that interval. Loss >1–2 psi = likely slow leak, stop.

Stage B (only if A is clean) — top up to ~40 psi, still below the 50 psi minimum. Wait 30–60 min, re-measure. Loss >1 psi = slow leak, stop.

Stage C (only if B is clean) — top up into your marked operating range (you gave the 50 psi minimum but not the upper bound — stay at or below the marked max; aim for the middle of the range, e.g., ~57–58 if the range is 50–65). Wait several hours or overnight, re-measure. Loss >1–2 psi over that window = stop.

Use the ankle rehab window to your advantage — let Stage C run overnight. There is no time pressure to get to 50 psi since you're not riding.

CONDITIONS MEANING SHOP INSPECTION, NOT "INFLATION PROVED IT"

Leave the bike unridden and book a shop visit if any of the following:

- Any finding from the visible-damage sequence above.
- The soapy-water / hiss test produces bubbles or an audible leak at any stage.
- Pressure drops more than 1–2 psi between any two consecutive rechecks.
- The tire was sitting underinflated for an extended period before today — a tire run very low can break sidewall casing cords, and that damage isn't always visible from outside.
- You can't positively rule out an embedded object. A thorn-sized hole in the tread is often only visible when you're looking for it; the mark is small.
- The bead won't seat evenly during reinflation.
- Any rim damage, dent, crack, or shifted rim tape noticed during step 4.

One final distinction worth stating plainly: "holds air when parked" is not the same as "safe to ride." Even after a clean Stage C, give the rear (and the front, which was already at 54) a final walk-around before your first post-rehab ride, and consider a shop inspection anyway — a tire that's been below its operating range with no obvious cause deserves a professional look, especially since you'll be loading your ankle rehab onto commuting decisions once you're riding again.

A wool throw with two small holes and one empty casing has three distinct problems bundled together: soil/biological residue (cleaning addresses), missing yarn at the holes (only rebuilding addresses), and the empty casing — a structural gap where yarn is gone but the surrounding fibers held shape, leaving a hollow tube (also only rebuilding or replacement addresses). Cleaning can't put fiber back.

OPTION 1 — PROFESSIONAL CLEANING ONLY
- Typical cash cost: $40–80 for a throw at a wool/wool-care specialist. Goes higher if the piece is oversized or has fringe/trim needing hand work.
- Resolves: soil, body oils, salts; the cleaner's process (heat, steam, or solvent) is incidentally lethal to moth eggs/larvae if any are present, so the textile comes back sanitized.
- Doesn't resolve: the two holes stay open; the empty casing stays an unfilled structural gap. The piece is cleaner but still damaged.
- Practical outcome: a fresh, hygienic throw that is visibly imperfect. Usable as-is only if you accept the holes; otherwise it's a holding action before a later repair or replacement decision.

OPTION 2 — CLEANING PLUS DARNING
- Typical cash cost: cleaning $40–80 plus darning. A general tailor/alterations shop typically charges $20–50 per small hole, but on a textured wool throw the rate climbs because matching yarn weight, color, and weave structure is finicky. A specialist textile conservator or reweaver is $80–200+ per repair. Realistic total: $100–400 depending on who does the work and how invisible you want the mend.
- Resolves: holes are closed, the empty casing is reinforced so it doesn't propagate, the piece is structurally whole. Cleaning still gives the soil/sanitization benefit.
- Doesn't resolve: most darns on a textured wool throw are visible on close inspection — yarn weight rarely matches perfectly and the reweave changes the local hand (slightly stiffer, sometimes a different sheen). On a smooth fine-gauge wool you can get near-invisible results; on a chunky or brushed throw expect to see and feel the mend. Also doesn't address whatever caused the damage — that lives separately from this comparison.
- Practical outcome: usable, structurally sound, materially longer useful life, original piece preserved. Visible repair unless you go to a high-end textile conservator and even then it may still show.

OPTION 3 — REPLACEMENT
- Typical cash cost: budget wool throws $40–100, mid-range $100–250, quality/heritage wool $250–600+. Cleaning cost is moot; you'd launder a new one gently at home.
- Resolves: holes, casing, soil, hand, appearance — all of them at once, with a full lifespan ahead.
- Doesn't resolve: doesn't recover the original (sentimental value, if any, or fit with existing décor). Highest cash outlay.
- Practical outcome: pristine, no compromises, but a different object.

SIDE-BY-SIDE

                     Cleaning only   Cleaning + Darning   Replacement
Low-end total        ~$40            ~$100                ~$40
Typical total        ~$60            ~$150–250            ~$150
High-end total       ~$100+          ~$400+               ~$600+
Holes closed         No              Yes                  Yes (new)
Casing resolved      No              Reinforced           Yes (new)
Visible mend         N/A             Usually yes          No
Original kept        Yes             Yes                  No
Useful life added    Modest          Long                 Full (new)

WHAT'S DELIBERATELY OUT OF THIS COMPARISON
- Cotton linens nearby. Monitor them on their own terms. Cotton isn't a keratin fiber and isn't a normal food source for the pests that eat wool, so observations on the linens translate poorly as either confirmation or refutation of anything about the throw. Treat the cotton check as a separate thread regardless of which option you pick — don't let findings there pull this decision in either direction.
- The cleaner's quote. The cleaner quoted you on cleaning the throw, not on diagnosing pests. Anything they noted about casings, holes, or fibers is textile observation, not a pest-control finding. So no pesticide, fumigation, or "infestation" inference should ride on this decision — that question is either answered elsewhere with appropriate evidence or doesn't apply. Don't let the quote do double duty.

If you want a one-line steer: replacement is the cleanest outcome if the throw has no particular value to you; cleaning + darning by a hands-on tailor/alterations shop is the right balance of cost and outcome if you want to keep it (a conservator is worth it only if the piece has real value); cleaning alone is a holding action, not a resolution.

The combination you describe — dry brown tips, mild droop on newer growth, dry top inch, free drainage, no standing water, no visible pests or residue — points most often to environmental/cultural stress from the move indoors rather than anything acute. Rosemary is Mediterranean in origin: it likes bright light, lean soil, and a dry-down between waterings. The conservative path is to stabilize the environment first and only escalate if conditions worsen.

WATERING
- Check before each watering: insert a finger 1-2 inches into the soil. If it feels dry at that depth, water; if any moisture is present, wait another day or two.
- When you do water, soak thoroughly until water runs freely from the drainage holes, then let it drain completely. Never let the pot sit in a saucer of standing water.
- In winter indoors, expect roughly every 7-14 days depending on pot size, soil mix, and how warm the room runs. Err toward less rather than more.
- Use room-temperature water. If your tap is very hard or heavily chlorinated, an occasional deep flush with filtered or rainwater helps leach mineral salts that accumulate at the root zone (salt buildup itself causes tip burn).

LIGHT
- South-facing is best in winter; east or west is workable. If the Cherrywood window is bright but mostly indirect, a full-spectrum grow light 6-8 inches above the plant on a 12-14 hour timer is a reasonable supplement — not required, but useful in February when daylight is short.
- Rotate the pot a quarter turn once a week so growth stays even.

DRAINAGE
- You already have free drainage — just confirm the pot is not sitting in drained water. Elevate it on pot feet or a pebble layer in the saucer.
- If you use a decorative cache pot, lift the inner pot out for watering, let it drain, then return it.

ACCLIMATION
- Skip repotting and skip fertilizer for now. The plant is in transition; pushing growth on a stressed root system works against you.
- Aim for the coolest spot you can comfortably give it: 55-65°F is ideal, with cooler nights (down to about 45°F) actually welcome. Keep it off cold window glass at night and away from any heat source.
- Skip misting. Indoor humidity of 30-40% is low for rosemary, but misting in cool conditions tends to cause more problems than it solves. Grouping with other plants or a nearby pebble tray is gentler.

MONITORING (next 2-3 weeks)
- Recheck soil moisture every 3-4 days to learn the rhythm; adjust your interval from what you observe, not from a fixed calendar.
- Existing brown tips will not green up — the goal is new growth coming in firm and aromatic.
- A brief perk-up after watering is normal; persistent droop at the same moisture level is a signal.

WHEN TO ASK A LOCAL PLANT PROFESSIONAL
- Sudden or widespread leaf drop
- Soft or mushy stems, especially near the soil line
- Persistent wilting despite appropriate watering
- Any white powdery or fuzzy coating, webbing, sticky residue, or a strong musty/rotting smell from the soil
- No new growth at all over 4-6 weeks despite the steps above
- Significant branch dieback (whole stems going brown and dry from the tips inward)

If you do reach out, a photo of the whole plant plus a close-up of the affected growth will speed up their assessment. And no diagnosis from me on pests or disease — just the watch-list above.

The block is already doing what tape would have done. It IS the stabilization, and the perimeter IS the margin. So the tape-free sequence is really about three working habits: keep washes inside your intended zone, treat the block edge as a hard line, and know the exact moment to back off.

PRE-PAINT CHECK

Inspect all four glued edges. Confirm the seal is flush, no raised fibers, no gap a wash could wick under.

Set the block on a flat, stable surface. A small foam board or sheet of glassine underneath helps if your table flexes or if you want to slide the block as you work.

Stage two tools within reach: a dedicated lift brush (soft, clean, kept thirsty) and a dry paper towel or blotter. The lift brush is your edge-rescue tool; it does not paint.

PAINTING SEQUENCE

1. Plan the quiet margin.
   Decide on a 6 to 10 mm bare-paper border all around before the first stroke. This is your permanent margin. Everything between the painting and the glue line is buffer. The buffer does not need tape; it just needs you to not paint there.

2. Stabilize without tape.
   The glued stack is already rigid. That is the whole point of a block over loose sheets.
   For heavy washes, rest your painting hand on a slip sheet so skin oils do not transfer.
   If you want a slight back-tilt to pull wash toward you, prop the FAR edge of the block on a pencil. Never shim the block itself, or you will bow the paper.

3. Control wash creep — bank and blink.
   Work wet-to-dry toward your quiet margin. Never work from the margin inward.
   Where you want the wash to halt, pre-dampen a narrow strip just inside that line with clean water only. The active wash will stop at the damp line because there is no longer dry paper to creep into.
   Where the wash meets your intended boundary, switch to the blot sequence you already use: 1 firm blot → light, broader stroke, then 2x to the seam; 20 second hold, 1 touch. The seam here is your dry buffer, not the block edge.
   If a wash creeps where you do not want it: within the 20 second window, use the lift brush dampened and blotted to wick pigment back toward wet. After dull, stop. Your standing rule covers this: no return after dull equals no bloom.

4. Edge-catch safety stop — when pigment reaches the block edge.
   This is the moment to halt, not to rescue. Go in this exact order:
   Lift the brush off the paper entirely. No more flow into that zone.
   With the lift brush damp, not wet, and blotted, draw pigment INWARD, away from the glue line. Move from clean toward loaded, never the reverse.
   One pass. Then stop. Rewetting will push pigment deeper, not retrieve it.
   If pigment has crossed under the glue line, press a dry towel against it briefly. Do not flood the area trying to chase it back.
   Leave the zone. Do not work it again today. The wetter you keep it, the deeper the pigment migrates.

5. Resolve quiet boundaries AFTER the wash is dry.
   When an edge is still bothering you after drying, the answer is value separation, not blending. A deliberate adjacent dark or light value will resolve the quiet into a clear edge. Re-paint only with a fully loaded brush on bone-dry paper.

POST-SESSION (only when the painting is finished)

Wait for full dry — overnight is safest on a block.

Insert a palette knife or letter opener between the top sheet and the next. Walk it gently around all four edges. The glue releases with light pressure; do not pry.

THREE REMINDERS FOR TODAY

The block's glued perimeter replaces tape. Trust it.

Your existing blot sequence already covers most boundary work — just point the seam at the dry buffer, not at the glue.

Edge catch equals stop and lift inward, exactly once. Do not flood, do not chase.

Auto-corrections to disable

For a true preservation master the scanner driver should be a passive digitizer, not an interpreter. Every "auto" that touches pixels before the file is written needs to be off.

Tone / exposure / white balance
  - Auto-exposure
  - Auto-tone / auto-levels
  - Auto-contrast
  - Auto-white balance / auto-color
  - Auto-gamma

Restoration / interpretation
  - Color restoration / faded-color recovery
  - Backlight correction
  - Skin-tone smoothing (some drivers ship with it on)
  - Auto red-eye

Sharpening / clarity
  - Any unsharp-mask, "clarity", or "enhance focus" applied in-driver

Noise / texture
  - Noise reduction (softens the actual grain of the film/paper, which is part of the artifact)

Dust and scratch removal — this one gets its own callout
  - Hardware IR-based cleaning: Digital ICE, SilverFast iSRD, VueScan IR Clean
  - Software dust-and-scratch filters in the driver

IR cleaning reads a separate infrared pass and masks what it thinks is dust. On silver-gelatin B&W prints and on Kodachrome (and most chromogenic slides with remnant coupler dyes) that IR pass is unreliable — it can erase fine silver grain and dye-coupler texture that are part of the original. Disable it. If dust work is needed, do it by hand on a derivative, not on the master.

Output controls that keep the master untouched

The discipline: the master is what came off the scanner. Every other file is a separate, named derivative.

File format
  - Master: uncompressed TIFF, or DNG if your pipeline accepts DNG as a true archival container. 16-bit per channel if the scanner supports it.
  - Never write the master as JPEG or any lossy format.
  - Derivatives are separate TIFFs (working) and JPEGs (delivery), never an overwrite of the master.

Bit depth and color space
  - Capture at the scanner's native depth (usually 16-bit).
  - Embed an ICC profile (the scanner's own, or a defined archival profile such as ProPhoto) into the master, but do not apply an output color transform during scan. The master is scene-referred, not output-referred.

Naming and folder layout
  - One folder per item. Master side read-only once written.
  - Master:  <itemID>_master_<YYYYMMDD>.tif
  - Working derivative: <itemID>_v01_<purpose>_<YYYYMMDD>.tif
  - Delivery derivative: <itemID>_v01_<YYYYMMD_Delivery>.jpg
  - The "v01" makes it obvious which file is master (v00 / _master) and which are derivatives.

Driver settings that enforce separation
  - In VueScan / Epson Scan / SilverFast: the "Save" tab writes to a specific master folder. The "Edit" / "Copy" path points elsewhere, or simply unused — let the master land, then open the master in Photoshop/Affinity and "Save As" any working copy.
  - Disable any "auto-replace original", "auto-import into library and apply auto-adjust", or driver-level overwrite behavior.
  - In Photoshop: open the master, immediately "Save As" a derivative. Never use "Save" back onto the master path.

RAW / DNG sidecar pattern (if the scanner outputs RAW)
  - Master is the RAW/DNG; every adjustment lives in an XMP sidecar next to it.
  - Derivatives are rendered as separate TIFFs/JPEGs from the sidecar, never by re-writing the master.

File-system guardrails
  - Once the master is written, mark the file read-only (chmod 444 or platform equivalent) and lock the master folder where the OS allows.
  - Checksum the master (sha256) and record it next to the metadata. If the checksum ever changes, the master has been altered.

Metadata sidecar
  - Capture-time metadata — operator, scanner model, settings actually used, light source, target, sleeve-note text — goes into a sidecar (text or XMP), not by re-processing the image. The metadata describes the unaltered capture.

One-line principle: capture once, write the rawest faithful file the scanner can produce, lock it, and from then on every adjustment is a new named file you can throw away without losing the original capture.

For the seven on the bench today the cleanest preflight is: open the driver, turn the list above off, set output to 16-bit uncompressed TIFF to a master folder you'll lock after the run, and confirm the master file actually arrived before you open anything in an editor.

Conservative short-term driving boundary

Until the driver-side blade is replaced, treat that streak as an obstructed sight line. The split rubber cannot lay a clean edge on the glass, so on the main sweep path you have a permanent film of water and road film that will smear, scatter headlight glare, and hide pedestrians, lane lines, and brake lights. Practical limits until fixed:

  * No driving in rain if you can avoid it. Park and wait, take transit, delay the trip.
  * If rain is unavoidable: daylight only, short familiar routes, surface streets (not highway), well below posted speed, extra following distance, and no night driving in any precipitation. Headlight glare off a water film in a streaked zone is the worst case — it is worse than the dry-day deficit.
  * Dry weather driving is fine for short errands, but treat the next rain as the trigger to either have the new blade on or to not drive.

Replacement sequence

  1. Confirm the size. Measure the old driver-side blade end-to-end, or look up year/make/model at the parts counter. Driver and passenger are usually different lengths — do not assume symmetric.
  2. Match the attachment. The connector at the blade end is one of several types: J-hook (most common), side pin, bayonet, pinch tab, or top lock. Match it to your arm, or buy an adapter kit.
  3. Buy one good blade for now. The passenger side is intact; you can replace both for even wear, but only the driver side is required to restore a safe sight line.
  4. Prep the glass. Lay a folded towel across the windshield under the wiper arm. If the arm slips while lifted, it can chip or crack the glass — the towel is cheap insurance.
  5. Lift the arm. Pull the arm up and away from the glass until it stays in the raised position. Some cars have a "service position" — ignition off, then tap the wiper stalk once with the key on to park them mid-screen before turning the key off.
  6. Angle the blade perpendicular to the arm so you can see the connector.
  7. Release the old blade. Usually a small plastic tab under the connector; press or slide it while pulling the blade down (toward the windshield) along the arm's hook until it slides free.
  8. Slide the new blade on. Push it up the hook in the reverse direction until the tab clicks. It should feel seated and not wiggle.
  9. Tug test. With the arm still raised, gently pull the blade away from the arm to confirm the lock has engaged. If it slides off, the connector type is wrong.
 10. Lower the arm carefully onto the glass. Hand-control it all the way down — do not let it snap.

What to verify after fitting (washer fluid on, dry glass first, then a wet test)

  * Full sweep, both directions. No streaks, no skipped arcs, no chattering, no hopping. A single missed patch across the driver's main view means the install is not acceptable.
  * Edge contact. Look along the blade while it sweeps — the rubber should sit flat. Lifting at one end, a bowed middle, or a corner that flips up all mean wrong size, wrong connector, or a bent arm.
  * No noise. Squeal or tick on every pass means the blade is the wrong length or the arm is pressing unevenly.
  * No windshield damage. Inspect the glass where the arm sat — look for a fresh chip or star, in case the arm dropped during the swap.
  * Passenger side unchanged. Confirm the intact blade still wipes cleanly. If both behave differently, the arm tension or geometry may be the actual fault — worth a shop visit.
  * Real-rain confirmation before relying on it. A garden-hose mist test on the glass is acceptable; an actual rainy-day drive is the true test. Do the first wet drive during daylight on a route you know.

When you should not drive in rain

  * Right now, with the split blade, period.
  * After fitting, until you have verified a clean two-direction wipe on wet glass.
  * After fitting, if any streak, skip, chatter, or lift persists — those symptoms mean the install is wrong, and the streak you have now is no safer than the one you are trying to fix. Recheck connector type and size; if both are right and the symptom remains, the arm itself is bent and needs a shop, not another blade.
  * Any time the wiper cannot clear the driver's primary viewing zone in one pass. A wiper that needs two or three passes to do its job is not legal-safe for rain driving; slow down or stop.

The first mistake is almost certainly a missing or broken cast shadow. Right now each segment of the key (bow, shaft, teeth) is probably sitting in its own little pool of cloth, which is exactly why your eye reads them as three symbols instead of one object. The cast shadow is what stitches bow-shaft-teeth into a single silhouette lying on the cloth — without it, the value pattern around each part is self-contained and the parts can't share a ground.

Before any highlights or cloth texture, paint ONE continuous cast shadow under the whole key. One shape, not three. It should:
- Start at the bow's far edge and run unbroken under the shaft to the tip of the last tooth
- Be darker at the contact points (bow's near curve, where the shaft meets the bow, the teeth biting into the cloth folds) and softer/lighter as it trails away
- Follow the contour of the folded blue-gray cloth — if a fold runs under the key, the shadow bends with the fold, which also helps the cloth start reading as a 3D surface and not a flat backdrop

A quick check before you commit: hold the painting at arm's length and squint. If the cast shadow reads as one connected footprint, the key will read as one object. If it still fragments into three little shapes, the shadow itself is fragmented and needs to be repainted as a single shape.

This also pairs with your standing rule about unresolved boundaries: the boundaries between bow/shaft/teeth stay quiet (no hard outlines), but the cast shadow does the value-separation work that makes the whole key pop forward as one form against the cloth.

Semantic problem. One field certifies owner-level state ("has the owner authorized and committed to this lifecycle state?"). The other certifies source-level release ("is the source connector authenticated, fresh, and allowlisted to publish?"). A connector-authenticated record is not the same object as an owner-authorized record. The two lanes stop being independently checkable, and the cert chain stops being auditable.

Operational problem. The collapse is structurally fail-open. If the source field is true and the owner field is unresolved, any consumer reading the collapsed boolean sees "ready" and acts. That is exactly the failure the gate is supposed to prevent — a connector-authenticated record presented as ready while owner-level permission is still open. It also destroys the owner-lane boundary, because once the fields are merged the per-lane freshness windows, signers, and certs are no longer separable. Downstream automations, exports, and customer-facing surfaces cannot distinguish "source OK, owner pending" from "fully cleared."

The fix is a derived display-only summary, not a replacement.

Practical split: cook two small batches instead of one big one. The cleanest way to keep Sam's tofu crisp and the vegetables non-watery is to leave both raw and ready in the fridge, then run a 5-6 minute stir-fry the moment Sam walks in. That avoids the reheating problem entirely.

Tonight's split (8 oz tofu, 1 head broccoli, 1/2 red pepper — roughly half each):

  Riley now
    - 4 oz tofu, cubed and patted very dry
    - ~half the broccoli, florets
    - 1/4 red pepper, sliced
    - ~3/4 cup rice

  Sam later (raw, refrigerated, cook when Sam arrives)
    - 4 oz tofu, cubed, patted dry, sealed container with a paper towel
    - remaining broccoli florets + 1/4 red pepper, cut, in a container
    - ~3/4 cup rice in a separate container
    - second jar of sauce (recipe below)


Rice — season it now and again at service
  Toss the warm rice with ~1 tsp sesame oil, a small splash of soy (start with 1 tsp per portion), and a few drops of lime. Salt to taste. Hold covered at room temp for an hour or two, or fridge + 30 sec microwave with a sprinkle of water. The rice holds better when you season it lightly and adjust at serving rather than drowning it in sauce up front — heavy liquid makes the grains clump and go mushy on hold.

Tofu (component A)
  Dry is everything. Press or pat the cubes with paper towels until the surface doesn't glisten. Toss with a pinch of salt and a thin coat of neutral oil or light sesame oil.
  Hot pan, medium-high, ~1 tbsp oil, lay cubes in without crowding. 3-4 min per side, golden and crisp. Don't move them early — let the crust set.
  Sauce off heat, just before serving: soy + rice vinegar + a few drops of sesame oil + minced garlic + grated ginger. Toss so it glazes, doesn't soak.

Vegetables (component B) — the no-watery rule
  The single most reliable trick: don't cook them until you're serving them. Raw + cut + refrigerated + brief high-heat stir-fry at the end beats cooked-then-held every time.
  Hot pan, oil, garlic + ginger 15 sec, broccoli first (needs 2-3 min), pepper next (1 min). Off heat: splash of rice vinegar and soy. Total veg time ~4 min.
  If you absolutely must pre-cook Sam's batch, spread it on a sheet pan in a single layer, loosely tented, in the fridge — and don't salt during the cook. Salt early = water out = soggy. Sauce at service, not before.

Sauce, per portion (mix in two small jars)
  1 tbsp soy sauce
  1 tsp rice vinegar
  1/2 tsp sesame oil
  1 tsp grated ginger
  1 small clove garlic, minced
  squeeze of lime

Buckle handling without flattening the damp sheet — the glued block is your ally here. The sheet stays put; only the block tilts.

Pre-wash check
  Confirm the first wash is dull to the back of a knuckle, not cool.
  Find the buckle's low edge by eye (a raking light reveals it). The pot's light edge must end up at the HIGH corner of your setup, not the low one.

Support and rotate
  Set the block on a damp paper-towel fold or a thin foam mat — grip enough that a tilt doesn't slide it.
  Wedge a small folded card or eraser under the corner opposite the buckle's low point. Target 5–10° of tilt, no more; the wash needs to settle, not run off the page.
  Confirm with one clean-water drop on a back margin: it should drift away from the light edge. If it drifts toward, reverse the wedge.

Water load
  Mix on the lean side — more water, less pigment — so the wash self-levels without needing volume.
  Brush: damp, not wet. Test on the back margin first.
  Two passes, your usual: light establishes, broad evens. Neither crosses into the reserved buffer.

Preserve the light edge
  Reserve a 1–2 mm dry buffer wider than the final edge.
  Approach from the side away from the light edge when you can; if you must cross toward it, stop the stroke short of the buffer and let the wash creep on its own — don't push it.
  Park a thirsty brush (clean, blotted damp-dry) at the working edge to catch any bead of moisture before it crosses into the reserved zone.

Stop conditions
  20-second hold, one touch. If the touch comes back stained or wet, the wash is still mobile — do not load more.
  If a bead forms against the reserved edge: pull it back with the thirsty brush, do not flood it.
  If a true puddle sits glossy after 20s: one firm blot, then leave it. No return after dull.
  If pooling keeps migrating toward the light edge: stop the session there. Let the sheet dry flat in the block — the buckle relaxes as it dries — and reset the tilt next round.

Do not
  Press the buckled area, flex the sheet, or weight the back.
  Rewet the dried wall wash to "fix" the edge — you'll just lift pigment into the buffer.
  Lift the block edge to "drain" the buckle; the tilt already does that without disturbing the sheet.

PREPARING
Turn the trousers inside-out. Find the original fold line (you said it's still visible) and the two ends of the original stitching. Thread your needle with about 24 inches of single-strand matching thread and knot the tail. Trim any loose thread tails from the old stitching flush with the fabric — don't cut the trouser.

PRESSING
Iron the opened area flat first to relax waviness in both the hem allowance and the leg. Then crease the hem allowance back along the original fold line with a steam pass, press it dry, and let it cool completely before pinning. A cool, crisp fold is what keeps the hem line true to the original.

PINNING
Pin the fold closed perpendicular to the edge, about every 1 to 1.5 inches along the opened section. Each pin should catch just one or two threads of the outer trouser fabric so it doesn't telegraph to the right side. Offset the pins slightly from the stitch line so the needle passes freely.

HAND-STITCHING
Where the original stitch holes survived, reuse them. Use a small running stitch: pick up one thread of the outer fabric at the fold, travel 3–4 mm through the inside of the hem allowance, exit at the next original hole, then pick up one thread again. Aim for 8 to 10 stitches per inch — that's the durable spacing for cotton. Keep tension even; the fold should just meet, not pucker. If a hole is missing, take a fresh tiny bite in the same spot.

KNOTTING
At the end of the run, take two small backstitches inside the fold to lock the thread. Then run the needle inside the fold allowance for 2–3 cm and bring it out, snip flush — the tail buries itself in the fold so it won't show or unravel.

CHECKING
From the inside, tug the hem gently along its length to confirm nothing slips. From the right side, hold the fabric up to a light — you should see no visible stitches, just the original fold line. Finish with a light press from the right side through a clean cotton cloth (a dish towel works) to set the hem. If you spot a pucker, ease that one stitch's tension before the final press.

Plan, in five phases. Each phase has an off-ramp so you can stop at any one of them.

PHASE 1 — LET IT DRY (no touch)

  Leave the sheet flat, face up, room air. Don't blot the spot, don't fan, don't tilt to drain. Beads will collapse on their own as water leaves; what matters is what they leave behind — a pale halo, a pigment-speckled patch, or nothing visible.

  Wait until the sheet is dry to the touch AND no longer cool. "Cool to the touch" still means damp.

PHASE 2 — INSPECT WITHOUT ABRADING

  Tilt the sheet under one low light source. Look for either:
    - a slight oily sheen — hydrophobic contaminant, usually a fingerprint, sometimes waxy residue
    - a matte halo where the surrounding paper has more sizing than the spot — opposite problem, localized sizing failure

  Then the breath test, no contact: breathe once across the area. Oil rejects condensation, so a fingerprint reads as a slightly drier patch against the fogged surrounding paper. This is the cleanest diagnostic you can run without touching the surface.

  Note which it is. The path in Phase 4 forks on this.

PHASE 3 — MINIMAL WASH TEST

  Room humidity, not a humid day. Clean brush, damp not loaded. Water only, no pigment.

  One touch on the spot, 20-second hold, no return. Same rule you already use — no return after dull.

  Beads form instantly and sit tight: contaminant is hydrophobic, it will not yield to wet work. Plan to integrate, not fix.
  Water sits and slowly spreads: sizing is intact, contaminant is mild. Test a 1:1 wash (water + small pigment) on a margin first, then on the spot, still one touch.

PHASE 4 — INTEGRATE OR PAINT AROUND

  Two paths. Both honor "no heavy paint."

  Path A — Integrate as texture.
    If the spot sits in a passage that could carry stippled dry-brush (foliage, weathered surface, fabric weave, dust, sand, stone), use a near-dry brush, light to broad in one pass, one touch. The natural beading will read as intentional variation rather than defect. Value separation holds because you're not laying film — only catching high points.

  Path B — Paint around it.
    Resolve the spot as kept-light negative space. Lay a slightly darker value immediately adjacent, within roughly 2× brush-width, using your seam technique. The darker neighbor makes the quiet spot read as intentional, not accidental. Same logic as "warm counter by value separation."
    If the passage must carry weight, leave the spot light and let the neighbor carry the value. Don't push pigment into the spot to force it darker — forced pigment will bead again and produce a more visible defect than what you started with.

PHASE 5 — HARD STOPS

  Stop the moment you see any of these, mid-pass:
    - paper surface pills, fuzzes, or lifts under the brush
    - loose fibers release into your rinse water
    - the sheet transmits light differently in the spot — localized thinning
    - gentle strokes leave a darker "polished" patch — sizing rub-off, not the contaminant

  Any of those means the sizing is failing. The right move is to stop wet work on that area, let it dry flat, and accept the passage as-is. More water or pigment against a failing sizing makes it worse, not better.

If the breath test in Phase 2 reads as a fingerprint — most likely cause at fingernail size — accept that the beading is permanent. Watercolor sizing has no good field fix for it. Paths A and B are the whole game from here.

  1. Slice into wedges or thick planks, not paper-thin. You want surface area to brown and enough body to hold shape.
  2. Wide skillet (10–12"), medium heat, 2 tbsp olive oil. When shimmering, lay fennel cut-side down in a single layer. Don't crowd — do two batches if needed; crowding steams it and you lose the sear.
  3. Salt. Leave it alone 3–4 min until you see a golden crust on the underside.
  4. Add the sliced garlic, dried herbs, and all the lemon zest. Stir once, 30 seconds — just to bloom.
  5. Add the cherry tomatoes and drained chickpeas, another small pinch of salt. 2 minutes, until tomatoes blister and start to break down.
  6. Splash in 2–3 tbsp of water (or broth if you have it). Cover, drop heat to medium-low, 3–4 minutes. This is the steam-finish — it cooks the center of each wedge without you touching them.
  7. Uncover, raise the heat briefly. You're aiming for a jammy gloss, not a puddle. If it's watery, give it another minute uncovered.

  Why this works: the sear builds flavor and gives the wedge enough structure to survive the next step; the brief covered steam finishes the inside; the final uncovered moment drives off water so the pieces don't collapse into mush. Stir gently — wedges should still look like wedges on the plate.

WHEN TO ADD FETA + LEMON

  - Lemon zest — early, with the garlic and herbs, so it blooms in the oil. Zest in fat becomes aromatic; zest in finished food reads raw and bitter.
  - Lemon juice — off heat, just before plating. Heat mutes citrus acid; you want the brightness to land fresh.
  - Feta — off heat, crumbled on top after plating. If you stir feta into a hot pan it melts into a cream sauce and you lose the textural contrast. As a top crumble it warms at the edges, holds its shape inside, and each bite self-assembles — warm-creamy + cool-clean.

  If you'd rather have a creamy glaze than a balanced crumble, you can crumble the feta in off heat and stir gently so the residual heat melts it over everything. Valid move, just less "balanced."

SEQUENCE (run in parallel)

  - Couscous: bring ~3/4 cup water or broth + pinch salt to a boil, pour over the couscous in a bowl, cover, rest 5 min, fluff with a fork, drizzle with a little olive oil.
  - While it rests, run the fennel/chickpea/tomato pan.
  - Plate couscous, spoon the fennel mixture on top, finish with the lemon juice, the feta crumble, and the reserved fennel fronds.

Approximate amounts are starting points — taste and adjust the lemon, salt, and feta at the end. The dish wants more acid than you think it does until you taste it.

A conservative sequence, no cutting or knotting:

  1. Lay the sweater flat on a hard, well-lit surface, right side up. Identify the loop apex and the "tight" side (usually one column over, where a stitch looks shortened or the fabric puckers).
  2. From the wrong side, push the blunt tapestry needle up through the center of the loop on the right side. Pass it through the open loop, not around it.
  3. Draw just enough needle through to seat the loop on the shaft (about 1–2 cm). The loop is now held by the needle, not by tension — your hands are off the yarn.
  4. Use the needle as a shuttle to move the loop sideways toward the puckered column. Lift each neighboring stitch one at a time and ease the loop's slack into it, working 2–4 columns each way. The face should flatten as the loop shrinks; stop as soon as it lies even.
  5. When the loop is only a few mm, ease the needle on through to the wrong side, drawing the remaining tail to the inside.
  6. On the wrong side, weave the tail into 2–3 adjacent stitches along the same row direction, and end inside the fabric. No knot. Don't trim — leave the tail tucked.
  7. Inspect before washing: rake light across the surface to check for residual pucker or ladder; gently stretch the panel once each way (wales, then course) and release, confirming it springs back flat and neighboring stitches sit even.

If at step 4 the fabric puckers elsewhere instead of flattening, the slack is moving the wrong direction — shift to the other side. If the yarn resists redistribution, stop; forcing it risks snapping an intact fiber.

Brothy tomato-lentil-pasta for two — a light, broth-forward version that comes together in about 25 minutes, mostly hands-off.

Approximate amounts:

  Olive oil          2 to 3 tablespoons
  Garlic             2 or 3 cloves, thinly sliced
  Dried herbs        ~1 teaspoon (oregano, thyme, or Italian seasoning)
  Cherry tomatoes    the whole pint, halved or roughly smashed
  Lentils            the whole can, drained and rinsed (see below)
  Short pasta        6 oz of the 8 oz — brothy means less pasta; save 2 oz
                     for another night
  Broth or water     4 to 5 cups (light vegetable or chicken; water is fine
                     if the tomatoes are good)
  Baby spinach       3 to 4 generous handfuls
  Lemon              1/2 a lemon for juice, plus a wedge per bowl
  Parmesan           a small wedge (~1 oz) to grate fresh at the table;
                     a parmesan rind dropped in while simmering is a bonus

Short pasta shapes worth picking if you have a choice: ditalini, small shells, or orecchiette work best in a broth — they hold liquid in their cups without turning the bowl starchy.

Should you rinse the lentils?
Yes. Canned lentils sit in starchy, sometimes slightly metallic packing liquid. Drain them in a fine-mesh strainer and rinse until the water runs clearer, then shake off the excess. Rinsing gives a cleaner flavor and lets you control the salt in the finished dish.

Method:

1. Warm the olive oil in a wide pot or deep skillet over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and dried herbs; cook gently 1 to 2 minutes until the garlic is fragrant and just turning pale gold. Don't let it brown — dark garlic reads heavy in a brothy dish.

2. Add the halved cherry tomatoes with a pinch of salt. Stir and let them break down for 5 to 7 minutes, pressing a few with the back of a spoon so they release their juice. You're aiming for a loose, jammy pan, not a thick sauce.

3. Pour in 4 cups of broth (hold the last cup in case you want it looser later). Add the parmesan rind if you have one. Bring to a steady simmer.

4. Add the pasta and cook until just al dente, stirring occasionally so it doesn't clump — about 8 to 10 minutes depending on the shape. The pasta should be swimming in broth, not sitting in a thick sauce. Splash in more broth if it's tightening up.

5. Stir in the rinsed lentils and warm through 1 to 2 minutes. Taste the broth and adjust salt.

6. Take the pot off the heat. Add the spinach in big handfuls and stir — the residual heat wilts it in under a minute. Squeeze in the lemon juice starting with half a lemon, then taste; depending on the tomatoes you may want more. Black pepper, more salt if needed.

7. Ladle into bowls. Top each with a generous grating of fresh parmesan, a small drizzle of raw olive oil (this is the brightness hit), and a lemon wedge.

How to keep the bowl bright rather than heavy:

  Spinach — add it off the heat. If you boil it, the color dulls and the flavor flattens. A minute of residual heat with the lid on is all it needs.

  Lemon — add it off the heat too, and in stages. Acid that boils loses its volatile aromatics and reads flat. Taste after each squeeze; you want a clean citrus lift on top of the tomato, not a sour note.

  Parmesan — don't stir grated parmesan into the pot. It clumps, clouds the broth, and turns the dish gluey. Either drop a rind in while the broth simmers (fish it out before serving) or, better, grate it fresh over each bowl at the table. The aroma at the moment of eating is what makes it taste bright.

Two small extras that help after a tasting shift:

  - A pinch of red pepper flakes with the garlic adds quiet warmth without weight.
  - If you have any basil or parsley, a small handful of torn leaves at the end is a clean, fresh finish.

The leftovers reheat well the next day — just add a splash of water or broth as you warm it, and finish with a fresh squeeze of lemon so it perks back up.

1. Rinse test. Hold one filmed glass under fresh water and rub the area with a clean fingertip or soft damp microfiber. If the film dissolves or smears off, it is surface residue and addressable. If the surface looks essentially the same after a thorough wipe — possibly iridescent, or microscopically rough instead of slick — it is most likely permanent etching from prior cycles. That is glass damage, not an appliance fault, so stop there and do not treat it as one.

2. Check rinse-aid level; refill if low or unknown. Low or missing rinse aid is the most common cause of this kind of cloudiness. Then confirm detergent actually dispensed during this load: the main-wash cup opened mid-cycle, the pod or powder is gone afterward, and no damp cake of detergent sits in the dispenser at cycle end. A pod stuck in the dispenser can film a whole load by itself. Note the current state without changing dosage yet.

3. Clean only the removable filter. If the machine has a user-removable bottom filter assembly — usually a cylindrical mesh that twists or lifts out — remove it, rinse it under the tap to clear food debris, and reseat it firmly. Skip this step if the model uses a self-cleaning filter with no user-serviceable cylinder; prying one out can damage the unit. No further disassembly, no spray-arm removal, no scrubbing pads, no vinegar or descaler on the glassware or the tub at this stage.

4. Run one short normal cycle with two of the filmed glasses, otherwise empty, on a standard program with the current detergent and rinse aid. At cycle end: if the film rinsed off in step 1, it should now be gone or clearly reduced; if it looks the same as before, that confirms prior etching, and the dishwasher did not cause anything new this run.

If residue was confirmed in step 1 and still shows after step 4, the next move is environmental — water hardness matched against detergent amount and rinse aid — not appliance repair, and not abrasive cleaning of the glassware.

Quick triage: ~1-inch seam, no squeaker, no hard parts, stuffing in place, asymptomatic — that's the favorable column. The decision is really about Kibo's history with plush toys and whether a hand-closed seam will actually hold up to him.

INSPECT (do this on a flat surface, good light, before deciding anything)

  - Measure the opening end-to-end along the seam. Anything past ~2 inches, or any branching/tear lines radiating from it, tilts toward discard.
  - Run a finger inside along the seam. You're checking for: (a) weakened adjacent stitching that's about to give way, (b) any small part (button eye, plastic nose, tag fastener) you missed, (c) foam pellets vs. polyester fiberfill — pellets are a harder pass.
  - Look at the fabric. Shredded/fluffed edges (frayed, fluffy white fuzz along the tear) means the seam will reopen under play; clean torn edges can usually be re-seated.
  - Sniff it. Musty/wet smell = bacteria in the stuffing; wash-and-repair is reasonable, but if the stuffing itself feels damp or clumped, replace the stuffing or discard.
  - Check stuffing condition. Clean polyester fiberfill, evenly distributed = workable. Matted, clumped, or visibly soiled = discard.

DECIDE: REPAIR OR DISCARD

Repair is reasonable only if ALL of these hold:

  - Opening is under ~1.5 inches with clean edges and no radiating weak points.
  - No small/hard component involved.
  - Kibo's pattern with plush toys is "loves and carries," not "rips open systematically." If he's a known de-stuffler, the seam will reopen within a session and you're back to square one plus a dog who's learned this toy is edible.
  - You can close it with a tight backstitch or a heavy-duty nylon thread zigzag, knot secured with a dab of fabric glue or a doubled knot pulled into the seam tunnel — not a surface stitch the dog can pick at.

Default to discard if any one of these is true:

  - Tear > ~2 inches, or multiple weak points along the seam.
  - Shredded/frayed edges, or foam-pellet fill.
  - He's previously eviscerated plush toys (predicts re-tearing, not re-bonding).
  - The toy is small enough that he could swallow a chunk of it whole if the seam gives further.
  - You can't close it tighter than the original factory seam.

For a bonded fabric toy (the fuzzy "shaggy" kind), even a perfect repair usually fails within a few play sessions because the fabric itself parts under teeth, not just the thread. Plush with a woven backing repairs much more reliably.

WATCH FOR THESE SIGNS (none right now — good)

  - Within the next 24–48 hours: repeated retching/dry heaving, vomiting (especially more than once), refusal of a meal he normally eats, or a noticeable drop in energy.
  - Stool changes: straining to defecate, no stool for >24 hours, or stool that's mucus-y or contains visible fabric/white fibers.
  - Abdominal signs: belly looks tight or distended, he's guarding his abdomen, or he's adopting a "prayer position" (front down, rear up) repeatedly.
  - Behavioral: restlessness, panting at rest, or suddenly not wanting to be touched.

Any one of those is a same-day vet call, with "possible foreign-body ingestion, recently had access to a plush toy with stuffing" as the history. A single isolated vomit or one skipped meal isn't an emergency on its own, but two or more of the above signs together, or vomiting that persists past 12 hours, is.

Practically: since stuffing is intact and nothing was ingested, you have a real window to inspect, repair or replace the toy, and resume normal play. If you do repair it, supervise the next play session rather than leaving it with him unsupervised — that's the single biggest variable in whether the repair holds.

Issues, in order of severity:

1. **Source-based differential treatment.** Telling users "because you came through paid search, you skip checks" creates two cohorts on different paths to the same end state. If those checks include anything functional — email/domain verification, security config, role assignment, DPA/terms acceptance, data residency — paid users land in incomplete or non-compliant workspaces while organic users get the full path. That's an audit and security problem, not just a UX preference.

2. **Attribution laundering.** Two paths means you can't compare funnels cleanly, you can't measure what the setup checks actually retain, and paid LTV/CAC math gets contaminated by accounts that skipped steps. Whoever sees clean paid conversion first will credit the ad for lift that's really just friction removal.

3. **The framing is the stakeholder's, not yours.** "A faster start" is launch-metric framing. The right question isn't "can we make paid users faster" — it's "are these checks skippable for anyone, and if so, why." If the checks have a purpose, source isn't a valid exemption criterion. If they don't have a purpose, remove them for everyone.

4. **The fact that Ines forwarded it is the tell.** She's flagging for review, not endorsing. Read the signal.

Before this moves, I'd want answers to:
- What specifically are the "standard setup checks"? List them.
- For each one: is it skippable for paid users only, or skippable period? On what evidence?
- Has security/legal signed off on a dual-path onboarding? (For B2B with workspaces, dual paths almost always surface a DPA or role-assignment gap.)

Cleaner alternatives if the underlying goal is real:
- Make the checks faster for everyone (parallelize, prefill, remove steps that don't earn their place).
- Defer non-essential checks to post-activation for everyone.
- Keep the welcome message but drop the bypass — "thanks for coming through paid, here's a shortcut to your workspace" without skipping verification.

1. Edge test (lowest-risk step). Touch only the outermost corner of the patch with a clean, dry rubber-cement pickup (or a clean fingertip). The corner is the thinnest dried film and should release first if it's going to release cleanly.

2. If it lifts clean, continue from that released edge inward, millimeters at a time. Roll the pickup along the surface — do not pull straight up. Straight-up pulls are the most common way fibers tear.

3. If a section resists, leave it and start from a different edge. Do not force.

Stop immediately if any of these appear:
   - paper fibers come up with the fluid
   - the surface scuffs, pills, or abrades
   - the surrounding wash lifts, bleeds, or cockles
   - the patch won't release at the corner at all

4. Escalation only if the dry edge test won't grab. With a small brush, apply a tiny amount of clean water to JUST the masking-fluid edge — keep it off the dry wash. Wait ~30s for the latex to soften, then lift with the pickup while still soft. Still roll, not pull.

5. If it still won't release cleanly, stop. Use the brand's own masking-fluid remover per its instructions, or check with the maker. Do not add heat, solvents, or rubbing.

Notes for your specific sheet:
   - The patch is near the outer edge and off the focal object — that's your margin, so use the outermost corner as your test point.
   - Never rub, scrape, heat, or erase; never pull straight up; never wet the surrounding wash directly.

# 1. Annual cost comparison

                              2 TB (current)   200 GB (offered)
  Annual price                $119.88          $35.88
  Monthly equivalent          $9.99            $2.99
  Headline savings if down    —                $84.00 / yr  (70.1%)

  Free room on plan           1,834 GB (89.5%) over by 14 GB (7.0%)

Hand check: 119.88 − 35.88 = 84.00. ✓  84.00 / 119.88 = 0.7007. ✓  214 − 200 = 14. ✓  14 / 200 = 7.0%. ✓

So the "savings" number is real but it assumes the 200 GB plan will actually accept 214 GB of data. Most consumer cloud-storage tiers do not silently truncate; the standard outcomes are: sync stops at the cap, new uploads fail, or the provider auto-upgrades and bills the difference. None of those match a clean $84/yr saving.

# 2. Why 214 GB does not fit 200 GB

Three honest reasons:

1. **The numbers don't fit, period.** 214 GB > 200 GB. The offered plan is smaller than what you currently have stored with that provider. A downgrade cannot be a like-for-like swap; it is a reduction that requires you to remove at least 14 GB (and, in practice, more, because the 200 GB figure is usually a *soft* cap where the first GB or two of overage still works but anything past it errors out — and even one failed upload breaks the 3-2-1 backup invariant for the files that didn't make it).
2. **Your usage is not flat — it's an active archive.** Per the P001–P027 working file, there are ~40 master TIFFs in an 8-photo Feb 14 prep plus undigitized backs, the Mom/Portland/Marcus sleeve-note work, and v01–v06 working derivatives that are *still being created*. Usage grows on this plan, it doesn't shrink. A 200 GB tier would be over the moment the next sleeve-note scan or v06 derivative lands.
3. **Masters are non-negotiable.** The locked-master + checksum + 3-2-1 workflow means every master TIFF must remain in cloud as one of its two offsite copies. Deleting masters to shoehorn into 200 GB would break the archive integrity rule and the established preserve-then-route principle in one stroke. The $84/yr saving would be paid for by destroying the property the plan is supposed to protect.

A 200 GB plan is also the wrong shape for the workload: you'd be paying for 200 GB of storage to hold 214 GB of masters + working + derivatives, with no room for the next capture batch.

# 3. Conservative renewal decision frame (preserve masters, keep headroom)

Goal: keep the May 2 renewal decision from being driven by the $84 headline and from forcing destructive file moves. Three options, in order of how conservative they are.

**Option A — Stay on the 2 TB plan. RECOMMENDED.**
- Cost: $119.88/yr, unchanged. ~$10/mo equivalent.
- Why: it already covers 214 GB with 1,834 GB of headroom (89.5% of the plan empty). That headroom is exactly what the archive needs — it absorbs the next undigitized batch, the next v06 working derivative, and the next sleeve-note scan without you having to re-decide storage every quarter. $84/yr saved on Option B is roughly the cost of one damaged master if a forced "delete to fit" goes wrong; the trade isn't worth it.
- Action: do nothing on May 2; auto-renew at $119.88 keeps the archive intact.

**Option B — Stay on 2 TB but switch to monthly billing instead of annual.**
- Same provider, same 2 TB cap. Cost rises to roughly $119.88/yr only if you prepay; monthly is typically ~$9.99/mo = $119.88/yr as well, or slightly more depending on the provider's monthly premium. Use this only if you want optionality (e.g., you expect usage to drop materially within 12 months). For an active, growing archive, prepay annual is the cheaper and simpler path.

**Option C — Genuine downgrade path, *not* by deleting masters.**
Only consider this if a hard budget reason forces the issue. The shape of a real downgrade is:
1. Move the **working derivatives (v01–v06, access copies, view-only JPEGs)** off the cloud tier entirely — onto the laptop + the existing external-drive copy that's already part of the 3-2-1 setup. Working files don't need a second cloud copy if they're checksummed and on two local media.
2. Keep **all masters** on whatever cloud tier remains, plus the external drive, plus the originals in sleeves. That keeps masters at three places even on a smaller plan.
3. After step 1, re-measure cloud usage. If it's now under, say, 160 GB with stable headroom, *then* the 200 GB plan is honest, and you've preserved masters. If it's still over, the downgrade isn't real and you stay on 2 TB.
4. Never delete masters, never delete to fit, never re-encode masters as JPEGs to save space (that destroys the archival master rule).

**Decision rule for May 2:**
- If there is no hard budget constraint: **auto-renew 2 TB annual at $119.88**. Done.
- If there *is* a hard budget constraint: do **Option C** (move working/access copies off cloud, keep all masters), not "delete to fit." If Option C doesn't get cloud usage comfortably under 200 GB, stay on 2 TB and address the budget question elsewhere.

The framing to keep in your head: the cloud plan is paying for **three guarantees** — masters are offsite, the archive has room to grow, and you don't have to make destructive decisions under a deadline. The $84/yr saving on the 200 GB plan would buy you none of those and would force you to break at least one. The conservative call is to renew the 2 TB plan and let the working files keep growing into the headroom that's already paid for.

Likely cause
The most common reason a $0 preferred-pharmacy copay shows up as a positive member price is that the pharmacy hasn't actually applied the plan to this fill yet — insurance card not scanned, plan not selected, or the claim hasn't been adjudicated. Sometimes the portal will show a cash/discount price until the bin/PCN/group is entered. A wrong plan being loaded (e.g., a commercial plan instead of the PDP) can also produce a positive copay.

Recommendation
- Do not pay the $18.50. Paying would create a real overcharge and a reimbursement chase instead of just fixing the adjudication.
- Stop checkout and confirm at the pharmacy counter (or via the portal) that Mom's Golden State Rx Saver is the active plan on the fill, with the correct BIN/PCN, before resubmitting the claim.
- After the plan is loaded and the claim re-runs, the member price should drop to $0.

Conservative sequence (before payment)

1. Confirm the script is actually queued at River Park, and confirm the pharmacy system shows the 2027 plan (not the 2026 one) on Mom's profile. The bin/pcn/group on the profile is what the claim will run against — if 2026 data is still loaded, every later step will be misleading.

2. Ask the pharmacist or tech to run the claim and read back the adjudicated copay before ringing anything up. A verbal "it should be $0" is not enough; only what the actual adjudication returns counts.

3. If the adjudicated copay is $0 at a preferred pharmacy, proceed to payment. If it is anything other than $0, or if the claim rejects, ask the pharmacy to leave the claim on hold (not reverse or delete it). A held claim still carries the reject codes and member/plan identifiers you will need for the next call.

4. Call Golden State Rx Saver member services with: pharmacy name and store phone, Rx number, drug and strength, fill date, adjudicated copay or reject code. Ask whether 2027 eligibility has propagated to network pharmacies, whether River Park is preferred for 2027, and whether lisinopril 10 mg adjudicates to $0 at a preferred pharmacy on this fill. Write down the reference number.

5. If the plan says coverage is correct and the pharmacy adjudication is wrong, ask the plan to push corrected eligibility, then ask the pharmacy to re-submit the held claim. Confirm the re-adjudicated copay is $0 before any payment.

6. If the plan says something different from the verified 2027 terms Riley cited (for example, a tier change or a delay in eligibility loading), ask the plan for the 2027 formulary tier and copay for lisinopril 10 mg, the 2027 preferred pharmacy list, and the document ID for the 2027 summary of benefits or formulary excerpt that applies. Keep the reference number.

7. If the path above is going to take longer than Mom's roughly 10 days of medication on hand, ask the pharmacist about a bridge or emergency supply. State pharmacy boards typically authorize a 72-hour (sometimes longer) emergency supply of a chronic maintenance medication; the pharmacist can dispense that without a new Rx while the claim is sorted. This is the continuity-preserving move.

8. Only pay when the claim adjudicates to $0 at River Park, or when Mom has a clear plan explanation of any non-zero amount and has chosen to pay it. Do not pay speculatively, and do not abandon the fill at one store if the chain can re-adjudicate correctly.

Continuity principle: do not skip doses, do not split tablets to stretch supply, and do not delay the refill further to "wait and see" whether the claim comes out right. The bridge-supply step exists precisely so verification and refill can happen at the same time.

Good news: a single tick found now, dog acting normally, is the lowest-risk scenario, but the sequence still matters because early mistakes (squeezing the body, twisting, folklore methods like heat/petroleum jelly) raise pathogen transmission. Kibo's last wellness was 4/24/27 with no findings, so the baseline is clean.

REMOVAL (fine-tipped/pointy tweezers, not blunt ones):
  1. Gloves if you have them; if not, wash hands before and after.
  2. Part the fur so you can see the mouthparts going into the skin.
  3. Grasp the tick as close to the skin as possible — at the head/mouthparts, not the swollen body.
  4. Pull straight up with steady, even pressure. Do not jerk, twist, crush, or squeeze the body. Twisting is the most common cause of mouthparts breaking off.
  5. If mouthparts stay in the skin: try once more with clean tweezers to pluck them. If they won't come out cleanly, stop — don't dig. Clean the site and let it heal; the small fragments rarely cause problems.
  6. Do not use heat, matches, alcohol, petroleum jelly, nail polish, soap, or essential oils to "make it let go." A stressed tick can regurgitate into the bite, increasing infection risk.

PHOTO + SPECIMEN PRESERVATION:
  - Take a clear close-up photo of the tick embedded BEFORE you pull it. This lets a vet later judge species (deer tick vs. dog tick vs. lone star), engorgement (how long it was feeding), and attachment site.
  - After removal, save the tick in a sealed ziplock or small jar with rubbing alcohol. That both kills and preserves it.
  - Label with: date (5/7/27), location on Kibo (left shoulder, outer), and ideally a coin/coin-sized reference in the photo for scale.
  - Refrigerate (not freeze) if you won't see the vet in the next day or two.
  - If you'd rather not keep it: flush it or seal it in a bag in the trash. Don't crush it with bare fingers.

CLEANING THE SITE:
  - Mild soap and warm water, then pat dry.
  - Or wipe with chlorhexidine (Hibiscrub) or diluted povidone-iodine (Betadine).
  - Avoid hydrogen peroxide on dog skin — it can irritate and slow healing.
  - Wash your own hands and tweezers with soap and alcohol afterward.

BITE-SITE SIGNS TO WATCH (next 1–14 days):
  - Increasing redness, swelling, warmth, or a lump that grows rather than shrinks.
  - Drainage, pus, scabbing, or crusting that doesn't resolve in 3–5 days.
  - An expanding ring or bull's-eye rash (harder to spot under fur; check by feel and parting hair). This is less common in dogs than in humans but does happen.
  - Local hair loss or persistent itch at the site.

SYSTEMIC SIGNS TO WATCH (typically 3–30 days out; some sooner, some later):
  - Lethargy, reduced play, "not himself."
  - Drop in appetite or water intake change.
  - Lameness, shifting-leg lameness, stiff gait, or joint swelling (classic Lyme / anaplasma).
  - Fever clues: warm ears, warm belly, shivering.
  - Vomiting, diarrhea.
  - Swollen lymph nodes (under jaw, in front of shoulders, behind knees).
  - Pale or tacky gums, bruising, or unusual bleeding.
  - Any breathing difficulty, cough, or collapse.
  - Neurological changes: head tilt, facial droop, sudden weakness, wobbliness, or — rare but classic — ascending paralysis starting in the hind legs.
  - Low platelet issues like nosebleeds or blood in urine/stool.

WHEN TO CONTACT THE VET (don't wait for a scheduled visit):
  - Any systemic sign above, especially lameness, lethargy with fever, vomiting, breathing trouble, or pale gums.
  - Bite site becomes hot, swollen, draining, or fails to heal in a few days.
  - Mouthparts retained AND site becomes inflamed or tender (rather than just a small dark speck).
  - You want species ID — bring the saved tick in; if it's a deer tick (Ixodes) and was attached long enough to engorge, the vet may discuss Lyme testing/timing.
  - You're unsure how long the tick was on. Ticks generally need ~24–48 hours of attachment before meaningfully transmitting Lyme/anaplasma; a freshly-found, flat tick is lower risk than a fully engorged one, but only a photo/specimen helps confirm.

CONTEXT WORTH FLAGGING IN PASSING:
  - Mid-May in most of the U.S. is peak tick activity. If Kibo isn't already on a prevention product (oral like Nexgard/Bravecto/Credelio, or a Seresto collar, or a newer isoxazoline), this is a reasonable prompt to ask the vet about one at the next visit, especially if walks are in wooded/grass edges.
  - The photo + saved specimen make a vet call faster and more useful if anything develops.

If you want, take the embedded-tick photo now before removal so you have it regardless of how the extraction goes.

Short answer: yes, home monitoring is still appropriate. What you’re describing — a small, firm, closed, non-tender bump at a documented tick-bite site, eight days out, with Kibo acting completely normally — fits a typical post-tick bite local reaction (sometimes called a “tick bite granuloma” or residual inflammatory nodule). At this size and behavior, it isn’t an emergency on its own.

What you’re already doing right
- Closed skin, no spreading redness/heat, no drainage, no bleeding, no pain on palpation
- Normal appetite, gait, and behavior
- No systemic signs (no feverish behavior, vomiting, weakness, breathing trouble)

That combination argues against local infection and against acute tick-borne illness at this moment.

What to keep doing
- Leave the bump alone: no picking, squeezing, scrubbing, soaking, or topical ointments
- A brief cone or a snug t-shirt layer if Kibo starts licking or scratching the shoulder
- Optional gentle wipe with dilute chlorhexidine or saline if it ever looks dirty, then pat dry
- Photograph the bump today (ruler or coin next to it for scale, dated) so you have a true baseline to compare against. That’s the photo you’d send later if anything changes.

Changes that should trigger a same-day vet call (send the photo first if you’re unsure)
At the bite site:
- Bump enlarges (especially past ~8–10 mm), becomes soft/fluid-filled, or stays a firm pea-size nodule past 3–4 weeks after the scab falls off
- New or returning redness spreading outward, heat, pain on touch, discharge (pus, crusting ooze), or the skin opens again
- Bleeding that returns or persists
- Persistent scratching or hair loss over the spot

In Kibo overall (the tick-borne illness window, typically 2–6 weeks post-bite, sometimes out to 6–8):
- Low-grade lethargy, “off” behavior, or reduced appetite that lasts more than ~24 hours
- Limping or shifting-leg lameness, stiffness, or reluctance to move
- Feverish behavior (warm ears/abdomen, panting at rest, shivering)
- Repeated vomiting, or any bloody/black/tarry stool
- New cough, gag, or unexplained rapid breathing at rest
- Dark, red, brown, or orange urine; yellowing of gums, inner ear, or whites of eyes; pale gums; unusual bruising
- Any sudden behavior change, weakness, stumbling, or collapse

Why this matters for timing
- Local site complications usually show up in days 1–14, so you’re in the window now and still looking at it daily is right.
- Tick-borne illness (Lyme, anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, RMSF, etc.) typically presents 2–6 weeks after the bite, with broader risk potentially out to 6–8 weeks. Your most recent routine wellness on 4/24/27 with no findings gives you a clean baseline to compare against.
- If it would ease your mind, your vet may recommend a baseline or screening 4Dx/Accuplex blood test around the 4–6 week mark (i.e., roughly early-to-mid June 2027) even if Kibo feels fine — worth asking at the next routine visit or by phone.

Bottom line
Stay the course. Watch the spot daily for any of the site-specific changes above, and watch Kibo’s overall behavior through the 6-week window for the systemic signs above. (two-value thumbnail, before the watercolor sheet)

0:00 – 2:00  Frame the thumbnail

7:00 – 9:00  Focal-read check
